# DeLawson — Design

Status: **draft, pre-implementation.** Nothing here is built. Sections marked
⚠️ are unresolved; they are collected again in §16.

Language: Rust.

## 0. How to read this document

**Nullius in verba.** No number in here stands on anyone's authority, Bob's included. Every design
and every figure is either justified from first principles in place, or labelled as a guess to be
confirmed. Where the two conflict, the arithmetic wins and the label gets updated.

| Label | Means |
|---|---|
| **Derived** | the arithmetic is shown where the claim is made |
| **Cited** | from a public source, with a link |
| **Guess** | a round number pending measurement; the numeric ones are collected in §4.7 |
| **Asserted** | stated from experience without derivation — usable, but flagged so it can be revisited |
| ⚠️ | unresolved; collected again in §16 |

**Performance claims carry a third thing**, per §1.6: achieved, the computed hardware bound, and the
fraction of bound. A throughput number without its ceiling is as much a liability as an unlabelled
constant, because it cannot distinguish good from merely better than the alternative.

**Section numbers are the keys, and this document is only ever grown at the end of a section.**
Cross references say §4.6.6.1, so inserting a section would renumber its siblings and silently
invalidate every reference to them. Appending within a parent instead keeps every existing number
correct — which is append-at-end beating insert-in-the-middle, in the document about append-at-end
beating insert-in-the-middle.

**That is the right trade and not a workaround** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17). It is the discipline
that makes a number a stable key, and its only cost is that reading order cannot be curated —
which costs nothing here, because a document this size is navigated by searching for the thing you
need, not read front to back. Named anchors would buy rearrangement, and rearrangement is not
wanted. What is wanted is §67's index of named invariants and terms, and numbers serve as its
targets perfectly well.

**That index now exists, as `INVARIANTS.md`** — the named invariants with what enforces each and what
would catch it being false, plus a term index pointing back the other way. It is a separate file
because it is *derived*: this document argues, and the catalogue collects. Two rules keep them
honest — an invariant's `Argued` list is ordered with **the canonical section first**, and the
catalogue admits only properties that could be falsified by an observation, so decisions, parameters
and derivations stay here in §0.1 where they belong.

The distinction matters because this document is long and will be read by people who cannot
re-derive it from scratch. An unlabelled number is a liability: in a year nobody can tell whether
it was computed or assumed.

**Inputs currently asserted rather than derived**, in rough order of how much rests on them:

Five public sources by Bob set the motivation and the scale, and are cited where used:
[the erasure-coding song](https://youtu.be/oak6U2yBy94) (§4.3.4.2),
[how AI should work](https://burtleburtle.net/bob/future/ai.html) (§1.0, §1.0.3),
[really big data centers](https://burtleburtle.net/bob/future/bigdata.html) and
[the dense torus core](https://burtleburtle.net/bob/future/dense.html) (§1.0.4), and
[the torus Dyson swarm](https://burtleburtle.net/bob/scifi/dyson.html) (§1.0.5).

| Input | Value | Where |
|---|---|---|
| Instance gone-and-not-yet-replaced | 10^-4 | §4.3.1 — **challenged in §4.3.1.1** |
| Reliability target | 10^-14 per window | §4.3.1 — given fleet meaning in §4.3.1.1 |
| Instance unavailable | 10^-3 | §4.3.1 |
| Placement slack | 4/3 | §5.6.1a — **now derived** from solver cost: `s/(s-1)` = 4 draws |
| Hint window | 10 minutes | §10.1 — should be a follower-lag budget |
| SSD seek/scan break-even | 40 KB | §7.1.1 — spans 4 KB-320 KB; the widest uncertainty here |
| EC group size for `(12+3)x(5+1)` | 90 or 108 cells | §4.3.3.2e — the 4/3 rule needs 108 to give 144 |
| Extent physical cap | 32 MB | §6 — bracketed from both sides, exact value a guess |
| Record sizes | 100 / 200 / 300 B | §4.7 |

### 0.1 Decided

The load-bearing decisions, so a reader need not reconstruct them from four thousand lines. §16 holds the
154 things *not* decided.

**Priorities and framing**

| | |
|---|---|
| Availability and reliability are **separate goals** with different remedies | §1.1 |
| **Data loss happens during disasters**, not steady state — a failed rollout beats a millennium of disk attrition | §1.1.1, §13.2 |
| Availability is promised **per record**, and is **time-bounded** — a timeout is part of it | §1.1, §5.11.2, §9.5 |
| **Throughput over latency**; job latency is the *maximum* over requests, so hedge at p99.9+ | §1.4, §9.5 |
| **Software should not matter**: if the hardware can do it, the software should deliver it | §1.6 |
| So the metric is **distance from the hardware bound**, never distance from a competitor | §1.6 |
| Every performance claim states **achieved, bound, and fraction** — a bare number is a liability | §1.6.1, §0 |
| The bound is for the work the design **chose** to do, so compression and EC are inside the rule | §1.6.3 |
| Fraction-of-bound targets **survive hardware changes**; absolute ones age out | §1.6.4 |
| Batched metadata is at **~5% of bound**, unbatched at **~0.5%** — both already meet the target | §1.6.2 |
| **~95% of hardware cost is disk**; that is cost composition and says nothing about space efficiency | §1.2, §12.7 |
| **Open source**, so storage can sit inside a compute cluster and egress fees — 48× the storage cost — vanish | §1.0 |
| Stable record numbers and keys make **external indexes permanently valid**, which is what shared AI memory needs | §1.0, §3 |
| The motivating case is public and specific: thousands of minds, 10,000 remember-test cycles/s each | §1.0.3 |
| So it wants **~10^7 metadata QPS** — 5× the demonstrated target, ~1/4 of the hardware bound | §1.0.3 |
| Latency bounds **depth** of reasoning; throughput bounds **breadth** — souls think in parallel, so §1.4 applies | §1.0.3 |
| Aggregate demand plausibly **exceeds one cluster**, which is a second reason for multiple stores | §1.0.3 |
| Depth is **per tier**, so the depth/breadth trade is really a **tiering** problem — DeLawson is one tier | §1.0.3.1 |
| DeLawson spans **8 orders of magnitude** of read latency internally and exposes none of it | §1.0.3.1 |
| **No reconstruct-for-read**: repair the whole group within the timeout, or flag it hot and fail | §9.8 |
| Because reconstructing for a read **does work the system does not persist** | §9.8, §1.6.4 |
| The **user sets the read timeout**, making availability-versus-latency their choice | §9.8 |
| Repair priority takes a third input: **read demand**, +1 global read applied after the swap | §13.4.0, §9.8 |
| Repair admission is a budget on **outstanding** reads+writes, returned on completion — the bin is the feedback loop | §13.4.3 |
| Bandwidth is a **whole-cluster** resource, so a **coordinator** hands out per-SN allocations | §13.4.4 |
| `grant = min(max(min(work, minimum), proportional), maximum)` — a floor, a share, and a self-DOS cap | §13.4.4 |
| Shared domains is why a coordinator is needed **and** why its per-SN ceiling rarely binds | §13.4.4.1 |
| A **tree of coordinators rooted at SN0**; two levels covers any real cluster | §13.4.4.2 |
| Recurring idiom: **a set of floors is a partition of a total** and must be validated as one | §13.4.4.3 |
| Sum the minimums to **a half or a third** of the total | §13.4.4.4 |
| **Equal sharing is pessimal**: with work and capacity fixed, the last completion is invariant, the earlier ones are free | §13.4.4.4, §5.12.4 |
| So compute **serializes at maximum parallelism** — 45% lower mean latency, 10× on staggered arrivals, same throughput | §5.12.4 |
| But bounded by Amdahl: run the **fewest concurrent jobs that saturates**, not literally one | §5.12.4.1 |
| The same rule cuts **temporary storage** by the same factor — Little's law makes it one win, not two | §5.12.4.2 |
| Which lands in **RAM**, the 5,000×-priced tier, because §5.12.2 wants working sets resident | §5.12.4.2 |
| Total scratch byte-seconds fall too, so finishing sooner **also costs less** | §5.12.4.2 |
| Compute is paid from a **bank of compute-hours**; a job starts when the balance covers its expected cost | §5.12.5 |
| Fourth instance of: **guaranteed allocations partition a total** — and an accumulating one needs a ceiling too | §5.12.5 |
| For compute, **quota and billing merge**: the balance is the quota, the hours spent are the record | §5.12.5.2 |
| The bank has a **ceiling, and charging stops there** — an unspent compute-hour costs the provider nothing | §5.12.5.1 |
| So storage bills **continuously** and compute bills **up to a cap**: same principle, different shapes | §5.12.5.1 |
| Rate buys **throughput**, ceiling buys **burst**; Σ rates bounds the steady state, Σ ceilings the transient | §5.12.5.1a |
| **Scheduled compute-hours** guarantee capacity at contention times, at a premium; unused ones fall into the bank | §5.12.6 |
| The premium prices the **opportunity cost**, so there is no use-it-or-lose-it — only the certainty is spent | §5.12.6 |
| **No overbooking**: Σ scheduled(t) ≤ cores at every instant — a calendar feasibility check, not a sum | §5.12.6.1 |
| Solvency uses the **average** scheduled load; the peak constrains only that instant | §5.12.6.2 |
| DeLawson's own recurring jobs are the **first customer** of scheduled compute | §5.12.6.2 |
| The floor staggers completion, so **whole users recover early** — worth more than partial recovery (§4.3.3.3) | §13.4.4.4 |
| Its cost is a **cap-limited tail**, which gives the per-SN maximum a second job | §13.4.4.4a |
| **Georeplication is a ship requirement**, and the only answer to §4.3.3.1's dominant loss term | §13.4.5 |
| It costs **1 at each end**, plus WAN — the first purpose the scalar ball bin cannot express | §13.4.5.1 |
| Re-encrypt at the **destination**; instances need not be byte-identical across clusters | §13.4.5.2 |
| Durability seconds must survive the trip; **`(path, record number)` is the portable name**, not the `DnId` | §4.6.3, §13.4.5.3 |
| `DnId`/`SnId` are **internal and cluster-local**; the path is the user-visible durable name | §4.6.3 |
| A hint is cluster-local by construction, and fails detectably across clusters — and detectably after a rewrite, since the extent's creation second is part of it | §4.6.3, §8.1.1a-10 |
| The georep destination gets a **dedicated directory**, so replicas cannot collide with local objects | §13.4.5.4 |
| So portability is relative to the replication root, and cross-cluster translation is **one prefix substitution** | §13.4.5.4 |
| Georep directories are **read-only permanently** — never promoted, so no offset-level split brain | §13.4.5.4 |
| Failover is a **copy by concatenation**, sharing sealed extents — metadata-only, zero space at copy time | §13.4.5.5 |
| Divergence is free: the shared base plus a private log is just §4.2 | §13.4.5.5 |
| The copy is placed at the **original path**, so source-built indexes resolve with no translation | §13.4.5.5a |
| Record numbers survive only if the **whole** object is copied in order | §13.4.5.5a |
| A permanently read-only replica is a mechanism that **resists the operator** (§4.3.4.2) | §13.4.5.4 |
| **Priority is door height, not a sort**: round-robin plus thresholds, so no heap over 2^31 items | §13.4.3.3 |
| Two doors per purpose: a **floor** admitted readily, then competition for the surplus | §13.4.3.1 |
| **Every door is below 10% remaining** — 1% for high priority, 9% for low; the bin runs nearly empty by design | §13.4.3.5 |
| Low priority therefore runs **only at idle**, and resolution improves under congestion | §13.4.3.4, §13.4.3.5 |
| The scheme is **work-conserving**: alone, any purpose reaches ~91%+ — doors arbitrate, they do not partition | §13.4.3.6 |
| So `sufficient` is a **floor, never a ceiling**; implementing it as a quota destroys that | §13.4.3.6 |
| So there is no expensive read to meter, and read billing can stay flat | §9.8.1 |
| Idle-time reconstruct-for-read is expressible as a **very high door** — but is **not worth building** | §9.8.2, §9.8.3 |
| Because a solve that writes its result **already exists** as repair with read-demand priority | §9.8.3 |
| The scale ambition is ~10^57 bits; DeLawson addresses ~10^26, so it is **10^31 short** and directional | §1.0.4 |
| Relative timestamps are why §1.3's rule survives a scale nobody designed for | §1.0.4, §4.6.3 |
| The intermediate scale is a **torus Dyson swarm** — 2^18 elements, so **inside** DeLawson's addressing | §1.0.5 |
| Its load-bearing property is **neighbours stay neighbours**, which is what lets placement never be revisited | §1.0.5 |
| Cluster diameter is a **choice of minimum communication time** — fast means small, slow means large | §1.0.5 |
| **Cluster diameter is free; ring diameter is not** — ~1,000 km at a 1 s failover target | §1.0.5 |
| The AI workload selects a **few km**, 300× tighter than consensus needs | §1.0.3, §1.0.5 |
| **StarMind** is a plausible near-term platform; a fast cluster is a circular section of the torus surface | §1.0.5.1 |
| In orbit the scarce resources are **launch mass and heat rejection**, so §1.2's basis changes and §12.1's rule does not | §1.0.5.1 |
| Every append records its **durability second**, so time-range queries work indefinitely — distinct from the minutes-long SCN snapshot horizon | §9.7 |
| **User code only on Compute; keys never where user code runs** | §1.5 |
| **A tenant is not a domain; a path is** — aliases falsify the tenant partition, so authorization attaches to the **directory** | §5.9.1a |
| Which is the unit §8.4.3 already uses for expiry, soft-delete opt-out and storage class — a fourth unit would have to justify itself | §5.9.1a, §8.4.3 |
| **No per-object ACL**: unbounded per-object metadata (§14.2), and S3 and GCS both shipped object ACLs and **deprecated** them for unauditability | §5.9.1a |
| If policy needs a grouping the tree does not express, **the tree is wrong** — cheap here, since a directory is derived and renames move nothing | §5.9.1a, §5.1.2.2 |
| **No deny rules**: composition is an alias AND the owner's ACL, and intersection is monotone, so any deny is a smaller grant | §5.9.1a, §5.1.1 |
| **Ownership is a tree; reachability is a graph** — everything structural runs on the tree | §5.1.1.1a |
| So **alias cycles are allowed**, bounded by keeping the aliases on the path and checking before recursing | §5.1.1.1a |
| Every object has a **canonical path**, the alias-free one; scrub and billing use only those | §5.1.1.1a |
| **Writable aliases** are allowed, and delete comes with write — so an alias's **grant** protects the target | §5.1.1.1a, §5.1.1.3 |
| The split is **Unix's hard-link against symlink**, and the canonical path is POSIX's `realpath` | §5.1.1.1b |
| Accounting on the owning tree is **AFS's volume quota**; **Tahoe-LAFS** shows the cost of cycles in the *reference* graph | §5.1.1.1b |
| The one different idea — a **per-viewer mount table** — forbids nesting, so it duplicates per worker | §5.1.1.1b |
| No-deny rests on **monotonicity**, not on how many policies compose — §5.1.1.1a unbounds the chain | §5.9.1a, §5.1.1.1a |
| Sharing one object is an **event with an expiry**, not durable state — a capability, not an ACL | §5.9.1a, §9.1.3.5 |
| The real boundary is **signed executables**, not absence of keys — which makes code signing load-bearing | §1.5 |
| **Extent decryption happens on the EN**; end-to-end encryption is a user-side option, not a product | §5.9.2, §7.2.3 |
| **AEGIS-128X2**, ~20 GB/s per core: encryption is 0.63 of a core at line rate where compression would be ~21 | §7.2.1 |
| The **AEAD tag is the checksum**, so every block is self-verifying before EC uses it as a repair source | §7.2.1 |
| Everything is encrypted **on the wire and on disk**; KS uses 256-bit | §7.2, §7.2.1 |
| Targets: **200k QPS** small metadata requests, **2M+ batched**, **per box** — both reached, the unbatched one **only just** | §1.4.0, §17.19.1 |
| ⚠️ **Between-session variance is ~23% where a three-trial spread is 0.6%**, so cross-session comparisons are worth ±25% | §17.19.2 |
| So a before/after must run **both arms in one session**, or a regression the size of the noise is invisible | §17.19.2 |
| The 10× gap says **nine tenths of the unbatched cost is messaging**; the ping ceiling is >64M QPS | §1.4.0 |
| Those figures are **end-to-end** — durable log write per message, encryption, compression, Nagle off | §1.4.0.1 |
| **Batching subsumes io_uring** on the network path: batching gave all the gains, io_uring was a regression | §1.4.0.1 |
| Read requests are logged because §12 requires **metering** them; batching is a billing mechanism too | §1.4.0.3 |
| **Batch depth is set by the compression window and the log write** — overhead amortization saturates at ~100 | §1.4.0.2 |
| Compression cuts **network and bytes written**, not just capacity, and the saving is realized per crossing | §7.1.3 |
| The gap is **repeated keyed compaction**, not compression — a **signed compute tier** is the likely home | §7.2.2.1 |
| Compaction frequency now trades **four** ways: write amp, read amp, hint validity, recompression CPU | §7.2.2.1 |
| So it pays for itself on HDD (threshold ~194 MB/s vs LZ4's 600) and does not on NVMe (~2.4 GB/s) | §7.1.3 |
| Compression **shortens every repair window**, so it improves durability, not only cost | §7.1.3 |
| A cluster may run **indefinitely** and lie dormant for eons — no absolute epochs, no work per elapsed time | §1.3 |

**Object model**

| | |
|---|---|
| Two flavors: **unkeyed** (64-bit record number, append only at the end) and **keyed** (sorted key, insert anywhere) | §3 |
| The asymmetry follows from counts being stable under update and tombstone but not insert | §3 |
| **Records are a store-layer primitive** — framing, record numbers, keys. The largest divergence from Cosmos | §1.4.5.1 |
| Five framings — `FixedLength`, `Nul`, `Lf`, `CrLf`, `LengthPrefixed` — declared at creation, **translatable on read and re-writable by coalescing**, so framing is not a durable property of the data | §8.2 |
| **Declared expiry**, defaulting to "never" but discouraged — the main lever on garbage | §8.5 |

**Structure**

| | |
|---|---|
| Four levels: object → streams → extents → instances | §4 |
| **Stored as lists, served as B-trees** — snapshot, Raft log, state machine | §4.4 |
| **Tail-only summaries may be synchronous; mid-tree summaries are lazy.** Why count-based addressing works at all | §4.5 |
| References are **node-local**: 4 B object→stream, 4 B stream→extent, 6 B extent→instance. No cluster-wide names in the data plane | §4.6 |
| Identity carries ownership: stream = `(DnId, StreamId)`, extent = `(SnId, ExtentId, creation second)` | §4.6.3 |
| Timestamps are **8-byte seconds compared by signed difference**, reinterpretable indefinitely | §4.6.3 |
| Position-dependent facts live in the **referrer**, not the target — forced by sharing | §4.6.2 |
| Extent = sealed **base** plus lazily-created **log**; compaction folds them | §4.2 |
| Extents seal on **either** limit: 4 GB logical or 32 MB physical | §6 |

**Durability**

| | |
|---|---|
| **4 instances while open, erasure-coded once sealed** | §4.3 |
| Four is really a decision to **relax the repair window**, not a reliability necessity | §4.3.1.1 |
| **Storage overhead = 1/(1 − survivable disaster fraction)**, achieved by MDS codes | §4.3.3 |
| Working assumption **Reed-Solomon, MDS, m = 4**; overhead chosen from disaster tolerance | §4.3.2 |
| Local codes trade minimum distance for locality, and are **patent-blocked until 2034** — **turbo codes** are the unencumbered fallback, at 1.5× and 2.5× instead of 1.333× and 2.333×, so the patent is worth **~$0.24/TB-month** | §4.3.2.1 |
| The two EC tiers are one **10×6 LRC** (1.333×) and its **data-duplicated variant** (2.333×) | §12.7.2.1 |
| The deliverable is a **catalog of codes with recommendations**, not one code; **turbo codes suffice for shipping** | §4.3.2.5 |
| Overhead is a **parameter**, not a discriminator — compare families at matched overhead | §4.3.2.5 |
| Codes are judged by **equivalence to 3× or 4× replication** — what customers already accept — under independent loss and under domain-loss-plus-independent-loss | §4.3.3.2a |
| The second instance buys **removal of repair from the read path**, not durability — minutes to readable instead of days | §12.7.2.1a |
| Erasure coding does not address **software bugs, admin error, or running out of space** | §4.3.4 |
| Utilization ≤ **1 − 1/D** is a *durability* requirement — a full cluster cannot repair | §4.3.4 |
| Repair must exceed the failure rate or loss is **certain**, not unlikely | §4.3.4.1 |
| **EC groups whole extents; it never splits them into fragments** — so reads never touch EC at all | §4.3.2.3 |
| Group members must be **byte-identical and of equal physical length**; SN owns the group | §4.3.2.3 |
| 1.333× and 2.333× are **one code with a different data-instance count**; the difference is availability, not durability | §4.3.2.4 |
| Repair bandwidth is a **network** number, not a device number — so the codec choice is **media-neutral** | §4.3.2.2a |
| All three candidate codes have **minimum distance 8**; the LRC wins on cell count and maximal recoverability | §4.3.3.2b |
| Product codes can be counted in **closed form** — no Monte Carlo needed for half the comparison | §4.3.3.2c |
| Equal-lossiness `f*` is a property of **(code, scheduler)** jointly, so the simulation needs the scheduler in it | §4.3.3.2c |
| Repair amplification is **not monotonic** in loss; it peaks at the first forced global solve | §4.3.3.2d |
| Domain requirements are `ceil(4k/3)` **per recovery set, at every nesting level** | §4.3.3.2e |
| Domain counts say where a code **reaches designed reliability**, not a minimum cluster size | §4.3.3.2e |
| Repair sorts by **amortized cost**, deprioritizing the single expensive class and letting it evolve | §13.4 |
| The greedy risk-per-byte order is the **wrong** order; the argument is over the population, not the group | §13.4.1 |
| The fast loop needs **no re-replication timeout** — duration is a priority input | §13.4.2 |

**Machines**

| | |
|---|---|
| **DN**, **SN**, **EN**, plus **FE**, **KS**, Compute, and the `delawson` client | §5, §5.9 |
| **Metadata is made reliable by consensus; bulk data by placement** | §5 |
| The **DN tier is self-hosted** in DeLawson keyed objects; the bootstrap root lives in **DN0's Raft state** | §5.5, §5.5.1 |
| **Two roots, not one**: the **object-locator** root is DN0's Raft state; the **topology** root is **KS** | §5.5.6 |
| KS owns tenant ids and ranges, the machine list, and **ring membership** — because a ring's membership cannot live in that ring | §5.5.6.1 |
| And because DN0's state is encrypted, so KS is up first: the fact naming DN0's members cannot be inside DN0 | §5.5.6.1 |
| **Leadership is not membership**: the ring holds who is primary, callers cache it, and a stale cache costs a **redirect** | §5.5.6.2 |
| Putting leadership in KS is the one arrangement that cannot work — failover must beat a timeout | §5.5.6.2, §16.12 |
| KS's state splits: keys **encrypted** behind the ceremony, topology **signed** and readable at once | §5.5.6.3 |
| Because the threat to topology is **integrity, not disclosure** — a forged domain map is a placement attack | §5.5.6.3 |
| **KS is on the change path, not the data path**, so a running cluster serves through a KS outage | §5.5.6.3 |
| ⚠️ **"Secure guarded" does not transfer to orbit**: physical attack gets much harder, and a local ceremony becomes impossible | §7.3.2.8 |
| So the ceremony moves to Earth and the key is **told** to a quorum member — the verifier is what makes that safe | §7.3.2.8 |
| Because **possession of the key is the authorization**, so the satellite needs no PKI and no trust root | §7.3.2.8 |
| ⚠️ Therefore **wire keys must never come from KS's locked half**, or a locked KS cannot accept the connection that unlocks it | §7.3.2.8, #91 |
| Latency is irrelevant on that path — §1.0.5's *cluster diameter is free, ring diameter is not*, one level out | §7.3.2.8 |
| Rings have 2n+1 voters but only **3 materialized members** — 3× RAM, not 7× | §5.7 |
| **Many rings per machine**; rings are a concurrency unit, not a capacity unit | §5.8 |
| **32-bit node ids**, bounded fan-out ~20,000, local indices in the data plane | §5.10 |
| SNs place on a **disk**, not an EN | §5.3.1 |
| Failure domains are **nested, never orthogonal**; slack 4/3 | §5.6 |
| Placement is **free-space-weighted random with rejection** — provably optimal, and self-balancing at any scale | §5.6.3, §5.6.4 |
| **No rebalancing.** Fullness is handled by redirecting writes; only DN range splits move anything | §5.11, §13.1.2 |
| **Default locality**: a directory's objects land on one SN | §5.11.1 |
| The intra-cluster network is **flat**, so there is no affinity mechanism | §5.12.3 |
| The **SN is not in the write path** | §8.1.3 |
| **Minimum viable cluster is one machine**; an unenforceable placement rule is simply **not enforced** | §5.6.7 |
| Placement is decided at write time and **never revisited**, so oscillation causes no churn | §5.6.7 |
| Achieved durability is therefore a **per-group** property, computed from placements, not from config | §5.6.8 |
| Independence **self-heals through compaction**, not through a rebalancer | §5.6.8 |
| Placement is a solver whose answer is **persisted in the instance list order** — steady state is verification | §5.6.9 |
| Therefore the instance list must **never be sorted or reordered** | §5.6.9 |
| Slack exists to make the **solve cheap** (`s/(s−1)` draws → 4 at 4/3) and to allow routing around bad domains | §5.6.1a |
| Raising the slack threshold **turns rules off** in mid-size clusters, so tune upward from the smallest | §5.6.1a |
| A **solver timeout** must defer and retry, never drop a rule | §5.6.10 |
| Verification is **incremental at 1 minute, unconditional at 1 hour**, riding the two sync loops | §13.1.10 |
| A dead EN cannot report its own disks, so the work list comes from a **scan**, bucketed by EN | §13.1.10.1 |

**Pipeline and keys**

| | |
|---|---|
| frame → **compress → encrypt** → replicate → seal → erasure-code. Both orderings are forced | §7 |
| Compression and encryption are **block-granular** at the index granule; the index points at **physical** offsets | §7.1, §9.3 |
| Keys: **daily master keys in KS only**, daily SN-master keys cached on ENs, extent keys derived. ~1 MB per century | §7.3 |
| **The EN does the on-disk crypto** — derives and caches a key per extent, encrypts and decrypts stored data, re-encrypts for the wire. Wire encryption is a self-contained layer the rest of the design ignores | §7.3.5, §17.5a |
| **Every tier sees some user data** — a DN compares user keys, an FE cuts records out of blocks — so the trust boundary is **DeLawson code against user code**, not tier against tier. Disk keys live only on ENs | §7.3.6, §1.5 |
| KS is unlocked by **operator secrets plus hardware** — the only step needing people | §7.3.2 |
| KS has a **ring**, so unlocking is a ladder: the boundary needing people is **the key being in no memory**, not quorum loss | §7.3.2.1 |
| A ring that lost quorum **heals itself**: membership is already committed, and quorums of successive configurations **intersect** | §7.3.2.2 |
| So a lone survivor must not act — its view may predate an **eviction** — but a quorum of its known configuration may | §7.3.2.2 |
| The ring stores a **verifier** for the unlocking key, so a wrong key fails loudly instead of producing garbage | §7.3.2.3 |
| Which is safe **only because the key is generated, never chosen** — a commitment to a passphrase is a brute-force oracle | §7.3.2.3 |
| The key store is **append-only and never prunes**: pruning a key deletes a day's data irreversibly | §7.3.2.4 |
| Ultimate recovery is **k-of-n shards** — surviving n−k losses and resisting k−1 colluders are the same knob, pulled opposite ways | §7.3.2.5 |
| And **shards are never stored with the hardware**, which is the only thing separating owner-recovery from thief-recovery | §7.3.2.5 |
| ⚠️ Automatic re-keying is a **key-extraction oracle** for physical access, and consensus cannot close it — membership speaks to identity, not integrity | §7.3.2.7 |
| **Splitting the secret does not help**: a member that can do the job can leak the job, so an envelope just moves the problem | §7.3.2.7 |
| The only structural fix is **threshold-sharing each master key across the ring**, affordable because KS is low-rate — undecided, §16.138 | §7.3.2.7 |
| Index granularity is `latency × bandwidth / 2` — **1 MB HDD, 20 KB SSD**, in *physical* bytes | §7.1.1 |
| Compression improves **HDD** read bandwidth and degrades **NVMe** read bandwidth; it is mandatory regardless | §7.1.2 |
| **An extent has exactly one media class**, because compression block size is durable and EC needs identical bytes | §7.4.2 |
| So a fast-read copy is a **tier or cache, never an instance**; migration is compaction with a new target | §7.4.2 |
| Every device-dependent constant lives in **one media-class table** in config | §7.4.1 |

**Writing, reading, syncing**

| | |
|---|---|
| Append blocks are atomic; **accepted / applied / durable**, with 3-of-4 a quorum | §8.1.1 |
| **Erasure coding forces byte-identical instances**, so an instance must **truncate above the durable watermark** on handover | §8.1.1a |
| The primary assigns a **logical** offset in a tiny serialized window; compress, encrypt and write happen outside it | §8.1.1a-2 |
| **Fixed-offset** appends supply their expected offset and are **exactly-once**; **assigned-offset** appends are **at-least-once**. The difference is duplicate prevention, not writer count — several writers may fix offsets. Prior art: **Azure append blobs**, same two modes, same rationale | §8.1.1a-3, §8.1.1a-5 |
| Logical offsets are **dense** — no padding, no holes — which is what makes the fixed-offset check, the reorder cache, and cumulative byte totals work | §8.1.1a-6 |
| **Unkeyed** objects have one unsealed extent, so the **object** logical offset is reportable; **keyed** objects have several, so only an extent-relative offset exists and it does not survive coalescing | §8.1.1a-7 |
| So compare-and-append is unkeyed-only; keyed objects get idempotency **from the key** | §8.1.1a-7 |
| An append block is a **byte range**, not a set of records; only a writer fixing its own offsets may leave a fragment | §8.1 |
| An append is bounded at **32 MB logical and 32 MB compressed**, equal on purpose so that incompressible data never fails the compressed cap; a *record* may be extent-sized, since it may span appends | §8.1.1a-2, §8.2.4 |
| No chunk padding: an append that will not fit **seals the extent short** | §8.1.1c |
| The quorum forces **broadcast, not a daisy chain** | §8.1.2 |
| **Soft delete** is a deferred decrement: 3-day window, timers in parallel across layers, opt-out per directory | §8.4 |
| Metadata must not **predecease** its data — which makes the heroics window for user deletes zero | §8.4.1d |
| Three sync loops: disk state **~1 min**, instance state **~1 hr**, DN→SN **days to months** | §13.1 |
| Sync is driven **from above**, one message per pair, with bucket counts negotiated **upward only** | §13.1 |
| Exactly two sync loops, because **only cross-tier references can drift** | §13.1.7 |
| Hot small objects need **caching plus a broadcast tree**, not more replicas | §9.6 |
| Appends stage in per-EN, single-copy **common extents**; four independent ENs are the durability | §8.1.4 |
| The receipt names the **final** extent; compression happens **upstream of the four-way fan-out** | §8.1.4, §8.1.4.1 |
| The durable watermark is set at **staging**, not at coalescing | §8.1.4.2 |
| 3-of-4 durability plus local coalescing gives **interior holes**, exactly detectable from the offset map | §8.1.4.3 |
| Staging is sized by **endurance, not capacity**; stage only small appends | §8.1.4.5 |
| Staging must be durable **with the power off**, so not DRAM | §8.1.4.5 |
| **The `delawson` client library compresses**, cutting append size across the internet | §8.1.4.1 |
| So initial compression is **never billed** by storage — it is the customer's CPU, or a compute job's | §8.1.4.1 |
| The 4 copies while open are **the four ENs' staging**, not 4 dedicated replicas | §4.3, §8.1.4.4 |
| Migration writes only the **1 or 2 instances EC needs** — write one, copy it — a **4× saving** | §8.1.4.4 |
| Common extents are the protection **until the EC group can protect itself** | §8.1.4.4 |
| So **recompression need never be deterministic**: exactly one node performs it | §8.1.4.4 |
| Prior art returns an offset only with **one** unsealed region (VSAM RBA); parallel writers always change the **name space** | §8.1.1a-9 |
| Three reference tiers: **durable** (key / record number), **hint** (`EnId`, extent name, row — a route a caller may hold, good for at least the hint window), and **none** (object offset) | §8.1.1a-10, §10.1 |
| Hints fail **detectably** because extent identity carries a creation second — Oracle's logical rowid pattern | §8.1.1a-10 |
| One key and one salt may cover **one** plaintext, so **within an extent an offset is written at most once, ever** | §7.2.4 |
| Therefore **a truncation seals the extent** — chosen over an IV epoch, which would need agreement in the write path and could be silently missed | §7.2.4, §8.1.1a |
| An instance may **mark itself broken and request a seal**; ***I* − *Q* + 1** of them force one, because the extent is then unappendable | §8.1.7.4 |
| A single instance may trigger one — sealing is universally safe, so the cost is **metadata churn**, damped at the SN | §8.1.7.4 |
| The mark is **durable and one-way**, and a marked instance fails every append **it sees** — so nobody counts, and the threshold is a consequence rather than a detector | §8.1.7.4.1 |
| **Seal requests exist at all three levels** — object, stream, extent — because concatenation needs sealed inputs | §6.4, §8.6.1 |
| For an **unkeyed** object that is one extent's work, since §6.3 and §8.1.1a-7 leave exactly one open extent | §6.4 |
| **Top-down**: close the container before its contents, or a concurrent append is still entitled to a new extent | §6.4 |
| **Ask the primary first, fall back to failure-mode sealing** — the fallback is slower *and* seals above the durable length | §6.4.1 |
| A requested seal **quiesces**, so it discards nothing; only handover and broken instances truncate | §6.4.1, §7.2.4 |
| **Every read names the object**, whatever else it names: the ACL is the object's, and no reverse edge recovers it | §9.1.3.4, §4.6.6 |
| A range start is the **object**, optionally **how far the caller already resolved**, and a **position**; a stale narrowing falls back to the object | §9.1.3.4 |
| A bare offset **snaps forward** to the next record boundary, so independently computed chunk boundaries are a **partition** — the Hadoop split rule | §9.1.3.4 |
| **Record + logical offset** is the only way to address the **interior of a record**, which a store for very large objects needs | §9.1.3.4 |
| A hint carries an unforgeable **capability** attesting `extent ∈ object` — asserting the pairing, or indexing extents by id, both fail | §9.1.3.5, §4.6.6 |
| The certificate **carries the authorization** — `(tenant, extent, write?)` — so no ACL is read at use time and both hops go | §9.1.3.5 |
| The **directory is used to mint it, not to check it**; that answers #81, since the ACL is not fetched at all | §9.1.3.5, §5.9.1a |
| ⚠️ Cost: a stale certificate authorizes for up to the hint window, and a quoted hint is no longer harmless | §9.1.3.5 |
| Which is tolerable on the assumption of **no security boundary inside a tenant** — an assumption, and load-bearing | §9.1.3.5, §16.145 |
| Because tenant-binding is what lets a scheduler **mint once and hand hints to many vertices** | §9.1.3.5, §8.1.1a-10 |
| Bounded because revocation stops **minting** at once, so nothing new can be obtained | §9.1.3.5 |
| **Stale certificates are accepted**, so removing a permission has a delay of the certificate lifetime | §9.1.3.5.2 |
| Which makes that lifetime a **security** parameter as well as a performance one, and §16.86 gains a second input | §9.1.3.5.2, §16.86 |
| ⚠️ A **broadcast** revocation is the third point on the curve, at the cost of an FE that must fail closed | §9.1.3.5.2, §9.6.2 |
| **Write is a plaintext flag that selects the signing key** — forging it changes which key is checked, so it fails | §9.1.3.5.3 |
| Which gives **two lifetimes**: long for reads where the DN load is, short for writes where the danger is | §9.1.3.5.3 |
| And scopes the **authority to grant** a write, since a holder of only the read key cannot mint one | §9.1.3.5.3, §7.3.1 |
| The hint stays **plaintext with the capability appended**, so an operator can act on a hint a user quoted | §9.1.3.5 |
| The signed form is **closed**: every field is in the answer, in the request, or ambient — else the request cannot be built | §9.1.3.5.4 |
| ⚠️ So it carries **identity, never a derived position** — signing a record number would put §17.16.2's three spaces inside the signature | §9.1.3.5.4 |
| A **128-bit tag** (16 bytes) and a **256-bit key**, by §7.2.1's own high-value-low-volume rule | §9.1.3.5.4 |
| ⚠️ Certificates are **~a quarter of a full answer**, which is why asking for them is an opt-in bit | §9.1.3.5.4, §9.1.3.11 |
| A position **may** be signed if its space is pinned by an identity in the same signature — so an **extent** offset could be | §9.1.3.5.4 |
| The birthday bound does not apply, since the attacker needs **one particular** extent — so 8 bytes would be sound | §9.1.3.5.4 |
| A budget is in **records, logical bytes or compressed bytes** — one named, all three reported; **one block always returns**, even past it | §9.1.3.6 |
| `object-info` is **extended, not replaced**, and bounded by **one entry limit** over objects + streams + extents (default **10,000**) | §9.1.3.7 |
| A batch answer leads with a **header**, and its continuation is an **index** — the caller already holds the list | §17.23 |
| It measures a name's cost **before** committing, stops at a **name boundary**, and always returns **at least one** | §17.23.1 |
| ⚠️ A batch **spans DNs**, so asking all of them for everything wastes up to **D times** the work — and wastes the expensive part | §9.1.3.12 |
| A batch is an **explicit list**, so routing is free and needs no round trip; what the FE lacks is each name's **cost** | §9.1.3.12, §9.1.3.1 |
| So: full ask to one DN, a **per-object summary** to the rest — one row per name, fixed work, no SN hop | §9.1.3.12 |
| That summary gives the **exact object count** elsewhere, and the first DN gets **limit − that count** | §9.1.3.12 |
| The detailed ask goes to the DN holding the **earliest names**, because the answer must be a prefix in the *caller's* order | §9.1.3.12 |
| The reservation needs **no round trip**: FE knows how many names it routed elsewhere, and each costs one entry | §17.24.3 |
| Round two takes a **contiguous run from the first unfinished name**, since that is where the caller will come back to | §17.24.3 |
| ⚠️ Every estimate is allowed to be wrong, because assembly **stops at the first name it does not have** | §17.24.4 |
| A shape's `next` means **where a listing would resume**, not where the rows asked for ran out | §17.24.2 |
| ⚠️ **Hash routing makes a batch cost D messages** — 46% slower over three DNs, and 63 requests per 100 names at a hundred | §17.24.5 |
| So contiguous **ranges** (#75) are what keeps a batch one request; a hash is the worst case by construction | §17.24.5 |
| It also tells a caller enough to **parallelize the rest itself**, which is §9.1.3.2's shape one level out | §9.1.3.12, §9.1.3.2 |
| **HDFS scans** its block list to find an offset — 2 × 10^9 blocks at 256 PB, the same number §14.1 reaches | §9.1.3.8 |
| Which is §4.5's rule with the counterfactual attached: locating by **record** is a descent, locating by **byte** is a walk | §9.1.3.8, §4.5 |
| **Streams carry flags**, and `updatable` is one — a *declared* guarantee, not an observed one | §9.1.3.9 |
| With it, and **tombstones retaining their original logical length**, the logical prefix sum is tail-only and may be exact | §9.1.3.9 |
| So the byte space behaves as the number space already does: a dead record keeps its **number and its width** | §9.1.3.9, §3 |
| Preserving a width **costs no space** — a logical offset is a name (§8.2.2), so compaction still reclaims the bytes | §9.1.3.9 |
| The snap rule ignores liveness, or a delete would move a partition boundary | §9.1.3.9, §9.1.3.4 |
| **Make the logic simple** → **reduce negation depth** → **name positively**; the last applies to all names, not just flags | §13.2.5.1, §4.1.1.0 |
| So flags are named for the **capability**, never its absence: `deletable`, not `undeletable` | §4.1.1.0 |
| A rollout parameter **defaults to the old behaviour** — "checked in off" is that rule for an *additive* feature only | §13.2.5.1 |
| So a *restrictive* feature's parameter is `deletes_allowed`, defaulting **true**: positive name, old behaviour, no thesaurus | §13.2.5.1 |
| Positive naming costs a negation at the **enforcement** site, so name for the **more frequent reading** | §13.2.5.1 |
| The **`LOff`/`COff` trick generalizes**: wrap same-typed values when a mix-up would be **silent** | §8.1.6.1 |
| And the sharpest test of silent is that the two **coincide in the cases a test would cover** | §8.1.6.1 |
| ⚠️ But **Rust charges more than C++** for it, so it is for clear benefits: `ROff`, `ObjectId`, `StreamId`, `ExtentId`, `Second` | §8.1.6.1 |
| An id mix-up is **loud as an address and silent as a map key**, which is most places | §8.1.6.1 |
| **Wrap values; group parameters.** A run of same-typed arguments wants a struct, as `AppendBlock` was | §8.1.6.1, §17.13.3 |
| ⚠️ `ROff` does **not** catch §17.16.2's three record spaces, and a partial fix that looks total is the risk | §8.1.6.1 |

**Coding rules**

| | |
|---|---|
| They have a home: **§18**, with four occupants, since a rule stated where it was argued drifts | §18, §16.141 |
| **Decompose the state**: m + n things is far less code than m × n, usually down to almost-independent booleans | §18.1 |
| Already done six times here — the `Want` bits, the capability flags, per-tier masks, nonce dimensions | §18.1.1 |
| And once by **removing** a dimension: a budget names one measure of three, never two | §18.1.1, §9.1.3.6 |
| For an **implication**, **normalize rather than validate** — then no illegal combination exists to test | §18.1.2 |
| An **exclusion** cannot be normalized away, and that is the kind wanting a negative test | §18.1.2 |
| Worth most is the **practice**; then that all pairs cost only **log n** cases; the tool is third | §18.1.3 |
| And the logarithm needs **complicated** test cases — one-thing-at-a-time suites pay the quadratic instead | §18.1.3 |
| The two knots here are the **append interface** (2,560 combinations, ~15 rows) and **stream properties** | §18.1.3 |
| ⚠️ **Lots of ways the tool fails to fit** — the practice survives them, the tool does not | §18.1.5 |
| **Nested dimensions** are worse than excluded ones: out-of-scope values are *meaningless*, not disallowed | §18.1.5 |
| When the knot grows, **add the feature to several random existing cases**, not regenerate | §18.1.5 |
| Because a suite that has been **run** is worth more than the array it came from — §5.6.9's persisted solver answer | §18.1.5, §5.6.9 |
| ⚠️ And the **term index is a first cut at which invariants interact**, so the pairs worth covering are already computed | §18.1.4, #92 |
| An index and a count sharing a type make the max count **2^64 − 1**, or **2^64 − 2** with a sentinel | §8.1.6.2 |
| Because **one past the end** must be representable, which §9.1.3's `next` computes on every answer | §8.1.6.2 |
| ⚠️ So §6's **4 GB** logical cap is one byte outside the `u32` enforcing it — the code is right, the doc is round (#89) | §8.1.6.2 |
| ⚠️ And `records = 0` already means *unknown* for an open extent, colliding with a real zero (#90) | §8.1.6.2 |
| Which is the best argument for the newtypes: the type owns the **sentinel** and the **boundary arithmetic**, at `u64`'s size | §8.1.6.2 |
| **Every space reserves a sentinel**, used or not: the bound comparison exists anyway, so it is nearly free | §8.1.6.3 |
| And uniform now beats a **format-contract change** later, which is what needing one later would cost | §8.1.6.3 |
| Sentinel at **`MAX` for measures** (zero is a real length) and at **`0` for ids** (allocated from 1, so free) | §8.1.6.3 |
| Because **double negatives read as emphasis of the negative** — a default of the language faculty, seen in novel languages | §4.1.1.0 |
| Withdrawing a capability is **deferred**, but the **official flag stays permissive** until cleanup completes | §4.1.1.1 |
| So the reliance rule is **unrepresentable to get wrong**: nothing can see a half-established restriction | §4.1.1.1 |
| **Enforcement is optimistic and reliance is conservative** — two views that want opposite biases | §4.1.1.1 |
| `off`/`henceforth`/`always` is **vocabulary for a transition**, not values in a record | §4.1.1.1 |
| The pattern is Oracle's `ENABLE NOVALIDATE`, which is **Bob's own feature** — so it is first-hand rather than matched from the literature | §4.1.1.1 |
| **`deletable`** is a second capability flag: withdrawing it bars *record* deletes, while dropping the whole stream stays possible | §9.1.3.10 |
| It buys **no log to probe** on every read, no deletion-driven compaction, and no churn against the repair reserve | §9.1.3.10 |
| ⚠️ Its cleanup pass is a compaction, and compaction must **preserve tombstone widths** — the two passes' natural implementations break each other | §9.1.3.10, §9.1.3.9 |
| Stream metadata has a **normal size plus a flag and extra structure** for the rare and the transient | §4.1.2 |
| Which makes the promise flags nearly free: only the middle state needs a cursor, and it is **transient by construction** | §4.1.2 |
| **Count the streams with extra structure** — if most have it, the normal size is wrong | §4.1.2 |
| **Restoring a capability is cheap, withdrawing it is deferred** | §4.1.1.1 |
| Large objects are built by **parallel partitions, sealed, then concatenated** | §8.6.1 |
| **Trilemma**: parallel bandwidth, dense stable offsets, monotone time index — pick two | §8.6.2 |
| The recursion to DN **attenuates** by fan-out; the rule is **spray per writer, not per request** | §8.6.4 |
| An object has a **sealed prefix** with dense numbering and a **growing frontier** addressed per stream | §8.6.6 |
| Non-monotone extent lists are pruned by **min/max durable-second intervals**, which fail safe by widening | §9.7.3 |
| Rewrites retain their inputs for the **hint window** (guess: 10 minutes) — retention, not compaction frequency | §10.1 |
| Append offsets are assigned in a **canonical length-stuffed space**, so they survive re-framing | §8.2.2 |

**Billing**

| | |
|---|---|
| Billing tracks **actual cost within 2× slack**, on every scarce resource | §12.1, §12.4 |
| For compute the slack binds on the **average** (~1.2× cost), not the instant — scarcity *is* cost | §12.1.1.2 |
| **Peak-to-mean is invariant to cluster size**: demand spikes are common-mode, so the LLN never smooths them | §12.1.1.1 |
| **Storage must not** be dynamically priced; a stored byte occupies a disk continuously | §12.1.1.3 |
| Reservations are the **hedge against spot peaks**, which is what their premium buys | §12.1.1.3, §5.12.6 |
| **No dithering of deletes**: the outstanding-delete limit already defers, and only when saturated | §8.5.1a |
| Back-pressure beats pre-emption whenever the pressure can be **measured** — §13.4.3.6's shape again | §8.5.1a |
| But **back-pressure fixes load; only dithering fixes phase** — so *do* dither recurring per-pair work | §13.1.9.1 |
| **Dither every recurring per-pair loop** — SN/EN warm, SN/EN cold, DN/SN — from a hash of the pair's ids | §13.1.9.1 |
| Alignment is the **default**, not an incident: things are created in batches, and cold start aligns everything | §13.1.9.1 |
| Aligned peak-to-mean ≈ **period / sync duration**, so the rarest loop (DN/SN) has the worst pathology | §13.1.9.1 |
| Deterministic, not random, so a **mass restart cannot re-align** them | §13.1.9.1 |
| §13.1.10's hourly verification budget **depends** on dithering; it is a precondition, not an optimization | §13.1.9.2 |
| **DN owns expiry**, via a secondary keyed index on **expiry second** — a prefix scan, no sweep | §8.5.1b |
| Costs ~5% more DN metadata and one insert per creation; **removes a correctness hole**, which decided it | §8.5.1b.0, §8.5.1b.2 |
| So **one** mechanism smooths deletion load, not three | §8.5.1b.2 |
| Expiry is a **trigger**, not a mechanism — it enters §8.4.1's deferred decrement | §8.5.1b.2 |
| Rule: **flatten what the design creates, price only what the world creates** | §8.5.1a |
| **Physical, not logical** bytes — forced by the same slack rule | §12.3 |
| A complex model with a **simple presentation**: top charges plus "everything else" while under 1% | §12.6 |
| Shared extents: **charge per billed reference = extent cost / number of billed references** | §12.6.3 |
| Total revenue is **invariant** under any regrouping of references, so sharing is not exploitable | §12.6.3 |
| Only the **shared** cost divides — each sharer pays its own reference's SN-memory cost in full | §12.6.3.1 |
| The denominator moves, so integrate **piecewise** from reference lifetimes rather than sampling | §12.6.3.2 |
| Unbilled (system) references mean real cost nobody is charged — track it in §12.7's chain | §12.6.4 |
| **Zero references is an orphan: a bug signal**, and the billing sweep detects it for free | §12.6.4 |
| **Billing is a job over snapshots**, never over live DN/SN/EN metadata — reproducibility demands it | §12.8 |
| Retain **outputs for years, inputs for weeks** | §12.8.1 |
| Soft delete's 3-day window is what makes **daily sampling exact**; the opt-out therefore needs a billing tombstone | §12.8.2 |
| Billing is **offline and exact**; quota is **online and approximate** | §12.8.3 |
| Metadata is snapshotted **daily, kept weeks, sampled weekly** for longer; jobs are **advisory** and SN validates | §13.5 |
| Snapshots are on the **intervention** path, not the recovery path | §13.5.3 |
| SN **must** know sealed physical size — seal, billing, and EC grouping each require it | §13.5.1 |
| Grouping keys on media, scheme, **size bin**, then **declared expiry**, then directory | §13.5.1 |
| Only **~58% of purchased disk** is billable; price lands near **2.6× raw disk cost** per byte | §12.7 |
| Worked prices: **$1.89 / $3.31 / $5.68 per TB-month** for 1.333× EC, 2.333× EC, 4-instance — **warm** storage, read immediately at HDD speed | §12.7.2 |

**Testing**

| | |
|---|---|
| **Self-concatenation** tests metadata scale — 2^31 extent references on 32 MB of real data | §15 |
| Hardest placement shapes are enumerable — a permanent suite asserting **latency percentiles, not success** | §5.6.10 |
| Budget: ~22 group placements/s per SN, so a group solve must clear **~10 ms** | §5.6.10 |

---

## 1. Goals

### 1.0 Purpose

**DeLawson is intended to be an open-source distributed data store.** Not a service with a source release
attached — the software itself, runnable by anyone, on their own hardware.

Three things follow, and they are the reason the design looks as it does.

**A motivating use case: shared AI memory**, set out at length in Bob's [*How I expect AI to eventually
work*](https://burtleburtle.net/bob/future/ai.html) (Cited). That means indexes maintained over shared
experiences in real or near-real time, and the awkward part of such a system is normally that indexes go
stale — references shift as the underlying store reorganizes. DeLawson's object model happens to remove that problem:

| | Gives |
|---|---|
| **Unkeyed objects append only at the end** (§3) | record numbers are **permanently stable**, so an external index entry of (object, record *N*) never needs revisiting |
| **Keyed objects are addressed by sorted key** (§3) | index entries by key are stable across inserts and compaction |

Both properties were derived for other reasons — §3's asymmetry falls out of cumulative counts being stable
under update and tombstone but not insert — and they turn out to be exactly what an index wants. §4.5 helps
too: the unkeyed record count is the one summary maintained *synchronously*, so a reader tailing an object
sees new records immediately rather than after a lazy update.

**Open source means storage can live inside the compute cluster, and egress fees vanish.** This is not a
minor saving. For 1 PB read once a month:

| | Cost per month | Multiple of storage |
|---|---|---|
| Storing it (DeLawson EC 1.333×, §12.7.2) | $1,890 | 1× |
| AWS egress at $0.09/GB | $90,000 | **48×** |
| GCS egress at $0.12/GB | $120,000 | 63× |
| …read four times a month instead | $360,000 | **190×** |

**For read-heavy analytics, egress dominates storage by one to two orders of magnitude**, and co-location
removes it entirely. Note §1.5 still forbids user code where keys are, so "inside the compute cluster" means
the same facility and network, not the same machines — which is enough, since egress is charged at the
provider boundary.

**And standalone it should still win on price.** §12.7.2.2 puts the warm, immediately-readable tiers at
2.8–3.2× under the cheapest immediate-read incumbent, which is the claim to defend: **better accessibility
per dollar than anything currently available**, not merely cheaper cold storage.

#### 1.0.1 What open source does to the billing sections

⚠️ §12 derives a price list, which reads oddly for a project given away. It survives the change of framing,
but its meaning shifts:

- For anyone **operating DeLawson as a service**, §12 is what it says it is.
- For an organization **running its own cluster**, §12 becomes **internal chargeback** — and the ADLS Gen1
  failure of §12.1 recurs in internal form. Teams pile into tiny streams when metadata is free whether or not
  money changes hands; the incentive does not care about the invoice.
- The **cost model** (§1.2, §12.7) is unconditionally necessary either way, since an operator who does not
  know their costs cannot size a cluster.

One genuine benefit: **open-source metering is verifiable.** A customer who can read the code can check that
the bill matches the rules, which is not true of any incumbent.

#### 1.0.2 Two tensions this purpose creates

⚠️ **Real-time indexes versus §1.4's throughput priority.** §1.4 says plainly that users who care about
individual request latency "are not who this is built for", and a cold point read costs four round trips
(§9.1). *Near*-real-time — seconds — is comfortable. Millisecond index lookups are not what this design
optimizes, and if shared AI memory needs them, that is a conflict to resolve rather than assume away.

**Historical queries are supported, at second granularity** — see §9.7. An earlier draft of this section said
they were not, conflating two different things: the SCN horizon (§4.3.4) bounds *transactional snapshots* to
minutes, but durability timestamps make "what did I do last Tuesday" and "scan all records added in [X, Y)"
answerable indefinitely. Second granularity rather than SCN granularity, which is ample for a memory
system.

- A single object may hold up to **2^64 records**.
- No single machine can hold such an object. Objects span many machines by
  construction, not as an optimization.
- **Tiny objects are equally expected**, in enormous numbers. Different users
  behave differently; the same system must hold a 30-record object and a
  2^64-record object without the small case paying for the large one (§11).
- **No per-record index anywhere.** An index with 2^64 entries is not
  storable, so record location must be computed from aggregate counts (or key
  ranges) plus a bounded scan.
- **Compression and encryption are automatic**, not opt-in (§7).
- **Billing tracks actual cost across every scarce resource** (§12) — bytes, but also
  stream, extent and object counts. Not a pricing detail: getting it wrong is what sank
  the one previous attempt to make this class of system user-visible.
- Sequential read throughput approaching the aggregate sequential bandwidth of
  the disks holding the object.

#### 1.0.3 What the motivating case actually demands

The AI page is specific enough to turn §1.0's motivation into requirements rather than a gesture. Its
load-bearing claims (Cited):

| Claim | Figure |
|---|---|
| Scale of sharing | *"thousands of souls reading and writing it simultaneously"* |
| Why pool at all | *"If you equipped 1000 AIs with processors and hard drives, and gave them the option of pooling their hard drives, pooling the hard drives is a large obvious win"* |
| Memory per mind | 1 TB to 100 TB |
| Thinking speed | a *remember-test-remember-test* cycle: ~50/s on disk, **~10,000/s on SSD** |
| Why not one store | speed of light forbids real-time access to a single central repository |

**The pooling argument is §1.0's co-location argument reached from the other direction**, which is worth
noticing: that page argues for shared storage from economies of scale among many minds, and §1.0 argues for
it from egress fees. Same conclusion, independent premises.

**Three requirements fall out. Derived.**

**Storage is not the binding constraint.** 1,000 minds at 100 TB each is 100 PB, against ~2 EB for a
1,000-EN fleet (§12.7.2). Comfortable by a factor of twenty.

**Metadata QPS is the binding constraint.** 1,000 minds × 10,000 cycles/s is **10^7 memory operations per
second** — five times §1.4.0's 2M batched target, and about a quarter of §1.6.2's ~40M/s hardware bound. So
the motivating case sits *between* what has been demonstrated and what the machine can do, which is exactly
the region §1.6 exists to make visible. It is also the strongest argument that §1.4.0's targets are a floor
rather than an ambition.

**And latency bounds depth, not throughput.** An earlier draft of this section had it wrong, so the
correction is worth stating plainly. **A soul is a set of goals and ongoing projects, and souls think in
parallel** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-16) — a soul is not a thread. So parallelism comes from *within* a mind as
well as from the number of minds, and §1.4's throughput-over-latency stance applies here like everywhere else.
There is no serial-workload exception.

What a single remember-test *chain* still gives is a bound on **depth**:

| | Set by | Scales with |
|---|---|---|
| **Throughput** — how much thinking happens | §1.4, batching, node count | souls × concurrent lines of thought |
| **Depth** — how far one line of reasoning gets per unit time | round-trip **latency** | nothing; it is `1/latency` steps per second |

A conclusion needing `N` sequential remember-test steps takes `N x latency` of wall clock no matter how much
hardware is thrown at it. At 100 µs a million-step chain is 100 seconds; at 10 ms it is nearly three hours.
**Derived.** So latency buys depth of reasoning, and throughput buys breadth.

**Which pushes the QPS estimate up rather than down.** §1.0.3's 10^7 assumed one line of thought per soul.
With `k` concurrent lines the demand is 1,000 × `k` × 10,000/s, so even modest concurrency puts it past
§1.6.2's ~40M/s bound for a single cluster. ⚠️ `k` is not given by the source and nothing here estimates it,
but the direction matters: **the shared-memory workload's aggregate demand plausibly exceeds what one cluster
can serve**, which is a second and quite independent reason the AI page insists on multiple stores.

#### 1.0.3.1 Memory is a hierarchy, so depth is per-tier

**There are different latencies at different levels** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-16), and the assistant writing
this document is an instance of it. Its own tiers, by observable behaviour rather than by any claim about
internals:

| Tier | Latency | Depth reachable |
|---|---|---|
| What is already in context | effectively free | thousands of steps |
| Reading a file in this repo | milliseconds | hundreds |
| Fetching a web page | seconds | a handful |
| Asking Bob | minutes to hours, and he may be asleep | one, maybe |

So §1.0.3's depth bound is **per tier**, not global. A line of reasoning that stays inside the fast tier goes
deep; one that must escalate goes shallow, and the escalation is what actually sets the pace.

**That dissolves §1.0.5's depth-versus-breadth trade into a tiering problem.** A soul does not choose one
minimum communication time — it has a fast small store *and* a slow large one, and spends the fast tier on
depth while using the slow tier for reach. Which is exactly what the AI page means by multiple memory stores
at different scales, and it means DeLawson is built to be **one tier in someone's hierarchy**, not the whole
of anyone's memory.

**DeLawson already has such a hierarchy internally, spanning eight orders of magnitude, and exposes none of
it. Derived:**

| Path | Added latency |
|---|---|
| Tiny object inlined in DN metadata, RAM-resident (§11) | network only |
| §9.6's cache at FE or EN | network only |
| Un-coalesced append, served from the EN staging index (§8.1.4) | network + SSD |
| Sealed extent on SSD | + ~100 µs |
| Sealed extent on HDD | + ~10 ms |
| Erasure-coded extent needing reconstruction, 1.333× tier (§4.3.2.4) | + 5 reads and a solve; §12.7.2.1a's worst case is minutes |

⚠️ **Nothing lets a caller ask which tier a read will come from**, and for a caller managing a depth budget
that is exactly the actionable fact: "will this be 100 µs or 10 ms?" decides whether to follow a line of
reasoning now or defer it. §9.5 gives timeouts and hedging, which handle the *consequences* of a slow read;
they do not let a caller avoid one. §4.3.2.4's availability tiers are already latency tiers in disguise — the
whole value of the second data instance is keeping reconstruction off the read path — so the design prices
this distinction without exposing it.

**And §12 should charge for it, which it currently does not.** A reconstruction read genuinely costs five
reads (§4.3.3.2d), so by §12.1 it should cost about five times a normal read. Billing per request without
regard to tier under-charges exactly the reads that are expensive, which is §12.2's failure mode in a new
place.

#### 1.0.4 The scale ambition, and the honest size of the gap

Bob's [*Really Big Data Centers*](https://burtleburtle.net/bob/future/bigdata.html) and
[*Dense Torus Core*](https://burtleburtle.net/bob/future/dense.html) describe the scale DeLawson is *aimed*
at — with his own caveat that it is "utterly wishful thinking that this particular code will go that far"
(Cited).

The dense core is a solar-mass rotating torus of 15 km hydrogen spheres at ~0.5 K, holding **1.2 × 10^57
bits**, computing 6 × 10^63 operations/second, lasting ~34 trillion years, with light-speed latency of 1.2 s
across a compact subset and 13 s across the whole.

**Quantifying the gap is more useful than admiring it.** Three scales, and they are far apart:

| | Elements or nodes | Bits | Where |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ship gate | 100,000 nodes | ~10^21 | §1.4.0, issue #26 |
| Addressable by design | 2^32 = 4.3 × 10^9 nodes | ~7 × 10^25 | §5.10 |
| **Torus Dyson swarm**, as simulated | 32 rings × 8,192 = **2^18** elements | — | §1.0.5 |
| The dense core | — | 1.2 × 10^57 | this section |

So DeLawson's addressing tops out about **10^31 short** of the dense core. **Derived.** It is not the design
that goes there, and saying so plainly is more useful than a hedge — the target is directional.

**The intermediate scale is a different story**, and it is the one worth taking seriously — see §1.0.5.

**But two parts of the design already come from the ambition, and that is why they look odd.**

**§1.3's refusal of absolute epochs.** The dense core's 34-trillion-year lifespan exceeds what an 8-byte
count of seconds can even express: 2^63 seconds is ~2.9 × 10^11 years, a hundred times short. §4.6.3's
timestamps survive anyway **because they are compared by signed difference rather than against an epoch**, so
the representation is reinterpretable indefinitely and only requires that two compared times be within ~1.5 ×
10^11 years of each other. A rule adopted for tidiness turns out to be the only reason the scheme survives a
scale nobody designed it for.

**The 2^64 records per object of §3.** At the ambition's scale a single object genuinely could exceed any one
machine, which is the premise §4's whole four-level decomposition rests on.

**And both pages agree on the thing that bounds this design's scope.** The AI page says speed of light
forbids one central repository; the dense core puts 1.2–13 seconds of light latency inside a *single*
structure. Against §1.0.3's 100 µs thinking budget, a mind cannot think across such a structure at all. So
**DeLawson is one memory store among many, not the global memory** — and moving memories between stores,
which the AI page describes as needing back-and-forth verification and questioning, is asynchronous, distinct,
and out of scope per §2.

#### 1.0.5 The intermediate scale, and the one property DeLawson actually needs from it

Between today's data centers and the dense core sits Bob's [torus-shaped Dyson
swarm](https://burtleburtle.net/bob/scifi/dyson.html) (Cited): satellites in elliptical orbits whose orbital
planes are rotated about an axis through the star but outside the orbital plane, sweeping out a torus.

**The load-bearing property is not the scale — it is that neighbors stay next to neighbors.** All satellites
share the same period, so the torus surface can be covered without collisions and **relative positions are
stable**, which is what makes tethers and mass exchange between neighbours possible at all rather than
requiring high-velocity rendezvous. Compared with a spherical swarm it also avoids the collapse at the poles
and the high-speed near-misses.

**And it already exists at small scale.** Starlink is one of these torus swarms, around Earth, keeping
neighbours next to neighbours, with the northward and southward paths separated by a few kilometres — so a
very flattened torus (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-16). That matters for how much weight to put on this row of the
table: the intermediate scale is engineering rather than speculation.

**Why a storage design should care.** §5.6.7 fixes placement at write time and **never revisits it**, and
§5.6.8 accepts that the fleet's realized independence is whatever the rules allowed when each extent was
written. That only works if the **failure-domain hierarchy is stable**. §13.1.10 already treats a disk being
rehomed to a different rack as an event that can invalidate an otherwise untouched placement — and in a naive
orbiting swarm, *every* neighbour relation churns continuously, so the hierarchy would never settle and
placement would need constant re-verification.

> **A neighbour-preserving topology is what makes "decide placement once and never revisit it" survive a
> moving substrate.** It is the orbital-mechanics analogue of §5.6.2's requirement that domains be nested
> rather than orthogonal.

**Two numbers that make this concrete rather than decorative. Derived.**

**The simulated swarm has 2^18 elements, and DeLawson addresses 2^32 nodes.** So unlike the dense core, this
scale is *inside* the design's addressing — with room for ~16,000 nodes per element before the 32-bit
identifiers of §5.10 run out. A coincidence of magnitudes rather than a design, but it identifies which of
the four rows above DeLawson is actually built for.

**A cluster's size is a definition, not a constraint.** You choose the **minimum communication time** you are
willing to call "close enough", and that choice fixes the diameter (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-16). Fast means
small, slow means large, and at slow enough you could take the whole solar system as one cluster.

| Minimum communication time | Diameter, in fibre at ~2/3 *c* | Deepest chain per second | What it serves |
|---|---|---|---|
| 100 µs | **~5-10 km** — a campus | 10,000 steps | §1.0.3's remember-test cycle |
| 10 ms | ~1,000 km — continental | 100 steps | consensus with ~1 s failover, see below |
| seconds | interplanetary | ~1 step | §1.4 batch work only |
| minutes to hours | the solar system | — | asynchronous transfer, not one store |

**So the diameter choice trades depth of reasoning against breadth of everything else.** A small fast cluster
reasons deeply over less data; a large slow one holds far more data and more nodes but advances any single line
of thought a hundred or ten thousand times more slowly (§1.0.3). That is the actual shape of the decision, and
it is not a storage tradeoff at all — it is a cognition one.

So §1.0.3's few-kilometre figure is not a bound on DeLawson — it is the diameter *the AI workload* selects,
and it is 300x tighter than anything the storage machinery itself needs. That is worth separating clearly,
because the two get conflated:

> **Cluster diameter is free. Ring diameter is not.**

§5.7's Raft rings need heartbeats, and an election timeout must comfortably exceed the round trip — call it
two orders of magnitude for stability. Targeting §5.7.1's fastest failover tier at ~1 second gives a round
trip of ~10 ms, or a **ring radius near 1,000 km**. **Derived.** Extents may sit anywhere the operator likes;
the *consensus* has to be local-ish, and §5.7's separation of consensus membership from RAM membership is
what makes that a workable division rather than a contradiction with §5.6's demand that ring members fail
independently.

At the slow end the machinery does not merely get slower, it stops applying: §13.1's one-minute liveness
loop, §9.5's timeouts, and Raft itself all assume round trips far below their own periods. A solar-system
"cluster" would be the multiple-stores regime the AI page describes — asynchronous transfer with
back-and-forth verification — which §2 puts out of scope. **The name still fits; the design does not.**

#### 1.0.5.1 StarMind is a plausible near-term platform

SpaceX's **StarMind** — the same flattened torus design as Starlink — is a plausible near-term deployment
platform for DeLawson (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-16). That makes §1.0.5 something other than a thought
experiment, and it is the reason to record it here rather than in a speculation appendix.

**How a fast cluster would be carved out of it:** take a roughly circular section of the torus *surface*, of
whatever radius the chosen communication time allows, **near the equator** (Asserted, Bob).

The neighbour-preservation property is what makes that work. The section is in constant motion, but because
all satellites share one period and neighbours stay neighbours, **the set of satellites in the section is
stable even though the section is moving.** Without that, a "cluster" would be a continuously changing
membership and §5.6.7's decide-placement-once rule would have nothing to hold onto.

⚠️ **It also invalidates §1.2's cost basis, though not §12's principle.** §1.2 puts ~95% of cost in disk plus
electricity plus rent, all terrestrial terms. In orbit, solar power is abundant and the scarce resources are
**launch mass** and **the ability to radiate heat** — the dense-core page names heat rejection as the limiting
factor on habitat design. So §12.7's chain from raw disk to a price per byte would need rebuilding on a
different basis.

That §12.1 survives unchanged is the point of having stated it as a principle: *bill proportional to actual
cost on every scarce resource* does not care which resources are scarce. A platform where mass and heat
rejection are the binding terms needs a new cost model and the same billing rule.

### 1.1 Availability and reliability are separate goals

Extents must be both:

- **Available** — readable *now*. Threatened by transient loss: a machine
  rebooting, a rack losing power, a network partition, an overloaded disk.
- **Reliable** — not lost *over time*. Threatened by permanent, correlated
  loss: several drives from one bad batch, one firmware bug, one datacenter.

They are not the same property and they do not have the same remedy.
Availability wants enough live instances reachable right now, and a read path
that will accept any of them. Reliability wants instances whose permanent-loss
events are independent, plus background repair and scrubbing to catch decay
before it accumulates.

#### 1.1.1 Data loss happens during disasters, not during steady state

**Asserted** (Bob, from experience): disasters come in all sizes, with larger ones rarer. Wait long
enough and something takes out 100% of a cluster; wait less long for 50%, and so on — **some power law,
R(≥s) ∝ s^-α, with α unmeasured.** Halving the size might multiply the rate by 5 (α ≈ 2.32) or by 10
(α ≈ 3.32); §4.3.3.1 shows that choice moves expected loss by ~6×, so it wants measuring rather than
assuming.

The consequence dominates everything else in this section: **steady-state disk failure is not where
data is lost.** §13.2 works a case — a failed rollout destroying 5% of a cluster costs ~3.2 extents,
against ~1 extent per 572 years per exabyte from ordinary disk failure. A single bad day beats a
millennium of attrition, and disasters are not rare enough to ignore.

So the reliability question is not "what is the per-window loss probability" but **"how large a
disaster survives, and how often is one that large?"** §4.3.3 works that out; it turns out to have an
exact and rather simple answer.

Two refinements to what "available" means:

- **It is promised per record, not per object.** A large object spans too many rings to be
  wholly reachable at one instant, while any single record is unaffected by how big its
  object is (§5.11.2).
- **It is time-bounded, not instantaneous.** Deciding something is unavailable means waiting
  for a timeout, and TCP's is ~20 seconds — ~40 with a retry, which is ~2,400× a normal
  read. A request that eventually succeeds after 40 seconds satisfies a naive availability
  definition and is useless in practice, so availability must be stated with a latency budget
  attached (§9.5).

Both push the same way on one point, and it is the origin of the machine types in
§5: **instances of an extent must sit in places that fail independently, and
the metadata describing an extent must not sit with the extent's own data.** A
failure that destroys the bytes must not also destroy the map to them.

### 1.2 The cost target

**Ignoring Compute, ~95% of DeLawson's cost should be disk, electricity, and rent.**
Everything else — server hardware, the metadata tiers, the software — fits in the
remaining ~5%.

⚠️ **This is a statement about hardware cost composition, not about space efficiency.** It says
disks dominate the bill; it says nothing about what fraction of purchased disk bytes end up as
billable customer data. That fraction is much lower — ~58% — and is worked out separately in §12.7.
Conflating the two is easy and was done in an earlier draft of this document: wasted *space* does not
come out of the 5%, it comes out of the 95%.

This is a **working assumption with room to move**, not a hard requirement: overhead
can be larger if it has to be. But it is worth stating as a goal, because it does real
work below and because the numbers it implies are sensitive to it (§5.3.1):

- It forces **tens to hundreds of disks per EN** (§5.3.1), because that is the only
  way a server's own cost becomes negligible against the storage attached to it.
- It keeps **ENs computationally cheap**, which constrains where the storage pipeline
  runs (§7.1).
- It bounds the **metadata tiers** to a small fraction of the fleet, which §14.5
  checks and finds comfortable.

⚠️ This is a prediction about a *healthy* workload, not an invariant, and it is emphatically
not a licence to bill only for bytes on disk — see §12.2, where doing so is what sank the
one previous attempt to make this class of system user-visible.

### 1.3 Longevity

**A cluster may run indefinitely, and may be dormant for geological spans and then be
brought back up.** Nothing in any persistent format may assume otherwise.

That rules out a family of designs that are otherwise natural:

- **No absolute end date.** Fixed-epoch counters that wrap into ambiguity are out;
  §4.6.3 compares timestamps modularly instead, so the interpretation can flip
  indefinitely and only extent *age* is bounded.
- **No work proportional to elapsed time.** Anything that marches forward one unit at a
  time must be lazy instead. Generating one key per elapsed day through a billion-year
  dormancy would mean 3.7 × 10^11 keys and 12 TB in a ring meant to hold a megabyte, so
  the key store is indexed by *active* days only (§7.3).
- **No assumption that the reader and the writer are contemporaries.** Persistent
  structures must be self-describing and versioned, because the code reading a record
  may be unrecognizably newer than the code that wrote it. Format evolution across such
  spans is a requirement, not a maintenance concern.

### 1.4 Throughput over latency

**DeLawson optimizes for throughput, and treats latency as a secondary good.** Good latency
is worth having when it is cheap; it does not win arguments against throughput.

The primary customer runs **big jobs composed of enormous numbers of small parallel
requests**. Such a user cares about when the *job* finishes and is indifferent to how long any
one of its zillions of requests took. Users who care about individual request latency exist
and are welcome, but they are not who this is built for.

That customer generates three distinct access patterns, and they want different things:
sequential scans (§9.4), scattered point reads (§9.1), and **one small object read by every
vertex of a job at once** (§9.6). The third is the one that breaks if treated as either of the
others.

The arithmetic behind the priority is Little's Law. Sustained throughput needs only
`throughput × latency ÷ request size` requests in flight:

| Sustained | Requests in flight at 17 ms, 32 MB | 1 PB job elapsed |
|---|---|---|
| 100 GB/s | 51 | 10,000 s |
| 1 TB/s | 507 | 1,000 s |
| 10 TB/s | 5,066 | 100 s |

A few hundred outstanding requests sustain a terabyte a second, so **concurrency is cheap and
per-request latency is hidden almost entirely.** Doubling latency while doubling concurrency
is a wash; halving throughput is not.

#### 1.4.0 The throughput targets, and what they imply

Two figures, both shipping requirements (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-15):

| Workload | Target |
|---|---|
| Small metadata info requests | **200,000+ QPS** |
| The same, **batched** | **2,000,000+ QPS** |

**Both have already been reached on this box** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-15): a prior
prototype of Bob's served 200k+ QPS of random object-info requests over **20 million tiny
objects** with the metadata resident in main memory on SN and DN, and 2M+ QPS for the same
workload **in batches of 1,000**. Per the clean-room rule in `CLAUDE.md`, that figure is
used here as an *existence proof* and nothing else — no design, structure, or constant is
taken from it.

So these are a **floor, not a stretch**, which changes how they should be treated: failing
them is a regression rather than a missed target. It also pins the workload definition —
