random object info, tiny objects, ~20 M of them, metadata RAM-resident — and answers a
question this section previously left open: the figures are **per box**, this box.

**The prototype's *ping* was ~1.4M QPS** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-16), which is a different number
from either row above and easy to confuse with them. The 200k figure is **ObjectInfo** — a request
that goes `laws` → FE → DN → SN and fetches one of 20 million object metadata records from RAM — so
it is four hops and a lookup, not a message. Ping is one hop and no work, and it ran seven times
faster. Both bars matter, and they measure different things: ping bounds the messaging layer, and
ObjectInfo bounds the messaging layer plus the metadata path built on top of it.

**Two different things are called batching here, and they must not be conflated**
(Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-16):

| | What it is | Where it appears |
|---|---|---|
| Transport coalescing | several independent messages pending on one connection leave in one syscall | how the ping reaches millions/s (§17.5) |
| An explicit batch request | one message that asks for 1,000 random objects at once | how ObjectInfo reached 2M QPS |

The 2M ObjectInfo figure was the second kind — a request that explicitly looked up 1,000 random
objects. The 10x it bought over 200k is therefore per-*request* amortization, not just per-message.
Transport coalescing is available to everything and needs no new message; an explicit batch API is a
design choice per operation.

**The 10x gap between the two ObjectInfo figures is the whole design content of those numbers.** The work itself
does not change; only the per-request message overhead is amortized. So the pair is really
one requirement on messaging.

**The two figures together split the cost**, which is more useful than either alone. With
`M` the per-message overhead and `W` the per-request work, a 1,000-deep batch amortizes `M`
to nothing, so `(M + W) / W = 10` gives **`M = 9W`: nine tenths of the unbatched cost is
messaging.**

Bob's instruction budget makes that concrete. Taking **~64 G instructions/sec** for the box:

| | Instructions per request | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Ping — the floor | **< 1,000** | so a pure ping ceiling is **> 64M QPS**; the prototype reached 1.4M |
| Batched lookup at 2M QPS | ~32,000 | an **upper bound** on `W` — see §1.4.0.1 |
| Unbatched lookup at 200k QPS | ~320,000 | `M + W`, so `M` ≈ 288,000 |

**Derived**, from Bob's 64 G figure and the two QPS numbers — but read §1.4.0.1 before
treating any of it as a measurement of work.

Note also what these targets are *not*: they say nothing about bulk bandwidth, and they
are about **metadata**. Bulk data is bounded by disks and the network, and is the subject
of §1.4.2.

#### 1.4.0.1 What the measured configuration included, and what it rules out

The two figures are **end-to-end, not in-memory-only** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-15). The
measured path included:

- a **durable log write to disk per message** — one write per 1,000-request batch;
- **encryption**;
- **message compression**, at the TCP level, with **Nagle disabled**;
- the lookup itself.

Amortized over 1,000 requests, encryption is ~20 instructions per request at §7.2.1's rate
and compression a few hundred, so neither is the bulk. But **the log write may be the actual
ceiling**: 2M QPS at one durable write per 1,000 requests is **2,000 log writes per second**,
and if each is a sync that is a device requirement, not a CPU one.

So the honest reading of 32,000 is **instruction-slots of wall-clock per request — an upper
bound on work, not a measurement of it.** A box waiting on `fsync` retires no instructions.
Whether the batched path is CPU-bound or log-bound is the first thing to determine, and it
decides whether there is headroom at all.

**Do not reach for io_uring on the network path.** Batching and io_uring amortize the same
thing — per-request syscall overhead — and in Bob's prototype **batching delivered all of the
gains and io_uring was a regression** (Asserted, Bob). Once a batch is 1,000 deep there is
nothing left for io_uring to amortize, and it brings its own cost. Batching was implemented
*in preparation* for io_uring and made it unnecessary. That negative result is worth keeping,
because io_uring is the obvious thing to try and trying it costs weeks.

⚠️ **io_uring for EN-to-SSD was still expected to help, and was never tried.** That is a
different problem — deep queues of independent device reads — and it is exactly §7.1.1's
observation that §1.4's zillions of tiny parallel requests keep SSD queues deep. Untested,
positive prior.

**Nagle must be off** wherever batches are built in userspace. Batching and then letting the
kernel coalesce adds latency to a decision already made.

`M` = 288,000 instructions remains the target for the unbatched path, but the remedy is now
known to be **batching**, not a faster syscall. That is still why the first milestone is a
ping benchmark: it establishes `M` for one message, which is what tells you the batch depth
needed to hide it.

**It is not memory-bound**, worth checking before assuming: 2M QPS at ~5 random cache-line
touches each is 10M misses/sec, well inside what 16 cores keep outstanding, and ~640 MB/s
against a box doing ~90 GB/s (§7.2.1).

#### 1.4.0.2 Batching has three motives, and they justify different depths

Batching is usually presented as syscall amortization. It is doing three jobs here, and **the overhead
argument is the one that saturates first** — which is why the measured configuration went to 1,000 deep
rather than stopping at 100.

Speedup at batch depth `b`, with `M = 9W` from above, is `10 / (9/b + 1)`:

| Depth `b` | Speedup | Share of the available 10x |
|---|---|---|
| 10 | 5.3x | 53% |
| 100 | 9.2x | **92%** |
| 1,000 | 9.9x | 99% |

**Derived.** So per-message overhead is essentially paid off by depth 100. The remaining factor of ten in
depth buys two other things:

**The durable log write.** At 2M QPS, one write per batch is 20,000 log writes/sec at depth 100 and
**2,000/sec at depth 1,000.** That is the difference between a device requirement that is awkward and one
that is easy, and per §1.4.0.3 the log is not optional.

**Enough data for compression to work with** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-15). The measured path compressed
messages, and compression needs a window: 1,000 small responses of ~100 B is ~100 KB, which compresses near
its asymptotic ratio, where a single 100 B message has no redundancy to find and may expand. So message
compression — which §7.1.3 shows is where the network saving comes from — is **only available at depth.**

That is worth stating as a design rule rather than an observation: **batch depth is set by the compression
window and the log write, not by overhead amortization.** Anyone tuning depth against a throughput graph
alone will stop at 100 and silently lose both.

#### 1.4.0.3 Billing is why a read request is logged at all

Logging a *read* looks like pure overhead until §12 is taken seriously. §12.1 requires
billing proportional to cost on **every scarce resource**, and §12.6.2 already prices
metadata request rate — so read requests must be **metered**, and metering that survives a
crash means a durable record.

So the log write in the measured configuration is not incidental overhead to be optimized
away: **it is the billing record.** What makes it affordable is exactly the amortization —
one write per 1,000 requests instead of per request — which makes **batching a billing
mechanism as much as a throughput mechanism.** The two motives point the same way, which is
rare enough to be worth noticing.

#### 1.4.1 But job latency is the *maximum* over requests

The priority does not make tail latency irrelevant — it changes which part of the tail
matters. A scan must read everything, so it waits for its slowest request, and with tens of
millions of requests the extreme tail becomes a certainty:

> A 1 PB scan issues ~3 × 10^7 requests. If one request in 10^6 stalls for a TCP timeout,
> ~30 of them do, and the job pays ~40 seconds.

So per-request tails matter *through the maximum*, not because any user is watching an
individual request. That is the real justification for the hedging of §9.5, and it also says
where to set it: hedging costs throughput in proportion to how often it fires, while the
benefit is a fixed saving, so the break-even depends on job length.

| Hedge at | Throughput cost | Wins for jobs shorter than |
|---|---|---|
| p95 | 5% | 13 minutes |
| p99 | 1% | 1.1 hours |
| **p99.9** | **0.1%** | **11 hours** |
| p99.99 | 0.01% | 111 hours |

**Hedge at a high percentile.** p95 would be the natural choice for a latency-first system and
is wrong here — it only pays for jobs under a quarter of an hour. p99.9 or beyond removes the
40-second stalls while costing a tenth of a percent.

#### 1.4.2 Read amplification becomes a first-order concern

Throughput-first does *not* simply favour coarser everything, which was my first instinct and
is wrong. Wasted bytes are wasted throughput, so read amplification is a throughput cost:

| Granule | Amplification for a 100 B record | Bytes moved by 10^9 point reads |
|---|---|---|
| 20 KB | 200× | 20 TB |
| 1 MB | 10,000× | 1,000 TB |

Granule size is therefore a **50× throughput factor** for point-read workloads, while being
nearly irrelevant to sequential scans, which read everything regardless. So §9.3's fine SSD
granularity is throughput-motivated, not latency-motivated — and the tension with compression
ratio in §7.1 is now a throughput-versus-cost trade on both sides rather than a
latency-versus-cost one. Sharpened, not settled.

#### 1.4.3 Prior art: GFS targeted the same customers

The [Google File System](https://research.google/pubs/the-google-file-system/) (SOSP 2003)
aimed at this same workload, and its assumptions section states the priority almost verbatim:
**"bandwidth is more critical than latency."** It also assumed *"component failures are the
norm rather than the exception"*, that *"appending is the dominant write operation"*, and that
overwrites are rare.

That is worth knowing for two reasons. It establishes the customer segment as real and
durable rather than a preference of this design; and where DeLawson agrees with GFS it is
converging on a tested answer, while where it differs the difference should be deliberate.

Agreeing:

| | GFS | DeLawson |
|---|---|---|
| Priority | bandwidth over latency | §1.4 |
| Failure model | failures are the norm | §1.1 |
| Write pattern | append-dominant, overwrite rare | §3, §4.2 |
| Chunk / extent size | 64 MB | 32 MB physical (§6) |
| Metadata in memory | master's RAM bounds capacity | SN's RAM bounds a stream (§14.1) |

The chunk size agreement is the more interesting one: two designs twenty years apart picked
tens of megabytes for the same reasons — amortize the seek, bound the metadata.

Differing, and why:

| | GFS | DeLawson |
|---|---|---|
| Metadata scale | **single master** | many DN and SN rings, bounded fan-out, 2^32 nodes (§5.10) |
| Durability | 3 replicas | 4 replicas derived from a 10^-14 target, then erasure coding (§4.3.1) |
| Consistency | relaxed | 3-of-4 quorum, applied-as-prefix, SCN consistent read (§8.1.1) |
| Namespace | flat pathname lookup table, no per-directory structure | `(parent dir id, name)`, so directory rename is O(1) (§5.5.4) |
| Billing | none — an internal system | a first-class design constraint (§12) |

The single-master limit is the one Google itself went on to fix with Colossus, and it is the
same limit §14.1 reasons about — metadata in memory bounds what one machine can address. GFS
accepted one such machine; DeLawson has many, which is what the fan-out and identifier work of
§5.10 buys. §1.4.4 compares Colossus directly, since it is the closer relative.

The last row is the one that most shapes this document. GFS and Cosmos were both internal
systems where metadata cost was *absorbed* rather than charged. §12.1 records what happened
when a system of this shape was exposed to paying users without billing for metadata, and it is
why billing here is derived from the cost structure rather than bolted on.

#### 1.4.4 Closer relative: Colossus

Colossus is GFS's successor and the nearer comparison. Per [Google's own
description](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/storage-data-transfer/a-peek-behind-colossus-googles-file-system):

> "Curators store file system metadata in Google's high-performance NoSQL database, BigTable.
> The original motivation for building Colossus was to solve scaling limits we experienced with
> Google File System (GFS) when trying to accommodate metadata related to Search. Storing file
> metadata in BigTable allowed Colossus to scale up by over 100x over the largest GFS clusters."

So yes — distributed metadata, in BigTable, and worth **over 100×** the largest GFS clusters.
The component mapping is closer to DeLawson than is comfortable:

| Colossus | DeLawson | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **Curators** — horizontally scalable metadata control plane | DN and SN rings (§5) | same fix for the same limit |
| Metadata in **BigTable**, which itself runs on Colossus | DN metadata in DeLawson keyed objects (§5.5) | same self-hosting choice |
| **D servers** — network-attached disks; data flows client↔D directly | ENs; the SN is not in the write path (§8.1.3) | same separation |
| **Custodians** — background balancing, RAID reconstruction, efficiency | background loops (§13.3) | same shape |
| **Client library** — the most complex component: software RAID, encoding schemes | undecided (§5.9.2) | see below |

Two of these are informative rather than merely reassuring.

**Colossus puts encoding in the client library**, and calls it the most complex component. That
is a real data point for §5.9.2, which is still open on where the storage pipeline runs.
DeLawson's cost target independently pushes the same way — §1.2 requires ENs to be
CPU-cheap — so client-or-FE-side encoding is both the economical answer and the one a
comparable system reached.

⚠️ **Colossus has a disk-space-balancing custodian, and §13.1.2 claims DeLawson needs no
rebalancing at all.** One of those is wrong, or they are solving different problems. The
likeliest reconciliation: free-space-weighted placement balances *space* prospectively and says
nothing about **read load**. A constantly-read extent makes its four disks hot regardless of how
full they are, and DeLawson currently has no answer for that — adding instances to hot extents
would be the natural one, which is still not *relocation*. Worth resolving before claiming the
absence of a rebalancer as a simplification.

Finally, the public description **does not address the bootstrap recursion** — BigTable runs on
Colossus while storing Colossus's metadata. §5.5.1's answer is derived here rather than
borrowed: the rings' Raft state is already a durable store that is *not* DeLawson, so the
bootstrap root lives in DN0's Raft persistent data and needs no separate component. It remains
the part of self-hosting with the least external precedent to check against.

#### 1.4.5 Direct ancestor: Cosmos

Cosmos began around 2004 and is where Bob spent twenty years (§1.4.3's customer description is
drawn from it). A public overview is Pat Helland and Ed Harris's [Stanford EE380 talk, October
2011](https://web.stanford.edu/class/ee380/Abstracts/111026a-Helland-COSMOS.pdf), and it is the
closest published relative to this design.

Scale, as of that talk: several hundred petabytes, tens of thousands of computers across many
datacenters, a couple of PiB ingested per day. Explicitly back-end batch analysis — the talk is
clear that Cosmos "does not support storage and computation needs for the Front-End."

Three layers:

| Layer | Contents |
|---|---|
| **SCOPE** | a SQL-like language, compiler and optimizer |
| **Execution** | Dryad — arbitrary DAGs rather than just map-reduce; a Job Manager placing work near its data; **Processing Nodes (PNs) hosting execution vertices** |
| **Store** | **streams** composed of **extents**, held by **Extent Nodes (ENs)**; **CSM**, the Cosmos Store Manager, handling names, streams and replication |

Store-layer specifics worth having: extents up to **2 GB**, replication across **3 different
ENs** per extent, and **compression and fault detection sited in the EN**.

**The vocabulary is the same because it is public.** DeLawson's `EN`, `stream` and `extent` name
the same things this talk names, and the resemblance at that level is traceable to a published
source rather than to anything else — which is exactly the provenance discipline this project
runs under (§ clean-room note in `CLAUDE.md`).

Where DeLawson agrees:

| | Cosmos | DeLawson |
|---|---|---|
| Streams composed of extents on ENs | yes | §4 |
| Append-only writing to the end of a stream | yes | §3 unkeyed flavor |
| Compression in the store layer | in the EN | §7 |
| Back-end batch as the target | explicit | §1.4 |
| Compute vertices consuming the store | PNs hosting vertices | §5.9 Compute, §9.6 |

Where it diverges, and why:

| | Cosmos | DeLawson |
|---|---|---|
| Metadata component | **CSM** — one manager for names, streams and replication | split into **DN** and **SN**, each a ring (§5) |
| Replication | 3 per extent | 4, derived from a 10^-14 target (§4.3.1), then erasure coded |
| Extent size | ≤ 2 GB | 4 GB logical **plus a separate 32 MB physical cap** (§6) |
| Record structure | **byte streams; structure lived in SCOPE** | **records are a store-layer primitive** (§3) |
| Compute allocation | Virtual Clusters with guaranteed capacity | undesigned |

CSM is the GFS-master-shaped component again, and DeLawson's split is the Colossus-shaped fix
(§1.4.4) applied to a Cosmos-shaped design.

#### 1.4.5.1 The real divergence: records live in the store

The largest difference is not a component but a layer boundary. **Cosmos's store layer was
byte-oriented.** Streams were "an unstructured byte stream of data"; record structure came from
*extractors* and *outputters* — SCOPE programs that parsed bytes into records on the way in and
flattened them back on the way out. Even Structured Streams, which added column and
affinity/clustering metadata and key-oriented access, were a SCOPE-layer construct: the talk
states outright that their on-disk representation "Is Only Visible to Scope."

**DeLawson pulls that boundary down.** Records are a storage primitive here:

- record framing is declared per object and translatable on read (§8.2);
- records are addressed by 64-bit record number or by sorted key (§3);
- the sparse index maps record numbers, not byte offsets (§9.3);
- and the whole addressing scheme rests on cumulative *record* counts (§4).

That is why DeLawson carries machinery Cosmos's store layer did not: framing options, keyed
objects, a record-granular index. It buys something specific in return — **a record is
addressable without a query engine.**

**Cosmos's own measurements argue for the change.** The VLDB paper (§1.4.5.2) reports that ad-hoc
jobs "typically spent 90% of their CPU in massively parallel extractors", most of it parsing
tab-separated values and sorting results. Moving record structure into the store aims squarely at
that number — though only at part of it:

| Extractor work | Removed by DeLawson? |
|---|---|
| Finding record boundaries | **yes** — framing is a store property (§8.2) |
| Re-sorting into key order | **yes** — keyed objects are already sorted (§3) |
| Parsing fields into typed columns | **no** — still a compute-tier job |

Two of three, then. Taking the third would mean column and schema awareness in the store, which is
what Structured Streams were and what this design has deliberately not taken on. §1's goal of 2^64 addressable records is a statement about
the store, not about a language on top of it, and none of §4's structure works if the store only
sees bytes.

⚠️ It also means DeLawson takes on a job Cosmos deliberately left to SCOPE, and the cost of that
is spread across §3, §4, §8.2 and §9.3 rather than sitting in one place. Worth being honest that
this is the single largest bet in the design relative to its ancestor.

#### 1.4.5.2 Cosmos, a decade later

A second public paper covers 2002–2021: [The Cosmos Big Data Platform at
Microsoft](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/the-cosmos-big-data-platform-at-microsoft-over-a-decade-of-progress-and-a-decade-to-look-forward/),
Power, Patel, Jindal, Leeka, **Jenkins**, Rys et al., VLDB 2021. Growth over that decade: **12×
servers, 188× logical data, 108× batch jobs**, at exabyte scale, with machine utilization
"exceeding 70% in most cases and 90% in many cases."

It also records specifics that bear directly on decisions made here.

**CSM was a Paxos ring of seven replicas, all holding metadata in RAM.** The paper describes
metadata kept "in a Paxos-protected ring with seven replicas that keep all metadata in RAM." That
is precisely the arrangement §5.7 rejects: 7× RAM to tolerate 3 failures, when only **three
members need the state materialized** and the rest can be log-only. §5.7's 3× is a direct
improvement on a documented predecessor rather than a hypothetical saving — and RAM is the
resource §12.2 shows costs ~5,000× disk, so the factor matters.

**Extents were 100 MB, "soon 250MB", compressed and stored in triplicate in different failure
domains.** The 2011 talk's 2 GB was a later figure, so the trajectory ran 100 MB → 250 MB → 2 GB.
DeLawson's 32 MB *physical* cap is smaller than any of them, with the growth absorbed by a
separate 4 GB *logical* cap (§6) — a split Cosmos did not have.

**The reliability model is the same one, stated the same way.** Each replica in a separate failure
domain so that "correlated hardware failures, such as power failures, do not cause the loss of
every extent replica"; a lost replica is replaced; and "data loss occurs when all replicas are
lost within the time window it takes" to do that replication. That is §4.3.1 and §5.6 exactly,
including the window framing — arrived at here independently and confirmed there empirically.

⚠️ **But their empirical answer was three replicas, not four.** The paper reports that data loss
"occur[s] with two replicas, but not with three replicas" — a decade of exabyte-scale operation
saying three suffices. §4.3.1 derives four from a 10^-14 target and a 10^-4 gone-not-replaced
assumption; production experience suggests one or both is pessimistic. The counter-argument is
that replication is transient in DeLawson — only open extents are replicated, everything sealed is
erasure-coded — so the fourth copy is cheap insurance rather than a third of the storage bill.
Worth knowing that the conservative choice is conservative *against measured practice*, not just
against a spreadsheet.

Two negative results are recorded too, which are worth more than they look: **2×2 replication**
(two copies in each of two clusters) "proved insufficient for availability during outages," and
plain two-replica extents "lost a trickle of data constantly."

### 1.5 One security invariant

**User code runs only on Compute machines, and decryption keys are never on a
machine that runs user code** (§5.9.1). Stated here because it constrains the
machine layout rather than following from it.

**The boundary is signed code, not absence of keys** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-15).
An EN holds keys and decrypts extents (§5.9.2); it is trusted because **ENs run no
user code and only signed executables.** So the fleet divides into two populations:

| Population | Runs | Holds keys |
|---|---|---|
| DN, SN, EN, FE, KS | **signed executables only** | yes |
| Compute | user code | **never** |

That makes "no keys where user code runs" a consequence of a simpler rule — *keys
live only where the executables are signed* — and it means **code signing is a
load-bearing security mechanism**, not an operational nicety. It also becomes a
placement constraint on work rather than only on data: anything needing plaintext
must run on a signed-code machine, which §7.2.2 shows is not free to satisfy.

### 1.6 Software should not matter

**If the hardware can do it, the software should deliver it and not get in the way** (Asserted, Bob,
2026-08-15). Message overhead, disk throughput, CPU consumption for compute — in each case:

> **The measurement is not how much better than competitors. The measurement is distance from the
> theoretical upper bound given the hardware.**

This is a stronger discipline than it sounds, and it is not the same as "be fast".

#### 1.6.1 It makes every performance claim two-sided

A number on its own is not a claim under this rule. Every performance figure needs a **computed hardware
ceiling beside it and the fraction stated**, because "3x better than the alternative" is compatible with
being at 1% of what the machine can do — and 1% is the interesting fact.

So the labelling discipline of §0 gains a companion: performance claims carry **achieved, bound, and
fraction of bound.** An unaccompanied throughput number is the same liability as an unlabelled constant.

#### 1.6.2 Applying it to the numbers already here

| Resource | Hardware bound | Where we are | Fraction |
|---|---|---|---|
| Trivial message (ping) | **>64M/s** — <1,000 instructions at ~64 G inst/s | unmeasured | — |
| Metadata lookup, batched | **~40M/s** — see below | 2M/s (§1.4.0) | **~5%** |
| Metadata lookup, unbatched | same | 200k/s | **~0.5%** |
| Bulk read per EN | **12.5 GB/s** — the NIC binds, devices give 20-400 (§4.3.2.2a) | unmeasured | — |
| Encrypt + authenticate | ~90 GB/s box | 20 GB/s on one core (§7.2.1) | 22% of the box, on 1/16 of it |
| Compress (LZ4) | ~90 GB/s box | 0.6 GB/s per core | **0.7%** |

The metadata bound: a lookup over 20 M objects touches perhaps 5 cache lines — a depth-4 B-tree plus the
record — so 320 B per lookup. Against ~90 GB/s peak at a realistic ~15% efficiency for random access, that
is **~40M lookups/s**. **Derived**, on a stated assumption about random-access efficiency that deserves
measuring rather than believing.

**So the batched metadata path is at roughly 5% of its bound, and the unbatched at 0.5%.** That is the
philosophy earning its keep: both figures already *meet* the shipping targets of §1.4.0, and this rule is
what says there is a 20x gap worth understanding anyway. §1.4.0.1 warns the gap may be mostly waiting on
the log rather than computing — which is precisely the kind of thing this discipline forces you to find out
instead of shipping past.

#### 1.6.3 The bound must be for the work the design chose to do

Read naively, "software should not matter" forbids compression: LZ4 at 0.7% of memory bandwidth looks like
the most egregious row in the table. But LZ4 is a heavily optimized implementation, so that 0.7% is what
the **algorithm** costs, not what the software wastes.

So the rule needs sharpening to be testable:

> Software may consume hardware to buy a **stated benefit**. It may not consume hardware for nothing. The
> bound is computed for the work the design has deliberately chosen, not for the least work imaginable.

That keeps compression (buys disk, §12.3), erasure coding (buys durability at low overhead, §4.3), and
encryption (§7.2, non-negotiable) inside the rule, while still condemning an extra copy, a per-request
allocation, or a syscall that batching could have amortized (§1.4.0.1).

It also means **the essential work per operation has to be written down** before a fraction-of-bound number
means anything. That is a real obligation, and it is where this rule does its work: naming the essential
work is what exposes the inessential.

#### 1.6.4 Work that is not persisted will be done again

A corollary sharp enough to be worth its own name, and §9.8 is the case that produced it:

> **Prefer doing more work once, and keeping it, over doing less work repeatedly and discarding it.**

Reconstructing an erasure-coded cell to satisfy one read costs 5-45 reads and leaves nothing behind; repairing
the whole group costs the same order and leaves the group repaired. Under §1.6's rule the first is the clearer
violation, because the hardware is spent and the fraction of *durable* benefit is zero.

This is not the same as "cache everything" — the persisted work has to be work someone will want again. It is
the reason §13.5's snapshots are worth their 0.08%, and the reason §9.6 caches hot objects rather than
recomputing them. Where it bites hardest is anywhere a read path is tempted to compute something it could
instead have written down.

#### 1.6.5 Two dividends

**Fraction-of-bound targets survive hardware changes; absolute targets do not.** §7.4 expects a decade-long
media transition and §1.3 expects the cluster to run indefinitely, so "2M QPS" ages badly where "5% of
bound" stays meaningful and keeps getting harder in the right way.

**A large gap is a defect, not a fact.** It should be filed rather than noted — which is why §1.4.0's 20x
gap is tracked as an issue even though the target it fails to reach is already met.

## 2. Non-goals

- Not a SQL database. No query language, no joins, no planner.
- No cross-object transactions.
- No general secondary indexes.
- No deduplication — per-extent encryption keys make cross-extent identity
  invisible, and billing by physical bytes removes the incentive.

---

## 3. Two object flavors

Fixed at creation; determines how records are addressed.

| | **Unkeyed** | **Keyed** |
|---|---|---|
| Address | 64-bit record number | sorted user key |
| Insert | **only at the end of the object** | anywhere, by key |
| Update | yes, count-preserving | yes |
| Delete | tombstone, count-preserving | tombstone |
| Positional access | yes, `O(log)` | no (§9.4) |

### 3.0 Why keyed objects are in the core rather than built on top

Keyed objects double a great deal of surface: every mechanism has a keyed story and an unkeyed one —
addressing, hints, compare-and-append, counts-as-statistics, the read path. It is fair to ask what that
buys over building a keyed index *as* an ordinary unkeyed object. The answer is that the surface is
mostly not theirs (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17):

- **DeLawson is to have updatable sorted indexes regardless.** They are wanted as a feature, not as
  scaffolding for something else — and they are where the hard parts live: ordered placement, insert in
  the middle, mutation, merging.
- **A keyed object is then a small step.** Storing the rows *in* the index rather than a reference to
  them elsewhere is Oracle's index-organized table, and **all the mechanism is already needed for the
  indexes themselves.** So keyed objects are close to free once indexes exist, and expensive only if
  you imagine building them first.
- **What index-only buys over index-plus-reference is locality for range scans**: the rows are already
  in key order where the scan is already reading, so a range is sequential instead of a chase per key.
- ⚠️ **And mutation is not optional anyway.** A right to erasure wants **deletes, and probably updates,
  of individual rows** — including in objects a user would call append-only. That forces change logs
  and extent merging into the design whether or not anything is keyed. So the machinery keyed objects
  are accused of requiring is machinery an append-only store already has to have.

The last two arrive from outside the storage argument, which is why they are easy to miss when weighing
the surface area: the expensive parts are wanted for other reasons, and what "keyed" adds on top of
them is small.

#### 3.0.1 Sorted by one key is the only updatable index

**The original aim was updatable indexes on embeddings, and the conclusion was against it** (Asserted,
Bob, 2026-08-17): **only sorted-by-a-single-key is updatable.** What that leaves is worth stating
precisely rather than being inferred:

- **Embedding indexes are generated stale and updated in passes.** They are rebuilt rather than
  maintained, which is a batch job and not a mutation on the write path.
- **Locality is approximated by combining sorted indexes.** The **intersection or union of several
  keyed indexes** gets a long way toward what an embedding index would give, using the one index type
  that *is* updatable rather than needing a second one that is not.
- **It is good enough because the consumer iterates.** Several passes of narrowing is **typical of deep
  thinking**, so approximate locality refined over iterations matches the shape of the work rather than
  falling short of it.

**The dividend is one updatable index type to build, not two**, and it is the one whose mutation,
ordering, repair and merging story the rest of the design already needs. An incrementally-updatable
nearest-neighbour structure has none of that in common with an ordered one: no key order to place by,
no range to scan, and its own crash-safety and rebalancing problem.

⚠️ **Nothing else in this document mentions embeddings**, and what a pass costs, how stale an index may
be before it misleads, and whether combining indexes is something the store answers or a job on Compute
are all unaddressed (#68).

#### 3.0.2 Updatable *secondary* indexes need transactions, so they come after the first release

⚠️ **An appended row spawns updates to the keyed indexes over it, which appears to require
transactions** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17). That is the line between two things that sound alike:

| | Atomicity needed | Because |
|---|---|---|
| **A keyed object**, updated | within one object | the rows *are* the index — index-organized, so one write changes one thing |
| **A secondary index** over another object | across two objects | appending a row and updating its index entry must not half-happen |

So the first release has **keyed objects and updates to them, and not updatable secondary indexes**
(Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17). That keeps the ship gate free of a transaction requirement, and it is a
real reduction rather than a deferral of difficulty: a keyed object needs no cross-object atomicity at
all.

**And it gives §16's transaction question a second, independent forcing reason.** It was valued for
dropping a ring from 3x RAM to 2x, and §9.1.3.1 added parallel pagination. This adds a third: without
transactions there are no updatable secondary indexes, so the feature that most obviously wants them is
blocked on the same thing.

⚠️ **Updatable sorted indexes are not on §1's ship gate**, and should be placed deliberately — with the
split above making that easier, since the part that needs no transactions is the part that could ship.

The asymmetry follows from one fact: **record counts are stable under update
and tombstoned delete, but not under insert.** An update replaces a record and
a tombstone leaves it present-but-dead, so every cumulative count in the object
is unchanged. An insert in the middle renumbers everything after it,
invalidating every cumulative count above the insertion point.

Therefore:

- **Unkeyed objects forbid mid-object insert.** Appends land at the end, where
  they touch no existing cumulative count. Record numbers are permanently
  stable and the count-based addressing of §9.1 works.
- **Keyed objects abandon counts as addresses.** Insert-in-the-middle is the
  point of them, so counts are unusably unstable and keys are the address.
  Counts are still maintained, but only as statistics — for `count`, for load
  balancing, for placement — never for lookup.

---

## 4. The logical decomposition: four levels

```
Object
  ├─ metadata (flavor, framing, device class, totals; inline records if tiny — §11)
  └─ streams[]     unkeyed: (stream_id, starting record number, cumulative logical + physical bytes)
       │           keyed:   (stream_id, first_key, cumulative bytes)
       Stream                        unit of capacity striping
         └─ extents[]  unkeyed: (extent_id, starting record number, cumulative bytes)
              │        keyed:   (extent_id, first_key, cumulative bytes)
              Extent                 unit of replication, sealing, compression, encryption, EC
                ├─ base              sealed, immutable
                ├─ log               unsealed, lazily created — updates, tombstones, keyed inserts
                └─ instances[]        replicas, or EC fragments after sealing
                     │
                     Instance        one contiguous block of bytes on one disk
```

Each level answers one question, searching on cumulative counts for unkeyed
objects and on first keys for keyed ones:

| Level | Question | Search key |
|---|---|---|
| Object | which stream? | starting record number / first key |
| Stream | which extent? | starting record number / first key |
| Extent | roughly where inside? | sparse index (§9.3) |
| Instance | which disks hold those bytes? | replica / fragment list |

The list in the diagram is the *stored* form; the *served* form is a B-tree
(§4.4). Which of the totals a level carries may be kept exact, and which only
lazily, follows a single rule — §4.5.

### 4.1 Streams

A stream exists **purely for capacity striping** — no semantic distinction, no
"index stream" or "log stream". An object small enough for one stream uses one
stream; streams are added as it grows.

A stream is the unit of assignment to a Stream Node (§5.2), and its ceiling is
what one SN can hold — see §14.

#### 4.1.1 A stream carries flags, and three kinds of them

**A stream has a number of flags** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-19). This is the canonical statement of
that; the individual flags are argued where their consequences are, and are collected here so the
field has one home rather than being rediscovered in four places.

⚠️ **They are not all the same kind of thing**, and the distinction decides whether a flag may be
turned off:

| Kind | Means | Reversible? | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| **state** | something that has happened | no, but only because the event cannot un-happen | `sealed` (§6.3) |
| **policy** | what the system should do | **yes** — a policy is meant to be changed | storage class (#74), soft-delete opt-out (§8.4), expiry (§8.5) |
| **capability** | whether something may ever happen to this stream | **yes**, and asymmetrically — see §4.1.1.1 | `updatable` (§9.1.3.9), `deletable` (§9.1.3.10) |

**A capability flag is the interesting kind, and it is new with those two.** What *withdrawing* one buys
is not a behaviour but an **omission**: because the thing can never happen, machinery that would have
coped with it can be skipped, and readers can rely on properties that would otherwise be unprovable.

##### 4.1.1.0 Flags are named for the capability, never for its absence

**Base flags are positive: `deletable`, not `undeletable`** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-19). ⚠️ **And this
is the bottom of a hierarchy rather than a rule of its own** (§13.2.5.1): *make the logic simple* →
*reduce the depth of negations* → *name things positively*. It therefore **applies to all names, not
only to flags.** The reason is capacity rather than taste:

> ⚠️ **Double negatives are read as emphasis of the negative, not as a positive.** It appears to be a
> feature of the built-in human language machinery — it shows up frequently in **novel** languages,
> which is the strong evidence, since a pattern that reappears in creoles is a default of the language
> faculty rather than a learned quirk of any one tongue.

So `!undeletable` does not read as *deletable*; it reads as *really not deletable*. A codebase with
negative flag names is asking every reader to fight their native parser at every negation, and the
mistakes are silent because the wrong reading is fluent.

**The rule states precisely as: a name must not itself be a negation** — no `un-`, no `no-`, no
`-disallowed`. That is narrower than "positive" and it is what actually matters, which is why `sealed`
passes: it is not morphologically a negation, so `!sealed` reads unambiguously even though the concept
is a restriction.

⚠️ **It is a strong default rather than an absolute**, and §13.2.5.1 works through the case that tests
it: a positive name costs a negation at the site that *enforces* the restriction, so the tie is broken
by which reading happens more often. For a capability that is *may I?*, which is why the positive name
wins here on the general rule rather than in spite of it.

⚠️ **And it is why this document's prose and the code's identifiers differ deliberately.** The sections
below argue about *updates being disallowed*, because that is the property being reasoned about; the
flag is `updatable`, because that is what will be read in a condition. Keeping both is better than
forcing either to serve the other.

##### 4.1.1.1 Withdrawing a capability is deferred, and the official flag stays permissive throughout

⚠️ **An earlier draft said a capability flag must be one-way — withdrawable and never restorable. That
is wrong in both directions** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-19).

> **Restoring a capability is cheap.** Withdrawing it is the slow one, and it is *deferred*: start
> refusing new operations, run a lazy cleanup pass over what is already there, and only then does the
> restriction hold of everything.

**But that is a description of a transition, not a three-valued flag** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-19), and
the distinction is what makes it safe. There will be many such flags and this will be done many times,
so the mechanism has to be uniform and cheap to read:

| | Says | Consulted by |
|---|---|---|
| the **official flag** — `deletable` | **still permissive** for the whole transition, flipping only when cleanup completes | **anything relying on the restriction** |
| a **per-purpose flag** in the extra structure (§4.1.2) | new deletes are being refused, and how far cleanup has reached | **enforcement**, and the pass itself |

⚠️ **So the reliance rule needs no discipline: it is unrepresentable to get wrong.** A reader consulting
`deletable` and finding it false may take every omission, unconditionally, because the flag does not
advertise the restriction until it is true of all the data. Nothing ever has to remember not to trust a
half-established promise, because nothing can see one.

**That splits two views that were being conflated**, and they want opposite biases:

| View | Bias | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **enforcement** | **optimistic** — refuse new operations at once | every operation refused now is one the cleanup pass will not have to clean |
| **reliance** | **conservative** — assume the capability remains | an omission taken too early reads over data that still violates the restriction |

**`off` / `henceforth` / `always` remain the vocabulary for describing where a transition has got to**,
and they are used that way throughout the sections below — but they are not flag values. The flag is
`deletable`; `henceforth` is a sentence about a stream, not a state in its record.

**Cited: this is Oracle's constraint state machine**, and the correspondence is exact rather than
loose. Oracle separates `ENABLE`/`DISABLE` from `VALIDATE`/`NOVALIDATE`, and the standard migration is
`ENABLE NOVALIDATE` — instant, and binding on new DML only — followed by a long `VALIDATE` over the
existing rows. ⚠️ **And the payoff lands in the same place**: Oracle's optimizer may only *rely* on a
constraint that is validated, because a novalidate one may be false of data already there. DeLawson's
omissions are the same — see below.

**Provenance, because it changes how much weight the analogy carries: `ENABLE NOVALIDATE` is Bob's own
feature — he proposed and implemented it** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-19). So this is not a pattern
matched from the literature and hoped to fit; it is one brought in first-hand by the person who built
it, which is why the three states and the reliance rule transfer as cleanly as they do. Where the two
differ, the difference is likely to be real rather than a misreading of someone else's design.

**Which is why the middle state has to be visible rather than internal.** The whole value of a promise
is what other machinery is allowed to skip on the strength of it, and at `henceforth` that machinery
must **not** skip anything:

| Omission | Safe at `henceforth`? | Safe at `always`? |
|---|---|---|
| skip the log probe on read (§9.1 step 3) | **no** — old tombstones may still be there | yes |
| trust an exact logical prefix sum (§9.1.3.9) | **no** — past updates may have shifted it | yes |
| treat hints as long-lived (§8.1.1a-10) | partly — no *new* rewrites from this cause | yes |

**And the loosening direction really is cheap**, which is what makes the whole thing tolerable to
operate: dropping back to `off` is a flag write plus abandoning the omissions, with no pass and no
cleanup. The escape from a promise made wrongly is therefore not "delete the stream" as an earlier
draft had it — it is simply to stop promising.

⚠️ **What loosening does cost is not paid by the store.** An external index built on offsets that were
exact stops being valid, and the store cannot rebuild it or even enumerate who holds one. So loosening
is cheap *mechanically* and expensive *contractually*, and those are different budgets — which is an
argument for the state being visible to readers, not for making the transition hard.

#### 4.1.2 A normal size, and a flag pointing at extra structure for the unusual

**Stream metadata has a normal size, plus a flag and extra structure for unusual cases** (Asserted,
Bob, 2026-08-19). The `henceforth` state and its cleanup progress live in the extra structure.

**Why a fixed normal size is the requirement and not a preference is §14.1.2's argument**: record size
decides *how many machines a given object needs*, because doubling the record doubles the fleet for the
same data. So the arithmetic is brutal and one-directional:

> A field needed by one stream in a thousand, held inline, is paid for by **all** of them. At §4.7's
> ~200 B stream record, sixteen bytes of rarely-used field is an 8% fleet tax on the metadata tier.

**So the rule is a two-line test**, and it admits exactly two kinds of field:

| Out of line if the field is | Example |
|---|---|
| **rare** — absent in the overwhelming majority | georeplication source (§13.4.5), a per-stream storage-class override differing from the object's (#74) |
| **transient** — present only during a transition | the `henceforth` state's **cleanup cursor**, and how far the pass has reached |

##### The transient case is the elegant one, and it makes the flags nearly free

⚠️ **Notice what the three states of §4.1.1.1 cost in the steady state: almost nothing.** `off` and
`always` are *the two ends*, and each is fully described by a couple of bits. Only the middle state
needs a cursor, a start time, and progress — and the middle state **exists only while a background pass
runs**.

| State | Needs extra structure? |
|---|---|
| `off` | no — a bit |
| `always` | no — a bit |
| `henceforth` | **yes** — the cursor, freed when the pass completes and the state becomes `always` |

**So the whole promise-flag feature costs a few bits per stream at rest**, and the machinery for
transitions costs nothing at all when nobody is transitioning. That is exactly the shape §14.1.2
demands, and it is a better outcome than either alternative — inlining the cursor would tax every
stream for a state almost none is in, and keeping it in a side table indexed by stream would cost a
lookup on a path that has to be cheap.

##### Prior art, and the vocabulary worth borrowing

**This is the resident-versus-non-resident split**, and several systems have converged on it:

| System | Shape |
|---|---|
| **Unix inodes** | direct block pointers inline, indirect blocks for large files |
| **NTFS** | small attributes **resident** in the MFT record, large ones spilled to extents — the closest analogue, and the clearest vocabulary |
| **Oracle** | a row that outgrows its block gets a pointer to a continuation piece |
| **ext4** | inline data for tiny files, extents otherwise |

None of them is novel and that is the point: the pattern is well understood, so what matters here is
the *policy* for what goes out of line rather than the mechanism for spilling it.

##### An escape hatch invites drift, so count it

⚠️ **The failure mode is not a bug but an erosion.** Once extra structure exists, every new rare field
goes into it and nobody re-examines whether the normal record is still the right size — or, worse,
fields drift out of *rare* into common while still being paid for out of line, one indirection at a
time.

**The check is cheap and should exist from the start: count the streams that have extra structure.**

- If that count is a small fraction, the split is doing its job.
- ⚠️ **If most streams have it, the normal size is wrong** — and the answer is to inline whatever became
  common, not to add another level.

That is a measurement rather than a rule, which is the right kind of guard for a policy that decays
slowly. §14.1.2's warning against re-baselining applies: the budget is there to be spent deliberately,
so the count is what makes "deliberately" checkable.

##### Where it lives is not settled

⚠️ Stream metadata exists in two places — the DN's stream-list entry and the SN's stream record — and
they want different things. **Declaration is the object's, so the DN's** (§9.1.3.9); **enforcement and
the cleanup pass are the SN's**, because the SN owns the extents whose tombstones get compacted and
whose lengths get summed. So the cursor plausibly belongs to the SN while the flag belongs to both,
which is one fact in two places and therefore something §13.1's sync loops have to reconcile
(§16.140).

### 4.2 Extents: base plus log

An extent is the unit of replication and immutability. Logically a **pair**:

- a **base**: sealed, immutable, in key order (keyed) or record order (unkeyed);
- a **log**: unsealed and appendable, holding updates, tombstones, and — for
  keyed extents — inserts falling in this extent's key range.

Reads merge base and log, newest version winning. **Compaction** folds the log
into a fresh base and drops the old pair (§10).

**The log is created lazily.** An extent only ever appended to has no log and
costs nothing for one. This matters: a full stream holds ~2^31 extents (§14),
and if each eagerly carried an open, fully-replicated log, the cluster's
open-extent count — the expensive, un-erasure-coded, in-memory-state-bearing
kind — would dwarf its sealed extent count. For append-mostly objects almost no
logs exist.

⚠️ Even lazily, an update-heavy full stream could want a log per extent. Lazy
creation makes the append-only case free and does nothing for the update-heavy
case, so open logs per stream need a hard bound with forced compaction when it
is hit. Open logs cost EN replicas and network, not just SN memory, so their
bound is far below the extent count.

### 4.3 Instances

- While open, the data is held on **4 independent ENs** in distinct failure domains
  and on distinct **disks** (§5.3.1). **4 copies**, for the reason below.
- After sealing, the extent becomes a cell in an erasure-coded group of **whole
  extents** (§4.3.2.3), with the number of *dedicated* instances set by the scheme:
  one at 1.333x, two at 2.333x (§4.3.2.4).

**Two corrections to earlier drafts, both from §8.1.4.**

**The four copies while open are the four ENs' own staging — their common extents —
not four dedicated replicas of the final extent.** Each is single-copy on its EN, and
the independence of the four ENs is the durability. So the migration to the final form
writes **only the 1 or 2 instances the scheme needs**, not 4 (§8.1.4.4).

**Re-encoding is not free of recompression.** EC itself operates on already-compressed,
already-encrypted bytes and so needs no keys — that part stands. But the migration from
common extents to dedicated ones **coalesces small appends and may recompress**, which
does need keys and CPU (§8.1.4.4).

#### 4.3.1 Why four instances and not three

Two operating assumptions, per instance:

| State | Fraction of the time |
|---|---|
| unavailable | 1/1,000 |
| gone, and not yet replaced | 1/10,000 |

The target is **at least 10^-14 reliability per average window between an instance being
lost and being replaced.** Data is lost when every instance is gone at once, so with *n*
instances the loss probability per window is (10^-4)^*n*:

| *n* | Loss per window | |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | 10^-12 | **fails the target by 100×** |
| **4** | **10^-16** | meets it with 100× margin |
| 5 | 10^-20 | overshoots; pays 25% more disk for it |

So four is not a round number — three misses by two orders of magnitude and five buys
margin nobody asked for.

⚠️ **The model is corroborated; the number is not.** Cosmos states the same failure model in the same
terms — replicas in separate failure domains, a lost replica replaced, data loss when all are lost
inside the replication window (§1.4.5.2). But its empirical finding was that **three replicas
sufficed** at exabyte scale for a decade. §4.3.1.1 works out why, and the answer is not that Cosmos
was lucky.

#### 4.3.1.1 What the target means, and which input to doubt

A probability "per average window" is not a quantity anyone can sanity-check. Converting it to a
fleet loss rate makes it checkable. A window opens when *one* instance is lost, so loss requires
the remaining *n*−1 inside that window:

> losses/year ≈ (extents) × *n* × AFR × *p_gone*^(*n*−1)

At 1 EB in 32 MB extents — 3.0 × 10^10 extents — and 1.5% AFR:

| Repair window *W* | Implied *p_gone* | 3 replicas | 4 replicas |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 h | 1.7 × 10^-6 | 1 loss per **255 yr** | 1 per 10^8 yr |
| 4 h | 6.8 × 10^-6 | 1 per **16 yr** | 1 per 1.7 × 10^6 yr |
| 12 h | 2.1 × 10^-5 | 1 per **2 yr** | 1 per 65,000 yr |
| **58 h** | **10^-4** | **13 losses per year** | 1 per **572 yr** |

Two things fall out, and the second is the important one.

**First, the 10^-14 target does have a sensible fleet meaning**: at 4 replicas and a 58-hour window
it is roughly one lost extent per 572 years per exabyte. That is a defensible number, so the target
survives being questioned.

⚠️ **Second, *p_gone* = 10^-4 is the input to doubt.** It implies a **58-hour repair window**, which
is lax — and a tighter one is cheap. Rebuilding a failed 20 TB disk inside an hour needs ~44 GB/s of
reads at 8× erasure-coding amplification, which is **0.18% of a 25 TB/s fleet**:

| *W* | Read bandwidth to hit it | Fraction of a 25 TB/s fleet |
|---|---|---|
| 1 h | 44 GB/s | 0.18% |
| 4 h | 11 GB/s | 0.04% |
| 58 h | 0.8 GB/s | 0.003% |

So **at a 1–4 hour window, three replicas already meet the target**, which is almost certainly why
Cosmos observed three sufficing. The fourth replica is not buying reliability that three plus prompt
repair could not; it is buying permission to repair slowly.

Which is still a reasonable trade — replication is transient (§4.3), so a fourth copy of open
extents costs little, while a tight repair window is a standing operational commitment. But the
honest statement is that **four instances is a choice to relax the repair window, not a
reliability necessity**, and the number to revisit is *p_gone*, not *n*.

**That exponent is entirely a claim about independence.** (10^-4)^4 assumes the four
failures are uncorrelated, which is exactly what the placement rules of §5.6 exist to
deliver. A correlated failure mode — one bad firmware revision, one power domain, two
instances on one machine's disks — collapses the exponent toward 10^-4 and the design
misses its target by ten orders of magnitude. The reliability figure is therefore a
statement about placement discipline, not about disks.

**Availability, separately.** A read needs one instance of four, so it is unavailable
(10^-3)^4 = **10^-12** of the time — *provided the four are tried promptly rather than
serially* (§9.5). Four copies give durability unconditionally, but they only give
availability if the read path can reach past a dead one faster than a TCP timeout. A write needs three of four applied (§8.1), which is
unavailable ~**6 × 10^-6** of the time — about 190 seconds per year per extent, and six
orders of magnitude worse than reads. That asymmetry is affordable only because a write
that cannot reach a quorum does not block: the extent is sealed short and a new one opened
(§13), which §6 already makes cheap by allowing extents to seal at any size.

Sealing and EC are also a **billing event**: 4 replicas of a 32 MB body bills as
128 MB; an 8+4 encoding of the same body bills as ~48 MB (§12).

⚠️ EC changes the read unit: what was one sequential read against a replica
becomes *k* fragment reads across *k* ENs, partly defeating the device tuning of
§9.3. Either align the fragment stripe with the index granularity, or retain one
full replica alongside the fragments for locality.

#### 4.3.2 Erasure-code parameters, and a patent problem

The §4.3.1 target applies to sealed data, which is erasure-coded rather than replicated, so the
code's parameters need the same arithmetic. A *k*+*m* code tolerates *m* losses and is lost at
*m*+1, so the loss probability is a binomial tail rather than a simple power — and **durability
depends on *m* alone, not on the storage ratio.**

That much is easy. The hard part is that plain Reed-Solomon **forces a choice between storage
overhead and repair traffic**, because reconstructing one lost fragment requires reading *k*:

| Code | Overhead | Repair amplification | Loss per window |
|---|---|---|---|
| 6+3 | 1.50× | 6× | 1.26 × 10^-14 — **fails 10^-14** |
| 8+4 | 1.50× | 8× | 7.9 × 10^-18 |
| 12+4 | 1.33× | 12× | 4.4 × 10^-17 |
| 20+4 | 1.20× | 20× | 4.2 × 10^-16 |

Note 6+3 fails the target, and earlier drafts of this document used it as the example. Beyond
that, every row buys cheaper storage with dearer repair. **Repair traffic is a throughput cost,
and §1.4 makes throughput the priority**, so this is not a free trade: across 2 EB at 1.5% AFR,
~30 PB is lost per year, and repair reads 240 PB/yr at 8+4 or 600 PB/yr at 20+4 — 7.6 GB/s
against 19 GB/s of continuous background traffic.

#### 4.3.2.1 Local codes dissolve the trade, and are encumbered

Codes with **locality** break the coupling: some parities cover only a small group of *r* data
symbols, so a single failure — the overwhelmingly common case — is repaired by reading *r*
fragments rather than *k*. Additional *h* "heavy" parities over all symbols preserve tolerance
to multiple simultaneous losses. **Repair amplification becomes *r*, independent of *k***, so
large *k* (cheap storage) and small *r* (cheap repair) stop being in tension.

*Maximally recoverable* codes are the strongest form: every erasure pattern that is
information-theoretically recoverable actually is. See ["Explicit Maximally Recoverable Codes
with Locality"](https://arxiv.org/html/1307.4150v2) — Gopalan, Huang, Jenkins and Yekhanin,
2013. Its Example 16 gives a [80,60,7] maximally recoverable local (60,4,4) code:

| | Overhead | Repair amplification | Loss per window | Fleet repair traffic |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| RS 8+4 | 1.50× | 8× | 7.9 × 10^-18 | 7.6 GB/s |
| **MR (60,4,4)** | **1.33×** | **4×** | ≤3.2 × 10^-19 | **3.8 GB/s** |

Better on three axes — cheaper storage, half the repair traffic, better steady-state durability.

⚠️ **But worse on the axis that turns out to matter.** An earlier draft of this section claimed
"better on every axis at once", which was wrong. Guaranteed disaster tolerance is (*d*−1)/*n*
(§4.3.3), and local codes **trade minimum distance for locality** — that is the fundamental tension,
not an artefact of this particular construction:

| | *n* | *d* | Overhead | Guaranteed survivable | MDS bound at that overhead |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| RS 8+4 | 12 | 5 | 1.50× | **33.3%** | 33.3% — achieved |
| MR (60,4,4) | 80 | 7 | 1.33× | **7.5%** | 25% — far short |

By the frequency law of §1.1.1 that is a **~32× higher loss rate** in the worst case. Since §4.3.3
shows disasters dominate loss, the local code is better precisely where reliability was already
adequate and worse precisely where it is lost.

To be fair to it: *maximally recoverable* means it recovers **every** pattern its structure permits,
so it does far better than 7.5% on disasters whose losses spread across local groups. If each local
group's fragments sit in distinct domains, a single-domain disaster costs one fragment per group and
every one is repaired locally — the ideal case. The real comparison therefore depends on the disaster
size distribution and on how domains map onto local groups, and deserves proper analysis rather than a
verdict either way.

#### 4.3.2.2 The codec choice is downstream of the repair-bandwidth budget

Repair amplification does not size the network, but it does set how fast a large outage recovers — and
those are very different regimes:

| | RS 8+4 (8× amplification) | Local *r* = 4 (4×) |
|---|---|---|
| Steady state, 100k disks | 7.6 GB/s = 0.03% of fleet | 3.8 GB/s = 0.015% |
| Rebuilding 120 PB after a 5% outage, at 25% of fleet | **44.9 h** | **22.5 h** |

In steady state neither figure is close to sizing anything; foreground traffic sizes the network
(§5.12.1). But in a large outage the amplification is applied to 5% of the cluster rather than to a
year's disk attrition, and **halving it halves the recovery window — which cuts degraded-window loss
~8×, since that loss goes as *W*³** (§13.2.2).

So the trade is three-cornered, and the network budget is what picks a corner:

- **A generous network** affords 8× amplification, so take the MDS code and its better disaster
  tolerance (§4.3.2.1).
- **A constrained network** makes locality valuable: it buys faster recovery, or equivalently a
  smaller fabric for the same recovery time — at the cost of guaranteed disaster tolerance.

⚠️ Which reframes the patent, more carefully than an earlier draft of this section did. It is not
"a repair-traffic optimization in a regime that was never the constraint" — repair traffic *is* the
constraint during outage recovery, which §13.2 shows is where loss actually happens. The patent blocks
one of the two ways to shorten that window; the other is buying more network. Whether that is worth
licensing therefore depends on the network budget, and the two are substitutes.

⚠️ **It is patented, and the patent does not expire until 2034.** Bob is a co-inventor, which
makes this easier to walk into rather than harder: the technique is familiar, the paper is
public, and neither of those makes it usable. This is a question for counsel, not for this
document — but it must be settled before any code is chosen, because the choice is baked into
every sealed extent and the §4.6.3 timestamp deadline means those live a very long time.

**There is an unencumbered fallback with similar statistics: turbo codes.** A little worse than the LRC,
but comparable in the properties that matter here, and not patent-encumbered. That changes the character of
the patent problem entirely — the alternative to licensing is not plain Reed-Solomon and its 8× repair
amplification, but something close to what was wanted.

**And the cost of not licensing can be priced.** Turbo codes raise the two overheads from 1.333× and 2.333×
to **1.5× and 2.5×** — the same absolute increment of 0.167× in both cases, so at §12.7.2's $1.42 per
physical TB-month the patent is worth a flat

> **~$0.24 per TB-month of avoided storage overhead**

which is +12.5% on the cheap tier and +7.1% on the dearer one. That makes licensing a straightforward
arithmetic question rather than a design one:

| Stored | Value of the patent |
|---|---|
| 100 PB | $284,000/year |
| 1 EB | **$2.84M/year** |
| 10 EB | $28.4M/year |

License it if it costs less than that; otherwise use turbo codes. Either way the design is unblocked, and
the unencumbered path still prices at $2.13 and $3.55 per TB-month — **2.8× and 1.7× under the cheapest
immediate-read incumbent** (§12.7.2.2).

⚠️ What is *not* quantified is the disaster-tolerance comparison. The MDS bound at 1.5× is 33% and at 2.5×
is 60%, but turbo codes will fall short of those as LRCs do (§4.3.2.1), and by how much is unknown. Since
§1.1.1 makes disasters the dominant loss mode, that gap could matter more than the $0.24 — it should be
measured before the choice is made on price alone.

⚠️ Note this reframes §4.3.2.1's comparison. The candidate is not "MDS Reed-Solomon versus a patented
local code" but "an LRC, or turbo codes if the patent bites" — and §12.7.2.1a shows the local structure buys
something the earlier analysis missed: with data extents duplicated, repair leaves the read path entirely,
which is what makes availability recover in minutes rather than days.

**Working assumption: Reed-Solomon, MDS, with the overhead chosen from disaster tolerance** — §4.3.3
makes overhead and survivable disaster fraction the same decision, and §4.3.3.1 makes it the dominant
reliability lever. *m* = 4 also satisfies steady-state durability, so 8+4 at 1.50× meets both; it is
used as the example throughout because it matches the overhead assumed elsewhere, so no downstream
figure changes.

Note the ordering this implies: **pick the disaster size to survive, which fixes the overhead, which
fixes *m*/*n*.** Repair traffic is then whatever *k* makes it, and is a throughput cost rather than a
reliability one.

#### 4.3.2.2a Repair bandwidth is a network number, which makes the codec choice media-neutral

The budget §4.3.2.2 spends is **network**, not device. Per EN at ~100 drives:

| | Device aggregate | NIC (100 GbE) | Repair bound |
|---|---|---|---|
| HDD | 100 x 200 MB/s = 20 GB/s | 12.5 GB/s | **12.5 GB/s** |
| SSD | 100 x 4 GB/s = 400 GB/s | 12.5 GB/s | **12.5 GB/s** |

**Derived.** The network already binds in an HDD fleet, by 1.6x. It binds in an all-SSD fleet by 32x. So a
media transition moves repair bandwidth by approximately nothing, and every repair-window figure in §4.3.3
is denominated in network bytes.

Two consequences.

**The codec decision has no hardware-driven expiry.** Both the constraint (network volume) and the saving a
local code buys (fewer bytes read to rederive) are denominated in the same unit, and neither depends on the
device. So the patent question of §4.3.2.1 — and its ~$0.24/TB-month price — is unchanged by the HDD-to-SSD
transition that §7.4 says is coming. It expires in 2034 and not before.

**Locality is worth more, not less, when the network binds.** The point of a local code is reading 6 nearby
blocks instead of 45 far ones, and that saving is priced in exactly the scarce resource. An earlier draft of
this section argued the reverse from a 20x device-bandwidth improvement that does not exist.

⚠️ In a *correlated* disaster the binding number is not any one NIC but the fleet's aggregate cross-section,
so a spine oversubscription ratio multiplies every repair window in §4.3.3 directly. §5.12.3 assumes a flat
intra-cluster network to argue affinity is unnecessary; **durability depends on that same assumption**, which
is a heavier load than it was introduced to carry.

#### 4.3.2.3 Erasure coding groups whole extents; it never splits them

An erasure-coded stripe is a **grid of whole extents**. A cell is one extent, not a fragment of one, and
parity is computed across cells. Nothing is ever split into shards and reassembled.

**Asserted** (Bob, 2026-08-15), and it is the single most consequential structural fact about EC here. Four
things follow.

**Reads never touch EC.** Data cells are stored whole and independently readable, so the read path is
identical for replicated and erasure-coded data. Erasure coding is purely a *repair-time* concern. That
removes reconstruction from §1.4.2's read-amplification budget entirely, and it is why §9.3's sparse index and
§9.1's three binary searches need no EC-aware variant.

**Instances must be byte-identical in stored form.** Parity is computed over the stored bytes of whole
extents, so the four instances of a cell must agree bit for bit — see §8.1.4, where this forces compression
and encryption to happen *upstream* of the fan-out to four ENs.

**Group members need equal physical length.** Extents seal on either the 32 MB physical bound or the 4 GB
logical bound (§6), so a logical-limit seal comes out short and arbitrary. Either pad every cell to a fixed
EC unit — pure waste, landing in §12.7's space-efficiency chain — or bin by size when forming groups. §13.5's
daily job does the latter, and that is its most immediately measurable win.

**A group spans unrelated objects, so deleting one member frees nothing.** Recomputing parity means reading
the whole group, so hard-deleting a cell inside a live group is deferred and batched. This is precisely
§12.7's "undeletable garbage" term, and it gives §8.4.1's deferred-decrement machinery a second consumer.

**SN owns the group** (Asserted, Bob). Group formation is therefore constrained to extents belonging to
streams on one SN. That is not an arbitrary restriction: it is what lets the repair priority sort of §13.4 and
the verification loops of §13.1.10 both run locally, with no cross-SN accumulator.

#### 4.3.2.4 The two variants are one code with a different data-instance count

The 1.333x and 2.333x figures of §12.7.2.1 are the same 10x6 grid, differing only in how many instances each
*data* cell gets. Parities always get one.

| Variant | Cells stored | Overhead |
|---|---|---|
| 1.333x | 45 data x 1 + 15 parity | 60 / 45 = **1.333x** |
| 2.333x | 45 data x 2 + 15 parity | 105 / 45 = **2.333x** |

**Derived**, and it reproduces both of Bob's figures exactly, which is the check that the reading is right.

Duplicating data cells buys a three-tier repair hierarchy:

| Loss | Repair path | Extents read |
|---|---|---|
| 1 of 2 data instances | copy the sibling | **1** |
| both data instances | local group | 5 |
| local group insufficient | global solve | 45 |

**And it explains the labels in §12.7.2.1.** "Always available" does not mean more durable — the code is the
same. It means a read can never be forced to do EC work: there is always a live copy. At 1.333x a lost cell
must be rederived before it can be served, hence "usually available, always reliable". The availability
difference between the two tiers is entirely about whether §4.3.2.3's promise — EC stays off the read path —
can ever be broken.

#### 4.3.2.5 The deliverable is a catalog with recommendations, not a code

**There will be a list of erasure codings to choose from, and DeLawson will recommend a few for different use
cases** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-15). So the question this section has been circling is misframed: it is not
"which code", it is "what is in the catalog, and what does each entry recommend itself for".

**Two families, and within each it is mostly parameters.** Rectangular LRC and turbo codes are structurally
different — one has local parities and maximal recoverability, the other is a product code decoded iteratively.
Inside either family, choosing dimensions and parity counts is a parameter sweep.

**Therefore overhead is a parameter, not a discriminator.** Nearly any overhead is reachable in either family:
§4.3.3.2b's `(27+3)x(5+1)` turbo code hits 1.333x, the same as the 10x6 LRC. What differs at equal overhead is
**reliability, repair reads, and domain floor** — which is exactly what §4.3.3.2c measures, and why the
comparison has to be done at matched overhead rather than across it.

**Each catalog entry must record**, so that a recommendation is justified rather than asserted:

| Field | Source |
|---|---|
| family and parameters | — |
| storage overhead | direct |
| minimum distance `d` | §4.3.3.2b, closed form for both families |
| minimum-weight uncorrectable pattern count | §4.3.3.2c, closed form for turbo, simulation for LRC |
| equal-lossiness point vs 4-instance data | §4.3.3.2c |
| common and worst-case repair reads | §4.3.3.2d |
| domain floor per recovery set | §4.3.3.2e |
| data-instance count, 1 or 2 | §4.3.2.4 |

**The recommendation axes are not just overhead.** A user or operator is really choosing along four:

- **overhead** they are willing to pay;
- **cluster size**, since a wide code silently under-delivers below its domain floor (§4.3.3.2e, §5.6.7);
- **whether a read may ever wait for reconstruction** — the 1-vs-2 data-instance choice of §4.3.2.4, which is
  an availability decision and not a durability one;
- **data lifetime**, since §8.5.3 argues short-lived data should skip erasure coding entirely.

**And turbo codes suffice for shipping** (Asserted, Bob). That is a scheduling fact worth recording plainly: the
patent question of §4.3.2.1, worth ~$0.24/TB-month, is a **later optimization and not a release gate.** The
catalog ships with an unencumbered family in it, and an LRC family can be added when the patent question is
settled — which is straightforward precisely because §4.3.3.2e already makes the scheme a recorded per-group
property with promotion done as compaction.

#### 4.3.3 What size of disaster survives, and what it costs

**Derived.** Given §5.6's placement — every fragment of an extent in a *distinct* failure domain —
a disaster confined to *m* domains destroys at most *m* fragments of any extent. So an *k*+*m* code
**survives any disaster confined to *m* or fewer domains, with certainty.** Not a probability: a
guarantee, provided the disaster respects the domain hierarchy.

In general a code tolerates *d*−1 arbitrary erasures, so its guaranteed survivable fraction is
(*d*−1)/*n*. Reed-Solomon is **MDS** — *d* = *n*−*k*+1 — which makes that exactly the parity fraction
*m*/(*k*+*m*), and gives a clean relation:

> **storage overhead = 1 / (1 − survivable fraction)**, for an MDS code

This is a **bound**, not an identity: MDS codes achieve it and nothing beats it. A non-MDS code of the
same overhead survives strictly less (§4.3.2.1 is the cautionary case).

| Code | Overhead | Survives a disaster of |
|---|---|---|
| 8+2 | 1.25× | 20% of the cluster |
| 10+4 | 1.40× | 29% |
| **8+4** | **1.50×** | **33%** |
| 8+8 | 2.00× | 50% |
| 4+12 | 4.00× | 75% |

Storage overhead *is* disaster tolerance, in a one-line correspondence. Surviving half a cluster
costs 2× — mirroring, essentially — and no in-cluster code survives 100%, which is what a second
cluster is for.

#### 4.3.3.1 Where expected loss actually comes from

An earlier draft of this subsection argued that loss is dominated by the *smallest* disaster
exceeding parity, on the reasoning that those are the most frequent. **That was wrong**, and the
error was treating loss as a step function. It is not: a disaster of size *s* destroys the fraction
of extents that lose more than *m* of their *n* fragments, which for an MDS code is

> **L(s) = P(X > m)**, where X ~ Binomial(*n*, *s*)

— a smooth curve, not a cliff. With disaster rate R(≥s) ∝ s^-α, expected loss is
∫ α·s^-(α+1)·L(s) ds, whose integrand goes as s^(m−α). For m > α that **increases** with s, so the
large disasters dominate after all:

| α (rate multiplier per halving) | Code | E[loss] ÷ R₁ | Median contributing *s* |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2.32 (5×) | RS 8+4 | 16.7 | **32%** |
| 2.32 (5×) | RS 8+8 | 4.6 | 58% |
| 2.32 (5×) | 3× replication | 3.4 | 36% |
| 3.32 (10×) | RS 8+4 | 101 | 20% |

R₁ is the rate of whole-cluster disasters. **Expected annual loss is of order R₁ for every code** —
which is the real conclusion: no in-cluster erasure code does anything about losing the whole
cluster, so the top of the distribution can only be addressed by **a second cluster.** In-cluster
parity buys the middle of the range.

⚠️ **The exponent is not known.** "Halving the size multiplies the rate by 5" was a shape, not a
measurement; 10× is equally plausible and changes E[loss] by 6×. Worse, **the integral diverges for
α > m**: at 3× replication (m=2) and α=3.32 the small end dominates and the model needs a floor —
the smallest real "disaster" being one disk. So **more parity both lowers loss and makes the
estimate well-behaved**, and the exponent needs measuring before any of these numbers are trusted.

#### 4.3.3.2 Comparing codes: the equal-lossiness point

Absolute loss figures are hard to judge and depend on an unmeasured α. **A better comparison, and
one independent of the frequency law: for what disaster size is a scheme exactly as lossy as
triplication?** Below that size it is better, above it worse.

| Scheme | Overhead | As lossy as 3× replication at | As lossy as 4× at |
|---|---|---|---|
| RS 8+2 | 1.25× | **never better** | never better |
| **RS 8+4** | **1.50×** | **s = 4.0%** | s = 0.13% |
| RS 8+8 | 2.00× | s = 30.5% | s = 20.5% |

This is far more informative than a durability probability. It says **8+4 beats triplication only for
disasters below 4% of the cluster** — and §13.2's failed rollout is 5%, already past it. 8+2 is worse
than triplication at every size despite costing 1.25×, so cheap parity is a false economy. 8+8, at
two-thirds the cost of triplication, is better than it for everything below 30%.

#### 4.3.3.2a How to evaluate a candidate code — the procedure, not yet the answer

**Not done here.** This records the method so the numbers can be produced when a code is actually chosen;
they are all calculable.

**The reference points are what customers already accept.** Almost all are happy with 3× replication and
essentially all would be happy with 4×. So the useful statement about any code is not an abstract
probability but **"equivalent to 3× or 4× replication at what loss rate?"** — and 3× fails at *p*³ while 4×
fails at *p*⁴, which makes the comparison a single equation.

Note this is the same equal-lossiness idea as §4.3.3.2 with a different independent variable: that section
crosses schemes against *disaster size s*, this one against *per-instance loss probability p*. They are
complementary — correlated loss and independent loss — and the second failure model below combines them.

**Two failure models to evaluate under:**

| | Model |
|---|---|
| 1 | Instant random loss of each instance with probability *p* |
| 2 | **One failure domain lost**, plus instant random loss of each surviving instance with probability *p* |

Model 2 is the one that matters, because §1.1.1 makes correlated loss the dominant mode and §13.2 shows a
domain-scale event is the realistic starting condition rather than a rare extreme.

**Method A — Monte Carlo.** Simulate both models across the code's matrix and find the *p* at which the
code's loss probability equals *p*³ or *p*⁴.

**Method B — back-of-the-envelope.** Count minimal uncorrectable patterns and equate. For the 10 × 6 LRC,
an uncorrectable pattern needs two rows and eight extents within them, giving

> C(10,2) × C(12,8) × *p*⁸ = *p*⁴  →  22,275·*p*⁴ = 1  →  ***p* ≈ 8.2%**

So that code matches 4× replication at a per-instance loss probability around 8%: below that it is better
than four copies, above it worse. The shape generalizes — (ways to choose the structural units) × (ways to
choose extents within them) × *p*^(losses needed) set equal to the reference — and it is cheap enough to do
for every candidate before committing to any.

**The turbo-code candidate to evaluate is a (5+1) × (12+3) matrix:**

| | |
|---|---|
| Grid | 6 rows × 15 columns = 90 cells |
| Data | 5 × 12 = **60** |
| Parity | 30 — each row a (12+3) code tolerating 3, each column a (5+1) tolerating 1, plus a 1 × 3 parity-of-parity corner |
| Overhead | 90/60 = **1.500×**, matching §4.3.2.1's turbo figure |

⚠️ Running these is what settles the open questions about turbo-code disaster tolerance and about whether the
LRC's thin guarantee (§12.7.2.1a) matters in practice. Both are arithmetic, not research.

#### 4.3.3.2b All three candidate codes have minimum distance 8

Before any simulation, the distances are computable and they are equal.

| Code | Overhead | Cells | Formula | d |
|---|---|---|---|---|
