| 10x6 LRC (45 data, 5 global, 10 local) | 1.333x | 60 | `n - k - ceil(k/r) + 2` = 60 - 45 - 9 + 2 | **8** |
| `(12+3)x(5+1)` turbo | 1.5x | 90 | product: `d1 x d2` = 4 x 2 | **8** |
| `(27+3)x(5+1)` turbo | 1.333x | 180 | product: 4 x 2 | **8** |

**Derived.** Every one of them survives any 7 losses and no more, guaranteed. So the differences between them
lie entirely in (a) how many cells there are to fail and (b) behaviour *beyond* d.

That settles the tempting middle option. `(27+3)x(5+1)` reaches 1.333x overhead with an unencumbered code —
the same overhead as the patented LRC — but it does so with **180 cells at the same distance 8**, twice as many
chances to accumulate the eight failures that kill a stripe. Bob's guess that it would be less reliable is
right, and §4.3.3.2c prices it.

It also isolates what the patent actually buys. At equal distance, the LRC has the fewest cells *and* is
**maximally recoverable** — its uncorrectable set is the information-theoretic minimum given the locality
structure, which no product code matches at any overhead.

#### 4.3.3.2c Product codes can be evaluated in closed form, with no Monte Carlo

§4.3.3.2a asks for pattern counting. For product codes that count is a combinatorial identity, so half the
comparison is free.

A product-code erasure pattern is uncorrectable by iterative row/column decoding exactly when it contains a
full rectangle of `d2` rows by `d1` columns in which every involved row and column exceeds its parity budget.
The minimum-weight uncorrectable patterns *are* those rectangles, so for an `(m1+r1) x (m2+r2)` code the count
of weight-`(r1+1)(r2+1)` failures is `C(m2+r2, r2+1) * C(m1+r1, r1+1)`.

| Code | Overhead | Min-weight uncorrectable patterns | Tolerable random loss vs 4-instance |
|---|---|---|---|
| `(12+3)x(5+1)` | 1.5x | C(6,2)·C(15,4) = 15 · 1,365 = **20,475** | **~23%** |
| `(27+3)x(5+1)` | 1.333x | C(6,2)·C(30,4) = 15 · 27,405 = **411,075** | **~13.5%** |

The equal-lossiness point of §4.3.3.2 solves as `f* = (k / N_8)^(1/4)`, setting per-data-cell loss equal to
4-instance data's `f^4`:

- `(12+3)x(5+1)`: `(60 / 20475)^(1/4)` = **0.233**
- `(27+3)x(5+1)`: `(135 / 411075)^(1/4)` = **0.135**

**Derived.** So buying 1.5x down to 1.333x with a turbo code costs **1.7x in tolerable loss fraction, or ~8.9x
more data lost at any given f.** That is the quantitative form of §4.3.3.2b's conclusion, and it is arithmetic
rather than simulation.

**Three caveats, all of which matter.**

1. It assumes uniform independent loss. §1.1.1 says the regime that actually destroys data is *correlated*, so
   this is the wrong model for the case we care most about — it is a code-comparison yardstick, not a
   prediction.
2. It assumes minimum-weight domination, which holds near break-even and fails badly above it.
3. Those `f*` values sit in a regime where **everything has already lost fractions of a percent**. Reading
   "13.5%" as "we tolerate 13.5% loss" would be badly wrong; at f = 0.135 four-instance data is losing
   `0.135^4` = 0.03% of itself, which by §4.3.3.3 may already be a total loss to the customer.

**And the yardstick is not a property of the code alone.** §13.4's repair scheduler changes how much data is
lost at a given f, so `f*` is a property of **(code, scheduler)** jointly. The pattern counting above stands
on its own and bounds the code; the equal-lossiness comparison between LRC and turbo cannot be done without
the scheduler in the loop, driven by a loss *process* over time rather than a single random loss fraction. Any
scoping of that work as "simulate the code" is scoped wrong.

#### 4.3.3.2d Repair cost per rebuilt cell, and where the peak is

For the 10x6 LRC, a row is 5 data + 1 local parity, so:

- **one** loss in a row is **0 global repairs** — the local parity solves it, 5 reads;
- **two** losses is **1 global repair** — solve one cell against the global parities, which drops the row to
  one loss and lets the local parity finish;

and in general the number of global repairs a group needs is

```
g = sum over rows of max(0, losses_in_row - 1)
```

A global pass costs ~45 reads regardless of `g`, because solving even one unknown against a global parity
touches all 45 data cells. So the cost per rebuilt cell is:

| Losses `m` | `g` | Reads | **Reads per fixed cell** |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 | 5 | **5.0** |
| 2 | 1 | 45 | **22.5** — the peak |
| 3 | 2 | 45 | 15.0 |
| 4 | 3 | 45 | 11.3 |
| 5 | 4 | 45 | 9.0 |
| 6 | 5 | 45 | 7.5 |
| 7 | 5 | 45 | **6.4** |

**Derived.** Two readings of this table drive §13.4.

**Repair amplification is not monotonic in loss fraction.** It is 5 at tiny loss (everything is a local
repair), spikes to 22.5 at the first forced global solve, then *falls* as more losses per group amortize the
same 45 reads. A measurement taken at "small failure" and at "big disaster" straddles the worst case and
reports that all is well.

**The most at-risk repairable group is nearly the cheapest.** 6.4 reads per cell at m=7 against 5.0 for a
local repair — a 1.29x penalty for repairing the thing that is one loss from unrecoverable. Risk-ordered
repair is therefore almost free at the top end, and the only expensive class is `g = 1`.

Turbo codes have the same shape with different constants: a column repair reads 5, a row repair reads 12, and
a pattern needing the full iterative solve reads up to 60 — worse than the LRC's 45, and an iterative
convergence rather than a one-shot solve. Combined with §4.3.3.2b and §4.3.3.2c, the patented code is better
on overhead, on the tail, and on domain floor (§4.3.3.2e) — and **identical in the common case**, where both
read 5. "We cannot use the LRC" costs 12.5% more space and a nastier worst case, not a slower steady state.

#### 4.3.3.2e What a code costs in failure domains

§5.6.1's 4/3 slack applies **per recovery set, at every nesting level at once**. For the
`(12+3)x(5+1)` turbo code (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-15):

| Recovery set | Members | x 4/3 | Domains needed |
|---|---|---|---|
| `(5+1)` row | 6 | 8 | **8** |
| `(12+3)` column | 15 | 20 | **20** |
| full stripe | 108 | 144 | **144** |

**Derived** that the rule is exactly `ceil(4k/3)` — the three figures reproduce as 8, 20 and 144. ⚠️ The third
only works if the stripe is 108 cells; `(12+3)x(5+1)` is 15 x 6 = **90**, which wants 120. Either the grid is
`(15+3)x(5+1)` = 18 x 6 = 108, or 144 should read 120. This needs settling because it is the figure that
decides where a code reaches its designed reliability.

Note what the slack is and is not. It inflates the **domain count requirement** without touching the 1.5x
space overhead — see §5.6.1, where the same ratio is derived from solver cost.

| Scheme | Overhead | Domains for designed reliability |
|---|---|---|
| 4 instances | 4x | **6** |
| 10x6 LRC | 1.333x | **80** |
| `(12+3)x(5+1)` turbo | 1.5x | **120-144** |

**These are not minimum cluster sizes.** §5.6.7 is explicit that an unenforceable rule is simply not enforced,
so every code works on one machine. The table says where a code **achieves its designed reliability** — below
80 domains a 10x6 LRC still functions and still returns data, it just does not deliver 1.333x-code durability.

**Which argues for a ladder rather than a code.** Adopters of an open-source store start small (§1.0.1), so
the durability scheme must be a recorded per-group property like media class (§7.4), with promotion between
rungs done as compaction-with-a-different-target (§10) — machinery that already exists. §4.3.3.2a's evaluation
procedure should then be run **per rung**, not once.

#### 4.3.3.3 "Lost" is a customer's judgement, not ours

**Asserted** (Bob): there is some fraction of loss at which a customer writes the remainder off as
unsalvageable, and **it varies by customer from about 1/1000 to 999/1000.** The upper end is not
hyperbole — people are still extracting text from the carbonized Herculaneum scrolls.

So the right metric is not "probability of losing an extent" but **the rate of disasters losing more
than the customer's write-off fraction *f***. That rate is R₁·s_f^-α where L(s_f) = *f*:

| Write-off fraction *f* | RS 8+4: disaster size that reaches it | Rate ÷ R₁ | 3× replication rate ÷ R₁ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.1% | 7.2% | **447** | 209 |
| 1% | 12.1% | 133 | 35 |
| 10% | 21.9% | 34 | 5.9 |
| 99.9% | 78.4% | **1.8** | 1.0 |

**A 250-fold spread in effective loss rate across customers, on identical storage.** The intolerant
customer and the Pompeii customer are not buying the same product, and no single durability number
describes both.

Two consequences:

- **Durability is a per-customer parameter**, so the design should expose overhead as a choice rather
  than fixing one code. §4.3.3 makes that a one-line correspondence — the customer picks a survivable
  disaster fraction and pays 1/(1−s) for it.
- **Which makes it billable**, and correctly so: higher durability *is* more physical bytes, so §12's
  billing-by-physical-bytes charges for it automatically with no new mechanism. A rare case where the
  cost model, the reliability model and the price list already agree.

#### 4.3.4 What erasure coding does not address

Bob has a song about this ("Erasure Coding", lyrics his, music Suno's), and it is a better summary of
the loss landscape than the preceding four subsections:

> *There is no clever coding or cost / That can guarantee no data loss …*
> *But there is no need to invoke vicious thugs / The biggest losses are from software bugs*
> *And fat-fingered admins who erase / There is no cure when you run out of space*

Three loss modes there that §4.3.1–§4.3.3 say nothing about, and all three are worse than the ones
they do cover.

**Software bugs.** §13.2's failed rollout is one shape of this and already dominates disk failure by
three orders of magnitude. It is not the only shape: a bug that corrupts on write, or deletes the
wrong extent, is not a disaster the domain hierarchy protects against, because it hits *logically*
rather than physically. Erasure coding is no defence at all — every fragment is dutifully consistent
with the corrupted data.

**Administrative error.** ⚠️ **The design currently has no protection whatsoever.** A delete is a
delete: §8.3 tombstones it, §13.1.7's sync loop propagates it, and the background loops reclaim the
space. Every mechanism cooperates efficiently in destroying the data. There is no soft-delete window,
no undelete, and no protection against an *authorized* deletion being wrong — which is the case that
actually happens. This is a real gap and probably the most serious one in this document, because it is
both common and completely unmitigated.

**Running out of space.** ⚠️ Worse than it sounds, and the song is precise: *there is no cure*. Repair
must **write** the reconstructed fragment somewhere, so a full cluster **cannot repair at all** — its
redundancy only decays, monotonically, until the data goes. So §13.2's utilization ceiling of
1 − 1/*D* is not a capacity guideline but a **durability requirement**, and running out of space is a
data-loss mode rather than an availability inconvenience.

#### 4.3.4.1 The stability condition

> *Erasure Coding stops random leaks / It's more like draining a bathtub, so to speak*
> *If fixes are faster than failures, data's preserved / Otherwise loss is certain and well deserved*

This is a condition the probability arithmetic of §4.3.1 quietly assumes and never states. Repair is
a queue: if its service rate falls below the failure arrival rate, the backlog grows without bound,
redundancy decays monotonically, and **loss becomes certain rather than unlikely** — no code helps,
because the code is not the thing failing.

For 100,000 disks at 1.5% AFR, 30 PB is lost per year, so repair must sustain **7.6 GB/s of reads** at
8× amplification. That is 0.03% of a 25 TB/s fleet — trivially affordable, but it is a **floor rather
than a target**, and it must be *guaranteed* rather than best-effort. §13.2.1's question of how much
bandwidth repair may take has an answer at the bottom end: never less than this, whatever else is
happening.

The in-flight backlog also needs somewhere to live — 41 TB at a 12-hour window, 198 TB at 58 hours —
which is small next to the 1/*D* reserve above, so the space rule is set by domain loss rather than by
ordinary repair.

#### 4.3.4.2 Two conclusions the song reaches first

The song is public, and performed: [*Erasure Coding*](https://youtu.be/oak6U2yBy94) (Cited).


> *Erasure Coding stops hardware leaks / But not admins or management freaks*
> *So: backup in several unrelated places / Immortality any 1 of n embraces*

**Independent clouds, not just independent domains.** §4.3.3.1 arrives at the same place by
arithmetic — expected loss is of order the whole-cluster disaster rate for every in-cluster code — but
the song's reason is better, because "management freaks" and administrative error are not in any
failure model. A second cluster under the same management protects against asteroids and not against
mistakes; a second *provider* protects against both.

> *Frequently no matter what you do / You find your worst opponent is you*
> *The safest place your data could have gotten / Is the one that you've forgotten*

Which is the design principle behind the gap above: the mechanisms most worth having are the ones that
resist the operator, and forgetting is the only such mechanism the system currently has.

> *Immortal data's impossible, tough, / But perhaps the end of time is good enough*

§1.3 sets the longevity goal at a cluster that may run indefinitely. This is the honest version of it.

### 4.4 Stored as lists, served as B-trees

The persistent form and the serving form differ:

| | Stored | Served |
|---|---|---|
| Stream | list of extents | B-tree in memory |
| Object | list of streams | B-tree in memory |

A list is the right thing to *write*: appends are cheap, the format is compact
(§14.1 depends on ~100 B per entry), and it is trivially scannable for the
rebuild-from-ENs path of §5.2. A B-tree is the right thing to *serve*: lookup is
a descent rather than a scan, and — decisively — **insert and split in the
middle are cheap**, which is what keyed objects need (§10) and what a flat
sorted array cannot give.

So an SN loads a stream's extent list from disk into a B-tree on assignment, and
serves from the tree.

#### 4.4.0 A DN's tree cannot be in memory, and keyed objects have no on-disk index yet

⚠️ **The table above says "B-tree in memory" and that is only true of the SN** (Asserted, Bob,
2026-08-17). The asymmetry is already in §5.1: SN state is bounded per stream by construction,
so an SN can afford to rebuild its tree from a list on assignment and hold it. **DN state is
disk-backed and grows with the object count, which nothing bounds** — so a DN cannot build its
index on the fly, and **its B-tree has to be on disk too**.

**Which exposes a gap: keyed objects have no on-disk index designed in** (Asserted, Bob,
2026-08-17). §10 makes a keyed object B-tree-*shaped* by splitting extents on key subranges, and
§4.4 gives the SN a tree over extent *position* — but nothing yet maps a **user key** to the
extent holding it. For a keyed object of millions of extents that map is itself large, paged,
and ordered: an index, on disk, with a root small enough to cache.

⚠️ **And it cannot be built on top of a keyed object, because it is what a keyed object is made
of.** Storing a keyed object's index in another keyed object needs that one's index, and so on.
This is §3.0's argument arriving a second time from a different direction: keyed objects are in
the core because the things they need cannot be layered over them. The index has to be
**intrinsic** — interior levels living in the object's own extents, with the root in its
metadata — and that is a piece of §3 that is currently missing rather than deferred.

**The requirement is general, which is why it is worth naming here rather than in §10.** A DN's
directory, a keyed object's key index, and §4.6.6.2's sweeps all want the same structure: an
ordered, paged, on-disk index whose interior nodes are stored in the same medium as its leaves.
Issue #73 tracks designing it once.

Because SNs and DNs are Raft rings (§5), the two forms fall into the standard
consensus arrangement, and the relationship between them is not a new problem:

| Form | Raft role |
|---|---|
| Stored list on disk | **snapshot** |
| Raft log | **journal** of mutations since the snapshot |
| In-memory B-tree | **state machine** |

Recovery is snapshot-then-replay, snapshotting truncates the log, and a new ring
member catches up by shipping the list and replaying. Scanning ENs to rebuild
(§5.2) sits behind all of this as a last resort.

### 4.5 Which summaries may be kept exact

Every level carries totals — record counts, logical bytes, physical bytes — and
they cannot all be maintained the same way. One rule decides it:

> **A summary that only ever grows at the tail may be updated synchronously all
> the way to the root. A summary of something that can change anywhere in the
> tree either should not exist, or is updated only lazily.**

A tail-only update touches just the rightmost spine of the B-tree — O(depth)
nodes, all of them already hot. A change in the middle would dirty an arbitrary
interior path and, worse, invalidate every prefix sum after it.

Applying the rule:

| Summary | Changes where? | Treatment |
|---|---|---|
| Unkeyed record count | tail only — appends only at the end (§3), and update and tombstone preserve count | **synchronous, exact, to the root** |
| Unkeyed logical/physical bytes | anywhere — a log append in a middle extent grows it | **lazy** |
| Keyed record count | anywhere — inserts land mid-tree | **lazy, or absent** |
| Keyed byte totals | anywhere | **lazy** |
| Extent instance list | anywhere — repair, re-encoding | not a summary; maintained directly |

Two consequences worth stating outright:

- **The addressing summary is the one that gets to be exact.** Unkeyed lookup
  needs cumulative *record counts*, which are precisely the tail-only quantity;
  it never needs cumulative bytes. That is not luck, it is why the count-based
  scheme of §3 works at all: the only summary on the critical path is the only
  one that can be maintained synchronously.
- **Byte totals — hence billing — are lazy.** See §12.

Lazy summaries are brought forward by the background loops of §13.3, not by the
write path.

### 4.6 References and reference counts

Both downward links in the hierarchy are **node-local 4-byte references to
reference-counted targets**, and they behave symmetrically:

| Reference | Lives in | Width | Population it must name |
|---|---|---|---|
| object → stream | a DN | **4 B** | streams a DN references |
| stream → extent | an SN | **4 B** | 1.7 × 10^9 extents per SN (§14.1) |
| extent → instance | an SN, within its fan-out | 6 B | a **disk** within an EN, plus a slot (§5.3.1) |
| global node id | cluster-wide, control plane | 4 B | 2^32 nodes (§5.10) |

Nothing in the data plane carries a cluster-wide name. Every reference is an index
into a population its holder already knows, sized to that population.

#### 4.6.1 Sharing at both levels

**An extent may be referenced by several streams, and a stream by several objects.**
The two are not equally common, though:

| Sharing | Frequency | Why |
|---|---|---|
| stream → extent | **rare** — assume 1 reference (§4.7) | only clones and packed extents |
| object → stream | **routine** | tiny objects are lumped into common streams (§11) |

So a common stream may carry a very large reference count while extents almost always carry
one. Sizing treats extents as privately owned; it must not treat streams that way.

What it buys:

- **Clone and snapshot cost metadata, not data.** Duplicating an object copies its
  stream list and increments stream refcounts — work proportional to the number of
  streams, not bytes. For a 0.4 PiB stream that is the difference between
  milliseconds and days. Sharing at the extent level does the same one level down.
- **Packed extents** (§11), where one extent holds several small objects, are
  naturally multiply-referenced.

What it costs:

- **Deletion becomes decrement**, with the background loops (§13.3) reclaiming at
  zero. Dropping an object frees nothing by itself.
- ⚠️ **Compaction of a shared extent cannot rewrite in place**, because the other
  referrers did not ask for it. It needs copy-on-write: compaction produces a private
  extent for the referrer that triggered it and leaves the shared one alone. So a
  clone's first write costs more than its steady state.
- ⚠️ **Key derivation must fix on the creating stream** (§7.3.3), since a shared
  extent belongs to several streams and "the stream id" is otherwise ambiguous.
- ⚠️ **Billing attribution is a policy question** (§12). Charging a clone and its
  original the full footprint double-bills; charging neither loses revenue; charging
  the creator makes clones free and holds the original hostage.

#### 4.6.2 Sharing forces position-dependent fields into the referrer

Sharing makes a structural rule unavoidable, and it is worth naming because it
explains the layout in §4:

> A shared thing may only carry facts true of it **wherever it appears**. Anything
> that depends on *where* it appears belongs to the reference, not the target.

Two objects sharing a stream will disagree about that stream's starting record
number — it might be the first stream of one object and the thousandth of another.
So the starting record number lives in the object's stream-list entry, never in the
stream record; likewise an extent's starting record number lives in the stream's
extent-list entry, and a keyed `first_key` in the referring entry too. Position-free
facts — physical size, key generation, instance locations — live with the target,
where they are shared for free.

This is why the §4 diagram puts the cumulative counts on the *entries* rather than in
the objects they point at. That was arbitrary-looking before sharing existed; it is
forced now.

#### 4.6.3 Identity: ownership is part of the name

Each level is **owned** by the tier above the bytes, and the owner is part of the
identifier rather than a field beside it:

| Thing | Owner | Full identifier |
|---|---|---|
| Stream | a DN | `(DnId, StreamId)` |
| Extent | an SN | `(SnId, ExtentId, creation second)` |

Extents are not guids. A full extent id is 12 bytes against a guid's 16, and **inside
the owning SN the `SnId` is implicit, so it costs 8** — exactly the extent-id field
already in the record (§5.10.4).

When an extent is shared across DNs, that happens **through two different streams**;
sharing is always mediated by the stream level, so an extent never has two owners.

**Why the creation timestamp.** It makes an `ExtentId` reusable without ambiguity. A
stale reference carrying an old second cannot match a new extent that reused the
number, which is the §5.10.4 naming-lifecycle problem solved by incarnation rather
than by refcounting — and solved with a clock instead of a persisted counter, so it
survives restarts for free and is legible when debugging.

Two safety requirements come with it:

- ⚠️ **An `ExtentId` must not be reused within the same second.** Cycle time is no
  help here — at any plausible creation rate the 2^32 id space takes days to years to
  wrap — so the hazard is purely an allocator handing the same number out twice in one
  second. That argues for a FIFO or least-recently-used free list rather than
  lowest-free allocation.
- ⚠️ **The issued second must never go backward**, or an NTP correction could
  manufacture a collision. The SN should keep the last second it issued in its Raft
  state and refuse to regress.

##### The portable name is the path, not the id

**The identifiers above are internal and cluster-local. The durable user-visible name is the path**
(Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-16). An earlier draft of this section read as though the id *were* the name, which is
wrong in a way that only shows up at the worst moment.

| | Name | Scope |
|---|---|---|
| Internal | `(DnId, StreamId)`, `(SnId, ExtentId, creation second)` | **one cluster** — two clusters collide |
| **User-visible** | `(path, record number)` for unkeyed, `(path, key)` for keyed | **portable** |

**§13.4.5's georeplication is what forces the distinction.** `DnId` and `SnId` are assigned per cluster, so a
replica cannot carry them; but §1.0's central promise is that external indexes never need rebuilding, and a
failover to the second cluster is precisely when a user cannot afford to rebuild every index they own. A path is
a sequence of names and is cluster-independent, so it survives the trip where an id cannot.

This costs nothing, because §5.5.4 already keys metadata by `(parent directory id, name)` rather than by the
path — so the path was never a stored identifier in the first place. It is resolved component by component, and
the components are portable even though the ids are not.

**Consequence for §8.1.1a-10's reference tiers:** the durable tier's names must be written with a path, and the
hint tier `(extent identity, row number)` is **cluster-local by construction** — a hint cannot survive
georeplication, and per §8.1.1a-10 it fails detectably, which is the correct behaviour rather than a gap.

##### The timestamp is 8 bytes of seconds, compared modularly

The daily SN-master key that encrypted an extent is **selected by its creation
timestamp** (§7.3), so the timestamp is load-bearing for decryption as well as for
identity. That makes its width a longevity decision, not a formatting one.

**8 bytes of seconds.** Inside the owning SN the id field is then `ExtentId` (4) plus
second (8) = **12 B**; the full form is 16 B, the same as a guid but structured and
meaningful.

Read as an unsigned counter from a fixed epoch, 8 bytes spans 585 billion years — 42×
the age of the universe — and then wraps, which would be an absolute doomsday: every
extent in the system becomes ambiguous at the same instant, and no amount of rewriting
beforehand helps the ones written just before it.

**So timestamps are compared by signed difference, not by magnitude.** The same bits are
interpreted as signed or unsigned according to era — equivalently, ordering is decided
by `(a − b)` taken as a signed 64-bit value. This is the technique behind TCP sequence
numbers and Linux's `time_after()`, and it changes the constraint qualitatively:

| | Absolute unsigned epoch | Signed-difference comparison |
|---|---|---|
| Cluster lifetime | 585 billion years, then dead | **unbounded** |
| The real constraint | replace everything before the epoch wraps | **no live extent older than ~292 billion years** (2^63 s) |
| Failure mode | everything breaks at once, unfixably | a single over-age extent, fixed by rewriting it |

That is the reconciliation between wanting 8 bytes and wanting a cluster that may run
essentially forever: the window stops being a doomsday and becomes a **rolling maximum
extent age** of ~292 billion years, 21× the age of the universe, which the age-driven
rewrite sweep (§13.3) satisfies trivially.

**The interpretation flips back and forth indefinitely.** Each flip is not a one-time
extension that eventually runs out; it is a periodic reinterpretation of the same 8
bytes, repeatable without limit. The only standing obligation is that live extents stay
inside one window — a bound on extent *age*, never on cluster age.

Two rules follow, and both are the kind that lie dormant for eons and then fail:

- ⚠️ **Never compare raw timestamps by magnitude.** Any `a < b` on the unsigned value is
  a latent bug. Only signed differences are meaningful.
- ⚠️ **Modular comparison is not a total order**, so a timestamp cannot be used naively
  as a sort key or B-tree key — it is only consistent among values within one window.
  Extents are keyed by `(SnId, ExtentId)` with the timestamp as a disambiguator rather
  than a sort key, so this is currently safe; it would stop being safe the moment
  something wanted to index by creation time.

Two safety rules from before still apply: an `ExtentId` must not be reused within one
second, which argues for FIFO or LRU rather than lowest-free allocation; and the issued
second must never go backward, so the SN keeps the last one it issued in its Raft state
and refuses to regress.

##### The same discipline applies to SCNs

Transaction sequence numbers (§5.7) have the identical problem on a **much shorter
wall-clock window**, because an SCN advances per transaction rather than per second. The
signed half-window, in years:

| Transactions/s | 6-byte | 8-byte | 10-byte |
|---|---|---|---|
| 10^3 | 4,500 | 2.9 × 10^8 | 1.9 × 10^13 |
| 10^6 | **4.5** | 2.9 × 10^5 | 1.9 × 10^10 |
| 10^9 | **0.0045** | 292 | 1.9 × 10^7 |

At a million transactions per second, 6 bytes is 4.5 years and 8 bytes is 290,000 —
where the same widths measured in seconds were geological. So width matters far more
here, and the comparison discipline is not optional.

What rescues it is that **the live SCN range is deliberately tiny**: SCNs are expected
to be valid for only ~10 minutes. Only open consistent reads and retained versions need
to be comparable, so capping validity caps the range, and the window bounds *version
age* rather than cluster age — exactly as with extents.

**SCNs are never persisted in cold data.** They live only in the short-lived replicated
extents — the open base and its log — and are **dropped when those are coalesced into a
sealed, erasure-coded extent** (§10). So an SCN's lifetime is bounded by how long an
extent stays hot, which is short by construction rather than by policy. This is the
strongest of the three reasons for the cap: the others bound the SCN range by choosing
to, while this one makes a long-lived SCN impossible to write down.

It also removes a per-record cost from the tier that holds essentially all the bytes. An
8-byte SCN beside a 100-byte record would be ~8% of logical volume — on the order of 80
PB across an exabyte — before compression; delta-encoding monotonic counters would claw
much of that back, but not storing them is exactly zero and depends on nothing.

⚠️ The API consequence is worth stating plainly: **consistent read has a horizon.** A
snapshot can be held for minutes, but there is no querying an object "as of last
Tuesday", because once coalesced there is one version and no SCN to select by. Any
time-travel feature would need a different mechanism entirely.

That cap is a large part of *why* the 10-minute figure exists. Headroom of a 6-byte SCN:

| SCN validity | at 10^6 tx/s | at 10^9 tx/s |
|---|---|---|
| **10 minutes** | 234,562× | **235×** |
| 1 hour | 39,094× | 39× |
| 1 day | 1,629× | **2× — exhausted** |

At a day of validity and a billion transactions a second, 6 bytes is gone. At ten
minutes it holds comfortably even there. **So the 10-minute cap is what makes a narrow
SCN viable at high transaction rates**, and the width and the cap have to be chosen
together.

Note the 10 minutes is **bracketed from both sides**, which is what makes it look like a
real design point rather than a round number: §5.7 needs a consistent read to last *long
enough* to write a checkpoint, while the SCN range and the coalescing lifetime both need
it *short enough*. The same shape as the extent record bracketed by reference width from
below and fleet size from above (§4.6.4), and the physical extent limit bracketed by seek
amortization and metadata volume (§6).

##### The hot tier absorbs the complexity

SCNs are the fourth thing to land on one side of the same line, which is worth naming as
a through-line rather than a coincidence:

| | Hot: open, replicated, mutable | Cold: sealed, erasure-coded, immutable |
|---|---|---|
| Durability | 4 replicas | *k*-of-*n* fragments |
| Structure | base **plus log** | base only |
| Versioning | **SCNs** | none |
| Mutability | appendable | fixed forever |

Every expensive or intricate mechanism lives in the small hot tier; the tier holding
essentially all the bytes stays simple, cheap, and immutable. Coalescing is the
transition, and it is where each of these is given up at once.

⚠️ SCN width and scope are undesigned. A Raft log index is a natural per-ring SCN and
needs no separate counter, but §2 rules out cross-object transactions while an object
spans many rings, so what an SCN is scoped to is not yet settled.

##### Two questions this settles

- **Who may authorize deleting a stream** (§13.1.8). The `DnId` *is* part of the
  stream's name, so a stream has exactly one owning DN by construction, not by
  convention. That is the safe form recommended there, obtained for free.
- **Key derivation is now stable against reassignment** (§7.3.3). Extent keys derive
  from the daily SN-master key of the SN that *created* the extent, and both the `SnId`
  and the day are immutable parts of the extent's name. Moving a stream to another ring
  cannot orphan its keys. Note the consequence: whoever decrypts must derive from the
  extent's own `SnId`, not from the SN currently serving the stream.
- The creation second also **subsumes the separate day index** §7.3.3 budgeted, since
  the day is the second divided by 86,400. One field, two jobs.

⚠️ Streams have no creation timestamp in this scheme, so `(DnId, StreamId)` is exposed
to exactly the stale-reference hazard the extent timestamp prevents. Stream churn is
far lower, so the pressure is milder — but the hazard is the same shape, and the
asymmetry looks unintentional. Worth confirming.

#### 4.6.4 Reference width brackets the record size from below

The 4-byte extent reference caps a machine at 2^32 extents, and the extent budget of
§14.1 is 171 GB, so:

| Extent record | Extents per SN | Share of 2^32 |
|---|---|---|
| 40 B | 4.27 × 10^9 | **99%** |
| 60 B | 2.84 × 10^9 | 66% |
| 100 B — the budget | 1.71 × 10^9 | 40% |
| 200 B | 0.85 × 10^9 | 20% |

**So the extent record cannot shrink below ~40 B** without a machine holding more
extents than 4 bytes can name. That is a floor, and §14.1.2 gives the ceiling from
fleet size — the record is bracketed from both directions, which is a more
comfortable position than a single guess.

**And the 4 bytes buy something beyond addressability: they are what the data
structures reference each other by.** §14.6.2 makes the case — an id rather than a
pointer is how a B-tree or a hash table over an arena is expressible in safe Rust at
all, and it happens to be half the width. Two independent reasons for the same
number, which is why it is not a figure to revisit lightly.

At the 100 B budget there is 2.5× headroom, and the itemized ~60 B (§5.10.4) still
leaves 1.5×. Worth knowing that shrinking records is not free: past a point it trades
metadata density for reference width.

#### 4.6.5 Size classes, and why a dedicated stream is the good case

**A DN treats small objects differently from big ones** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17):

| Object | Held as | Described by |
|---|---|---|
| **tiny** | inline records | the DN, which holds the bytes (§11) |
| **small** — one append's worth | **a small range in a particular stream, created by a single append** | **the DN alone** |
| **large** | its own extents in its own stream | the DN, then its SN |

⚠️ **The reason is garbage, not read performance** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17). Put positively:
**the good thing about a dedicated stream is that it has no garbage.** When the object goes, the whole
stream goes with it — every extent is reclaimable at once, with nothing to compact and nothing to
copy.

A shared stream is the opposite: deleting one small object leaves a hole inside extents that other
objects still need, so nothing can be reclaimed until either everything in the extent is dead or
somebody rewrites it. That is §10's compaction work and §8.5's garbage, arriving for a reason that has
nothing to do with the object being deleted being large. **Sharing is what turns a delete into a
future rewrite**, and a dedicated stream is what turns it into a free.

**So the trigger is not a size estimate but an observation** — two of them, and both are evidence
rather than prediction:

- **A big append goes straight to a dedicated stream.** One append that large is proof enough.
- **A second small append also triggers a dedicated stream.** An object appended to twice is an object
  that grows, and a growing object in a shared stream is the case that makes garbage later. The
  one-append object is the one that shares, because it is the one that will never fragment.

**And nothing has to be got right at the time**, which is what makes an observation-based rule safe:
**extents and streams can be rewritten later to compact things** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17). An
object that started shared and turned out to be large is tidied by the same machinery that compacts
anything else, so the cost of guessing wrong is deferred work rather than a wrong structure.

#### 4.6.6 The reverse edge is a count, not a list

Reclamation needs to know when the last reference to an extent or a stream goes away, which
raises the question of whether the target should track **who** refers to it or merely **how
many** do. **It keeps a count** (Decided, Bob and reasoning here, 2026-08-17).

⚠️ **A count costs nothing per reference, and a list costs everything.** The count lives in
the *record* — 2 to 4 bytes of §4.7's 100-byte extent record — while a list of referrers is a
second structure the size of the forward one, doubling the largest thing the system stores.
The forward references stay 4 bytes either way, so this is not a trade between two widths; it
is a trade between a field and a whole index.

The two counts are not the same size, for §4.6.1's reason: an extent's is almost always 1 and
fits 16 bits, with saturation refusing further sharing rather than wrapping, while a common
stream carries one reference per tiny object lumped into it and needs 32.

**What actually asks a reverse question, and what it really needs:**

| Use case | Needs | Why a list is not the answer |
|---|---|---|
| Deletion and GC | the count | decrement, reclaim at zero — §4.6.1 |
| Compacting a shared extent | nothing | copy-on-write, driven *forward* from the referrer that triggered it |
| Billing a shared extent | the count | computed forward per object, divided by the count; the other referrers are never named |
| Checking invariants | the count | a forward mark-and-sweep recomputes every count, so **counts are auditable and repairable** — a list is one more thing that can be wrong |
| Debugging "what stream is this extent in?" | — | the metadata snapshot answers it for anything over a day old, and under a day the writer is still there |
| Authorizing a direct `(EnId, extent, record)` hint | — | ⚠️ **not the count, and not a list either — see the correction below** |
| ⚠️ Reporting what a permanent loss destroyed | genuinely reverse | see below |
| Impact of a planned decommission | genuinely reverse | same shape, and nobody minds if it takes an hour |

**The general rule underneath most of those rows: wanting a reverse lookup usually means
context was thrown away that could have been carried.**

⚠️ **An earlier version of this paragraph offered the hint as the clean example of that rule, and
it is the one row where the rule does not close the question** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-19). It said
that authorizing a hint appears to need extent → object until you put the stream in the hint, at
which point the question disappears. **It does not disappear**, for two reasons that survive putting
anything at all in the hint:

- **A hint carried by a caller is asserted, not proved.** A caller may name any extent beside any
  stream. Believing the pairing is believing the caller, and checking it is the extent-list search
  the hint existed to avoid — which the SN cannot even do quickly, since its list is ordered by
  record number and not by extent id (§9.1).
- **It is two edges, not one.** Extent → stream is the cheap one; **stream → object** is still
  wanted, because the ACL governs the object, and it crosses the DN → SN boundary this section's
  last paragraph explains cannot hold a maintained reverse edge.

**The count is still right and a list is still wrong** — the fix is neither. It is to make the
carried context *unforgeable*, which §9.1.3.5 does with a capability, and which needs no reverse
structure on any tier.

The one row that is real is **reporting a permanent loss** — when a quorum is gone for good,
every affected user is owed a list of what they lost, which is extent → stream → object for
millions of extents at once and wants to be current rather than a day stale. That is answered
by a **sweep, not an index**: the event is rare, §14.1 keeps this data in RAM, and one pass
over a stream table is minutes. Paying for a permanently maintained structure to make a rare
batch question fast is the wrong trade. Issue #71 tracks building the sweep.

**And for object → stream there is a second, harder argument.** §13.1.7 fixes the loop
inventory at exactly one sync loop per tier boundary. `stream → extent` lives inside one SN
ring and is atomic under Raft, so a reverse edge there would at least be *maintainable*; but
`object → stream` crosses DN → SN, so a stream holding the objects that reference it would be
cross-tier state that drifts, needing reconciliation by the very loop §13.1.6 already runs to
find orphan streams. That loop works off counts. Giving it a list to reconcile as well would
be a second copy of its own job.

##### 4.6.6.1 Each count lives with the references it counts

**An extent's count of referring streams lives in the SN, and a stream's count of referring
objects lives in the DN** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17). The second means the DN holds a record
of its own **keyed by `StreamId`** — a thing the DN has that is not an object and not a copy
of the SN's stream, existing so that the many objects lumped into one common stream (§11) have
somewhere to be counted. An object's stream list points at it, and it points at the stream.

Each count therefore sits in the same tier as the references it counts, which is what makes it
maintainable: a reference and the count of it change under one ring's Raft, so they cannot
disagree across a message that was lost.

⚠️ **§5.11.3.4 refines this into two levels, and improves it.** Once a range is a ring, the
`StreamId` record lives in the **range** and counts that range's objects, while the **SN** counts
how many *ranges* reference the stream. So the SN is told a count after all — of ranges, not of
objects — and it is the single place that observes zero, which is the tier that has to delete the
stream anyway.

**A stream referenced from two DN rings would otherwise have no single place for its count** —
objects lumped into a common stream (§11) are naturally co-located, but a clone into another part
of the directory tree may not be. Two answers, at different levels. **A cross-ring clone copies**
(Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17), so the case does not arise for clones, and §5.1.1.2 explains why that
is affordable: aliases cover what made cross-ring sharing attractive. **And where sharing is
wanted anyway — concatenate — the two-level count handles it**, with the SN aggregating range
references so that nothing has to track objects across rings.

##### 4.6.6.2 Counts get scrubbed

**A count is a cache of a truth held by the referrer** (§13.1.7), so it can be wrong, and
periodically it is recomputed and repaired (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17). This is the payoff of
choosing a count over a list: the truth is still there in the forward references, so a scrub
is a mark-and-sweep that can restore it. A list, once wrong, has no such recovery — you would
be reconstructing it from the same pass anyway.

⚠️ **The two ways a count can be wrong are not equally bad, and the scrub must not treat them
alike.**

| Error | Consequence | How the scrub may act |
|---|---|---|
| count too **high** | space leaks, and §13.1.6's leverage makes a leaked count expensive | correct it freely — the worst case is that reclamation happens |
| count too **low** | **live data is freed** | never act on this alone |

A scrub that computes a lower number than the record holds has not proved the record wrong; it
may have missed a reference that moved during the pass. So lowering a count has to be
conservative — an epoch or generation that makes "unchanged for the whole pass" checkable, or
two agreeing passes, or the clock of §13.3 rather than an immediate free.

**And the scrub is the same walk as the loss sweep of §4.6.6.** Both visit every forward
reference once and ask something about it. One traversal, several consumers, is the shape to
build — issue #71.

##### 4.6.6.3 How lazy each of these may be

Three things here are deliberately deferred — the scrub above, §5.1.1.1's alias bit, and
reclamation at zero references — and they do **not** get the same latitude.

| Deferred thing | May lag by | What the lag costs |
|---|---|---|
| §5.1.1.1's alias bit | **a day, easily** | an alias refused that would have been legal |
| A refcount scrub | a day | nothing, while counts are only too high |
| **Reclamation at zero references** | ⚠️ **not a day** | real storage, unbilled |

**Reclamation may be lazy but it cannot be very lazy** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17): *"I could
see waiting a day before aliasing a higher directory, but not waiting a day for garbage to stop
being billed."*

**This is §12.1's principle, not a separate rule.** Billing must track actual cost within
slack, in *both* directions — and unreclaimed garbage is cost without billing, which is the
direction §12.1 says makes the service go broke. Deleted bytes still on disk are the purest
form of the divergence: the customer's meter stops on its own, because billing walks forward
from live objects (§4.6.6) and a gone object stops appearing, while the disk stays full.
§8.4.1's retention window is the case where the two *do* track, which is precisely why the
customer pays for it.

⚠️ **Short-lived data with soft delete opted out is where the ratio blows up**, and it is the
case that sets the requirement. Steady-state garbage is *churn rate × reclamation lag*, which
bears no relation to how much live data the tenant has: a workload writing and deleting a
petabyte a day carries a petabyte of garbage at a one-day lag while being billed for almost
nothing. So the promptness requirement is set by **the shortest-lived data the system accepts,
not by average behaviour**. And a tenant who opted out of the retention window asked not to
have their deleted data stored; keeping it a day anyway makes the opt-out a fiction.

**So the budget derives rather than being invented**: reclamation must be prompt enough to hold
garbage inside §12.1's slack, which on a high-churn opted-out workload means near-prompt and on
an archive means almost anything. Stating it as "reclaim within N hours" would set the wrong
variable — the number that matters is how far cost has drifted from billing, and time is only
one of its inputs.

### 4.7 Working budgets

Every number below is **a guess, to be replaced by measurement**. They are collected
here so the sizing arguments have one source, and so that refining one of them is a
single edit rather than an archaeology exercise.

Treat them as **budgets to spend against, not totals to re-derive.** The itemized
content of a record will drift upward as flags, timestamps and checksums accumulate;
that is what the headroom is for, and re-baselining every downstream calculation on
each increment produces numbers obsolete by the next revision.

| Budget | Value | Where it is used |
|---|---|---|
| Extent metadata record | **100 B** | §14.1 — itemized at ~60 B so far (§5.10.4) |
| Stream metadata record | **200 B** | §14.1 |
| User object metadata record | **300 B** | §14.2 |
| References per extent | **1** | §4.6.1 — more is supported but rare |
| References per stream | **many** for lumped streams, 1 for dedicated | §4.6.1, §11 |
| Extent / stream reference width | **4 B**, node-local | §4.6 |
| Extent physical size | 32 MB compressed | §6 |
| Extent logical size | ≤ 4 GB | §6 |
| Instances per open extent | 4 | §4.3 |
| SN / DN machine RAM | 256 GB | §14.1 |
| SN RAM split | **1/3 streams, 2/3 extents** | §14.1 — varies wildly by tenant |
| Placement slack | 4/3 | §5.6.1 |
| Fan-out per machine | ~20,000 | §5.10 |
| Compression ratio, when assumed | 4× | §12, §14.2 |
| Billing slack — how far a billed dimension may sit from true cost | **2×** | §12.1, §12.3 — **now derived** in §12.4.1: it is the count of dimensions in an additive bill |

The SN RAM split deserves its own warning: **it will vary wildly between tenants and
in production**, because it encodes an assumed mix of object sizes (§14.1.1). It has
to be a soft allocation that rebalances, not a partition fixed at build time.

#### 4.7.1 What the placeholders actually cost

**Measured, 2026-08-17**, and the gap is worth knowing before anyone sizes a test
against it. The reference width above is **4 bytes**: a stream's extent list and an
object's stream list hold node-local references, and the ~100 byte record itself
lives once in a table those references point into.

| List | Budget per entry | Today | 2^32 entries, today |
|---|---|---|---|
| An SN stream's extents | 4 B | **80 B** — 64 B inlined plus a 16 B instance list | 344 GB |
| A DN object's streams | 4 B | **56 B**, inlined | 241 GB |

⚠️ **40 B until 2026-08-20**, when the DN's stream record took a creation second and a
stream's sizes (§17.25.1). Four fields for the space of two, since `records` stopped being an
`Option<u64>` in the same change — but it is still 16 bytes on a list this table exists to
warn about, and **it moved the 2^32 figure from 172 GB to 241 GB.** The size test is what
sent this edit here (#9).

⚠️ **Both lists inline the whole record where the design says reference**, so they
cost twenty and fourteen times the budget. That is a property of §14.6's placeholders and
not of the design — but it decides what a large-stream or large-object test can reach
on real hardware, so it is the number to size against until the segmented array and
the B-tree land. At 4 bytes a 2^32-entry list is 17 GB; at 80 it is a machine's worth
of RAM per stream.

The SN also pays what the table above cannot show: the instance list is a **separate
allocation per extent**, so 2^n extents are 2^n allocations, each rounded up and given
a header. Real RSS is above the computed figure and the packed form has none of it.

---

## 5. The physical decomposition: machine types

The logical levels of §4 do not all live in the same place. Splitting them is a
reliability requirement, not an optimization (§1.1). Three machine types carry
the storage hierarchy itself; §5.9 adds the four that surround it.

| Node | Holds | Replication | Why separate |
|---|---|---|---|
| **DN** — Directory Node | The directory hierarchy and user object metadata, including each object's stream list, and inline records for tiny objects | **Raft ring** | User metadata can exceed the data itself; a distinct workload with a distinct size |
| **SN** — Stream Node | Per stream: the extent list. Per extent: the instance list | **Raft ring** | Must not sit with the bytes it maps |
| **EN** — Extent Node | Extent instances: contiguous blocks of bytes on disk | none — instance placement *is* its redundancy | The bytes themselves; the only tier that scales with raw capacity |

```
client ──▶ DN            resolve path → object metadata → which stream?
       ──▶ SN            which extent? → which instances?
       ──▶ EN            the bytes
```

The asymmetry in the replication column is the heart of the design. **Metadata is
made reliable by consensus; bulk data is made reliable by placement.** Consensus
is the right tool for small mutable state that must be exactly right, and the
wrong tool for petabytes — so DNs and SNs are Raft rings, while an extent's
redundancy comes from having several independently-placed instances (§4.3) and,
once sealed, erasure coding. Both mechanisms nonetheless need members placed in
independently-failing domains, which is why §5.6 serves both.

### 5.1 DNs — Directory Nodes

As in GFS, user objects live in a **directory hierarchy**, and DNs track the
directories as well as the objects.

The critical sizing fact: **user metadata cannot be RAM-resident by default.**
Because enormous numbers of tiny objects are expected, and every object carries
identity, path, times, flavor, framing, counts, byte totals, an ACL reference,
and a stream list — well over a hundred bytes before any records — **the
metadata can be larger than the data it describes.** For a 30-byte object it is
larger by several times.

So DN state is **disk-backed, loaded and cached in RAM on demand**. This is the
opposite of the SN arrangement below, and the difference is not incidental: SN
state is bounded per stream by construction, while DN state grows with the
object *count*, which nothing bounds.

DN state is a large, sorted, key-addressed collection that must be paged from
disk and cached — which is exactly the keyed object of §3. **It is therefore
stored in DeLawson keyed objects, with a bootstrap root outside.** See §5.5.

⚠️ The directory hierarchy brings semantics only partly designed: path
resolution and rename are addressed by the key choice in §5.5.4, and listing a
directory with a billion entries by the virtual directories of §5.1.2, but
permissions and quotas are not. Billing (§12) also attaches naturally to
directories and accounts rather than to bare objects.

#### 5.1.1 Aliases: another tenant's directory inside your tree

**A DN has aliases** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17). Given the privilege to do it, you can attach
another tenant's directory into your own tree, and it appears as if it were yours. What it is
not is a copy or a transfer of ownership:

- **The data has one official owner**, who is the only party that may write or delete it.
- **An alias is read-only**, always, however the aliasing tenant's own permissions read.

That asymmetry is what makes aliases cheap, and several hard questions fall out of it rather
than having to be answered:

| Question | Answer, because an alias is a read-only view |
|---|---|
| Does an alias pin storage? | **No.** It is not a counted reference (§4.6.6), so it cannot appear in any refcount |
| What happens when the owner deletes? | **The alias dangles**, which is the owner's right — deletion is theirs |
| Who pays? | **The owner.** Nothing aliased counts against the reader's quota |
| Whose ACL governs a read? | The **owner's**, checked at the target; the alias only says the reader may look |

⚠️ **The read-only row is superseded by §5.1.1.1a**: writable aliases are allowed, which Bob wants for many
workers sharing one object while each keeps private scratch — and which turns out to be what lets the tenant
stay the unit of trust (§16.145). Read-only survives as the sensible **default** for a grant, not as a rule.

⚠️ **An alias is the one directory reference that needs a name bigger than a ring.** §4.6's
rule is that nothing in the data plane carries a cluster-wide name — every reference is
node-local, an index into a population its holder knows. An alias breaks that by construction,
because it points at a directory another ring owns. So it is not a `StreamId` or an object
reference; it is a distinct kind of entry carrying a global target, and the DN has to treat it
as one.

It leaves open **what a reader sees during the owner's writes**, since an alias reads live
data rather than a snapshot. Cycles are handled by §5.1.1.1.

##### 5.1.1.1 No alias may point into a tree that contains aliases

⚠️ **Superseded by §5.1.1.1a** (Bob, 2026-08-19): cycles are now *allowed*, bounded by cycle detection
on traversal, and the machinery below — the two bits, the sweep, the upward walk, the move rules — goes
with the rule. **Kept because the reasoning is what §5.1.1.1a had to answer**, and because the
asymmetric-error argument about greedy-set-lazy-clear is worth keeping wherever a bit like it reappears.

A tree with aliases in it is a graph, so listing, recursive delete, quota walks, the §4.6.6.2
scrub and §71's sweep all have to cope with cycles — unless cycles are impossible. **They are
forbidden by construction** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17): *an alias may not point at a directory
whose subtree contains an alias.*

**That is enough, and here is why.** Under the rule, an aliased directory's subtree contains no
aliases, so the only things reachable from an alias target are ordinary directories and
objects: reachability from a target is exactly its subtree, and a subtree of a tree has no
cycle. There is no traversal to bound and no visited set to carry.

**Enforcing it takes two checks, not one**, because the rule is a property that has to survive
later edits as well as hold at creation.

| Check, when creating an alias at *P* pointing at *D* | Cost |
|---|---|
| **(a)** No ancestor of *P* is itself aliased | walk up from *P*, O(depth) reads of a per-directory count of inbound aliases |
| **(b)** *D*'s subtree contains no alias | O(1), against a per-directory **bit** meaning "an alias is somewhere beneath me" |

(b) is the rule as stated. ⚠️ **(a) is what keeps it true afterwards** — without it, someone
adds an alias *inside* an already-aliased subtree and (b)'s guarantee for the older alias
quietly stops holding. (a) needs no maintenance at all: it reads a bit in each
directory on the way up, and depth is small.

**"Beneath me" is a boolean, greedily set and lazily cleared** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17) —
not a count. Nothing ever asks *how many* aliases are beneath a directory; (b) asks only
whether there are any. So:

- **Setting** walks up from the new alias's parent and **stops at the first ancestor already
  set**, because every ancestor of a set directory is set. The walk therefore only ever climbs
  through clear bits, and **the root is written once — for the first alias in the cluster**,
  not on every creation. Which is what stops alias creation from being a way to DOS the root.
- **Clearing** is done only by a sweep that has established there is no alias beneath.

⚠️ **The two errors are not symmetric, which is §4.6.6.2's rule again.** A bit left set refuses
an alias that would have been legal; a bit cleared wrongly permits an alias into a tree that
has one, which is the cycle this section exists to prevent. Greedy-set-lazy-clear puts every
error on the safe side, and a boolean cannot drift the dangerous way at all: it is never
lowered except by proof, where a count can be driven low by one missed decrement.

**Why this is a bit and §4.6.6's refcounts are numbers** is worth being explicit about, since
they look like the same problem. It is **how urgent the zero is**. Reaching zero references
must free storage promptly, and making every delete wait for a sweep would leave a cluster's
worth of space uncollected — so that one pays for a real count. Nobody is waiting to alias a
tree they just cleared, so this one does not.

So a directory carries **two bits' worth of alias state**: aliases beneath me, and aliases
pointing at me. Neither is a number.

**Moving a directory is a create and a delete of the same shape.** Moving a subtree that
contains aliases sets its new ancestors eagerly, by the same stop-at-the-first-set walk, and
leaves the old chain to the sweep — and a move that would place an aliased directory under
another aliased directory is refused by check (a).

##### 5.1.1.1a Cycles are allowed, and the canonical path is what counts

**The rule set** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-19), replacing §5.1.1.1's prohibition:

| | |
|---|---|
| **cycles of aliases** | **allowed** |
| every object has a **canonical path** | the one with no aliases in it |
| **writable aliases** | allowed |
| **recursive delete** — a type of write | traverses, and **stops at cycle detection** |
| **recursive directory listing** | traverses, and **stops at cycle detection** |
| **§4.6.6.2's scrub** | **only pays attention to canonical paths** |
| **billing** | leaning to **canonical paths only** — which still count several streams referencing one extent and several objects referencing one stream, but do not count an alias as a new set of references |

**One idea organizes all of it, and it is worth stating on its own:**

> **Ownership is a tree; reachability is a graph.** Aliases add ways to *reach* an object and change
> nothing about what *owns* it — so everything structural runs on the tree, and only traversal has to
> cope with the graph.

⚠️ **That is why forbidding cycles was never necessary.** §5.1.1.1 forbade nesting so that five
traversals would not meet one; the rule set above lets them exist and gives each traversal the right
answer instead — the two that follow the user's view bound themselves, and the two that account for
things never leave the tree.

##### The canonical path exists and is unique, which is what makes this work

**Every object has exactly one.** An object sits in exactly one directory, and a directory sits in
exactly one parent, so the alias-free path is its parent's canonical path plus its name — unique by
induction, and it exists because the ownership hierarchy is rooted.

**And no canonical path can be part of a cycle**, since a cycle needs an alias and a canonical path has
none. So the structure everything structural depends on is a **tree**, whatever the alias graph does
above it.

##### Detecting the cycle: the aliases on the path so far

**Keep a list of the aliases traversed on the current path and check a new one against it before
recursing** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-19).

Ordinary depth-first detection, and the **path** set rather than a global visited set is the right thing:
a cycle is re-entering something you are already inside. ⚠️ **It is exact in both directions**, which
neither alternative is:

| | Refuses legal structures | Permits a cycle |
|---|---|---|
| a **depth cap** (symlink `ELOOP`) | **yes** — a legitimate deep chain | no, by refusing depth |
| **levels**, aliases pointing strictly downward | **yes** — anything the declared order did not foresee | no |
| **the path set** | **no** | **no** |

⚠️ **And §5.1.1.1 had the costs the wrong way round.** Its argument for forbidding nesting was that
*"there is no traversal to bound and no visited set to carry."* The set is a handful of entries on a
stack, held per traversal and stored nowhere. **The rule it justified costs two bits per directory, a
greedy-set-lazy-clear discipline, a sweep to clear them, an upward walk on every alias creation, and
special handling for moves — all of which the new rules delete.**

**A cycle also leaks nothing**, which removes the last worry: an alias is not a counted reference, so a
loop of them holds no storage and keeps nothing alive.

##### 5.1.1.1b Prior art: the split is Unix's, and the accounting is AFS's

**§5.1.1.1a's design is the mainstream answer**, worth establishing because the rule set looks permissive
next to what it replaced.

⚠️ **The tree/graph split is exactly Unix's hard-link/symlink split**, and Unix drew the line in the same
place for the same reason:

| | Counted? | Cycles | DeLawson's equivalent |
|---|---|---|---|
| **hard link** | yes, an inode refcount | **impossible** — forbidden to directories, precisely because they would make the namespace a graph and break `..`, `fsck` and recursive delete | a shared **stream or extent** (§4.6.1), counted by §4.6.6 |
| **symlink** | **no** | **allowed**, bounded at resolution | an **alias** |

**So "ownership is a tree, reachability is a graph" is the rule Unix already lives by** — and forbidding
hard links to directories was the same instinct §5.1.1.1 had, correctly applied to *references* and
wrongly extended to *views*. **The canonical path also has a standard name**: POSIX `realpath()` is
exactly "resolve every symlink and give me the alias-free path".

##### Accounting: AFS charged the volume, not the mount point

**AFS mounts volumes into a namespace and charges quota to the volume**, so mounting one elsewhere does
not move who pays. That is §5.1.1.1a's canonical-path billing in different words, from a system that ran
at scale for decades — a volume is the owning tree, a mount point is the alias.

⚠️ **The sharper comparison is Tahoe-LAFS, because it shows what DeLawson avoided.** Tahoe's directories
are capabilities embeddable in one another, so its cycles are in the **reference** graph — and refcounts
cannot collect a cycle, so Tahoe uses **leases with expiry** instead. **DeLawson keeps refcounts precisely
because its cycles are confined to the view graph**, which is what "an alias is not a counted reference"
buys. The load-bearing consequence of the decomposition, demonstrated by a system that paid the other way.

##### The one genuinely different idea, and why it does not fit

**A per-viewer mount table**: Plan 9 builds a namespace per process from binds, and HDFS's ViewFs does the
same with a client-side mount table mapping paths to namenodes. **Cycles become impossible by
construction**, because each viewer's table is flat and finite rather than nested.

⚠️ **It fails the requirement directly.** A flat table means each worker names the shared foundation
itself — `/shared → gorilla:/`, `/foundation → other:/` — so **every worker's table repeats every
entry**, which is *"that shouldn't be duplicated per worker"* exactly. **Nesting is what stops the
duplication and a flat table is what forbids nesting**; they cannot both be had.

**Two more that do not transfer**, recorded so nobody re-derives them:

- **Content-addressed pinning** (git submodules): a cycle would need something containing the hash of a
  thing containing its own hash, so cycles are impossible. It works because a submodule names an
  *immutable version*, and an alias is a live view.
- **No hierarchy at all** (S3, GCS): cross-account access is policy plus roles, with no mounts to alias.
  A data point about necessity rather than an option, since §5.1 has a real hierarchy.

##### Two things worth borrowing

- **A depth cap *underneath* the path set.** Unix has `ELOOP` **as well as** visited sets in tools,
  because a tool that forgets its set should still terminate. It costs nothing when the set works and
  turns a hang into an error when a traversal is written wrongly — §17.12.1's structural instinct applied
  to a backstop.
- ⚠️ **`realpath` as a user-visible operation.** If canonical paths decide who is charged and what the
  scrub examines, then *"what is the canonical path of this"* is a question with consequences. POSIX
  exposes it; DeLawson probably should (§16.148).

##### 5.1.1.2 Aliases are why a cross-ring clone may copy

§4.6.6.1 left open what to do about a stream referenced from two DN rings, which has no single
place to keep its count of referring objects. **Settled: a cross-ring clone copies rather than
shares** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17).

That looks expensive — §4.6.1 says clone's whole point is costing metadata rather than data,
and copying gives that up. It is affordable because **aliases take the common case away.** The
usual reason to want another ring's data in your tree is to *read* it, and an alias does that
for nothing. What is left for a copying clone is the case where you genuinely want your own
writable, independently-owned duplicate — and for that, copying is not a workaround but the
correct semantics.

So the sharing rule ends up simple: **share inside a ring, copy across one, alias when reading
is all you wanted.**

##### 5.1.1.3 Whether an alias may be writable, and what the read-only rule was carrying

⚠️ **§5.1.1 asserts an alias is read-only always, and that is stronger than what is needed** (Asserted,
Bob, 2026-08-19): *"I know they need to be able to be read-only, but I don't immediately see a problem
with allowing them to be writable as well."*

**The use case is specific**: splitting one tenant into several that can all write *almost* the same
things. **Many workers on a gorilla, each with its own private scratch space** — shared write access to
the big thing, private write access to their own.

##### The strongest argument for it comes from somewhere else entirely

**Writable aliases are what let the tenant stay the unit of trust**, and that matters because
§9.1.3.5's certificate binds the tenant:

| The gorilla-plus-scratch case, built as | The boundary between workers is | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| **one tenant**, per-principal directory ACLs (§5.9.1a) | **inside** a tenant | §16.145's assumption breaks, so the certificate must bind a **principal** — and §8.1.1a-10's scheduler can no longer mint once and hand hints to many vertices |
| **several tenants**, writable aliases onto the shared thing | **between** tenants | the assumption holds, and the scheduler case survives |

So this is not only a convenience. ⚠️ **Without writable aliases, the first serious multi-worker
workload forces an intra-tenant boundary, and that boundary is what §16.145 says would cost the hint
design its coarse binding.** Two features that look unrelated are the same decision seen twice.

##### Writable means writable, and delete comes with it

⚠️ **A draft of this section proposed the narrower change — appendable but not deletable — and that is not
what is meant.** Bob counts **recursive delete as a type of write** (§5.1.1.1a), so a writable alias
carries deletion too.

**Which puts a hazard in plain sight**: a recursive delete on a worker's own tree would reach through its
alias and delete the shared project. That is not what anyone wants, and **the traversal rule is not what
prevents it** — cycle detection bounds termination, not authority.

**What prevents it is the alias's own grant.** §5.9.1a's intersection already governs: an operation
through an alias must be permitted by *both* the alias's grant and the owner's ACL. So an alias granting
append-only refuses the recursive delete, and one granting delete permits it because somebody said so.

⚠️ **So the vocabulary of a grant becomes load-bearing** where it was not before — read, append, write,
delete are now distinctions an alias has to be able to express, and **read-only remains the right
default** (§16.146). Bob's original instinct survives as a default rather than as a rule, which is
usually where a too-strong rule should end up.

##### The four answers §5.1.1 derived from read-only, re-examined

| Question | Under an appendable alias |
|---|---|
| Does it pin storage? | **Unchanged.** Still not a counted reference (§4.6.6), and an append lands in the *owner's* tree where the owner's counts already cover it |
| What happens when the owner deletes? | ⚠️ **Sharper than before.** The alias dangled and took someone else's data with it; now it takes **the worker's own output** |
| Who pays? | ⚠️ **The real cost — see below** |
| Whose ACL governs? | **Unchanged.** The owner's, checked at the target, intersected with the alias's grant (§5.9.1a's `ALIAS-READS-INTERSECT` extends to writes unchanged) |

**Billing is well defined, and an earlier draft of this paragraph said otherwise.** It claimed §12.6.3
could not attribute a write made through an alias. **It can**: §5.1.1.1a settles that billing counts
**canonical paths only**, and data written through an alias sits under the owner's canonical path — so it
bills to the owner, which is the same answer §5.1.1 already gave.

⚠️ **What is open is whether that is the right *policy*, not whether it computes.** Granting write access
through an alias is granting spend on your own quota, and that is a coherent thing to mean — it is what
lending a credit card means. The alternative attributes to the writer, which needs an alias to become
something §12 counts and gives up the property that makes an alias free (§16.146).

##### And §5.1.1.2's rule survives, with a third clause

A writable alias is **not** a substitute for the copying clone. §5.1.1.2 keeps copying for *"your own
writable, independently-owned duplicate"*; this adds **shared-writable, single-owner**, which is a
distinct semantic rather than a cheaper version of that one. Nor does it reopen §4.6.6.1's refcount
problem, since it creates no reference.

##### ⚠️ The alternative worth pricing: invert the alias

**The gorilla case may not need writable aliases at all**, and the alternative is faster:

> Each worker **owns** its scratch and appends there — private, uncontended. The gorilla's owner holds a
> **read-only** alias onto each worker's scratch and **concatenates** (§8.6.1).

That is §8.6's answer to this exact workload, and it gets §8.6.1's parallel bandwidth instead of
§8.1.1a-8's **~200 MB/s per-object ceiling**, which is one disk's worth because one extent is open. **The
shared-write version runs straight into that ceiling**, and §1.0's motivating case — many writers into
one object — is precisely why §8.6 exists.

| | Bandwidth | Visibility |
|---|---|---|
| **writable aliases**, all appending to the gorilla | one open extent, so ~200 MB/s (§8.1.1a-8) | **immediate** |
| **inverted**: private scratch, owner concatenates (§8.6.1) | parallel across workers | **at the concat** |

**So the question is whether the gorilla needs live shared appends or eventual assembly.** If eventual,
the inversion serves it with mechanisms that already exist — read-only aliases and #84's seal, then
concat — and is faster. If visibility must be immediate, writable aliases are the answer and the
throughput ceiling is the price, which is §8.6.2's trilemma rather than anything new.

#### 5.1.2 Virtual directories

**User directories vary from empty to many millions of children, and that does not scale**
(Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17). Nothing about a user's naming has to be balanced, so a directory is
the wrong unit for anything the DN has to size — statistics, pagination, splitting, placement. A
**virtual directory** is the unit that is: a bounded piece of the name space that the DN
maintains, sized by the data rather than by the user.

Two forms were considered, and **the prefix form is chosen** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17):

| Form | A virtual directory is | Boundaries |
|---|---|---|
| start-to-end | an arbitrary lexicographic range | chosen — they can sit anywhere |
| **prefix** | a prefix of the name space, **not required to end at a `/`** | drawn from a fixed lattice |

So `a/b/c/dingo` might fall in the virtual directory `a/b/c/di`. Its advantage is being **purely
nested** within the directory structure: splitting a prefix *P* yields the predetermined children
*P*+*c*, so any two virtual directories are either nested or disjoint. There is no policy decision
at split time, no way for repeated splitting and merging to leave boundaries in awkward places, and
combining several of them to describe an actual directory is a sum rather than a reconciliation.

⚠️ **The scale varies by at least 256x**, because splitting at a byte boundary multiplies the
count by the alphabet — likely 16 to 65536 children (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17). Reasoned here: the
radix is a free parameter and only *bytes* make 256 natural. Any **fixed** radix keeps boundaries
predetermined, so splitting on a nibble would give 16x variance for one more level of depth. Worth
measuring the real byte distribution per depth before fixing it, since path names use perhaps 40 of
the 256 values and use them very unevenly.

⚠️ **And skew, not variance, is the failure mode.** The 256x figure assumes the discriminating byte
discriminates. Real sibling names share long prefixes — `part-000000001`, `2026-08-17T…` — so a
split at the next position can leave almost everything in one child. **A virtual directory's prefix
must therefore be allowed to be any length**, so a split jumps straight to the first position where
names actually differ. That is a radix tree with path compression rather than a fixed-depth trie,
and it is a requirement rather than an optimization: Bob's billion-children case is exactly the
generated-name shape that defeats the uncompressed version.

##### 5.1.2.1 Splitting and merging rename nothing

**Virtual directories split and merge** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17): insert a billion children into
a user directory and they split as the children arrive; delete them all and they merge back. So
boundaries do move — the value of the prefix form is not that they are fixed.

**What the prefix form gives instead is that a virtual directory's name is derived, not allocated.**
Its name *is* its prefix. So a split and a merge rename nothing and renumber nothing, and no stale
name is left behind for anyone to hold. The contrast that makes this concrete is the range merge of
§5.11: two ranges have to renumber `StreamId`s when they merge, precisely because those ids were
handed out independently by each side. A virtual directory's contents are named by user keys, so
there is no id space to reconcile — children collapse into their parent and that is the whole
operation.

⚠️ **The cycle needs hysteresis.** Split at *N* and merge below *N*/2 or lower; splitting and
merging at one threshold makes a workload hovering there thrash, and Bob's insert-a-billion-then-
delete-them-all pattern crosses it twice.

##### 5.1.2.2 A directory is derived, not stored

**The virtual directory tree may be coarser than the user directory tree** (Asserted, Bob,
2026-08-17). One virtual directory may span many actual directories; the requirement is not
containment but that **the user directory tree can be derived from it**.

That is what makes the pathological shape affordable. A tree of `a/a/a/a/a`, `a/a/a/a/b`,
`a/a/a/b/a` … is millions of directories with two children each, and giving each of them a record
is precisely the scaling problem this section exists to avoid. Deriving them costs nothing, because
**the tree structure is already in the names**: the `/`s say what the directories are.

So the rule is: **a directory needs a stored record only when it carries something not derivable
from its children's names.** In practice that is an annotation, or anything the directory holds in
its own right — permissions, quota, owner, timestamps.

**Listing then becomes a prefix scan that skips whole subtrees**, which is exactly S3's `prefix`
plus `delimiter=/` — public prior art for both the semantics and the fact that they scale, from a
store that also has no real directories. ⚠️ **It puts a hard requirement on the on-disk index of
§4.4.0**: listing the children of `a/a/a/` must not scan every descendant, which for two children
and a billion descendants is catastrophic. The index needs **seek-to-successor-of-a-prefix** —
having seen `a/a/a/a/`, jump past everything beneath it to the next distinct child. That constrains
the node format, so it belongs to that index's design rather than to whoever writes listing.

##### 5.1.2.3 Annotations are hidden children, and the marker is `_`

**A user's annotation of a directory has to be preserved** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17) — a
directory marked for georep, or aliased (§5.1.1), and others in future. Deleting such a directory
because it became empty loses information the user put there.

⚠️ **And an annotated directory has to be a virtual-directory boundary, because annotations are
inherited.** Georep or an alias applies to everything beneath, so a virtual directory straddling
that path would hold children with two different answers. The prefix form satisfies this by
construction — every directory path is itself a prefix, so forcing a cut there selects a member of
the lattice rather than inventing one. A start-end scheme would need a separate list of forced
boundaries maintained beside the data. Annotating a directory therefore *splits* its virtual
