directory, and un-annotating merely permits a later merge; neither renames anything.

**The annotations are stored as hidden children** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17), which is close to
forced: once directories are derived rather than stored, there is nowhere else to put them. One
mechanism — a name and a record — and three things follow for free:

- **emptiness solves itself**, since the directory has a child;
- **deletion solves itself**, since removing the last annotation correctly ends the directory;
- **a new kind of annotation costs a name, not a schema change** — quota, retention and ACLs later
  are more children rather than more fields.

**The marker is `_`** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17). It has to be **printable**, because a user
asking to see hidden things must be able to read the names back and type them; and `.` is already
overused. There is no standard here — the Unix leading `.` is a convention in `ls` and the shells
rather than anything a filesystem enforces, and the Hadoop ecosystem hides `_` and `.` when
enumerating inputs — so the choice is between conventions, not against one.

⚠️ **Hidden must mean omitted from a default listing, never absent.** This is what makes `_`
*preserve* Hadoop's semantics rather than collide with them (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17): `_SUCCESS`
and `_temporary` are already invisible as data to the tools that write them, so hiding them here
gives them the treatment they already expect. But those tools then **test for `_SUCCESS` by exact
name** to check job completion, so a point lookup, a `stat`, and an explicit show-hidden listing
must all still find it.

| Design | A user writing `_SUCCESS` |
|---|---|
| a **reserved** prefix | ⚠️ refused — Spark cannot write it, outright breakage |
| **hidden but writable** | legal, hidden by default, found by name — and Hadoop's intent is preserved |

**DeLawson's own annotations therefore need a reserved sub-prefix rather than a list of reserved
names.** Reserving exactly `_georep`, `_alias` and so on means the reserved set grows with every
annotation kind added, and each addition breaks whichever user already used that name. Reserving
one component — `_delawson/…` — is fixed forever and leaves the rest of the `_` space to users.

**Which repairs the objection to Hadoop's version rather than repeating it.** The complaint against
`_` and `.` in Hadoop is that a *display* convention was given *semantic* force, so a user's
legitimate `.config` silently disappears from a read. Keeping `_` presentational, with the
semantics confined to a narrower reserved sub-prefix, means nothing a user writes ever changes
meaning — only whether it shows up by default.

**So the emptiness test is "no children at all", not "no visible children".** A directory holding
only `_SUCCESS` must not be reclaimed. ⚠️ What remains open is the truly empty case: whether
`make-directory` on its own leaves anything behind, or whether a directory exists exactly when
something is under it. The DN serves `MakeDirectory` and `RemoveDirectory`, so the operations exist
and the semantics have to be chosen rather than discovered.

**One thing this buys elsewhere.** §5.11's range splits want to fall at tenant or directory
boundaries, so that a split does not cut through a set of objects that get concatenated together.
Virtual directory boundaries are a ready-made supply of cuts already aligned with the name
hierarchy, so a range split that lands on one costs nothing extra.

### 5.2 SNs — Stream Nodes

An SN holds, for each stream assigned to it, the **extent list**, and for each
of those extents, the **instance list** — where the copies are.

These two are on the same node type deliberately: there is no known use case
that demands the extent-list-per-stream and the instance-list-per-extent live
on different machines, and keeping them together makes a lookup one hop instead
of two.

What must *not* be co-located is either of them with the instances themselves.
That separation is the reliability requirement of §1.1: an EN failure destroys
bytes, and the map to the surviving copies has to outlive it.

A stream's ceiling is what one SN ring member can hold (§14.1). A maximal object
therefore spreads its streams over many SNs — necessarily, since no single
machine can hold them all.

**An SN is a Raft ring, not a machine** — and only three of its members hold the
extent list in RAM at all (§5.7). Losing one member costs capacity headroom, not
availability; ring members are placed in independently-failing domains by §5.6,
for the same reason extent instances are.

Note what this means for §14.1: a materialized member holds the *whole* extent
list, so the stream ceiling is set by the share of one machine's RAM that this
ring gets — and since a machine hosts many rings (§5.8), that share is a small
fraction, not the whole.

**Self-describing extents remain worth having as a backstop.** Each instance
should carry a header with its extent id, stream id, starting record number, and
byte totals, so that an extent list is reconstructible by scanning ENs. With a
Raft ring this is no longer the primary durability mechanism — it is the recovery
path for losing a whole ring at once, which is exactly the correlated failure
§5.6 exists to make unlikely but cannot make impossible. It also gives an
independent check on the ring's state, which matters most for the metadata tier
(§5.5.3).

### 5.3 ENs — Extent Nodes

ENs store extent instances and nothing else: a contiguous block of compressed,
encrypted bytes per instance. They are the only tier that scales with raw
capacity, and the only tier that erasure coding and repair touch.

Because ENs hold ciphertext (§7), repair, re-encoding, and scrubbing all run
without key access.

#### 5.3.1 SNs place on disks, not on ENs

**An SN chooses a disk, not a machine.** It tracks which instances sit on each disk
of each EN it can reach, so an instance reference names `(EN, disk, slot)` rather
than `(EN, offset)`.

That costs nothing, because the disk byte is paid for by the locator shrinking. A
slot index within one disk needs 3 bytes where a byte offset within a whole EN
needed 4:

| Component | Width | Covers |
|---|---|---|
| local EN index | 2 B | ~20,000 ENs in the fan-out set (§5.10) |
| disk index | 1 B | 256 disks — a 1 PB EN of 20 TB disks has 50 |
| slot index | 3 B | 16.7 × 10^6 slots — a 100 TB disk holds 3.0 × 10^6 extents |
| **Instance reference** | **6 B** | unchanged from the previous per-EN encoding |

**The cost target sets the disk count.** Per §1.2, server hardware must be ≤5% of an
EN's total cost. With *S* the server cost and *D* a disk's lifetime cost — the drive
plus its share of electricity and rent — that requires:

> *S* / (*S* + *nD*) ≤ 0.05, i.e. **n ≥ 19·(S/D)**

| *S/D* — server cost in disk-equivalents | Disks required | Within a 1-byte index? |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | 57 | yes |
| 6 | 114 | yes |
| 8 | 152 | yes |
| 13 | 247 | barely |
| 20 | 380 | **no** |

So "tens or hundreds" is right, and which end depends entirely on how a bare storage
server prices against a disk. A cheap server against expensive disks lands in the
tens; anything like a conventional server needs well over a hundred.

A **third bound** comes from the NIC: 150 disks at 200 MB/s is 30 GB/s against 25 GB/s for
2 × 100 GbE, so past ~125 disks a sequential scan is network-limited rather than disk-limited
(§5.12.1). All three bounds — cost from below, disk index from above, NIC from above — land in the
same neighbourhood, which is mild corroboration that a hundred-and-something is the right answer.

**How hard this bites depends on the overhead target**, which §1.2 holds loosely. For
an overhead fraction *f*, the requirement is *n* ≥ ((1−*f*)/*f*)·(*S/D*), and a 1-byte
disk index caps *n* at 256:

| Overhead *f* | Disks needed | Largest *S/D* a 1-byte index allows |
|---|---|---|
| 5% | 19 × (*S/D*) | 13.5 |
| 10% | 9 × (*S/D*) | 28.4 |
| 15% | 5.7 × (*S/D*) | 45.2 |

So this does couple a metadata format decision to the business model — but softly.
At a strict 5% a bare server may cost at most ~13 disk-equivalents before 1 byte of
disk index stops sufficing; letting overhead drift to 10% doubles that headroom to
~28, which is comfortably beyond any plausible server-to-disk ratio. **The 1-byte
index is safe unless both the 5% target is held strictly and servers are expensive
relative to disks.** Worth watching rather than worrying about.

Why bother tracking disks at all: **a disk is the innermost failure domain.** One
disk dying should cost the instances on that disk and nothing else. Without
per-disk tracking, a single failed disk is indistinguishable from a failed EN, and
repair would rebuild the machine's whole complement instead of one disk's worth.
Per-disk placement also stops two instances of one extent landing on two disks of
the same machine, which would satisfy a naive "different disk" rule while sharing a
power supply, a controller, and a kernel.

### 5.4 Three spreading requirements, of two kinds

| Requirement | Level | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Instances of one extent on ENs in distinct failure domains | extent → instances | Reliability and availability (§1.1) |
| Members of one Raft ring in distinct failure domains | SN and DN rings | A ring whose members fail together is not a ring |
| Streams of one object on distinct SNs | object → streams | Capacity: no machine holds them all |

The first two are the same problem — place *n* things so they fail
independently — and are solved by one mechanism, §5.6. The third is arithmetic,
not reliability, and conflating it with the others would be a mistake: a
placement policy good for correlated-loss avoidance is not automatically good
for spreading capacity.

### 5.5 The DN tier is self-hosted

**Decided: DN metadata lives in DeLawson keyed objects, with a bootstrap root
outside DeLawson.** Building a separate store for it would duplicate
compaction, replication, erasure coding, compression, and encryption — for a
workload the keyed object already is.

#### 5.5.1 The resolution chain has fixed depth

Self-hosting invites infinite regress: an object's metadata is in an object,
whose metadata is in an object. It must terminate at a fixed, small depth.

| Level | What | Where its own locator lives |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | **Bootstrap root** — in **DN0's Raft persistent state** | the ring's own consensus storage, not DeLawson |
| 1 | **Partition map** — a keyed object: key range → metadata object | level 0 |
| 2 | **Metadata objects** — keyed objects: object key → object metadata | level 1 |
| 3 | **User objects** | level 2 |

Three hops, not recursion. Same shape, and for the same reason, as BigTable's Chubby file →
root tablet → METADATA tablets → user tablets.

**The root needs no new component.** Every ring is a Raft ring (§5.7), and **ring state is made
persistent by Raft — a log and snapshots on local disks — not by DeLawson.** So a
non-self-hosted durable store already exists in the system, and the bootstrap root is simply
distinguished content in the Raft state of a distinguished DN ring, **DN0**. Nothing has to be
invented, deployed, or operated separately.

Its content is what a DN would otherwise supply for level 1: the partition map's object id, its
stream list (stream ids plus SN locations), its totals, and its key identifier. The partition
map is small — a million partitions at ~300 B is ~300 MB, comfortably one stream — so **the root
is a few kilobytes and changes almost never**, which is trivial for a Raft snapshot to carry.

This is what dissolves the recursion, and it is the piece Colossus's public description leaves
unexplained (§1.4.4). The layering is three deep and acyclic:

| Layer | Made durable by |
|---|---|
| DN metadata, user objects | DeLawson objects |
| Object locators — the bootstrap root | **DN0's Raft state** |
| Raft state | local disks, replicated across ring members |

#### 5.5.1.1 Cold start has a definite order

Because ring state is itself encrypted at rest (§5.9.1), the sequence matters, and it is
acyclic only because KS is keyed differently from everything else:

| Step | What comes up | Unlocked by |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **KS ring** | operator secrets plus hardware devices (§7.3.2) — the only step needing humans |
| 2 | **DN0 ring** | keys from KS; decrypts its Raft state |
| 3 | The **bootstrap root**, read from DN0's Raft state | — |
| 4 | Partition map → metadata objects → user objects | keys from KS |
| 5 | **SN rings**, loading extent B-trees from their snapshots | keys from KS |
| 6 | **ENs**, reporting disks (§13.1) | no keys needed to serve ciphertext |

KS's own state is encrypted under the human-and-hardware unlocking key rather than under a
DeLawson key, which is precisely what breaks the circle. Everything else can then be keyed from
KS without any structure needing to read itself.

Level 2 is partitioned rather than one global object mainly to bound contention
and blast radius; a single keyed object could hold the whole namespace as far as
capacity goes (§14.3).

#### 5.5.2 Damping the write recursion

The hazard: a user write updates metadata, which is a write to a DeLawson
object, which updates *its* metadata, which cascades. A cascade to the root on
every append would be fatal.

Two dampers exist already, and one problem needs a decision.

- **Extent churn does not propagate at all.** An object's extent list lives on
  its SN, not in DN metadata (§5.2). So a metadata object sealing, splitting, or
  compacting extents never touches the level above it. This is the main damper,
  and it is free — a consequence of putting extent lists on SNs rather than in
  object metadata.
- **Stream growth barely propagates.** Level 1 needs updating only when a level-2
  metadata object gains a *stream* — every ~64 PiB (§14.1). Effectively never.
- **The cascade terminates after one level**, by the rule of §4.5. Writing a
  user object's new record count into DN metadata is an *update* to an existing
  level-2 record. An update is count-preserving (§3), so the level-2 metadata
  object's own record count — the only summary maintained synchronously — does
  not change at all. What does change is its byte totals, and those are lazy by
  §4.5. So the propagation stops: one level up, and no further. The feared
  cascade to the root cannot happen.

- ⚠️ **Write amplification into the metadata tier is a separate problem**, and
  it survives. Even without a cascade, updating DN metadata on every user append
  is one metadata write per data write. The remedy is the same as §4.5's
  treatment of byte totals: keep the authoritative live count on the SN, which
  already maintains it exactly and synchronously for addressing, and let the DN
  copy be a lazily-refreshed cache. Then a steady stream of appends touches no
  DN at all.

  Recommended, not decided — but note the recommendation now rests on write
  amplification alone, not on any risk of unbounded recursion.

Nothing else in DN metadata is volatile: the stream list is append-only, because
a stream's starting record number never changes once assigned (§3).

#### 5.5.3 Circular failure

Self-hosting means a DeLawson outage can prevent recovering DeLawson. Three
requirements follow:

- The **bootstrap root must be durable and available independently** of
  DeLawson — it cannot be stored in the thing it bootstraps.
- **Metadata extents must be identifiable on ENs.** §5.2 already wants
  self-describing instance headers so SN state can be rebuilt by scanning ENs;
  those headers should also carry a flag marking metadata extents, so a
  disaster-recovery scan can rebuild the metadata tier **first**, before anything
  that depends on it.
- **Metadata objects want their own placement policy**: more redundancy, maximal
  spread, and possibly replicas retained rather than erasure-coded (§4.3), since
  metadata reads are frequent, small, and latency-critical in a way bulk data is
  not.

⚠️ The key hierarchy has the same circularity: metadata objects are encrypted
(§7), so their keys must be obtainable without reading metadata. The root must
anchor the key hierarchy, not just the object hierarchy.

#### 5.5.4 What the metadata key should be

| Key | Listing a directory | Renaming a directory | Path resolution |
|---|---|---|---|
| Full path | prefix scan | rewrites every descendant key | one lookup |
| `(parent dir id, name)` | prefix scan on parent id | one entry changes | one lookup per component |

**Recommended: `(parent directory id, name)`.** Renaming a directory with a
billion descendants must not be a billion-record rewrite, and prefix scans still
make listing cheap because keyed objects are sorted. The cost is a lookup per
path component, bounded by path depth and highly cacheable.

⚠️ Not decided.

An earlier draft argued that georeplication escalated this to a requirement, because
failover would re-root a replica's subtree and that rename would be a full-dataset
rewrite under a full-path key. **That argument is withdrawn**: §13.4.5.5 replaces
promotion-by-rename with copy-by-concatenation, which creates new directory entries
rather than renaming existing ones and is equally cheap under either key. The renaming
argument above stands on its own merits and is unaffected.

#### 5.5.5 Two dividends

- **Metadata gets compression, erasure coding, and repair for free.** Object
  metadata is highly repetitive — sibling paths, adjacent timestamps, identical
  flavor and framing — so it should compress several-fold, and it is
  erasure-coded once sealed. This materially shrinks the "metadata can exceed
  data" problem of §14.2: true in logical bytes, much less true in physical ones.
- **Billing metadata becomes measurable** rather than estimated, because it is
  physical bytes in real objects (§12).

#### 5.5.6 There are two roots, and only one of them is the bootstrap root

⚠️ **§5.5.1, §16.1 and §16.2 have been conflating two different root facts**, and separating them
settles both of Bob's expectations at once (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-19):

| Root | Answers | Lives in |
|---|---|---|
| the **object-locator root** — §5.5.1's bootstrap root | *where is the partition map object* | **DN0's Raft state**, as §5.5.1 has it |
| the **topology root** | *what machines exist, what rings they form, what failure domains they sit in, what tenants exist and which ranges they own* | **KS** |

**KS owns the topology root** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-19): tenant ids and ranges, the official list of
machines, and the membership of every ring. §16.2 guessed the bootstrap root would hold the
failure-domain hierarchy; it cannot, and the reason is a circularity rather than a preference.

##### 5.5.6.1 Ring membership cannot live in a ring, and that decides it

**A Raft ring keeps its own membership in its log** — configuration changes are log entries — so a
*running* ring knows who its voters are. But two moments are not covered by that, and both are
ordinary:

- **Forming a ring** needs an initial configuration from somewhere outside it. There is no log to read
  before there is a ring.
- **A member that has lost its disk** needs to be told which ring it belongs to before it can catch up.

⚠️ **And §5.5.1.1's cold start makes DN0 unavailable for this by construction.** DN0's Raft state is
encrypted, KS holds the key, so KS comes up first — step 1 before step 2. Anything DN0 holds is
therefore unreadable at the moment ring membership is needed, **including DN0's own membership.** So
the fact that says which machines form DN0 cannot be inside DN0.

**KS is the only component that is both earlier than every ring and durable outside DeLawson**, which
is the same property §5.5.1.1 already relies on to break the key circle. It needs no new component for
the same reason the bootstrap root needed none — and it is already the registrar (§17.7, #36), so it
already knows which processes are alive and where. The official list is the durable half of something
it half-does.

**Derived, and small.** Nothing here is a capacity question:

| | At 100,000 nodes |
|---|---|
| Machines — id, address, failure-domain path, media classes at ~64 B | **~6 MB** |
| Rings — ~10 per machine (§5.8.1), 7 members at 4 B | **~4 MB** |
| Master keys | ~1 MB per century (§7.3) |
| Tenants and ranges | the largest term, and still megabytes per million tenants |

##### 5.5.6.2 Three tiers of freshness, and the primary is in the fastest

**Something else caches who the current primary of each ring is** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-19), and the
split is the point rather than an optimization:

| Fact | Changes | Home |
|---|---|---|
| **membership** — who may vote | on decommission and repair: minutes to months | **KS**, authoritative |
| **leadership** — who is primary now | on failover, which §16.12 requires to complete **faster than a timeout** | **the ring itself**, in its own consensus state |
| **cached leadership** | whenever the cache is wrong | **whoever is talking to the ring** |

⚠️ **Putting leadership in KS would be the one arrangement that cannot work.** Failover must beat a
timeout (§16.12 makes ring size the lever for exactly this), and routing every failover through a write
to a single distinguished component — then every subsequent read through a hop to it — makes the thing
that must be fastest depend on the thing that must be most careful.

**A stale leadership cache costs a redirect, and that is the whole cost.** This is the fourth instance
of a pattern already load-bearing three times over, which is the strongest argument for it:

| | Authoritative and slow | Operational and fast |
|---|---|---|
| §5.7 | consensus membership | RAM membership |
| §5.6.9 | the persisted placement decision | verification |
| §17.13 | the SN's extent list | the FE's remembered open extent — "losing it costs asks, not correctness" |
| here | KS's membership | the ring's leadership, cached by callers |

**Cited**: this is the ordinary Raft client contract — a follower answers "not the leader" with a hint,
and the client retries — and the same shape as Bigtable's and HBase's client-side location caches.

**Topology reads want caching for the same reason.** §5.6 needs the failure-domain hierarchy on every
placement decision, and §5.6.10 budgets ~22 group placements per second per SN; across a thousand SNs
that would be tens of thousands of reads per second aimed at one component. Since topology changes
almost never, every tier caches it, and **a topology epoch number is what lets a cache notice it is
stale** — carried on messages that already flow, rather than polled.

##### 5.5.6.3 The unlock ceremony must not gate topology, so KS's state splits in two

⚠️ **This is the real cost of the decision, and it has a clean answer.** §7.3.2 has KS unlocked by
operator secrets plus hardware — the only step needing humans. If topology also lives in KS, then after
a power event **nobody could enumerate the machines until a human arrived**, which would put a ceremony
in front of automated recovery.

**The resolution is that topology is not a secret.** Machine lists, ring membership, tenant ids and
ranges are operational facts, not confidential ones — so:

| Half of KS's state | Protected how | Available |
|---|---|---|
| **master keys** | encrypted under the human-and-hardware key (§7.3.2) | after the ceremony |
| **topology and registry** | **signed, not encrypted** | as soon as the process starts |

⚠️ **Signed rather than merely plaintext, because the threat is integrity and not disclosure.** A
forged machine list or failure-domain hierarchy is a placement attack: it would let an attacker make
four instances land in one domain while every rule appeared satisfied (§5.6.8 makes achieved durability
a per-group property computed from placements, so nothing downstream would notice). Confidentiality
buys nothing here; authentication is the whole requirement.

**What this buys is an availability posture worth stating plainly: KS is on the change path, not the
data path.** With KS down, no new keys are issued, no process registers, and no topology changes — but
ENs already cache the SN-master keys they need (§7.3.1) and no read or write consults KS, so a running
cluster keeps serving. That is the right thing for a component that needs a human to start.

##### 5.5.6.4 What would move it

Bob's expectation is that these may move if they are too much for KS or find better homes. Nothing
above suggests capacity is the problem — the state is megabytes and the request rate is low once
everything caches. **Two things would change the answer:**

- ⚠️ **If KS turns out to need a Raft ring of its own** (and §5.5.1.1's step 1 says "KS ring", so it
  probably does), then it has consensus storage and the topology root is simply distinguished content
  in it — exactly the argument §5.5.1 makes for the bootstrap root living in DN0's. That is not a move,
  it is the same answer with the mechanism named.
- **If tenant ranges turn out to be hot**, they belong with the thing that resolves names rather than
  with the thing that holds keys. #75 is already reconsidering how a DN range is named across split and
  move, and if a range becomes a frequently-consulted mapping it is a level-1 fact (§5.5.1's partition
  map) rather than a topology fact. The test is whether it changes with data or with the machine
  inventory.

### 5.6 Failure domains and placement

Reliability (§1.1) requires instances that fail independently. A Raft ring wants
the same thing for a different reason: a ring whose members fail together is not
a ring. **Extent-instance placement and ring-member placement are therefore one
problem**, and one mechanism should serve both.

#### 5.6.1 Slack

To place *n* independent things, use a failure-domain type that has at least
**slack × n** domains. Slack is configurable; the default is **4/3**.

| *n* | Domains required |
|---|---|
| 3 instances | 4 |
| 4 instances | 6 |
| 5-member ring | 7 |
| 7-member ring | 10 |

With exactly *n* domains there is no freedom at all: one domain down — planned
or not — and there is nowhere to put a replacement, so the group stays degraded
until that domain comes back. Slack buys somewhere to re-place, which is what
turns repair from *waiting* into *work*.

#### 5.6.1a What slack is actually for, and why the ratio is 4/3

The paragraph above gives the wrong rationale. **Slack is for making the solve cheap and for preventing
hardware hotspots** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-15) — not for reserving somewhere to re-place.

**The solve cost has a closed form.** Placing the *last* of *k* members into *n* = *s·k* domains, a random
draw hits an unused domain with probability `(n-k)/n = (s-1)/s`, so the expected number of draws is
`s/(s-1)`:

| Slack *s* | Expected draws for the hardest member |
|---|---|
| 1 | infinite — a perfect matching, and one domain down makes it infeasible |
| 5/4 | 5 |
| **4/3** | **4** |
| 3/2 | 3 |

**Derived**, and it is what makes 4/3 principled rather than round: it buys a four-draw expected solve for the
hardest member of a recovery set. At zero slack §5.6.3 is not sampling at all — it is a matching problem with
essentially one solution up to permutation, which goes infeasible the moment a domain is unavailable.

**And it is what gives free-space weighting any power.** With no slack there is no choice to make, so §5.6.3's
weighting is decorative and a full, slow, or degraded domain still gets its share. Slack is the ability to
route *around* a bad domain while still satisfying the rule. That is a balance-and-availability argument, not
a durability-reserve one.

**The ratio has a counter-pressure, which sets the search direction.** Slack cannot be turned up for free,
because domains cannot be manufactured: "4/3 slack" means *do not enforce a rule unless the cluster has 4/3x
the domains the recovery set needs* (§5.6.7). Raising the threshold makes solving cheaper and simultaneously
**turns rules off in mid-size clusters**, weakening independence exactly where it is already thinnest. So the
correct tuning procedure is to start at the smallest slack that solves acceptably and raise only until the
time budget of §5.6.10 is met — never higher. That is the opposite of how a knob like this is usually tuned.

#### 5.6.2 Nested, not orthogonal

Domain types must be **nested** — each a refinement of the one above, forming a
single hierarchy. Cross-cutting, orthogonal domain types are **a bug**.

The cost of getting this wrong, using 3 instances with 4 power domains and 4
software-deployment domains:

| | Where instance 3 may go | Fraction of cluster |
|---|---|---|
| **Orthogonal** (a 4×4 grid) | must differ from both predecessors in power *and* software: 2 powers × 2 softwares = 4 of 16 cells | **1/4** |
| **Nested** (software within power) | satisfying the coarse constraint satisfies the fine one automatically: 2 of 4 power domains | **1/2** |

The general shape: with *d* orthogonal types of *k* domains each, the *i*-th
instance may be placed in `((k−i+1)/k)^d` of the cluster; nested, it is
`(k−i+1)/k` **regardless of d**. For the case above the sequence is
1, 0.75, 0.5 nested against 1, 0.5625, 0.25 orthogonal.

**Orthogonality costs an exponent.** That is not merely inelegant: shrinking the
candidate set slows repair, worsens balance, and can make placement impossible
in a cluster that is already partly degraded — exactly when placement matters
most. Nesting keeps the constraint linear no matter how many domain types are
added, which means new domain types (a new firmware tier, a new network fabric)
can be introduced without compounding cost.

#### 5.6.3 Choosing a disk: weighted random, then reject

Domain independence says where an instance may *not* go. It does not say which of the
survivors to pick, and picking badly fills disks unevenly — which wastes capacity, since
a full disk is unusable even while its neighbours are half empty.

**So placement is proportional to free space.** The mechanism reuses the sync loop that
already exists:

1. The once-a-minute disk-liveness sync (§13.1) also reports **fullness per disk**.
2. A once-a-minute summary builds a **cumulative table of free bytes** over all disks the
   SN can currently reach.
3. To place an instance, pick a **uniformly random byte** in the total free space and
   **binary search** the table for the disk containing it.
4. If the placement rules already exclude that disk's domain, **retry**.

The cost is negligible. An SN reaching 407 ENs of 150 disks tracks ~61,000 disks — a
477 KB table, rebuilt each minute, and 16 comparisons per placement. At *G*=64 it is
~244,000 disks, 1.9 MB, and 18 comparisons.

Retries are few, because the rules only exclude domains already used. With the six domains
slack requires for four instances (§5.6.1):

| Placing instance | Fraction allowed | Expected picks |
|---|---|---|
| 1st | 1.00 | 1.0 |
| 2nd | 0.83 | 1.2 |
| 3rd | 0.67 | 1.5 |
| 4th | 0.50 | 2.0 |

**Rejection sampling is exactly right here, not an approximation.** Sampling from a
free-space-weighted distribution and discarding disallowed draws yields precisely the
free-space-weighted distribution *conditioned on* the allowed set — which is the
distribution wanted. No correction term is needed.

Two further properties worth noting:

- **It is provably optimal, not a heuristic.** Maximizing the time until the *first*
  disk fills means equalizing every disk's time-to-full: with free space *f_i* and write
  rate *r_i*, equal *f_i*/*r_i* under Σ*r_i* = *R* gives *r_i* = *R*·*f_i*/Σ*f_i* — exactly
  proportional to free space, and uniquely so.
- **What converges is exhaustion, not fullness.** Since d*f_i*/d*t* ∝ −*f_i*, free space
  decays exponentially and *ratios are preserved*: a newly added disk stays proportionally
  emptier rather than catching up. All disks approach exhaustion together, which is the
  property worth having — no disk is full while its neighbours have room.
- **It is indifferent to the rule set**, so the same machinery serves erasure coding,
  whose placement rules differ from 4-instance replication (§4.3) — only the rejection
  predicate changes.

⚠️ Weighting and constraints do interact: if one domain is markedly emptier than the rest,
weighted picks concentrate there and are rejected more often. The retry count stays
bounded but rises, and the effect is worst exactly when the cluster is lopsided — after
adding a rack, say. Worth measuring rather than assuming.

#### 5.6.4 The cluster balances itself, at any size

Something falls out of §5.6.3 that is worth stating on its own, because it is the property
that makes the scheme viable at scale: **SNs never coordinate with each other, and the
cluster balances globally anyway.**

Each SN sees a random ~20,000 of the ENs — random, but stratified so its view is spread
evenly across the finest tracked failure domain. It weights placement by the free space it
observes, and that is the whole algorithm. No SN knows another exists.

**The ENs are the communication medium.** When one SN fills the ENs it can see, their free
space falls, so their weight falls in the tables of every *other* SN that shares them.
Those SNs shift elsewhere, which raises pressure on their remaining ENs, which lowers those
weights for a third set of SNs. The adjustment propagates through the overlap graph without
a single message between SNs — the fullness measurement *is* the signal.

**Why it lands on the global optimum.** Because each SN's fan-out is an unbiased sample of
the cluster, its local free-space distribution is an unbiased sample of the global one. An
SN allocating proportionally to its local sample therefore allocates proportionally to
global free space in expectation, and the sum over all SNs is the globally optimal
allocation of §5.6.3 — reached by purely local decisions. This is why the stratification
matters: it is what keeps the sample unbiased across domains, and a clustered or correlated
view would bias the aggregate.

**The algorithm is scale-free.** Per-SN cost is a 477 KB table and 16 comparisons per
placement, and *neither changes when the cluster grows* — an SN's work depends on its
fan-out, not on the fleet. Adding ENs or SNs requires no re-partitioning, no rehashing, and
no global recomputation.

> **The 2^32 node limit is a consequence of identifier width, not of the algorithm.** The
> algorithm itself works arbitrarily large.

And raising that limit is cheap, thanks to the local-reference design of §4.6: global node
ids appear only in the control plane and in the per-SN fan-out tables (78 KB each), never in
the 10^9-entry extent lists, which use 2-byte neighbourhood-local indices. Widening the
global id touches small structures only. **The data plane is already size-agnostic.**

Feedback delay is not a concern. The table is a minute stale at worst, and one SN writing
at 5 GB/s spread over 61,000 disks moves each by ~4.9 MB per minute — 0.000025% of a 20 TB
disk. Weighting is also proportional rather than threshold-based, so there is no edge to
oscillate around.

#### 5.6.5 What nesting costs

**Planned disruptions must be serialized.** Software deployments and large
planned outages cannot run at the same time.

⚠️ The placement arithmetic above is verified; this operational constraint is
asserted from experience and its precise argument should be written out before
anyone relies on it. The mechanism appears to be that nesting collapses every
domain type onto one hierarchy, so "at most one domain intentionally down"
becomes a single global budget shared by every kind of planned work, rather than
one budget per orthogonal dimension.

#### 5.6.6 A concession that is a known defect

⚠️ Orthogonal software-deployment domains may be supported anyway, because that
is how clusters are built today. This is a compatibility concession and a known
defect, not a design choice, and it should be labelled as such wherever it is
configurable — it costs the exponent in §5.6.2.

#### 5.6.7 An unenforceable rule is not enforced, and the minimum cluster is one machine

**The minimum viable cluster size is 1 machine** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-15). If a placement rule cannot find
a domain type with enough domains, **the rule is not enforced.** It does not fail, and it does not block the
write.

- In the degenerate single-machine case, 4-instance reduces to 1-instance and EC's two copies per data extent
  reduce to one.
- As the cluster grows and more domain types acquire enough domains, 4-instance placement and the rules of
  §4.3.3.2e start making use of them, with no migration required.
- Because domains are **nested** (§5.6.2), a rule whose natural domain type is too small degrades to the
  finest nested type that does have enough domains. Orthogonal domains could not express that fallback, which
  is one more instance of §5.6.2's "orthogonal is a bug".
- **All placement rules are enforced independently.** Each is a separate filter, applied or skipped on its own.

**This is the adoption path, not a concession.** §1.0's purpose is an open-source store, and people evaluate
those on one machine before deploying them. A cluster that refused to write until it had 80 failure domains
would never be evaluated at all. An earlier draft of this section argued that placement should fail loudly
rather than degrade; that is wrong for placement rules, and right only for the distinct case in §5.6.10.

**Oscillation causes no churn**, for two reasons that both hold:

1. A placement spread over 80 domains still satisfies the rule vacuously at 79, and still satisfies it on the
   way back to 80. The predicate is monotone in the right direction.
2. More fundamentally, **placement is decided at write time and never revisited** for rule reasons — which is
   the same fact §13.1.2 states as "there is no rebalancing". Nothing moves, so oscillation cannot move it.

#### 5.6.8 Therefore achieved durability is a per-group property, not a cluster property

Because placement is fixed at write time and never revisited, a five-year-old cluster holds extents placed
under many different sets of enforceable rules. **"How durable is my data" cannot be read off the
configuration** — it has to be computed from actual placements.

That is what §13.5's daily job should audit: the *realized* independence of each EC group, not a prediction of
feasibility. It is also the input §4.3.3.2c's simulation actually needs, since a real fleet is a mixture of
independence levels rather than a single one.

**And independence self-heals opportunistically, without a rebalancer.** Extents written during a dip below a
threshold keep their weaker placement, but compaction, media migration (§7.4) and code promotion (§4.3.3.2e)
rewrite extents anyway, and a rewrite places under whatever rules are enforceable *then*. The fleet drifts
toward better independence as a side effect of work it already does. Nobody should later add a rebalancer to
accomplish this.

⚠️ On a single machine with ~100 disks, **disk is a domain type with plenty of domains**, and §5.3.1 already
places on disks rather than ENs with a 1-byte disk field for exactly that reason. So four instances on four
disks of one machine is expressible and protects against the most common failure there is. Collapsing to
1-instance whenever the *EN-level* rule is unenforceable gives that up. The reading taken here is that the
collapse happens when the **finest** type is also exhausted — one disk, or few enough that the rule fails at
disk level too. If the intent is to collapse at the EN level regardless, the reasoning needs recording,
because the difference is 4x in space.

#### 5.6.9 Placement is a solver whose answer is persisted, so the steady state is verification

Placement *is* a constraint solve (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-15) — the earlier claim in this section that it is
merely a sequence of independent filters is wrong. What keeps it cheap is that **the solution is persisted in
the order of the instance list**, so the recurring cost is verification rather than search:

- **Solve once**, when the extent is created or when it converts from 4-instance to EC.
- **Verify** thereafter: rebuild the rules and check they are obeyed, with no attempt to re-derive an ordering.
- **Repair is an incremental single-slot solve** against an already-valid assignment — one filtered
  weighted-random draw per §5.6.3, not a stripe-wide search.

**The rules are little hash tables**, indexed by `ExtentId & (tablesize - 1)`, and verification looks for
collisions. `ExtentId` is dense and system-assigned, so it is already well distributed and no real hash
function is needed. Table sizes follow §4.3.3.2e's thresholds — 8, 32, 256 — so they are stack-allocated,
cache-resident, and verification is O(members) per rule with no sorting and no set allocation.

**Collision-freedom comes from the stored assignment, not from the hashing**, and the arithmetic shows it must:
six members into an 8-slot table are all distinct with probability `8·7·6·5·4·3 / 8^6` = **0.077**, so a random
slot would collide 92% of the time. **Derived.** The mask is how the table is *indexed* cheaply; the ordering
is what makes it collision-free.

**Two invariants this creates.**

**The instance list's order is semantic.** The per-extent list of 6-byte references (§5.3.1) carries the
solution in its positions, and position also gives the EC cell role of §4.3.2.3 for free. So the list must
never be sorted, deduplicated, or reordered for lookup speed. That is exactly the kind of locally-harmless
optimization someone applies to a small unsorted array, so it belongs as an assertion next to the type.

**Collision-freedom and slack are different checks.** Verifying no collisions says the current assignment is
valid. It says nothing about whether the next repair will *find* a free slot, which is a count of available
domains, not a collision test. Both are cheap; conflating them produces a fleet that verifies clean right up to
the moment it cannot place a replacement.

#### 5.6.10 Both cadences are guesses gated on measurement, and the two gates are separate

4/3 and the one-minute loop of §13.1 are guesses. The real test is to implement and time it, with **the cadence
gated on verification speed and the slack gated on solve speed** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-15). The two are
independent: verification is O(members) regardless of slack, and the solve does not care how often verification
runs.

**The most frequent hard solve is the 4-instance-to-EC conversion**, which places a whole group plus its
parities. Its rate is derivable: at 1 TB/s cluster ingest and 32 MB physical extents, ~30,000 extents seal per
second, forming ~670 EC groups/s, or roughly **22 group placements per second per SN** at ~30 SNs. To hold that
under a quarter of a core, a full group solve must come in under **~10 ms**. **Derived**, and loose enough that
a reasonable rejection-sampling implementation should clear it by a wide margin — which is itself worth
confirming, because failing it by 10x would mean something structural rather than something tunable.

The requirement is that placement be **solvable nearly always for all cluster shapes, and very fast on
average.** For any code there are a handful of hardest shapes, where several placement rules are tight against
the slack at once. Those are enumerable, so they should be a permanent regression suite: domain counts sitting
exactly at each threshold of §4.3.3.2e, several rules tight simultaneously, skewed free space, one domain full,
one domain down.

**The suite's assertions must be on latency percentiles, not on success.** The failure mode being guarded
against is not a wrong answer; it is a solve that takes ten seconds under a shape nobody tested. A suite that
asserts only "placement succeeded" passes straight through it.

**And a solver timeout must not be handled like insufficient domains.** These need opposite treatment:

| Condition | Nature | Correct response |
|---|---|---|
| Not enough domains | permanent, a property of the cluster | drop the rule (§5.6.7) |
| Solver out of time | transient, a property of load | **defer and retry** |

If they share a code path, a load spike permanently degrades the independence of everything written during it,
and per §1.1.1 that is discovered during the disaster.

#### 5.6.11 Affinity was considered and rejected

**Decided against** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17). Recorded at length because it is a reasonable idea
with real prior art, so it will be proposed again.

**What it would have been.** A keyed index or a large concatenated object is built by many vertices
each writing its own partition; the partitions are concatenated, with an index of partition locations,
and a reader reads individual partitions. Affinity would place the corresponding extents of related
objects together so that a vertex — or a join — found its inputs in one place. The instances of any one
extent could go anywhere; what would be constrained is that *the others match*.

**It has been built before.** The nearest is **CoHadoop** (Cited:
[CoHadoop: Flexible Data Placement and Its Exploitation in Hadoop](http://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol4/p575-eltabakh.pdf),
Eltabakh, Tian, Özcan, Gemulla, Krettek and McPherson, PVLDB 4(9), 2011), which adds a file-level
**locator** to HDFS and colocates the blocks of files sharing one, best-effort, with a locator table in
the namenode. MPP databases get the same effect by hash-distributing tables on a shared key so joins
are local; Spanner gets it declaratively by interleaving child rows in the parent's storage.

**Three reasons against, and they are independent:**

1. ⚠️ **Erasure coding will purposely break it.** EC needs the cells of a stripe far apart, and the
   natural grouping — extents of one stream, §13.5.1's easy case — is exactly the set affinity wants
   together. So affinity is undone deliberately by a mechanism that has to run, which means paying for
   it twice: once to establish and once to lose.
2. **It buys nothing if the network is flat.** §5.12.1 makes the intra-cluster network carry everything
   anyway, and for the case that matters most — a vertex free to choose which extents it reads —
   locality is already free by partitioning *from* the placement (§5.12.0). Affinity would only serve
   the stages whose input set is fixed in advance, and those are the stages that must gather across the
   network regardless.
3. ⚠️ **It ties data to spots that were good places for data months or years ago, causing hotspots.**
   This is the general one: **an affinity group is a persistent constraint derived from a transient
   condition.** The cluster it was right for is not the cluster that exists later — machines are added,
   filled, removed — while free-space-weighted placement is continuously rebalancing against exactly
   that drift. Affinity fights it, with stale information, for ever.

**And three more that fell out while working it through**, kept because they generalise: a cross-object
affinity group can attract **unbounded** data to one spot, and a loose granularity does not help since
it spreads a fixed amount of data rather than capping how much arrives; affinity must be honoured **at
repair** or it decays at the rate disks fail, making repair a second component that has to understand
it, and EC grouping a third; and it **correlates loss across objects**, so a domain failure takes the
same partition of everything rather than a scattering.

**What replaces it.** For reading, nothing is needed: partition the extents by where their instances
already are, and place the vertices to match (§5.12.0). For gathering, the network — which is what
§5.12.1 already assumes and §5.12.3 already stakes the design on.

**The general rule worth keeping** even though the feature is not: **a placement constraint derived
from a transient condition becomes a hotspot.** Anything that pins data relative to a decision made
earlier is competing with the balancer, and losing slowly.

### 5.7 Ring composition: consensus membership is not RAM membership

Raft tolerates *n* failures with 2n+1 members. Materializing the served B-tree
(§4.4) on all of them would cost **7× RAM at n=3** — and RAM is the resource that
bounds a stream (§14.1), so that is 7× the most expensive thing in the system.

That is not hypothetical: Cosmos's CSM did exactly this, keeping metadata "in a Paxos-protected
ring with seven replicas that keep all metadata in RAM" (§1.4.5.2). What follows is a direct
improvement on a documented predecessor.

It is also unnecessary. **Consensus needs 2n+1 voters; only three members need
the state materialized.**

| Role | Count | Cost | Job |
|---|---|---|---|
| Primary | 1 | CPU + RAM | serves reads and writes; holds the B-tree |
| Hot backup | 1 | RAM | always up to date; the designated next primary |
| Checkpoint writer | 1 | RAM | takes write locks to write checkpoints, without stalling the primary |
| Log-only members | 2n+1 − 3 | disk | store the Raft log and vote; materialize nothing |

At n=3 that is **3× RAM instead of 7×**, with four cheap log-only members
supplying the remaining durability and votes.

The third materialized member exists because writing a checkpoint — the on-disk
list form of §4.4 — needs a consistent view of the tree, which means taking write
locks. Doing that on the primary or on the always-current hot backup would stall
serving, so it gets a member of its own.

⚠️ **That third member is removable.** Given transactions and a consistent read
that can be held for ~10 minutes, the single hot backup could write its checkpoint
from a snapshot without taking write locks, bringing the cost to **2× RAM**. The
ten minutes is roughly checkpoint size over write bandwidth: at ~500 MB/s it is a
checkpoint of ~3 × 10^11 bytes, about one machine's full memory. Note that §5.8
shrinks checkpoints by orders of magnitude, which makes this optimization easier
rather than harder.

The same ten minutes is also an *upper* bound from a different direction — it keeps
the live SCN range small enough for a narrow sequence number (§4.6.3) — so the figure
is squeezed from both sides rather than chosen.

#### 5.7.1 Primary switchover has three quality tiers

| Case | Client uncertainty | Requires |
|---|---|---|
| Scheduled: known next primary, known time | **milliseconds** | switchover planned in advance |
| Known next primary, unplanned time | one wrong guess, then correct | a designated successor |
| Ordinary Raft election | wait for the winner to catch up | nothing |

The third case is the expensive one, and the role split above is why: **a log-only
member elected primary must materialize the whole B-tree from checkpoint plus log
before it can do anything.** So elections must prefer materialized members
strongly — and the hot backup is exactly that, a designated successor that is
already current. The cheap tiers are not optimizations bolted on; they are the
normal path, and ordinary election is the fallback.

### 5.8 Many rings per machine

A metadata machine should hold members of **many** rings in different roles:
primary for some, hot backup for others, checkpoint writer for a few, log-only for
many more. Two reasons:

- **Cost amortization.** Expensive roles (CPU for primaries, RAM for materialized
  backups) and the cheap one (a log on disk) mix on every machine, so no machine
  is all-expensive and none sits idle.
- **Core utilization.** Write work within a ring is serialized, so one ring keeps
  only so many cores busy. To use *C* cores a machine needs several rings in a
  primary role. **Ring count per machine is set by core count** — and by how much of
  a ring's work is serialized, which is a number nobody has measured (§5.8.2).

**What serializes it is the process-wide exclusive lock** (Asserted, Bob,
2026-08-17): **work persisted to the ring is done under the exclusive side** of
§14.6.3's global shared/exclusive lock. So this is not a ring-specific mechanism
sitting beside the metadata structures' locking — it is the same lock, and persisting
a mutation is one of the operations §14.6.3 requires to be enumerable. **Bob's
expectation is around 10 rings per machine.**

#### 5.8.1 Rings are a concurrency unit, not a capacity unit

**A ring serves many streams.** *P* is chosen for cores and cost amortization, and
has nothing to do with how much a stream may hold — the two are independent, and an
earlier draft of this section wrongly tied them together by assuming one stream per
ring (§14.4).

What *P* does bound is **failover cost**, because an elected log-only member must
materialize everything its ring serves before it can act. At 500 MB/s, a ring
holding a 1/*P* share of a machine's 171 GB extent budget takes:

| Primary rings/machine | Ring's share of the extent budget | Materialize time |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 171 GB | ~5.7 min |
| 16 | 10.7 GB | ~21 s |
| 64 | 2.7 GB | ~5.3 s |
| 256 | 667 MB | ~1.3 s |

So many rings per machine is what makes §5.7.1's expensive tier — an ordinary
election won by an unmaterialized member — tolerable rather than frightening. It
also makes checkpoints cheap, which is exactly what the 2×-RAM optimization in §5.7
needs: holding a consistent read for seconds is a far easier promise than holding
one for ten minutes.

Stream size, separately, is bounded by the machine's whole extent budget — see
§14.1.

⚠️ So *P* is a real design parameter, not a tuning knob: it trades core
utilization and failover speed against stream-list size. It wants choosing
deliberately, and it interacts with the extent-entry size that §14.1 still needs
measured.

### 5.9 The rest of the fleet

Four more machine types surround the storage hierarchy.

Naming convention: **the three storage-hierarchy tiers end in `-N`** — DN, SN, EN
— **and the surrounding services do not**, so FE and KS read as outside the
hierarchy at a glance. Names stay plain and descriptive rather than clever, so
that a wide range of people can work on the code comfortably.

| Type | What it is | Holds keys? | Runs user code? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **KS** — Key Store | A Raft ring holding the daily master keys (§7.3); ~1 MB per century, unlocked by humans and hardware | **yes — and only here** | no |
| **FE** — Front End | Checks user authorization; coordinates clients talking to the other machines | yes, transiently | no |
| **Compute** | Runs user code. Eventually, not initially | **never** | **yes** |
| **`delawson`** — client | Library and CLI, talks to FE over the internet | see §5.9.2 | it *is* user code |

KS is a Raft ring for the same reason SNs and DNs are (§5): keys are small mutable
state that must be exactly right, which is what consensus is for and what bulk
replication is not. Unusually among the rings, KS's state is *tiny* — about a
megabyte per century (§7.3) — so its ring exists purely for reliability and
availability, never for capacity.

#### 5.9.1 The security boundary

> **User code may only run on Compute machines, and decryption keys may never be
> on a machine that runs user code.**

The boundary is drawn at *keys*, not at *bytes*, and that is the right place:
plaintext is one object's worth of exposure, while a key is every extent under it.
The blast radius differs by orders of magnitude, so the two deserve different
containment.

What falls out of the invariant:

- **ENs hold keys, but narrowly scoped ones.** They cache daily SN-master keys
  (§7.3.1), so an EN compromise is not limited to ciphertext — but it is bounded on
  two axes, to the days and the SNs whose keys that EN happens to hold, and it
  never yields a master key. Repair, re-encoding, and scrubbing still need no keys
  at all (§7), so those background loops stay outside the crypto path.
- **Compute machines receive plaintext, never keys.** User code may read what it is
  authorized to read; it may not hold the capability to decrypt anything else.
- **SNs and DNs need keys for their own state, not for user data.** Their
  checkpoints and logs are on disk and so are encrypted, and DN state is itself
  DeLawson keyed objects (§5.5) — but neither needs a user object's data key.

⚠️ **Compute-near-data and decrypt-at-FE pull against each other.** If only a
trusted tier may decrypt, and Compute may not, then every byte Compute reads
traverses a decryption tier — which is exactly the bandwidth funnel that
compute-near-storage exists to avoid. Enforcing the boundary by process or enclave
isolation *on* the Compute machine would fix the bandwidth problem, but the
invariant as stated is machine-level and excludes it. Either the invariant relaxes
to a hardware-isolation boundary, or the decryption tier's bandwidth has to scale
with Compute's input rate. This needs deciding before Compute is built, not after.

#### 5.9.1a What authorization attaches to: the directory, not the tenant and not the object

⚠️ **"Each tenant is their own domain" was the working model and aliases falsify it** (Asserted, Bob,
2026-08-19): an object under an alias is readable by its owning tenant *and* by whoever the alias was
granted to, so the tenant is not a partition of anything.

**The replacement is one sentence: a tenant is not a domain, a path is — and a tenant root is just a
distinguished path.** Everything below follows from that, and most of it was already decided for other
reasons.

**The unit of policy is the directory**, and this is a consistency argument rather than a new choice.
§8.4.3 and §16.27 already make the directory the unit for **expiry grouping**, **soft-delete opt-out**
and **default storage class**. Three policies already ride it; authorization riding the same unit costs
nothing new to explain, and a fourth unit would have to justify itself.

An object's policy is its nearest ancestor directory's, which is the POSIX and ADLS inheritance rule.

##### Per-object authorization: the industry shipped it and retreated

**There is no per-object ACL** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-19, and the prior art agrees emphatically).
Two independent arguments, and the second is unusually strong evidence:

- **Cost, on the one tier whose count is unbounded.** §14.2 makes DN object count the thing with no
  ceiling, and §9.1.3.3 already refused to store per-object *counts* on exactly that ground — "it costs
  space per object, on the one tier whose object count is unbounded". An ACL body per object is a much
  larger version of the same mistake. An ACL *reference* is affordable (§5.1 has one); a distinct
  policy per object is what is being refused.
- **Cited: S3 and GCS both shipped per-object ACLs and then deprecated them.** AWS made "bucket owner
  enforced" the default, which **disables object ACLs entirely**; GCS calls object-level ACLs legacy
  and recommends uniform bucket-level access. That is a natural experiment run twice at enormous scale,
  and both ran it backwards. The failure mode was not cost but **unauditability**: nobody can answer
  "who can read what" when the answer is scattered across 10^12 objects, and the well-known public-data
  incidents were per-object ACL confusion rather than deliberate grants.

**And a general principle falls out**, which is the useful part when a case seems to demand per-object
policy:

> If policy needs a grouping the directory tree does not express, **the tree is wrong, not the policy
> model.**

That is affordable advice here in a way it would not be elsewhere, because §5.1.2.2 makes a directory
*derived rather than stored* and §5.11.3.1 makes splitting and merging rename nothing — so
restructuring to match a policy boundary is cheap. Where it is not cheap, §5.1.2's virtual directories
express a grouping without moving anything.

##### The three cases that look like they need per-object, and what serves them

|Case | Better answer |
|---|---|
| **Share one object with an outside party** | a **time-bounded capability** (§9.1.3.5's machinery, attesting authorization instead of membership). Revocable by expiry, auditable as an issuance, and **zero per-object metadata** — this is S3 presigned URLs, and DeLawson already has the shape |
| **Quarantine one object** found to hold something it should not | **move it.** A rename into a quarantine directory is cheap (§5.11.3.1) and uses the unit that already exists |
| **Per-record entitlements** — medical or per-subject data | not an authorization problem at this layer. Either an object per entitlement class, or the user encrypts before sending and pays for it in physical bytes (§7.2.3) |

**The first row is the one worth noticing**, because it says the per-object case is real and the ACL is
the wrong mechanism for it: a share is an *event with an expiry*, and an ACL is *durable state*.
Modelling an event as state is what produced the auditability problem above.

##### Negative authorization: not needed, and the reason is structural

**There are no deny rules** (Asserted, Bob and reasoning here, 2026-08-19). The question is not taste,
it is whether policy composes from independent sources:

| | Needs deny? | Because |
|---|---|---|
| **AWS IAM** | **yes** | policies arrive from many places at once, so a guardrail is only enforceable if it can override a grant made elsewhere |
| **Kubernetes RBAC** | **no**, by choice | "purely additive" was chosen for comprehensibility |
| **POSIX ACLs** | no | a mask narrows; nothing denies |
| **DeLawson** | **no** | see below |

**DeLawson's composition is already an intersection, and intersection needs no deny.** §5.1.1 settles
that a read through an alias is governed by **the owner's ACL, checked at the target**, with the alias
only saying the reader may look. That is an **AND** of two gates, and AND is monotone: narrowing either
side narrows the result, so any restriction expressible as a deny is expressible as a smaller grant.
Deny earns its keep only where composition is a union.

⚠️ **An earlier draft leaned on the composition depth being capped at two**, since §5.1.1.1 bounded an
alias chain at one hop. **That cap is gone** — §5.1.1.1a allows nesting, because two levels of sharing
cannot express a shared foundation under a shared project.

**The argument that matters survives untouched**: no-deny rests on intersection being **monotone**
(§5.9.1a), which holds for any number of terms. Only the comprehensibility claim weakens, and it weakens
to something workable — **explaining a refusal means reporting a chain rather than a pair**, and the
chain is known exactly, because §5.1.1.1a's path set is the list of what was traversed.

##### What this leaves open

- ⚠️ **Where the ACL is fetched from is still §16.129 / #81**, and unaffected by any of the above. That
  question is about *hops*, not about *granularity*.
- ⚠️ **Whether a capability may ever attest authorization** rather than only membership. §9.1.3.5 was
  since revised: the certificate **does** carry authorization (`(tenant, extent, write?)`), so a
  bounded revocation lag is already accepted there. ⚠️ **That makes the question narrower rather than
  moot** — what a share adds is a bearer who is *not* the named tenant, which is the property §9.1.3.5
  keeps by binding the tenant. So it is still a separate mechanism, and §16.135 is about whether the
  bearer may be someone with no standing at all.
- **Whether a tenant needs any representation at all** beyond being a path with a quota and a bill
  attached. Nothing above requires one, which is a hint that "tenant" is a billing concept rather than a
  security concept — but §12's quota accounting may want it, and that has not been checked.

#### 5.9.2 Where decryption happens: on the EN

**Decided: extent decryption happens on the EN** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-15). Neither
option this section previously weighed is taken.

| Decrypt at | Why not |
|---|---|
| FE | FE bandwidth would have to carry all bulk data, which §5.12.1 already shows is the expensive shape |
| Client | Pushes keys out of the datacenter, and makes DeLawson's own compression and coalescing impossible |

**It follows from §1.5's sharpened boundary.** ENs run only signed executables and no
user code, so holding keys there does not violate the invariant — and it puts
decryption at the one place that already touches every byte, so no tier has to be
sized to carry bulk plaintext it would not otherwise see. §7.2.1 shows the CPU cost is
a fraction of a core.

Two things this makes possible that FE-decrypts did not:

- **Reads are served from the EN directly**, with no decryption tier in the path, which
  is what §1.4.2's read-amplification budget assumes.
- **The EN can act on record framing during coalescing** (§8.2.1), which needs
  plaintext.

**End-to-end encryption remains available to the user, as a user-side choice.** Anyone
who wants it may encrypt before sending, and DeLawson will store the result faithfully
(Asserted, Bob). What it costs them is stated in §7.2.3 — it is not free, and the price
is charged automatically rather than administered.

### 5.10 Node identifiers and bounded fan-out

**DN, SN, and EN identifiers are 32 bits**, so the design scales to 2^32 of each.

That immediately rules out a full mesh. There are only 65,536 ports per IP and a
usable ephemeral range of ~28,000, so a machine can hold on the order of 10^3–10^4
connections. Against 4.3 × 10^9 nodes, **a machine can see roughly one part in
400,000 of the cluster.** Connectivity is therefore deliberately partial:

> Each SN ring talks to only some ENs; each EN talks to only some SNs.

#### 5.10.1 How much fan-out is needed

Let *F* be the ENs an SN can see and *G* the SNs an EN can see. An SN machine's
rings map a fixed quantity of instance bytes, and each visible EN devotes roughly
`capacity/G` of itself to any one SN, so `F/G = instance bytes per SN ÷ EN
capacity`.

The instance bytes per SN machine come from §14.1. A machine's extent budget of
171 GB at ~100 B holds **1.7 × 10^9 extent records**, but it is *primary* for only
about a third of the rings it materializes (§5.7) — the other roles do not talk to
ENs — so it drives ~5.7 × 10^8 extents, which at 32 MB and 4 instances is
**~76 PB of EN capacity to reach**. Note this is **independent of P**: more rings per
machine means proportionally smaller streams, so the extent count a machine holds is
set by its RAM, not by how that RAM is divided.

| EN capacity | *F/G* | *F* at *G*=4 | *G*=16 | *G*=64 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 100 TB | 764 | 3,054 | 12,217 | 48,867 |
| 1 PB | 76 | 306 | 1,222 | 4,887 |
| 3 PB | 25 | 102 | 407 | 1,629 |

*G* is the free choice, and it is the one that matters: **sharing is what gives
repair and balance somewhere to go.** With *G*=1 each EN answers to a single SN,
which is a static partition — cheap in connections, but a dead EN can only be
replaced from a pool of one SN's making, and a reassigned stream finds no ENs it
may talk to.

The table's real lesson: **EN capacity buys sharing.** At 100 TB per EN, *G*=16
needs 18,000 connections and is out of reach; at 1 PB per EN the same sharing costs
~1,800 connections and is comfortable. Fan-out policy and EN sizing are one
decision, not two.

Helpfully, **the cost target pushes the same way.** §5.3.1 derives tens to hundreds
of disks per EN from the requirement that server hardware be ≤5% of cost; at 150
disks of 20 TB that is a 3 PB EN, where *G*=16 costs only ~407 connections and *G*=64
still only ~1,600. Two independent arguments — reliability wanting sharing, economics
wanting few servers per byte — converge on large ENs.

#### 5.10.2 Neighborhoods must be domain-diverse, and randomly chosen

§5.6 requires instances in slack × *n* independent failure domains. Those domains
must now exist **within the F ENs an SN can see**, not merely somewhere in the
cluster. A neighborhood of 2,000 ENs that all share a power domain satisfies the
connection budget and violates the reliability requirement.

So fan-out sets are not arbitrary subsets: **each neighborhood must span at least
slack × n domains at every level of the nesting hierarchy** (§5.6.2). Slack is
likewise a neighborhood property, not a cluster property — repair re-places within
the neighborhood, so it is the neighborhood that must retain spare domains after a
loss. This is a materially stronger requirement than the cluster-wide version, and
it is the one that actually has to hold.

Beyond diversity, the set should be a **random** selection, stratified to spread evenly
across the finest tracked failure domain. Randomness is what makes each SN's view an
unbiased sample of the cluster, which is what makes the self-balancing of §5.6.4 land on
the global optimum. A clustered or systematically-assigned neighborhood would satisfy
domain diversity and still bias placement.

#### 5.10.3 Reassignment needs mutable fan-out

⚠️ If a stream moves from one SN ring to another (§13), the new ring must be able
to reach the ENs already holding that stream's extents. Otherwise the move requires
copying every byte. So either reassignment is confined to rings with compatible
neighborhoods, or **fan-out sets must be mutable** — which means connection churn
during recovery, exactly when the system is already busy.

This is the same shape as the key-derivation trap in §7.3.3: a mutable assignment
being used where a stable identity is needed. Both want deciding together.

#### 5.10.4 Bounded fan-out means 2-byte references, not 4-byte

The 32-bit identifiers are for **cluster-wide naming** — topology, configuration,
the control plane. They need not appear in per-extent metadata at all.

Because an SN can reach at most ~20,000 ENs, and 2 bytes addresses 65,536, an
instance's EN can be named by a **neighborhood-local index**. The global 32-bit id
appears exactly once, in the SN's fan-out table: 20,000 entries × 4 B = **78 KB**,
once per table rather than once per reference.

| Field | Bytes |
|---|---|
| extent id — `ExtentId` (4) + creation second (8), `SnId` implicit (§4.6.3) | 12 |
| starting record number | 8 |
| cumulative logical bytes | 8 |
| cumulative physical bytes | 8 |
| key generation and flags | 2 |
| 4 × instance reference (2 B local EN index + 1 B disk + 3 B slot) | 24 |
| **Total** | **62 B** |

The day index §7.3.3 needs for key derivation is not a separate field: the creation
second already carries it.

The same argument applies to any reference whose fan-out is bounded: DN and FE
references from an SN are likewise ≤20,000, so they too are 2-byte local indices.
**Global ids are control-plane; local indices are data-plane.**

The intra-EN locator can likely shrink too. If it is a slot index rather than a byte
offset, 3 bytes addresses 2^24 slots, which at 32 MB per extent covers a 512 TiB EN
— bringing the entry to **56 B**. Worth confirming against the EN sizing that §5.10.1
already ties to fan-out.

Two compounding effects, because §14.1 shows the stream list grows as the *square*
of entry size: the 8 bytes saved by local indices frees ~10 GB of RAM on every SN
machine, *and* takes ~22% off the largest metadata structure in the system. Larger
streams also mean fewer of them, which shortens every stream-list descent.

The itemized total is not a new baseline. **§14.1 keeps 100 B as the budget**,
because flags, timestamps and fields not yet identified will consume the headroom;
what the local-index encoding buys is room to add them, not a smaller number to
quote.

⚠️ **The cost is a naming-lifecycle problem.** A local index is only meaningful
relative to a table, so:

- The fan-out table is critical state and must live in the ring's Raft state
  (§4.4), snapshotted and logged like everything else.
- **A local index must not be reused while any extent entry still references it.**
  Retiring an EN and admitting a replacement into the same slot would silently
  re-point every extent that named it. That needs reference counting, or a
  generation number in the slot, or append-only slot allocation with compaction.
- §5.10.3's mutable fan-out becomes harder: reassigning a stream to another ring
  means its entries' local indices refer to the wrong table. The cheap fix is to
  make the table **travel with the stream** — 78 KB is nothing next to the extent
  list — which argues for the index namespace being per-stream rather than per-ring.

⚠️ Per-stream or per-ring index namespace is undecided, and it is the same
stable-identity-versus-mutable-assignment question as §5.10.3 and §7.3.3. All three
now want deciding together.

---

### 5.11 Fullness is handled by redirecting writes, never by moving data

Every tier fills up eventually, and the design's answer is the same at each: **stop writing
there and let the existing contents age out.** Nothing is relocated to make room.

| Tier fills | Response | Movement required |
|---|---|---|
| **EN** | Its weight in the free-space table falls to zero, so placement stops choosing it (§5.6.3) | **none — automatic** |
| **SN** | The DN directs *new streams* for that range to a different SN | **none** |
| **DN range** | Split the range, or rebalance | **yes — but metadata only** |

⚠️ **Deployment domains also cap utilization.** After losing one domain the survivors must hold
everything, and they are (1 − 1/*D*) of the capacity — so **the cluster can never exceed
1 − 1/*D* full** and still absorb the loss. At 20 domains that is 95%; at 10 domains, 90%; at 4,
just 75%. The domain count is therefore a capacity decision as well as a blast-radius one
(§13.2).

The EN case needs no mechanism at all: free-space weighting already stops writing to a full
disk, because a disk with no free bytes has no weight. Fullness handling and load balancing
are the same code.

The SN case needs one fact tracked — **the DN knows how full its SNs are** — and then
redirection is a placement decision for new streams. Existing streams on the full SN may
still grow, but growth of existing streams is minor next to the creation of new ones, so the
redirect is effective almost immediately. Eventually those streams age out and the SN
recovers capacity without anything being copied.

Only the DN range case forces movement. And note where it lands: **movement is required
exactly where it is cheapest.**

| | Volume | Medium | Movement needed? |
|---|---|---|---|
| EN | bulk data, PB per machine | disk | never |
| SN | metadata, 256 GB per machine | **RAM** — ~5,000× disk (§12.2) | never |
| DN | metadata | disk | **yes** |

The requirement to move is *inversely* correlated with the cost of moving. Splitting a DN
range is a metadata operation on disk-resident state, and it reuses the split machinery keyed
objects already need (§10). Had the SN tier been the one requiring rebalancing, it would have
meant relocating RAM-resident state — the most expensive bytes in the system.

#### 5.11.1 Default locality, and why

**User ranges map to a DN, and the DN maps them to an SN**, so by default **objects in the
same directory land on the same SN.** That is deliberate: it minimizes the number of rings a
directory depends on.

A directory whose objects sit on one DN and one SN is unavailable only if one of *two* rings
is down. Spread the same objects across a hundred SNs and it is unavailable if any of a
hundred and one is:

| Rings depended on | *p* = 10^-5 per ring | *p* = 10^-6 |
|---|---|---|
| 2 (default locality) | 2 × 10^-5 | 2 × 10^-6 |
| 101 (spread over 100 SNs) | 1 × 10^-3 | 1 × 10^-4 |

Fifty times worse, for no benefit — the capacity is the same either way. Spreading is
something to do when *forced* by size, not by default.

#### 5.11.2 Whole-object availability degrades with size; per-record does not

The corollary is uncomfortable and worth stating plainly. A large object is forced to span
many SNs (§14.1), so its dependency set grows with it:

| Operation | Rings touched | Depends on object size? |
|---|---|---|
| Read one record | 1 DN + 1 SN + its ENs | **no** |
| Read the whole object | every SN it spans | **yes, linearly** |

At any plausible ring availability, **a maximal object of ~4 × 10^6 streams is never wholly
available at one instant** — with *p* = 10^-6 the expected number of unavailable streams is
still ~4. Per-record availability, meanwhile, is unaffected by object size.

So the availability contract has to be **per record, not per object**, and whole-object
operations — scans, migrations, verification sweeps — must be **resumable rather than
atomic**, tolerating parts being briefly unreachable and returning to them. That is a
requirement on the API and on §13.3's loops, not a defect: for objects this large there is no
alternative, and §9.4's scan design already walks streams in order rather than needing them
simultaneously.

#### 5.11.3 A range is a ring

**A DN range gets its own Raft snapshot and log, and therefore its own ring** (Asserted, Bob,
2026-08-19) — one ring per range, except transiently while splitting or merging. That keeps a
ring's data contiguous, and it is what lets a range split when both its neighbours are busy,
because the split creates a *third* ring in the middle rather than pushing work sideways.

⚠️ **The consequence to absorb first: a machine is no longer the owner of a key span — a ring
is.** A physical DN hosts members of many rings, placed wherever there is capacity, so "which DN
owns this range" stops having a single answer. An earlier draft of this section concluded that a
DN must therefore support multiple noncontiguous ranges; with a ring per range the question
dissolves instead, because nothing about a range's identity refers to a machine.

**And moving a range becomes a membership change**, which is a thing §13 already does. The planned
handover between old and new owner is Raft's own leadership change, so it needs no term number of
its own — Raft has one. Replacing a failed member and rebalancing a range away from a hot machine
become the same operation.

##### 5.11.3.1 A name may not encode a placement decision

**References to a stream are `(range, StreamId)` and never `(DN, StreamId)`** (Asserted, Bob,
2026-08-17). `StreamId`s are only unique within a range, so the lookup is a mapping rather than an
array — and naming the machine would bake in a placement that rebalancing changes. This is §4.6's
rule again: every reference is an index into a population its holder knows, never a machine
address.

**Inside an SN, though, the reference is the array slot** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17), with
`(range, StreamId)` interned to it — exactly §14.6.5's arrangement for extents, where an external
name reaches an internal index through a hash and everything internal uses the index. The payoff
is the same: **a range split rekeys hash entries and touches no stream record**.

##### 5.11.3.2 Splitting is cheap, merging is not, and both move the smaller side

**A split gives every stream to exactly one child range**, so ids need not change: it is a rekey
plus, with a ring per range, populating the new ring with the subrange's state.

⚠️ **A merge unions two id spaces that can collide, so it must renumber** — and a `StreamId` is
named by the DN's objects, making merge a bulk reference rewrite where split is a rename of keys.
Splits and merges are always within one DN's neighbourhood (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17), so both
sides are reachable, but the asymmetry is real and it decides how each should be built.

**Both operations should move the smaller side.** A split creates the new ring for the smaller
piece and leaves the bulk in place; a merge renumbers the smaller participant. That bounds the
work by the smaller of the two in both directions.

**⚠️ Merging is certainly needed, and the case that needs it is the cheap one** (Asserted, Bob,
2026-08-17). The workload is a conveyor: there is usually a hot spot that **grows in alphabetical
order, moving along with the alphabetic end**, and a month or a year later that data is deleted
from the trailing end. So the ranges wanting merging are the emptied ones —

| Case | Renumbering cost |
|---|---|
