| the range is **empty** | **none** — no streams, so no collisions. It is a *deletion*: drop it and give its span to a neighbour |
| the range is **near-empty** | renumber only the smaller side — the streams actually present, not the span |

which means **the expensive general merge, two full ranges unioning two full id spaces, may never
need building.** What is load-bearing is *noticing* that a range has emptied.

**The transient is the part to design.** While splitting or merging, a range is not exactly one
ring. Raft supplies the clean shape: populate and catch up the new ring while the old one still
serves, then cut over at a known index, so there is a single instant at which the old ring stops
answering for that span. ⚠️ The alternative — both answering for a window — is where read-your-
writes questions live, and §16 item 11 already flags the interaction with in-flight writes.

##### 5.11.3.3 What sets the size band, and why the ends are measured differently

| End | Set by |
|---|---|
| **minimum** | **concatenate locality** — concatenating extents inside an SN is cheap, and across ranges it becomes the DN concatenating multiple streams, so it is cheaper to talk to one SN. **Plus per-ring overhead**, now that a range is a ring: a leader, heartbeats, a snapshot and log, and state-machine RAM on every member |
| **maximum** | **what one ring member can hold** — the same shape as §14.1's per-SN bound, and it bounds §4.4.0's per-range index too |

**Finding the DN is a B-tree walk over ranges, which lets ranges be pretty small** (Asserted, Bob,
2026-08-17) — but note that argument *relaxes* the minimum rather than setting it. Two things set
it, and **the larger binds**; both want measuring rather than guessing.

**A DN may map one range to several SNs, though it should prefer one** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17),
because a single object lives in a single range and can be large enough that its streams must span
SNs — which §5.2 already requires of a maximal object.

**And the split point is deferred** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17). Splitting at the alphabetic end
minimizes the number of splits, but risks a small range if the pattern does not hold; a size band
wider than 2× permits splitting in the middle and 3× permits the 2/3 mark, avoiding ranges that are
too small from the start. **Derived:** if a range splits at *M* and no piece may fall below *m*, the
most asymmetric split allowed is **f ≤ 1 − m/M** — 1/2 at a ratio of 2, 2/3 at 3. So the band width
is not an independent knob; it *is* the split policy. ⚠️ And the ratio only means something once both
ends are expressed in one unit, which they are not yet: one is locality, the other capacity.

Two things not yet decided that would settle it: **split points preferring tenant or directory
boundaries** — since what the minimum defends is not size but not cutting through objects that get
concatenated together, and §5.1.2's virtual directories are a ready supply of such cuts — and
**choosing the split point from observation**, since a range knows where its own recent inserts
landed and can split at its right edge only when they were overwhelmingly there.

##### 5.11.3.4 A stream may be referenced from several ranges, and the counts are two-level

**Concatenate lets an object reference streams in any SN holding that tenant's data, so a stream may
be referenced from multiple ranges** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17). Rather than copy to avoid that —
which would make user concatenate cost storage sometimes and not others, for space that need not be
spent — **the SN's stream knows it is referenced by several ranges, and the DN/SN sync of §13.1 is on
the range-stream reference rather than on the stream.** A range knows which DN it belongs to, and the
handoff when ranges rebalance touches nothing about the stream.

**Which amends §4.6.6.1's counts into two levels**, and the arrangement is better than what that
section settled on:

| Reference | Counted in | Why it is safe there |
|---|---|---|
| object → stream | **the range** | same ring as the objects doing the referencing |
| range → stream | **the SN** | one place that sees zero, and the tier that must delete the stream anyway |

⚠️ **This is not the distributed termination §4.6.6.1 feared.** Each range independently decides it
no longer references a stream and says so once; the **SN aggregates**. There is a single point that
observes zero, so nothing has to agree with anything, and it survives rebalancing because a
range-stream reference does not care which DN the range currently sits on. §13.1.7's drifting
cross-tier reference is therefore **`range → stream`**, not `object → stream`.

**A tenant reading another tenant's aliased stream (§5.1.1) copies if it concatenates that into an
object it owns** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17), so sharing never crosses a tenant boundary.

**And a stream holds one tenant's data, which the DN can assure** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17).
Multi-tenant streams would answer the zillion-tenants-with-one-tiny-object abuse, but §12.4.3's base
tenant charge answers it too and costs nothing: single-tenancy is what makes §7.3.3's key derivation,
§12's attribution and the plain statement "this stream belongs to a tenant" all simple, and pricing
gives them up for nothing.

⚠️ **One thing this makes load-bearing:** finding the ring that serves a key needs a directory from
ranges to rings, and that directory cannot itself be range-partitioned without recursing. It points
at §5.5's bootstrap root — already §16 item 1 — which is now on the path of every DN lookup rather
than only of startup.

---

### 5.12 Compute: undesigned, but the network already binds

Compute is largely undesigned, and **Virtual Clusters (§1.4.5) are unlikely to be the route** —
Cosmos's model of guaranteed capacity per group plus free use of idle capacity is one answer, not
the only one. What follows is what can already be said without designing it.

**The bounded fan-out pattern probably applies.** §5.10's answer to "*n* machines cannot all talk
to *m* machines" is not specific to SN↔EN, and Compute has the same shape: a vertex needs a
handful of ENs and a handful of peers, not all of them. Expect the same three ingredients —
random stratified neighbourhoods, local indices rather than global ids, and rejection against
placement rules.

#### 5.12.0 The prior art, for when this is designed

**SCOPE is what this layer looked like last time**, and Bob is one of its authors (Cited:
[SCOPE: Easy and Efficient Parallel Processing of Massive Data Sets](http://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol1/1454166.pdf),
Chaiken, Jenkins, Larson, Ramsey, Shakib, Weaver and Zhou, PVLDB 1(2), 2008): a declarative language
over rowsets with **no explicit parallelism**, a small extensible operator set, a cost-based optimizer,
and a job manager scheduling the resulting graph.

**Noted and not pursued.** ⚠️ **Compute is deliberately out of the picture at present** (Asserted, Bob,
2026-08-17) — *the store itself is a big enough can of worms* — so this is a pointer to where the
answer will be found, not the beginning of an answer. The same paper's storage material is used where
it belongs, in §8.1.4.1.

⚠️ **One line of it bears on a storage assumption, and there is an answer.** The paper says *"A unit of
computation generally consumes a small number of collocated extents"* — Cosmos deliberately
**collocated** the extents a computation would consume, where §5.12.3 argues DeLawson needs no
affinity. Both can hold, because **the order of the two decisions can be reversed** (Asserted, Bob,
2026-08-17):

> **You could co-locate compute to storage if a vertex is free to read any set of extents — partition
> the extents by instance location, then place vertices near each shared location. That does not work
> if a vertex has to read a set of extents fixed beforehand.**

Collocating extents *for* a computation constrains placement, and placement has other masters — free
space, failure domains, repair (§5.6, §13.4). **Choosing the partitioning *from* the placement
constrains nothing**: the store places extents for its own reasons, the scheduler reads where they
landed, and every vertex gets a local set by construction.

**So this is a requirement on the store rather than a Compute decision to make now**, and the store can
already meet it: **instance locations have to be visible**, which is exactly the `EnId` in §8.1.1a-10's
hint and what #61 wants `object-info` to expose. A scheduler partitioning by location is the same
caller as a job holding hints, asking the same question.

Where a vertex's input set *is* fixed in advance — a join on a partitioning key, a sort where a vertex
owns a range — that does not apply, and affinity would be the alternative. It was considered and
rejected (§5.6.11); those stages cross the network.

#### 5.12.1 The security invariant makes the network carry everything

Cosmos and Dryad placed **computation close to its data** — the talk is explicit that the
execution engine is "responsible for the placement of the computation close to the data it
reads." **DeLawson cannot do that**, because §1.5 forbids user code on any machine holding
decryption keys, and ENs hold them (§7.3.1).

So every byte a job reads crosses the network, always. That is a real cost this design pays and
its ancestor did not, and it is why cluster size is bounded by network bandwidth rather than by
anything else:

| | Aggregate delivery | Compute uplinks needed to absorb it |
|---|---|---|
| 100 ENs | 2.5 TB/s | 200 × 100 GbE |
| 1,000 ENs | 25 TB/s | 2,000 × 100 GbE |

**Bounding a cluster geographically and by network bandwidth is therefore not a convenience, it
is forced.** Buy more EN disk bandwidth than the fabric can deliver to compute and the disks sit
idle. The corollary is that the fabric must be flat within that bound — §5.12.3 costs it out and
finds it affordable, which is what lets topology be ignored thereafter.

The same balance appears inside one machine, and it is a **third independent bound on disks per
EN**: 150 disks at 200 MB/s is 30 GB/s, while 2 × 100 GbE is 25 GB/s. Disks outrun the NIC by
1.2×, so sequential scanning is NIC-limited at that disk count. §5.3.1 bounded disks per EN from
below by the cost target and from above by the 1-byte disk index; the NIC bounds it too, and
lands in the same neighbourhood.

#### 5.12.2 L-shaped jobs, and what "compact" should mean

Jobs are often **L-shaped**: a huge parallel read that discards most of its input through
filtering and aggregation, then a long churn on what remains. Not a guess — the VLDB paper
describes it directly: extract vertices "discard most of the data, aggregate most of the rest, and
then later vertices spend a long time churning that remaining data" (§1.4.5.2). The question is
whether the remainder wants to be *compact*.

It does — but **"compact" means RAM-resident in aggregate, not co-located on few machines.** The
gap that matters is not network topology, it is memory versus network, and that gap survives any
fabric:

| | Bandwidth |
|---|---|
| Local RAM | ~100 GB/s |
| 100 GbE NIC | ~12.5 GB/s |
| Local NVMe | ~7 GB/s |

RAM is ~8× a 100 GbE link, so **no amount of bisection bandwidth makes fetching a working set as
fast as already having it.** Which resolves the worry: the goal is not to squeeze phase 2's data
onto a few nearby machines — that would sacrifice the CPU parallelism phase 2 needs — but to have
it *resident* across whatever nodes are churning on it.

The number that decides everything is the filtering ratio:

| Remainder | Against 1,000 nodes × 256 GB = 256 TB | Phase 2 becomes |
|---|---|---|
| 1 TB | 0.4% of RAM, 1 GB per node | a **memory** workload; storage is out of the loop |
| 500 TB | does not fit | a **storage** workload — 100 iterations is 50 PB of re-reads |

So the design implication is not about placement at all: **phase 2 is cheap when the remainder
fits in aggregate compute RAM and expensive when it does not**, by a factor of the iteration
count. If it does fit, the network carries only whatever the algorithm itself needs — shuffles
and reductions — and DeLawson is not in the loop.

⚠️ Which suggests the useful thing for DeLawson to offer Compute is not locality-aware placement
but a way to know, and to report, whether a job's remainder will fit. That is a scheduling input
nobody has designed.

#### 5.12.3 No affinity, because the network is flat

⚠️ **Narrower than it reads, and now settled.** A vertex free to choose *which* extents it reads is
local by construction — partition the extents by instance location and place the vertices to match
(§5.12.0) — so a flat network is not what makes reading work. Affinity, the alternative, was considered
and **rejected** (§5.6.11). So what a flat network is load-bearing for is the stages with a
fixed-beforehand input set: joins on a partitioning key, sorts where a vertex owns a range, anything
that gathers.

Cosmos built placement affinity for joins — affinitized extents mapped to the same racks, so a
vertex "joining two affinitized streams could join them by their affinitized keys without reading
cross-rack data", kept in sync by an Affinity Service (§1.4.5.2). DeLawson has nothing equivalent,
and deliberately so.

**Affinity is a mechanism for avoiding network. If the network is flat, it buys nothing.** Cosmos's
affinity was worth a service because its topology had a cross-rack penalty worth dodging. DeLawson
assumes instead that **intra-cluster network is flat** — full bisection, no topology to exploit —
which makes co-partitioning an optimization with nothing to optimize.

That assumption has to be paid for, and it is affordable because network is not close to the
dominant cost. For one EN over five years:

| | Cost |
|---|---|
| 150 disks at ~$250 each (capital, power, space) | ~$37,500 |
| Full-bisection 100 GbE per server — NIC, leaf port, spine share, optics | ~$2,500 |
| Network as a fraction of total EN cost | **~6%** |

So the strategy is: **make the network sufficiently beefy, then ignore it.** Against a strict 5%
overhead target that is tight — network alone would consume the whole non-disk budget — and at the
10% §1.2 allows for, it is comfortable. Either way it is single-digit percent of a cluster whose
cost is disk, which is what makes "ignore the topology" a sound engineering position rather than
wishful thinking.

⚠️ It is an **assumption, and worth recording as one.** If a cluster ever spans a boundary the
fabric cannot flatten — separate buildings, an oversubscribed uplink, a metro link — then topology
becomes visible again and affinity comes back with it. §1.2's geographic bound is what keeps that
from happening, so the two are the same decision seen from different ends.

This also completes a chain worth reading in one place:

> §1.5 forbids user code where keys are → so all reads cross the network (§5.12.1) → so the
> network must be flat and beefy → so cluster size is bounded by what can be affordably
> flattened (§1.2) → and given a flat network, affinity and co-partitioning buy nothing.

---

#### 5.12.4 Scheduling: maximum parallelism, because equal sharing is pessimal

**Compute should strive for maximum parallelism once a job is started** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-16). The argument
is the same one §13.4.4.4 makes about repair bandwidth, and seeing it twice in unrelated places is the reason to
state it as a principle.

Ten jobs, ten processors, ten minutes of compute each:

| Policy | Each job finishes at | Mean latency | Last finishes at |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Fair**: one processor each | 10 min, all of them | **10 min** | 10 min |
| **Serialize at full parallelism** | 1, 2, 3 … 10 min | **5.5 min** | 10 min |

**Derived.** Same throughput, 45% lower mean latency, identical worst case. And with jobs arriving staggered at
one-minute intervals, each finishes one minute after it arrives — **a 10x latency improvement at identical
throughput.**

> **When total work and total capacity are fixed, every allocation finishes the last job at the same time. Only
> the distribution of earlier completions differs — and equal sharing is the pessimal choice.**

That is the same statement as §13.4.4.4's, where pure proportional allocation makes every SN finish
simultaneously so no user recovers early. Repair and compute are the same problem with different nouns.

**Note this is not §1.4's throughput-versus-latency trade.** §1.4 declines to sacrifice throughput for latency.
Here nothing is sacrificed: the latency distribution improves for free, so §1.4's priority does not forbid it and
in fact has nothing to say about it.

##### 5.12.4.1 Bounded by the job's own parallelism, so "one at a time" is not the rule

⚠️ The table above assumes a job can use all ten processors. Amdahl bounds that: a job with serial fraction *s*
cannot exceed a speedup of `1/s`, so a job that can only occupy two processors leaves eight idle if run alone —
which §1.6 forbids.

So the rule is not "one job at a time". It is:

> **Run the fewest concurrent jobs that still saturates the resource.**

That degrades to one at a time when a single job can saturate, and to many when jobs are narrow. It also means the
scheduler needs each job's *parallelism profile*, not just its total cost — and nothing here says how that is
obtained. Declared by the submitter, measured from history, or discovered by ramping.

##### 5.12.4.2 And it cuts temporary storage by the same factor

Better still: if each job needs 1 GB of scratch, then ten jobs at one processor each hold **10 GB
simultaneously**, where serializing at full parallelism holds **1 GB** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-16). Peak
temporary storage is `concurrent jobs × temp per job`, and §5.12.4.1's rule minimizes exactly that first factor.

**The latency win and the storage win are the same win, by Little's law. Derived.** With `L` jobs in flight, `λ`
the throughput and `W` the latency, `L = λW`. Throughput is fixed by assumption, so any reduction in latency is a
proportional reduction in jobs in flight, and temporary storage is proportional to jobs in flight:

| Policy | `W` | `L = λW` | Peak scratch |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fair, one processor each | 10 min | 10 | 10 GB |
| Serialize at full parallelism | 1 min | **1** | **1 GB** |

So this is not a second benefit stacked on the first. It is the same improvement measured in a different unit,
which is why they cannot be traded against each other.

**Total consumption falls too, not only the peak.** Each job holds its scratch for a tenth as long, so billable
byte-seconds go from 100 GB-min to 10 GB-min — a 10x reduction in what §12.3 charges for. **So the user who wants
their job to finish sooner also pays less for scratch space**, with no policy required to align those. §12.1's
pattern once more.

**And it can decide feasibility, not just cost.** A cluster with 5 GB of scratch cannot run the fair schedule at
all, while the serialized one needs 1 GB. That is a stronger claim than "cheaper": the wrong policy makes a
workload impossible rather than expensive.

**§5.12.2 makes this the most valuable of the three effects.** That section argues the phase-2 working set must be
**RAM-resident in aggregate**, because no fabric closes the ~8x gap between local RAM and a 100 GbE link. Fewer
concurrent jobs means fewer simultaneous working sets competing for RAM — and §12.2 prices RAM at ~5,000x disk per
byte. So the factor-of-*L* saving lands in the **most expensive resource in the system**, not in scratch disk.

⚠️ **This assumes temp storage per job is independent of how wide the job runs.** True for data-parallel work
where intermediate data scales with *input* rather than with worker count — §5.12.2's filter-then-churn shape is
exactly that. False where every worker keeps a full working copy, in which case widening a job multiplies its
scratch and the saving evaporates. Which case a job is in is part of the parallelism profile §16 already needs
(question 122), so it is one question rather than two.

#### 5.12.5 Compute-hours in a bank account

**Compute should hand out compute-hours; accounts accumulate them and may start a job when the balance covers its
expected cost** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-16).

That makes admission a **local balance check** rather than a global negotiation, which matters because §5.12.4
wants jobs started promptly and at full width. And it is what makes maximum parallelism affordable: a job that
will occupy the whole cluster for a minute must first have banked the equivalent, so bursts are pre-funded rather
than arbitrated.

**It is the design's third scheduling idiom**, and they are worth distinguishing:

| Resource | Idiom | Where |
|---|---|---|
| Repair bandwidth within an SN | thresholds — doors on a bin | §13.4.3 |
| Repair bandwidth across SNs | floor plus proportional surplus | §13.4.4 |
| **Compute** | **token bucket — accumulate a rate, spend in lumps** | here |

**And the same constraint appears for the fourth time.** §13.4.3.4's sufficient amounts, §13.4.4.3's minimums,
§16's question about their partition — and now:

> **Σ accumulation rates ≤ total capacity**, or the bank is insolvent in the long run and balances are promises
> that cannot be kept.

**Derived.** A balance cap is needed too, and for a different reason: rates summing correctly still permits every
account to hoard for a month and burst simultaneously, which exceeds capacity instantly. Rates bound the long-run
average; a cap bounds the burst. At this point the recurrence is established enough to state as a rule: **any set
of guaranteed allocations is a partition of a total, and must be validated as one — and if the guarantee
accumulates, it needs a ceiling as well as a rate.**

##### 5.12.5.1 The ceiling, and why charging stops when it is reached

**The accumulated balance has a ceiling, and the customer stops being charged once it is reached** (Asserted, Bob,
2026-08-16).

**That is not generosity, it is §12.1.** Billing must be proportional to *actual cost*, and §12.1 is explicit that
over-charging is as much a failure as under-charging because competitors undercut it. So ask what an unspent
compute-hour costs the provider:

| Resource | An unused reservation costs | So billing is |
|---|---|---|
| Storage | a disk, occupied whether read or not | **continuous** |
| **Compute** | **nothing** — an unspent hour occupies no processor | **stops at the ceiling** |

**Derived.** Compute-hours are not a stored good. Charging to accumulate them past a cap would bill for something
that costs nothing to hold, which §12.1 forbids in the same breath as under-billing metadata. And it means the two
resources genuinely have different billing *shapes* — which is what "bill every scarce resource" looks like when
done properly rather than uniformly.

**What is actually being sold** is then clear: the **accumulation rate** buys long-run throughput, and the
**ceiling** buys burst size. Two dials, and they correspond exactly to the two constraints below. A customer sitting
at their ceiling has bought all the burst they are entitled to, and there is nothing further to sell them until they
spend some.

**No exploit**, by the §12.6.3 check: holding an unspent balance is free, but spending it restarts the charging as
the bank refills, so over any long period a customer pays rate × time for what they consumed. The only free thing
costs the provider nothing.

##### 5.12.5.1a The two constraints do different jobs

| Constraint | Bounds |
|---|---|
| **Σ accumulation rates ≤ capacity** | the **steady state** — long-run demand cannot exceed what exists |
| **Σ ceilings** | the **transient** — the largest simultaneous burst, in total work |

**Derived.** If every account is at its ceiling and all burst at once, aggregate demand is `Σ ceilings` of work,
which is *served* rather than refused — it simply drains over `Σ ceilings / capacity` of wall clock. So the system is
stable with a bounded overshoot, and §5.12.4's serialization is what keeps that drain's latency distribution sane.

⚠️ Which leaves the sizing question rather than the structural one: how large a simultaneous burst is acceptable,
since that and not solvency is what `Σ ceilings` decides.

##### 5.12.5.2 Two things the bank forces a decision about

⚠️ **Overrun.** Admission tests the *expected* cost, and estimates are wrong. Killing a job at its estimate is
harsh and makes estimation adversarial; allowing unbounded debt invites abuse. The middle option — let the job
run, let the balance go negative, and refuse **new** starts until it recovers — preserves work already done and
self-limits, but needs a bound on how negative.

**Quota and billing merge here, unlike everywhere else.** §12.8.3 insists billing be offline and exact while quota
is online and approximate. For compute the bank balance *is* the quota and compute-hours consumed *are* the
billing record — one quantity doing both jobs. That works because compute is consumed in large lumps, where §12.8's
per-request metering needed the split precisely because requests are tiny and numerous. Worth stating so nobody
"fixes" the inconsistency.

#### 5.12.6 Scheduled compute-hours, for predictable recurring load

**Customers may schedule actual compute-hours for recurring work, at a somewhat higher price than normal
compute-hours. Unused scheduled hours become normal unused hours in the bank account. The system may not reserve
more scheduled compute at any instant than it has actual cores** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-16).

That is what lets a customer guarantee their predictable load has compute available **at high-contention times** —
the case §5.12.5.1a admits the bank alone cannot cover, since when everyone bursts together the drain is served but
slowly.

**The premium is correct under §12.1 rather than a revenue grab.** A reservation consumes the provider's ability to sell
that instant to anyone else, whether or not the customer uses it, so it has an opportunity cost even when idle —
and §12.1 says price the cost. What makes the product fair is that **the premium buys the guarantee while the
underlying hours survive**: unused, they fall back into the bank, so there is no use-it-or-lose-it. The customer
loses only the certainty they turned out not to need.

⚠️ Except at the ceiling. A customer already at their §5.12.5.1 balance cap who does not use their scheduled hours
**loses them**, because there is nowhere for them to convert to. That produces a sensible incentive — do not
over-schedule when your bank is already full — but it is a surprise, and it should be stated in the product rather
than discovered in an invoice.

##### 5.12.6.1 No overbooking makes the constraint a calendar, not a sum

Every previous instance of the partition rule (§13.4.3.4, §13.4.4.3, §5.12.5) has been a scalar: a set of floors
summing within a total. This one is different:

> **Σ scheduled(t) ≤ cores, for every instant t.**

**So admission is a feasibility check over an interval, not a comparison of two numbers**, and the ledger is
time-indexed. Two consequences follow. **Derived.**

**Recurring reservations must be stored as rules, not expanded instances.** "Every day at 03:00 for twenty
minutes" has no last occurrence, so expanding it is unbounded. The reservation is a period, a phase, a duration and
a width.

⚠️ **Feasibility over periodic patterns is the harder half.** Admitting a new reservation means finding the peak of
a sum of periodic step functions, which is exact only over the least common multiple of all periods — and mixed
hourly, daily and weekly periods make that large. Quantizing to a slot grid and checking one LCM window is the
obvious approach; bounding the admissible periods to divisors of a day is the cheaper one. Undesigned.

**Refusing to overbook is the conservative choice and worth keeping.** Providers normally overbook reservations
because utilization is never 100%, trading a rare broken promise for more revenue. Declining that is consistent
with §1.1's general refusal to promise what cannot be delivered: a reservation that sometimes fails is not a
guarantee, and this design's whole availability argument rests on distinguishing the two.

##### 5.12.6.2 How the two products fit inside one capacity

The bank's rates and the reservations both draw on the same cores, and they constrain capacity at different time
scales. Separating them is what keeps both promises honest:

| Requirement | Constraint | What it protects |
|---|---|---|
| **Solvency** | Σ bank rates + *average* scheduled load ≤ capacity | the bank's long-run promises |
| **Peak** | Σ scheduled(t) ≤ cores | the reservation guarantee at that instant |

**Derived.** Note it is the *average* scheduled load that enters solvency, not the peak — a reservation occupying
every core for one minute a day is 1/1440 of capacity in solvency terms, while being total at that minute.

⚠️ **But at a peak instant, best-effort work gets `cores − Σ scheduled(t)`, which may be zero.** That is the same
structural starvation as §13.4.3.4 and acceptable for the same reason, provided it is bounded — which argues for a
**cap on the reservable fraction** of the cluster, so bank-account holders always have something. Otherwise a
sufficiently popular reservation slot makes the bank's accumulation rate a promise that is briefly worthless.

**And DeLawson is its own first customer.** §13.5's daily snapshot, the billing job (§12.8), EC grouping (§13.5.1)
and the independence audit (§5.6.8) are exactly predictable recurring load. So the system should hold scheduled
reservations for them — and §12.6.4 requires that cost to be tracked rather than absorbed silently, which makes the
system's own reservations the first entry in that ledger.

#### 5.8.2 How many cores a ring process can use is the number to measure

**There will be some average number of cores a ring process can use before the
exclusive-lock work leaves the others idle, and it has to be measured** (Asserted,
Bob, 2026-08-17). It is Amdahl's law with the serial fraction being whatever share of
a ring's work is persisted:

| Share under the exclusive lock | Cores one ring process can use | Rings to fill 32 cores | To fill 64 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 5% | 20 | 2 | 3 |
| 10% | 10 | 3 | 6 |
| 20% | 5 | 6 | 13 |
| 35% | 2.9 | 11 | 22 |
| 50% | 2 | 16 | 32 |

**Derived.** So the three numbers — the exclusive share, cores per ring process, and
rings per machine — are one relation with one unknown. An earlier draft of this section
asserted "one ring keeps about one core busy", which is the 100% row and much too
pessimistic.

**The estimate to design against: cores per ring process is probably between 2 and 50,
and 8 is a good guess** (Guess, Bob, 2026-08-17). Reading the relation from that side:

| Cores per ring process | Implied exclusive share | Rings to fill 32 cores | To fill 64 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2 — the pessimistic end | 50% | 16 | 32 |
| **8 — the guess** | **12.5%** | **4** | **8** |
| 50 — the optimistic end | 2% | 1 — one ring more than fills it | 2 |

Which is consistent with around ten rings per machine on a machine of a few dozen
cores, and it says what the range costs: at the pessimistic end a machine wants a few
dozen rings and pays §5.8.1's failover and stream-list costs for them; at the
optimistic end one or two rings would fill the machine and role mixing (below) becomes
the binding reason for more.

⚠️ **And it varies by user** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17), because what share of the
work is persisted is a property of the workload: a read-heavy tenant persists almost
nothing and fills many cores per ring, a write-heavy one fills few. So *P* is not one
fleet-wide number derived once — **which is a third argument for many rings per
machine**: a machine holding rings for many tenants sees the average of their mixes
rather than one tenant's, so the number it should be configured with is stable even
though the per-ring figure is not.

⚠️ **The measurement is not "how fast is a ring".** It is the *share* of the work that
has to be serialized, because that is what bounds the parallelism however fast each
part is. A ring twice as fast with the same share fills the same number of cores.

**And role mixing wants several rings for a second, independent reason.** A machine is
primary for a ring or it is not, so with one ring its CPU load is feast or famine. The
count of primary roles is binomial, so the swing narrows as 1/√*R*:

| Rings per machine | Primary roles, mean (ring of 5) | Spread |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.2 | 200% |
| 5 | 1.0 | 89% |
| 10 | 2.0 | **63%** |
| 40 | 8.0 | 32% |

**Derived.** Which says something useful about *why* the answer is around ten rather
than around one hundred: the smoothing is a diminishing return, and by ten the swing
is already a third of what a single ring gives, while §5.8.1's failover cost and the
stream-list cost both keep rising with *P*.

## 6. Size limits and sealing

An extent seals when it hits **either** limit, whichever comes first:

| Limit | Value | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Logical | **4 GB** | An intra-extent logical offset fits in 32 bits. |
| Physical | **32 MB compressed** (initial guess) | Bounds compaction cost, repair granularity, and open-extent memory. |

Also bounding the physical limit from below: it must stay **above ~8 MB** so an
HDD seek is small relative to scanning the extent. A seek plus rotation is
~10 ms; 32 MB at ~150 MB/s is ~213 ms, so the seek is under 5% overhead. At
8 MB it is ~19%.

**Consequence: extent size is data-dependent.** Which limit binds depends
entirely on compressibility:

| Data | Ratio | Binds first | Logical span | Physical |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Incompressible (already-compressed media) | ~1× | physical | ~32 MB | 32 MB |
| Typical text / structured records | ~3–4× | physical | ~100–130 MB | 32 MB |
| Highly redundant (logs, sparse columns) | ~30× | physical | ~1 GB | 32 MB |
| Pathologically redundant | ≥128× | **logical** | 4 GB | ≤32 MB |

So **the physical limit binds almost always**, and the 4 GB logical cap is
reached only past a 128:1 ratio. The logical cap is best understood not as a
normal sealing trigger but as the guarantee that keeps intra-extent logical
offsets 32 bits wide.

A single object can therefore hold wildly heterogeneous extents — a 32 MB span
beside a 1 GB span — so nothing may assume uniform extent size. All navigation
is by cumulative totals (§4), which is indifferent to this.

### 6.1 EC recovery cost is probably what limits it, and 32 MB is a guess

The table above lists three reasons for an upper bound — compaction cost, repair granularity, and
open-extent memory. **Of those, EC recovery cost is probably the limiting one, and 32 MB compressed
is a guess until it can be measured** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17).

The reason it is the binding side is that **an extent is the unit of repair**. A fragment belongs to
one extent, so repairing a loss reads *k* fragments of that extent (§4.3.2) and cannot read less.
Total recovery bandwidth for a dead device is the same whatever the extent size — the same bytes come
back either way — but the *unit* is not, and three things follow from the unit rather than the total:

- **Exposure is per group, and it ends when that group's repair finishes.** §13.2.2's loss estimate
  is driven by how long an individual group sits degraded, not by when the fleet-wide recovery
  finishes, and losses go as the cube of that window.
- **A repair is the smallest thing that can be scheduled, retried, or interrupted.** §13.4 sorts
  repairs by amortized cost; a coarser unit is a coarser sort, and work lost to an interruption is
  a whole unit.
- **Nothing may reconstruct on the read path** (§9.8), so a repair's latency is not hidden behind a
  read — it is the whole of the recovery for that group.

Pushing the other way, and already derived: an extent must stay **above ~8 MB** so an HDD seek
amortizes (above), and it must stay **large** so that SN metadata per byte stays affordable (§14.1)
— halving the extent size doubles the extent records for the same data, and §14.1.2 says record
count is what decides how many machines an object needs.

#### 6.2 The physical cap bounds the first write, not the extent for life

**32 MB compressed is a bound on what a sealing extent may accumulate, not a property an extent keeps**
(Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17). Recompression during coalescing (§8.1.4.4) or compaction (§10) may leave an
extent larger than the cap, and that is fine: the cap exists to bound what one extent costs to write,
repair and hold open, and once the bytes are written none of those are decided by it any more.

⚠️ **So nothing may treat it as an invariant.** Two places in this document lean on extent size in ways
worth re-reading with that in mind: §4.6.4's address arithmetic, which sizes a slot from extents per
device, and §4.3.2.3's requirement that **EC group members have equal physical length** — a
recompression that changes one member's size has to preserve that, which makes "recompress freely" and
"members are equal" two constraints that meet. Neither is broken by the soft cap, but both are stated
elsewhere as though the cap were fixed.

**And the obvious prior-art comparison is not like-for-like** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17). Cosmos's
extents were *"typically a few hundred megabytes"* (Cited: [SCOPE](http://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol1/1454166.pdf),
§2.1), and **that limit is logical, as almost everyone's is, since almost nobody compresses.** So it
compares against DeLawson's **4 GB logical** cap, which is an order of magnitude larger — not against
the 32 MB compressed one.

⚠️ **What is unusual is that a compressed cap exists at all.** It is a second limit, on a quantity most
systems do not have separately, and it exists because the costs it bounds are costs in *stored* bytes:
EC recovery reads *k* stored fragments, compaction rewrites stored bytes, an open extent occupies
stored bytes. A store whose logical and stored sizes coincide needs one cap for both. **So what #50 is
measuring is the stored-byte bound**, and the logical cap can stay where it is.

⚠️ **So the number is bracketed by two measurements neither of which has been made.** What would
replace the guess: repair time for one extent as a function of its size on the target media,
including the code's read amplification, and how well repair parallelizes as the unit shrinks —
against the seek-amortization floor (#6) and the metadata cost per byte. 32 MB is a placeholder
sitting between two bounds, chosen because it is comfortably inside both, and #50 is the work of
replacing it.

---

### 6.3 What it means for a *stream* to be sealed

**A stream is sealed if it is not allowed any more appends or concatenates** (Asserted, Bob,
2026-08-17). That is a statement about permission, not about fullness — and it is the definition to
keep, because fullness is only one of the reasons it happens.

**The reason it makes sense is the middle of an object.** An unkeyed object is append-only, and §3's
whole argument is that record numbers must be stable: an insert in the middle renumbers everything
after it. An object made of several streams therefore has exactly one stream that may take an
append — the last — and **every stream before it is sealed by construction**, because appending to a
middle stream would insert records into the middle of the object.

Two things follow, and the second is what the implementation rests on:

- **Sealing is what makes the next stream's numbering safe.** Once a stream is sealed with *R*
  records starting at object-local record *F*, the stream after it starts at *F* + *R* and that never
  moves. A stream that could still grow would make every record number above it provisional.
- **A sealed stream's record count is knowable, and an open one's is not.** So a DN can say which
  stream holds record *N* for all the sealed ones by arithmetic, and for the last one it can only say
  "at or past its first record" and let the tiers below answer. That asymmetry is not an
  implementation shortcut; it is what "sealed" means.

**And concatenation is covered by the same word.** §8.6.1 builds an object by concatenating sealed
streams, so a stream that is a *source* is unaffected — but a sealed stream may not be a *target*, for
the same reason it may not take an append: it would renumber what follows.

Why a stream seals in the first place is a separate question with a separate answer: its SN's memory
is what bounds how many extents it can hold (§14.1), so a stream fills. `extents.per_stream` is that
limit, and on a test cluster it is set low so a stream sealing is the common path (§17.12).

### 6.4 Sealing on request, at all three levels

**There are requests to seal an object, its streams, and its extents** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-19).
Sealing so far has been something that *happens* — an extent fills (§6), a stream runs out of extents
(§6.3), an instance breaks (§8.1.7.4). This is sealing because somebody asked.

**It exists because concatenation requires sealed inputs** (§8.6.1). That is not a nicety: §8.6 makes
parallel-partitions-then-concatenate the only way to build a large object at aggregate bandwidth, so
a writer that has finished a partition needs a way to say so. Without a seal request the writer's
options are to wait for the partition to happen to fill or to leave the extent open for ever, and
neither is a way to finish a job.

**And for an unkeyed object it is one extent's worth of work, which is the whole payoff of two earlier
decisions.** §6.3 makes every stream before the last sealed by construction, and §8.1.1a-7 gives an
unkeyed object exactly one unsealed extent. So:

| Sealing | Unkeyed | Keyed |
|---|---|---|
| an **extent** | its primary seals it | the same |
| a **stream** | mark it closed, then seal its **one** open extent | the same |
| an **object** | mark it closed, then its **one** open stream, then that stream's **one** open extent | several unsealed extents at once, so a fan-out |

**So the three levels are one path with different starting points**, and only keyed objects make it a
recursion worth worrying about. The partial-failure question below is correspondingly small for
unkeyed and real for keyed.

**Top-down, and the order is not a preference.** Mark the container closed *before* sealing its
contents, because the other order races: seal the open extent first and a concurrent append asks the
SN for the next one, which it is still entitled to give. Closing the object stops new streams,
closing the stream stops new extents, and only then is there a fixed thing to seal. Same direction as
§13.1's sync loops, for the same reason — the level above is what can still create work.

#### 6.4.1 Ask the primary first, and fall back to failure-mode sealing

⚠️ **A seal request must try the normal path before the SN-coordinated one** (Asserted, Bob,
2026-08-19): ask the primary of each open extent to seal the ordinary way, and only fall back to
§8.1.7's failure-mode sealing if that does not work.

**The cost argument is the obvious one.** The normal seal is the primary saying where the extent ends,
which it knows because it assigned every offset — one hop. Failure-mode sealing is a quorum read:
poll the instances, discard the smallest *I* − *Q* responses, take the order statistic, and coordinate
the result at the SN. Several round trips and a decision, against one hop and an answer.

**And a user-triggered seal is not a failure**, which is why the cheap path usually works. Nothing has
gone wrong; a writer has finished. The primary is almost certainly alive, because the request arrives
on the heels of appends it was just serving.

**The stronger argument is that the fallback produces a worse answer, not merely a slower one.**
§8.1.7.1 shows failure-mode sealing never seals *below* the durable length but may seal *above* it —
which is a commitment to repair up to that length rather than a claim the bytes are there. A normal
seal has no such gap: the primary knows the durable length exactly, so it seals exactly there.

| | Round trips | Seals at | Leaves behind |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Normal**, via the primary | one | the durable length, **exactly** | nothing |
| **Failure-mode**, via the SN | several | at or **above** it | a repair obligation, and possibly a hole to fill |

So trying the cheap path first **costs nothing when it works and loses nothing when it does not**,
which is the shape that makes a fallback unambiguously right rather than a tuning question. What is
left to choose is how long to try before giving up, which is §8.1.7.2's question and not a new one.

**A requested normal seal quiesces the extent rather than cutting it.** The primary stops accepting
appends, lets the ones in flight settle, and seals at the durable length that results. So it discards
nothing, truncates nothing, and has no interaction with §7.2.4 at all — which is worth saying because
"seal" now names two operations that look similar and differ in exactly that respect:

| Trigger | Discards anything? |
|---|---|
| a request (§6.4), or an extent filling (§6) | **no** — it seals where the bytes already stop |
| handover or a broken instance (§7.2.4, §8.1.7.4) | **yes**, above the durable watermark, which is why that path must seal |

⚠️ **A writer racing a seal loses, and there is no way to be kind about it.** An append accepted but
not yet durable when the seal lands is refused, and the writer cannot retry into the next extent
because the stream is closed and cannot be given one. That is the correct outcome — the object is
being sealed, so appends to it are ending — but it is user-visible, and a writer that wants a clean
finish should stop appending before asking.

**Seal requests are idempotent.** Sealing something already sealed succeeds and reports what it came
to, because a retry after a timeout is the ordinary case and the fallback above makes timeouts
expected.

⚠️ **What a partial seal answers is undecided.** A keyed object with many unsealed extents may seal
most and fail one, and "ok" is wrong while a bare failure throws away the work that succeeded. The
shape §9.1.3 already uses — say what was done and what to ask for next — looks right, and idempotence
is what makes retrying the whole request cheap. Left open (§16.134).

## 7. The storage pipeline

Every extent body goes through the same pipeline, and the order is forced:

```
records → framing → compression → encryption → replication → (seal) → erasure coding
```

- **Compress before encrypt.** Ciphertext is incompressible, so the reverse
  order gives no compression at all — and ratio is what the customer is billed
  on (§12).
- **Encrypt before erasure-code.** EC is linear over whatever bytes it is given,
  so encoding ciphertext lets repair and re-encoding proceed on ENs with no
  access to keys.

### 7.1 Block alignment

Whole-extent compression and whole-extent encryption would both destroy random
access: you cannot decompress or decrypt from the middle. So both operate on
**blocks**, and the block boundary is what the sparse index points at (§9.3).
One granule is one compression unit and one encryption unit:

- read the extent's index, find the granule containing the target,
- read exactly that granule from an EN, decrypt it, decompress it, scan it by
  framing.

Granule size is therefore a three-way decision — index density, compression
ratio (larger blocks compress better), and read amplification (larger blocks
waste more per point read) — not the purely device-driven choice §9.3 describes.

⚠️ The device-tuned granularities of §9.3 (1 MB HDD, 20 KB SSD) were chosen for
seek amortization alone — §7.1.1 derives them. 20 KB is small enough to hurt
compression ratio noticeably, and ratio is billable. The SSD granularity may need
to rise, or compression blocks may need to span several index granules.

Because block size is device-dependent and larger blocks compress better, **the
compression block size is a durable property of the extent** — which is what makes
media class durable too, and forbids mixed-media extents (§7.4.2).

**The cost target constrains where these stages run.** §1.2 requires ENs to be
computationally cheap — a server carrying 150 disks cannot also carry the CPU to
compress at line rate, since that CPU would blow the 5% budget it is supposed to fit
inside. **So compression should not run on ENs.** Encryption is a weaker case, since
AES-NI is cheap enough to plausibly survive the budget, which matters because §7.3.1
has ENs caching keys and therefore doing crypto. That asymmetry — compression
elsewhere, encryption possibly on the EN — is a constraint on §5.9.2's open question,
not an answer to it.

#### 7.1.1 Where the granularities come from: seek cost equals scan cost

The device figures §9.3 uses are not arbitrary. The break-even byte count is

```
B = access_latency x sequential_bandwidth
```

— the point at which the time to seek equals the time to scan the bytes you skipped.

| Device | Latency | Bandwidth | Break-even | Index interval | Min read |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| HDD | ~10 ms (seek + rotation) | ~200 MB/s | **2 MB** | 1 MB | 1 MB |
| NVMe SSD | ~10 us | ~4 GB/s | **40 KB** | 20 KB | 20 KB |

**Derived**, reproducing Bob's 2 MB and 40 KB.

**The interval is half the break-even, and "half" has a reason.** Once scan time falls below seek time, halving
the index interval again cuts total read cost by at most a third while doubling index size. At half break-even
the seek is 2/3 of the read and further densification buys almost nothing. The same number falls out from the
opposite direction: if a seek is being paid at all, read at least half break-even so it is amortized. Two
independent arguments landing on one number is why this is a design point rather than a taste.

**The HDD figure is robust; the SSD figure is not.** HDD spans 1-3 MB across plausible drives (5-13 ms,
200-250 MB/s) — +/-50%, safe to build on. SSD spans **4 KB to 320 KB**, an 80x range: 10 us is Optane-class or
a very good NVMe at queue depth 1, NAND NVMe is 80-100 us (giving 320 KB), and at high queue depth a modern
drive reaches full bandwidth at 4 K random, pushing break-even down to the page size. Since §1.4 has DeLawson
issuing zillions of tiny requests in parallel, **queues will be deep**, which argues the effective figure is
well below 40 KB. ⚠️ This is the number to measure earliest; it is the only one in this section that spans two
orders of magnitude across defensible assumptions.

**Intervals must be measured in physical bytes, not logical.** The trade is about bytes crossing the device,
and compression ratios span 1x to 128x (§12.3), so a logical-interval index would give wildly different
physical scans per object. §9.3 already stores physical offsets; this is the reason.

**The index sizing then works out with a symmetry worth noticing.**

- **HDD, 1 MB interval, 32 MB extent** — 32 entries, ~384 B per extent. That is ~4x the ~100 B SN extent budget
  of §4.7, so it cannot live on SN; it lives in the extent, EN-side. Per EN at 2 PB / 32 MB = 62.5 M extents
  that is ~24 GB, which is affordable to **cache in EN RAM** — and worth caching, because a cold read that
  fetches the index first costs two seeks and doubles the expensive thing.
- **SSD, 20 KB interval** — ~1,600 entries, ~19 KB per extent: 0.06% space overhead, far too much to cache
  broadly. So it stays on the device and is fetched on demand, which is fine precisely because SSD seeks are
  cheap.

The device with the expensive seek gets the small cacheable index; the device with the cheap seek gets the large
index it can afford to fetch. Both fall out of the same ratio, so this is not a coincidence to be maintained by
hand.

#### 7.1.2 Compression improves HDD read bandwidth and degrades SSD read bandwidth

Compression helps *bandwidth* only when the decompressor is faster than the device it is feeding. Reading `B`
logical bytes at ratio `r` with decompression speed `D` takes `B/(r·BW) + B/D`, which beats `B/BW` exactly when

```
D > BW · r/(r-1)          (at r = 2: D > 2·BW)
```

| Device | Bandwidth | Threshold *D* at r = 2 | LZ4, ~4 GB/s/core |
|---|---|---|---|
| HDD | 200 MB/s | 400 MB/s | **wins**, ~10x over |
| SATA SSD | 550 MB/s | 1.1 GB/s | **wins** |
| NVMe | 4 GB/s | 8 GB/s | **loses** |

**Derived**, and it confirms Bob's statement that no codec is fast enough to improve SSD read performance —
zstd at ~1-2 GB/s loses even on SATA. The general rule, which is what should be recorded rather than the
verdict, is that **compression helps when device bandwidth is below about half the decompressor's speed**. Over
a build measured in years the device side moves and the codec side does not.

**This does not make compression optional.** DeLawson compresses regardless, for capacity and for §12.3's
physical billing. What the arithmetic says is that on an SSD, compression is simultaneously a capacity win and a
bandwidth loss — and that is **not a conflict the system has to adjudicate**, because physical billing already
makes it the user's economic choice: declining compression costs them more physical bytes and buys them
bandwidth. One more case where billing proportional to cost removes a policy decision instead of adding one.

#### 7.1.3 Compression usually pays for itself, because the bytes move more than once

§7.1.2 asks only whether compression beats a *single* device read, and on that test NVMe fails it. That is
the wrong test. **Compression reduces network traffic and the bytes written to HDD or SSD as well**
(Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-15), and the saving is realized every time the compressed bytes move or are stored.

Counting the crossings a logical byte actually makes:

| Crossing | Times | Medium |
|---|---|---|
| client to primary | 1 | network |
| primary broadcast to four ENs (§8.1.2) | 4 | network |
| write to device | 1 | disk |
| reads over the object's life | *E* | disk |
| repair reads (§4.3.3.2d) | rare, large multiplier | network |

So the break-even compression speed is the single-crossing threshold **divided by the number of times the
saving is realized**. Writing `C` for compression speed and using `r = 2`:

> win iff `1/C < (1 - 1/r) x [ 4/W_net + 1/W_write + E/W_read ]`

| Device | Threshold `C` | LZ4 compress, ~0.6 GB/s/core |
|---|---|---|
| HDD, 200 MB/s, `E` = 1 | **~194 MB/s** | **wins by 3x** |
| NVMe, ~2-4 GB/s, `E` = 1 | **~2.4 GB/s** | loses by 4x |

**Derived.** Two things worth noticing in those numbers.

**On HDD the disk dominates and the network is almost irrelevant** — 5 x 10^-9 s/byte for the two disk
crossings against 3.2 x 10^-10 for all four network crossings, a factor of 15. So the network argument does
*not* rescue compression on fast devices: on NVMe the two terms are comparable and both are small, which is
why the conclusion matches §7.1.2's rather than overturning it.

**But `E` is the term that decides it**, and `E` is a workload property, not a hardware one. Warm storage
read a few times over its life pushes the HDD threshold well below 194 MB/s, at which point even zstd pays.
An object written once and never read pays nothing back at all. ⚠️ Nothing in the design measures `E`, and
§13.5's snapshots are where it would come from.

**And compression improves durability, which is not a cost argument at all.** §4.3.2.2a shows repair is
network-bound, and a repair window is bytes-to-move divided by bandwidth. Compression cuts the numerator
directly, so it shortens every repair window in §4.3.3 by the compression ratio. That is a rare event per
byte, so it barely registers in a steady-state cost ledger — but §1.1.1 says data loss happens during
disasters, and during a disaster it is the only term that matters.

⚠️ **This weakens §7.1's conclusion that compression must not run on ENs, and the tension should be
resolved rather than left implicit.** That conclusion rests on compressing at NIC line rate, which needs
~21 cores. But per §8.1.4.1 each byte is compressed **once cluster-wide**, by the primary, not once per
instance — so an EN's compression load is its share of ingest, which §8.1.4.5 puts at ~63 MB/s sustained.
That is **0.1 of a core**, not 21. The 21-core figure binds only if bursts to line rate must never be
throttled, and §1.4 says throughput is what matters and a burst may queue. Per §0, the arithmetic wins and
the label gets updated: either §7.1's rule needs restating as "must not compress at line rate", or the
sustained-rate case needs a reason it is wrong.

### 7.2 Encryption details

- Block-granular mode with a per-block IV/tweak derived from
  `(extent_id, block_index)`, so blocks are independently decryptable and
  identical plaintext in two places does not yield identical ciphertext.
- Keys are per-extent, but **derived, not stored** — see §7.3.
- Sealed extents are immutable, so keys never need rotation in place; **rotation
  happens by rewriting during compaction** (§10), which is a rewrite anyway.
- Decryption happens **on the EN** (§5.9.2), which runs only signed executables (§1.5).
- **Everything is encrypted on the wire and on disk.** Not only extent bodies: all
  messages are encrypted too (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-15).

#### 7.2.1 AEGIS-128X2, and why encryption is free where compression is not

**The working codec is AEGIS-128X2**, measured by Bob at **20 GB/s on a single core**,
with the whole 16-core box topping out near **90 GB/s** — so the box saturates well
below 16x one core, as a memory-bandwidth ceiling rather than a compute one. It is an
AEAD, so it **authenticates and encrypts in one pass**.

**That settles the cost question §7.1 left asymmetric**, and the arithmetic is worth
writing out because the two stages differ by two orders of magnitude:

| Stage | Per-core throughput | Cores at 12.5 GB/s line rate | Cores at 63 MB/s sustained |
|---|---|---|---|
| AEGIS-128X2 encrypt+authenticate | ~20 GB/s | **0.63** | 0.003 |
| LZ4 *compression* | ~0.6 GB/s | **~21** | **0.1** |

**Derived.** Encryption fits §1.2's 5% server budget at *either* rate, which is why
§7.3.1 can safely cache keys on ENs. Compression fits only at the sustained rate — see
§7.1.3, which argues the sustained column is the relevant one because each byte is
compressed once cluster-wide rather than once per instance, and flags the tension with
§7.1's rule as needing resolution.

**KS uses 256-bit keys and 256-bit encryption** (Asserted, Bob) — deliberately overkill,
because the master keys are the most important secrets in the system and the volume
protected by them is negligible, so the stronger primitive costs nothing. Bulk extent
and message encryption stays at 128-bit. See §7.3.

**Authentication in the same pass is a larger dividend than the speed**, and it removes
a layer the design would otherwise have needed:

- **The AEAD tag is the checksum.** No separate CRC layer, and no question about whether
  the checksum covers what the encryption covers.
- **Every stored block is self-verifying**, which is exactly what EC repair needs: a
  corrupt source is detected *before* it is used to rederive a lost cell, so corruption
  cannot propagate into parity (§4.3.2.3).
- **§13.1.9's cold sweep gets its detector for free**, and an exact one rather than a
  probabilistic one.
- **§4.3.4 observes that erasure coding faithfully preserves corrupt data.**
  Authentication is what separates "faithfully preserved" from "correct", so this
  partially answers it — for corruption in flight or at rest, though not for logical
  corruption written by a bug through the normal path.

The tag must be **per block**, not per extent, or random access is lost and §7.1's
argument for block granularity collapses.

#### 7.2.2 Recompression has no machine to run on

**Recompression needs significant CPU *and* a node running only signed executables**
(Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-15). Those two requirements do not currently intersect:

| Candidate | CPU to spare? | Signed-only? |
|---|---|---|
| EN | **little** — §7.1, §1.2 give it almost none | yes |
| Compute | yes | **no** — it runs user code (§1.5) |
| DN, SN | some, but sized for metadata rings (§5.8) | yes |
| FE | undesigned | yes |
| **A signed compute tier** — Compute's shape without user code | yes | yes |

⚠️ So the fleet **as originally specified** had no machine with both properties. That is a
gap and not a detail, because §10 makes compaction the place where recompression, EC
re-encoding, key rotation, media migration and code promotion all happen, and every one of
them needs plaintext and CPU.

**Bob's phrasing names the likely resolution**: the work is done by the EN "or some other
signed DeLawson equivalent of a compute node" (2026-08-15). That last is a real machine
type rather than a hedge — **Compute's hardware shape without Compute's user code**, and
therefore permitted to hold keys under §1.5. It is the bottom row of the table above.

#### 7.2.2.1 The gap is narrower than it first looked

Two findings shrink it, and what remains is worth naming precisely.

**Initial compression is not in the problem at all.** §8.1.4.1 puts it in the `delawson`
client library, so no compression happens on the ingest path inside the datacenter.

**Migration recompression fits on the EN.** The common-to-dedicated migration (§8.1.4.4)
recompresses each byte **once**, at the ingest rate — ~63 MB/s sustained per EN
(§8.1.4.5), which is ~0.1 of a core for LZ4. §7.1's 21-core objection was computed at NIC
line rate, which this is not.

| Job | Times per byte | Cores per EN, sustained |
|---|---|---|
| Initial compression | — | **0**, it is the client's (§8.1.4.1) |
| Migration recompression | once | **~0.1** |
| Repeated keyed base-plus-log compaction | many | multiplies with compaction frequency |

**So the live gap is repeated compaction of keyed objects**, where the same bytes are
rewritten every time a log merges into a base, and CPU scales with compaction frequency
rather than with ingest. That is also the case §8.1.1a-10 shows is already trading against
hint validity, so compaction frequency now has a **fourth** term: write amplification, read
amplification, hint hit rate, and recompression CPU.

It should be settled before compaction is built, because it decides what compaction *is*:
a background loop on an existing tier, or a machine type of its own.

#### 7.2.3 A user who encrypts first pays for it, automatically

Users are welcome to encrypt before sending (§5.9.2). The consequences are not
prohibitions, they are prices:

- **Their data will not compress**, so they pay more physical bytes under §12.3 — which
  is the correct outcome rather than a penalty, and needs no policy to enforce.
- **DeLawson cannot re-frame their records** during coalescing (§8.2.1), so the
  read-path translation §8.2.1 wants to remove stays.
- **Their records are opaque to Compute**, so §5.12's near-data work cannot see them
  without the user's own keys.

That is the §12.1 pattern once more: billing proportional to cost turns what would have
to be an administered restriction into a self-enforcing trade.

#### 7.2.4 One key and one IV may cover one plaintext, which makes an offset write-once

**The same key and salt may never be used twice for different data** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-19).
This is the AEAD rule rather than a DeLawson choice, and it is not a degradation when broken: under
a nonce-respecting construction, IV reuse across two plaintexts leaks their XOR, and AEGIS's
nonce-misuse profile also hands over the ability to forge tags under that key.

**Most of the requirement is already met by construction**, which is worth stating before the hole:

| Level | Distinct because |
|---|---|
| across days | the daily master key is fresh (§7.3) |
| across SNs | the SN-master key is derived per SN (§7.3) |
| across extents | the extent key is derived from `(SnId, ExtentId, creation second)` (§7.3.3), and the second makes even a reused id a different key |
| across blocks in an extent | `block IV = f(extent id, block index)` (§7.2) |
| across wire segments | a connection prefix, a direction byte and a segment counter — §17.5a settled this and stated the invariant explicitly |

So the whole question reduces to one: **can a block index be used twice, for different data, within
one extent identity?**

⚠️ **It can, in exactly one place: truncation above the durable watermark** (§8.1.1a). Handover
discards a suffix nobody agreed to, and subsequent appends then land at offsets the discarded blocks
occupied — **same extent identity, same block index, different plaintext.** The severity is not
softened by those bytes being unreadable to users:

| | |
|---|---|
| The discarded ciphertext | was written to disks, and up to 3 of 4 instances may hold it |
| The replacement ciphertext | goes to the same offsets, under the same key and the same IV |
| What an attacker needs besides the two | **nothing** — the XOR of the ciphertexts is the XOR of the plaintexts |
| Who reads whole instances anyway | §13.1's sync loops and EC repair (§4.3.2.3) |

**Three fixes, and they are not equally good:**

| Fix | Cost |
|---|---|
| an **epoch** in the IV derivation, bumped per truncation, recorded with the extent | ⚠️ every instance must agree on the bump — consensus on a value in the write path, which is what §8.1.3 keeps the SN out of the path to avoid. An instance that missed a bump reuses the IV, so the failure mode is silent |
| a **per-block nonce carried with the block** rather than derived | 16 B per block on the wire and on disk, and it must be stored to decrypt — it stops being derived, which is the property §7.3 is built on |
| **a truncation seals the extent** | one extra extent per handover event |

**Settled: sealing** (Asserted, Bob and reasoning here, 2026-08-19). §8.1.1c already establishes that
sealing an extent short is free and preferable to padding, and §6 permits sealing at any size, so
this needs no new mechanism — only a new trigger for one that exists and is exercised. And it
converts a cryptographic side condition into an invariant that is local, checkable, and stated
positively:

> **Within one extent identity, an offset is written at most once, ever.**

**That invariant is worth more than the rule that motivated it**, which is the argument for
preferring it to the epoch:

- it is what makes §8.1.1a-3's fixed-offset exactly-once check sound — the check compares content at
  an expected offset, which presumes the offset has one history;
- it is what makes a sealed extent's bytes a function of its name, which is what EC's byte-identical
  instances need (§4.3.2.3);
- it needs no field, no agreement, and no bump that can be missed. Nothing can silently violate it,
  because the only thing that could is now required to seal.

⚠️ **What it costs, stated plainly: a flapping primary produces short extents**, and extent count is
what bounds an SN's memory (§14.1). So this couples primary stability to metadata growth where
before it did not. The coupling is bounded by the handover rate, which #56 has to settle regardless —
but the cost now falls on a different budget than it did, and #56 should hear about it.

**And the rule applies upward, to anything else under a cluster-wide key.** §9.1.3.5's capability
authenticates and encrypts nothing, so it has no keystream to leak — but it is built from the same
primitive, so it **carries a salt in its plaintext prefix** rather than resting on an argument that a
fixed nonce is safe for MAC-only use. `(FE id, monotone counter)` suffices and needs no RNG: the FE
id is 2 bytes by §5.10.4, and seeding the counter from the clock means a restart cannot repeat one.
That is §17.5a's construction reused, and reusing it is the point — **a nonce discipline that is
stated once and applied everywhere is the only kind that survives**.

### 7.3 The key hierarchy: daily, derived, and scoped by SN

Per-extent keys are right, but *storing* them is arithmetically impossible. At 32
bytes each:

| Keys for | Count | Stored size |
|---|---|---|
| Extents in a 1 EB physical cluster | 3.0 × 10^10 | **954 GB** |
| Extents in one maximal object | 5.5 × 10^13 | **1.75 PB** |
| Objects, if a trillion tiny ones exist | 10^12 | **32 TB** |

None of those can live in a consensus ring. So the hierarchy stores almost nothing
and derives the rest:

```
daily master key         randomly generated, one per day
                         lives ONLY in KS; on KS disk, encrypted at rest
  → daily SN-master key  = derive(daily master key, SN)
                         cached on ENs
    → extent key         = derive(the correct daily SN-master key, extent)
      → block IV         = f(extent id, block index)        (§7.2)
```

Master keys are **random, not derived** — there is no key above them, which is
what makes the layer below unrecoverable without KS.

**The authoritative key store is kilobytes.** One random key per day:

| Active days | Keys | Size |
|---|---|---|
| 1 year | 365 | 12 KB |
| 10 years | 3,650 | 117 KB |
| 100 years | 36,500 | **1.2 MB** |

A century of master keys is about a megabyte, and — unlike the tenant-keyed scheme
this replaces — the figure does not depend on how many customers or objects exist.
Old daily keys must be kept as long as any extent encrypted under them survives,
which this makes free.

⚠️ **Keys are generated lazily, and the store is indexed by *active* day, not elapsed
day.** §1.3 allows a cluster to lie dormant for geological spans; marching one key
forward per elapsed day through a billion-year dormancy would mean 3.7 × 10^11 keys and
12 TB in a ring sized for a megabyte. A day with no extent creations needs no key, so
the store must be sparse and populated on demand.

#### 7.3.1 Two-dimensional scoping bounds the blast radius

**ENs cache daily SN-master keys.** This corrects §5.9.1: ENs are not keyless, and
an EN compromise is not limited to ciphertext.

But the exposure is bounded on two axes at once:

| Axis | Bounded by | Effect of a compromise |
|---|---|---|
| Time | daily rotation | only the days whose keys are cached |
| Space | per-SN derivation | only extents of the SNs whose keys are cached |

And critically, **the master keys never leave KS**, so no number of compromised ENs
ever yields the ability to derive a key for a different SN or a different day.
Deriving downward is easy and deriving upward is impossible, which is what makes
caching the middle layer acceptable.

#### 7.3.2 KS is unlocked by humans and hardware

Master keys are written to KS disks encrypted, under an **unlocking key derived
from a combination of operator-entered secrets and hardware devices**. That is the
true root of trust — and it is deliberately not something a machine can produce
alone.

Consequences worth being explicit about:

- **Cold start requires human action.** If every KS machine restarts at once, the
  master keys on disk cannot be decrypted until operators supply their secrets and
  the hardware devices are present. There is no fully automatic recovery from a
  total KS outage, by design. This is a security choice being paid for in
  availability, and it should be an owned decision rather than a discovered one.
  ⚠️ **But "total" is narrower than it reads, and §7.3.2.1 is the ladder.** The
  boundary is whether *any live process still holds the key*, not whether the ring
  has quorum — a ring that lost quorum heals itself without people, because
  membership is already committed and quorums of successive configurations
  intersect (§7.3.2.2). The ceremony is for the case where every member restarted.
- **There are two independent roots, and only one needs people.** §5.5.1's bootstrap root
  anchors the *object* hierarchy and lives in DN0's Raft state, so it needs no ceremony; the KS
  unlocking key anchors the *key* hierarchy and does. Since ring state is itself encrypted,
  KS must come up first — §5.5.1.1 gives the full cold-start order, which is acyclic precisely
  because KS is keyed by humans rather than by KS.

##### 7.3.2.1 A ladder of failure scales, and the boundary is memory rather than quorum

**KS has a ring** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-19), which turns "cold start requires human action" from one
blunt statement into four cases with very different costs. Each rung's price is proportional to how
rare it is, which is §1.1.1's shape — disasters, not steady state — applied to the key hierarchy.

| Scale | Recovered by | People? |
|---|---|---|
| **a member** returns, quorum live | **the ring unlocks it directly**: membership is a committed fact, so the quorum already attests that machine belongs | **no** |
| **quorum lost**, but some live process still holds the key | wait for a quorum of the last-known membership to assemble, then re-key them | **no** — see §7.3.2.2 |
| **every member restarted**, so the key is in no memory anywhere | present the unlocking key to a member, which **confirms it is the right one** | yes, whoever holds the key |
| **the organization gone**, hardware intact | reconstruct the unlocking key from **k of n shards** | yes, k custodians |

**The first rung is what makes ordinary operation automatic**, and it works because the ring already
knows something an outsider would have to be told: **membership is a committed fact** (§5.5.6.1), so a
returning member's right to be re-keyed is established by the quorum rather than by a human vouching
for it.

⚠️ **What that implies is worth stating rather than inferring: after the ceremony, the unlocking key —
or something equivalent — is live in KS members' memory.** It has to be, or a quorum could not hand a
returning member what it needs. That is the cost of rung one, and it sets the real boundary further down
the ladder: **the ceremony is needed when the key is in no memory anywhere**, not when quorum is lost.

⚠️ **It is also an oracle.** Rung one hands keys to a machine on the strength of committed membership,
which cannot speak to whether that machine's hardware was modified while it was down. §7.3.2.7 works
through the attack, why splitting the secret does not help, and the one structural answer.

##### 7.3.2.2 Losing quorum need not need people, and the reason is that quorums intersect

⚠️ **An earlier draft of this section put the ceremony at quorum loss, and that is wrong** (Asserted,
Bob, 2026-08-19, correcting it). **A still-up member has its own list of what machines are in the ring,
so it can refuse to hand out the key until a quorum of those machines is up, and then hand it out.**

The draft's mistake was conflating two different things a quorum is needed for:

| | Needs a live quorum? |
|---|---|
| **Committing a new membership change** — admitting a machine that was not a member | **yes** |
| **Acting on a membership already committed** — re-keying a machine the log already says belongs | **no.** Any surviving member has that in its log |

So the attestation a returning member needs **already happened**, before the outage. Nothing new has to
be decided, and a survivor is applying an old committed decision rather than making a fresh one.

**But a lone survivor must still not act alone, and the reason is staleness rather than authority.** Its
log may predate a committed change — most sharply, an *eviction*: if the ring removed a machine because
it was compromised, a member with a stale log still lists it, and handing the key out on that view
hands it to exactly the machine the ring expelled.

**Waiting for a quorum of the last-known membership fixes that, by the property Raft is built on:**

> **Quorums of successive configurations intersect.** So any quorum assembled from a known
> configuration necessarily contains at least one member that knows about any change committed after
> that configuration.

Which means the assembled group can elect a leader, discover the current committed membership — the
most up-to-date log wins, which is ordinary leader election — and *then* re-key whoever actually
belongs. The stale view is corrected before it is acted on, rather than being trusted or refused.

**So the ladder's second rung is automatic**, and that materially improves the availability posture: a
KS ring can lose quorum and still heal itself with no human, provided one process stayed up. The
ceremony is for the case where that is not true.

⚠️ **Two things this needs, and the second is a real gap:**

- **A survivor holding the key must refuse everything while it waits**, and the wait is unbounded. That
  is correct — it makes nothing worse — but it must be *observable* that KS is waiting-and-savable
  rather than broken, or an operator will start the ceremony unnecessarily, or worse, rebuild.
- ⚠️ **This is only as strong as machine authentication.** "A quorum of those machines is up" is
  meaningless if an attacker can stand up four processes claiming to be four members. So a machine's
  identity has to be cryptographically established, and the credential that does it cannot be behind
  the key it is trying to obtain. §5.5.6.3's signed topology is the right half of KS for it to live in,
  but nothing yet says what a machine's identity actually is (§16.137).

##### 7.3.2.3 The ring stores a verifier, so a wrong key fails loudly

**An authentication for the unlocking key is stored in the ring's snapshot and log** (Asserted, Bob,
2026-08-19), so anyone with the key can tell it to a member and the member can confirm it is the right
one. Without this, a wrong key is indistinguishable from a right one until something downstream
produces garbage — and "downstream" here is every extent in the cluster.

⚠️ **The verifier is safe only because the unlocking key is generated rather than chosen**, and this is
the one place the scheme could be got dangerously wrong. A commitment to a secret, stored where it can
be read, is an **offline brute-force oracle**: an attacker holding a KS disk can test candidates without
touching the cluster.

| Verifier commits to | Then it is |
|---|---|
| a high-entropy **generated** key | harmless — there is no candidate set to search |
| a human-chosen passphrase | **a brute-force oracle**, and worse than having no verifier at all |

So the rule is narrow and absolute: **the unlocking key is generated, never chosen**, and §7.3.2's
operator-entered secrets are *shares of a generated key* rather than passwords. A slow KDF in the
verifier is worth having as defence in depth, but it is not what makes this safe.

##### 7.3.2.4 Every day's master key is recoverable, because a lost key is lost data

**All daily master keys are on disk encrypted, so a whole-ring outage loses neither the current nor any
past key** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-19). The emphasis on *past* is the load-bearing half, and §7.3.3 says
why: an extent's key derives from the master key of **the day it was created**, so a master key that
cannot be recovered is every byte written that day, gone permanently.

**So the key store is append-only and never prunes**, which is a durability invariant rather than a
retention policy: pruning a key deletes data, silently and irreversibly, at a moment nobody is
watching. §7.3's sizing makes it free — one random key per day is **~1 MB per century** — so there is
never a reason to consider it.

##### 7.3.2.5 The last rung must be possible, and that is a feature and a threat at once

**If everyone suddenly dies and someone else gains access to all the KS hardware, it should be possible
for them to unlock it** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-19) — shards buried under eleven mountains, fetch at
least six. Difficult on purpose, and *possible* on purpose.

**k-of-n does two jobs at once**, which is why it beats a full backup of the key:

| | What it buys | Bounded by |
|---|---|---|
| losing **n − k** shards | survives the disaster | how large k is |
| needing **k** custodians to agree | no one person can be coerced, and no one person can defect | how small k is |
