Those pull opposite ways, so k and n trade in the same shape as §4.3.3's "what disaster size do we
design for" — and 6-of-11 survives five losses while resisting five colluders.

⚠️ **The property is simultaneously the capability an attacker wants.** "Whoever holds the hardware can
eventually unlock it" is exactly what an adversary who has stolen the hardware would like to be true.
What keeps it a feature is that the hardware is **not sufficient** — k shards from k separated places
are needed too. Which makes one operational rule load-bearing, and it is the easy one to violate by
convenience:

> **Shards are never stored with the hardware**, nor all in one jurisdiction, nor all reachable with
> one person's credentials.

That is the whole difference between "recoverable by its owners after a catastrophe" and "recoverable
by whoever takes the disks", and nothing in the cryptography enforces it.

##### 7.3.2.6 A dividend from §5.5.6.3: recovery starts before the custodians arrive

§5.5.6.3 splits KS's state into a **locked** half (master keys) and an **unlocked** half (topology and
registry, signed rather than encrypted). That was decided so a human ceremony could not gate automated
recovery, and it pays off exactly here: on the bottom two rungs, **a KS ring can come up far enough to
serve the machine list and ring membership while the key custodians are still travelling.**

So the slowest rung overlaps with useful work — rings can re-form and the cluster can establish what
exists — and only operations that genuinely need plaintext wait. With one undivided encrypted store,
every recovery step would queue behind a journey.

##### 7.3.2.7 A tampered member is a key-extraction oracle

⚠️ **Rung one is an oracle for anyone with physical access** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-19): take a member
down, modify its hardware to leak what it is given, bring it back up, and the ring re-keys it
automatically, because committed membership says it belongs. Saying so plainly is better than implying
the ladder is airtight.

**Why consensus cannot close it.** Committed membership answers *is this machine a member*. It cannot
answer *has this machine been tampered with*, and no amount of agreement makes it able to — the ring's
knowledge is of identity, and the attack is on the integrity of something the ring cannot observe. Rung
one exists so a routine reboot needs no human, and from the ring's side a routine reboot and a
malicious one are the same event.

⚠️ **And splitting the secret does not help, which is worth recording because it is the obvious first
idea** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-19). The tempting move is an envelope: keep the unlocking key for the
ceremony only, wrap a store key with it, and hand a returning member less than the root. It fails,
because a KS member writes a new master key every day and therefore needs the store key to function —
so the store key becomes an equal problem, and the exchange buys almost nothing.

The general form is the useful statement, and it applies to any variant of the idea:

> **A member that can do the job can leak the job.** There is no credential that lets a machine serve
> master keys without being able to exfiltrate them, so partitioning *what protects* the secret cannot
> reduce what a functioning member must hold.

**So the only structural fix is to make no single member hold anything usable**, and that is threshold
cryptography rather than key management: **share each master key across the ring so that serving one
requires k members to cooperate**, and no member ever assembles a whole key.

| | One tampered member leaks |
|---|---|
| today's design | **every master key in existence** |
| threshold-shared | **one share**, which is nothing. It takes k tampered members |

**It is the same primitive as §7.3.2.5's k-of-n shards, applied to the running system rather than only
to disaster recovery** — and the two would want the same k, since they are answering the same question
about how many custodians can be compromised at once.

**And it is affordable here specifically because KS is a low-rate component.** A key fetch is once per
SN per day per EN (§7.3.1), not per request, so multiplying each fetch by k participants costs messages
in a place with no throughput requirement. This is the same argument §7.2.1 uses about encryption being
free where compression is not: the cost lands where there is room for it.

⚠️ **What it costs is complexity in the component that must never be wrong**, and that is a serious
objection rather than a footnote. Threshold schemes have subtle failure modes, KS is the root of trust,
and a bug there is unrecoverable in a way a bug elsewhere is not. §16.138 holds the decision.

**If threshold is not taken, this is an accepted risk and should be named as one**: an attacker with
physical access to one KS machine, the ability to modify it below the attestation boundary, and the
patience to let it be re-admitted, obtains every master key and therefore every byte in the cluster.
Three things narrow it without closing it, and none is cryptographic:

- **Attestation** forces the attacker below the measured boundary — from soldering a wire onto a
  working machine to defeating the boot chain or tapping the memory bus. Not a new component: §1.5
  already makes code signing load-bearing, #23 records it as unspecified, and §16.137's machine
  identity is the same question. A TPM measures code and not the bus, so DMA interposers and cold-boot
  attacks survive it.
- **Loud re-keying.** A re-key cannot be refused, since reboots are routine, but every one can be
  logged with the member, how long it was absent, and its attestation — turning a silent compromise
  into one with a record.
- **An absence threshold.** A member gone longer than some period, or whose attestation changed, goes
  to the ceremony rather than being re-keyed automatically. That prices the attack in availability
  instead of closing it, and it is a policy knob rather than a mechanism.

##### 7.3.2.8 Unlocking from a different planet, which the verifier makes possible

**KS assumes secure guarded machines, and a likely deployment is satellites** (Asserted, Bob,
2026-08-19) — §1.0.5's torus swarm and §1.0.5.1's StarMind are both orbital. ⚠️ **What "secure
guarded" means there is not known**, and the honest answer is that the term does not transfer: some of
what it usually buys gets much stronger and some of it disappears.

| | On the ground | In orbit |
|---|---|---|
| Physical access by an adversary | the thing guards exist to stop | **far harder, and highly detectable** — a rendezvous is observable, which §7.3.2.7's attack needs to be not |
| Physical access by an **owner** | routine | **impossible**, so no ceremony can be performed locally |
| A compromised machine | can be inspected, or destroyed | neither, and it cannot be recovered |
| Bit flips | rare enough to ignore here | radiation, which matters below |

**So the threat model inverts rather than worsening**: the attack §7.3.2.7 could not close becomes very
hard, and the ceremony that closes everything else becomes impossible to perform where the machines are.

##### The consequence, and it is a good one

**The verifier of §7.3.2.3 lets the ceremony happen somewhere else entirely** (Asserted, Bob,
2026-08-19): keep a known secure guarded machine on Earth, assemble the unlock key there, open a
connection to a known quorum member in orbit, and **tell it the key.**

⚠️ **What makes that safe is that the secret is self-authenticating.** The satellite does not have to
decide whether to trust the caller, and therefore needs no PKI, no certificate chain and no notion of
which Earth machines are legitimate:

> **Possession of the unlock key *is* the authorization.** The verifier turns "do I trust this
> connection" into "is this the right key", which is a strictly easier question and one the member can
> answer alone.

That is the whole reason §7.3.2.3 is worth more than fail-fast convenience. Without a verifier, remote
unlock would need the satellite to authenticate the unlocker — which needs a trust root, which is the
problem being solved.

##### Two requirements it imposes, one already met and one not

⚠️ **The unlock path must work while KS is locked, so it may not depend on anything KS's locked half
holds.** That is §5.5.1.1's acyclicity argument moved one level outward, and it is **currently
satisfied**: the wire key comes from configuration (`messaging.key`), not from the master-key hierarchy,
so a locked KS can accept an encrypted connection.

**That property is worth protecting explicitly, because the natural-looking improvement destroys it.**
Deriving wire keys from KS's own hierarchy would be tidier, would remove a shared secret from a config
file — and would make a locked KS unable to accept the connection that unlocks it. **It is exactly the
circle §5.5.1.1 exists to break, and it would be reintroduced as a cleanup.**

⚠️ **Forward secrecy is not met, and this cannot be used in anger until it is.** Today
`messaging.key` is one symmetric key in a configuration file, so **a recorded session plus that file
yields the unlock key** — and an interplanetary link is the easiest thing in this design to record. The
unlock connection needs a per-connection ephemeral exchange, which the wire layer does not have (#91).

##### Where the crown jewel goes, and why the distance does not matter

**The guarded machine moves from the data to the ceremony**, which is a concentration of risk and a
reduction in count: one guarded place instead of every KS site. **§7.3.2.5's k-of-n keeps it
transient** — the Earth machine need not *hold* the key, only assemble it while k custodians present
shards, so the crown jewel exists for the duration of an unlock and not as a standing target.

**And the latency is irrelevant on this path**, which is what makes the scheme work at any distance.
§1.0.5 already has the rule: *cluster diameter is free; ring diameter is not.* The ladder of §7.3.2.1
splits along exactly that line:

| Rung | Where it happens | Speed needed |
|---|---|---|
| a member returns; quorum lost but the key is live | **in orbit, within the ring** | fast — it is the ring re-keying itself |
| every member restarted; the organization gone | **from Earth** | none — a light-minute either way is nothing against a human ceremony |

So an 8-minute round trip at 1 AU costs nothing where it lands, and the fast rungs never leave the
constellation.

⚠️ **One orbital hazard is specific to the verifier**: radiation bit flips. A corrupted verifier
**rejects a correct key**, turning a recoverable outage into an apparently unrecoverable one — and it
is stored in the ring's snapshot and log, which is where a rare corruption would sit unnoticed for
years. It wants redundancy of its own, and checking it against a copy is not the same as checking a key
against it (§16.143).

#### 7.3.3 What the extent entry must record

Deriving an extent's key needs the *correct* daily SN-master key — the right day, and
the right SN. **The extent's own identifier supplies both, at no extra cost.** A full
extent id is `(SnId, ExtentId, creation second)` (§4.6.3), so:

- the **day** is the creation second divided by 86,400 — no separate day-index field;
- the **SN scope** is the `SnId` of the SN that *created* the extent.

Both are immutable parts of the extent's name, which closes a trap an earlier draft
flagged: if derivation had keyed on *which ring currently serves the stream*, then
reassigning a stream (§13) would orphan every key for its existing extents. Naming the
creating SN makes derivation stable against reassignment by construction.

⚠️ The consequence is that **whoever decrypts must derive from the extent's own `SnId`,
not from the SN serving it.** After a reassignment those differ, and a cache keyed on
the serving SN would fetch the wrong master key.

#### 7.3.4 What this hierarchy does not give

⚠️ **There is no cryptographic tenant isolation.** Keys are scoped by day and SN,
not by customer, so two tenants' extents on one SN for one day derive from the same
SN-master key. Isolation rests on FE authorization (§5.9) and on keys never
reaching user code (§1.5) — not on separate key material. That is a coherent
position, but it forecloses customer-supplied keys and weakens any "we cannot read
your data" claim, so it interacts directly with §5.9.2.

#### 7.3.5 Settled: the EN does the on-disk crypto, and the wire is a separate layer

An earlier draft left this open — "which machine performs which stage is undecided and
determines where plaintext exists". It is decided (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17):

- **The EN derives and caches the on-disk encryption key for each extent**, from the
  daily SN-master key it holds and the extent's own name (§7.3.3), and **it does the
  encryption and decryption of on-disk data.** Nothing above it needs a disk key, ever.
- **It re-encrypts what it sends over the wire**, so a block leaving an EN is protected
  by the wire layer rather than by the key it was stored under.
- **Wire encryption is self-contained and ignorable by the rest of the design**
  (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17). It protects a hop and nothing else depends on it — which
  is why §17.5a can settle its own questions (per-segment sealing, nonce discipline,
  batch boundaries) without any of them reaching this section.

**Two keyed layers, doing different jobs**, and the important part is that they meet only
inside an EN:

| Layer | Key | Protects | Terminates at |
|---|---|---|---|
| **On disk** | derived per extent, cached by the EN | data at rest, for as long as it is stored | the EN, both directions |
| **On the wire** | per connection (§17.5a) | one hop, for the length of that hop | each end of each hop |

⚠️ **So compressed user data is visible at every hop that terminates a wire segment**,
which is the FE as well as the EN. That is what the earlier warning was about and it has
not gone away: **compression is not confidentiality.** What is now settled is narrower and
still worth having — *disk* keys live only on ENs, so a machine that is not an EN cannot
read stored data even if it holds bytes, and an EN's exposure is bounded to the days and
SNs whose keys it caches (§7.3.1).

---

#### 7.3.6 Every tier sees some user data; the boundary is code, not tier

Collecting the answers, because they arrived one at a time and the summary is the useful
form. **A DN has to see plaintext in order to do keyed objects** (Asserted, Bob,
2026-08-17): a keyed lookup is a comparison against **user keys**, so the keys are in the
metadata and the metadata is user data. And a DN already holds object *names*, which are
user data too.

| Tier | Sees | Because |
|---|---|---|
| **client** | everything | it is the user's data, and it compresses and checks it (§7.5) |
| **DN** | object names, and **user keys** for keyed objects | a keyed lookup is a key comparison (§9.2) |
| **SN** | `first_key` per extent, for keyed objects | choosing an extent is the same comparison one level down |
| **FE** | compressed bytes always; **plaintext** when a caller asks for part of a block | somebody has to cut the piece out (§9.1.2) |
| **EN** | stored bytes, and their plaintext transiently | it does the on-disk crypto (§7.3.5) |

⚠️ **So "where does plaintext live" has no single answer, and it was the wrong question.**
Every tier sees the part of the user's data it needs to do its job, and the design has never
depended on any of them not seeing it. What it depends on is narrower and checkable:

- **Disk keys live only on ENs** (§7.3.5), so a machine that is not an EN cannot read stored
  data even if it holds the bytes.
- **No tier runs user code** (§1.5), which is why every tier can be trusted with what it
  sees. That is the actual trust boundary — **DeLawson code against user code, not tier
  against tier.**
- **Compute is therefore the boundary that matters**, and §5.12 already draws it the right
  way round: Compute machines receive plaintext and never keys, because they are the one
  place user code runs.

Which also explains why §7.5.3 keeps the CRC out of stream and extent metadata even though
that metadata is already full of user data: the objection is not that a tier would see it
but that **one tenant would see another's**, since staging extents mix tenants. Tenancy and
trust are different boundaries and only one of them runs along tier lines.

### 7.4 Media classes, and why an extent has exactly one

**There will be an HDD-to-SSD transition, and the fleet will be mixed for a decade.** §12.7.2's drive lives ten
years, so anything purchased now is in service into the mid-2030s. If SSD manufacturing overbuilds and its price
falls to HDD's, there is no motive to buy HDD and it goes away (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-15) — but gradually. So
**media class is a permanent configuration axis, not a migration event.**

#### 7.4.1 Every device-dependent constant belongs in one table

The constants of §7.1.1, §7.1.2 and §9.3 are **per media class**, not global: index interval in physical bytes,
minimum read size, compression block size, the staging bypass threshold of §8.1.4, whether compression is a
read-bandwidth win, and repair bandwidth. Those belong in a single device-class table in the config, populated
by measurement — not as five constants scattered through the code. That is cheap now and unpleasant in year
three, and it is a decision for the config schema being built first.

#### 7.4.2 An extent has exactly one media class, and so do all four of its instances

**Mixed-media extents are not supported** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-15). The derivation:

1. Minimum read size is per-media — 1 MB HDD, 20 KB SSD (§7.1.1).
2. Compression block size must be at least the minimum read, and larger blocks compress better (§7.1), so the
   optimal block differs by ~50x between media.
3. EC operates on stored bytes, so instances must be byte-identical in stored form (§4.3.2.3). Different block
   sizes make that impossible, and re-deriving parity from decompressed content would need keys on the parity
   path and full decompression.
4. Therefore compression block size is a **durable property of the extent** — unlike record framing, which
   §8.2.1 explicitly says is *not* — and so is media class.
5. Therefore all four instances are same-media.

Encryption reinforces the same conclusion: block boundaries and IV structure would also have to match (§7.2).

**Five consequences, all mild, which is a sign this is the natural constraint.**

- **A fast-read copy is a tier or a cache, never an instance.** §9.5's hedging stays within one media class.
  Cross-media speedup must be a separate object or an explicit cache, which is honest about its cost instead of
  hiding it. ⚠️ An earlier draft proposed one SSD instance plus three HDD instances per extent; that is
  unavailable, and the reasoning above is why.
- **Media migration is compaction with a different target.** Rewriting an extent at a new block size is what §10
  already does, so migration is a policy input to an existing loop rather than new machinery — and it inherits
  the retention rule of §10.1 automatically, since it is a rewrite.
- **Placement filters by class before selecting.** §5.6.3's free-space-weighted choice with rejection sampling
  runs *within* a class.
- **A media class cannot be piloted.** The 4/3 slack and the independence rules must be satisfiable inside the
  class alone (§5.6.1a, §4.3.3.2e), so introducing SSD means introducing a placement-viable footprint of it, not
  a few drives per rack.
- **The same logical object costs different physical bytes on different media**, because block size changes the
  ratio. Under §12.3's physical billing that is automatically correct rather than a special case, but it does
  mean media must be a **visible, priced attribute** — a user cannot be surprised by their bill changing after a
  migration they did not request.

#### 7.4.3 What the transition does not change

- **Repair bandwidth**, which is a network number either way (§4.3.2.2a) — so the codec choice, and the patent
  question, are media-neutral.
- **Compression as a requirement**, since capacity dominates cost whichever device holds it (§12.3).
- **Extent size**, which is governed by SN RAM (§14.1) rather than by the device.

The exposure is entirely in the constants, which is the good case — provided they are constants in a table and
not constants in the code.

### 7.5 The CRC is the user's guarantee, and it is theirs to compute

Encryption already detects tampering and corruption on the wire and on disk — an AEGIS tag fails to
open a segment that has changed a bit (§7.2.1). **That is enough for the system's own purposes and it
is not enough for the user's**, because it only ever covers a byte range the system already accepted.
What the user wants to know is that the bytes DeLawson stored are the bytes the user's *buffer* held,
including through everything that happened between the two.

**So an append takes the CRC of its logical append block, in the user's chosen row format, as an
optional argument** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17). Optional, because a caller that does not care should
not pay; given, it is a promise the store then keeps.

#### 7.5.1 What the CRC is over, and what that buys

**The logical bytes, framed the way the writer framed them.** Not the compressed form and not the
encrypted form, because those are the system's representations of the data rather than the data. Which
means the CRC survives every representation change the pipeline makes, and is what makes the guarantee
end-to-end rather than hop-to-hop.

The sequence a caller gets is worth spelling out, because it is what makes the guarantee stronger than
a checksum computed by the store:

1. The caller computes the CRC **on its own buffer**.
2. The caller does **its own validation** of that buffer — whatever it means by correct.
3. It passes **both the buffer and the CRC** to append.

Step 2 is the one that matters. A checksum the store computes on arrival certifies whatever arrived; a
checksum the caller computes before its own checks certifies what the caller *meant*, and any
corruption between the caller's memory and the store's acceptance shows up as a mismatch instead of as
durable wrong data.

#### 7.5.2 The client compresses out of place, then re-verifies

**The `laws` client compresses the buffer — not in place — and then verifies that the buffer still
matches the CRC** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17). Compression belongs to the client rather than to an FE
(§8.1.4.1), which is what makes this possible at all. The order is the point: compressing out of place leaves
the original intact to be re-read, so **a corruption that happened before or during compression is
caught by the mismatch.** Compressing in place would destroy the evidence.

That places one CRC computation and one verification on the client's append path, which is affordable
because the CRC is far faster than anything it sits beside. The implementation is
[crc64nvme](https://github.com/bobjen/crc64nvme) — a port of the Cosmos 64-bit CRC, authorized by
Microsoft, bitwise compatible with the CRC Azure uses — taken as a dependency rather than copied, and
one we own, so an ARM branch is our work to do rather than somebody's to wait for.

**Measured here, three trials over 512 MB:**

| Build | Throughput |
|---|---|
| baseline `x86-64` | 4.8, 4.4, 4.8 GB/s |
| `-C target-cpu=native` | 13.9, 13.9, **14.6 GB/s** |

**Measured, 2026-08-17**, and the two builds produce identical CRCs, so this is purely how fast the same
answer arrives. A **3x** difference from one compiler flag is worth knowing about, and it is a flag with
a deployment consequence: `native` bakes in the build machine's instruction set, so a fleet needs a
named floor or runtime dispatch rather than this (#62).

**And it is fast at the sizes an append block actually comes in**, which is the number that decides
whether the guarantee is affordable — a store of enormous objects still writes 50-byte records:

| Append block | Per call | Rate |
|---|---|---|
| 16 B | **2.6 ns** | 6.1 GB/s |
| 44 B — one small record | **5.6 ns** | 7.9 GB/s |
| 256 B | 15.9 ns | 16.1 GB/s |
| 4 KB | 233 ns | 17.6 GB/s |
| 64 KB | 3.7 µs | **17.7 GB/s** |
| 32 MB — the cap | 2.4 ms | 13.9 GB/s |

**Measured, 2026-08-17.** There is no startup cost to speak of: the small sizes are slower per byte only
because they are short, not because anything is being set up (§7.5's tables are built once per process).
So the CRC is **5.6 ns on the smallest append and 2.4 ms on the largest** — against a request that takes
microseconds and a 32 MB write that takes hundreds of milliseconds. It is noise at both ends, which is
what makes it reasonable to put on every append rather than offering it as a premium.

The peak is in the middle, at 4-64 KB, and the fall to 13.9 GB/s at 32 MB is memory rather than
arithmetic — worth noting only so that the two figures above are not read as inconsistent.

⚠️ **The tables are built once per process** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17). Initialization is the
expensive part, so there is one CRC per process, built on first use — a caller constructing one per
append would pay setup per call and get right answers while doing it, which is the kind of mistake that
never shows up as a bug.

#### 7.5.3 It travels with the compressed block, and is checked on the way out

**The CRC accompanies the compressed block throughout**, and **whenever a compressed block is
decompressed the CRC is checked** — a mismatch is corruption, reported as such rather than returned as
data. So the check happens at every point where the logical bytes exist again, which is the only place
it can mean anything.

On the read path that place is **whoever decompresses** — the client if it may hold whole blocks, the FE
if it may not (§9.1.2). The client is the better answer, because then the same machine that computed the
CRC going in checks it coming out and nothing in between looks inside.

**The EN never checks a CRC**, and could not: it holds what the writer compressed, it does not
decompress, and it may hold no keys. A check there would work only for as long as nothing compresses,
and would then fail on every append.

**Coalescing computes new CRCs** (§8.1.4.4, §10), and this is the subtle part: a CRC is over logical
bytes *in a row format*, and coalescing may change the row format (§8.2.1). **So what is recorded is
the CRC and the row format it was computed over.** A stored CRC without its framing is not
interpretable, and re-framing without recomputing would silently invalidate every one of them.

The chosen implementation helps here in a specific way: it can **concatenate two CRCs in O(log n)**
without rescanning the bytes. So coalescing that merely joins blocks *in the same row format* can
combine their CRCs arithmetically, and only a coalesce that re-frames has to read the data to
recompute.

⚠️ **The CRC is not exposed in object info** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17), and the reason is a tenancy
boundary rather than tidiness: **an EN's common extents combine tenants** (§8.1.4), so **stream and
extent metadata is not protected information.** A CRC is derived from user bytes, so putting one where
cross-tenant metadata lives would leak a fingerprint of one tenant's data to another. It belongs with
the block, inside what is encrypted — never in the metadata that describes where the block is.

**The block itself is single-tenant, though**, and so is a coalesced extent: an append block comes from
one writer, and coalescing works only within one tenant's extents (§9.1.2). It is the staging extents
that mix, which is why the boundary falls between a block and the metadata about it rather than between
a block and its neighbours.

## 8. Writing

### 8.1 Append blocks

The unit of write is an **append block**: a byte range applied to the target extent atomically — the whole
range becomes visible or none of it does.

⚠️ Note "byte range", not "set of records". A block may contain **record fragments** at either end, since with
a writer that fixes its own offsets a record may span appends (§8.2.2). So a record becomes complete only when every append
carrying part of it is durable, and atomicity is a property of the byte range rather than of the records inside
it. An earlier draft said "0..n records, all its records become visible or none do", which is true only when
appends happen to be record-aligned.

**Fragments belong to fixed-offset appends.** A record spanning two appends needs those appends to be
consecutive in the extent, which a writer can only know if it fixed the offsets itself — so
**assigned-offset appends must be record-aligned** (§8.1.1a-3), since two of them interleaving would split
each other's records. What makes a fragment safe is not that there is one writer but that the writer knows
where its bytes landed.

An append returns its **logical offset in the extent** as a locator, plus the record number of the first
complete record it contains (unkeyed) and the extent it landed in.

#### 8.1.1 Accepted, applied, durable

An extent has a **primary EN** among the ENs holding its instances, and that primary runs
the append protocol. Three states, and the distinctions matter:

| State | Means | Scope |
|---|---|---|
| **accepted** | a machine has received the append | one machine |
| **applied** | it *and every append before it* are on disk on that machine | one machine |
| **durable** | the primary EN knows **3 of 4** instances have applied it | the extent |

**Applied is a prefix property, not a per-append flag.** An append is applied only once
all its predecessors are also on disk, so each instance's state collapses to a single
watermark and durability is the watermark reached by at least three of the four. That is
what makes the bookkeeping cheap enough for a tier that must stay CPU-poor (§1.2): the
primary tracks four numbers per open extent, not a set of outstanding appends.

**Three of four is the default, not a constant.** Both numbers are configuration — `[extents]`
`instances` and `quorum` — so 3 of 5 or 4 of 5 are a config change and not a code change (Asserted,
Bob, 2026-08-17). What the code must not permit is a quorum that fails the overlap argument below, and
it refuses to start rather than allowing it.

**Three of four is a quorum, and that is load-bearing.** Any two 3-subsets of a 4-set
overlap in at least two members, so a new primary that polls any three instances is
guaranteed to see every durable append. Primary handover needs no separate reconciliation
protocol — the intersection does it. Had durability been 2 of 4, two disjoint pairs could
each hold a "durable" append the other had never seen.

#### 8.1.1a Parallel appends: what GFS does, and why it cannot be copied

Multiple clients appending to one object is the case worth studying, because §1.0's motivating use case —
many writers recording shared experiences — is exactly it.

**GFS's answer is `record append`.** It "allows multiple clients to append data to the same file concurrently
while guaranteeing the atomicity of each individual client's append", and the mechanics are close to
DeLawson's: the client pushes data to all replicas of the last chunk, the primary assigns the offset, and the
secondaries are told where it went. Serialization at a primary, as in §8.1.1.

But the semantics are much weaker, deliberately:

| GFS property | Consequence |
|---|---|
| The offset is "of GFS's choosing" | the client learns where its record landed; it cannot specify |
| **"append-at-least-once semantics"** | a failed append is retried, so **duplicates** occur |
| A record that will not fit pads the chunk | **gaps**, and records never span chunks |
| Records limited to **¼ of chunk size** | bounds worst-case fragmentation from that padding |
| **"GFS does not guarantee that all replicas are bytewise identical"** | replicas may differ; regions are "defined interspersed with inconsistent" |

Readers cope by application convention — records carry checksums so padding can be skipped, and unique IDs so
duplicates can be dropped.

**DeLawson cannot adopt this, and erasure coding is the reason.** GFS reads a whole replica, so divergent
replicas are survivable: each read is self-consistent even if two reads differ. Erasure coding is not so
forgiving. Reconstruction combines fragments computed from *different machines*, so if those machines held
different byte sequences the reconstruction yields garbage — and §7.2's per-block IVs derived from
`(extent_id, block_index)` mean even the ciphertext must match exactly.

> **Erasure coding forces byte-identical instances. Replication does not.**

⚠️ An earlier draft of this line said erasure coding therefore forces *exactly-once append*. It does not, and
the distinction matters. A duplicate appended at a **fresh** offset leaves every instance holding the same
byte sequence — it merely contains the record twice. What GFS suffers from is different: a failed attempt
leaves bytes at an offset on *some* replicas, and the retry lands elsewhere, so the replicas genuinely diverge.

DeLawson avoids that with a truncation rule rather than with exactly-once semantics:

> **On primary handover, an instance must truncate anything above the durable watermark** (§8.1.1).

Since "applied" is a prefix property, an instance that applied an append which never reached quorum is holding
a suffix nobody agreed to. Discarding it restores byte-identity. This is Raft log truncation in another guise,
and it is what makes the prefix-watermark design sufficient for erasure coding.

The second reason for wanting exactly-once is §1.0's stable-index property. An index entry of (object, record *N*) is only permanently
valid if record numbers are unique and never shift. At-least-once appends would give the same logical record
two numbers, and padding would leave gaps — which does not break correctness so much as destroy the one
property that made DeLawson attractive for indexed data in the first place.

#### 8.1.1a-2 How the append actually works

**The primary chooses the offset when the append arrives at the extent, and that is the only serialized part.**
Everything expensive happens afterwards:

| Stage | Serialized per extent? |
|---|---|
| Assign the offset | **yes** — a lock and some arithmetic |
| Compress, encrypt, write to disk, replicate | no |
| Report the offset back once durable | no |

That ordering is what keeps per-extent serialization from being a throughput limit, and the margin is large:

| Append size | Serialized | Pipeline work at 500 MB/s | Serialized fraction |
|---|---|---|---|
| 32 MB | ~100 ns | 64 ms | 1.6 × 10^-6 |
| 1 MB | ~100 ns | 2 ms | 5 × 10^-5 |
| 4 KB | ~100 ns | 0.01 ms | 1.3 × 10^-2 |

Note the offset assigned in that window must be a **logical** position, since the compressed size is not yet
known. Physical placement is determined afterwards and recorded in the sparse index (§9.3) — which is why §4
carries logical *and* physical cumulative totals rather than one.

**An append is bounded at 32 MB logical *and* 32 MB compressed** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17, correcting
his own earlier revision — the original draft of this section had it right). The reason is the case that
otherwise fails:

> **You do not want appends failing because they exceed the compressed limit, and 32 MB of
> incompressible logical data does not compress.**

So the two caps are equal on purpose. If the logical bound were 4 GB like a record's, a caller could
send 4 GB of incompressible bytes that cannot fit a 32 MB compressed cap however the system tries — and
the failure would arrive *after* the caller had done the work, for a reason the caller could not have
predicted without knowing its own compression ratio in advance. With both at 32 MB, an append that a
caller can measure is an append that fits.

⚠️ **And the compressed limit is soft.** It bounds what is accumulated on first write and nothing after
that (§6.2), so an append at the cap that compresses badly is not refused for missing it by a little —
which is the other half of not making callers predict ratios.

A **record** is still bounded by an extent rather than by an append (4 GB logical, §8.2.4), because a
record may span appends. So the three bounds are not one number after all: an append is the smallest of
them, and it is smallest precisely so that it can never be the thing that fails.

⚠️ **The append half of that may yet come down, because a message is not an extent** (Asserted, Bob,
2026-08-17). A frame is capped at 1 MB and a sealed segment at 8 MB, both to stop a peer making the far
side allocate what it asks for — so a 32 MB append needs either a larger cap, a multi-frame append, or a
lower append limit. The last is the cheap one, and a writer wanting a large record can still build it from
several appends (§8.2.3), so the choice is about how many receipts a writer gets rather than what it can
write. #53.

**A large append becomes several device writes, and stays one append.** 32 MB compressed is ~213 ms of HDD
at 150 MB/s, and holding a disk for that long delays everything queued behind it — so the primary may cut
the write into pieces to interleave with other work. That is invisible to the writer: §8.1's atomicity is a
property of the byte range, so the watermark advances only when every piece has landed, and a reader never
sees half an append however many writes it took.

**Durability returns the offset as a locator**, so a writer learns exactly where its data landed.

#### 8.1.1a-3 Fixed-offset append gives exactly-once, for free

⚠️ **An earlier draft called this "single-writer mode", and that is the wrong name** (Asserted, Bob,
2026-08-17). What distinguishes the two modes is **whether duplicates are prevented**, not how many writers
there are: **several writers may append at fixed offsets**, and what they get is not duplicates but
*mismatch failures* — a writer whose expected offset has been filled by somebody else is told so, and retries
against the new end. Duplicates are *allowed* in the other mode, not required in this one. So the modes are
named for who fixes the offset (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17):

| Mode | Offset | Duplicates |
|---|---|---|
| **Fixed-offset append** | the writer supplies the offset it expects | **prevented** — the offset plus the content is the token |
| **Assigned-offset append** | the primary assigns it on arrival | possible — a retry gets a fresh offset |

A writer that wants exactly-once **tracks the offset it expects and includes it in the append.** The primary
then compares:

| Case | Result |
|---|---|
| Expected offset = actual next offset | append proceeds |
| Expected offset already filled, **same length and same data** | **succeeds** — the retry is recognized as a duplicate |
| Expected offset already filled, different length or data | **fails as a mismatch** |
| Expected offset beyond the current end | held in an out-of-order cache (below) |

That third row is the idempotency mechanism, and it needs no producer identifier or sequence number: **the
offset plus the content is the token.** This is not a new idea — it is
[Azure's `Append Block` conditional append](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/rest/api/storageservices/append-block),
for the same stated reason (§8.1.1a-5). A retry re-sends the same bytes at the same place and is absorbed;
a genuine conflict is detected rather than silently ordered.

So the two modes differ in exactly the way GFS's does not offer:

| | Offset | Semantics | Suits |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Fixed-offset** | supplied by the writer | **exactly-once**, with conflict detection | anything relying on stable record numbers (§1.0) |
| **Assigned-offset** | assigned by the primary | **at-least-once** — a retry gets a fresh offset, so duplicates are possible | merge and producer-consumer patterns, as in GFS |

⚠️ Worth being explicit that assigned-offset appends are at-least-once, and for the same reason GFS's are:
with no expected offset there is nothing to compare a retry against. Users wanting stable external indexes
should fix their offsets; users letting the primary assign them must tolerate duplicates exactly as GFS's
do — and a writer chooses per append, since the difference is one argument rather than a mode the object
is in.

#### 8.1.1a-4 The out-of-order cache, and why only one mode needs it

A writer pipelining several fixed-offset appends may have them arrive out of order, so **an EN receiving an append
from beyond the current end can cache it, ordered by offset, in case the gap fills.** That is what lets a
writer keep many fixed-offset appends in flight rather than waiting for each to be placed — which matters, since
§1.4 makes throughput the priority and a stop-and-wait writer would be latency-bound.

**Assigned-offset appends need no such cache**, because the offset is chosen on arrival and gaps never occur.

⚠️ The cache needs a **bound** and a **timeout**: memory is finite, and a gap left by an append that never
arrives must not pin cached data indefinitely. Both are undesigned, and together they set how far ahead a
writer may pipeline.

#### 8.1.1a-5 Prior art: Azure append blobs

**The two-mode append of §8.1.1a-2 and §8.1.1a-3 is not novel. The prior art is Azure append blobs**, whose
[`Append Block` operation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/rest/api/storageservices/append-block) has both
modes and gives the same reason for them.

The service appends at the end and returns `x-ms-blob-append-offset`, "the offset at which the block was
committed, in bytes" — the primary assigning the position and reporting it back. The conditional header
`x-ms-blob-condition-appendpos` supplies an expected byte offset, succeeding "only if the current offset matches
that specified by the client" and otherwise failing 412. Microsoft's stated purpose is DeLawson's exactly:

> "Clients that use a single writer can use this header to determine whether an `Append Block` operation
> succeeded, despite a network failure."

Their advice for many writers matches §8.1.1a-3 too — Azure's word for a fixed offset is a *conditional*
header, and they note it works but hurts throughput, so "for the
highest concurrent append throughput, applications should handle redundant appends and delayed appends in the
application layer", by adding "epochs or sequence numbers in the data". Which is also GFS's advice (§8.1.1a).
**Two independent designs reached the same split: conditional append for one writer, at-least-once plus
application dedup for many.**

Where DeLawson differs: Azure caps an append blob at **50,000 appends** and ~4.75 TiB. DeLawson has no
append-count ceiling because extents seal and roll (§6) — the cap is a consequence of Azure's blob being one
addressable unit rather than a list of extents.

| System | Who assigns the offset | Client may specify it? |
|---|---|---|
| **Azure append blob** | the service, returned in the response | **yes** — `appendpos`, 412 on mismatch |
| **GFS `record append`** | the primary chunkserver, "at an offset of GFS's choosing" | no |
| **Kafka** | the partition leader, base offset in the produce response | no — idempotency via producer id and sequence |
| **HDFS** | nobody — a single lease-holding writer knows the length already | n/a |
| **Ceph RADOS** | the primary OSD serializes object ops (append is one) | compare-and-set primitives exist |
| **Oracle `ROWID`** | the system, on insert, and returned to the client | no |

⚠️ The Ceph row is from recollection rather than a checked source; it should be verified before being relied on.

#### 8.1.1a-6 Density is load-bearing, and most of these lack it

Oracle's `ROWID` is a system-determined locator handed back to the client, which is the same shape — but **it
has holes.** Row numbers skip deleted rows, blocks are not packed full, and the space is sparse throughout.
GFS's offsets have holes too, from the padding of §8.1.1c.

**DeLawson's logical offsets are dense**, and three separate mechanisms depend on it:

| Mechanism | Why density is required |
|---|---|
| The fixed-offset check (§8.1.1a-3) | the writer must **predict** the next offset — impossible if the system may skip |
| The out-of-order cache (§8.1.1a-4) | it assumes gaps are *temporary*, from reordering. A permanent hole would never fill and the cache would never drain |
| Cumulative logical byte totals (§4) | logical offsets must be additive to be searchable |

This reframes §8.1.1c. Sealing an extent short rather than padding it looked like a space nicety; it is
actually what **keeps offsets dense**, and therefore what makes the compare-and-append protocol possible at
all. GFS could pad because its clients never predicted an offset; DeLawson's do.

⚠️ **But sealing short still breaks predictability across an extent boundary**, and the design has not said
which token the writer compares:

| Token | Predictable by the writer? |
|---|---|
| Offset **within the extent** — as described in §8.1.1a-2 | no: the writer cannot know when the extent rolls |
| Offset **within the object**, dense across extents | **yes**, always computable from what it has sent |
| The pair *(extent, offset)* | yes, at the cost of one failed round trip per roll — the failure tells it the new extent |

The pair is workable, since a roll happens only every 32 MB or so and one wasted round trip per roll is
negligible. But an object-wide offset needs no failure at all, and the choice should be deliberate rather than
implied.

Worth noting a fourth shape: **sequencer-based shared logs** such as Corfu hand out positions from a tiny,
fast, serialized token service and let clients write the data directly to storage. That is §8.1.1a-2's
separation of the serialized window from the data path taken to its conclusion — the sequencer *is* nothing but
the critical section. If per-extent offset assignment ever became a bottleneck, that is the shape to borrow.

#### 8.1.1a-7 Which offset is reportable depends on the object flavour

| | Unsealed extents | Reportable offset |
|---|---|---|
| **Unkeyed** (append at end) | exactly one — the tail of the last stream | **object logical offset** |
| **Keyed** (insert in middle) | several at once | **extent-relative only** |

For an unkeyed object,

> object logical offset = sum of sealed extent logical lengths + offset within the tail extent

is **well defined, dense, stable, and writer-predictable**. There is exactly one place appends can land, so the
prior sum is fixed.

**Keyed objects insert in the middle and therefore have several unsealed extents at once**, so no such sum
exists. Only the **extent-relative** offset is available, and §10's coalescing can rewrite an extent into other
extents and take its offsets with it.

**So compare-and-append is an unkeyed-object mechanism.** Keyed objects do not need it: an insert names a key,
so re-inserting the same key with the same value is naturally idempotent and with a different value is an
update. **The key is the position**, and idempotency comes from key comparison rather than from an offset token.

One addition worth stating plainly, because it applies to both flavours: **offsets are never a durable
reference.** Only record numbers and keys are (§4.6.3, §8.1.1a-10).

#### 8.1.1a-8 The cost: one open extent bounds the per-object append rate

Having exactly one unsealed extent is *what makes* the object offset well defined, and it serializes appends
through one extent whose instances sit on one disk each.

| | |
|---|---|
| Per-object append rate | **~200 MB/s** — one disk's write bandwidth |
| Against a 1,000-EN fleet's read capability | ~125,000x lower |
| Aggregate, 10,000 objects appending | 2 TB/s — unaffected |

**Derived.** The ceiling is per-object, not fleet-wide, which is fine for most workloads and awkward for exactly
the one §1.0 names: many writers recording shared experiences into one object, wanting both a single ordered
sequence and stable references. §8.6 works that conflict through and finds it is a trilemma rather than a
choice.

⚠️ **And the ceiling comes from the promise, not from the storage** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17). It is one
disk's bandwidth because the append returns `(object, row)` immediately, which needs one place deciding the
order. **A writer willing not to be told its row straight away could be served at an SN's throughput instead
of a disk's** — many disks rather than one, which is orders of magnitude.

So this is an option to offer rather than a limit to live with. What it costs is exactly what §8.1.1a-9
argues against making the *default*: an answer that arrives later, order fixed at extent creation rather than
at seal, and head-of-line blocking behind the slowest concurrent writer. **Those objections are decisive for
a default and not for a choice** — a writer bulk-loading can accept all three, and a writer that wants a
stable reference in hand cannot. The design should let the writer say which it is.

#### 8.1.1a-9 Prior art for the receipt: VSAM returns it, POSIX does not

Two questions were asked separately and have opposite answers.

**Is there a standard append interface that returns the offset?** Yes, and it is old. **VSAM ESDS**: a `PUT` to
an entry-sequenced data set appends at the end and **returns the record's RBA to the application, and that RBA
is constant thereafter**, usable as a direct-access address (Cited: [IBM, relative byte
addresses](https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/epfz/6.1.0?topic=sets-relative-byte-addresses-rba); [IBM CICS: KSDS,
ESDS, RRDS](https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/cics-ts/5.5.0?topic=control-vsam-data-sets-ksds-esds-rrds)). That is
compare-and-append's receipt, from the 1970s. The SQL analogue is Oracle's `INSERT ... RETURNING ROWID` and the
identity-retrieval family: the system picks the address, the response reports it, the address is durable.

**POSIX is the opposite.** `write(2)` under `O_APPEND` atomically positions at end-of-file, but returns the byte
*count*, never the position; obtaining the position needs a separate racy `lseek`/`fstat`, and NFS cannot even
provide the atomic append underneath it (Cited: [POSIX
`write`](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/functions/write.html); [appending from multiple
processes](https://nullprogram.com/blog/2016/08/03/)).

**Are there systems with several unsealed tails, where the object offset becomes known only later?** None found.
Every system that permits parallel unsealed regions **removes the global offset from the write response rather
than deferring it**, in one of two shapes:

| Shape | Systems | Position name space |
|---|---|---|
| **Compound id** | Pulsar / BookKeeper | `MessageId` = (ledgerId, entryId); one ledger open at a time |
| | Kafka | offsets are per-*partition*; a topic has no offset at all |
| | Iceberg positional deletes | `(file_path, pos)` — row position within a data file, never table-wide (Cited: [Iceberg spec](https://iceberg.apache.org/spec/)) |
| **Two-phase** | S3 / Azure / GCS multipart upload | `UploadPart` returns an ETag against a part *number*; byte layout is defined by `CompleteMultipartUpload` |
| | BigQuery Storage Write API | pending streams have **per-stream offsets starting at 0**; table order is defined atomically by `BatchCommitWriteStreams` (Cited: [batch load](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/write-api-batch), [intro](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/write-api)) |

And everything that *does* return an offset synchronously has exactly one unsealed region: GFS `RecordAppend`,
Azure append blob `AppendBlock` (§8.1.1a-5), Kafka's single active segment per partition, Corfu's sequencer
(which assigns *before* the write).

**So the eventually-known-offset interface is unattested** (Guess, from absence — absence is not proof, but the
consistency is a signal: everyone who needed the parallelism paid for it by changing the name space, not by
deferring the answer). Three reasons it is worse than it looks, all Derived:

1. **Order must be fixed at extent *creation*, not seal**, or the sum of prior lengths never converges. So
   extent slots would be allocated eagerly and filled lazily, committing extent count before the bytes exist.
2. **Resolution is head-of-line blocked.** One stuck unsealed extent leaves every append after it unresolvable,
   indefinitely. Offset availability becomes coupled to the slowest concurrent writer rather than to your own
   durability — a promise with no time bound, which §1.1 argues is the worst kind here.
3. **Two answers over time for one append** is a cache-invalidation problem pushed into every client and every
   external index, which is precisely what §1.0 promises not to have.

**Conclusion.** The append response carries the address the system can guarantee forever — the compound
`(stream, record number)` for unkeyed data, the key for keyed — and never a position in a name space that has
not been decided yet. §8.6 shows the eventually-known object offset is still real, but as a consequence of
*sealing* rather than a promise made at append time.

#### 8.1.1a-10 Three tiers of reference lifetime

| Tier | Reference | Known | Lifetime |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Durable** | `(object, key)` keyed; `(stream, record number)` unkeyed | immediately | forever |
| **Hint** | `(extent identity, row number in extent)` | immediately | **until that extent is rewritten** |
| **None** | object offset, or object row number for keyed data | never | — |

Row number within an extent **is** stable and can be returned immediately; what makes it a hint rather than a
name is that §10 may rewrite the extent (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-15).

**The hint in full is `(EnId, (SnId, ExtentId, creation second), record number)`** (Asserted, Bob,
2026-08-17) — an instance to ask, the extent's whole name, and the row in it. The EnId is what makes it a
route rather than a description: holding one, an FE goes **straight to an EN**, skipping the DN and the SN.

Three things follow:

- **It serves both object flavours.** A row within an extent is as well defined for keyed records as for
  unkeyed ones, so insert-in-the-middle data gets the same hint — which is the point of the middle tier
  existing at all, since keyed objects have no durable positional address (§3).
- ⚠️ **It removes the DN and SN hops, not the FE hop.** Authorization lives at the FE (§5.9), so a hint
  used *by* an FE on a user's behalf preserves it, while a user reaching an EN directly would skip it. That
  makes "who may hold a hint" a different question from "who may use one", and the first has a much easier
  answer.
  ⚠️ **But the hop removal as stated here does not hold, and §9.1.3.5 is the correction** (Asserted, Bob,
  2026-08-19). An FE authorizes an *object* and a hint names an *extent*, and nothing in the tuple above
  binds them — so proving the hint belongs to the object it is presented with costs exactly the DN and SN
  descents the hint was meant to skip. The tuple therefore needs a fourth part, an unforgeable
  **capability** attesting `extent ∈ object`, and the fields listed here are the *plaintext prefix* it is
  appended to.
- **It is what the user is given, not only what the FE keeps** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17). The motivating
  shape is a job scheduler: **ask once up front, hand the hints to the vertices, and let them use them as
  the job runs.** So `object-info` has to return enough for a caller to construct hints — extent names,
  their instances, and their record ranges — rather than only the stream-level answer it gives today
  (#61).

**What makes the middle tier safe rather than dangerous is already in §4.6.3**: extent identity is
`(SnId, ExtentId, creation second)`, so a rewritten extent has a **different identity**. A stale hint therefore
fails **detectably** — a clean "that extent is gone" rather than a silent read of whatever now occupies the slot.
If extent ids were reused, the same hint would be a corruption vector. The creation second, introduced to
disambiguate reuse after deletion, is what licenses returning extent-relative row numbers at all.

**Oracle solved exactly this, for exactly this reason.** A secondary index on an index-organized table cannot use
a physical rowid "because of the inherent movability of rows in a B\*-tree index", so it stores a **logical rowid
= primary key + a physical guess** at the block address. On lookup the guess is tried; if the block is not what
was expected it falls back to the primary-key search, and the logical rowid stays valid regardless. Oracle even
meters the decay: `PCT_DIRECT_ACCESS` in `DBA_INDEXES` is the percentage of guesses still valid, and partition
maintenance is called out as invalidating them wholesale. (Cited: [Oracle: speeding up index access with
IOTs](https://docs.oracle.com/cd/A97630_01/appdev.920/a96590/adg07iot.htm); [Oracle 26c: indexes and
IOTs](https://docs.oracle.com/en/database/oracle/oracle-database/26/cncpt/indexes-and-index-organized-tables.html);
[Foote, the logical rowid guess component](https://richardfoote.wordpress.com/2012/04/26/iot-secondary-indexes-the-logical-rowid-guess-component-part-i-lucky/).)

That is the pattern for DeLawson keyed objects verbatim: an external index stores the key and *may* cache
`(extent, row)` as a hint; on miss it re-resolves by key. Keyed objects therefore need no new mechanism — the key
lookup is the recovery path that has to exist anyway.

**Hint lifetime is a compaction-policy number.** With base-plus-log (§4.2), a hint into the base dies at every
compaction and a hint into the log dies when the log merges, so expected validity is about the compaction
interval. That makes compaction frequency a **three-way** trade rather than two-way: write amplification, read
amplification, and hint hit rate. It argues for exposing a `PCT_DIRECT_ACCESS` analogue per object, since an
index whose guesses have all gone stale is silently paying double lookups — and §12.1 says a cost that real
should be visible.

**Hints are a keyed-object optimization specifically.** For unkeyed objects the durable reference is already a
direct address and the fallback is exact and cheap (§9.1's three binary searches), so they barely need hints.
Keyed is where positions move.

#### 8.1.1b What others do, and what DeLawson still needs

| System | Approach to concurrent append |
|---|---|
| **GFS** | serialize at the primary, at-least-once, duplicates and padding pushed to the application |
| **HDFS** | **single writer** per file, lease-held — avoids the problem rather than solving it |
| **Apache BookKeeper** | single writer per ledger, with fencing on failover |
| **Kafka** | partition leader assigns offsets; an idempotent producer (producer id + sequence number) gives exactly-once |
| **Azure append blobs** | concurrent appends with an append-position conditional header for optimistic concurrency |
| **Ceph RADOS** | append ops serialized by the primary OSD |
| **S3** | historically no append at all — whole-object PUT |

The pattern: either restrict to one writer, or serialize at a primary and then choose between at-least-once
(cheap, GFS) and exactly-once (needs an idempotency token, Kafka).

**DeLawson is structurally in the Kafka position but has not specified the token.** §8.1.1 gives a primary EN,
a total order per extent, and a prefix watermark; §8.1.2's 3-of-4 intersection lets a new primary learn the
durable point. What is missing is the retry case: if an append is applied by two instances and the primary
then dies, a client retry could append it a second time, and nothing in the design prevents that.

**Resolved, and more cheaply than Kafka's answer.** §8.1.1a-3 gets exactly-once from the expected offset plus
a content comparison, so no producer identifier or sequence number is needed — the request already carries
everything required to recognize its own retry. Kafka needs a token because its producers do not track
offsets; a DeLawson writer fixing its own does.

What remains open is not exactly-once but **truncation on handover** (§8.1.1a) and the **bound and timeout on
the out-of-order cache** (§8.1.1a-4).

#### 8.1.1c One thing DeLawson gets for free: no padding

GFS pads a chunk when a record will not fit and caps records at a quarter of the chunk to bound the resulting
fragmentation. **DeLawson needs neither**, because extents may be sealed at any size (§6) — an append block
that will not fit simply seals the extent short and starts a new one, which is the same mechanism §13 already
uses when an EN fails mid-write.

That is a direct payoff from variable-size extents. GFS's chunks were fixed at 64 MB, so the only way to keep
a record whole was to waste the tail; DeLawson's are bounded but not fixed, so the tail is simply shorter.

⚠️ A bound on append-block size is probably still wanted, for the same reason GFS had one: a very large block
arriving at a nearly-full extent wastes the remainder. The difference is that the waste is bounded by the
block size rather than by the chunk size, and it lands in §12.7's garbage term rather than in silent padding.

#### 8.1.2 The quorum forces broadcast, not a daisy chain

The primary must send each append to all three secondaries **in parallel**. Chain
replication — primary → S1 → S2 → S3 — would defeat the quorum entirely.

The reason is that a quorum only buys straggler tolerance if the writes are *issued*
concurrently. Under broadcast, durability arrives when the second-fastest of three
secondaries applies, so one slow node costs nothing. Under a chain, reaching three of four
means passing *through* the first two secondaries in sequence, so every straggler is on the
critical path and a stall at S1 blocks S2 and S3 as well:

| | Mean latency to durable (iid apply times, mean 1) |
|---|---|
| Broadcast — 2nd fastest of 3 | 1/3 + 1/2 = **0.83** |
| Chain — first two in sequence | 1 + 1 = **2.00** |

The tail matters more than the mean. With 1% of nodes running 10× slow, a chain is hit by a
straggler 2.0% of the time, while broadcast needs *two* of three to be slow and is hit
0.03% of the time — a **67× rarer** slow tail. Given that 3-of-4 exists precisely to avoid
waiting for the slowest instance, pairing it with a topology that serializes them would be
self-defeating.

What broadcast costs is egress *distribution*, not egress total. For a 4 MB append block
both put 12 MB on the wire; the chain spreads it one hop per node while broadcast puts all
12 MB on the primary's uplink. Fleet-wide that evens out, because every EN is primary for
some extents and secondary for others — so the concentration bounds per-extent burst
throughput rather than aggregate capacity.

#### 8.1.3 The SN is not in the write path

Worth stating explicitly, because it is easy to assume otherwise: **the SN places
instances and records where they are, then gets out of the way.** The append protocol runs
between the client or FE and the primary EN, and the SN is not consulted per write.

Two things depend on this:

- **The SN's memory budget survives.** §14.1 has one SN mapping ~76 PB of EN capacity from
  256 GB of RAM, which is only possible because it never touches a byte of it.
- **The cost target survives.** §1.2 needs writes to be handled by the tier that already
  owns the disks, not by an extra hop through a metadata machine.

The SN does learn of the outcome, but lazily: extent size and byte totals are the mid-tree
summaries §4.5 keeps lazy, and the sync loops of §13.1 reconcile the rest.

#### 8.1.4 EN-internal staging: common extents

Appends do not land directly in their final extent. Each EN has its own **common extents**, likely on SSD, which
absorb arriving appends; the EN tracks the offsets those appends will occupy in their **final** extents, and
coalesces into the final extents immediately. **The `(extent, offset)` returned by an append names the final
extent, never a common extent** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-15).

**Common extents are single-copy and purely EN-internal.** Each of the four ENs stages independently, and *that*
is the durability: four staging copies on four ENs chosen for failure independence (§5.6) have identical exposure
to the four final instances. So the SSD needs no RAID and no replication of its own, and an EN that loses its
staging device is repaired by the ordinary instance-repair path (§13.1) — no new failure mode, no new mechanism.

**What it buys.** Small appends destined for many different final extents would otherwise be small random writes
to HDD, at ~100 IOPS. Batching them into one sequential staging write and then one batched sequential write to
the final extent converts random IOPS into sequential bandwidth. Since §1.2 puts 95% of cost in disk, HDD IOPS is
exactly the scarce resource worth spending a cheap device to protect.

**Address assignment is decoupled from data placement.** The final extent and the offset within it are chosen by
the primary when the append arrives (§8.1.1a-2), so the address is known before the bytes reach their final home.
The EN-local index from `(final extent, offset range)` to staging location is bounded by *un-coalesced* appends
only, so it is small, and it is the read path's authority: a read of a recently-appended offset consults it before
touching the final device. That is what makes §8.1.1a-10's hint valid immediately on write rather than a
forward-dated promise.

##### 8.1.4.1 The client compresses, which is as far upstream as it goes

**Settled twice.** An FE compressing each append block was considered and rejected on 2026-08-17:
**"client compressing is better than FE compressing"** (Asserted, Bob). What the client version keeps
is below; what an FE version would have cost is compression CPU inside the datacenter on the ingest
path and append size across the internet. Neither version troubles §4.3.2.3's byte-identical
instances, since one compressor is one compressor wherever it sits — the argument is about where the
CPU and the bytes are, not about reproducibility.

**And it settles who checks the user's CRC** (§9.1.2). A client that compresses is a client that has
the codec, so it can decompress what comes back and compare it against the CRC it computed going in.
**Nothing between the two ever looks inside.**

**Append blocks are compressed by the `delawson` client library** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-15).

**And there is published prior art for exactly this, from a store that did it** (Cited:
[SCOPE](http://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol1/1454166.pdf), §2.1, Chaiken, Jenkins, Larson, Ramsey, Shakib,
Weaver and Zhou, PVLDB 1(2), 2008, of which Bob is an author):

> *"Append blocks are stored in compressed form with compression and decompression done transparently
> at the client."*

Worth citing for two reasons beyond agreement. **A distributed store that compresses is rarer than it
should be**, so the practice is hard to source at all — and **Cosmos is otherwise sparsely
documented**, which makes a peer-reviewed sentence about it one of the few public references there is.
Where this document would otherwise re-derive the practice, it can point at somebody having run it.

The same section describes three more decisions this document reached again independently: *"The data
within an extent consist of a sequence of append blocks. The block boundaries are defined by
application appends… contain a collection of application-defined records"* (§8.1, §8.2), *"concurrent
writers are serialized by the system"* (§8.1.1a-8), and *"regularly scrubbed to protect against bit
rot"* (§13). The client
library is DeLawson code, so this is not user code doing it — and it **reduces append size across the
internet**, which is the one link in the chain nobody controls the cost of.

That is strictly further upstream than "at the primary", and it settles a constraint this section previously
derived the hard way. §4.3.2.3 requires byte-identical instances, and four ENs compressing independently would
not produce them; compressing once at the client makes every staging copy identical for free. Three dividends:

- **no compression CPU inside the datacenter on the ingest path at all**, which sidesteps §7.1's objection
  rather than paying it;
- **no bit-reproducibility requirement on the codec**, so codecs and levels may vary per client and be
  upgraded;
- **the primary still learns the compressed size on arrival**, so it can assign the physical offset and detect
  the 32 MB physical seal bound at the same moment it assigns the logical one (§6).

**So the common extent holds append blocks compressed however the client compressed them**, which means
heterogeneous codecs and levels sitting side by side. Normalizing that is one of the jobs of the migration in
§8.1.4.4.

**It also takes the compression CPU off DeLawson's ledger entirely** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-15), and §12
handles both cases with no new mechanism:

| Client location | Whose CPU | How it is billed |
|---|---|---|
| Outside the cluster | the customer's own machine | **not billed at all** — DeLawson never spent it |
| A Compute node (§5.12) | the cluster's | **billed to the compute job**, which is already metered |

So the storage price of §12.7 does not have to carry compression CPU in either case, and the incentives come
out right without a policy: an external client that compresses hard pays fewer physical bytes and spends only
its own cycles, while a Compute-node client faces a real trade between compute charges and storage charges and
can optimize it. §12.1's pattern once more — cost-proportional billing turning a policy question into an
arithmetic one for the user.

**Recompression is different, and must be billed**, because it *is* DeLawson's CPU (§8.1.4.4). That splits the
ledger cleanly: initial compression is the client's cost and unbilled, recompression is the cluster's cost and
metered.

⚠️ Two consequences worth deciding rather than inheriting. **§12.3 bills physical bytes**, so a client that
compresses badly is billed for it until recompression fixes it — which makes recompression latency a billing
input, not only a space one. And a client that declines to compress is indistinguishable from one whose data is
incompressible, which is fine for billing and awkward for capacity planning.

##### 8.1.4.2 The durable watermark is set at staging, not at coalescing

*Durable* (§8.1.1) is reached when 3 of 4 ENs have the append in staging or final storage. So the
second-granularity durability timestamp of §9.7 and the retention window of §10.1 both key off **staging** time,
and coalescing latency is invisible to both. The alternative — timestamping at coalesce — would make time-range
query boundaries depend on background-loop scheduling, which is not a property anyone should have to reason
about.

##### 8.1.4.3 3-of-4 durability plus local coalescing produces interior holes, not short tails

Each EN coalesces on its own schedule, deterministically given the same appends at the same offsets. But
durability is 3-of-4, so the fourth EN may legitimately have missed an append — and because offsets are
primary-assigned, that append is a **hole in the middle** of its final extent, not a truncated tail. §8.1.1a
frames pre-EC reconciliation as truncation above the durable watermark; it is actually **hole-filling and
truncation**.

The saving grace is that primary-assigned offsets make hole detection **exact and cheap**: a gap in the offset map
is a gap, with no byte comparison. So before seal, the primary confirms all four instances cover the offset range
contiguously and any EN with gaps fetches them from a peer. **That is a required pre-EC step** and should be named
as one rather than discovered.

##### 8.1.4.4 Migration from common extents to dedicated ones

The transition is not a copy. It **coalesces small appends and may recompress** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-15) —
normalizing the heterogeneous client compression of §8.1.4.1, and turning many small append blocks into the
block structure §7.1 wants for random access.

**And it writes only the instances the scheme needs.** If EC needs 1 or 2 dedicated instances (§4.3.2.4), write
only those — **write one and copy it to make two** — and **keep the common extents until the EC group can
protect the data itself.**

| | Migration writes | Protection during the window |
|---|---|---|
| Earlier draft: 4 replicas, then EC | 4x | the 4 dedicated replicas |
| This: 1 or 2 instances | **1x or 2x** | the 4 ENs' common extents |

**Derived saving: 4x on the migration write at 1.333x, 2x at 2.333x.** The common extents are already durable
across four independent ENs, so writing four dedicated copies buys nothing that already-durable staging does
not provide.

**Copy, do not re-derive, for the second instance.** §4.3.2.3 requires the two to be byte-identical, and a byte
copy guarantees that where two independent recompressions would not. This is the dividend that matters most:
**recompression never needs to be deterministic**, because exactly one node ever performs it. That removes a
constraint §8.1.4.1 previously had to design around.

⚠️ **The retention requirement this creates is the part to get right.** Common extents cannot be released until
the group's parity exists, so staging retention is set by **how long a group takes to complete** — which is a
policy choice, not a data-availability limit:

- **Data is available fast.** An SN covering ~34 ENs sees ~2.1 GB/s of ingest, so the 45 data cells of a 10x6
  group (~1.44 GB at 32 MB physical) accumulate in **under a second**.
- **But §13.5.1 forms groups in a daily offline job.** Waiting for it means retaining a **day** of ingest —
  ~5.5 TB per EN against the ~1.8 TB device §8.1.4.5 sizes for endurance. **The device is 3x too small.**

So one of three things must be true, and it should be decided rather than discovered:

1. **Prompt online grouping** completes stripes in seconds, with the offline job advising only future
   groupings. §13.5.1 already notes that grouping extents within a single stream is easy; the hard part it
   solves is cross-directory optimality, which is exactly the part that can wait.
2. **Write more instances up front** to release staging early — trading the 4x write saving back for staging
   capacity.
3. **Size staging for retention** rather than endurance, which changes §8.1.4.5's rule and its cost.

Option 1 looks right, and it suggests the general shape: **protect promptly with a cheap grouping, optimize
later by regrouping** — except that regrouping rewrites parity, so its cost is not zero and the choice is not
obvious.

##### 8.1.4.5 Sizing is set by endurance, not capacity

Every ingested byte passes through the staging device once, so DWPD binds rather than GB. Using §12.7.2's
20 TB/$923 drive and ~100 drives per EN (2 PB raw, ~$92k), filling that over a year is ~63 MB/s sustained, or
5.5 TB/day — at 3 DWPD, ~1.8 TB of SSD, **under 0.1% of the EN's disk cost**. Even a 16x burstier assumption
stays inside §1.2's 5% budget. **Derived.** The sizing rule is therefore "endurance at sustained fill rate", not
"capacity for N seconds of buffer", and the two give very different answers.

**So stage only small appends.** An append near the 32 MB physical bound gains nothing — it is already a
sequential write — so writing those through directly cuts staging wear to the small-append fraction, which is the
only fraction that needed the IOPS conversion. The threshold is a per-media-class constant (§7.4.1).

**Staging must be durable with the power off.** An earlier draft proposed DRAM staging on an all-SSD EN, on the
grounds that four independent ENs each holding one copy give the same exposure as four final instances. **That is
rejected** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-15): *durable* means durable with the power off, and DRAM is not, however many
machines hold it. Independence across ENs addresses uncorrelated failure; a power event is not the only way to
lose volatile state, and losing an accepted append is exactly what §8.1.1's watermark promises cannot happen.

So on an all-SSD EN the choice is to stage on the SSD and accept writing each byte twice, or to stage on some
other non-volatile device. The arithmetic above sizes the first: at the sustained fill rate, doubled wear is
still inside §1.2's budget, so the simple answer survives.

This also removes the motivating case for making **power** an explicit nested failure domain. It may still be one
for other reasons — a correlated power event is a disaster in the §1.1.1 sense — but nothing in the write path now
depends on it.

##### 8.1.4.6 An extent known to age out quickly is never coalesced at all

**If it is known that an extent will age out quickly, never write the coalesced version**
(Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17). This is §8.5.3's argument one level down, and it is the stronger
version of it: coalescing is a rewrite whose cost is amortized over the data's remaining life,
so for data with almost no remaining life the right amount of rewriting is none. What is saved
is the whole migration write of §8.1.4.4, the recompression CPU that goes with it, and the
garbage both leave behind.

**Declared expiry decides it, exactly as it decides encoding.** An object with a one-day
expiry (§8.5.1) already skips the encode queue; the same declaration should skip the coalesce.
One signal, two decisions, neither of them a guess.

Two consequences, and the second is the awkward one:

- ⚠️ **Data that is never coalesced is never self-describing.** §8.1.5.1 makes coalescing the
  moment an extent becomes interpretable on its own, so skipping it leaves that extent
  dependent on its disk's journal for the whole of its life rather than for a window. The
  journal's blast radius is therefore not purely transient, which is an argument for #46's
  second copy rather than against it.
- ⚠️ **It keeps the data on the staging device for its lifetime.** Appends land in common
  extents (§8.1.4), so an extent that is never migrated is one that never leaves them.
  §8.1.4.5 sizes staging by *endurance* at ~1.8 TB, and §8.1.4.4 already finds that device 3x
  too small to *retain* a day of ingest. So the rule has a lifetime threshold set by staging
  capacity and not by the amortization argument: skipping the coalesce is free for data that
  ages out in minutes and unaffordable for data that ages out in a week, with the crossover
  set by a device sized for something else (#47).

### 8.1.5 What an EN keeps on disk: a journal of extent metadata, per disk

The bytes of an extent are on a disk; what says which extent they belong to, and at what
offsets, has to be somewhere too. **That is a journal of extent metadata, one per disk**
(Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17), and it is an ordinary journal in the §4.4 sense — the same shape
Raft state has, for the same reason:

| Part | Holds |
|---|---|
| **Snapshot** | the disk's extent metadata as of a moment |
| **Log** | every change since |

**A new snapshot is written when the log gets big.** Nothing more elaborate: the log bounds
recovery time, and rewriting the snapshot is what shortens it again.

#### 8.1.5.1 Only coalesced extents are self-describing

This is the part that decides how much the journal matters. **A coalesced extent should be
self-describing** — it carries enough of its own metadata to be read without asking anything
— **but a freshly written, un-coalesced extent is interpretable only with that disk's
journal** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17).

⚠️ **So the journal sharpens a claim made in three other places.** §5.2, §5.5.3 and §8.4.1's
heroics path all say that a disaster is recoverable by scanning ENs for self-describing
extents. That is true of the coalesced ones. For everything written since the last
coalescing, the scan finds bytes it cannot interpret, and the disk's journal is the only thing
that says what they are. The recovery story therefore has two halves, and the second one is
