new: **coalesced data is recoverable from the data itself, recent data is recoverable from the
journal.**

And the exposure is per disk rather than per extent: **every un-coalesced extent on a disk
depends on that one file.** Which makes it tempting to keep the journal on *two* different
disks in the EN — a cheap, purely local piece of redundancy for something whose loss costs
much more than it does — and that is worth deciding rather than assuming (#46).

#### 8.1.5.2 Where the implementation starts

**An EN begins with a vector of extents and a vector of appends, in memory** (Asserted, Bob,
2026-08-17). That is enough to get the command working end to end, and the journal comes
after — the same stand-in bargain as DN's in-memory object index (§17.5g), and the same
caution: nothing about the in-memory version is evidence about what the durable one costs.

#### 8.1.5.3 When transactions arrive, the EN's part of them lives in the journal

**Not being attempted yet: system change numbers and transactions.** But the place they will go is
already decided, and it is worth writing down because it constrains the journal being designed now:
**the EN's portion will be purely in the disk journal, never in the final extents** (Asserted, Bob,
2026-08-17).

Two things follow, and both are about what *not* to build:

- **The extent format does not grow a change number per record.** Extent bodies stay pure data, so
  what gets compressed, encrypted, erasure-coded, repaired and shipped between clusters carries no
  transaction state — and coalescing (§8.1.4.4) has nothing extra to preserve.
- **The journal has to have room for it.** It is already the thing that makes a recent extent
  interpretable (§8.1.5.1); it will also be the thing that says what is visible. A journal format
  that can only describe extents and offsets would have to be replaced, so it should not be designed
  as though extent metadata were all it will ever hold.

### 8.1.6 Logical and compressed positions are different types

**It is very easy to confuse logical and compressed values in append code, since both are 32-bit,
so they are separate types and the compiler is what catches it** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17). A
logical position counts the bytes a writer wrote; a compressed one counts the bytes that were
stored. An extent is capped well inside 32 bits either way, so nothing but a type distinguishes
them — and they are *equal* in exactly the case that hides the mistake: while nothing is
compressing yet.

The vocabulary is worth pinning down, because this document has used two words for one thing:
what §4.5 and §8.1.1a-2 call a **physical** position is what the code calls a **compressed**
one. Same space, and the sparse index (§9.3) is what relates it to the logical one.

⚠️ **And adopting the types immediately found a gap: an append carries no logical length, so the
receipt cannot report a logical offset.** §8.1.1a-2 requires the locator returned to a writer to
be logical, and §8.1.1a-7 makes the reportable offset a property of the object flavour. But the
client compresses (§8.1.4.1), so what reaches the primary EN is already compressed and its
logical size is known only to the client. The EN therefore has nothing to compute a logical
position from, and what it returns today is a compressed one wearing the wrong name. **The append
has to carry the logical length**, and until it does the receipt is only correct because nothing
compresses (#48).

#### 8.1.6.1 The same trick applies elsewhere, and one test says where

**`LOff` and `COff` are an instance of something general, and it can be done for other values**
(Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-19): wrap same-typed quantities that mean different things, and argument
mismatches become compile errors instead of wrong answers.

**The marginal cost is already near zero**, which is what makes it worth being systematic about:
`common/src/offset.rs` defines both types from one `space!` macro, so a third is a line, and the wire
conversions come with it.

##### The test for when it earns its keep

Not every pair of same-typed values wants a type. The criterion is in §8.1.6's own argument, and it is
sharper than "these are different things":

> ⚠️ **Wrap them when a mix-up is *silent* — and the sharpest form of silent is that the two coincide
> in exactly the cases a test would naturally cover.**

`LOff` and `COff` are equal while nothing compresses, which was every test written before compression
existed. That is not a fact about offsets; it is the shape of the hazard.

⚠️ **And the criterion has to be applied strictly, because Rust charges more for this than C++ does**
(Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-19). There is no implicit conversion to lean on, so a wrapped value needs an
impl or a `.get()` at every arithmetic operation, comparison, format and wire crossing — where a C++
strong typedef can stay largely transparent. **So the technique is for cases with a clear benefit, not
for every quantity that has a name.**

| Candidate | Type today | A mix-up is | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| **`ROff`** — a record number or count, beside `LOff` and `COff` | `u64` | **silent**: §9.1.3.6's three measures are records, logical bytes and compressed bytes, and only two of them have types | **yes** |
| **`ObjectId`, `StreamId`, `ExtentId`** | `u64` | **silent** — see the correction below | **yes** |
| **`Second`** (and a day) for key derivation (§7.3.3) | `u64` | **silent and unrecoverable** — a *derived* key looks valid either way, and §7.3.2.4 makes a key you cannot reproduce that day's data gone | **yes** |
| **entries / bytes** for the answer limit (§9.1.3.7, §16.132) | `u64` | silent while entries are uniform | once the limit exists |
| `DnId` / `SnId` / `EnId` | `u32` | mixed: loud as an address, silent as a map key | lower |

**`ROff` is the cheapest of these and the most obviously missing**, because `common/src/offset.rs`
already generates `LOff` and `COff` from one macro and §9.1.3.6 names *three* measures. Two have types
and the third is a bare `u64` — so `Covered { records, logical, compressed }` mixes typed and untyped
fields, and `Budget::met` compares a count against a byte total by writing the comparison correctly
rather than by being unable to write it wrongly. **The evidence that the type is wanted is that a test
was written instead**: `a_budget_is_met_only_in_its_own_space` exists precisely because 500 logical
bytes must not satisfy a 500-compressed-byte budget, which a type would refuse to compile.

##### ⚠️ Correcting the claim that id mix-ups fail loudly

An earlier version of this section rated the id types low priority on the grounds that a swap fails
loudly. **That is true only while an id is being used as an address, and false where it is a map key**,
which is most places:

| | Swapping two ids |
|---|---|
| `format!("SN{n}")` to pick a peer | **loud** — the request goes to a machine that refuses it |
| `self.at.get(&(sn, id))` in the EN | **silent** — the lookup simply misses, and the EN then creates a fresh extent for what it thinks is a new name |

`EN::place(sn: u32, id: u64, created: u64)` is the example: the last two are adjacent, same-typed, and
swapping them uses a timestamp as an extent id. The map misses, a second extent appears, and nothing
says anything. So the correction reverses the priority — **ids belong on the list**, as Bob's had them.

##### A run of same-typed parameters wants a struct, not five newtypes

⚠️ **The worst hazard in the code today is not solved by typing values at all.** `SN::close` takes
`dn: u32` and then **five consecutive `u64`s** — `stream, id, records, length, second`. Every swap
among them compiles, and several would be silent.

**§17.13.3 already solved this shape once, and the answer was a struct**: `AppendBlock` exists because
"two processes each counting positions in a list pass their own unit tests while disagreeing with each
other". A parameter list is the same failure with the compiler in the room. So:

> **Wrap the *values* when two spaces could be confused; group the *parameters* when a signature has a
> run of them.** They are different fixes for different mistakes, and the second is cheaper per unit of
> risk removed.

##### ⚠️ `ROff` does not catch §17.16.2's bug, and it must not be thought to

The highest-severity mix-up in this system's history is object-local against stream-local against
extent-local record numbers — §17.16.2, where all three origins are zero until an object outgrows its
first extent and **139 of 200 reads failed** the moment one did.

**`ROff` makes all three the same type.** Distinguishing them needs a per-container type —
`ObjectRecord`, `StreamRecord`, `ExtentRecord` — and that is a far more invasive change, because a
record number appears in `Described`, `Located`, `Open`, `Held`, `Extent`, `Append` and `Landed`, each
in a different space. Under Bob's cost rule that is not obviously worth it.

**So the honest position: this work does not address §17.16.2, and that bug stays covered by a test** —
`a_record_number_survives_the_trip_through_three_spaces`, plus any read that crosses a seal. Saying so
matters more than it might seem, because the danger of a partial fix is the confidence it creates:
`ROff` everywhere would make the read path *look* type-safe while the conversion that actually broke
remained a matter of getting the arithmetic right.

#### 8.1.6.2 One type for an index and a count costs one value, and a sentinel costs another

**Because the same type serves as an index and as a count, the maximum count is not 2^64** (Asserted,
Bob, 2026-08-19): it is **2^64 − 1**, or **2^64 − 2** if 2^64 − 1 means *no value given*. The same
applies to every other space.

The arithmetic, once, because it is easy to be off by one about being off by one:

| | With no sentinel | With `MAX` meaning none |
|---|---|---|
| largest **count** | 2^64 − 1 | 2^64 − 2 |
| largest valid **index** | 2^64 − 2 | 2^64 − 3 |
| what **one past the end** is | 2^64 − 1, which is the count | 2^64 − 2 |

**One past the end is why the count loses a value even without a sentinel.** It is not a curiosity:
§9.1.3's `next` is *the record to ask for after this answer*, which after the last record is one past
the end, and `first_record + records` is computed all over the read path. A count of exactly 2^64 would
make that expression unrepresentable at the top of the range.

⚠️ **For capacity this is immaterial and for the contract it is not.** Nobody will store 2^64 records.
But §0's rule is that an unlabelled number is a liability, and "64-bit record number" (§3) invites the
reading that the limit is 2^64 — which is wrong, and wrong in the direction that only shows up at the
boundary, where nothing is ever tested.

##### ⚠️ It exposes a cap this document states in a form the type cannot hold

**§6 says an extent seals at "4 GB logical", and `LOff` is 32 bits.** 4 GB is 2^32; the largest value a
`u32` holds is 2^32 − 1. So the cap as written is exactly one byte outside the type that enforces it.

**The code is right and the document is round.** The EN's check is
`extent.logical_end.plus(logical).is_err()`, with the comment that this is "the 4 GB logical cap
enforcing itself through the type rather than by a constant" — so what is enforced is
**logical_end ≤ 2^32 − 1**, a cap of 4 GiB *minus one byte*. The section boasting that the type enforces
the cap is the section stating a cap the type cannot represent, which is a pleasing kind of wrong.

Two ways out, and the choice is not obvious: **restate the cap as 2^32 − 1** and accept an unlovely
number in §6, or **widen `LOff`** and let 4 GB be exactly 4 GB. §14.1.3's argument that a compressed
length is four bytes inside §4.7's budget is about `COff`, not `LOff`, so widening is not free either
(#89).

##### ⚠️ And a sentinel already exists, spelled as zero, where it collides

Today an extent still being appended to reports **`records = 0`** to mean *count unknown* — the SN says
"the record count is zero unless the extent is sealed", and the FE reads it back as
`self.records > 0 && …`. **That is the sentinel Bob is proposing, chosen at the wrong end of the
range**, and zero is a value a count can legitimately take:

| An extent with `records == 0` | Is |
|---|---|
| still open | count unknown |
| sealed holding nothing | a real count of zero |

The second is excluded today by other means — the FE treats `records == 0 && length == 0` as *this
block will not fit an extent of its own* and refuses — so nothing is currently broken. **But the
encoding cannot distinguish them**, so the exclusion is a property of the surrounding code rather than
of the value, and it has to keep being true.

##### Which is the strongest argument for the newtypes so far

Put together, this is a better case for `ROff` and friends than catching mix-ups was:

- **The type owns the sentinel.** `ROff::NONE` is `MAX`, `is_none()` asks, and nothing has to remember
  that zero is special — because it stops being special.
- **The type owns the boundary arithmetic.** `LOff::plus` already returns an error rather than wrapping,
  with the comment that running out of positions "is the extent being full, which is a reason to seal it
  and not a reason to wrap". One-past-the-end and the sentinel are exactly the same kind of rule, and
  they belong in the same place.
- **And it costs no memory, which `Option` would.** `Option<u64>` is 16 bytes where a sentinel is 8, and
  §4.7 budgets ~100 bytes for an extent record — so the niche-free encoding matters against a budget
  §14.1.2 says decides how many machines an object needs. A newtype gives `Option`-like ergonomics at
  `u64`'s size.

#### 8.1.6.3 Settled: every space reserves a sentinel, used or not

**Every one of these types gets a sentinel** (Decided, Bob, 2026-08-19), and the argument is marginal
cost rather than need:

> **A comparison has to happen anyway** to keep the maximum length representable — so comparing against
> `MAX − 1` instead of `MAX` is the same instruction, and reserving the value is nearly free even where
> nothing uses it.

**And the uniformity is the real prize**, because the alternative is a migration. A space that reserves
nothing today and needs a sentinel tomorrow has to lower its documented maximum, which is a change to a
format contract — the kind §13.2.5 needs a parameter and an upgrade path for. Reserving now costs one
value; reserving later costs a version.

##### Where the sentinel sits differs by kind, and both are provably safe

| Kind | Sentinel | Why there | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| **measures** — `ROff`, `LOff`, `COff`: counts, lengths, offsets | **`MAX`** | zero is a length a caller can legitimately mean, so it cannot be the absence | one value |
| **ids** — `ObjectId`, `StreamId`, `ExtentId` | **`0`** | ids are allocated from **1** (`next_object`, `next_stream`, the SN's `Naming`), so zero is already impossible | **nothing** |

**So the rule is uniform in kind rather than in literal value**, and the id case is genuinely free: it
needs no headroom for one-past-the-end either, because nothing computes one past an id. §17.12's batch
answer already relies on this, marking an absent name with a zero id — `Described::missing()` — so the
convention exists and this only names it.

##### Done for the two spaces that exist

`LOff` and `COff` now carry `NONE`, `MAX`, `is_none()` and `is_some()`, and the checked constructors
refuse a length equal to the sentinel rather than letting it become one. **One existing test reversed**,
which is the useful part:

```
assert!(LOff::new(u32::MAX - 1).plus(LOff::new(1)).is_ok());   // was
assert!(LOff::new(u32::MAX - 1).plus(LOff::new(1)).is_err());  // is
```

That sum used to be allowed and produced a length **equal to the sentinel** — a full extent whose
logical end reads as *no value*. Nothing could reach it, since §6's cap bites long before, but it is the
exact shape of the bug the reservation prevents.

⚠️ **It also tightens §6's cap by one more byte**, which sharpens #89 rather than settling it: the
largest logical extent is now 2^32 − 2. Restating §6's "4 GB" as 2^32 − 2 is honest and ugly, so #89's
third option — **a round cap comfortably below the type's ceiling** — looks better than it did. The cap
is a guess (§0) rather than a derived figure, so lowering it to a number with headroom costs capacity
nobody is using and buys arithmetic nobody has to check.

**The first row is the one to do, because the bug is not hypothetical.** §17.16.2 records it: three
numbering spaces meet on the read path, all three are zero until an object outgrows its first extent,
and **139 of 200 reads failed** the moment one did. §17.18 and §17.19 then found the same *class* of
defect twice more in one afternoon — an FE patching a field by position, and a benchmark chopping an
answer by an assumed width.

**And it would replace a comment with a compiler.** The FE carries this warning today:

> ⚠️ **`within` twice and `origin` are only correct as a set.** Both first-records are zero until an
> object outgrows its first extent, so a version that drops either one passes everything that never
> leaves that extent and then fails most reads.

With typed spaces, `within` becomes two distinct conversions — object→stream and stream→extent — and
`origin` the only way back. Dropping one stops compiling, so that paragraph describes a property of the
types instead of a rule somebody has to hold in mind. §17.12.1's lesson again: **structural rather than
careful.**

##### What it does not fix

⚠️ **A newtype prevents *mixing* spaces and does nothing about being wrong *within* one.** An
`ExtentRecord` off by one is still off by one, and §17.16.2's bug had both faces. So this narrows the
class rather than closing it, and the test that reads past the first seal is still what catches the
rest.

**Tracked in #86**, and it belongs to the coding rules §16.141 says have no home.

### 8.1.7 Sealing when an instance is down

The normal seal is the primary's: it assigns the offsets, so it knows where the extent ends. **When
instances are down the SN coordinates it instead** (#55), and the algorithm is Bob's, 2026-08-17:

> **Seal at the minimum accepted length over all responses, discarding the smallest response.**

⚠️ **And "the smallest response" is really "the smallest *I* − *Q* responses", because the quorum is
configurable** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17). With four instances and a quorum of three that is one
response discarded; **with three of three it is none, so the rule is plainly the minimum**; with five
of three it is two. One rule, and the two numbers in `[extents]` say what it means:

| Instances | Quorum | Discard | Responses needed |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | 3 | 1 | 2 |
| 3 | 3 | 0 | 1 |
| 5 | 3 | 2 | 3 |
| 5 | 4 | 1 | 2 |

⚠️ **A quorum must be more than half, and the configuration is refused if it is not.** Two quorums
have to overlap or two disjoint sets could each hold an append the other never saw — 3 of 4 overlap in
two, while **2 of 4 do not overlap at all** and 3 of 6 do not either. §8.1.1 argues this; the config
now enforces it rather than trusting whoever edits the file.

**And none of this is new: it is a quorum read, the same algorithm as Paxos and Raft** (Asserted, Bob,
2026-08-17). The order statistic is the giveaway — **Raft advances its commit index to the largest
index a majority of its followers have matched**, which sorted is the same (*I* − *Q* + 1)-th smallest
this rule takes (Cited: [Raft](https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf)). The overlap requirement is Paxos's
intersection argument, and "a new primary polls a quorum and sees everything committed" is leader
election with the log names changed.

That is worth stating rather than glossing, for two reasons. A reader who recognizes the mechanism can
stop looking for what is different about it — **nothing is** — and inherit its failure modes and its
proofs instead of re-deriving them. And where DeLawson *does* differ from a consensus log, the
difference is not in the quorum but in what is being agreed: byte ranges in an extent rather than
entries in a log, so the "index" is a length and the record rules of §8.2.3 sit on top of it.

#### 8.1.7.1 Why the second-smallest is the right statistic

Sort the accepted lengths of the four instances, *a* ≤ *b* ≤ *c* ≤ *d*. Discarding the smallest and
taking the minimum of the rest is **b**, the second-smallest — and *b* is exactly the largest length
that three instances have, since *b*, *c* and *d* all reach it and only *c* and *d* reach *c*. So
with every instance answering, **the rule computes the durable length exactly**.

In general it is the (*I* − *Q* + 1)-th smallest, which is the largest length *Q* instances have.
**Derived, and checked exhaustively** for 3-of-3, 4-of-3, 5-of-3, 5-of-4, 6-of-4 and 7-of-5 over
every combination of lengths and every subset of responders: **never below the durable length in any
case, exactly right whenever every instance answers, and the overshoot shrinks with each extra
response.**

With one instance missing, *b* is computed from three responses and the absent instance's length *m*
is unknown. Then:

| *m* | True durable length | The rule seals at |
|---|---|---|
| ≥ *b* | *b* | *b* — exact |
| between *a* and *b* | *m* | *b* — too long by *b* − *m* |
| < *a* | *a* | *b* — too long by *b* − *a* |

**So the rule never seals below the durable length, and may seal above it.** That asymmetry is the
right way round, and it is the whole reason the rule is shaped this way:

- **Sealing below would discard an append that was acknowledged as durable.** Unacceptable at any
  price.
- **Sealing above keeps bytes that were accepted but never promised.** At least one live instance has
  them, so sealing there is a *commitment to repair up to that length* rather than a claim that it is
  already there — and §8.1.4.3's hole-filling is the step that already exists to do it.

#### 8.1.7.2 When to stop waiting

Two stopping rules, and they answer different questions:

- **Stop as soon as the computed length matches a durable length any responder reported** — which
  needs only *I* − *Q* + 1 responses, two in the shipped shape. An instance's reported durable length
  is a length it knows reached a quorum, so a match is proof rather than inference, and no further
  opinion can improve on proof.
- **Otherwise wait a very short time — of order 100 ms — once a quorum of responses is in.** The usual
  cause of failure-mode sealing is one instance being down, so **a quorum of responses will nearly
  always arrive, and the ones after it are what turn an upper bound into the exact answer.** Every
  byte of overshoot is a byte repair has to move to make good, so a little waiting buys a tighter
  seal.

⚠️ **The grace period has to stay far below a TCP retry**, which is §16's open question 14: the whole
point of seal-short is that one dead EN must not stall a writer for a timeout. 100 ms is comfortably
inside that, and it is a knob rather than a constant for exactly that reason.

#### 8.1.7.3 It composes with the record rules for free

The seal point still has to land on a record boundary (§8.2.3 rule 1), so the computed length is
trimmed back to the last complete record at or below it. **That trim cannot lose anything
acknowledged**, because §8.2.3's second gate means an append that closed no record was never durable
in the first place. So failure-mode sealing needs no record surgery and no special answer to the
writer about half-written records — the rules that removed the split in §8.2.4 remove it here too.

#### 8.1.7.4 An instance may mark itself broken and ask for a seal, and *I* − *Q* + 1 of them force one

**An instance of an extent can mark itself broken and request a seal** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-19).
This is the other direction from §8.1.7: there, something outside notices instances are down and
coordinates a seal; here, an instance that knows something nobody else can — a device error, an
unreadable journal — says so.

**And *I* − *Q* + 1 of them make the seal compulsory, by arithmetic.** An append needs *Q* instances
to apply it, so with *B* broken the healthy count is *I* − *B* and appends are impossible exactly when

> *I* − *B* < *Q*, that is **when *B* ≥ *I* − *Q* + 1**.

At four instances and a quorum of three that is **two**: two broken instances leave two healthy, and
two can never be three. **Derived.** So at that point the extent is not merely degraded, it is
*unappendable*, and leaving it open is a lie — every subsequent append would fail after waiting for a
quorum that cannot form.

⚠️ **That is the same *I* − *Q* + 1 as §8.1.7.1's order statistic, and not by coincidence.** *I* − *Q*
is how many instances may be lost while a quorum survives; the +1 is one too many. §8.1.7.1 counts up
to it to find the durable length, and this counts to it to find that there is no more length to come.
Two uses of one threshold, which is a hint that it is the real quantity and the two rules are one
mechanism seen from either end.

**Whether a *single* instance may trigger a seal: yes, and it costs metadata rather than correctness**
(Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-19, and nothing here contradicts it). The reason no contradiction appears is
that sealing is already the universally safe response — §6 permits sealing at any size, §8.1.1c makes
sealing short free rather than wasteful, and §7.2.4 has just made it the answer to truncation as well.
Three things argue for allowing it:

- **It is information nobody else has.** An instance that has read a bad block knows it before any
  sync loop could infer it, and the alternative is waiting for the fact to be rediscovered from
  outside.
- **It shortens a fragile window.** An extent with one broken instance is one failure away from
  unappendable. Sealing converts it into something repair can work on — EC grouping and
  re-replication both want sealed extents.
- **It composes with everything already decided.** The seal length comes from §8.1.7's order
  statistic, and instances holding more than that truncate — which seals, per §7.2.4. A broken
  instance's own reported length is safe to include: reported low it is likely among the *I* − *Q*
  discarded, and reported high it seals above the durable length, which §8.1.7.1 shows is the
  tolerable direction.

⚠️ **The cost is churn, and its blast radius is every extent that instance holds.** A flapping EN
that seals on each wobble produces short extents across all of them, and extent count is what bounds
an SN's memory (§14.1) — so this lands in §16.133's budget alongside handover, from a second
direction. **The SN is the natural place to damp it**, because it already records every seal
(§8.1.7), so a threshold or a rate limit there needs no new participant. What must not happen is an
EN deciding unilaterally *and* unboundedly.

**One thing it must do besides asking**: an instance that has marked itself broken stops counting
toward the quorum for new appends immediately, or the primary keeps waiting on it. Requesting the
seal and withdrawing from the quorum are the same act, and separating them would leave appends
stalling against an instance that has already said it cannot help.

##### 8.1.7.4.1 Nobody counts: the threshold describes what happens rather than causing it

**If an instance durably marks itself as requesting a seal, and thereafter fails any further append
it sees, then *I* − *Q* + 1 such instances prevent a quorum for any further append** (Asserted, Bob,
2026-08-19). That is the mechanism, and it is better than the rule it replaces.

**"Appends it sees" is the exact obligation, and the exactness is what makes it cheap.** A marked
instance does not have to prevent appends, observe them, or know they happened — it answers *no* to
what arrives at it and nothing else. It has no duty toward an append it never receives, which is
just as well, since an instance that has declared itself broken is the last thing that should be
required to notice something.

⚠️ **The arithmetic above stops being something anything implements.** Read as a rule, *B* ≥
*I* − *Q* + 1 needs an observer: something has to learn how many instances are broken, decide the
threshold is met, and act — which is a detector with a staleness window, a race against instances
marking themselves concurrently, and a question about who runs it. Read as a *consequence*, none of
that exists. Each instance refuses appends locally, and appends stop reaching quorum **because they
cannot**, not because anyone noticed. The threshold is then a description of when appends start
failing, and §8.1.7's ordinary coordinated seal — which is already what happens when appends fail —
takes it from there.

**That is the same shape as three other things already decided**, which is why it is worth naming: the
quorum intersection needs no reconciliation protocol (§8.1.1), placement needs no rebalancer because
the answer is persisted (§5.6.9), and the waiters need no ordering discipline because they live under
the lock (§17.12.1). In each case a rule that would have needed an enforcer became a consequence of
where a fact is kept.

**Durably is load-bearing, and it is the one part that costs something.** A mark held only in memory
is cleared by a restart, and an instance that comes back accepting appends would take offsets its
peers have long since moved past — writing different bytes where the extent already has some, which
is exactly the §7.2.4 hazard the rest of this section exists to prevent. So the mark belongs in the
EN's per-disk extent journal (§8.1.5), beside the extent metadata that already has to survive a
restart to be interpretable at all.

⚠️ **And it is a one-way door.** Nothing clears the mark, because there is no safe way back: an
instance that resumed appending after being skipped would have a hole it cannot fill and a durable
length its peers disagree with. Repair is the way back, and repair works on a *sealed* extent — which
is what the mark brings about.

### 8.2 Record framing

An object declares a framing at creation, and **appends are stored in the format the writer gave
them**, by default:

| Framing | Boundary | Overhead per record |
|---|---|---|
| `FixedLength` | every record the same declared width | **0 B** |
| `Nul` | terminated by `0x00` | 1 B |
| `Lf` | terminated by `\n` | 1 B |
| `CrLf` | terminated by `\r\n` | 2 B |
| `LengthPrefixed` | a fixed-width length precedes each record | 4 B |

`LengthPrefixed` and `FixedLength` are the framings permitting arbitrary binary content; the
terminator framings require that the terminator not appear inside a record, and exist so that
existing line- and NUL-delimited data can be stored and scanned without a rewrite.

**Boundary bytes count towards the logical length.** A 100-byte record in `CrLf` is 102 logical
bytes, and §4's cumulative logical byte totals include the framing.

#### 8.2.1 Framing is a representation, not a property of the data

A reader may **ask for a different framing than the writer used**, and DeLawson translates. The
translation is arithmetic rather than a scan, because the overhead per record is a constant for a
given format:

> logical_B = logical_A − *N*·overhead_A + *N*·overhead_B

and *N*, the record count over the span, is exactly what §4's cumulative counts already carry. So
converting a logical length between framings is **O(1)** — another use for an index built for
addressing.

Most users write and read in the same format, so this is the exception rather than the rule. But
it also means **coalescing may change the stored framing** (§10), and therefore:

> **Framing is not a durable property of the data.** The records are the data; the framing is how
> they happen to be laid out at the moment.

The motive for re-framing during coalescing is to match the *dominant read* format and take the
translation off the read path. Saving space is a weaker motive than it looks: at 100-byte records
`LengthPrefixed` costs 3.85% of logical bytes and `CrLf` 1.96%, but framing bytes are about as
predictable as data gets — an identical terminator every hundred bytes — so compression removes
most of that before it reaches the physical bytes anyone is billed for (§12.3).

#### 8.2.2 Zero-length appends break the fixed-offset check

⚠️ `FixedLength` with a declared width of **zero** is degenerate in a way that collides with
§8.1.1a-3: every record occupies 0 logical bytes, so an append of any size advances the logical
offset by nothing, and **two appends share an offset**. The fixed-offset check then cannot tell a
retry from a new append, which is precisely what it exists to do.

**Resolved: the append offset is always determined in a canonical length-stuffed space** (Asserted,
Bob, 2026-08-15), independent of how the append is actually formatted.

> The offset assigned at accept is computed as if the append were **length-stuffed**, where every
> row's length field occupies **4 bytes** of logical space. The append's real format is a separate
> field in the append header.

**This makes no assumption whatever about row content.** A zero-width fixed-length row still consumes
4 logical bytes, so `FixedLength(0)` stops being degenerate and no framing mode needs forbidding.

The invariant the check actually needs is still worth stating:

> **Every fixed-offset append must advance the logical offset strictly.**

but the only way left to violate it is an append containing **zero records**, permitted by §8.1. That
is a property of the individual request rather than of the object's declared framing, so it is
detectable at accept and cheap to reject — a far narrower restriction than disallowing a framing mode.

**The larger payoff is that logical offsets become invariant under re-framing**, which removes a
contradiction between §8.2.1 and §8.1.1a-7 that would otherwise have been latent. §8.2.1 permits
coalescing to change the stored framing; §8.1.1a-7 defines the object offset as the sum of sealed
extent *logical* lengths. If logical length were measured in the stored framing, re-framing an extent
during compaction would silently shift every offset above it — destroying exactly the density and
stability §8.1.1a-6 says three mechanisms depend on. A canonical space decouples the two: **framing is
a representation, and now so is the physical byte position; only the canonical offset is a name.**

**What it costs, and what it does not.**

- **4 bytes per row of canonical space**, whatever the stored framing. At 100-byte records that is 4%
  inflation of the logical space; at 8-byte records, 50%.
- **Nothing in billing**, because §12.3 bills physical bytes and the canonical space never reaches a
  disk.
- **Something in sealing**: §6's 4 GB *logical* cap is consumed in canonical bytes, so an extent of
  very small records seals at fewer physical bytes than a naive reading suggests. Worth stating
  explicitly, since the two limits of §6 are meant to bracket a known range.
- **No new work on the append path.** The primary must parse the append per its declared framing to
  compute canonical lengths — but it already has to parse it to maintain the cumulative record counts
  of §4, and §8.2.1 shows converting a logical length between framings is O(1) given the record count.
- **A 4-byte length field caps a row at 4 GB**, which coincides with §6's logical extent cap. Those two
  agreeing is a consistency check, not a coincidence to be relied on.

**An earlier draft suggested using the record number instead, and that does not work.** Appends may contain
**record fragments** — a writer that fixes its own offsets may reasonably let a record span appends — so an
append boundary need not fall on a record boundary. A record number therefore does not identify an append: two
appends can both begin inside record 5, and distinguishing them needs *(record number, offset within the
record)*, a two-part token strictly worse than the single logical byte offset.

So **the logical byte offset is the right token precisely because it is record-agnostic**, and the
zero-width-fixed-length case is a genuine corner that simply needs forbidding rather than designing around.

#### 8.2.3 An extent holds whole records; an append need not

Four rules, all Bob's, 2026-08-17, and they are not the same rule at different scales:

1. **An extent contains whole records.** Sealing is where this is enforced, and the boundary is the
   extent's, not the append's.
2. **A record may cross append blocks.** §8.2.2 already relies on this — a writer fixing its own offsets
   controls where its bytes land, so an append boundary need not fall on a record boundary.
3. **A terminator framing's data may not contain its terminator**, and **the `laws` client is what
   checks it.** The client is the last place that holds records *as records* before they become a byte
   stream; after that, a stray `\n` in `lf` data is not a violation anybody can detect — it is simply
   two records. Checking where the information still exists is the only place the check means anything.
4. **Every framing can face a partial record** — including `fixed`, where a block ending part-way
   through the declared width is a partial record found by arithmetic rather than by a missing
   terminator. What differs between framings is not whether a fragment can happen but whether a
   reader can **resynchronize**: a terminator framing can find the next boundary by scanning, while
   `fixed` and `length` are interpretable only from a known record boundary. So rule 1 is strictest
   for those two — a boundary lost in `fixed` or `length` data is unrecoverable rather than merely
   awkward — and it is why the seal boundary must land on a record end.

⚠️ **The consequence for durability is the sharp one: an append whose trailing record is incomplete
cannot be reported durable until a later append completes that record.** Bytes being on three of four
disks is not enough, because half a record is not a record — so the append that *started* a record
waits for the append that finishes it. Two things follow:

- **A receipt can wait on a subsequent append**, not merely on the instances. §8.1.1's watermark is
  about bytes; this is a second gate in front of it, and an append satisfies both or is not durable.
  A writer that stops mid-record has an append that never completes, which is correct: it never
  wrote a whole record. It is also what keeps an extent from sealing mid-record, which §8.2.4 turns
  into the reason nothing ever has to be split.
- **An append's receipt covers the records it completed**, which may include one begun by an earlier
  append. Record numbers are assigned to complete records, so they are assigned in the append that
  finishes them.

#### 8.2.4 One rule removes the split: a block ends on a boundary, or holds no boundary at all

The obvious reading of the rules above is that sealing must sometimes **split the final append and
discard half a record**, leaving an append that committed some of its records and not others — an
outcome that is neither a success nor a failure, and that a writer seeing only "ok" or "error" would
either lose data over or duplicate data over. That is what an earlier draft of this section
concluded, along with the observation that a writer can avoid it by ending every append on a record
boundary.

**But it can be removed rather than mitigated** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17):

> A record may fail to end in its append block **only if it began at the start of that block, or in
> an earlier one.**

Equivalently, and this is the form to check: **an append block either ends on a record boundary, or
contains no record boundary at all.** A block may be all whole records, or it may be a slab of bytes
wholly inside one record — never three records and half of a fourth.

**Why that removes the split.** It makes every append block indivisible *and* placeable:

- A block that **ends on a boundary** can go wholly into the current extent or wholly into a fresh
  one. §8.1.1a-2 already bounds an append at 32 MB logical precisely so it always fits a fresh
  extent, so the primary's choice is free.
- A block that **holds no boundary** belongs to a record that is still open, and rule 1 of §8.2.3
  keeps a whole record in one extent — so the extent cannot seal until that record closes.

Put together: **an extent seals between records, and therefore between blocks.** Nothing is ever cut,
no append is ever divided, and the partial-commit answer is not needed because the state it described
cannot arise. The deferral rule of §8.2.3 is what enforces the second bullet — an append that closes
no record is not durable yet, and an extent with an open record is not sealable yet, which are the
same fact seen from the writer's side and the extent's side.

**So a record's maximum size is an extent's maximum size** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17): **4 GB
logical, and 32 MB compressed on first write.** Rule 1 keeps a whole record in one extent, so the
record cap cannot be anything else — and since a record may span appends, the cap is *not* the 32 MB
logical append bound of §8.1.1a-2. A writer may build a record out of many appends, up to what an
extent holds; what it may not do is send one of them larger than 32 MB.

⚠️ **And the compressed half of that is soft: it bounds the first write, not the extent for ever**
(Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17). If later recompression (§8.1.4.4, §10) makes an extent larger than
32 MB, that is fine — nothing needs to hold the extent under the cap once the bytes are in it. See
§6.2, because anything that reads the cap as an invariant is reading it wrongly.

**And the check belongs in two places, for different reasons.** The `laws` client frames the record it
is given, so what it sends always ends on a boundary and the rule is satisfied by construction. The
primary EN checks it anyway, because the rule is what makes sealing simple and a writer talking to the
protocol directly must not be able to break that.

### 8.3 The three mutations

| | Unkeyed | Keyed |
|---|---|---|
| **Insert** | appended to the object's tail extent; allocates the next record number | written to the log of the extent whose key range covers the key |
| **Update** | `(local record number, new bytes)` appended to that extent's log | `(key, new bytes)` appended to the log |
| **Delete** | tombstone for the local record number, appended to the log | tombstone for the key, appended to the log |

Update and delete never touch the base, never change any cumulative record
count, and never reopen a sealed extent. Insert is the only operation that moves
counts, which is why unkeyed inserts are confined to the object's end.

### 8.4 Deletion, and soft delete

§4.3.4 identifies administrative error as the most serious unmitigated loss mode: a wrong-but-authorized
delete is executed faithfully by tombstoning (§8.3), propagated by the DN→SN sync (§13.1.7), and
completed by the background loops. Soft delete is the answer, and most of the machinery already exists.

#### 8.4.1 It is a deferred decrement

Streams and extents are reference-counted (§4.6.1), so **retaining a deleted object is simply not
decrementing yet.** A delete marks the object's DN record deleted with a *reclaim-after* timestamp; the
background loops (§13.3) perform the decrement when the window expires.

The important consequence is that **a soft-deleted object still holds its references**, which keeps
every existing invariant intact:

| Mechanism | Why it is unaffected |
|---|---|
| DN→SN sync (§13.1.7) | The DN still references those streams, so they are not orphans and are not reclaimed |
| Orphan detection | Unchanged — a retained delete is a live reference, not a leak |
| Compaction (§10) | Unchanged; tombstones within a live object are a separate matter (§8.3) |
| Billing (§12) | Retained bytes are physical bytes, so they bill automatically |

That last row is a feature: the customer holding a retention window pays for it, with no new metering.
It is also §12.6's "uncompacted garbage" question arriving with a clear answer — **yes, they pay**,
because the bytes are really there and really theirs.

#### 8.4.1a Two failure sources, and why they need the same window

Soft delete guards against two quite different things:

- **A software bug issuing deletes**, which can originate in **any layer** — FE, DN, SN or EN. A bug
  saying "delete everything" is not exotic; it is the ordinary shape of a bad deploy.
- **A user deleting the wrong thing**, which is the common case and the one users can describe.

⚠️ **Do not build a window where maintainers can recover by heroics but users cannot recover directly.**
That regime looks like protection and is actually a staffing trap: every accidental deletion becomes a
support ticket, and the maintainers end up spending all their time on manual recovery instead of on the
system. **So undelete must be a user-facing operation over the whole window**, not a privilege exercised
on the user's behalf.

Heroics are still needed, but for the other case. When a *bug* did the deleting, the user may not know
what vanished, may not be able to name it, and the layer that would serve the undelete may itself be the
one that malfunctioned. That is genuinely a staff operation — acceptable because it is rare, where user
error is not.

#### 8.4.1b Three days, and a brake

The window is set by human response time, and **three days is the maximum needed, not a floor.** The
worst case is a failure on Friday evening, seen Monday morning. A Thursday failure is noticed by Friday,
so it needs one day. Nothing needs more than the weekend.

That holds because **the intervention required is trivial: stop hard deleting.** A maintainer does not
need to diagnose anything or restore anything within the window — only to hit the brake, after which the
data sits safely while the actual fix is worked out at leisure.

⚠️ Which makes the brake a **requirement**: there must be a single, immediate, cluster-wide switch that
halts all hard deletion, usable by someone who knows nothing yet except that something is wrong. Without
it the three days are not usable, because diagnosis does not fit in them.

#### 8.4.1c Every layer needs a window, and the timers must run in parallel

Since the bug can be in any layer, **every layer must retain** — a layer that hard-deletes immediately on
instruction destroys the data regardless of what the layers above kept.

Done naively that multiplies: FE waits three days then tells DN, which waits three days then tells SN, and
so on. Four layers, **twelve days**, and since **the real cost is EN retention** — the ENs hold the bulk
data, everything above is metadata — that is four times the storage it needs to be.

**The fix separates the timer from the authorization:**

> On delete, **soft-delete propagates to every layer immediately**, and each layer starts its own timer at
> once. A layer may hard-delete only when it has **both** received a hard delete from above **and** its own
> timer has expired.

All timers therefore run concurrently and expire together, so the total is one window rather than one per
layer — 12 days becomes 3. The conjunction is what keeps it safe: the timer alone would allow premature
deletion, and the hard delete alone would let a buggy layer force an immediate purge.

#### 8.4.1d The heroics window for user deletes is zero

The two-phase arrangement has a property worth naming, because it is exactly what §8.4.1a demands and it
falls out rather than being engineered: **for a user delete there is no interval during which the data
exists but the user cannot recover it themselves.**

The reason is an ordering. The DN holds the user-facing metadata *and* drives the hard-delete GC, so it
necessarily still has the soft-deleted record at the moment it issues the hard delete. Therefore:

| Interval | Data on ENs | User can undelete | Heroics needed |
|---|---|---|---|
| Before the DN's timer expires | yes | **yes, via the normal API** | no |
| After the hard-delete cascade | no | no — it is genuinely gone | impossible |

There is no third row. Contrast the arrangement that would produce one: if the DN discarded its record
first and the ENs retained afterwards, then in between the bytes would exist on disk with no metadata
pointing at them — unrecoverable through the API, recoverable only by scanning ENs. That is precisely the
staffing trap of §8.4.1a, and it is avoided by the invariant

> **metadata must not predecease the data it describes.**

Which the design satisfies for free, since the metadata holder is the one that initiates the deletion.

**The bug case is different, and that is what the lower layers' timers are for.** A bug that destroys DN
metadata directly, bypassing soft delete, *does* create a heroics window — metadata gone, EN data still
present — and recovering from it means scanning ENs for self-describing extents (§5.2). So the two
mechanisms divide cleanly by failure mode:

| Mechanism | Serves | Failure mode |
|---|---|---|
| The DN's soft-deleted record | **users**, directly | someone deleted the wrong thing |
| The lower layers' independent timers | **maintainers**, by heroics | a bug deleted metadata it should not have |

Same window length, no overlap wasting space, and no gap creating the trap. Each layer's retention is doing
a different job.

#### 8.4.2 The window must resist the operator

> *Frequently no matter what you do / You find your worst opponent is you* — §4.3.4.2

⚠️ **A soft delete that the deleting authority can also hard-delete is decoration, not protection.** If
an admin can delete an object and then shorten its retention window, or purge it outright, the mechanism
defends against nothing that actually happens. So the design property that matters is not the window's
existence but its **immutability**:

- the window may be **lengthened** by anyone who can write the object;
- it may be **shortened or waived only by a different authority** than the one that performed the delete
  — ideally not by a single principal at all;
- and the reclaim-after timestamp must live where the deleter cannot reach it.

Everything else here is bookkeeping. This is the part that makes it a safeguard.

#### 8.4.3 What the window costs, and why it must scale with lifetime

The cost is best expressed against **data lifetime**, not against a churn rate:

> retained-deleted fraction = **window ÷ average data lifetime**

| Data lifetime | 1-day window | 3-day window |
|---|---|---|
| 1 day | 100% | **300%** |
| 1 week | 14% | **43%** |
| 1 month | 3.3% | 10% |
| 1 year | 0.3% | 0.8% |
| 10 years | 0.03% | 0.08% |

⚠️ **Three days is very long for data that lives a week**, which is the common case for the date-partitioned
workloads of §8.5 — and an earlier draft of this section hid that by expressing the cost as churn × window,
which quietly assumed year-long lifetimes and produced a reassuring 0.8%.

**Scaling the window down does not work.** An earlier draft proposed window = min(3 days, lifetime ÷ 10),
which gives 1-day data a 2.5-hour window. That is useless, and the reason is worth stating: **protection is
not continuous in window length.** §8.4.1b sets the window by *human response time*, so a window shorter
than about a day buys nothing at all — nobody notices, nobody brakes. There is no "proportionally less
protection"; there is useful and there is useless, with a cliff between them.

**So the choice is binary, and it belongs to the user: opt out of soft delete, per object or per directory.**

| Declared lifetime | Cost of the full 3-day window | Reasonable choice |
|---|---|---|
| 1 day | **300%** | opt out |
| 1 week | **43%** | opt out |
| 1 month | 10% | either |
| 1 year | 0.8% | keep it |
| 10 years | 0.08% | keep it |

Below about a month the full window costs more than 10% and the decision is real; above it the cost
disappears and there is no reason to opt out.

**Opting out is not accepting risk so much as using a different recovery path.** Short-lived data is
usually *derived* — cooked outputs, staging, intermediates — and its recovery mechanism is **re-running the
job**, which is almost always cheaper than 300% standing storage. Long-lived data tends to be
source-of-truth and not regenerable, which is exactly where the window earns its cost. So the two ends of
the lifetime range have different recovery mechanisms available, and the opt-out is how a user says which
one applies.

The default is **protected**, with opt-out explicit — the same shape as §8.5's expiry defaulting to "never".
But the encouragement runs the other way: "never" forfeits something and is discouraged, whereas opting out
of soft delete on regenerable intermediates is the *right* answer and should be easy to express.

⚠️ **Per-directory is the granularity that matters**, and it converges with two other decisions: §8.5's
expiry grouping is directory-shaped because of the `yyyy/mm/dd/hh` pattern, and §5.11.1's default locality
already puts a directory's objects on one SN. **The directory is emerging as the natural unit of policy** —
lifetime, soft-delete opt-out, and placement all attach to it. Worth designing deliberately rather than
letting three mechanisms each invent their own scope.

⚠️ And it is not free space it consumes — **it eats the repair reserve.** §4.3.4 makes utilization
≤ 1 − 1/*D* a durability requirement, because a full cluster cannot repair, and retained deletions sit
inside that headroom. At 20 domains the reserve is 5%, so **the aggregate retained fraction has to stay
under that** — which the opt-out largely delivers by itself, since the workloads with punishing overheads
are precisely the ones that will opt out.

But it is not guaranteed by the opt-out, only made likely by it. A tenant with month-scale data and no
opt-out sits at 10% and exceeds the reserve alone. So retention still needs **admission control against
the reserve**, and it remains coupled to the utilization target and to *D* — the sort of interaction
discovered during an incident if it is not designed.

### 8.5 Expiry, and why it is the main lever on garbage

**Undeletable garbage exists only when deletion is not atomic.** An extent whose contents all die at
once is simply dropped; an extent with some records dead and some live cannot shed the dead ones without
a rewrite (§12.7). So the question is not how to reclaim garbage but **how to arrange that data dies
together.**

Two cases already do:

- **Streams are deleted atomically** — a stream is dropped whole, so it leaves nothing behind.
- **Objects created the same day in the same directory are usually deleted the same day**, which is a
  strong regularity rather than a coincidence.

That second point generalizes into a pattern worth designing for. The canonical shape — familiar from
Oracle date partitions — is **`yyyy/mm/dd/hh` directories, each written during one hour and deleted
exactly a week or a month or a year later.** Data with a known, shared death date is the common case, not
the exception.

#### 8.5.1 Declared expiry

**So users should tell us when data should be deleted.** An **expiry** is part of an object's metadata,
and the default is **"never" — officially discouraged.** Discouraged rather than forbidden: "never" is
sometimes the truth, but it is the answer that forfeits everything below.

What a declared expiry buys:

| | With expiry | Without |
|---|---|---|
| Placement | co-locate objects sharing an expiry, so extents die whole | mixed lifetimes per extent |
| Garbage | ~0 | ~5% of all disk (§12.7) |
| Compaction | none needed for expiry — the extent is simply dropped | rewrite to reclaim |
| Deletion cost | O(metadata) | O(data) |

This is the strongest available lever on the §12.7 efficiency chain, and it costs nothing but an API
field and the discipline to group by it.

#### 8.5.1a The midnight spike needs no dithering, because the delete limit already defers

§12.1.1.1 lists a deletion spike at midnight GMT as a demand feature to be priced around, and part of it is
self-inflicted: humans declare expiry at day boundaries — "keep this 30 days" means midnight, not 03:47 — so
expirations pile onto one instant, worldwide, every day.

**An earlier draft proposed dithering the hard-delete time forward by a deterministic per-object offset to spread
that work. Rejected** (Bob, 2026-08-16): there is a limit on outstanding extent deletions, and **GC simply defers
deletes when the limit is already hit.** No pre-emptive spreading is needed.

**And the rejection is right for a reason worth keeping**, because dithering is an appealing idea that will be
proposed again. It is the difference between a static partition and a work-conserving threshold — §13.4.3.6's
distinction, arriving in a second place:

| | When the fleet is idle | When it is saturated |
|---|---|---|
| **Dithering** | delays anyway, and the customer is billed for the delay | delays |
| **Outstanding-delete limit** | **no delay at all** | defers, exactly as much as needed |

**Derived.** Dithering pays its cost unconditionally to buy smoothing that is only ever needed under contention; the
limit is free when there is nothing to smooth. Back-pressure beats pre-emption whenever the pressure can be
measured, and here it can.

**Two dividends of not dithering.** The declared expiry is honoured as closely as capacity allows rather than
deliberately missed, so the "not before" reading of expiry is not required for *this* purpose. And there is only
**one** smoothing mechanism to reason about instead of three, so nothing can compound (an earlier draft flagged that
hazard; it no longer exists).

**The general rule survives the specific proposal's rejection**, and it is the part to remember: §12.1.1 shows
peak-to-mean is invariant to cluster size, so a spike the design cannot flatten must be priced around forever.
Flatten what the design creates — but prefer measuring the pressure to guessing at a spread.

⚠️ **This argues against dithering *load*, not against dithering *phase*.** §13.1.9.1 dithers SN/EN cold syncs, and
correctly: that work is recurring, so a spike there stays in phase and repeats indefinitely, which back-pressure
cannot fix. Expiry deletes are one-shot, so the queue drains and there is no phase to break. The two rules look
contradictory and are not.

#### 8.5.1b How DN finds what to expire, given that its metadata is on disk

**DN is in charge of expiring user objects** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-16). That is the natural owner — DN holds the
object metadata carrying the declared expiry — but it creates a problem the SN tier does not have.

**DN metadata is mostly on disk** (§14.2), so the GC pass that would naively do the expiring is slow: **once a day
or slower.** Expiring on that schedule would mean an object declared for 30 days lives 31, which is not prompt
enough to be called honouring the declaration.

**Decided: DN keeps a secondary index of objects keyed by expiry second** (Bob, 2026-08-16). §5.5 already stores DN
metadata in DeLawson *keyed* objects, so this is one more keyed object and no new machinery. Finding what to expire
is then a **prefix scan** of a sorted structure — everything with key ≤ now — rather than anything requiring a
sweep.

**The write cost is small. Derived:** one extra keyed insert per object creation, and a delete-plus-insert when an
expiry changes. An index entry is an expiry second plus an object reference, ~16 B against the ~300 B of object
metadata in §4.7 — about **5% more DN metadata**, which is inside the noise of a tier §12.2 already prices as the
cheap one.

##### 8.5.1b.0 The alternative, and why it lost

The natural alternative — and the first proposal — was a **heap prioritized by expiry date, holding objects that
expire before the next GC pass, refilled by that pass**, double-buffered so the sweep fills the next window while
the current one drains. It needs no write-path maintenance at all, which is its whole appeal. It lost on three
counts:

**1. It only works if the GC period is far shorter than object lifetimes.** The heap holds one GC period's worth of
expirations, so its size is

> `heap entries ≈ objects × (GC period / mean object lifetime)`

For a DN holding ~10^9 objects at ~16 B per entry — an expiry second plus an object reference — **Derived**:

| Mean lifetime | GC period | Heap entries | Heap size |
|---|---|---|---|
| 30 days | daily | 3.3 × 10^7 | ~530 MB |
| 7 days | daily | 1.4 × 10^8 | ~2.3 GB |
| **1 day** | daily | **10^9 — every object** | ~16 GB |

⚠️ **And short lifetimes are expected.** §8.4.1b notes that three days is already long for users who typically
delete within a week, so the middle row is the realistic case and the bottom row is not far-fetched. As the ratio
approaches 1 the heap degenerates into a copy of the whole object set and saves nothing.

**2. Its sizing depends on a number nobody knows.** Whether the heap is 530 MB or the entire object set turns on
the lifetime distribution, so choosing it would mean betting on unmeasured customer behaviour. The index has no
sizing constraint to get wrong.

**3. It has a correctness hole that the index does not**, and this was decisive. See §8.5.1b.2.

An index is maintained on write, so it is never a snapshot and never stale. A heap refilled by a sweep is both.

##### 8.5.1b.2 The hole the index closes

**An object created after a sweep passed its position can expire without ever being in the heap.** A sweep is a
snapshot; anything created — or re-dated — afterwards is invisible to it until the next pass. The symptom is data
silently outliving its declaration, which is the one failure mode expiry exists to prevent.

A heap design can patch this: DN is the creator, knows the expiry, and can insert directly into the live heap when
the expiry falls inside the current window. But it is precisely the case such a design forgets, and it has to be
got right in two places rather than one.

**An index has no snapshot and therefore no hole.** Creation writes the index entry; a prefix scan for key ≤ now
finds it. That is the strongest of the three reasons above, because the other two are about cost and this one is
about correctness.

**Deletion load is smoothed by one mechanism, not three.** §8.5.1a rejects dithering, and the index has no pop
schedule to tune, so the outstanding-extent-deletion limit is the only thing spreading the work — which is what
§8.5.1a argues is the right shape anyway.

Note that expiry needs no new teardown path: DN expiring an object enters §8.4.1's deferred decrement, which
releases stream references, then extent references, then the bytes. Expiry is a *trigger*, not a mechanism.

#### 8.5.2 Extent size is a weak lever by comparison

**Guess** (Bob): doubling extent size increases garbage by ~3%. Taken literally that is
G ∝ E^0.043 — an extremely flat power law:

| Extent size | Garbage |
|---|---|
| 1 MB | 4.3% |
| **32 MB** | **5.0%** |
| 1 GB | 5.8% |
| 4 GB | 6.1% |

**Across the entire plausible range — 1 MB to 4 GB, twelve doublings — garbage varies only 1.4×.** So
shrinking extents is a poor way to fight garbage, and expiry grouping (5% → ~0) is worth roughly thirty
times more than the whole extent-size range.

Usefully, that removes a constraint from an already over-constrained number: §6's 32 MB physical cap is
bracketed by seek amortization, metadata volume, the 4-byte reference floor, and NIC bandwidth, and it
turns out **garbage need not be in that list.**

⚠️ Worth noting the guess is unverified and its shape matters more than its value. If doubling extent
size increased garbage by 30% rather than 3%, the conclusion inverts and extent size becomes the primary
lever. Cheap to measure once anything is running.

#### 8.5.3 Short-lived data should skip erasure coding

**Data that will be deleted within a day — perhaps within a week — should not be erasure-coded at all.
It can stay 4-replica.**

That has a derivable break-even, because encoding is a rewrite whose cost is amortized over the data's
remaining life. Encoding one 32 MB extent moves ~80 MB of I/O and saves ~80 MB of standing storage
(4 replicas at 4× against 8+4 at 1.5×). The break-even lifetime is the ratio of I/O cost to storage cost,
which depends on how busy the disks are:

| Disk duty cycle | I/O capacity over a 5-year life | Break-even lifetime |
|---|---|---|
| Saturated | 31.6 PB | **1.2 days** |
| 30% busy | 9.5 PB | 3.9 days |
| 10% busy | 3.2 PB | **11.6 days** |

So "a day, or maybe a week" is right, and the width of the range is honest — it is set by disk utilization
rather than by anything the storage layer controls.

Three consequences:

- **Declared expiry makes this decision automatically.** An object with a one-day expiry never enters the
  encode queue, which saves the I/O *and* the garbage *and* the compaction.
- It answers part of §12's seal-to-encode latency question: for short-lived data the right latency is
  **infinite** — never encode it.
- ⚠️ It cuts the other way for billing. 4-replica storage costs 2.7× erasure-coded storage (§12.3), so
  short-lived data is legitimately dearer per byte-day. That is correct — it *is* more expensive — but it
  means the price list needs a durability-and-lifetime dimension rather than one figure per byte.

---

### 8.6 Parallel ingest into one object

§8.1.1a-8 leaves a conflict: one unsealed extent is what makes the object offset well defined, and it caps a
single object at one disk's write bandwidth. §1.0's motivating case wants both. This section resolves it, and the
resolution is that **the three properties people want are a trilemma, not a menu.**

#### 8.6.1 Concatenation of sealed streams is the mechanism

The way to build a large object with one writer's ordering is to **write many partitions in parallel, each
with its own writer, seal them, then concatenate them into one object** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-15).

This is strictly better than the deferred-offset interface §8.1.1a-9 rejects, and for a reason worth stating:
**concatenating sealed streams computes the offsets you would have deferred, synchronously, at a moment you
choose.** All inputs have known logical lengths, so the splice is metadata-only and the resulting object offsets
are dense, stable and final immediately — no head-of-line blocking, no two-answers-over-time, no promise without a
time bound. It also reuses machinery §15.1 already assumes exists, since self-concatenation is how large test
objects are built.

Two costs, both bounded:

- **References taken before the concatenation are invalidated by it** — partition *k*'s records shift by the sum of
  prior record counts. But **stream-relative** record numbers survive, because concatenation splices streams
  unchanged. That is §8.1.1a-9's compound id arriving on its own, and it matches §4.6.3, where `(DnId, StreamId)`
  is already the durable name.
- **N partitions contribute N short tail extents.** That is §10's existing job.

#### 8.6.2 The trilemma

Multiple unsealed tails do **not** rescue the time-range property, which is the thing that makes them look
attractive. §9.7's binary search works because durability seconds increase monotonically down a single-tail extent
list; concurrent tails interleave in time, so the list stops being sorted and the search degrades to a scan.
Multiple unsealed tails do not remove the fan-out — they hide it inside one object.

And parallel concatenation has the same defect: partitions written *simultaneously* have overlapping timestamp
ranges, so the concatenated extent list is not monotone either. Concatenation preserves monotonicity only when the
partitions are time-**disjoint** — hourly segments written in sequence, which is segmentation rather than
parallelism.

| Want | Mechanism | Loses |
|---|---|---|
| parallel bandwidth + dense stable offsets | parallel partitions, then concatenate | timestamp-monotone extent list |
| parallel bandwidth + monotone time index | N objects, one tail each | single-object dense offsets |
| dense offsets + monotone time index | one writer, one tail | parallelism (~200 MB/s) |

**Derived.** All three in one object is not available, and this is independent of any interface choice. It is the
sharp form of open question 36.

#### 8.6.3 Fan-out on read is the right thing to pay for

The objection to N objects is that a `[X, Y)` reader touches many of them. That costs less than it appears under
§1.4's own stance: 1,000 binary searches issued in parallel cost **one round trip of latency**, not 1,000, because
§1.4.1 makes job latency the maximum. What they really cost is 1,000x the metadata *request rate* — which §12 says
must be billed, and is therefore a priced resource rather than a hidden one.

What the client should not have to do is know the 1,000 object names. So **time-range becomes a directory-level
operation**, pruned by the interval summaries of §9.7.3 before any fan-out happens.

#### 8.6.4 The recursion up to DN attenuates rather than repeating

If ingress exceeds one SN, it must be sprayed across streams on multiple SNs. The worry is that recording those
streams overwhelms DN the same way. It does not, because update rate divides by the fan-out at each level:

| Level | Unit added | Rate at 1 TB/s ingress |
|---|---|---|
| EN | bytes | 1 TB/s |
| SN | extent (<=4 GB logical / 32 MB physical) | ~30,000/s |
| DN | stream (>=1 PB) | ~1 per 1,000 s |

A stream holds ~262,144 extents at the 4 GB logical cap, so **SN-to-DN update rate is ~10^5-10^6 : 1**. And DN's
per-stream cost is a 4-byte reference plus a cumulative count — ~12 B, not the 200 B the *SN* pays (§4.7). A
10,000-stream frontier is ~120 KB in the DN object. **Derived.** The 200 B/stream figure is what makes tiny
streams a billing catastrophe on SN (§12.2); it is not what DN pays.

**So DN is overwhelmed only if the streams are fragments**, which gives the design rule:

> **Spray per writer, not per request.** A writer picks its stream once and stays on it.

Then DN traffic is one entry per writer, ever. Round-robin per append makes DN's update rate equal the request
rate and kills it. That stickiness is already forced by fixed-offset compare-and-append (§8.1.1a-3), so it is not
a new constraint. And per §12.1 the enforcement should be **price, not quota**: bill stream count and DN entry
count and fragment-spraying becomes the expensive way to write — §12.2's lesson applied prospectively instead of
retroactively.

#### 8.6.5 What genuinely recurses is the summary, not the load

A DN object's stream list carries the **cumulative record count per stream**. The moment two streams are growing at
once, that is a mid-tree summary in §4.5's sense — it changes below the tail, not at it — and §4.5 already forbids
maintaining it eagerly.

So record numbers are unavailable over the growing region for a **summary-rule** reason, which is a cleaner and
more durable argument than a load argument because it does not depend on any of the numbers above.

#### 8.6.6 The shape that follows: a sealed prefix and a growing frontier

Given §8.6.5, the two options collapse toward each other — "N separate objects" is "one object" with the fan-out
list held in a directory instead of inside an object. Both fan out on read, but the stream list is one object,
RAM-resident, ~12 B/entry, already on the read path, where a directory needs an enumeration plus N object metadata
lookups. So a single object wins, with two explicit regions:

| | Sealed prefix | Growing frontier |
|---|---|---|
| Streams | sealed, lengths final | N, one SN each, sticky writer |
| Addressing | dense object record number, binary searchable | `(stream, record number)` only |
| Time range | monotone per stream, binary search | min/max durable-second interval, prune by overlap |
| Cumulative counts | materialized | must not exist (§4.5) |

Streams convert from frontier to prefix as they seal, and the cumulative counts are materialized lazily at that
point by §13.3's background loops. So the eventually-known offset is real, but it is a consequence of **sealing**
and never a promise made in an append response — which is where §8.1.1a-9's prior art pointed.

⚠️ An object's *total* record count is unknown while the frontier is open, so the 2^64 record numbering of §3 is
dense only over the prefix. A reader asking "how many records" gets "at least K, plus N open streams". That is
honest rather than broken, but it is a user-visible consequence that should be decided deliberately rather than
discovered.

## 9. Reading

### 9.1 Unkeyed: locating record *N*

0. **FE**: the `delawson` client sends the request; FE authorizes it against the
   object's ACL and coordinates the hops below (§5.9).
1. **DN**: resolve the path, read the object metadata, descend the stream B-tree
   (§4.4) on starting record number → stream *S* and a stream-local record number.
2. **SN** holding *S*: descend the extent B-tree → extent *E* and an
   extent-local record number; read *E*'s instance list.
3. If *E* has a log, check it for a newer version or tombstone. If found, done.
4. Otherwise binary search *E*'s sparse index → nearest preceding checkpoint.
5. **EN**: read that granule from any instance and **return the whole compressed
   block**, even when the caller asked for less.
6. **Whoever extracts**: decrypt, decompress, check the CRC, parse forward by framing,
   and take the record the caller wanted. That is the client if it may hold whole
   blocks, and the FE if it may not — §9.1.1.

⚠️ **An earlier draft had the EN doing steps 5 and 6 together — decrypting, parsing and
returning one record. That is the wrong division** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17): **the EN
returns whole compressed blocks and it is up to whoever asked to extract the exact
requested data.** Two independent reasons, and either alone would settle it:

- **ENs are CPU-poor by design** (§1.2 puts the money in disks, not cores), and
  decompressing and parsing on the tier that owns the disks spends the resource that
  tier does not have.
- **A block is the unit an EN deals in.** Its business is bytes and offsets; what a
  record is belongs above it, which is why a read needs no framing argument at all.

⚠️ An earlier version of this paragraph said an EN *cannot* look inside a block because
it holds no keys. That is wrong: **ENs do cache daily SN-master keys and do decrypt**
(§7.3, §5.9.2). Returning whole blocks is a division of labour, not an inability — and
the next section is a check that depends on the EN being able to look.

#### 9.1.1 The EN checks the auth code on every read off disk

**An EN reads a block off a disk, and the block is encrypted, so it has an auth code to check —
and it should check it on every read off disk** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17). A tag that does not
verify means those bytes on that device are corrupt, and the EN is the one place that can say so.

**Off disk, not per client read**, and the distinction is real rather than pedantic because **an EN
will have a small cache of recently read data** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17). A block already in
memory has nothing new to learn from being re-verified — that would spend CPU on the hot path to
re-detect a fault RAM has its own defences against — while a block coming off a device is exactly
where media corruption appears. So the check is attached to the device read, and a cache hit costs
nothing at all.

**That cache holds blocks as stored**, which is to say encrypted and compressed, because that is
what an EN has and what it hands back (§9.1). So it needs no keys to serve a hit, adds no place
plaintext sits, and costs exactly its bytes — the cheapest possible shape for a cache, and the
reason a *small* one is worth having even on a tier that must stay CPU-poor.

It is affordable for the reason §7.2.1 gives: AEGIS is nearly free, so verifying costs about what
reading cost, and an EN is already paying that.

**This is a different check from the user's CRC, and the difference is what makes it worth having**
in addition:

| | Covers | At | Says |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Auth code** | one encrypted block, as stored | the EN, on every read off disk | *this instance's copy is bad* |
| **CRC** (§7.5) | the writer's logical bytes, end to end | whoever decompresses | *something between my buffer and here is wrong* |

⚠️ **The EN's check is the one that localizes, and localizing is what makes corruption
actionable.** A failed tag names an instance, so the read can be retried against another and the
bad copy repaired by the ordinary path (§13.1) — the user never sees it. A CRC mismatch says only
that something is wrong somewhere, which is the right guarantee to offer and a poor place to start
an investigation. The two layers are detection and diagnosis, and neither substitutes for the other.

#### 9.1.2 How far the block travels decides who checks the CRC

**If an FE can return whole compressed blocks to the client, then the client is what checks
the CRC** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17) — **unless there is a security reason insisting the FE
does it.**

The client is the better answer wherever it is available, and the reason is symmetry: the
client compressed the bytes and computed the CRC going in (§7.5.2), so a client that
decompresses and checks going out is comparing its own buffer against its own promise, with
**nothing in between ever needing to look inside**. No tier spends CPU on it, no tier needs
keys, and the guarantee covers the FE as well as everything below it. A check at the FE
covers everything below the FE and takes the FE's word for the rest.

**The candidate security reason turns out not to apply** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17), and the
reason is a constraint that was already true rather than one that had to be added:

| | Tenants |
|---|---|
| An **append block** | **one** — a block comes from one writer |
| An EN's **common extent** | many, since staging combines whatever arrives (§8.1.4) |
| **Coalescing** | within one tenant's extents only, so a dedicated extent is single-tenant |

So a whole append block is one tenant's data by construction, and handing one to a client
leaks nothing. **The end-to-end version stands**: the client may hold whole blocks and check
its own CRC, and no tier between it and the disk has to look inside.

And the capability question settles the same way: **the client compresses** (§8.1.4.1), so the
client has the codec and can decompress what comes back. So the answer is the strong one —
**the client checks its own CRC** — and it holds all the way down.

⚠️ **But an FE has to see plaintext whenever the user asked for part of a compressed block**
(Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17), because somebody has to decompress it and cut the requested piece
out, and there is nobody else between the EN and the caller. So the two shapes are not a global
choice — they are a property of each read:

| The caller asks for | Then | The FE sees | The CRC is checked by |
|---|---|---|---|
| **a whole block** | the FE passes it through | compressed bytes | **the client**, end to end |
| **part of a block** — one record | the FE decompresses, extracts, returns the piece | **plaintext** | the FE |

**Which means the client should be able to ask either way**, because the right answer differs
per read rather than per deployment. A scan will use every byte of a block, so asking for blocks
wastes nothing and keeps the check end to end. A point read of a 50-byte record out of a 256 KB
block would ship the whole block across the internet — the one link §8.1.4.1 says nobody controls
the cost of, and the one §12 bills for — to use 0.02% of it.

⚠️ **And that is a real limit on the guarantee, worth stating plainly rather than in a footnote:
a caller that asks for part of a block gets the FE's word that the CRC matched.** The end-to-end
version is available — ask for the block — and it costs egress. A user who wants both cheap point
reads and an unbroken chain of custody cannot have them from the same request, and knowing which
