one they bought is better than assuming.

**What survives regardless**: no tier in the middle spends CPU on *compression* on the write path,
and no tier above an EN ever needs a *disk* key (§7.3.5). What does not survive is any claim that
the FE holds nothing readable — it terminates a wire segment, so it sees compressed bytes on every
read and plaintext on some, and **compression is not confidentiality**. §9.6.1's cache asymmetry is
narrower than an earlier version of this section claimed: an FE cache adds no *new* kind of
exposure, which is not the same as adding none.

⚠️ **"Any instance" holds for a sealed extent, and not for an unsealed one — and the reason is
the watermark, not the data** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17). Below the durable length every instance
has everything, contiguously; **interior holes exist only above it, on every instance including the
primary** (§8.1.4.3 is about that region). So the bytes are not what differ. What differs is that
**a secondary may hold a stale durable length**, and would answer a read against the wrong
watermark — refusing or truncating something that is in fact durable. The primary is the instance
that knows what the durable length is, so an unsealed extent is read there.

That makes spreading unsealed reads a question of getting the watermark to the secondaries rather
than of copying data, which is a much cheaper problem than it first looks (#54).

Two B-tree descents, one small log probe, one index search, one granule read —
but spread over four machine types, so a cold point read costs **four round
trips** including the authorization hop. Sealed extents are immutable, which makes almost everything above
cacheable at the client: the object's stream list changes only when the object
grows, and an extent's instance list changes only on repair or re-encoding. A
warm client goes straight to the EN.

#### 9.1.3 How much one answer may carry, and how a caller asks for the next of it

**`object-info` does not return enough to be useful for bulk reading, and it should not try to
return everything.** Today it answers with an object and one stream (§17.12); a caller building
hints (§8.1.1a-10) needs the extents, their instances, and the record range of each. But an
object can hold 2 × 10^9 extent references (§14.1), so "all of them" is not an answer that can be
sent.

**So there is a limit on the number of objects plus streams plus extents either `object-info` or
`batch-object-info` may return, and hitting it succeeds** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17). It does
not fail and it does not truncate silently: it answers with a **range** and says which range it
answered. Reading a huge object is then many range requests, which is the same shape as any
paginated interface and is why **ranges are worth implementing before the limit matters** — a
limit with no way to ask for the next piece is just a smaller failure.

⚠️ **And there is a real difficulty in the middle of that** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17): **a
caller with a fixed-size buffer does not know how many rows to ask for**, because it does not
know the row sizes. Every way of naming an end has the same flaw:

| Ask for | Problem |
|---|---|
| *n* rows | *n* rows might be a byte or a gigabyte |
| up to logical offset *X* | an offset is not a durable reference (§8.1.1a-7), so it may not land where the caller expects |
| from row *R* to *R* + a logical offset | the start is durable and the end is not, so the caller cannot say where it stopped |
| from row *R* to *R* + a compressed offset | the same, in the other space |

**The way out is to stop using an offset as a resume point and use it only as a budget.** A
request names a **durable start and a byte budget** — "from row *R*, at most *N* bytes" — and the
*answer* says which rows it contains and **what row to ask for next**. Then:

- the start is always a record number, which is stable for ever (§3, §8.1.1a-10's durable tier);
- the end is a byte count, which the caller chooses to fit the buffer it actually has;
- the continuation is a row number the system computed, so the caller never has to work out
  where its last fetch ended — which was the whole difficulty.

That is the ordinary shape of a paginated read, and the reason to spell it out is that the
tempting version — resume from where the bytes stopped — is the one that breaks, because
**offsets are the tier of reference that is allowed to move** (§8.1.1a-10). A caller resuming
from an offset is resuming from a hint; a caller resuming from a row is resuming from a name.

#### 9.1.3.1 Resuming from a row is serial, and consistent read is what makes it parallel

⚠️ **The scheme above works and it is serial**, which for a large object is the whole cost: each
request waits for the previous answer to learn where to start. A caller reading a terabyte in
megabyte pages makes a million round trips end to end, and the latency of every one is exposed.

**Consistent read removes the dependency, because it makes the boundaries computable** (Asserted,
Bob, 2026-08-17). Given a consistent view of an extent, its contents cannot change under the read —
so chunk *k* is bytes *k*·*N* to (*k*+1)·*N* by arithmetic, and **the caller can issue every request
back to back without waiting for any answer.** Fixed logical chunks or fixed compressed chunks,
either way: what matters is that the caller *computes* the boundaries instead of discovering them.

**And it fits comfortably inside the hint window** (§10.1, at least ten minutes), so the extents and
instances the caller was given stay valid for the length of such a read.

That is a second, independent argument for consistent read. §16's open question values it for
dropping a ring from 3x RAM to 2x — the largest cost saving identified so far. **This is a latency
argument rather than a cost one**: it turns a paginated read from serial into parallel. Two unrelated
reasons for the same feature is a strong position to be in.

**Parallelism across extents is the other axis**, and it needs no new mechanism: different extents
are on different ENs, so a caller holding the extent list can read them at once. Within one extent,
consistent read is what unlocks it; across extents, the extent list already does.

⚠️ **`batch-object-info` has the same problem and no such fix.** A caller cannot pre-slice its list
of names into requests that will each fit an answer, because the answer size per object depends on how
many streams and extents that object has — which is the thing it is asking about. So issuing a run of
batch lookups asynchronously is guesswork in a way that reading an extent is not, and the guess is
unbounded: one object might contribute a hundred thousand extents to the answer.

**That is the same problem a job scheduler has**, one level up: partitioning work across vertices
needs the object sizes, and the sizes are what the lookups are for. §5.12.2 already names telling a
job whether its remainder fits as the most useful thing DeLawson could tell a scheduler; this is the
same gap arriving during *planning* rather than during execution.

#### 9.1.3.2 A partial answer that carries complete counts

Two things together reduce that to one round trip.

**A caller works from a queue rather than a chain** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17): split the objects
into ranges, put the ranges in a queue, issue asynchronous requests for whatever is in it, and when
an answer reveals more work, **put that at the end of the queue.** Discovery does not disappear, but
it stops being the critical path — the pipe stays full while it happens, and the depth of the chain
stops mattering because nothing waits on any particular answer.

**And an answer says how much it did not tell you** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17). An answer that is
partial in *detail* can still be complete in *counts*:

| The answer carries | Even when |
|---|---|
| how many **streams** the object has | it can only describe the first one |
| how many **extents** the stream has | it returns only some of their metadata |
| which range of extents this answer covers | that range is a small part of them |

**That is what makes the rest trivial.** With the total extent count in hand, a caller computes every
subsequent request by arithmetic — the same trick as §9.1.3.1's fixed chunks, applied to metadata
instead of data — and the queue keeps them all in flight. So the shape is **one round trip to learn
the shape, then everything else at once.** The counts are cheap to include: they are maintained
already, because billing needs them (§12.8).

**Multiple streams should be rare** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17), which is why the stream count is
worth carrying even though it is almost always one: a single stream reaches **51 PiB** before an SN's
memory bounds it (§14.1), so an object needs a second only when it is enormous. The extent count is
the interesting number in nearly every case, and the stream count is there so that the rare case is
not a surprise.

#### 9.1.3.3 The first round of discovery is the directory listing

**A query over many objects will usually be preceded by a directory listing from the DN, and that
listing is where the first round of discovery would naturally happen** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17) —
so a caller planning work over a directory could learn the shape of all of it in one answer, before
asking about any object in particular.

**If the numbers are there to give.** The accuracies would differ by where each lives:

| From a listing | Accuracy | Because |
|---|---|---|
| streams per object | **exact** | the DN allocates them, so it owns the count (§17.12) |
| extents per stream | **stale** | extents are the SN's, learned lazily (§8.1.3, §4.5) |
| records or bytes per stream | **stale** | same, and for the same reason |

**Stale would be the right accuracy for what it is for.** Partitioning work across vertices needs
sizes to within a factor, not to the byte: a scheduler balancing 10,000 objects does not care that one
has grown by three extents since the summary was written. Demanding exactness would put §13.1's sync
loops on the critical path of every job that plans, which is the coupling lazy summaries exist to
avoid.

⚠️ **But whether a DN should hold those counts at all is undecided** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17):
**it is extra metadata, and metadata that changes.** The objection is sharper than it sounds, because
it is three objections:

- **It costs space per object**, on the one tier whose object count is unbounded (§14.2). Per-object
  bytes are the scarce thing there in a way they are not anywhere else.
- **It has to be maintained**, so a growing object eventually dirties its DN summary — which puts
  metadata writes on the DN in proportion to appends, and keeping the DN out of the write path is
  most of what §8.1.3 is for.
- **Stale *and* maintained is the worst pair**: paying to keep something that still cannot be
  trusted, which invites callers to trust it anyway.

**Settled: nowhere, and nothing is stored** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17). §13.5's metadata snapshots do
carry these numbers, and they are **too stale for a job or for `laws dir` to use** — a planner wants
last minute, not last night.

**So a listing is implemented the way `object-info` is: it walks down the tiers as far as it has to
go.** No DN-side summary to maintain, no staleness to explain, and the cost is round trips rather
than metadata — paid by the caller that asked, in proportion to what it asked about.

**And how far it has to go depends on the object's size class** (§4.6.5), which is what makes this
affordable rather than merely correct:

| Object | Described by | Round trips |
|---|---|---|
| tiny, inlined | the **DN alone** — it holds the records | one |
| small, one append's worth | the **DN alone** — it holds the stream and the range | one |
| large, owning its stream | the DN, then its SN, whose extent list is the interesting part | two |

**The cheapest objects are the cheapest to describe**, which is the right way round given that §14.1.1
expects the population to be dominated by tiny ones. **A directory of small objects is answered
entirely by the DN**, because a small object is a range in a stream and the DN has both — the walk
stops at the first tier for everything except the objects big enough to have an extent list worth
sending.

So the discovery has three rounds and each is cheaper than it looks:

1. **Estimates for a whole directory**, once, from wherever they live.
2. **A lookup per object it decides to read**, giving exact counts and the first range of extents
   (§9.1.3.2) — all of these in flight at once, since step 1 said how many to expect.
3. **The ranges**, computed by arithmetic from the exact counts, also all at once.

**Nothing in that chain waits on a number it could have estimated**, which is the property worth
keeping when any of it is implemented. Note that step 1 is the only one whose *home* is in doubt: steps
2 and 3 are answered by the tiers that own the data, and their counts are exact because they are asked
of whoever maintains them.

**Two consequences worth noting before it is built:**

- **The budget is a logical byte count, and the caller cannot know the compressed size in
  advance** — so a request naming a logical budget may come back with more or fewer compressed
  bytes than expected. Whichever space the budget is in, it bounds one of the two and not the
  other, and which one the caller cares about depends on whether it is buying network or memory.
- **A range answer is a hint, not a name.** The extents and instances in it are the middle
  reference tier, valid for at least the hint window (§10.1) — so a caller that pages slowly must
  expect to re-ask, and one that pages a huge object should expect its early pages to have aged
  out by the time it finishes.

#### 9.1.3.4 A start is the object, plus how far the caller already resolved, plus a position

§9.1.3 settled the *end* of a range: a budget, not an address. This settles the *start*, which needs
more room than a record number, because the whole point of handing a caller extents (§9.1.3.2, #61)
is that it should not then have to re-derive what it was just told.

⚠️ **Every read names the object, whatever else it names** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-19). That is not
redundancy and it is not politeness to the API:

- **Authorization is per object and lives at the FE** (§1.5, §5.9, §9.1 step 0). The FE checks the
  object's ACL and *then* forwards, so a request naming no object could not be authorized at all.
- **The object cannot be recovered from a stream or an extent.** The edges run downward, and §4.6.6
  makes the reverse edge a *count* rather than a list on purpose. A stream may also be referenced by
  more than one object (§4.6.1, §5.11.3.4), so even paying for a reverse index would not give a
  unique answer.

So a stream or an extent in a request is **an optimization on top of the object, never a substitute
for it**, and a start is three things:

| Resolved as far as | What it saves | What it costs when stale |
|---|---|---|
| **the object** only | nothing — §9.1's ordinary walk | — |
| a **stream** of it | the DN's descent over the stream list | fall back to the object |
| an **extent** of that stream | the DN's descent *and* the SN's | fall back to the object |

⚠️ **A stale narrowing is recoverable rather than fatal, and that is entirely because the object is
always present.** This is Oracle's logical rowid exactly (§8.1.1a-10): a durable name plus a physical
guess, where the guess is tried and the name is the fallback. A start naming only an extent would
have no fallback, and could not be authorized either.

**The position, for an append-only object, is one of three:**

| Position | Means | Tier (§8.1.1a-10) |
|---|---|---|
| **record number** | that record's first logical byte | **durable** — good for ever |
| **record number + logical offset** | that many logical bytes past that record's start, possibly *inside* it | **durable** — a rewrite moves neither part |
| **logical offset** alone | that many logical bytes into whichever container was named | below |

**The two offset forms are not redundant, and what separates them is which one snaps.** Naming a
record says *I know where the records are, and I want a byte inside this one*; naming only an offset
says *I do not know where the records are, so put me at the next one*.

- **Record + offset is exact, and may land mid-record.** That is its purpose: §1.0's objects are very
  large, one record may be far bigger than any caller's buffer, and a record number alone cannot say
  where inside it to resume. Nothing else in the design addresses the interior of a record.
- **A bare offset snaps forward**, to the first record beginning at or after it.

⚠️ **The snap rule has to be fixed rather than merely documented, and §9.1.3.1 is why.** Vertices
computing adjacent chunk boundaries by arithmetic resolve them *independently*. Under a
"nearest boundary" or implementation-defined rule, adjacent chunks would sometimes overlap and
sometimes leave a gap, and **neither vertex could detect either**. Snapping forward always makes
independently computed boundaries a partition: the vertex holding a chunk reads past its end to
finish its last record, and its neighbour starts after that. (Cited: this is the Hadoop input-split
rule, adopted for the same reason.)

**Why the narrowing dimension exists at all is §4.5**, and this is the load-bearing paragraph:

> A descent on **record numbers** is an index lookup, because the unkeyed record count is the one
> summary §4.5 permits to be exact and synchronous to the root. A descent on **byte counts** is not,
> because logical and physical byte totals are explicitly lazy.

So a caller naming a stream or an extent is **supplying the prefix sum the store declines to
maintain**. That is the same division of labour as §9.1.3's — the caller brings the budget, the
system computes the continuation — with the caller also bringing the part it was already given.

⚠️ **`(object, logical offset)` looks like it contradicts two earlier sections, and does not.**
§8.1.1a-7 calls the object logical offset "well defined, dense, stable and writer-predictable" for
unkeyed objects, while §8.1.1a-10 files it under the tier called **none**. Both are right, about
different properties:

| | |
|---|---|
| Is it **stable**? | **Yes**, for append-only data — appended logical bytes never move, and compacting append-only extents has no tombstones to drop, so logical content is preserved exactly |
| Is it **cheaply resolvable**? | **No** — that needs a prefix sum of logical lengths, which §4.5 keeps lazily |

**A stable address the store cannot cheaply resolve is a different defect from an unstable one**, and
it has a far better remedy. For an append-only object the lazy sums are **exact over the sealed
prefix and merely behind at the frontier** (§8.6.6): a sealed extent's logical length never changes,
so "lazy" here means *short*, never *wrong in the middle*. An object-relative logical offset therefore
resolves exactly everywhere except the growing tail — and at the tail the answer says where it
actually started, which §9.1.3.2 already obliges it to do.

**Keyed objects get none of that**, which is the conclusion §8.1.1a-7 reaches from the write side:
interior inserts change logical lengths anywhere (§4.5), so no prefix sum over a keyed object is ever
exact. Their start space is a different cross product, and this is a placeholder for its shape rather
than a design of it:

| Keyed start | Note |
|---|---|
| (object \| stream \| extent, **key**) | the durable form, and the one a caller should normally use |
| (**extent**, **row**) | §8.1.1a-10's hint tier exactly — valid until that extent is rewritten |

#### 9.1.3.5 A narrowing must be proved, not asserted, so the hint carries a capability

⚠️ **The spec §8.1.1a-10 gives for a hint has a hole, and it is fatal to the hop it claims to save**
(Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-19). A caller presents an extent; the FE authorizes an *object*; **nothing
binds the two.** The consequences compound:

| | |
|---|---|
| Proving `extent ∈ object` structurally | DN (object → streams) then SN (stream → extents) — **precisely the two hops the hint exists to remove** |
| Doing it at the SN | the extent list is searchable by **record number**, not by extent id (§9.1), so membership-by-id is a scan of up to 2 × 10^9 entries (§14.1) |
| Indexing by extent id instead | a per-extent reverse entry on the one tier §14.1 says is memory-bound — the trade §4.6.6 already refused |
| Sending `(object, row)` alongside `(extent, row)` | no help: the object-relative row is the thing whose resolution costs the hops |
| Putting the **stream** in the hint (§4.6.6's earlier answer) | no help either: an asserted pairing is only as good as the caller, and `stream ∈ object` is still the DN's to answer |

**So the binding cannot be recomputed cheaply, and it must therefore be carried unforgeably.**
Whoever first resolved object → stream → extent did the full walk anyway; it mints a **capability**
attesting that this extent is in this object, and a later FE **verifies the capability instead of
repeating the walk.**

⚠️ **The certificate carries the authorization, and an earlier draft of this section had it backwards**
(Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-19). It said the capability attests *membership only, never authorization*, so
that the FE would still evaluate the object's ACL and nothing could go stale. **What that costs is the
hop the hint exists to remove**, and Bob's version does not pay it:

> **The signature covers `(tenant, extent, write?)`, and it means: this tenant may read — or write —
> this extent.** The FE checks that the certificate matches the current tenant and the current extent,
> and that is the whole check.

**So the directory is used when *constructing* the signature, not when evaluating it.** The FE evaluates
the directory's policy (§5.9.1a) once, at mint time, to decide whether to issue; at use time nothing is
resolved and no policy is read. That is what makes it two hops saved rather than one — and it answers
§16.129 / #81, which asked where the ACL is fetched from precisely because that decides whether a hint
saves the DN round trip or only the SN one. **It is not fetched at all.**

⚠️ **It cannot be transplanted, which is why binding the extent is enough.** A draft of this paragraph
worried that a certificate for one extent could be presented alongside a request naming a different
object, and concluded the *directory* had to be in the signature too. That was a misreading: the extent
is in the signature, so the certificate authorizes exactly that extent, and there is no second path for
the FE to consult and be misled by.

##### What it costs, stated plainly

**A stale certificate authorizes reads — and writes, if it carries that right — for a while after a
policy change** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-19). That is the ordinary capability trade, and the draft's
whole argument was an attempt to avoid it that cost more than it saved.

| | Bounded by |
|---|---|
| how long a revoked tenant keeps access | the certificate's **expiry**, which is the hint window (§10.1) |
| how much it keeps access to | **only extents it already holds certificates for** |

**The second row is what makes the lag tolerable.** Revocation stops the *minting* at once, so a revoked
tenant cannot obtain a certificate for anything new — and §10.1's window is ten minutes, not a session.

**A hint is no longer harmless to quote, and that matters less than it first appears** (Asserted, Bob,
2026-08-19): *"I don't see how to avoid stale certificates without forcing a trip to DN... I don't know
of a use case where there is a security boundary between a tenant and itself, so the security aspect
isn't bothering me so far."*

Possession plus being the named tenant is access — but it is useless to a *different* tenant, so what
leaks stays inside the boundary that already had it.

⚠️ **That is an assumption rather than a fact, and it is worth naming because the model can express its
opposite.** §5.9.1a attaches policy to the **directory**, and a directory's ACL names principals — so a
tenant whose principals have different grants (`/a` but not `/b`) *does* have an internal boundary, and a
certificate binding only the tenant would cross it.

**And the assumption is load-bearing rather than merely comfortable**, which is the reason to write it
down:

| Certificate binds | §8.1.1a-10's scheduler case | Intra-tenant policy |
|---|---|---|
| the **tenant** | **works** — mint once up front, hand the hints to every vertex | not enforced |
| the **principal** | breaks, or forces the vertices to share one principal | enforced |

§8.1.1a-10's whole motivating shape is *ask once, hand the hints to the vertices, let them use them as
the job runs.* **Tenant-binding is what makes that possible**, so narrowing to a principal would cost the
feature the certificate exists for. The two are not independent choices, and if a use case for an
intra-tenant boundary appears, that is the price (§16.145).

**What survives is the operator's side of §7.3.2.8**, and it survives because it never rested on the
membership-only claim: the prefix is plaintext, so an operator reading a hint from a bug report can see
which extent it names and go look **with their own authority**. That came from the readability decision,
not from what the certificate asserts.

##### 9.1.3.5.2 Stale certificates are accepted, which makes the lifetime a security parameter

**Settled** (Decided, Bob, 2026-08-19): *"I don't see how to avoid stale certificates without forcing a
trip to DN to see the current state of directories, so I do accept stale certificates, which means
removing permissions has a delay of however long certificates last."*

⚠️ **So one constant now answers to two unrelated requirements**, and §0's discipline says that is worth
flagging rather than leaving for whoever tunes it:

| The certificate's lifetime *L* bounds | Wants *L* |
|---|---|
| how often a caller must go back to the DN to re-mint | **long** — that trip is the one the certificate exists to avoid |
| how long a removed permission keeps working | **short** — it is the revocation delay, exactly |

**The trade is quantifiable, which is the useful part**: the DN load a hint saves is proportional to
1/*L*, and the revocation delay is *L*. There is no value that is good at both, so the number is a
policy choice and not a tuning one — and §16.86 already asks what the hint window should be, from a
completely different direction (how far a follower may lag). **It now has a second input pulling the
other way**, and the two need reconciling before either is fixed.

⚠️ **And the two need not be the same number.** A hint stops being *useful* when its extent is rewritten;
a certificate stops being *safe* when policy changes. Setting the certificate's expiry shorter than the
hint window is possible — the route stays valid while the authorization is re-minted — and it costs
exactly the DN trips that shortening *L* implies. So decoupling them buys nothing by itself; it only
makes the trade explicit in two places instead of one.

##### The option Bob's framing leaves out: push the revocation

**A delay of *L* is what waiting for expiry costs. It is not the only way to revoke.** §9.6.2 already
wants a **broadcast tree** for getting one fact to many consumers quickly, and "forget certificates for
this tenant, or this directory" is that shape of fact.

| | Revocation delay |
|---|---|
| wait for expiry | always *L* |
| broadcast, expiry as the backstop | ~a broadcast, and *L* only if the broadcast fails |

⚠️ **What it costs is the property that makes an FE cheap.** §17.14's reasoning is that what an FE
remembers can be lost without harm — *"losing what is remembered costs asks, not correctness."* **A
revocation list breaks that**: an FE that has lost one would honour a certificate it should refuse. So a
restarted FE would have to **fail closed** — rejecting certificates until it has re-synced — which is
the ordinary certificate-revocation problem and its ordinary cost.

**So this stays an option rather than a decision.** It is worth having written down because the choice
is not between "accept *L*" and "pay a DN trip per read": there is a third point on the curve, it reuses
machinery the design already wants, and its price is a specific and well-understood loss (#94).

**The hint stays readable, with the capability appended** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-19), which is a
requirement rather than an encoding preference: **an operator debugging a complaint must be able to
read a hint a user quoted and go look at that extent under their own privileges.** An opaque or
encrypted handle would make the user's own bug report unactionable.

| Part | Contents | Form |
|---|---|---|
| **the hint** | `StreamId`, `(SnId, ExtentId, creation second)`, the extent's first record, the row | **plaintext**, versioned, printable |
| **the certificate** | write flag, **salt**, expiry second, key version, tag | appended suffix |

##### 9.1.3.5.4 The signed form is closed, and contains identity only

**A certificate is verified from other plaintext in the read request, so that plaintext has to be in the
`object-info` answer too — or the request cannot be constructed** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-19).

⚠️ **That is a closure requirement, and it determines the field list rather than leaving it to taste.**
Every signed field must be obtainable at *mint* and again at *verify*, from something the caller was
given and hands back:

| Signed | At mint, from | At verify, from |
|---|---|---|
| the **tenant** | the request being authorized | the connection's credentials — **ambient**, so it is in neither the answer nor the request |
| the **extent name** `(SnId, ExtentId, creation second)` | the SN's `ExtentRow` | the read request, which the caller built from that row |
| the **write flag** | the grant being exercised | the certificate's own plaintext, and it selects the key (§9.1.3.5.3) |
| the **salt**, **expiry**, **key version** | the mint | the certificate's own plaintext |

**Which closes**: `ExtentRow` already carries the extent name (§17.21's shape), and everything else is
either ambient or inside the certificate. Nothing signed is missing from either end.

##### ⚠️ And two things must *not* be signed

**The first record must not be**, and the reason is §17.16.2's bug class rather than anything about
certificates:

> A record number exists in **three numbering spaces** — object-local, stream-local, extent-local — and
> the FE converts between them. **Signing one of them puts the conversion inside the signed form**, so a
> mint and a verify that disagree about which space produce a valid certificate that fails to verify, or
> worse.

**It is not needed either.** The extent name *is* the identity; the first record is arithmetic a caller
does with it, and a caller that lies about it gets wrong record numbers back and harms only itself. So it
stays in the plaintext hint, where it is useful, and out of the signature, where it is a hazard.

**Nor the stream id.** `(SnId, ExtentId, creation second)` is already globally unique (§4.6.3), so adding
the stream is one more field that must match for no gain — and one more thing to disagree about.

**The rule that falls out needs stating carefully, because the blunt version is wrong** — and Bob's next
observation is what sharpens it:

> **A signed form may carry a position only in the coordinate space of an identity it also carries.**

**The extent's first record fails that test**, which is why it comes out: after the FE's conversion it is
*object-local*, and the object is not in the signature — so nothing in the signed form pins which space
the number is in. ⚠️ **And it cannot be fixed by signing the extent-local version, because that is always
zero.** The quantity is inherently cross-space, which is exactly why it was the wrong thing to sign.

##### Which says what a finer-grained certificate would look like

**If authorization is ever wanted for an offset rather than a whole extent, it would be an *extent*
offset** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-19), *"since the hint is by extent"*. That passes the rule cleanly:

| A signed position, measured in | The space is pinned by | Sound? |
|---|---|---|
| **extent**-local records or bytes | the extent name, already in the signature | **yes** |
| **stream**-local | the stream, which is not in the signature | no |
| **object**-local | the object, which is not in the signature | no |

**So the extension is available without disturbing anything**: a certificate could bound a range inside
the extent it already names, in any of §9.1.3.6's three spaces, and remain closed and unambiguous. That
is not a feature being added here — only a door being left unlocked, and the rule above is what keeps it
so.

⚠️ **And it puts a requirement on `object-info`**: a caller can only construct such a hint if it was told
the extent's **base offsets** in the space it wants to bound. §17.21's `ExtentRow` must therefore carry
all three. **It now does** — and the SN answers `UNKNOWN` for the logical one, because nothing records
it yet (#94).

##### Sizes: a 16-byte tag, and a 256-bit key

**Yes, 16 bytes — a 128-bit tag.** And the two numbers should differ, which is the part worth being
explicit about:

| | Choice | Why |
|---|---|---|
| the **tag** | **128-bit**, 16 bytes | already absurd overkill: forgery is an *online* attack, rate-limited by the FE and detectable on every failure, so 2^-128 per attempt is not the binding constraint |
| the **key** | **256-bit** | §7.2.1's own rule. It reserves 256-bit for KS *"because the master keys are the most important secrets in the system and the volume protected by them is negligible, so the stronger primitive costs nothing"* — and a cluster-wide daily key held by every FE is the **widest key in the system** protecting a few dozen bytes per certificate. Both halves of that argument apply exactly |

⚠️ **The tag is where the answer size goes, and it is a lot.** At §9.1.3.7's 10,000-entry limit the
certificates are 34 B × 10,000 ≈ **340 KB of a 1.4 MB answer — about a quarter of it.** Which is
precisely why §9.1.3.11 makes `Detail::Capabilities` an opt-in bit: **a caller planning work needs the
extents and their record ranges, and not the routes**, so it should not pay for routes it will not use.

**Truncating the tag to 8 bytes is defensible, and the reason the obvious objection does not apply is
worth recording** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-19): *"I was going to object to 8-bit being reasonable due to
the birthday attack, but that doesn't apply here — it's for a particular extent not a group of
extents."*

**That is the right distinction.** A birthday bound would bite if a collision were *useful*: an attacker
who found any two messages sharing a tag could substitute one for the other. Here the attacker wants a
certificate for **one specific extent** — the one it means to read — so it cannot accept whichever extent
it happens to collide with. The attack is targeted guessing at 2^-b per attempt, not 2^-b/2, and every
attempt is an online verification the FE rate-limits and can count.

| | Work |
|---|---|
| birthday, if a collision were useful | 2^32 at an 8-byte tag |
| **targeted guessing, which is the real attack** | **2^64**, online and detectable |

**So the choice is a straight trade rather than a security question**: 8 bytes saves about 6% of a full
answer, and 16 bytes buys margin in a parameter where margin is cheap. Left at 16 with the reasoning
recorded, so the saving is available if answer size ever binds.

**The salt is §7.2.4's rule, not a belt-and-braces measure.** One key and one salt may cover one
plaintext, and a cluster-wide daily key (§16.130) is the widest key in the system — so the mint
carries `(FE id, monotone counter)` rather than resting on an argument that a fixed nonce is safe
for MAC-only use. It needs no RNG, and seeding the counter from the clock means an FE restart cannot
repeat one.

**The path is the right thing to bind to**, per §4.6.3: it is the portable durable name, and it is
what the ACL is attached to. Binding the object *id* instead would force a DN lookup to translate,
which is the hop being saved.

**What it costs to verify is nothing worth measuring.** §7.2.1 puts AEGIS at ~20 GB/s per core, so a
26-byte tag is noise against the request it authorizes — the same argument that licensed checking an
auth code on every read off disk (§9.1.1).

##### 9.1.3.5.3 Write: a plaintext flag that selects the key

**Settled** (Decided, Bob, 2026-08-19): *"Write can be handled by including a plaintext flag of whether
write is allowed, and that flag can choose which signature key to check with."*

That is better than either of the two obvious answers — a flag inside the signed message, or two
separate keys — because it is both, and the flag is what makes the two keys usable without a lookup.

⚠️ **And the flag being plaintext is not a weakness, which is the neat part.** Forging it defeats itself:

| An attacker with | Flips the flag to | The verifier then | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| a **read** certificate | write | checks against the **write** key | the tag was made with the read key, so it **fails** |
| a **write** certificate | read | checks against the **read** key | likewise **fails** |

**So the flag needs no protection from the MAC to be unforgeable in effect** — changing it changes which
key is checked, and the signature was made under exactly one of them. Covering it in the MAC anyway is
free and worth doing as defence against an implementation that verifies with the wrong key, but it is not
what makes the scheme sound.

**One certificate suffices**, provided the rule is stated as *the operation sets the minimum authority*
rather than *the flag sets the operation*:

- a **write** request needs a certificate whose flag says write, verified under the write key;
- a **read** request accepts either, since a write certificate implies the read.

Without that, a tenant with write access would need two certificates for one extent.

##### Two keys means two lifetimes, which §9.1.3.5.2 wanted

⚠️ **This is the dividend, and it was not the motivation.** §9.1.3.5.2 makes the certificate lifetime a
security parameter, with revocation delay pulling it short and DN load pulling it long — one number, no
good value. **Two keys make it two numbers**, rotated independently:

| | Wants a lifetime |
|---|---|
| **read** certificates — common, and a stale one leaks a read | **longer**, because that is where the DN load is |
| **write** certificates — rarer, and a stale one writes to an extent policy says it may not | **shorter**, and it costs little because there are fewer |

**So the trade can be made twice, differently**, and the dangerous half can be made safe without paying
for it on the common path. Rotating the write key invalidates only write certificates.

**And it scopes the authority to grant**, which is §7.3.1's blast-radius reasoning one level up: a
component holding only the read key cannot mint a write certificate whatever bug it has. That was the
argument for two keys before the flag made them cheap to use.

##### The primitive is still unchosen

⚠️ **What signs it is not settled and should not be guessed here** (#93). The requirement is statable:
an unforgeable tag over a short message, verifiable by any FE from a key it already holds, cheap on every
hint read (§7.2.1 makes that easy), and versioned so it can change — which §9.1.3.5's 2-byte key version
already allows for.

**§7.2.4's key-and-salt restriction is already handled**, and two keys make it easier rather than harder:
the certificate carries a `(FE id, monotone counter)` salt whether or not the primitive needs a nonce, and
the salt space is now per-key. A deterministic MAC over distinct messages would not have needed one;
carrying it anyway is what §8.1.6.3's *reserve it whether or not you use it* buys.

**Three failures, and they are distinguishable**, which settles #61's fourth question:

| Symptom | Means | The caller should |
|---|---|---|
| MAC does not verify | forged, expired, or the object was renamed | re-resolve from the object |
| MAC verifies, extent's creation second does not match | that extent was rewritten (§10) | re-resolve from the object |
| both fine, row absent | there is no such record | not retry |

⚠️ **Two things this needs that do not exist yet.**

- **A key.** Any FE must verify what any other FE minted, so this wants a **cluster-wide daily key**
  from KS. §7.3's hierarchy is scoped by *SN* and day, deliberately (§7.3.1), so this is a new scope
  rather than an existing key used differently — small, but it is an addition to §7.3 and not a
  consequence of it. Daily rotation also bounds a token's life independently of its expiry field.
- ⚠️ **How many hops this actually saves depends on where the ACL is fetched from**, which is not
  decided. §5.1 has the object record holding an ACL reference, which would put authorization at the
  DN — and then the DN hop survives for authorization no matter what a hint carries, and the
  capability's saving is the SN hop plus the DN's *descent* rather than the DN round trip. §9.1
  counts the authorization hop separately from the DN hop, which suggests the intended answer is a
  cached or separately-held ACL, but nothing says so. **The ACL's home is now load-bearing for the
  hint story**, which it was not before.

**Prior art, and it is the ordinary shape.** S3 presigned URLs, Kerberos service tickets and
capability systems generally all carry an unforgeable statement rather than re-deriving it at the
point of use. What is slightly unusual here is how *little* the token says: not "the bearer may
read this", only "this extent is inside this object". The narrow claim is what removes the
revocation problem, and it is the whole reason the scheme is cheap.

#### 9.1.3.6 Three measures, and why a request may name only one

A budget is a number in one of three spaces. All three are wanted, by different callers, for reasons
that do not overlap:

| Budget in | Bounds | Enforced by | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| **records** | nothing physical — a count | the record counts, already exact (§4.5) | free |
| **logical bytes** | the caller's **decompressed buffer** | summing `logical` over the blocks returned | free |
| **compressed bytes** | the **network and the disk read** — what §12.3 bills and §5.12.1 makes scarce | the bytes the EN hands back | free |

**All three are free to enforce, which is why there is no reason to offer only one.** The logical
case is the one that looks impossible: a block is opaque below the client (§8.1.4.1), so it seems
only a decompressor could bound logical bytes. But the writer's logical count travels beside every
block *precisely because* nothing below can recompute it (§8.2, §17.16.1), and summing numbers you
were handed costs nothing.

**A request names exactly one, and the answer reports all three actually returned.** It may not name
two, because a caller cannot know the compression ratio in advance (§9.1.3.3) — a request bounding
both logical and compressed bytes would routinely satisfy neither, with no rule saying which to
honour. **The default is logical**, because the buffer is the thing a caller is certain about; a
caller sizing a network transfer or estimating a bill names compressed instead.

⚠️ **Only one of the three bounds the bill, and it is not the intuitive one** (Asserted, Bob,
2026-08-19). §12.3 bills physical bytes, so **the record count is very nearly uncorrelated with what
a read costs**: one record and a million cost about the same if they arrive in the same 2 MB. Three
consequences, and the first is the one a caller has to be told:

- **A budget in records gives no cost control at all.** It is a convenience for a caller reasoning
  about its own data, not a lever on its bill. A caller that wants the bill bounded must name
  **compressed** bytes, and that is the only measure that does it.
- **A budget in logical bytes is barely better**, because the ratio between logical and compressed is
  the data's property rather than the caller's choice. It bounds memory, which is what it is for.
- **So the answer must report the compressed figure whatever was asked for**, which is already the
  rule above — and this is the reason it is not merely tidiness. It is the only number in the answer
  that tells the caller what just happened to its bill.

That asymmetry is worth stating because the three measures otherwise look interchangeable, and they
are interchangeable for *bounding an answer* and not at all for *bounding a cost*.

⚠️ **One block always comes back, even past the budget.** A block is the unit an EN deals in (§9.1),
so a budget below the first block's size would otherwise return nothing — for ever, on every retry,
which is a livelock wearing back-pressure's clothes. The budget is therefore a **stopping rule
applied after the first block**, and the overshoot is bounded by one block, which §8.1.1a-2 bounds
at 32 MB.

⚠️ **32 MB is a poor thing to promise a caller with a 64 KB buffer**, and the remedy is not here: it
is #53, how large a block may be on the wire. What this section fixes is that the overshoot is
**bounded and reported** rather than silent — the three measures in the answer are what a caller
must believe, not its own budget.

#### 9.1.3.7 What `object-info` must answer with, and the one limit over the whole answer

**Settled: `object-info` is extended, rather than joined by a second operation** (Asserted, Bob,
2026-08-19). #61 leaned the other way, on the grounds that extent detail would make every lookup pay
for what most lookups do not want. **The limit below dissolves that objection**: with a cap on
entries per request, a caller wanting the object alone asks for no extents and pays exactly what it
pays today. A separate operation would then buy nothing an argument does not.

The answer has three levels, and the fields at each are set by what a hint needs (§9.1.3.5, #61):

| Level | Fields |
|---|---|
| **the object** | id, flavour, framing, creation second — and the **counts** below |
| each **stream** returned | `StreamId`, its `SnId`, its first object-local record, its record count once sealed, its extent count |
| each **extent** returned | `(SnId, ExtentId, creation second)`, its instances **primary first**, its first stream-local record, its record count, its compressed length, whether it is sealed, and **its capability** (§9.1.3.5) |

The extent row is the hint plus what planning needs: the name, so a stale one fails loudly (§4.6.3);
the instances, so it is a route rather than a description; the ranges and lengths, so a caller can
compute chunk boundaries without asking again (§9.1.3.1); and the capability, without which none of
it may be used.

**And the counts, which are what make a partial answer useful** (§9.1.3.2): streams per object,
extents per stream, records per stream. An answer complete in counts and partial in detail lets a
caller compute every remaining request by arithmetic rather than discovering them one at a time.

**The limit is one number over entries of all three kinds together** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-19) —
objects plus streams plus extents. One number rather than three, because what has to be bounded is
the *answer's size*, and a per-kind cap lets a single pathological object evade the total. It is a
configured knob, a request may name a smaller cap of its own, and **hitting it succeeds** (§9.1.3):
the answer says which range of each level it covered, and what to ask for next.

**Default: 10,000 entries.** Derived, from the answer it produces and the batch it must not break:

| | |
|---|---|
| An extent entry | 3 name fields, 4 instances, 3 ranges and lengths, a flag, a 34-byte capability (§7.2.4) ≈ **~140 B** in the current encoding |
| 10,000 of them | **~1.4 MB**, well inside `MAX_SEGMENT_BYTES` (8 MB), so an answer never needs segmenting |
| §1.4.0's measured batch — 1,000 objects, one stream each | **2,000 entries**, leaving room for objects averaging five entries |

⚠️ **What the limit says at the top end is that enumerating a whole large object is the wrong
request.** §14.1 allows 2 × 10^9 extent references in one object: 2 × 10^5 requests, and ~260 GB of
answers. So **`object-info` takes a range as well** — the same (start, budget) shape as a read, with
the budget in entries — and a scheduler asks about the partition its vertex will read rather than
about the object. A caller that genuinely wants every extent of a 10 PB object wants §13.5's
snapshots, not this path.

**`batch-object-info` stops at a name boundary wherever it can**, and mid-object only when one object
alone exceeds the limit. The continuation is then *the next name*, with an extent range only in the
mid-object case, which keeps the common answer a simple prefix of the list asked about.

⚠️ **That breaks a property the current answer has**: today a batch pads a missing name with zeros so
the answer lines up positionally with the request (§17.12). Once an answer may be short, position is
no longer enough — it has to say **how many of the names it covered**, and a caller reading it the
old way would silently attribute one object's metadata to a different name.

#### 9.1.3.12 A batch spans DNs, and a one-entry summary is what bounds the first one's budget

⚠️ **A batch of names is not one DN's business** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-19). Names route to DNs by the
namespace partition (§5.5.1, §5.11.3), so a thousand names can touch many — and §17.23's implementation
asks exactly one, which a single-DN test cluster hides completely.

**But note what a batch is not** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-20): *"there may eventually be a command that
does an objectinfo of everything in a directory, but BatchObjectInfo is not it."* A batch carries an
**explicit list** of names, optionally a range per name. So the FE does **not** have to discover which
names exist or where they live — it holds the list and the partition map, and groups them by DN with no
round trip at all (§16.150 for the directory-wide command, which is a different problem).

> **What the FE does not know is what each name will *cost*.** §9.1.3.1: a batch cannot be pre-sliced
> because the answer size per object is the thing being asked about. Routing is free; **budgeting is not**.

**Three ways to spend one entry limit (§9.1.3.7) across D DNs:**

| | Cost |
|---|---|
| **serially**, DN after DN | slow — a round trip per DN, §9.1.3.1's serial chain one level up |
| **in parallel**, each asked for everything | ⚠️ up to **D times too much work**, and all but one answer's worth is discarded — and the discarded part is the *expensive* part, since extents cost an SN hop each (§17.22) |
| **asymmetrically** — the full ask to one, a **per-object summary** to the rest | one round trip, and the others' work is fixed at one row per name |

##### The cheap tier is a per-object summary — not a stream list

⚠️ **My first draft of this had the later DNs return their stream lists, and that is more than is needed**
(Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-20): *"ask later DNs for only a per-object summary, not even their lists of
streams."*

**Which is better on both sides of the trade:**

- **The work is fixed, not variable.** A stream list is per-object variable-length; a summary is one row.
  A DN with a thousand names in the batch does a thousand table lookups and stops, with no SN hop
  (§17.20) and no per-object fan-out (§17.22).
- **It is exactly what the budget needs.** Every name the answer covers costs **at least** its own object
  row — one entry, by §9.1.3.7's accounting over objects + streams + extents. So the summary yields the
  **exact count of objects the later DNs contribute**, and:

> **the first DN is given the limit *minus* that count.** It cannot then expand streams and extents so
> greedily that there is no room left for the later DNs' rows.

**And the reservation errs in the recoverable direction.** One entry per name is a *lower* bound on that
name's cost, so subtracting it can leave the first DN a smaller budget than it could have used — never a
larger one. **Under-spending is fixable in a second round; over-spending is not**, because the only way
back from an over-full answer is to throw work away. If the first DN does not fill `limit − count`, ask
again with detail.

##### Why the first DN is the one holding the earliest names

**Because §9.1.3.7 makes the answer a prefix of the request and the continuation an index**, which is what
lets a caller slice its own list. ⚠️ **A prefix in the caller's order is not a prefix in any DN's order**:
if names 1, 3, 5 live on one DN and 2, 4, 6 on another, filling greedily from the first alone yields
1, 3, 5 — not a prefix of anything, and not describable by an index. So the detailed ask goes to whichever
DN owns the earliest names, and the quota is spent in the caller's order.

##### And even if it stops there, the caller can finish the job itself

⚠️ **One step of the above is unnecessary, found on building it** (§17.24.3): the summaries are not
what tells the FE how much to reserve. A summary costs exactly one entry per name and the FE knows how
many names it routed elsewhere *before it sends anything*, so the reservation needs **no measuring round
trip** and round one is one parallel wave. What the summaries are for is sizing **round two**.

**The most useful thing about the cheap round trip is what it tells the caller** (Asserted, Bob,
2026-08-19): *"even if this doesn't need to go on to other DNs, it tells the user enough information for
them to be able to parallelize fetching the remaining batch infos themselves."*

That is §9.1.3.2's shape — **one round trip to learn the shape, then everything else at once** — arriving
one level out. §9.1.3.2 applies it within an object's answer, using exact counts so a caller can compute
its remaining requests by arithmetic. This applies it *across* a batch: the summaries say which names
exist and what each will cost, so a caller can slice the rest into requests that will each fit and issue
them all together.

⚠️ **Which raises the question of whether the FE should do the asymmetric fan-out at all.** Two answers,
and they are not exclusive:

| | Suits |
|---|---|
| the **FE** does it | a caller that wants one request and one answer, and does not want to know about DNs |
| the **caller** does it, from the summaries | a caller with many batches in flight, which can pipeline across them — and it has the context to order the work, which the FE does not |

**§9.1.3.1 already found that batch lookups cannot be pre-sliced** because the answer size per object is
the thing being asked about. **The counts are what removes that**, and they remove it for the caller as
well as for the FE — so the second row may be sufficient and the first is a convenience (§16.149).

#### 9.1.3.8 Prior art: HDFS supports 256 PB files and scans to find an offset

**HDFS supports files up to about 256 PB, and reportedly finds the block containing a byte offset by
scanning the block list from the beginning** (Bob, 2026-08-19, from public reports).

⚠️ **Cited with a caveat**: the behaviour is widely reported and matches the data structures HDFS is
known to use — a NameNode `INodeFile` holds a flat array of blocks, and `getBlockLocations(src, offset,
length)` walks it accumulating sizes until the running total passes the offset. The **client** then
caches the returned list and binary-searches it locally, so the scan is per metadata call rather than
per read. That reading is from memory and has not been checked against the source here; **#85 is the
obligation to discharge it**, and it should be discharged before anything is built on the details. The *shape* is what matters and the shape is not in doubt.

**The arithmetic is the point, and it is the same number DeLawson reaches:**

| | |
|---|---|
| 256 PB at HDFS's 128 MB default block | **2 × 10^9 blocks** |
| §14.1's limit on extent references in one object | **2 × 10^9** |

**Not a coincidence.** Both are what you get when a per-object metadata array grows until linear
anything becomes intolerable, and both tiers arrive there from opposite directions — HDFS from a large
fixed block size, DeLawson from a small one (§6's 32 MB) and a much larger object.

**Why HDFS has to scan is instructive, because it is an absence rather than a mistake.** Blocks are
nominally fixed-size, so offset ÷ block size would be arithmetic — but append and `concat` can leave a
file with non-uniform blocks, so the general case cannot use it. And there is no maintained prefix sum
over block sizes to descend instead. **With neither arithmetic nor an index, a scan is what is left.**

**This is §4.5's rule with the counterfactual attached**, and it is worth having the counterfactual:

> §4.5 makes the *addressing* summary the one that gets to be exact, and says "that is not luck, it is
> why the count-based scheme of §3 works at all". HDFS is what the other choice looks like.

DeLawson locates by **record number**, which §4.5 keeps exact and synchronous to the root, so §9.1's
descent is a B-tree lookup (§4.4) rather than a walk. That is the whole difference, and HDFS is
evidence that the alternative is not merely theoretically worse — it shipped, at a scale where it
matters, and the cost is real.

⚠️ **And it lands squarely on the one thing DeLawson has *not* solved.** §9.1.3.4 admits that a descent
on byte counts is not an index lookup here either, because §4.5 keeps byte totals lazily. So **for
offset addressing, HDFS's problem is DeLawson's problem** — and §9.1.3.4's answer is to avoid the
question rather than to solve it: address by record, or supply the container and let the caller
contribute the prefix sum the store declines to maintain.

**But there is a subclass where it could be solved, and HDFS is what makes it worth naming.** §4.5 keeps
logical bytes lazy because they can change anywhere — an update rewrites a record to a different length,
which shifts every offset above it. **An object that has never been updated has no such case**, so its
logical prefix sum is tail-only, and by §4.5's own rule a tail-only summary may be exact to the root:

| Object | Logical prefix sum | So a bare offset is |
|---|---|---|
| unkeyed, **never updated** | **tail-only, so it may be exact** | a B-tree descent |
| unkeyed, updated | changes mid-object | lazy — scan or bracket-and-walk |
| keyed | changes anywhere (§8.1.1a-7) | never exact |

⚠️ **The first row is probably the common case for the motivating workload** — §1.0's shared AI memory
is append-only by construction, and so is every log-shaped object. So the pathology HDFS lives with may
be avoidable for most objects, at the cost of maintaining one more exact summary and a flag saying
whether it is still trustworthy. §9.1.3.9 settles how; what HDFS supplies is the evidence that the case
was worth examining rather than dismissing.

#### 9.1.3.9 A stream flag buys exact offsets, provided a tombstone keeps its width

**Streams will carry a number of flags, and `updatable` can be one of them** (Asserted, Bob,
2026-08-19) — withdrawn, so that updates are refused. That is what makes §9.1.3.8's subclass a *declared* property rather than an observed one,
which matters: a reader can be told the guarantee holds, instead of the store having to notice that no
update has happened yet and hope none does.

**The condition Bob attaches is the load-bearing half: deletes must leave tombstones that retain their
original logical length.** With it, the three mutations of §8.3 line up exactly as the prefix sum needs:

| Mutation | Effect on the logical prefix sum | |
|---|---|---|
| **insert** — at the tail (§3) | grows the end only | tail-only, so §4.5 permits an exact summary |
| **update** — rewrites a record, possibly to a different length | shifts every offset above it | **the flag forbids it** |
| **delete** — a tombstone that keeps the slot's width | **none** | nothing moves |

**So the byte space behaves exactly as the number space already does**, and that coherence is the real
argument for it. §3 has counts stable under update and tombstone, so a deleted record keeps its record
*number*; this says it also keeps its **width**. One rule, two spaces, and neither has holes that move.

##### Preserving a width costs no space, because a logical offset is a name

⚠️ **The obvious objection is that reserving width for dead records makes compaction pointless, and it
does not** — because §8.2.2 already makes the logical offset a **canonical name space** rather than a
measure of what is stored, with the sparse index (§9.3) mapping it to physical positions.

| | Reclaimed by compaction? |
|---|---|
| the tombstoned record's **physical bytes** | **yes** — the index simply maps nothing there |
| its **logical width** | no, and it costs nothing: a gap in a numbering is not a gap on a disk |

And §12.3 bills **physical** bytes, so the user is not charged for the hole either. The cost is entirely
in the index having a region with no mapping, which it must already tolerate.

⚠️ **But it is an obligation on §10 that would not otherwise exist, and it is easy to violate.** The
natural implementation of compaction — fold the log into the base and write out the surviving records —
silently closes the gaps and shifts every offset above. **Compaction must preserve the widths of
tombstoned records**, and nothing about compaction makes that obvious, so it wants to be a checked
invariant rather than a remembered one.

##### Trusting the sum needs the valid state, and the snap rule must ignore liveness

Two consequences that are easy to get wrong:

- ⚠️ **The exact sum may only be trusted once `updatable` is actually false** (§4.1.1.1). The flag stays
  true for the whole transition, so this needs no care: while the recomputation pass runs, nothing says
  the sums are exact. Setting the flag is O(1) and binds new writes at once, but an object updated in the past
  has a prefix sum that is already wrong — so the background pass that recomputes it is what makes the
  guarantee true, exactly as Oracle's optimizer may only rely on a validated constraint. Loosening the
  flag again is cheap for the store and expensive for whoever built an index on the offsets.
- ⚠️ **§9.1.3.4's snap-forward must go to the next slot boundary, live or not.** If it skipped
  tombstones, then **deleting a record would move a partition boundary** — two vertices that computed
  adjacent boundaries before and after a delete would overlap or leave a gap, which is precisely the
  property §9.1.3.4 fixed the snap rule to guarantee. So the snap is computed on the numbering, and
  skipping dead records is the reader's job afterwards.

##### What else the flags field is for, and one question left

**Bob says flags, plural, and the design already has occupants for the field**: `sealed` is one (§6.3),
#74 puts the **storage-class policy** on the stream, §8.4 has soft-delete opt-out, and §8.5 has expiry.
So this is not a field invented for one purpose — it is a field that already had tenants and now has a
named one.

⚠️ **Where the flag is declared is not quite settled.** The guarantee a reader wants is about an
**object** — *can I trust offsets here* — while enforcement has to be per **stream**, because that is
where records live and where the SN can refuse an update. The natural reading is declared on the object
at creation and carried onto every stream it is given, which leaves one case to think about: §5.11.3.4
lets a stream be referenced from more than one place, so **a shared stream with the flag set constrains
all of its referrers, and a shared stream without it cannot be used by an object that wants the
guarantee** (§16.139).

#### 9.1.3.10 Withdrawing `deletable`, and the compliance claim it encodes

**`deletable` is another such capability** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-19), and what motivates withdrawing
it is a compliance observation rather than a performance one:

> **GDPR requires deletes of user data, but a stream with no user data will never have a GDPR delete,
> and can be marked as knowing that.**

⚠️ **What it must mean, precisely, or it is a compliance hazard rather than a feature.** Withdrawing
`deletable` bars **record-level** deletion within the stream. It does **not** make the stream itself
undeletable — dropping the whole object or stream stays possible, and must, or a flag meant to be
irrelevant to erasure law would create the exact problem it claims not to have.

| | Allowed with `deletable` withdrawn? |
|---|---|
| tombstone one record (§8.3) | **no** |
| delete the whole object or stream (§8.4) | **yes** |
| expiry firing on the whole object (§8.5) | **yes** |

**What the withdrawal buys is omission** (§4.1.1), and the list is longer than it looks, because
record deletion is what several mechanisms exist to cope with:

- **No tombstones, so no log.** §4.2's extents are base plus a lazily-created log; a stream taking
  neither updates nor deletes never creates one. So §9.1's step 3 — *if the extent has a log, check it
  for a newer version or a tombstone* — is skipped on every read.
- **No deletion-driven compaction.** §10 folds base and log; with no log there is nothing to fold.
  Rewriting for storage-class migration and re-encoding survives (§7.4.2), so extents still move — but
  the routine cause is gone.
- **No churn against the repair reserve.** §8.4.3 and §16.42 make retention window × churn consume the
  1 − 1/D headroom §4.3.4 needs for repair. Deletes are that churn.
- **The soft-delete machinery does not apply** at record level — §8.4's deferred decrement, the
  three-day window, §8.4.1b's hard-delete brake all exist to make record deletion safe.

⚠️ **And with both capabilities withdrawn, hints get much longer-lived**, which is the dividend worth noticing.
§8.1.1a-10 makes hint lifetime "a compaction-policy number", since a hint dies when its extent is
rewritten. A stream that never updates and never deletes is rewritten only for tiering, so **its hints
outlive §10.1's ten-minute window by a wide margin** — moving §8.1.1a-10's middle reference tier close
to the durable one, for exactly the objects least likely to change.

##### The cleanup pass is what "validate" means here, and it differs per flag

§4.1.1.1's three states are not an abstraction over these two flags; each has a concrete pass, and they
are different work:

| Withdrawing | Refusing new operations begins | The pass that lets the official flag flip |
|---|---|---|
| **`updatable`** | refuse new updates | **recompute** the logical prefix sums, which past updates may have shifted |
| **`deletable`** | refuse new deletes | **compact away** the existing tombstones and logs, after which there is no log to probe |

**So "lazy cleanup" is literal for deletes and figurative for updates** — one removes data that violates
the promise, the other recomputes a summary the violations invalidated. Both are background passes over
the stream, and neither blocks the O(1) start of refusing new operations.

⚠️ **Which means the deletes pass has an interaction worth flagging: it is a compaction, and compaction
must preserve tombstone widths** (§9.1.3.9). Compacting away a tombstone's *bytes* is the point;
compacting away its *slot* would shift every offset above it and break the other flag's guarantee. The
two passes therefore have to agree, and the natural implementation of each breaks the other.

##### Getting the claim wrong

Withdrawing `deletable` asserts a fact about the **data** — that it holds nothing anyone may demand the
erasure of — and that is a judgement by whoever creates the stream, which the store cannot check. If it
turns out wrong, the remedy is cheap by §4.1.1.1: **restore `deletable` and delete the record.** Nothing
has to be rebuilt, because restoring a capability costs only the omissions.

**So the default is off, and setting it is a deliberate act.** It is right for derived data, telemetry,
indexes and aggregates — the things that are regenerable and hold nobody's personal data — and wrong by
default for anything else.

### 9.2 Keyed: locating key *K*

Identical in shape, with `first_key` comparisons replacing starting record
numbers and the sparse index mapping `key → offset`. The log probe is not
optional here: keyed logs hold inserts, so a key absent from the base may still
exist.

### 9.3 The sparse index

One checkpoint approximately every **1 MB** for HDD-backed extents and **20 KB**
for SSD-backed extents — half the point at which seek cost equals scan cost, which
§7.1.1 derives as `latency x bandwidth`. On an HDD the seek dominates and there is
no point indexing finer than what you would read anyway; on an SSD there is much
less seek to amortize, so finer granularity pays.

**Checkpoints record physical offsets** — positions in the compressed, encrypted
body, which is what a reader actually seeks to. A checkpoint is
`(local record number or key, physical offset)`, optionally with the logical
offset if callers need logical positions.

Cost, at a 32 MB physical extent and 8-byte checkpoints:

| Device | Granularity | Checkpoints | Index size | Overhead |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| HDD | 1 MB | 32 | ~256 B | 0.0008% |
| SSD | 20 KB | ~1,600 | ~13 KB | 0.04% |

Device class is a property of the extent — necessarily so, per §7.4.2 — so an object
migrates between tiers extent by extent, as a rewrite (§10).

### 9.4 Scans

A full scan ignores the index: walk the stream list in order, the extent list in
order, read each extent at full device bandwidth, merging its log. Because
streams sit on distinct SNs and their extents on many ENs, scans of a large
object parallelize across the cluster naturally.

Keyed objects support ordered and range scans by key but **not** positional
access — "the 10,000,000th record" is unanswerable, because counts are
statistics rather than addresses (§3).

**What a caller actually sends to scan a range is §9.1.3.4's start and §9.1.3.6's budget**, and what
it needs in hand to send them is §9.1.3.7's answer. This section is the physical shape of a scan; those
are its interface.

---

### 9.5 Timeouts, and using the options

**Redundancy is an availability benefit only if it can be used before a timeout expires.**
That is not automatic, and getting it wrong turns four copies into a durability feature with
no latency benefit at all.

The scales are brutally mismatched:

| | Duration |
|---|---|
| Typical EN granule read (HDD seek + 1 MB) | ~17 ms |
| TCP timeout | ~20 s |
| TCP timeout with one retry | ~40 s — **~2,400× a normal read** |

So a reader that tries one instance, waits for TCP to give up, retries, and only then tries
another has a worst case of tens of seconds per instance. Four instances tried serially is
worse than one.

**The remedy is hedging: issue to a second instance after a short delay rather than after a
failure.** §4.3's four instances (and, after sealing, *n* fragments of which any *k* suffice)
are exactly the options needed:

| Hedge after | Worst-case read | Improvement over serial retry |
|---|---|---|
| 25 ms | ~42 ms | ~960× |
| 50 ms | ~67 ms | ~600× |
| 100 ms | ~117 ms | ~343× |

And it is nearly free, because only the slow tail is ever duplicated. Hedging at the p99 of
read latency duplicates 1% of reads; at p99.9, 0.1%. The extra load is a knob with a
well-understood cost, unlike the 40-second stall it replaces.

**Set it high — p99.9 or beyond.** §1.4.1 works out why: under a throughput-first priority the
cost of hedging is proportional while the benefit is a fixed saving, so p95 only pays for jobs
under a quarter of an hour, while p99.9 pays for anything under eleven.

Two places this generalizes:

- **Metadata reads have fewer options.** A record read touches one DN ring and one SN ring
  (§5.11.1), and unlike the EN layer there is no second ring to ask. The options inside a
  ring are its members: the hot backup is current by construction (§5.7), so it can serve a
  hedged metadata read. That trades a little staleness for a large latency bound — and
  because sealed extents are immutable, most metadata answers cannot go stale in a way that
  matters.
- **The write path already hedges structurally.** Broadcast plus a 3-of-4 quorum (§8.1.2)
  means a straggler or a dead instance costs nothing: the quorum arrives from the fast three.
  What still needs a timeout budget is the decision to give up and seal the extent short
  (§13), and that budget must sit far below 40 seconds or a single dead EN stalls a writer
  for a TCP timeout.

⚠️ Hedge delays are undesigned. They differ per tier — an EN granule read, a metadata
lookup, and a client-to-FE request over the internet have different normal latencies by
orders of magnitude — so a single global value will be wrong everywhere.

---

### 9.6 Hot small objects: caching and broadcast

A third access pattern, distinct from the sequential scans of §9.4 and the point reads of §9.1:
**one small object read by an enormous number of consumers at once.** The motivating case is
Compute — a big job ships tiny executables and config files to every one of its zillion
vertices.

Read amplification here is the job's vertex count, and that is not survivable by ordinary means:

| Vertices | Total read for a 50 MB executable | Served from 4 instances on 4 disks |
|---|---|---|
| 10,000 | 0.5 TB | 625 s |
| 100,000 | 5 TB | 1.7 h |
| 1,000,000 | 50 TB | **17.4 h** |

A job whose vertices should start in seconds cannot spend seventeen hours distributing its own
binary. And replication does not rescue it: sustaining this from disk would need hundreds of
thousands of disks for one 50 MB file.

Two mechanisms are needed, and they address different parts of it.

#### 9.6.1 A cache, at FE or EN

Caching removes the *disk* from the path. A machine serving from RAM at ~10 GB/s does the work
of fifty disks, so ~83 caching machines could distribute 50 TB in a minute — viable where 400,000
disks is not.

Where it lives is a real trade:

| | Caches | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| **EN** | ciphertext granules | already has the bytes; a few GB of RAM is nothing against 3 PB of disk; **adds no new plaintext location** | still costs a network hop per consumer |
| **FE** | whole small objects | already on the path for authorization; removes the EN hop entirely | FE holds **plaintext** (§5.9.2), so it is a new place plaintext sits |

⚠️ Undecided. The security asymmetry is worth weighing: an EN cache of ciphertext creates no
new exposure, while an FE plaintext cache does.

**Part of it is already settled: an EN will have a small cache of recently read data** (Asserted,
Bob, 2026-08-17) — the top row of the table above, in miniature. It holds blocks as stored, so it
needs no keys, adds no plaintext location, and a hit also skips the auth-code check of §9.1.1. What
remains open is the *large* cache for hot objects, which is a different question from a small one for
recently read blocks.

**Two things narrow that** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17). **The FE is a cache** — that is what it is
for, beyond authorization and coordination. But **an extent is usually read once**, and a cache of
read-once data is only a cost, so it is *unclear that the FE is the right cache for hot extents*
specifically. What the FE is unambiguously the right cache for is what §17.13 already does with it:
**where records live**, which is metadata, is small, and is asked about repeatedly even when the bytes
behind it are not.

**And for several of the motivating cases there will be another mechanism** — spreading a configuration
to the vertices of a job is §9.6.2's broadcast, not a cache, and a job that has been handed hints
(§8.1.1a-10) needs neither. So the hot-object cache question should be settled *after* those exist,
since they remove much of what would otherwise justify it.

#### 9.6.2 Broadcast, which is the actual fix

Caching reduces the cost per consumer; it does not change the fact that the total is *N* × *S*
flowing out of a small number of machines. **Broadcast changes who provides the bandwidth.**

Distributing through a tree among the job's own vertices — each receiving vertex forwarding to
*f* others — moves the bottleneck from a handful of EN disks to the compute fabric's own NICs:

| Fan-out | Depth at 10^6 vertices | Source sends | Elapsed at 10 Gbps |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | 9 | 200 MB | ~1.4 s |
| **10** | **5** | **500 MB** | **~2 s** |
| 32 | 4 | 1.6 GB | ~5.1 s |

**17.4 hours becomes ~2 seconds** — a ~26,000× improvement — and the source reads the object
*once*. The total bytes moved are unchanged; what changes is that they move across links which
scale with the job, rather than across the four disks that happen to hold the extent.

So DeLawson needs a **broadcast tool for Compute**, not merely a faster read path.

Three things fall out:

- **It does not violate the key boundary.** Vertices forward *plaintext* to other vertices of the
  same job, all of which are already authorized for it (§1.5). No keys move, so peer distribution
  is compatible with the invariant — worth stating, since it superficially looks like a breach.
- **Billing stays honest by itself.** Reads are a billed dimension (§12.4), and a broadcast job
  performs one read rather than a million. That is not a discount — it is what the job actually
  costs, since the fan-out consumed compute-fabric bandwidth rather than storage. The incentive
  and the cost point the same way.
- **This is not the hot-spot problem of §1.4.4.** Read hot spots are unpredictable and gradual,
  and their remedy is more instances. This is predictable, job-scoped, and all at once, and its
  remedy is a tree. Conflating them would produce the wrong mechanism for both.

### 9.7 Time-range queries

**Every append records the second in which it became durable**, and that makes history queryable long after
the SCN horizon of §4.3.4 has passed.

| | |
|---|---|
| Granularity | **one second** — not SCN granularity |
| Assigned | **per append**, not per record; many appends share a second |
| Semantics | the moment the append became **durable** (3-of-4 applied, §8.1.1), not when it was received |
| Stored | as a **table** in the EN's extent index or append header — *not* interleaved with the records |

Keeping it out of the records matters: at 8 bytes per entry it would otherwise be a per-record tax on
data whose records may be 100 bytes, and §12.2 shows what per-record overheads cost at scale.

#### 9.7.1 Why it is nearly free for unkeyed objects

For an append-only object, **record number and durability time both increase monotonically**, so a time range
maps to a *contiguous* record range. A time-range scan is therefore a binary search of the timestamp table
followed by an ordinary record-range read — the same shape as §9.3's sparse index, one dimension over.

That is another payoff from §3's append-only-at-the-end rule, which was adopted to keep cumulative counts
stable and keeps turning out to buy things: stable external indexes (§1.0), synchronous record counts (§4.5),
and now cheap time-range scans.

**Table size** is one entry per second in which an append became durable, so it depends on fill *rate* rather
than on volume:

| Fill rate | Time to fill a 32 MB extent | Entries | Table |
|---|---|---|---|
| 10 MB/s | 3 s | 3 | negligible |
| 1 MB/s | 32 s | 32 | 0.3 KB |
| 100 KB/s | 320 s | 320 | 2.6 KB |
| 10 KB/s | 3,200 s | 3,200 | 26 KB |
| 1 KB/s | 32,000 s | 32,000 | **256 KB — 0.8% of the extent** |

⚠️ So a **slowly-written extent accumulates a large table**, because it stays open for hours. A time-based
sealing trigger would bound it — sealing after an hour caps the table at 3,600 entries, ~29 KB, comparable to
