the sparse record index. There are independent reasons to want one anyway, since §4.2 makes open extents the
expensive kind. But it cuts the other way too: hourly sealing of a 1 KB/s stream produces 3.6 MB extents,
nine times as many extents as filling them would, and §12.2 prices extent metadata. Undecided, and it is a
genuine three-way trade between table size, open-extent cost, and metadata volume.

#### 9.7.2 Keyed objects, and what compaction must preserve

Keyed objects insert in the middle, so record number is **not** monotonic in time and a time range does not
map to a contiguous range. The timestamps are still recorded per append, so the query is answerable by
locating the appends in the window — but it is a scan over candidate extents rather than a binary search, and
its cost has not been worked out.

⚠️ **Compaction must carry durability timestamps forward.** A timestamp is a property of the record, not of
its current location, so a rewrite that dropped it would silently destroy history — and §10 rewrites
everything eventually. That is easy to get right and easy to forget.

---

#### 9.7.3 Interval summaries, for when the extent list is not monotone

§9.7.1's binary search depends on durability seconds increasing down the extent list. §8.6.2 shows that any form of
parallel ingest breaks that monotonicity — several unsealed tails interleave in time, and so do concurrently
written partitions that are later concatenated. So the search has to be replaced, not merely tuned.

**Keep `(min durable second, max durable second)` per extent, per stream, and per object**, and answer a range
query by pruning on interval overlap instead of by binary search.

**The reason this is legal under §4.5 is better than "it is cheap".** An interval **only ever widens**, so a stale
or conservative value costs a wasted read and never a wrong answer. Fail-safe summaries can be maintained lazily by
§13.3's loops with no correctness argument about ordering — which is exactly the property §4.5's rule exists to
select for.

It is also not novel: this is what Parquet column statistics and Iceberg manifest pruning do. And it **degrades
gracefully in the right direction** — if writes happen to be sequential, the intervals are disjoint and pruning is
exactly as good as the binary search it replaced.

Per-object intervals are what make §8.6.3's directory-level time-range query cheap, since fan-out then only reaches
objects whose interval overlaps the requested range.

### 9.8 A read that would need reconstruction does not reconstruct

**Policy: reconstruct-for-read never competes with repair** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-16). If a read needs a
missing cell, rebuilding just that cell to satisfy the read is **not** done at the expense of other work — but
it is permitted when nothing else wants the bandwidth, via a purpose with a **very high door** in §13.4.3's
sense (§9.8.2).

The reason is throughput, and it generalizes:

> **Reconstructing for a read does work the system does not persist.** Five to forty-five reads are spent, one
> read is served, and nothing is left behind — so the next read of the same cell pays it again.

Instead, three things happen:

1. **Repair the whole group, if that fits within the timeout.** Repairing persists the work, so the cost is
   amortized over every future read of the group instead of charged to this one. The read then succeeds from
   repaired data.
2. **Otherwise flag the EC group as hot.** That bumps its repair priority by **one global read**, applied
   *after* §13.4's 0-global-versus-1-global swap, and puts it in a queue for immediate reprocessing by GC.
3. **If the bumped priority still does not meet the bar, it waits for the next GC pass.**

**The user sets the timeout** (Asserted, Bob), which makes the choice theirs: a long timeout says *I will wait
for the group to be repaired*, a short one says *fail fast*. That is §1.1's argument — availability includes
waiting for a timeout — turned into a per-request control rather than a system-wide constant.

**Why bumping *after* the swap is exactly right.** §13.4 deliberately deprioritizes the `g = 1` class so that
it evolves into cheaper, higher-priority states, and the justification for that deprioritization is that
**nobody is waiting.** A hot flag is the statement that somebody is. So the swap encodes absence of demand and
the bump encodes its presence, and applying the bump afterwards is what keeps both arguments intact. A `g = 1`
group flagged hot jumps from last place into the descending region — the largest single move the priority
function can make, which is appropriate since it is the only class where demand and cost disagree.

#### 9.8.1 Three consequences worth stating

**It sharpens what §4.3.2.4's "usually available" means.** Not "slower to read" — a read of a missing cell in
the 1.333x tier **fails, or waits for repair**, at the user's choice. So the availability difference between
the two EC variants is a difference in *time to first successful read*, and §12.7.2.1a's minutes-versus-days
figure is a repair-queue latency, not a reconstruction latency.

**It removes the expensive read**, which resolves most of §16 question 108. If reads never reconstruct, then
every read is either cheap (data present) or unserved — there is no 5x-cost read to meter, so read billing can
stay flat and §12.6.2 needs no tier term. The expensive work is repair, which is system work benefiting every
future reader. ⚠️ The one exception is case 1 above: a user with a long timeout triggers a whole-group repair,
so they pay latency for work that benefits everyone else. Whether that is charged, unpriced, or credited is
undecided.

**It closes a read-amplification attack.** Without this policy, repeatedly reading a degraded group would force
45 reads each time — a 45x amplifier available to any caller. With it, the first attempt triggers one repair and
every later read is cheap.

⚠️ **Does the hot bump accumulate?** If a hundred readers hit the same degraded group, a single +1 may still
leave it below the bar, and it starves while demand mounts. Accumulating the bump makes read demand a real
weight; not accumulating keeps §13.4's ordering simple and bounded. A decaying accumulation is the obvious
compromise and is not obviously correct. Undecided.

Note that §9.5's hedging cannot help here: at 1.333x there is one instance to read, so there is no second
target to hedge to. Hedging is a 2.333x-tier mechanism (§4.3.2.4).

#### 9.8.2 …except at idle, where the objection stops applying

The argument against reconstruct-for-read is a **throughput** argument: hardware spent, nothing persisted
(§1.6.4). Under contention that is decisive. At idle it is empty — §1.6 says allocated bandwidth left unused is
wasted, so spending idle bandwidth on a non-persisted read costs nothing and serves a user.

So reconstruct-for-read becomes a **purpose with the highest door of any**, and the admission mechanism
reconciles the two concerns with no separate policy: real work drives the level down, the highest door stops
being cleared, and read reconstruction stops. Exactly the desired behaviour, obtained from a threshold rather
than from a rule.

**Its door belongs above the 1-9% band, and it is the only purpose for which that is true.** Two reasons, both
Derived:

- **The level moves slowly** (§13.4.3.4). A door inside the narrow band would let read reconstruction hold
  bandwidth that newly-arrived repair work cannot reclaim promptly. The one purpose whose work is *discardable*
  should also be the one that yields with the most margin.
- **It is the only preemptible purpose.** Abandoning an in-flight read reconstruction costs nothing — the caller
  simply gets the failure it would have got anyway. Abandoning a repair means the work must be redone. So it is
  safe to give this purpose a hair trigger, and unsafe to give one to anything else.

The consequence for §4.3.2.4's availability tiers is a better story than §9.8.1 told: a degraded read in the
1.333x tier fails **under load** and succeeds **at idle**, automatically, with the user's timeout (§9.8) deciding
how long they are willing to find out.

⚠️ **But if you have paid for the solve, why not write the result?** A global solve costs ~45 reads; writing the
rebuilt cell costs 1 more and makes the work permanent — 2% for a durable benefit, which §1.6.4 says take every
time. And having solved, there is no reason to rebuild only the cell that was asked for rather than every
recoverable cell in the group.

Follow that through and "reconstruct for read" collapses into **ordinary repair with read-demand priority**,
which §13.4.0 already provides. Which leaves a genuine question rather than a rhetorical one: **is there a case
where the solve is possible but the write is not?** Plausibly yes — placement may be unsolvable, the group may be
mid-regrouping (§16 question 104), or the target media class may be full (§5.11). If those are the only cases,
then non-persisting reconstruction is a narrow fallback and not a general mode, and its door can be set
accordingly.

#### 9.8.3 Disposition: available, and not worth building

**Decided: do not build it** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-16 — "I doubt it's worth the coding effort"). The section
above stays because the reasoning is what justifies the omission, and because the same reasoning is what someone
would have to overturn to add it later.

The argument for leaving it out is stronger than effort-versus-value, and §9.8.2 is what makes it so:

| | |
|---|---|
| Read-triggered solve **that writes its result** | already exists — ordinary repair with read-demand priority (§13.4.0) |
| Read-triggered solve that **discards** its result | needs new code, and §1.6.4 says writing costs 2% more for a durable benefit |
| So the new code buys | only the cases where the solve is possible and the **write** is not |

Those cases — unsolvable placement, a group mid-regrouping, a full media class — are narrow, and in each of them
the right answer is probably to fix the blocking condition rather than to serve a read from work that is thrown
away. So the feature is not merely low-value; **the case for it nearly closes on inspection.**

What remains true and worth keeping is the general lesson, which §13.4.3.6 states: because the admission
mechanism is work-conserving, **a purpose whose work is worthless under load but harmless at idle can be
expressed as a very high door rather than as a policy.** That pattern will come up again for something that *is*
worth building.

## 10. Compaction

Compaction reads a base plus its log and writes a fresh base with updates
applied, tombstones dropped, and (keyed) inserts merged in key order, then
atomically swaps the pair in the SN's extent list.

- **Extent membership of a stream changes over time.** Extent *position* within
  a stream is unstable; extent *identity* must be a stable unique id that
  outlives position.
- **Keyed compaction can split.** If the merged result exceeds either limit of
  §6 it becomes two extents covering two key subranges, spliced into the extent
  list. This makes keyed objects B-tree-shaped — one log level per base,
  splitting on overflow — rather than LSM-shaped with many levels.
- **Unkeyed compaction never splits or renumbers.** Update and tombstone
  preserve count, so the new base covers exactly the record-number range the old
  one did and everything above it is untouched. Purely local.
- Compaction is a rewrite, so it is also where EC re-encoding, device-class
  changes, recompression, and **encryption key rotation** happen.
- Compaction is a **billing event**: it reclaims the physical bytes held by
  superseded versions and tombstones (§12).

⚠️ Compaction policy — triggers, write-amplification budget, split throttling —
is not designed. Billing makes it sharper than usual: the schedule directly
determines a customer's bill.

### 10.1 Rewrites must retain their inputs for the hint window

§8.1.1a-10's middle tier — `(extent identity, row number in extent)` — is invalidated by exactly one operation, and
compaction is it:

| Operation | Invalidates a hint? |
|---|---|
| Replication/repair (§13.1's fast loop) | No — new *instances*, same extent identity |
| EC on seal | No — physical layout changes, logical row number does not |
| Tail truncation above the durable watermark | No — pre-seal |
| **Coalescing / base-plus-log compaction** | **Yes** |
| Hard delete | Yes, and correctly so — the record is gone |

The goal is exact ordering, for a bounded window after write, without a key lookup — the SCN-granularity tier that
§4.6.3 contrasts with second-granularity timestamps. Current guess: **10 minutes** (Guess).

⚠️ **And it is a promise made to users, not an internal convenience** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17). A hint
is handed out — to a job scheduler, which hands it to vertices that use it while the job runs — with the
guarantee that it **holds for at least that window**. So the retention rule below is part of the contract:
a rewrite that released its inputs early would not merely lose a cache hit, it would break something a
caller was told it could rely on. The floor is what makes the hint usable by anyone who cannot re-ask
cheaply.

**Three things make that nearly free.**

**Test the seal second, not the creation second.** An extent open for an hour has its last write at seal time, so the
predicate is `now - seal_second >= 600`. No new field: the seal second is the maximum of the per-extent durability
timestamps §9.7 already stores, and unsealed extents cannot be compaction inputs anyway.

**Constrain reclamation, not compaction frequency.** A flat rule would forbid a hot keyed object from compacting its
log every 30 seconds for read amplification. But compaction may write its new base whenever it likes provided the
*inputs stay resolvable* for the window after their seal. So the requirement is a **minimum retention on superseded
extents** — the deferred-decrement shape §8.4.1 already uses for soft delete, with a different timer — and
compaction frequency stays purely a read-amplification decision.

**The cost is disk, not SN RAM.** Bounded by the window times the compaction output rate, held on the tier that
§12.2 prices at 1/5000th of RAM.

**What the window does not promise.** It promises *not rewritten*, not *not deleted*. A hint into hard-deleted data
must fail, and with §8.4's soft-delete opt-out it can fail in well under 10 minutes. That is correct behaviour.

**And it does not deliver cluster-wide SCNs.** An SCN is a total order; `(extent, row)` is an address. Within one
stream it *is* a total order — extent position in the stream, then row within extent — but across the N frontier
streams of §8.6.6 there is no order at all. So the honest guarantee is two-tier:

- **per-stream, exact ordering, for the window** — via `(extent, row)`, no key lookup, no ambiguity;
- **globally, second granularity, forever** — via durability timestamps (§9.7).

That is what a Kafka partition offers, so it is defensible to advertise, but it is not "SCNs for 10 minutes" and
must not be described that way.

⚠️ 10 minutes is a guess, and the real number should be derived from what it budgets: **how far a tail-following
consumer may lag behind its writer before it must fall back to a key lookup.** Framed as a follower-lag budget it
becomes measurable; framed as a round number it stays a guess forever.

---

## 11. Small objects

Three regimes by size, which map cleanly onto the node types of §5:

| Regime | When | Storage | Streams and extents of its own |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Inline** | very small | records live inside the object's metadata record | none |
| **Lumped** | small | **shares a common stream with many other objects** | none of its own |
| **Packed** | below half a max-sized extent | shares one extent with other objects; the extent carries a directory of its occupants | shares |
| **Dedicated** | above that | its own streams and extents | yes |

**Lumping is the load-bearing case.** Tiny objects are gathered into common streams rather
than each getting a stream, which is what keeps stream counts — and therefore SN memory
(§14.1) and the DN sync (§13.1.3) — proportional to *bytes* rather than to *object count*.
Without it, a trillion tiny objects would mean a trillion streams.

**Self-hosting (§5.5) changes what "inline" means.** Since DN metadata is itself
stored in DeLawson keyed objects, an inline object's records end up as bytes in a
*metadata* extent on ENs. There is no "DN only" regime — nothing is stored
outside the object hierarchy except the bootstrap root.

The small-object win is real but differently explained: an inline object has no
stream, extent, or instance **of its own**, and instead rides along in metadata
extents shared with thousands of other objects' metadata. So inline is really a
special case of packing, obtained for free — and with better locality than
explicit packing, because an object's metadata and its records land in the same
place.

⚠️ This blurs the boundary between the inline and packed regimes. If inline
already packs via the metadata object, what does the explicit packed regime add
beyond a larger size bound? Possibly nothing, in which case two regimes suffice:
inline-in-metadata, and dedicated. Worth resolving before either is built.

The half-extent threshold guarantees a packed object never straddles an extent
boundary: at most half of a maximum extent, at least two objects fit and any
packable object fits whole.

⚠️ "Half a max-sized extent" is ambiguous now that §6 gives two maxima. Half of
4 GB logical and half of 32 MB physical are very different; since the physical
limit almost always binds, the packing threshold is presumably ~16 MB physical.
Needs confirming.

⚠️ Packing collides with billing and compression. A packed extent is compressed
as a unit, so per-object physical size is **not additive** — two objects that
share substrings compress better together than apart, with no principled way to
attribute the saving. Either compress each packed object independently (losing
ratio, and ratio is billable) or attribute physical bytes proportionally to
logical size (approximate, and customers can notice). Deleting one packed object
also leaves garbage until the shared extent is compacted, and packed objects
share an EC fate.

---

## 12. Billing and metering

### 12.0 DeLawson ships a cost model, not a price list

**The operator sets the coefficients** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-19):

> "Part of my purpose of choosing billing that makes it easy to lower bills arbitrarily close to
> costs, and making it open source, is that I want DeLawson to get used. If a cluster operator
> wants to make a higher profit, they set the coefficients — they can multiply their costs all by
> X if they want to. They can even overcharge some things but not others. Business decision on
> their part, and it is always a business in some sense, because actual clusters do cost money to
> run."

So what this section designs is **metering**, and a table of coefficients over it. The dollar
figures worked through in §12.7 are calibration and sanity checks against the market — they are
not the product, and nothing in the code should treat them as more than defaults. "It is always a
business in some sense" covers the internal case too: an organization running its own cluster is
doing chargeback rather than sales, and it turns the same knob.

**Everything downstream reads differently once that is clear:**

- ⚠️ **The 2× slack of §12.4.1 is the error an operator cannot tune away.** Multiplying every
  coefficient by X changes the level and not the shape, so a dimension whose *shape* is wrong
  stays wrong at every price. That is what the design owes: not the right price, but a set of
  dimensions no coefficient has to apologise for.
- **Being able to drive a bill close to cost is the adoption lever of §12.1.0**, made operational.
  The floor stays a real constraint — clusters cost money — but the design's job is to leave as
  little unavoidable margin between price and cost as it can, and let the operator decide how much
  to add back.
- **Charging above cost on some dimensions and not others is intended, not abuse.** It is how an
  operator discourages a workload their hardware is bad at, and it is a faster instrument than
  §12.4.2's refusals for anything that is merely expensive rather than pathological.

⚠️ **The risk this creates is that an operator can set a coefficient to zero**, which reintroduces
§12.1's ADLS Gen1 failure inside their own cluster — the free dimension is the one users find. The
code should make that possible and not easy: **ship non-zero defaults for every metered dimension,
and say something when a dimension is metered but priced at zero.** An operator choosing to eat a
cost is fine; an operator not noticing they have is the failure mode.

### 12.1 The governing principle

> **Billing must be proportional to actual cost, within some slack.** Bill too little and
> the service goes broke; bill too much and a competitor undercuts it.

Both bounds are real, which makes billing accuracy a two-sided constraint rather than a
revenue-maximizing exercise. It also makes it a *design* constraint: the price list has to
be derivable from the cost structure, so any resource the design makes scarce must be
something the design can meter.

**This has a precedent worth taking seriously.** Cosmos was made user-visible once, as
**ADLS Gen1**. It did not bill for user metadata — and users responded exactly as the
incentive invited, piling into enormous numbers of extremely tiny streams. Nothing about
that behaviour was unreasonable; it was the cheapest way to use the product as priced.

#### 12.1.0 The two bounds are not symmetric: the floor is a constraint, the ceiling is a lever

The principle above reads as two equal bounds. **It is not** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-19):

> "If DeLawson can store the same data in less space and pass the savings on to customers, using
> less space makes DeLawson more likely to get used. DeLawson billing just has to assure the
> cluster owner doesn't go broke in the process."

So the **floor** — do not go broke — is the constraint to satisfy, and the **ceiling** is not a
constraint at all but the **lever**: efficiency is meant to arrive at the customer as a smaller
bill, because that is what makes the store worth choosing. Every byte not stored is a byte not
charged for.

⚠️ **Which settles the logical-versus-compressed question that §12.3.3 leaves open, and settles
it the other way from the precedents.** Under logical billing the savings *cannot* reach the
customer: compression, coalescing and erasure coding would all improve the owner's margin and
nothing else, and the customer would see the same bill a non-compressing competitor charges and
have no reason to prefer this store. **Billing physical bytes is the mechanism by which "store
it in less space" becomes a benefit the customer can see.** It is a competitive requirement, not
an accounting preference.

**And physical billing tracks cost by construction, which is what protects the floor.** §12.3.3's
table shows revenue per physical byte swinging 13.5× under logical pricing, entirely on
properties of the data the price list never mentions. Bill the physical byte and that swing is
zero: an incompressible tenant occupies more and pays more, a compressible one occupies less and
pays less, with no need to guess a compression ratio in advance. The 2× slack is spent on things
that genuinely vary rather than on hedging against the data.

**It also prices every efficiency decision the design already makes.** Compression (§8.1.4.1),
coalescing (§8.1.4.4), erasure coding versus replication, and the storage class of §74 all change
the physical footprint — so under physical billing each becomes a customer-visible, priced choice.
A tenant asking for four instances pays roughly three times one accepting 12+4, which is roughly
the truth.

⚠️ **What is left of the floor risk is therefore not storage at all.** Physical billing
self-corrects on bytes, so the places an owner can still go broke are the dimensions it does not
capture: metadata, operations, and the transient double footprint during compaction. §12.1's own
cautionary tale is exactly one of those — ADLS Gen1 did not bill metadata — so that is where the
attention belongs, not on the byte.

#### 12.1.1 Compute prices must vary, and the slack rule binds on the average

**Compute pricing will break the 1x-2x rule in both directions — lower when capacity risks going unused, higher at
peak demand — while still averaging about 1.2x cost** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-16).

##### 12.1.1.1 The law of large numbers does not rescue this

**Demand is not uniform, and no cluster is large enough to make it uniform.** That is the load-bearing claim, and it
is worth stating formally because the intuition runs the other way. Write each customer's demand as

```
demand_i(t) = a_i · f(t) + noise_i(t)
```

Summing over *n* customers, the noise averages out — its relative variance falls as `1/sqrt(n)` — but the common
term `f(t) · Σa_i` **scales with *n* exactly as the mean does.** So:

> **Peak-to-mean is a property of the workload's time structure, not of the cluster's size. Growing the cluster
> does not smooth demand.**

**Derived.** The spikes are common-mode, not independent: a deletion spike at midnight GMT every day, weekends
quieter than weekdays, end-of-year busier than the rest. Averaging only works on what is independent, and none of
those are.

##### 12.1.1.2 Varying prices are *more* faithful to §12.1, not less

The rule says proportional to **actual cost**. Ask what actual cost is at a given instant:

| State | Actual cost of serving one more compute-hour | Average cost is |
|---|---|---|
| Capacity idle | **marginal** — electricity, a small fraction of amortized | far too high |
| Capacity scarce | **opportunity** — the work displaced | too low |

So average cost is the right answer at neither extreme, and **a fixed price was always the approximation.**
Selling idle capacity below average cost but above marginal cost is profitable rather than charitable — the
alternative is zero revenue on hardware that costs the same either way, which §1.6 calls waste.

At peak, the usual objection is that a competitor undercuts you. But the peak is common-mode, so **every provider
is scarce simultaneously** and there is no trough elsewhere to undercut from. That is uncomfortable and it is the
honest reading.

**So restate the rule rather than abandon it:**

> §12.1's slack binds on the **average** price paid over time, not on the instantaneous price. The accountable
> figure is ~1.2x cost on average; the instantaneous price is free to track scarcity because scarcity *is* cost.

##### 12.1.1.3 What must not vary, and what it costs

**Storage must not be dynamically priced.** A stored byte occupies a disk continuously, so its cost has no
time structure to track. Compute has one because a processor-second unused is gone. The design therefore has three
billing shapes, and their differences are §12.1 applied faithfully rather than inconsistently:

| Resource | Shape | Where |
|---|---|---|
| Storage | continuous, stable price | §12.3 |
| Compute bank | accumulate at a rate, **charging stops at the ceiling** | §5.12.5.1 |
| Compute at the margin | **time-varying with scarcity** | here |

⚠️ **The cost is predictability, and this is the second source of it.** §16's question about sharing volatility is
the first. §12.6 promises a simple presentation, and a bill that moves with the clock strains that — so the price
must be **published and derived from observable utilization**, because an unpredictable price gives customers no
way to shift load and therefore fails at the one job it was introduced to do.

**And §5.12.6's reservations are the hedge, which retroactively explains their premium.** A scheduled compute-hour
costs more than a normal one precisely because it is **insurance against peak spot prices** as well as a capacity
guarantee. Customers with flexible work take the spot price; customers with predictable work buy certainty. The two
products compose rather than compete.

### 12.2 Why "bill for bytes" is not enough

The arithmetic of that failure mode is stark, because **RAM costs roughly 5,000× per byte
what disk does** — and the gap is nothing like the ~200× a naive comparison of purchase
prices suggests. Building it up per GB over a five-year life:

| | DRAM | HDD |
|---|---|---|
| Capital | $3.00 | $0.010 |
| Power | $1.53 | $0.0013 |
| **Server amortization** | **$23.44** | $0.0020 |
| Redundancy | ×3 materialized ring members (§5.7) | ×1.5 erasure code |
| **Total** | **~$84** | **~$0.020** |
| | | **ratio ~4,200×** |

Purchase price is the *smallest* of the three terms. What dominates is server
amortization — a machine's worth of CPU, board and chassis spread over 256 GB of RAM,
against the same machine spread over 3 PB of disk — and then the ring triples it. So ~5,000×
is the right order, and the figure the billing model must use.

At that ratio:

| | |
|---|---|
| A minimal stream: 200 B stream record + 100 B extent reference | 300 B of SN RAM |
| Disk-equivalent cost | **1.5 MB** |
| Break-even user payload, at 4 instances | **~375 KB** |

**A stream holding less than ~375 KB costs more in metadata than in data**, and the
underbilling grows without bound as the payload shrinks. The average stream of §14.1.1 holds
128 MB, comfortably 341× above break-even — but the abuse case is not marginal. A user who
fills one SN's stream budget with 1 KB streams consumes 128 GB of SN RAM, worth **640 TB of
disk**, while billing for 1.7 TB. **Underbilled 375×.** The workload cheapest for the user is
ruinous for the operator, so it is the workload the pricing selects for.

#### 12.2.1 DN metadata is far less dangerous, and that is why lumping matters

The severity is entirely about *which medium* holds the metadata. DN metadata lives on disk
(§5.1), so its ratio against user data is ~1 rather than ~5,000:

| Metadata | Medium | Cost of one record | Break-even payload |
|---|---|---|---|
| Stream, on an SN | **RAM** | 300 B × 5,000 | **~375 KB** |
| Object, on a DN | disk (300 B, 4× compressed, 1.5× EC) | ~112 B | **~112 B** |

**The stream case is ~3,300× more dangerous than the object case.** Which is the real
justification for lumping (§11): gathering tiny objects into common streams moves their
metadata cost out of the RAM-backed stream tier and into the disk-backed DN tier. It is not
merely a way to keep stream counts down — it is a change of medium, and therefore of cost by
three and a half orders of magnitude.

It also says something about where to worry. A trillion tiny objects is a manageable DN
problem. A trillion tiny *streams* is an unmanageable SN problem, and the difference between
those two sentences is the whole reason §11 exists.

### 12.3 Physical, not logical, is the same rule

Billing by physical rather than logical bytes is not a separate decision — it is §12.1
applied to compressibility. **The slack is 2× by default**, and the gap between logical and
physical is the compression ratio, which §6 puts anywhere from 1× to 128×:

| Data | Ratio | Error if billed logically |
|---|---|---|
| Incompressible media | 1× | inside slack |
| Typical text and records | 3.5× | 1.8× outside |
| Logs, sparse columns | 30× | 15× outside |
| Pathological | 128× | 64× outside |

The extremes are 128× apart, so **no single logical price can sit within 2× of cost for
everyone.** Set it for compressible data and incompressible customers are massively
underbilled; set it for incompressible data and compressible ones leave for a competitor.
Physical billing is forced, not preferred.

The same test catches something else. A byte of extent body costs 4× as much held as four
replicas as it does at 1.5× under an 8+4 erasure code — a **2.67× ratio, which exceeds the
2× slack.** So billing cannot apply a flat per-byte rate across durability states: whether
an extent is still replicated or already encoded has to be metered per extent, which is why
§12.5 treats the seal-to-encode latency as a real quantity rather than an implementation
detail.

#### 12.3.1 Prior art: BigQuery offers both models

**BigQuery** — not Colossus, though BigQuery is built on it — offers exactly this choice:
["two storage billing models: logical (uncompressed) and physical
(compressed)"](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/storage_overview). The details
are more instructive than the mere existence:

| | BigQuery's arrangement |
|---|---|
| Granularity | per **dataset** |
| Default | **logical** |
| Switching | 14-day cooldown between changes, 24 hours to take effect |
| Time travel and fail-safe | **included** under logical, **charged separately** under physical |

Offering a choice looks at first like adverse selection — every customer picks whichever is
cheaper, so the provider collects the *minimum* of the two. But it is better than that.
Let *R* be the physical price per byte divided by the logical price per byte. A customer with
compression ratio *c* prefers physical when *c* > *R*, so revenue per physical byte tracks
min(*c*, *R*):

| *R* | Billing error across all compression ratios | |
|---|---|---|
| 1.5 | 1.5× | inside 2× slack |
| 2 | 2× | inside 2× slack |
| 4 | 4× | outside |

So **the price ratio caps the error.** Two models with *R* ≈ 2 sit inside the 2× slack,
where pure logical billing was unbounded — the choice converts an open-ended error into a
bounded one. That is a real mechanism, not a giveaway. (I have not verified BigQuery's
actual *R*; the page above defers pricing elsewhere.)

The catch is that the bound holds **only for customers who optimize.** A customer left on
the logical default with 30×-compressible data is overcharged ~15× against an *R*=2 physical
rate. So the scheme is really a non-compliant default plus an escape hatch, and its accuracy
is conditional on customer attention. The 14-day cooldown and the differing time-travel
treatment are what stop the escape hatch from being gamed continuously.

**DeLawson's position: physical only.** Error 1× for everyone, no customer decision, no dual
accounting, no cooldown rules, and nothing that depends on whether a customer read the
pricing page. The dual model is worth knowing about as a demonstration that physical billing
is commercially viable — customers accept it — rather than as a pattern to copy.

#### 12.3.2 Prior art: ADLS Gen1 priced per GB and never mentioned compression

The other shipped precedent points the same way, and it is worth being careful about how
much of it is known. Three steps, of decreasing solidity:

| | Standing |
|---|---|
| ADLS Gen1's overview **never mentions compression** | **Cited** — [the archived page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/azure/data-lake-store/data-lake-store-overview), copied into `delawson-notes/reference/` because it is retired and may disappear |
| **Azure lists prices in GB**, and ADLS Gen1 presumably billed the customer the same way | **Guess**, Bob, 2026-08-19 — the general Azure pricing convention, not a recollection of that product's price list |
| So it billed **logical** bytes and kept the compression win | reasoned here, from the two above |

⚠️ **And the unit is the weaker half of the evidence, not the stronger.** A store billing
compressed bytes would also quote a price per GB — "per GB" says nothing about *which* GB. What
carries the argument is the **silence**: §5.12.0's SCOPE paper says Cosmos stores data
compressed, so a product that compresses, charges by the GB, and never mentions compression is
almost certainly not charging for the compressed byte. A provider billing compressed bytes has
to explain compression, because the customer cannot otherwise predict the bill; one billing
logical never has to bring it up.

The page's silence is broad, which weakens the inference a little further — it also says nothing
about consistency, durability, block size or quotas. But **two of two precedents default to
logical**, since §12.3.1's BigQuery offers both and defaults that way too. So DeLawson billing
compressed bytes is the unusual choice, and §12.9's fifth question — whether the billed figure
is reported back, and at what granularity — is live rather than a detail.

⚠️ **And it exposes a hazard that logical pricing is simply immune to.** Under compressed
billing the customer's bill moves when *we* change something: a better codec, a different
compaction schedule, a re-encoding. §10 already records that compaction is a billing event and
that "the schedule directly determines a customer's bill" — under logical billing that sentence
does not exist. Whatever is chosen, the customer must not be able to attribute a bill increase
to a provider decision they did not ask for and cannot see.

#### 12.3.3 What logical pricing costs a store that compresses

**Azure Data Lake Storage charges $0.01 per GB per month for cool data** — **Cited**, read off
[the pricing page](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/pricing/details/storage/data-lake/) by Bob
on 2026-08-19. Prices there are tiered by volume across Hot, Cool, Cold, Archive and Premium,
with separate transaction charges per 10,000 operations, and the page covers **Gen2**. ⚠️ Its
figures are rendered by JavaScript and come back as placeholders to an automated fetch, so this
is a number a person has to re-read rather than one a script can check.

**Turn the crank on it.** At $0.01 per *logical* GB per month, revenue per **physical** GB
depends entirely on properties of the customer's data that the price list never mentions.
**Derived:**

| The customer's data | Physical bytes per logical GB | Revenue per physical GB/month |
|---|---|---|
| compresses 6×, stored in triplicate | ⅙ × 3 = **0.50** | **$0.020** |
| incompressible, stored in triplicate | 1 × 3 = **3.00** | **$0.0033** |
| compresses 6×, 12+4 erasure coded | ⅙ × 1.33 = **0.22** | **$0.045** |
| incompressible, 12+4 erasure coded | **1.33** | **$0.0075** |

⚠️ **Compression alone spreads revenue per physical byte 6×, and the whole table spreads it
13.5× — against §12.1's slack budget of 2×.** The direction is that the customer whose data
compresses pays six times as much per unit of resource actually consumed. Erasure coding makes
it worse rather than better, because it shrinks the physical footprint the logical price is
spread over.

**So the customer's rational move is to compress before storing** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-19):
*"Customers hopefully learn through the network that they need to build their own compression
layer for anything stored there."* Doing so moves them from the first row of that table to the
second, at a sixth of the price per byte they actually occupy.

**Which is §12.1's ADLS Gen1 metadata lesson a second time.** There, not billing metadata taught
users to pile into tiny streams; here, billing logical bytes on a store that compresses teaches
them to compress client-side. Both times the users behave reasonably and the price list is the
thing at fault.

##### 12.3.3.1 DeLawson is already at the endpoint, which answers §12.9's fifth question

**§8.1.4.1 has the client compressing.** So DeLawson arrived, by another route, exactly where
logical pricing drives a customer — and two things follow.

**First, there is no internal compression win to keep.** A logical price list flatters a provider
who compresses privately and pockets the difference; DeLawson gave that up when it moved
compression to the client. Pricing as though the win existed would be pricing something the
design does not have.

**Second, and more useful: the main objection to billing compressed bytes dissolves.** §12.9's
fifth question worries that the billed figure is "compressed size, which the customer cannot
directly control". ⚠️ **But when the client compresses, the customer computed that number** — it
travels in the append, and §17.16 measured the client checking it against the CRC. A customer who
chose the codec and measured the result can predict the bill exactly, which is the property
logical pricing was there to protect.

What stays outside their control is only what the store does *afterwards* — §8.1.4.4's
coalescing, §10's recompression and re-encoding. That is a far smaller surface than "the
compressed size", and it is what §12.9 should actually be asking about.

### 12.4 The rule that follows

> **Every scarce resource must be a billed dimension, or users will arbitrage the free
> one.**

| Resource | Cost driver | Must be billed as |
|---|---|---|
| EN disk | physical bytes × instances × time | **bytes stored** |
| SN RAM | stream records + extent **references** (§12.6.2) | **stream count and extent-reference count** |
| DN storage | object records (§14.2) | **object count** |
| Network and CPU | appends, reads, syncs | **operations** |

⚠️ **§1.2's "95% of cost is disk" must not be read as licence to bill only for disk.** That
figure is an *outcome* of a healthy workload, not an invariant. Bill only for bytes and the
workload shifts until metadata dominates cost — at which point 95% is simply false. The
cost model is a prediction conditional on the billing being right, not a justification for
simplifying it.

The slack in §12.1 is what makes this tractable: dimensions need not be exact, only close
enough that no arbitrage is worth chasing. **The default slack is 2×** (§4.7). Being 30× out
on one workload is fatal, because that is the one users will find — and §12.3 shows the same
2× test is what forces physical billing and per-extent durability metering.

#### 12.4.1 Where the 2× comes from: it is the price of an additive bill

**The 2× is derived, not chosen** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-19), and knowing the derivation says
when it applies:

> "If you bill reads by both seek and scan, you can add `A*seeks + B*scans` to get a bill and
> have A and B so pure-seek and pure-scan is profitable. But that causes double billing at the
> middle where `A*seeks = B*scans`. The 2× slack lets you give a simpler bill (pure addition).
> The 2× is soft."

**The arithmetic.** A read consumes two things that can each saturate a device first — seeks and
scanned bytes — so what a workload really costs is set by whichever binds: `cost ≈ max(seeks/S,
bytes/B)` in units of a whole device. Pick the coefficients so that a pure-seek workload and a
pure-scan workload each pay for the device they occupy, and the bill is `seeks/S + bytes/B`. At
the extremes bill and cost agree exactly. **At the crossover, where the two terms are equal, cost
is ½ and the bill is 1 — an overbill of exactly 2×.** **Derived.**

**So the 2× buys pure addition.** A customer can be handed `A × seeks + B × scans`, see which term
dominates, and act on it. The exact bill would be `max(A × seeks, B × scans)` per request, summed
— which is not much harder to compute but is much harder to explain, cannot be decomposed into
"what did I pay for", and behaves strangely when a customer's mix changes within a billing period.

⚠️ **And it generalizes in a way worth knowing before adding a billed dimension: with an additive
bill over *n* dimensions that can each bind, the worst case is *n*×, not 2×.** The 2 is the count
of dimensions in the formula, not a property of seeks or of bytes. So a third billed dimension in
the same sum widens the required slack to 3×, which is a real argument for keeping the number of
dimensions in any one formula small — and it answers §12.9's sixth question, which asks whether 2×
is right for every dimension: the figure belongs to the *formula*, not to the dimension.

**What makes it soft** is that `max` is only the right cost model when the two resources do not
contend. Seek time and transfer time genuinely add on a spinning disk, where they share one head,
so there the additive bill is nearly exact and the slack is nearly 1×. On a device where IOPS and
bandwidth are closer to independent, `max` is the better model and the full 2× applies. Which
makes the slack a **per-media-class** figure rather than a constant, and something §3's media
tables could eventually carry a measured value for.

#### 12.4.2 Refusing a pathology is cheaper than billing it

**A third way to keep the bill simple: raise an error for pathological usage, so that pathology
never needs a dimension of its own** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-19) — for example disallowing more
than five iterations of `A' = A + B` concatenation.

**This is the dual of §12.4.1 and it is strictly cheaper.** Each dimension added to an additive
bill costs another 1× of slack; a limit costs none, because it removes the case rather than
pricing it. So for any pathology that is **rare, identifiable, and cheap to check at the moment
of the operation**, a limit beats a dimension outright.

**And some pathologies cannot be billed at all.** Repeated derivation is the example: each
`A' = A + B` roughly doubles what the object references, so *n* customer operations can produce
2^*n* of something. No linear price tracks an exponential, so there is no coefficient that makes
the bill both fair at *n* = 1 and survivable at *n* = 60. A limit is not the cheap option there,
it is the only one.

⚠️ **The design already uses this technique elsewhere without naming it.** §5.1.1.1 forbids an
alias pointing into a tree that contains aliases — so cycles are impossible rather than detected,
and no traversal anywhere needs a visited set or a depth bound. Same shape: refuse the pathology
once, at one place, and every later mechanism gets to assume it away. §6's size limits are the
same move again, which is why extent sizing arithmetic works at all.

**What it costs, and it is not nothing:**

- ⚠️ **A limit is a compatibility commitment.** Raising one later is easy; lowering it breaks
  users. So it has to be generous enough never to catch legitimate use and tight enough to
  exclude the pathology — and if those two ranges are not clearly separated, a limit is the
  wrong instrument and the thing really does need metering.
- **It should be a feature parameter** (§13.2.5), so it can be moved without a deploy, and any
  limit a full ring must agree on is read by the primary and sent.
- ⚠️ **The check has to be designed in, not added later.** "More than five iterations" is only
  answerable if an object carries its **derivation depth** — a small counter that a concatenate
  sets to `max(depth(A), depth(B)) + 1`. One byte in the object record, and it is unrecoverable
  retroactively: an object made before the counter existed has no depth to compare.

**The error is also the better teacher.** §12.1's ADLS Gen1 story is a lesson in how users learn
from a price list, and an invoice is slow feedback that arrives once a month at somebody who did
not write the code. A refusal arrives at the caller, in the failing request, with the limit named.

#### 12.4.3 A base charge that dominates the pathology is the other way to avoid a dimension

§12.4.2 removes a pathology by refusing it. **The other move is to absorb it: set a floor charge
high enough that the pathological case is already paid for** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-19) —
*"making sure base tenant cost is greater than the cost of a single object… then you don't have
to charge separately for the constraint that streams can't combine multiple tenants."*

**The constraint in question is §11's**: a stream holds one tenant's data (§5.1.2 and #75), which
means a tenant storing one tiny object still occupies a stream, an extent, and instances of that
extent. Under per-byte billing that tenant pays nearly nothing and costs a fixed amount, which is
§12.2's whole argument arriving at the smallest possible scale.

**And the exposure is exactly one object's worth, which is why a flat charge closes it.** Lumping
(§11, §4.6.5) puts a tenant's *later* small objects into common streams they already own, so
single-tenancy only bites at the **first** object. The floor is therefore per tenant, not per
object — a number that a base charge can dominate outright, where a per-object overhead could not.

**What that number is made of is metadata, not bytes**: an object record, a stream record, an
extent record and its instances — order a kilobyte of the RAM-resident state §14.1 budgets, which
§12.7 prices far above disk. So the base charge is computed from §14's budgets rather than from
the customer's data, and in absolute terms it is small.

**Three techniques, then, for keeping a bill short**, and only the first costs slack:

| | Costs |
|---|---|
| add a billed dimension | ⚠️ another 1× of slack (§12.4.1) |
| refuse the pathology (§12.4.2) | a compatibility commitment, and a check designed in from the start |
| **a base charge that exceeds it** | ⚠️ a higher entry price for everyone |

⚠️ **That last cost pulls against §12.1.0's adoption argument** — the whole point of passing
savings on is being easier to choose, and a floor charge is the one price a prospective user meets
first. The mitigation is that it only has to exceed *one object's* cost rather than anything
proportional, so it can be small enough not to deter, and it is worth checking that it stays that
way rather than becoming a general-purpose revenue floor.

### 12.5 What the design already makes visible

- **Compression works for the customer, not just the fleet.** Ratio divides the bill, which
  is why compression must precede encryption (§7) and why shrinking compression blocks for
  index density is not a free trade (§7.1).
- **Sealing and EC cut the bill ~2.7×** (4 replicas → 8+4), so the latency between sealing
  and successful encoding is money. That needs an explicit target and a decision about who
  absorbs the cost of the gap.
- **Compaction reclaims billable bytes**, so the compaction schedule sets part of the bill —
  as does the DN→SN sync cadence, since each missed delete leaks an orphan stream pinning
  ~1.74 PB (§13.1.8).
- **Lumping tiny objects into common streams** (§11) is what makes the small-object case
  billable at all: without it every tiny object would carry a full stream's metadata cost,
  which is precisely the ADLS Gen1 failure reappearing from the object side rather than the
  stream side.
- **Metering must be per-object over time** — bytes × instances × duration, plus the counts
  above — surviving failures and double-counting nothing during repair, re-encoding, and
  compaction, where old and new bases briefly coexist.
- **The billed quantity is a lazy summary.** By §4.5, physical byte totals change anywhere
  in the tree and so are maintained lazily by the background loops of §13.3 — the exact,
  synchronous summary is the unkeyed record count, which nobody is billed for. Billing
  therefore reads an eventually-consistent figure. Tolerable for metering integrated over a
  month; it means a customer's *instantaneous* usage query is either stale or must be
  answered by summing live extent totals on the SNs on demand.

### 12.6 A complex model, presented simply

Closing every arbitrage means many billed dimensions (§12.4), and many dimensions mean a
bill nobody wants to read. Those are separable problems: **the model is complex, the
presentation need not be.**

A bill is a **sum of charges**. A summary shows **the top few charges plus "everything
else"**, and collapses the tail only when that tail is below **1% of the total**. Precisely:

> Sort the charges descending and show the **smallest prefix whose complement sums to under
> 1%**.

The "sums to" matters. Collapsing every *individual* item under 1% would let twenty
half-percent charges vanish into a tenth of the bill — the threshold has to apply to the
remainder as a whole, not item by item.

#### 12.6.1 It adapts to the workload, which makes it diagnostic

The point is that the same rule produces a one-line bill for ordinary use and an itemized
one for strange use, without anybody choosing which. Extent references are the example:
usually negligible, dominant if you do something weird.

Take 1 PB of erasure-coded data, illustratively:

| | Stored bytes | Extent references | Summary |
|---|---|---|---|
| Normal workload | 99.96% | 0.04% | **1 line item** + everything else at 0.04% |
| Same data, cloned 1000× | 71.6% | **28.4%** | **2 line items** |

The clone adds no bytes at all — every extent is shared (§4.6.1) — but multiplies extent
references a thousandfold, and references are what consume SN memory. So the cost appears
from nowhere as far as stored volume is concerned, and the bill surfaces it automatically
the moment it matters.

That is a **diagnostic** property, not merely a cosmetic one. A customer who accidentally
builds a pathological workload learns it from their own bill, in the line item that names
the mechanism, rather than from a support conversation weeks later. And a dimension that is
invisible in the common case cannot be quietly forgotten by whoever implements the meter,
because the summary rule will expose it as soon as some customer finds it.

#### 12.6.2 The cost driver is extent *references*, not extents

Worth making explicit, since it is what the example turns on. An extent shared by *n*
streams has **one** extent record but ***n*** entries in ***n*** extent lists, and it is the
list entries that occupy SN memory. So:

> SN memory ∝ stream records + **extent references**

§14.1 counts "extent records" and is right only because §4.7 assumes one reference per
extent. Under heavy sharing the two diverge without limit, and it is references that must be
metered and that bound a stream. The §15.1 self-concatenation test is the extreme case —
2^31 references to a single 32 MB extent — which is a useful consistency check: **the
workload that stresses the system hardest is also the one the billing model charges most
heavily for.** If those two ever disagreed, one of them would be wrong.

#### 12.6.3 Sharing divides the charge among billed references

Sharing sealed extents (§4.6.1, §13.4.5.5) means **refcounts that cross tenants**, so a rule is needed
(Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-16):

> **charge per billed reference = extent cost / number of billed references**

Two tenants sharing an extent each pay half. **Total charged equals total cost exactly** — not within §12.1's 2x
slack but exactly — which is what makes it the only cost-proportional option:

| Alternative | Failure |
|---|---|
| Charge every referrer in full | over-bills by *n*; breaks §12.1's slack for *n* > 2 |
| Charge only the creating referrer | the creator subsidizes everyone, and their delete leaves nobody paying |
| Charge nobody until sharing resolves | loses revenue, and sharing may never resolve |

**It is not exploitable**, which is worth checking since §12.2 exists because of an exploit. Creating a thousand
dummy tenants to reference your data divides your share by a thousand and creates a thousand shares of the same
size, so an attacker who owns all of them pays exactly what they paid before. **Total revenue is invariant under
any regrouping of references.**

##### 12.6.3.1 Only the shared cost divides

This is the refinement §12.6.2 forces, and getting it wrong would under-bill sharing badly. An extent shared by
*n* streams has **one** extent record and ***n*** list entries. So:

| Cost component | Divided? |
|---|---|
| The extent's physical bytes on disk | **yes**, by the number of billed references |
| **Each reference's own SN-memory entry** | **no** — every sharer has its own, and pays for it in full |

**Derived.** So the charge is `(extent disk cost / n) + (own reference's metadata cost)`, and since §12.2 prices
SN memory at ~5,000x disk per byte, the second term is not a rounding error. Sharing an extent does not share the
reference to it — which is exactly §12.6.2's point, and it means heavy sharing reduces a tenant's *byte* charges
while raising the fleet's *metadata* charges. The §15.1 self-concatenation case is the limit: 2^31 references
paying 1/2^31 of one extent's disk cost each, plus full price for 2^31 references.

##### 12.6.3.2 The denominator moves, and two consequences follow

⚠️ **A tenant's bill depends on strangers' behaviour.** When someone else copies an object that shares your
extents your bill falls; when they delete, it rises. Total revenue is invariant so this is not a correctness
problem, but it is a **predictability** problem, and §12.6's simple presentation has to survive a customer asking
why their bill moved when they changed nothing. Not resolved here.

**And a co-tenant's delete raises your bill**, which also means "delete to save money" works less well than
expected under sharing — §8.4.1's deferred decrement frees nothing until the last reference goes.

**Billing must integrate over a changing denominator**, piecewise rather than by sampling. §12.8's daily snapshots
would get the denominator wrong for part of any day in which sharing changed — but §12.8.2 already retains
creation and deletion seconds for references, so the denominator at any instant is **computable exactly** from
reference lifetimes rather than sampled. That is the same mechanism that made daily existence-sampling exact, used
a second time.

#### 12.6.4 Unbilled references, and orphans as a bug signal

**Not every reference is billed.** System data — DN metadata, §13.5's snapshots, the bootstrap chain — holds
references that belong to no tenant. An extent whose references are all unbilled has **no** billed references, so
nobody is charged and the cost is real: it lands in §12.7's chain as system overhead, where §12.7's ~58%
space-efficiency figure already accounts for its kind. **Billing must track that cost rather than ignoring it**,
or the price per byte sold is understated.

**An extent with *zero* references of any kind is orphaned, and should not exist.** §8.4.1's refcount reaching
zero is what triggers reclamation, so an orphan means the decrement was lost or the reclaim never ran.

> **Orphaned data is a bug signal, not a billing category.** Its bytes must be counted, and its existence must
> raise an alarm.

**And the billing job is the orphan detector, for free.** Computing per-reference charges requires enumerating
every reference to every extent — which is precisely the sweep that finds extents with no references at all. So
§13.5's job gains a correctness check as a by-product of a revenue calculation, with no extra pass. That is the
same fusion argument as §13.1.10's verification riding the instance sync, and it is worth making explicit because
the two jobs would otherwise be written by different people at different times.

### 12.7 From raw disk to a price per byte

The 95% of §1.2 is about cost composition. **Space efficiency is a separate and much larger effect**,
and pricing has to account for it: the bytes you sell are far fewer than the bytes you buy.

| Stage | Factor | Cumulative |
|---|---|---|
| Purchased raw disk | — | 100% |
| Installed — bought a year before use, ~10-year life | ×0.90 | 90% |
| Powered and healthy — some fraction always down | ×0.95 | 85.5% |
| Net of system metadata, historical copies, and analysis of it | ×0.90 | 77% |
| Filled to target | ×0.80 | 61.6% |
| Net of undeletable garbage | ×0.95 | **58.5%** |

**Guesses**, all of them, per §0 — but the shape is what matters: **only about 58% of purchased disk
bytes are billable.** At 10% of disks down rather than 5% it is 55%.

Two of these deserve comment:

- **Undeletable garbage** is structural, not sloppiness. An erasure-coded extent with some records
  deleted and others live cannot shed the dead ones without a rewrite; a stream lumping many small
  objects (§11) cannot release one object's space until compaction. ~5% is a guess, and it is the term
  most under the design's control — but **not via compaction or extent size.** §8.5 shows the lever is
  **declared expiry**: group data by when it dies and extents die whole, taking this term toward zero.
  Extent size moves it only 1.4× across its entire plausible range.
- **Soft-deleted data is not in this table at all**, because it is **billed** (§8.4.1). It occupies
  space and earns revenue, so it is neither overhead nor waste. It does still consume the repair
  reserve (§8.4.3), which is a durability constraint rather than an efficiency one.

#### 12.7.1 Setting the price

**Asserted** (Bob): aim for usable disks ~80% full, but **price to be profitable at 66% full**, and
target billing at ~**1.2× costs** on average. Underbilling is fatal, overbilling is survivable, and
the surplus funds capacity growth and the people who keep it running.

Pricing on the conservative fill gives a billable fraction of 48.2% rather than 58.5%, so:

> price per billable byte = 1.2 × (1 / 0.95) ÷ 0.482 ≈ **2.6 × the raw disk cost per byte**

| | Multiple of raw disk cost |
|---|---|
| Total hardware cost | 1.05× |
| Revenue at the 80% fill target | 1.53× |
| **Realized margin** | **1.45×** |

So the stated 1.2× becomes ~1.45× in practice, because pricing assumes 66% fill while operations aim
at 80%. That gap is deliberate headroom, not optimism: it absorbs the guesses above being wrong in the
unfavourable direction, and every factor in the efficiency chain is a guess.

The useful thing to carry away is the **2.6×**. It is the bridge between §1.2's cost model and §12's
price list, and it means a customer's per-byte price is dominated not by disk cost but by everything
between a purchased disk and a billable byte.

### 12.7.2 A worked cost, in dollars per GB-month

**Inputs**, all current market figures rather than guesses: a 20 TB HDD at **$923**, 10-year life, **16 W**
kept busy continuously, at **$0.27/kWh** covering electricity and rent together.

| One disk over 10 years | |
|---|---|
| Capital | $923.00 |
| Electricity and rent | $378.69 |
| **Total** | **$1,301.69** — 29% of it is power and rent |
| Per month | $10.85 |
| **Per raw TB-month** | **$0.542** |

Applying §12.7's efficiency chain (58.5% billable) and the 5% non-disk hardware:

> **cost = $0.98 per physical TB-month**

and pricing on the conservative 66% fill with the 1.2× margin of §12.7.1 gives **$1.42 per physical
TB-month** — the 2.62× factor that section derives, arrived at independently here.

| Scheme | Overhead | Cost $/TB-mo | Price $/TB-mo | Price $/GB-mo |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4-instance replication | 4.000× | 3.90 | **5.68** | 0.00568 |
| EC 2.333× — always available and reliable | 2.333× | 2.28 | **3.31** | 0.00331 |
| EC 1.333× — usually available, always reliable | 1.333× | 1.30 | **1.89** | 0.00189 |

#### 12.7.2.1 What the two EC tiers actually are

An earlier draft guessed these were Reed-Solomon 3+4 and 12+4. They are not — they are **one LRC and a
two-instance variant of it**, which behaves quite differently.

**The 1.333× code is an LRC shaped as a 10 × 6 matrix:**

| | Count | Placement |
|---|---|---|
| Data extents | **45** | rows 1–5 × columns 1–9 |
| Global parities | **5** | column 10, rows 1–5 |
| Local parities | **10** | row 6, one per column |
| **Total** | **60** | overhead 60/45 = **1.333×** |

Each column is a local group of six, so a single loss is repaired by reading the other five: **5 reads +
1 write = ~6 operations per recovery.**

**The 2.333× code is the same thing with the data extents duplicated:** 2 × 45 + 5 + 10 = **105**, overhead
2.333×. Repair gets much cheaper, because a lost data extent is now a copy rather than a reconstruction —
1 read + 1 write. Averaged over the 90 data instances and 15 parities that is **~2.4 operations per
recovery**, against 6.

#### 12.7.2.1a Why one takes days and the other minutes

The operational gap after losing a tenth of the cluster is not 2.5× — it is about three orders of magnitude:

| | Time until affected data is readable again |
|---|---|
| 1.333× | **days** |
| 2.333× | **minutes** |

Repair traffic does not explain that, and the reason it does not is the interesting part. **The
two-instance variant does not need to repair before it can serve reads.** The surviving instance of each
data extent is immediately readable, so restoring availability is a matter of re-pointing reads; the
reconstruction that restores *durability* then proceeds in the background with nobody waiting on it.

The 1.333× code has no such luxury. A lost data extent has no surviving copy, so it must be reconstructed
from its column *before the first read of it can be answered* — which puts the whole multi-day repair on
the critical path for availability.

So this is §1.1's separation of availability from reliability turning up as **two recovery timescales**:

| | Availability restored | Durability restored |
|---|---|---|
| 1.333× | days — coupled to repair | days |
| 2.333× | **minutes — decoupled** | days, in the background |

Which is a better justification for the extra 1× of overhead than "more copies." **What the second instance
buys is not durability but the removal of repair from the read path.** That is also the honest content of
"always available" versus "usually available" — much sharper than a fragment-count comparison.

⚠️ Two caveats. The LRC's *guaranteed* disaster tolerance is bounded by the Gopalan Singleton-like bound —
*d* ≤ *n* − *k* − ⌈*k*/*r*⌉ + 2 = 8, so at most 7 arbitrary erasures, **11.7% of fragments** against the 25%
an MDS code of the same overhead would give (§4.3.3). The 10%-outage case is therefore *just* inside the
guarantee, which is tighter than it looks. And "minutes" assumes hot data — the re-pointing is cheap, but a
tenth of the cluster's worth of metadata still has to be updated to reflect the new instance locations.

#### 12.7.2.2 Sanity check against the market

⚠️ An earlier draft compared these tiers to Glacier Deep Archive and GCS Coldline. **That comparison is
unfair to DeLawson**, because those tiers buy their price with retrieval latency, retrieval fees, and
minimum storage durations. **This is warm data, not cold data:**

| | Read behaviour |
|---|---|
| **EC 1.333×** | usually **100% readable immediately at HDD speed** — the exception being while recovering from a major outage (§12.7.2.1a) |
| **EC 2.333×** | **almost always** 100% readable immediately at HDD speed |

So the right comparison set is providers that also serve reads immediately:

| | $/TB-month | |
|---|---|---|
| **DeLawson EC 1.333×** | **1.89** | usually immediate, HDD speed |
| **DeLawson EC 2.333×** | **3.31** | almost always immediate, HDD speed |
| **DeLawson 4-instance** | **5.68** | immediate |
| Backblaze B2 | 6.00 | immediate; egress free to 3× storage |
| Wasabi | 6.99 | immediate; no egress fee, 90-day minimum |
| S3 Standard-IA | 12.50 | immediate; retrieval fee, 30-day minimum |
| Cloudflare R2 | 15.00 | immediate; no egress fee |
| GCS Standard | 20.00 | immediate |
| S3 Standard | 23.00 | immediate; no minimum, no retrieval fee |

Against the cheapest immediate-read incumbent, B2 at $6:

| | vs B2 | vs S3 Standard |
|---|---|---|
| EC 1.333× | **3.2× cheaper** | 12.2× |
| EC 2.333× | **1.8× cheaper** | 6.9× |
| 4-instance | 1.06× — parity | 4.0× |

⚠️ **Treat that as a question, not a boast.** Undercutting the cheapest incumbent threefold is either a real
advantage or a sign the cost model is optimistic, and since every factor in §12.7's efficiency chain is a
guess, the second deserves weight. Two specifics: B2 reportedly runs a wider Reed-Solomon code with *lower*
storage overhead than 1.333×, so the advantage cannot be coming from the code — it would have to come from
disk density (§5.3.1's 150 disks per server) and cost discipline. And these are list prices; negotiated
large-customer pricing is lower, so the real gap is smaller than the table.

**If SSD latency and throughput are wanted, that is a different product at a different price.** Device class
is already a per-extent property (§9.3), so the design accommodates it without change. On media capital
alone — $46/TB for these HDDs against roughly $60/TB for QLC or $120/TB for enterprise NVMe — the same tiers
would land near $2.50–$7.40 or $4.90–$14.80 per TB-month, before accounting for the very different power,
density and endurance profiles. **HDD is the default because §1.4 wants throughput per dollar, not latency.**

### 12.8 Billing runs offline, over snapshots

**Billing is a job over the snapshotted metadata of §13.5. It does not read DN, SN, or EN metadata
directly** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-15).

The decisive reason is **reproducibility**: a disputed invoice must recompute to the same number, which
requires an immutable, retained input. Walking live metadata gives a bill with no well-defined instant,
non-reproducible by construction. It would also put a full-fleet aggregation over ~6x10^10 extents on the
serving path once a day.

#### 12.8.1 Retain outputs for years, inputs for weeks

Billing retention is set by the dispute and audit window, which is far longer than §13.5's few weeks — but
weekly samples cannot reproduce a *daily* charge, and extending daily snapshot retention to cover an audit
period would be expensive. The bill and its per-object intermediate aggregates are orders of magnitude
smaller than the metadata they came from, so: **keep computed charges and intermediates for years, raw
snapshots for weeks**, and answer old disputes from the retained aggregates rather than by recomputation.

That also decides what the intermediates must contain — otherwise discovered during the first dispute.

#### 12.8.2 Daily sampling is not integration, and soft delete is what closes the gap

Metering storage from a daily snapshot would make an object created and deleted between two snapshots
**free**, and timed create/delete cycles are then unbounded abuse — exactly the failure mode §12.1 exists
to prevent.

**§8.4.1b's three-day soft-delete window is longer than the one-day snapshot interval**, so anything that
lived and died between snapshots is still present as soft-deleted in the next one, carrying a creation
second (§4.6.3) and a deletion timestamp. Byte-seconds are therefore **exactly computable, not sampled**.
Soft delete, built for disaster heroics, is what makes daily billing exact.

**Except for the opt-out.** §8.4's per-object opt-out hard-deletes immediately, and such an object can slip
entirely between snapshots. So **opting out of soft delete must not opt out of a minimal billing
tombstone** — id, physical size, creation second, deletion second, durability class, media class — retained
until the next snapshot. A few dozen bytes. Without it, the opt-out added for users with one-day data is
also a free-storage exploit.

#### 12.8.3 Billing is offline and exact; quota is online and approximate

These will be conflated. A spend cap or capacity quota cannot run off a snapshot, since a tenant can blow
through it within a day, so enforcement needs a live, cheap, deliberately inexact mechanism — documented as
**not** the billing path. Both are needed and neither substitutes for the other.

#### 12.8.4 The job runs on Compute, and DN inlines tiny objects

⚠️ That combination is a §1.5 problem. §11 inlines small object bodies in DN metadata, so a DN metadata
snapshot puts **plaintext user data** into a file that Compute jobs read — and Compute is where user code
runs. Billing needs only the *length* of those bodies.

So the snapshot must either exclude inline bodies or keep them encrypted under a key Compute does not hold.
Worth catching before implementation, because "snapshot the DN metadata" is the obvious approach and it
quietly moves user data across the one boundary the design says must never be crossed.

### 12.9 Open policy questions

1. Do customers pay for **uncompacted garbage** they created by overwriting, when DeLawson
   chooses the compaction schedule?
2. Do they pay for the **transient double footprint** during compaction and re-encoding?
3. How are **shared streams and extents** attributed between a clone and its original
   (§4.6.1)? Charging both double-bills; charging neither loses revenue.
4. How are **packed objects** attributed (§11)?
5. Is the billed figure — compressed size, which the customer cannot directly control —
   reported back to them, and at what granularity?
6. Whether **2× slack** (§4.7) is right for every dimension, or whether some — network,
   operations — can tolerate more.

Note question 3 in the old list — whether metadata is billed — is no longer open. It must
be (§12.3).

---

## 13. Consistency, membership, and failure

- **Durability** on write comes from replicating an append block to all open
  instances on their ENs before acknowledging. Sealing is the commit point that
  fixes content.
- **EN failure on an open extent**: seal the extent short and open a new one.
  This removes replica repair from the write path entirely, and is cheap
  precisely because §6 makes extent size variable anyway.
- **EN failure on a sealed extent**: background fragment reconstruction over
  ciphertext, never blocking a write, never needing keys.
- **SN or DN member failure**: absorbed by the ring (§5.7), but the cost depends on
  *which* member. Losing a log-only member costs a vote. Losing the primary
  triggers switchover, cheap if scheduled or if the hot backup takes over (§5.7.1).
  Losing the hot backup is the one that quietly matters — it removes the cheap
  switchover path until a replacement is materialized, so restoring it should be
  prompt rather than lazy.
- **Loss of a whole SN ring**: the streams it served are unaddressable even with
  every EN healthy. This is now the worst failure in the design, and §5.6 exists
  precisely to make it improbable — a ring is only as independent as its
  placement. The recovery path is scanning ENs for self-describing extents (§5.2).
- **Loss of a whole DN ring**: worse, because of self-hosting (§5.5.3) — recovery
  must start from the bootstrap root and rebuild the metadata tier first.

⚠️ How a stream is reassigned from a failed ring to a fresh one, and how cluster
membership and domain topology are themselves distributed, are undesigned. Note
the topology is not static: §5.6 depends on knowing the domain hierarchy, so that
hierarchy is itself critical configuration that has to live somewhere reliable —
plausibly the bootstrap root (§5.5.1).

### 13.1 Sync loops

Reality diverges from metadata, and three loops reconcile it. Their cadences differ by
five orders of magnitude, and the principle behind that is worth stating:

> **Sync frequency follows the rate at which reality can diverge, not the importance of
> the data.**

| Loop | Cadence | Volume per sweep | Why that cadence |
|---|---|---|---|
| SN → EN, **disk state** | **~1 minute** | ~1 MB (16 KB/s) | Disks go up and down constantly, and placement needs fresh free-space figures (§13.1.1) |
| SN → EN, **instance state** | **~1 hour** | ~46 GB (13 MB/s) | Individual instances vanishing or corrupting is far rarer than a disk cycling |
| DN → SN | **a day to a month** | ~156 MB (1.8 KB/s daily) | No hardware failure can make a DN's view of a stream wrong; cost is set by distinct streams, not objects (§13.1.3) |

All are **driven by the upper tier** — the SN asks the EN, the DN asks the SN. The tier
holding the metadata is the one that knows what ought to exist.

#### 13.1.1 Why the fast loop carries disks, not instances

The two SN→EN loops differ by the size of what they enumerate, and the gap is enormous:
an SN reaching 407 ENs sees ~61,000 disks but drives ~2.3 × 10^9 instances — **37,000
instances per disk.**

| Per-minute sweep of | Volume | Rate |
|---|---|---|
| all disks | ~1 MB | **16 KB/s** — trivial |
| all instances | ~46 GB | **760 MB/s** — out of the question |

So the once-a-minute message carries **disk-level state only**: up or down, and free
bytes. Instance enumeration moves to the hourly loop, where the same 46 GB is 13 MB/s.

**What the fast twitch is for is replication — replacing instances that have gone
missing.** When a disk goes down, the instances on it are no longer protecting anything,
and §4.3.1's reliability figure is explicitly *per window between an instance being lost
and being replaced*. Shortening that window is the whole point.

How much window there is to spend depends on disk failure rates, since the assumed
`p_gone` = 10^-4 is just window ÷ mean time to failure:

| Disk AFR | MTTF | Repair-window budget | Consumed by 1-minute detection |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1.5% | 67 yr | 58 hours | 0.03% |
| 5% | 20 yr | 17.5 hours | 0.10% |
| 10% | 10 yr | 8.8 hours | 0.19% |

So detection is nearly free against a budget measured in hours. It is not *instant*, though:
with a 20-second timeout, a dead disk is known 20 seconds after the fact at best, and ~80
seconds at worst if a probe is missed first — 0.25% of even the tightest repair budget. What
actually consumes the window is moving the data: re-replicating a failed 20 TB disk needs 1.4 GB/s aggregate
to finish in 4 hours, or 0.23 GB/s in a day — spread across the fan-out, either is
comfortable.

Which raises the obvious question: if the budget is hours, why detect in a minute? Because
detection feeds three different reactions on different timescales:

| Reaction | When | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Stop directing reads there | immediately | a dead disk costs read latency, not durability |
| Stop placing new instances there | immediately | otherwise appends fail |
| Begin re-replication | **after a delay** | most down disks come back, and re-replicating one costs 20 TB of traffic |

**Detect fast, react slowly.** Since disks cycling up and down is routine (far more common
than an instance actually disappearing), the expensive reaction has to wait out the
transient while the cheap reactions happen at once. A loop that detected slowly could not
separate the two.

#### 13.1.2 There is no rebalancing

Worth stating flatly, because most storage systems have a rebalancer and this one does not:
**data is never moved to even out utilization.** The only bulk movement is when an EN is
removed from the system, and that is decommissioning rather than balancing.

Nothing accumulates that would need correcting. Free-space-weighted placement (§5.6.3) is
*prospective* — it directs new writes to where there is room, and §5.6.3 shows that is the
unique allocation which exhausts all disks simultaneously. Imbalance never builds up, so
there is nothing to go back and fix. The self-balancing of §5.6.4 is balance by *steering
writes*, not by relocating bytes.

§5.11 generalizes this to every tier, including what happens when one actually fills.

That absence is a large simplification: no rebalancer to schedule, to rate-limit against
foreground traffic, or to reason about interacting with repair and compaction.

⚠️ **The claim covers space, not load.** Colossus has a disk-space-balancing custodian
(§1.4.4), which suggests prospective placement is not the whole story. The gap is probably
**read hot spots**: a constantly-read extent makes its instances' disks hot regardless of
fullness, and free-space weighting is blind to that. The natural remedy is *adding* instances
to hot extents rather than moving anything, which would preserve "no relocation" while
admitting that "no rebalancing" was too strong.

The cadence also has to match **the SN's own scan of its extents**, ideally once a
minute and once every five minutes at worst, since a stale free-space table is useless if
nothing consults it. That scan is memory-bandwidth bound, not I/O bound:

| Scanned | In 1 minute | In 5 minutes |
|---|---|---|
| the SN's primary share, 5.7 × 10^8 records | 0.95 GB/s | 0.19 GB/s |
| all roles, 1.7 × 10^9 records | 2.85 GB/s | 0.57 GB/s |

Comfortable on a modern machine — but only because records are compact and laid out for
sequential access (§4.4). At 100 B per record a full scan walks 57–171 GB of memory;
pointer-chasing through a structure that size would not finish in a minute. **The scan
