cadence is what makes the record-size budget and the list-shaped layout load-bearing**,
not merely tidy.

#### 13.1.3 DN → SN is about streams, not objects

**The DN sync enumerates the streams a DN references, not its objects.** That distinction
is what makes the loop cheap, because **tiny objects are lumped together into common
streams** (§11) — so the number of distinct streams a DN references is far smaller than
its object count.

| Objects per DN | Objects per stream | Distinct streams | Sweep | Daily |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 10^12 | 1 (large objects) | 10^12 | 20 TB | 232 MB/s |
| 10^12 | 1,000 | 10^9 | 20 GB | 232 KB/s |
| 10^12 | 128,000 | 7.8 × 10^6 | **156 MB** | **1.8 KB/s** |

A 128 MB average stream (§14.1.1) holding kilobyte objects lumps ~128,000 of them, so the
bottom row is the expected case: a sweep of a couple of hundred megabytes, trivial at any
cadence. An earlier draft of this section costed the sweep at object granularity and
concluded the cadence was limited by DN paging bandwidth. That was wrong by up to five
orders of magnitude.

⚠️ **This only holds if the DN maintains a set of referenced streams.** Deriving that set
by reading every object's metadata would put the object count back on the critical path
and restore the 300 TB figure. So the DN needs its referenced-stream set as durable state
alongside the objects, which is a requirement rather than an optimization.

So why is the cadence still a day to a month rather than a minute? Not cost — §13.1.6 gives
the reason: nothing this loop guards against happens on a fast timescale, because no
hardware failure can make a DN's view of a stream wrong. The cadence is set by how much
orphan leakage is tolerable (§13.1.8), not by what the sweep costs.

#### 13.1.4 One message per pair, driven from above

**Sync is per pair — SN/EN, DN/SN — not per disk or per object.** One message covers
the whole pair and is *internally* structured by the substructure below it. That keeps
the message count proportional to the fan-out (§5.10) rather than to fan-out × disks,
which at 150 disks per EN is a 150-fold difference in chatter for no gain.

**The upper tier drives.** The SN asks the EN; the DN asks the SN. The tier holding the
metadata is the one that knows what ought to exist.

#### 13.1.5 Cold sync bucketing, negotiated

A cold sync enumerates everything, and one message may not hold it. Bucketing differs
between the two pairs, because only one of them has a natural substructure to split on:

| | SN → EN | DN → SN |
|---|---|---|
| Step 1 | one message | one message |
| Step 2 | **sets of disks** — a real substructure of the EN | — |
| Step 3 | **hash within a disk** | **hash of `StreamId`** |

An earlier draft claimed a neat parallel here, with objects grouping a DN's streams the way
disks group an EN's instances. That was wrong: the DN sync is about streams, and tiny
objects *share* streams (§13.1.3), so objects are not a partition of the stream set at all.
DN → SN has no physical middle level and buckets straight by hash.

How much splitting each needs:

- **SN → EN.** An SN drives ~2.3 × 10^9 instances (§5.10.1); at a 3 PB EN with *G*=16 that
  is ~5.6 million per pair, **~112 MB** at 20 B each. One whole 20 TB disk digests to
  ~12 MB, so a pair reaches step 3 only when the SN owns a large fraction of one disk — a
  low sharing factor or unusually large disks. At *G*=16 the per-disk share is ~0.75 MB and
  step 2 suffices.
- **DN → SN.** With lumping, a DN's whole sweep is on the order of 156 MB (§13.1.3) spread
  across its SNs, so most pairs fit in one message and hash buckets are needed only for the
  largest.

**Bucket count is negotiated, and only upward:**

- The **upper tier estimates** the bucket count from what it knows — it has the count
  already, so the estimate is free and usually right.
- The **lower tier may raise it in its first response** if that estimate is too low, and
  the upper tier retries with the larger count.

The asymmetry is the interesting part, and it is not arbitrary. The lower tier may
legitimately hold *more* than the upper tier knows about — orphans, which are a large part
of what the sync is for (§13.1.8) — so only it can discover the estimate was short.
Allowing increases only makes the negotiation monotonic and terminating: at worst one extra
round trip, with no possibility of two parties oscillating between sizes.

#### 13.1.6 What each sync is actually for

The two loops have different centres of gravity, and it is worth being precise because
an earlier draft of this section had the DN→SN emphasis backwards.

**DN → SN is mostly about confirming deletes.** Its dominant job is assuring that the SN
really did delete the streams the DN told it to. That is the common case and the
expensive one.

**An orphan stream wastes space permanently**, and the leak is far larger than the
record itself. Nothing else in the system will ever notice it:

- no DN asks about it, because no object references it;
- the SN cannot tell it is unreferenced — it just holds a stream record;
- and its extents still carry a reference from it (§4.6.1), so extent reclamation will
  not touch them either.

So an orphan stream **pins everything beneath it forever**. A 200-byte leaked stream
record at the §14.1 stream size holds down ~1.3 × 10^7 extents, four instances each:
**~1.74 PB of disk, pinned by 200 bytes of metadata** — a leverage ratio of ~10^13.
That is the whole justification for the loop existing, and it is why "quite slow" must
still mean "reliably completes".

#### 13.1.7 Why there are exactly two sync loops

Because **only cross-tier references can drift.** Within one tier a Raft ring makes
updates atomic, so its internal references are consistent by construction; across a
tier boundary there is a message that can be lost.

| Reference | Crosses a tier? | Can drift? | Sync loop |
|---|---|---|---|
| **range** → stream (§5.11.3.4) | DN → SN | **yes** | DN → SN |
| stream → extent | inside one SN ring | no — atomic under Raft | none needed |
| extent → instance | SN → EN | **yes** | SN → EN |

That is the complete explanation for the loop inventory: one per tier boundary, and none
in the middle. It also reframes reference counts — **a refcount is a cache of a truth
held by the referrer**, and where the referrer is in another tier, the cache can be
wrong. The sync is what reconciles it.

#### 13.1.8 Divergence runs in both directions

| Divergence | Meaning | Action |
|---|---|---|
| SN holds a stream no DN references | **orphan stream** — a failed delete or abandoned create | reclaim; this is the common case (§13.1.6) |
| EN holds an instance the SN never mentions | **orphan instance** — a failed delete, an abandoned write, or state a ring lost and rebuilt | reclaim the space |
| SN expects an instance the EN lacks | lost to disk failure or corruption | repair — re-replicate or reconstruct |
| DN references a stream the SN lacks | **data loss**, not mere unavailability — the ring was the sole authority | escalate; nothing routine fixes this |

The last row is rare rather than routine: it needs a whole ring to lose state, which
§5.6 exists to prevent. But it is the one divergence with no remedy, so the loop should
raise an alarm rather than attempt a repair.

⚠️ **Deleting on the strength of one DN's silence is dangerous, and sharing makes it
worse.** Streams may be referenced by objects on *different* DNs (§4.6.1), so one DN
failing to mention a stream does not mean nobody references it. A wrong deletion here is
unrecoverable — it destroys live customer data — so the safe forms are:

1. **Each stream records an owning DN**, the single authority for its reference set, and
   only that DN's sync may authorize deletion. Cross-DN sharing then means a shared
   stream still has one home.
2. Or the SN must hear from *every* DN that could reference the stream before deleting,
   which is a quorum problem across an unbounded set.

(1) is much the simpler, and it is the recommendation, but it constrains how stream
sharing works and needs settling alongside §4.6.1.

#### 13.1.9 Warm sync and cold sweeps

Cold sync is the full enumeration above. **Warm sync covers only what changed**, so it
is small regardless of fleet size and can run far more often. The cold sweep exists to
catch what the warm path missed — silent corruption, dropped messages, state lost in a
ring failure — and its cadence is a bandwidth decision:

| Full cold sweep every | Digest bandwidth per SN |
|---|---|
| hour | ~13 MB/s |
| day | ~0.5 MB/s |
| week | ~0.08 MB/s |

Even hourly is affordable in bulk terms. What makes it affordable is that it is a
digest exchange rather than a per-instance protocol: the same sweep as individual RPCs
would be tens of thousands per second.

⚠️ Better still, compare a **hash tree per disk** and descend only where the digests
differ, making steady-state cost proportional to *divergence* rather than to instance
count. Divergence is normally zero, so that is the difference between a full sweep and
almost nothing. Undesigned; this is where it belongs.

The liveness loop has no such problem: one message per EN per minute across the fan-out
is a few hundred messages a second, and each is a small per-disk status vector.

#### 13.1.10 Two verification tiers, riding the two sync loops

§5.6.9 makes the steady-state cost of placement *verification* rather than search. That verification has to fit
inside the sync loops, and whether it does is entirely a question of cadence.

**A full pass is expensive.** Per SN at 2^31 extents there are ~36 M EC groups, each needing ~60 instance lookups;
at 60 x 100 B = 6 KB per group that is ~215 GB touched per pass, or ~20 s at 10 GB/s sequential — and 200 s+ if
the accesses are scattered rather than group-ordered. **Derived.**

| Cadence | Full-pass cost |
|---|---|
| 1 minute | 33-330% of a core — infeasible |
| **1 hour** | **0.5-5% of a core — free** |

So the two tiers map onto the two loops of §13.1.7, and neither needs a new mechanism:

| Loop | Cadence | Scope of verification |
|---|---|---|
| **SN/EN liveness** (per-disk status vector) | ~1 minute | only EC groups with a member on a disk whose state changed |
| **SN/EN instance sync** (per-instance enumeration) | ~1 hour | **everything, unconditionally** |

**The fast loop's job is unavailable disks.** That is what the frequent loop is really for (Asserted, Bob,
2026-08-15); it catches domain-topology changes — a disk rehomed to another rack, two racks merged into one power
domain, an EN reassigned — only incidentally, and those would not justify a one-minute cadence on their own. But
they are real, and they are why a placement that nothing has touched can develop a collision: they are the reason
the slow tier must be unconditional rather than incremental.

**The slow tier is nearly free because it rides a walk that is happening anyway.** The hourly per-instance sync
already enumerates every instance, so verification adds table operations to an existing traversal, and because that
sync covers every EN once per hour, "verify everything" falls out of dirty-marking as each EN reports in — no
separate scan, and the work spreads across the hour instead of arriving as a burst.

**This gives SN-local EC grouping (§4.3.2.3) a second justification.** It was already about keeping §13.4's
priority sort local; it also keeps the verifier local, since a group's members are all extents the same SN owns. If
groups spanned SNs, neither loop could verify a group from one partner's report.

##### 13.1.10.1 Finding the affected extents when the EN cannot tell you

The fast tier needs "which extents have an instance on the disk that just changed", and there are three candidate
answers. Two of them are wrong.

**A reverse index on SN is too expensive.** At ~625,000 extents per disk (20 TB / 32 MB) and ~3,400 disks per SN,
an `(EN, disk)` to extent index is ~8.5 GB of SN RAM — the tier §12.2 prices at 5,000x disk, competing with the
extent metadata that already owns 2/3 of it (§14.1).

**Asking the EN does not work in the case that matters.** The EN does hold the disk-to-extent mapping on its own
cheap storage, and for a single failed disk on a *live* EN it can simply report the list. But **if the disk is down
because the EN is dead, the EN cannot respond** — and an EN death takes every one of its disks down at once, which
is the largest repair event there is. An answer that only works while the reporter is healthy is not an answer.

**So: ask the EN when it is alive, and scan when it is not.** SN's extent metadata names the EN in every instance
reference (§5.3.1), so the work list is recoverable by enumeration — and enumeration is a pass SN already knows how
to do, because it is the same walk as the hourly full verification above. **An unreachable EN triggers an
out-of-band run of that pass.**

- Cost: the same 20-200 s as a full pass.
- Against a repair budget measured in hours (§4.3.1.1), that is comfortable.
- **Bucket by EN, so one pass serves every currently-dead EN.** A failed rollout kills 5% of the fleet at once
  (§13.2); it should cost one scan, not one scan per EN.
- No reverse index is needed at all — not in RAM, not on disk.

**This puts a real latency requirement on the full pass**, and not merely an amortized one: it is also the
critical path for the largest repair event. 200 s is fine; 2,000 s would not be. That is the number §5.6.10's
measurement should report first.

##### 13.1.9.1 Dither the phase of every recurring per-pair loop

**Dither the SN/EN cold syncs, the SN/EN warm syncs, and the DN/SN syncs** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-16). That covers
every recurring per-pair loop in §13.1, so it is one rule rather than three exceptions:

| Loop | Period | Pairs |
|---|---|---|
| SN/EN liveness (warm) | ~1 minute | one per EN in the fan-out |
| SN/EN per-instance sync | ~1 hour | one per EN |
| SN/EN cold sweep | hour to week (§13.1.9) | one per EN |
| DN/SN sync | day to month (§13.1.3) | one per SN |

**Why alignment happens.** An EN reimage restarts every cold sync against that EN at the same instant. But that is
only the most visible cause — **things are created in batches**, so alignment is the *default* rather than a rare
event:

- cluster cold start (§5.5.1.1) begins every loop at once, so a fresh cluster is entirely in phase;
- a cluster expansion brings up a batch of SNs or ENs together;
- a rolling deployment restarts a domain's worth of processes together.

So an un-dithered system is not "occasionally aligned by an incident". Its **initial condition is aligned**, and
nothing pulls it apart.

**Why the spike is the wrong thing to worry about.** §8.5.1a rejects dithering for expiry deletes and this section
requires it here; the rules only look contradictory:

| | Expiry deletes (§8.5.1a) | Recurring syncs (here) |
|---|---|---|
| Work shape | **one-shot** — each expiry happens once | **recurring**, per pair |
| Does the spike self-perpetuate? | no; the queue drains and it is over | **yes** — the phase persists indefinitely |
| Cost of dithering | delayed reclamation, and §12.8.2 bills for it | **~none** |
| Right answer | **back-pressure**: defer under load, free when idle | **dither the phase** |

> **Back-pressure fixes load. Only dithering fixes phase.** Neither substitutes for the other: dither so the steady
> state is spread, and let back-pressure absorb the transient that remains.

**The longest-period loops are the worst affected and the hardest to diagnose.** When *N* pairs are aligned, the
instantaneous load is *N* syncs at once against a spread of *N* per period, so the peak-to-mean ratio is
approximately **period / duration of one sync** (Derived; the durations below are guesses):

| Loop | Period | One sync | Aligned peak-to-mean |
|---|---|---|---|
| Warm liveness | 1 min | ~1 ms | ~6 × 10^4 |
| Cold sweep | 1 week | ~1 s | ~6 × 10^5 |
| **DN/SN** | 1 month | ~1 s | **~2.6 × 10^6** |

So DN/SN — the loop it would be most tempting to leave alone, being the rarest — has the worst pathology. It is also
the one where the cause is least likely to be noticed, since observing the pattern takes a month. **That is the
argument for dithering by default rather than in response to a measurement.**

**Dithering costs nothing on any of these loops.** A sync's timing is arbitrary: §13.1.9 says the cold sweep exists to
catch what the warm path missed, so shifting one pair by up to a period changes only the detection latency for silent
corruption, which is already period-scale. Delaying a *delete* costs a customer money; delaying an audit costs
nothing.

**Dither deterministically, from a hash of the pair's identifiers** — `(SnId, EnId)` or `(DnId, SnId)` — into the
period. Not from a random draw, for a reason that matters more than it looks:

- **Deterministic is stable across restarts**, so a rolling deployment, or the very reimage that caused the
  alignment, cannot re-align anything. A per-process random offset spreads correctly and then re-randomizes on every
  restart, giving up predictability for no gain.
- **Both ends can compute it**, so the schedule needs no negotiation and fits §13.1.4's one-message-per-pair,
  driven-from-above shape.
- It is legible when debugging, which is §4.6.3's stated reason for preferring a clock to a counter.

**Implement it once, at the scheduling layer**, keyed on the pair and the period — not separately in each loop.
There are four loops today and the fifth will forget.

##### 13.1.9.2 §13.1.10's cost estimate depends on this

Worth making explicit, because it is a dependency and not a bonus. §13.1.10 concludes that unconditional verification
is affordable at hourly cadence — 0.5-5% of a core — on the grounds that "the work spreads across the hour instead of
arriving as a burst". **That spreading is exactly what dithering provides.** Without it, every EN reports at the same
moment and the hourly pass arrives as the un-amortized 20-200 s burst that §13.1.10 rejects at one-minute cadence.

So dithering is a **precondition** for the verification cadence, not an optimization applied afterwards.

⚠️ One minor consequence for §13.4.4: with phases spread, no two SNs' work reports come from the same instant, so the
coordinator sees a rolling picture rather than a synchronized one. That is smoother and therefore better, but it
compounds the staleness §13.4.4.3 already flags — a proportional share is computed from reports taken at different
times as well as at different ages.

### 13.2 Recovering from a failed rollout

A worked case, because it turns out to be the dominant data-loss mode rather than a footnote.

Take a 1,000-EN cluster of 3 PB each — 3 EB raw, 80% full, so 2.4 EB used — with **20 software
deployment domains**, and suppose a rollout destroys one domain: **5% of the cluster.**

#### 13.2.1 How long it takes

120 PB must be reconstructed. At 8+4 erasure coding that means **reading 960 PB**, because
rebuilding one fragment reads eight (§4.3.2):

| Fleet read bandwidth given to repair | Recovery time |
|---|---|
| 100% | **11.2 h** |
| 25% | **1.9 days** |
| 10% | 4.7 days |

The 100% row is not available in practice. 960 PB in 11.2 hours is 23.8 TB/s, which *is* the fleet
(§5.12.1) — recovery at full tilt means the cluster does no customer work at all. So the honest
answer is **two to five days**, set by how much throughput you are willing to stop selling.

#### 13.2.2 The degraded window is the real cost

With 12 fragments spread over 20 domains, a domain holds a fragment of **60% of all extents**, so
60% of them run at 11-of-12 for the duration. Each then needs 3 more losses to be lost, and over a
45-hour window ordinary disk failure supplies them at *p* = C(11,3)·(*W*/MTTF)³:

> **~3.2 expected extent losses per failed rollout.**

Compare the steady state of §4.3.1.1: about one loss per 572 years per exabyte. **A single failed
rollout costs more data than a millennium of ordinary disk failure.** Disk AFR is not the thing to
worry about.

#### 13.2.3 It improves as the fourth power of domain count

Both terms shrink with more, smaller deployment domains: the affected fraction goes as 1/*D* and the
recovery window goes as 1/*D*, and losses go as the cube of the window — so **expected losses scale
as *D*^-4.**

| Domains | Domain size | Recovery at 25% | Extents affected | Expected losses |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 20 | 5% | 1.9 d | 60% | **3.21** |
| 40 | 2.5% | 0.9 d | 30% | 0.19 |
| 100 | 1% | 0.4 d | 12% | ~0.002 |
| 200 | 0.5% | 0.2 d | 6% | ~0.0001 |

Doubling the domain count cuts expected loss **sixteenfold**. **Deploy in ~1% increments, not 5%.**
Nothing about the storage design has to change; it is a rollout policy.

⚠️ **Failure domains and deployment increments are different things, and the table above conflates
them.** A *failure domain* (§5.6) is a unit of correlated failure that fragments must be spread
across, and §4.3.3 wants those coarse — few enough that a real disaster is confined to *m* of them.
A *deployment increment* is how much software is pushed at once, and this section wants those fine.
They are independent: deploy in 1% increments *within* one failure domain, and both goals hold at
once. The right reading of the table is that the *increment* should be ~1%, not that there should be
100 failure domains.

#### 13.2.4 Three things this connects to

- **It is the same operation as decommissioning.** §5.11 identified EN removal as the only case
  requiring bulk movement; a failed rollout is that case arriving unplanned, so the machinery is
  shared and there is no separate recovery path to build.
- **It is why planned disruptions must be serialized** (§5.6.4). Two domains down at once doubles
  the affected fraction and squares nothing — it makes extents lose *two* fragments, and the loss
  exponent drops from 3 to 2. That is not a marginal worsening.
- **The erasure code matters twice over.** A local code with *r* = 4 (§4.3.2.1) reads 480 PB instead
  of 960, halving recovery time — and since losses go as the cube of the window, cutting expected
  losses ~8×. The patent blocking it until 2034 therefore costs recovery time and rollout risk, not
  just steady-state repair bandwidth.

#### 13.2.5 A new feature is a parameter, checked in off

**Every new feature is protected by a parameter, checked in disabled, and enabled once it is fully
deployed** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17). Two reasons, and they are different from each other:

- **The members of a ring must behave the same.** A rollout is gradual by design (§13.2.3 wants ~1%
  increments), so for the length of it the ring is running two binaries. If the *binary* is what
  decides whether a feature is on, the members disagree for the duration of every deployment. If a
  parameter decides, they agree throughout, and the switch is thrown once when every member can
  honour it.
- **A live site needs a switch that is not a rollback.** When a new feature turns out to be the
  thing that is broken, turning it off is a parameter change; rolling back the binaries is §13.2's
  dominant data-loss mode. The cheap remedy has to exist, because the expensive one is dangerous.

⚠️ **A parameter the ring must agree about is read by the leader and sent to the members** (Asserted,
Bob, 2026-08-17), not read by each member from its own configuration. A configuration change reaches
the fleet the same gradual way a binary does, so at any moment during one the members' files disagree
— and a member that consults its own copy makes a decision the ring did not make. Reading it once,
where the decision is made, and carrying it with the request is what makes "the ring agreed" true
rather than probable. **The same rule holds for an extent's instances**: the primary reads it and it
travels with the append, exactly as the creation second does (§8.1.5).

**In tests the default is the other way round: the mock configuration is checked in with the new
feature on** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17). The tests should exercise what the code is going to do, so
the checked-in cluster file and the checked-in test configuration deliberately disagree — off in the
fleet, on in the tests — and a test that wants the old path turns it off explicitly. Since §15.3.2
puts the test defaults in one routine, flipping one is one edit rather than a sweep.

**And the parameter is temporary.** Once it has been constant-on in the fleet, the parameter *and the
old code it protects* are deleted, the next version or a later one. That deadline is the point: an
old path kept behind a parameter nobody ever turns off is untested code that still runs somewhere,
and *n* of them make 2^*n* combinations nobody has tried. The switch buys a safe deployment, not a
permanent second implementation.

**Not yet, though** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17): none of this is needed until something is
*persisted*, and perhaps not until the code is released publicly. Nothing in memory survives a
deployment, so there is no old state for a new binary to disagree with, and every process in this
cluster is replaced at once. So the absence of any such parameter today is correct rather than an
omission — the first one arrives with the first thing written to a disk that outlives the process
that wrote it.

⚠️ **After a public release, the upgrade graph sets the removal deadline.** A released system gets
upgrade rules of the form *to go from X to Z you must pass through Y*, and those intermediate major
versions are what decides when a parameter may go: **a feature may not be removed while a supported
upgrade path still runs a version that needs it.** So "the next version or later" is a floor set by
tidiness before release, and a constraint set by the upgrade graph afterwards — the two are the same
rule at different stages, and the second one is not negotiable by whoever is tidying up.

##### 13.2.5.1 "Checked in off" is a proxy; the rule is "defaults to the old behaviour"

⚠️ **This section and §4.1.1.0's naming rule conflict, and it is a real conflict rather than a
confusion** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-19): *"if the feature is disallowing something, that conflicts with
the positive-name rule, and I end up going to the thesaurus to try to find a positive name for
disallowing whatever it is, or flipping a coin on which rule to obey."*

**First, the rule §4.1.1.0 belongs to, because it is larger than flag names** (Asserted, Bob,
2026-08-19):

> **Make the logic simple** → **reduce the depth of negations** → **name things positively.**

Each is an instance of the one above it, the naming rule **applies to all names and not only to
flags**, and the reason is capacity rather than taste: humans misread double negatives and are
hopeless at triple and quadruple ones. ⚠️ **That rule has no home of its own in this document**, which
is a gap — it is a coding standard, and there is no section for those (§16.141).

##### What does not work: renaming the gate after its machinery

An earlier draft of this subsection claimed the conflict dissolved if the gate were named for the
mechanism it switches on — `stream_capability_flags` rather than `disallow_deletes` — since machinery
is always a positive noun. **That is available and it is not free**, so it is recorded as a technique
rather than a resolution:

| | Says |
|---|---|
| `disallow_deletes` | exactly which behaviour changes |
| `stream_capability_flags` | that a mechanism exists |

**The second is vaguer, and vagueness has a cost paid at the worst moment** — by whoever is looking for
the switch that will stop deletes being refused, while it is happening. Trading specificity for
positivity is sometimes right and never free.

##### What does work: the rollout rule was stated as a proxy

**"Checked in disabled" is not the requirement; it is what the requirement looks like for an *additive*
feature.** The requirement is:

> **A new feature's parameter defaults to the behaviour that was there before it.**

That is what §13.2.5's two arguments actually need — a not-yet-upgraded configuration supplies no
value, so the default is what the old fleet gets, and it must be the old behaviour. **"Off" is merely
what that means when the feature adds something.** For a feature that *takes something away*, the old
behaviour is the permissive one:

| Feature | Parameter | Default | Ends at |
|---|---|---|---|
| a truncation seals the extent (§7.2.4) — **additive** | `seal_on_truncate` | **false** | true |
| streams may bar record deletes (§9.1.3.10) — **restrictive** | `deletes_allowed` | **true** | false |

Both are named positively, both default to the old behaviour, and **neither needed a thesaurus.** The
bind came from reading "off" as the rule instead of as an example of it.

##### The residual conflict is real, and it is between the two halves of the naming rule

⚠️ **Naming positively can *increase* negation depth at the point of use**, which is the general rule
fighting its own special case:

| | At the enforcement site | At the query site |
|---|---|---|
| `disallow_deletes` | `if disallow_deletes` — **depth 0** | `if !disallow_deletes` — depth 1 |
| `deletes_allowed` | `if !deletes_allowed` — depth 1 | `if deletes_allowed` — **depth 0** |

So there is no naming that is shallow everywhere, and the arbitration follows from the top of the
hierarchy rather than from the naming rule:

> **Name for the reading that occurs most often**, since that is what minimizes total negation depth.

For a capability, the common question is *may I?* rather than *must I refuse?* — enforcement happens in
one place and queries happen everywhere — so the positive name wins on the general rule, not despite
it. **Where that is not true of some particular flag, the general rule says to name it the other way**,
and §4.1.1.0's prohibition on `un-` and `-disallowed` is a strong default rather than an absolute.

⚠️ **And where a name genuinely cannot be made shallow, the negation depth is a signal about the
logic rather than about the name.** Two or more negations meeting in one expression usually means a
predicate is missing: give the compound condition a positive name of its own and the depth collapses.
That is the top rule doing the work the bottom one could not.

### 13.3 Background loops

Everything the write path is not allowed to do synchronously has to happen
somewhere. That somewhere is a set of **background garbage-collection loops**,
and by now the design has accumulated a substantial list of work for them:

| Work | Deferred from | Why it cannot be synchronous |
|---|---|---|
| Bringing lazy summaries forward | §4.5 | Byte totals change anywhere in the tree |
| Compaction: fold logs into bases | §10 | Rewrites an extent; also reclaims garbage |
| Erasure coding after sealing | §4.3 | Encoding a sealed extent takes time and bandwidth |
| Dropping replicas once EC is verified | §4.3 | Must not race the encode |
| Fragment reconstruction after EN loss | §13 | Must never block a write |
| Scrubbing and checksum verification | §1.1 | Catches decay before it accumulates |
| Reclaiming garbage in packed extents | §11 | A deleted packed object leaves a hole |
| Encryption key rotation | §7.2 | Happens by rewriting during compaction |
| **Age-driven rewrite of over-age extents** | §4.6.3 | Compulsory: no live extent may be older than the ~292-billion-year comparison window, or its identity and key selection become ambiguous |
| Refreshing the DN's cached counters | §5.5.2 | Otherwise one metadata write per data write |
| Re-placing instances and ring members | §5.6 | Restoring domain independence after a loss |
| The SN's own once-a-minute extent scan | §13.1.1 | Finds extents wanting repair, sealing, encoding or re-placement; memory-bandwidth bound |
| Raft snapshotting | §4.4 | Truncating the log must not block mutations |
| Rebuilding a ring's state from ENs | §5.2 | Disaster recovery, inherently slow |

Two observations. First, most of these are *the same operation* — compaction
rewrites an extent, and while rewriting it can re-encode, re-key, re-compress,
change device class, and reclaim garbage in one pass. Scheduling them jointly
rather than as independent loops is likely to matter.

Second, the loops are how the design pays for the §4.5 rule. Deferring
mid-tree summary maintenance is only sound if something eventually does it, and
the lag is directly visible in billing (§12) and in any `count` on a keyed
object.

⚠️ Loop scheduling, prioritisation, and rate limiting are undesigned, and they
compete with foreground traffic for exactly the resources — EN disk bandwidth
and SN memory — that the foreground path needs.

---

### 13.4 Repair scheduling: sort by amortized cost, not by risk

§4.3.3.2d shows repair cost per rebuilt cell spikes at `g = 1` — one global repair needed — and falls monotonically
above it. That shapes the scheduler.

**Always fix a whole EC group.** The 45 reads are being paid anyway, so write as many rebuilt instances as
possible from them (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-15). This is why more at-risk repairs have *lower* amortized cost: 6.4
reads per cell at m = 7 against 5.0 for a purely local repair, a 1.29x penalty for repairing the group that is one
loss from unrecoverable.

**The priority order inverts the obvious one:**

1. groups needing **0 global repairs** — local, cheap, high volume;
2. groups needing **2 or more** global repairs, **descending** by count — both more at risk and cheaper per cell;
3. groups needing **exactly 1** global repair — last.

**And the deferred class is drained by evolution rather than by scheduling.** Ignored `g = 1` groups accumulate
further losses and thereby become higher-priority *and cheaper*, while the `g = 0` groups get fixed quickly and so
never evolve into `g = 1` in the first place. The policy shapes the population: it drains the cheap end and lets
the middle drift into the cheap-per-cell high end, so the 22.5-reads-per-cell peak is rarely paid.

**It is safe by construction, which is not obvious.** The single deprioritized class, `g = 1`, is also the *least*
at-risk of the classes needing global work — it needs six more losses to reach `d = 8`. The only way it worsens is
to escalate to `g >= 2`, which places it in the descending-priority region. Escalation *is* the promotion
mechanism, so the deferred population cannot drift into a blind spot and no deadline override is required.

**Efficiency improves with disaster severity**, which is backwards from most schedulers and worth stating so nobody
"fixes" it. Severity is what converts `g = 1` groups into `g = 4` groups, and that conversion is the source of the
amortization. The bad case is a slow trickle, where `g = 1` groups sit at peak cost and never escalate — and in a
slow trickle there is spare network and nobody cares. It is efficient precisely in the regime where efficiency
binds.

**Turbo codes have the same pattern** with different constants (§4.3.3.2d), so the policy is not code-specific.

#### 13.4.0 Read demand is the third input to priority

The priority function takes three things, not one:

| Input | From | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `g`, global repairs needed | §4.3.3.2d | the base ordering, with the `g = 1` swap |
| unavailability duration | §13.4.2 | separates transient from permanent, replacing a timeout |
| **read demand** | §9.8's hot flag | **+1 global read, applied after the swap** |

Demand belongs there for the same reason cost does: a group somebody is trying to read is a group whose repair
delivers more value per byte moved. And it is what makes §9.8's refusal to reconstruct-for-read acceptable —
without a demand term, a degraded group nobody has prioritized could stay unreadable indefinitely while the
queue works on groups at lower risk.

#### 13.4.1 The greedy order and the throughput-optimal order disagree

Strictly by marginal risk reduction per byte read, a `g = 1` group is ~1/f times more likely to lose data than a
`g = 0` one, so at f = 1% greedy risk-per-byte ranks it ~22x above the local repairs and would fix it **first** —
the naive ordering. **Derived.** The ordering above wins only through lookahead over the population's evolution.

This is a case where the myopic optimum is the wrong answer, so the reasoning belongs next to the code. A priority
function read without the dynamics looks like a bug, and will be "optimized" back to the greedy order.

#### 13.4.2 The fast loop needs no re-replication timeout

The obvious implementation carries a constant — wait N minutes before re-replicating a down disk — to avoid
churning on reboots, which take every disk on an EN down at once. It is unnecessary. **Unavailability duration is
just another input to the same priority function**: one missing instance with the disk down two minutes ranks below
one missing with the disk down two hours.

Then transient failures resolve by **never reaching the front of the queue**, which is the same drain-by-evolution
dynamic as above, running in the opposite direction. Three dividends:

- one continuously re-sorted queue instead of a fast loop with a timeout plus a disaster scheduler;
- §13.1's one-minute cadence sets *detection* latency, and the queue sets repair latency;
- an EN reboot generates no repair work at all, rather than work that must be cancelled — and there is no constant
  to tune wrong.

#### 13.4.3 Admission control: the ball bin

§13.4 says how repairs are *ordered*. This says how they are *admitted*, and the two are less similar than
they sound (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-16).

Each SN has an allocation of **outstanding repair bandwidth, measured in extent reads plus writes.** When a
repair is scheduled its cost is **removed** from the available pool; when it completes, the cost is
**returned**. Where that allocation comes from is §13.4.4 — it is not a per-SN constant.

| Repair | Reads | Writes | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| Copy one missing instance | 1 | 1 | **2** |
| Replace 2 of 4 missing | 1 | 2 | 3 |
| Replace 3 of 4 missing | 1 | 3 | 4 |
| EC local group repair (§4.3.3.2d) | 5 | 1 | 6 |
| EC global solve, `m` = 2 | 45 | 2 | **47** |
| EC global solve, `m` = 7 | 45 | 7 | 52 |
| Vacating an EN scheduled to go down | 1 | 1 | 2 per extent, x very many |
| **Reconstruct for read**, discarding the result (§9.8.2) | 45 | **0** | 45 |
| **Georeplication**, receiving (§13.4.5) | 0 | 1 | 1, plus WAN |
| **Georeplication**, sending (§13.4.5) | 1 | 0 | 1, plus WAN |

**Derived** from §4.3.3.2d, and SN can estimate every one of these because it knows the instance state and the
group's shape. The 26x spread between a copy and a global solve is the range the thresholds below have to
discriminate over. At 32 MB physical per extent (§6), a budget of *N* outstanding is about *N* x 32 MB in
flight, which is what makes the unit physically meaningful rather than notional.

##### 13.4.3.1 The mechanism

Think of a **bin of balls**, where the balls are unused bandwidth and the **level** is how much is free. Each
purpose has a **door** at some height in the wall of the bin. If the level of balls is above a purpose's door,
GC may spend bandwidth on that purpose. Lower door means higher priority.

**There are two doors per purpose, plus a *sufficient* amount for that purpose:**

| Condition | Door used | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| the purpose is using **less** than its sufficient bandwidth | the **lower** door | admitted readily |
| the purpose is already using **at least** its sufficient bandwidth | the **higher** door | admitted only when there is plenty spare |

So every purpose gets easy access up to a guaranteed floor and then competes for the surplus. That is a
minimum guarantee plus best-effort above it, expressed as two numbers per purpose instead of as a scheduler.

**GC sweeps every item round robin** — every extent, every EC group — and grants bandwidth to anything that
needs repair and whose door the current level clears.

##### 13.4.3.2 Why the "outstanding" framing is better than a rate limit

**Because cost is returned on completion, the mechanism self-corrects under congestion.** A congested fleet
completes repairs more slowly, so costs stay deducted for longer, so the level stays low and fewer new repairs
are admitted. A rate limiter would keep injecting work at the configured rate and would need a feedback loop
and a tuning constant to avoid it. Here there is neither: **the bin is the feedback loop.**

It also means the budget is denominated in something real. Outstanding reads plus writes is what the network
and the disks are actually spending, which is the §4.3.2.2a bottleneck, and it makes a copy and a global solve
directly comparable without a conversion factor.

##### 13.4.3.3 Ordering is thresholds, not a sort

This is the part most likely to be implemented wrong. §13.4's priority ordering is **not** realized by keeping
a sorted queue:

- **Priority is door height.** A group's `g`, its unavailability duration (§13.4.2) and its hot flag (§13.4.0)
  determine which door it must clear.
- **Round robin gives everything a chance to try.** No heap, no re-sorting as state changes underneath — which
  matters at 2^31 extents and ~36 M EC groups per SN, where maintaining a sorted structure would cost more than
  the repairs.
- **Order within a priority class is sweep order**, i.e. arbitrary, and that is fine.

**The sweep period is therefore the repair latency floor** for anything discovered by the sweep. That argues
for fusing this pass with §13.1.10's hourly verification pass, since both walk every item and one walk can do
both. §9.8's hot flag is the out-of-band fast path that exists precisely because an hour is too long to wait
when somebody is reading.

##### 13.4.3.4 Starvation is accepted, and bounded by the sufficient amounts

**Lower doors can starve upper doors**, because the ball level changes only slowly — a burst of high-priority
work holds the level down long enough that low-priority purposes never get a turn. That is intended, not a
defect: during a disaster, low-priority work *should* stop.

What bounds it is the sufficient amounts, and that gives a design constraint worth checking:

> **If the sum of all purposes' sufficient allocations does not exceed the total, no purpose can be starved
> below its sufficient level.** If the sum exceeds the total, starvation below the floor becomes possible and
> the guarantees are nominal.

**Derived.** So the `sufficient` values are not independent knobs — they are a partition of the allocation, and
they should be validated as one.

##### 13.4.3.5 Every door is near the bottom: below 10% remaining

**All doors, high and low, sit below 10% bandwidth remaining** — high priority perhaps **1% remaining**, low
priority perhaps **9%** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-16). So the bin is nearly empty almost all the time, and every
distinction the mechanism makes happens inside the last tenth of the headroom.

**That is deliberate, and it follows from §1.6.** Allocated repair bandwidth left unused is wasted hardware, so
the target state is *nearly all of it committed*. The doors are not there to hold the level up; they are there
to decide who gets the last sliver.

**Notation: always state these as *percent remaining*, near 0 — never as percent allocated, near 100.** Two
reasons, and the second is the load-bearing one:

- *Remaining* is the quantity the mechanism actually compares. The ball level **is** remaining bandwidth, so a
  door expressed in remaining needs no mental inversion at the comparison site.
- In the remaining framing, **a lower number means a lower door means higher priority** — the ordering reads
  monotonically. In the allocated framing the sense flips: 99% allocated is the *high*-priority door, and any
  reader or implementer who forgets that inverts the entire priority scheme. It is a one-character bug with a
  data-loss failure mode.

⚠️ And read "9% remaining" as remaining out of the *repair allocation*, not out of the fleet. The allocation is
itself a cap on what repair may take from foreground work, so a nearly-empty bin says nothing about cluster
utilization. These get conflated and the mistake alarms in the wrong direction.

**It creates a resolution requirement, and this needs checking. Derived.** Doors 8 percentage points apart, with
the lowest at 1%, cannot be distinguished unless the level resolves much finer than one repair. The largest
single cost is ~52 (a global solve at `m` = 7), so for 1% to mean anything the allocation *A* must satisfy

> *A* ≳ 100 × 52 = **~5,200 outstanding units**, i.e. ~166 GB of repair data in flight per SN at 32 MB each.

Whether that is reachable depends on how long a repair holds its cost, by Little's law — outstanding = rate ×
latency:

| Repair completion latency | Outstanding at ~42.5 GB/s of repair | Doors distinguishable? |
|---|---|---|
| 0.16 s (one extent at full disk rate) | ~210 units | **no** — one global solve is 26% of *A* |
| 5 s (repair queued behind foreground work) | ~6,600 units | yes |

**Which is a second, less obvious dividend of the outstanding-work framing:** the mechanism's *resolution*
improves under exactly the congestion it exists to manage, because slow completion raises the outstanding count.
In a quiet fleet the level sits near the top, everything clears every door, and the door structure is
irrelevant — which is correct, since there is nothing to arbitrate.

⚠️ But it means **the allocation must be sized for the congested case**, not the quiet one. If *A* is a few
hundred units, a single global solve vaults past every door at once and the two-door structure is decorative.
That is a concrete thing to validate once repair exists.

⚠️ **And §9.8's hot flag needs a reserved floor, not just a low door.** At 1% remaining, a low door is barely
cleared by anything, so "immediately reprocessed by GC" is not delivered by door height alone. Hot repair should
have its own *sufficient* allocation under §13.4.3.1, so that it is admitted through the lower door of its own
purpose rather than competing for a sliver.

##### 13.4.3.6 The scheme is work-conserving: alone, any purpose gets at least 90%

**This is why the doors must sit near the bottom, and it is the property that makes the mechanism sound**
(Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-16). Since even the highest door is below 10% remaining, a purpose with no competition
keeps being admitted until the level reaches its own high door — so it consumes **91% to 99% of the allocation**
depending on which door that is.

> **Every purpose can use at least 90% of the bandwidth if no other purpose is competing for it.**

**So the doors arbitrate contention; they do not partition capacity.** That is the difference between this and
the obvious alternative, and the obvious alternative is worse:

| | Idle-capacity behaviour |
|---|---|
| Static partition — each purpose reserved *X*% | bandwidth sits **unused** when only one purpose has work |
| Doors near zero remaining | any purpose alone reaches ~91%+ |

Static partitioning would leave allocated repair bandwidth idle whenever the mix of pending work is lopsided,
which is precisely the waste §1.6 forbids. **Placing every door near zero remaining is what makes the scheme
work-conserving without a scheduler.**

**Therefore `sufficient` is a floor, never a ceiling**, and this is the likely implementation error. Exceeding
its sufficient amount does not cap a purpose — it only moves it from its low door to its high door, and the high
door is still near the bottom. A purpose that has plenty of work and no competition sails past `sufficient` and
keeps going. Anyone who implements `sufficient` as a quota has built the static partition in the table above and
lost the property this section exists to state.

**And work-conservation and starvation are the same choice seen from two sides. Derived.** Both follow from
placing all doors near zero:

- **alone** — the level stays high enough to clear even a high door, so a purpose reaches ~91%+;
- **under contention** — high-priority work holds the level near the bottom, so higher doors are essentially
  never cleared and low-priority work does not run.

So §13.4.3.4's starvation is not a defect to be fixed but the contended-case face of the property that gives
full utilization in the uncontended case. What keeps it from being unbounded is the `sufficient` floors, which is
why §16 question 111 treats them as a partition to be validated rather than as knobs.

**That is stronger than "low priority can starve"** — it is "low priority does not run except at idle", and the
right response is to make sure nothing correctness-critical is filed under low priority.

⚠️ **Vacating a scheduled-down EN is the one purpose with a deadline**, and thresholds cannot express
deadlines. Every other repair type is "sooner is better"; a decommission has a date, after which the machine
leaves whether or not its data was copied off. Either it gets the lowest door unconditionally, or it needs a
door that descends as its deadline approaches. Undecided, and it is the case where getting admission control
wrong loses data rather than merely delaying repair.

### 13.4.4 The allocation is handed out centrally, because bandwidth is a cluster resource

**Repair bandwidth is a whole-cluster resource, determined by the network** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-16). §13.4.3
treats an SN's allocation as given; this is where it comes from.

**Why it cannot be partitioned per SN.** Every SN's ENs are spread across the same power domains, software
deployment domains and racks — that is what §5.6 requires of placement. So all SNs draw on the same network
cross-section and are in direct competition. There is no static division that is both fair and work-conserving.

**A central coordinator.** SNs report how much work they have; the coordinator hands out bandwidth
proportionally, with a floor and a ceiling:

```
grant = min( max( min(work_requested, minimum), proportional_share ), maximum )
```

Reading the inner part: if an SN wants less than its minimum it gets what it asked for; otherwise it gets its
minimum, or its proportional share if that is larger. **So the minimum is a floor and the proportional share is
the surplus** — the same shape as §13.4.3.1's two doors, one level up. That recurrence is worth noticing: the
same floor-plus-compete idiom arbitrates purposes within an SN and SNs within a cluster, so the starvation and
work-conservation reasoning of §13.4.3.6 transfers directly.

**The maximum exists because an SN can DOS itself.** An SN granted a very large share could schedule enough
repair to saturate its own ENs and ring, damaging the foreground work it is there to serve. The cap is
self-protection, not fairness, and it is the one term that is *not* about sharing.

#### 13.4.4.1 The maximum costs work-conservation, and the same premise pays for it

⚠️ The cap breaks the property §13.4.3.6 establishes at the SN level. If damage concentrates on a few SNs, then
`(SNs with work) × maximum` may be less than the cluster total, and bandwidth sits idle — which §1.6 forbids.

**But the premise that forces central coordination is the same one that makes this rare. Derived.** Because every
SN's ENs are spread over all domains, any domain-scoped disaster — a failed rollout (§13.2), a power event, a
rack loss — damages **every SN roughly equally**, so every SN has work and the cap does not bind. Even a single
EN's death spreads, since §5.10 gives an EN a fan-out of thousands of SNs. Concentration would require something
SN-scoped, such as one ring's own failure.

So the two facts are one fact: *shared domains* is why a coordinator is needed **and** why its ceiling is
affordable. Worth stating, because the cap looks like a work-conservation bug in isolation.

#### 13.4.4.2 A tree of coordinators, rooted at SN0

For clusters with very many SN rings a single coordinator will not do, so it becomes a **tree — and SN0 is always
the root** (Asserted, Bob).

That reuses §5.5.1's convention rather than adding a mechanism: instance 0 of a machine type is the well-known
anchor, as DN0 already is for the bootstrap root, so nothing new is needed to discover the coordinator.

**The tree is shallow. Derived.** At §5.10's fan-out of ~20,000 children:

| Levels | SNs coordinated |
|---|---|
| 1 | 20,000 |
| 2 | 4 × 10^8 |
| 3 | 8 × 10^12 — beyond the 2^32 node limit of §5.10 |

So two levels covers any realistic cluster and three covers the design limit. Each level adds a round trip, but
reporting is periodic rather than per-repair and grants change slowly (§13.4.3.4), so the depth costs nothing.

#### 13.4.4.3 Two consequences to settle before it is built

⚠️ **What an SN does when the coordinator is unreachable.** Falling back to the **minimum** is the safe answer:
it guarantees forward progress on repair without risking oversubscription of a network nobody is arbitrating. But
that only holds if

> **Σ minimum over all SNs ≤ total cluster bandwidth.**

Otherwise the minimums are nominal *and* a coordinator outage oversubscribes the network. That is the third time
this document has met the same constraint — §13.4.3.4's sufficient amounts, §16 question 111, and now this — so
it is an idiom with a recurring bug: **a set of floors is a partition of a total, and must be validated as one.**

⚠️ **What "work to do" means, and how stale it is.** The natural unit is §13.4.3's outstanding reads plus writes,
and an SN learns its backlog from the round-robin sweep of §13.4.3.3. So a report is only as fresh as the sweep
period, and proportional shares are only as accurate as that. If sweeps take 20-200 s (§13.1.10) then grants lag
by that much, which is fine for a slow-moving level and possibly not fine at the onset of a disaster — exactly
when proportions change fastest.

Note also that the cluster figure being arbitrated is a **network cross-section**, not a sum of NICs.
§4.3.2.2a's warning applies: a spine oversubscription ratio divides the total that the coordinator has to give
away.

#### 13.4.4.4 What the minimum buys: users recovered early, at almost no cost

**Set the sum of minimums at about a half to a third of the total** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-16). Then watch a
failed rollout delete 5% of the cluster (§13.2).

**Before.** Not all bandwidth is handed out. SNs with work are running at up to **20x their minimum**, because
the surplus has few claimants.

**At the onset.** Every SN's demand suddenly exceeds its minimum, so every floor is claimed. With the minimums
summing to a third, the remaining two thirds spread over everyone is **about 2x the minimum each** — so every
SN drops to roughly **3x its minimum**, down from 20x. **Derived.**

**Then the cascade.** SNs are not equal: §5.11 fills older SNs and redirects writes to newer ones, so an SN's
repair work is proportional to the data it holds, and the 5% loss hits all of them evenly. So **small SNs finish
long before big ones.** A finished SN asks for only the work it needs, far below its minimum — and the formula's
`min(work_requested, minimum)` term hands the rest back rather than reserving it. That bandwidth flows to the
SNs still working, whose share climbs in an accelerating progression — 3x, 5x, 8x, 13x, back to 20x their
minimum — until they finish too.

**What this buys is the recovery-time *distribution*, and the effect is larger than it looks. Derived:**

> Under **pure proportional** allocation, share ∝ work, so every SN's completion time is `ΣW / T` — **they all
> finish at exactly the same moment.** Nobody is recovered until everybody is.

That makes pure proportional allocation *pessimal* for the metric that matters, and the floor is what breaks the
tie. Since §1.1 promises availability **per record** rather than per cluster, and §1.4.1 makes a job's latency
the maximum over its requests, a user whose data all sits on small SNs goes from "recovered at the very end" to
"recovered early" — and their max drops with it.

**The same result appears in compute scheduling** (§5.12.4), which is the reason to trust it: with total work and
capacity fixed, the last completion is invariant and only the earlier ones are free to arrange, so equal sharing
is pessimal in both places.

**And §4.3.3.3 explains why completing *some* users fully beats partially completing all of them.** A
fully-recovered user is unambiguously fine; a 95%-recovered user may consider the remainder unsalvageable. So
the staggered distribution is not merely nicer, it converts users from *possibly ruined* to *definitely fine*,
one SN at a time.

##### 13.4.4.4a The honest cost: the cap lengthens the tail

Bob's account says total recovery finishes when the big SNs finish, so the minimum rule is free — "unless they
are capped by the bandwidth where they would DOS themselves". That caveat is the whole cost, and it is worth
stating precisely because the mechanism looks free otherwise.

**Utilization is what determines total time.** Total work `ΣW` over total bandwidth `T` gives `ΣW / T` *provided
the bandwidth stays fully used.* The reallocation above keeps it fully used while enough SNs still have work.
But two things happen together at the end:

- floors diverted bandwidth away from big SNs mid-recovery, so they have **more work left** at the end than pure
  proportional would have left them;
- by then **few SNs remain**, and each is limited by the per-SN maximum of §13.4.4.

So if `k` SNs remain, each capped at `C`, utilization is `kC / T`, and the tail runs at that fraction. **Pure
proportional has no such tail**, because everyone finishes together. So the minimum rule does not cost nothing —
it trades a **longer tail for much earlier completion of most users.** Almost certainly the right trade, given
§4.3.3.3, but it should be recorded as a trade rather than as a free lunch.

**It also gives the per-SN maximum a second job, and a way to set it.** §13.4.4 introduces the cap purely as
self-DOS protection. Here it turns out to bound the recovery tail: a higher cap shortens the tail and a lower one
lengthens it. So the cap is not "as low as is safe" — it is the largest value an SN can absorb without damaging
its foreground work, which makes §16 question 116 a measurement worth doing rather than a policy to be guessed.

### 13.4.5 Georeplication is another large consumer of bandwidth, and a ship requirement

**Georeplication from other clusters is required before going public** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-16), and it is a
major bandwidth purpose alongside repair.

**The design already proved it necessary and had not listed it as a requirement.** §4.3.3.1's arithmetic shows
expected loss is dominated by whole-cluster disasters for *any* in-cluster code, and §4.3.4.2 reaches the same
place from the song: erasure coding stops hardware leaks but not administrators. So georeplication is the only
answer to the dominant loss term, and everything in §4.3 is a second-order refinement by comparison. Promoting it
to a ship gate corrects an omission rather than adding a feature.

#### 13.4.5.1 It is the first purpose that consumes a different resource

§13.4.3's bin holds one kind of ball: extent reads plus writes against the intra-cluster network cross-section.
Georeplication does not fit that shape.

| | Source cluster | Destination cluster |
|---|---|---|
| Reads the extent | **1** | — |
| Writes the extent | — | **1** |
| WAN bandwidth | shared, and neither cluster's local resource | |

**So a georeplicated extent costs 1 at each end rather than 2 at one end** (Derived) — and the binding resource
may be the WAN link, which appears in neither cluster's cross-section figure.

⚠️ **That makes the allocation multi-dimensional, and §13.4.3/§13.4.4 are scalar.** A single number cannot
express "plenty of WAN, no local write bandwidth" or the reverse, and both states occur. Either the coordinator
arbitrates a vector, or georeplication is admitted against whichever resource is scarcer with the other treated
as a constraint. This is the first place the one-dimensional ball bin is inadequate, and it will not be the last.

**WAN is also the most expensive bandwidth in the system.** §1.0 puts cloud egress at 48x the monthly cost of
storing the data it moves. Whatever the transit arrangement between two clusters, §12.1 requires georeplication
to be billed on the resource that actually binds — and that is the one term in §12 where the price per byte moved
dwarfs the price per byte stored.

#### 13.4.5.2 Crossing a cluster boundary crosses a key boundary

§7.3 scopes keys by SN and by day precisely to bound blast radius, and §7.3.1 makes that scoping
two-dimensional. A second cluster is outside all of it.

| Approach | Problem |
|---|---|
| Share master keys between clusters | destroys §7.3.1's blast-radius argument, and the second cluster exists to be independent |
| Re-encrypt at the source before sending | needs plaintext and CPU on a signed-code machine — §7.2.2's homeless job |
| **Send over the encrypted wire, re-encrypt at the destination** | destination ENs already hold keys and run signed code (§1.5, §5.9.2) |

The third looks right and costs least. Its consequences: instances are **not** byte-identical across clusters,
which is fine because EC groups are per-cluster (§4.3.2.3); and the same logical data occupies different physical
bytes in each cluster, so §12.3's physical billing legitimately differs between them.

⚠️ **Compression may or may not survive the trip.** If the destination's media class matches, the source's
compressed blocks ship as-is and save WAN bandwidth. If it does not, §7.4.2 makes compression block size a
durable, media-specific property — so cross-media georeplication requires recompression, which is §7.2.2's
missing machine yet again.

#### 13.4.5.3 What must survive the trip, and one thing that currently cannot

**Durability timestamps must be preserved.** §9.7's per-extent durability second is a property of *the data*, not
of the cluster that holds it. If a replica re-stamped on arrival, §9.7's time-range queries would answer
differently on each cluster and §1.0's "what did I do last Tuesday" would depend on which replica you asked.

⚠️ **But identity as defined cannot survive it.** §4.6.3 makes ownership part of the name — a stream is
`(DnId, StreamId)`, an extent is `(SnId, ExtentId, creation second)` — and those ids are **cluster-local**. Two
clusters will collide. So either identity gains a cluster component, or replicated data is re-identified on
arrival.

**Re-identifying breaks §1.0's central promise at exactly the wrong moment.** The whole point of §1.0's stable
record numbers and keys is that external indexes never need rebuilding — and a failover to the second cluster is
precisely when a user cannot afford to rebuild every index they own.

**Resolved: the durable user-visible name is the path**, and §4.6.3 now says so. `(path, record number)` and
`(path, key)` survive georeplication where `(DnId, ObjectId, record number)` does not.

#### 13.4.5.4 The destination gets a dedicated directory

**A georeplication destination should have a dedicated directory, so replicated data cannot collide with
anything local** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-16). Three things follow.

**No collision, and multiple sources coexist.** Each source cluster lands under its own subtree, so the local
namespace is untouched and a destination can hold replicas of several clusters at once without a naming
authority between them.

**Portability is relative to the replication root.** The prefix means the absolute path differs between
clusters — `/x/y` on the source, `/georep/A/x/y` on the destination. So the portable name is precisely
`(path relative to the replication root, record number)`, and translating between clusters is **one prefix
substitution**. That is a world away from re-identifying every object: a client library or an index consumer can
do it mechanically, and it is the same operation for every object rather than a per-object lookup.

**Failover is a re-rooting, and §5.5.4 is what makes it cheap.** Promoting a replica means moving
`/georep/A/x/y` to `/x/y`. Under §5.5.4's recommended `(parent directory id, name)` key that is **one metadata
change**; under a full-path key it would rewrite every descendant record. §5.5.4 marks that choice as not
decided and recommends it on renaming cost alone — **georeplication turns the recommendation into close to a
requirement**, because the rename in question happens during a disaster, under time pressure, on the entire
replicated dataset.

**Georep directories are read-only permanently** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-16). They are never promoted. If you
want a writable version you **copy** — see §13.4.5.5.

That removes a hazard rather than deferring it. A promoted-in-place replica would have to accept appends under
§8.1.1a-3's fixed-offset compare-and-append at offsets the old primary may also have used, which is split-brain
at the offset level. An always-read-only replica cannot have that problem.

It is also a mechanism that **resists the operator**, in §4.3.4.2's sense: a replica that is structurally
incapable of being written cannot be corrupted by the destination cluster's users or by a bug in them. Given that
§4.3.3.1 makes cross-cluster replication the answer to the *dominant* loss term, the copy being immune to local
mistakes is most of its value.

#### 13.4.5.5 Failover is a copy, and the copy is nearly free

**Copy by concatenation, sharing the sealed extents** (Asserted, Bob). §8.6.1 already makes concatenation a
metadata-only splice of sealed streams, and §4.6.1 already allows an extent to be shared between streams. So this
is a composition of two existing mechanisms and not a new one.

**Concatenation requires streams and extents to be sealed**, which a replica satisfies: it holds committed data.
⚠️ Unless georeplication streams live appends, in which case the replica's tail extent is unsealed and cannot be
shared by reference — it must be copied by value or left behind.

**Divergence is free, because §4.2 already has base plus log.** The writable copy is a base-plus-log where the
**base is shared by reference and the log is private**, so further edits become different change logs for the
different streams. Nothing new is needed for copy-on-write; it falls out of the structure already there.

##### 13.4.5.5a The copy restores the original path, so indexes work verbatim

This is better than the promotion-by-rename story §13.4.5.4 sketched, and worth being explicit about.

| Access mode | Path | What an index built on the source needs |
|---|---|---|
| Read the replica in place | `/georep/A/x/y` | one prefix substitution (§13.4.5.4) |
| **After failover, copy to** | **`/x/y`** | **nothing — the original path resolves** |

Because the copy is placed at the source's own path, `(path, record number)` from cluster A resolves on cluster B
with no translation at all. **Derived.** So the prefix substitution is only needed for reading a replica *before*
failover, which is the case where a user is deliberately looking at a replica and knows it.

**Record numbers survive only if the whole object is copied, in order.** Concatenating the same sealed streams in
the same sequence reproduces the same cumulative counts and therefore the same record numbers (§8.6.1). Copy a
subset, or reorder, and that guarantee is gone — so "copy for failover" and "copy a slice for analysis" are
different operations with different promises.

##### 13.4.5.5b Three consequences

**Space cost is zero at copy time**, growing only with divergence. That is the copy-on-write dividend, and it
means a failover costs metadata proportional to stream count rather than anything proportional to data volume.

**The replica stays intact and can keep tracking the source.** After failover the original cluster may come back
and keep pushing; the replica continues to mirror it while the copy is the new authority. Two divergent lineages
then exist deliberately, and reconciling them is the user's problem rather than the system's — which is the right
allocation, and is only available because the replica was never promoted.

⚠️ **Shared-extent billing stops being a policy detail.** §12.9 already lists it as open; failover makes it
load-bearing, because immediately after a copy two objects reference one set of extents and one of them may belong
to a different tenant. Charging both fully double-bills; charging neither loses revenue; splitting requires
knowing the sharers. This now needs an answer before georeplication ships.

### 13.5 Metadata snapshots, and the jobs that run over them

**System metadata is snapshotted daily and kept for a few weeks, with once-a-week samples kept longer** (Asserted,
Bob, 2026-08-15). Compute jobs run over the snapshots. This is the substrate for several things that must not run
against live DN/SN/EN state.

#### 13.5.1 EC grouping is computed offline

§4.3.2.3 requires group members to share a media class, an EC scheme, and a physical length; grouping them by
likely co-deletion additionally requires knowing which objects sit in which directory, **which only DN knows**. So
a job reads the snapshot, computes groupings, and tells SN which of its extents to group.

**SN must know sealed physical size.** ⚠️ This was previously unclear; it is not optional, for three independent
reasons. Something must decide and durably record the 32 MB physical seal (§6); §12.3 bills physical bytes, so
DN's per-object charge aggregates from SN's per-extent sizes; and grouping needs it. 32 MB needs 25 bits, so it is
4 bytes inside §4.7's ~100 B budget. The primary EN computes it — it compresses before broadcasting (§8.1.4.1) —
and reports it at seal, which cannot wait for the hourly instance sync because seal is a durable metadata
transition.

**The grouping key**, in decreasing order of confidence:

| Term | Why |
|---|---|
| media class, EC scheme | hard requirements (§7.4.2, §4.3.2.3) |
| **physical size bin** | the immediately measurable win — drives `sum(max - size)` padding waste toward zero |
| **declared expiry bucket** | §8.5.1 is an *explicit statement* of when data dies, so a group ages out in a narrow window and reclamation is nearly free |
| directory | the fallback co-deletion proxy, for data with no declared expiry |

Expiry beats directory because directory is only a proxy for co-deletion and expiry is a declaration of it.

#### 13.5.2 The job is advisory; SN validates

SN checks every proposed group against its own invariants — same media class, same EC scheme, compatible sizes, and
per-recovery-set independence with slack (§4.3.3.2e) — and rejects violations.

That keeps the trust boundary right under §1.5, since the job runs on Compute, where user code lives and no keys
are held. And it means a buggy or hostile optimizer costs **efficiency, never durability** — the same principle as
§5.6.10's refusal to let a transient condition weaken independence permanently.

#### 13.5.3 Snapshots are on the intervention path, not the recovery path

They will look exactly like a backup, and someone will eventually write a recovery procedure that depends on
yesterday's snapshot. **Normal recovery is §5.5.1's Raft state and three acyclic durability layers.**

What snapshots are genuinely load-bearing for is the human-intervention window: §8.4.1b requires an operator to
decide "stop hard deleting" within three days, and a daily snapshot is precisely what tells them what existed
before the bug ran. So they are load-bearing for heroics and must not be load-bearing for correctness. That is a
constraint worth stating rather than leaving to inference.

#### 13.5.4 Sizing, and why they should be deltas

At 1,000 ENs x 62.5 M extents x 100 B, one full snapshot is ~6.25 TB. Daily for three weeks plus weekly for five
years is ~1.6 PB against a ~2 EB fleet — **0.08%**: acceptable, but not noise. **Derived.**

Successive snapshots are nearly identical, and DN metadata already lives in keyed DeLawson objects (§5.5), so a
snapshot is a consistent read of a keyed object and **deltas are the natural form**, cutting that by one to two
orders of magnitude. Either way it is system overhead that belongs in §12.7's 58% chain explicitly, rather than
appearing later as unexplained shrinkage.

#### 13.5.5 One artifact, several consumers, so the schema is a contract

Billing (§12.8), EC grouping, capacity forecasting, and the realized-independence audit of §5.6.8 all read the same
snapshot. So the schema must be **self-describing and versioned**, and old snapshots must stay readable by newer job
code. Cheap now; expensive in year three.

The independence audit is worth calling out because nothing else can do it: placement is fixed at write time and
never revisited (§5.6.7), so a cluster that has been quietly placing badly for a year looks identical to a healthy
one — until the disaster it was supposed to survive (§1.1.1).

## 14. Does the metadata fit? (sizing)

Three tiers, three different answers, and the binding constraint turns out to be
the width of the record number rather than storage at any level.

### 14.1 SN: a machine's RAM, split between streams and extents

An SN serves stream and extent records from RAM, and that is what bounds both. Using
the budgets of §4.7 — 256 GB per machine, split **1/3 for stream records at 200 B
and 2/3 for extent records at 100 B** — and taking the worst case for capacity,
`compressed = physical`, so an extent's logical span equals its 32 MB physical size:

| | Budget | Record | Capacity |
|---|---|---|---|
| Stream records | 85 GB | 200 B | **4.3 × 10^8 streams** |
| Extent references | 171 GB | 100 B | **1.7 × 10^9 references** |

(References, not extents: a shared extent has one record but an entry in each referring
stream's list, and the entries are what occupy memory — §12.6.2. The two are equal only
under §4.7's assumption of one reference per extent.)

A stream is bounded above by the whole extent budget: one stream monopolizing a
machine reaches 1.7 × 10^9 × 32 MB = **51 PiB**. Any lower cap is policy, not a
constraint. Note this is a property of the *machine*, not of the ring — §5.8.1
corrects an earlier draft that tied stream size to rings per machine.

Compression relaxes it further: at a 4× ratio the same extent count spans 4× the
logical bytes.

#### 14.1.1 The split encodes an assumed workload mix

The two rows above imply an average of just **4 extents per stream** — 128 MB of
logical data per stream. That is not a claim about how a large object is striped; it
is a claim about the *population*, and it is consistent with §1's expectation of
enormous numbers of tiny objects, each holding one stream with a handful of extents.

The average and the maximum differ by nine orders of magnitude, and both are real:

| Stream size | Extents | What has this shape |
|---|---|---|
| 128 MB | 4 | the average, dominated by tiny objects |
| 0.4 PiB | 1.3 × 10^7 | a stream of a large object |
| 51 PiB | 1.7 × 10^9 | one stream owning a machine's whole extent budget |

**So the split cannot be a static partition.** A tenant with a billion tiny objects
would exhaust the stream budget while the extent budget sat idle; a tenant with one
enormous object would do the reverse. Bob's own caveat is that the ratio varies
wildly by tenant even in production, so it has to be a soft allocation over one pool,
rebalanced as the mix shifts.

⚠️ Soft allocation raises a question a fixed split does not: what happens when a
machine's mix shifts far enough that it can no longer hold what it has been assigned?
Streams must migrate, which is §16's reassignment problem arriving from a new
direction — driven by workload drift rather than failure.

#### 14.1.2 Sensitivity

The ceiling scales inversely with record size. **The §4.7 budgets stay the planning
figures** — 100 B and 200 B — even though the fields itemized so far reach only ~60 B
(§5.10.4), because flags, timestamps and fields nobody has identified yet will consume
the headroom. Budget and spend deliberately; do not re-baseline on each increment.

| Extent record | Extents per SN | One-stream ceiling | Share of the 4-byte reference (§4.6.4) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 40 B | 4.3 × 10^9 | 128 PiB | 99% — the floor |
| 60 B — itemized so far | 2.8 × 10^9 | 85 PiB | 66% |
| **100 B — the budget** | 1.7 × 10^9 | 51 PiB | 40% |
| 200 B — a long `first_key` inlined | 0.85 × 10^9 | 26 PiB | 20% |

What the extent record controls is **how many machines a given object needs**: at
200 B rather than 100 B every stream costs twice the SN memory, so the fleet doubles
for the same data. It does not affect the object's stream list, which depends on the
stream record and the chosen stream size instead.

⚠️ Inlining a generous keyed `first_key` is therefore a fleet-sizing decision, not a
metadata-format detail. That is the argument for a bounded key prefix with
disambiguation-by-read.

⚠️ The 200 B stream budget is the **stream record on its SN**. The object's *stream-list
entry* on a DN is a different and smaller thing — a 4-byte reference, a starting record
number, cumulative byte totals — and has no budget yet. Sizings that quote a stream-list
size use 200 B as a deliberately loose upper bound; a real figure would shrink them
severalfold.

#### 14.1.3 Two fields worth their memory: compressed length, and which disk

Two things about SN metadata were left iffy: **whether an extent record tracks its compressed
length, and whether the SN keeps a reverse index from instances to the disk they are on.**
**Bob leans to both, on the grounds that SN metadata is well under 1% of EN cost** (Asserted, Bob,
2026-08-17), and that is checkable rather than a feeling:

| | |
|---|---|
| One SN's extent budget (§14.1) | 1.7 × 10^9 references × 32 MB = **54 PB** of EN capacity |
| EN cost for that, at §12.7.2's $923 / 20 TB drive and disk being 95% of it | **$2.64M** |
| A 256 GB metadata machine | ~$4,000 to $10,000 |
| **SN as a share of the EN capacity it maps** | **0.15% to 0.38%** |

**Derived.** So the suspicion is right by a factor of three to seven, and a 1% budget would leave
about **4x** headroom over a $6,000 machine.

⚠️ **But cost is not the constraint the extent record is under**, so that headroom is not a licence
to spend. §14.1.2 is the binding argument: record size decides *how many machines a given object
needs*, because doubling the record doubles the fleet for the same data. What the cost check
establishes is narrower and still useful — **the 100 B budget is not under dollar pressure**, so
these two fields should be judged on whether they fit inside it, which they do. The itemization of
§5.10.4 reaches ~60 B; a 4-byte compressed length and a disk identifier per instance take it to
~72 B, inside the budget and not a reason to raise it (§14.1.2: budget and spend deliberately, do
not re-baseline).

**What each one buys:**

- **Compressed length** is what makes an extent's *cost* knowable. Billing is physical bytes
  (§12.3), and repair scheduling by amortized cost (§13.4) is arithmetic on bytes moved — both of
  which are compressed bytes, not logical ones. It is also what retires an assumption: §14.1's
  capacity table takes the worst case `compressed = physical` precisely because nothing records
  the truth. Four bytes, and by §8.1.6 it is a `COff` and not interchangeable with a logical one.
- **Which disk an instance is on** answers the question a disk failure asks: *which instances were
  on it?* Repair is the dominant term in every loss calculation (§13.2, §4.3.3.1), and the window
  starts with enumerating what was lost. Without this the SN cannot answer at all — the disk is
  below the granularity anything records.

⚠️ **The form of the reverse index is the part still to settle** (#49). Recording a disk identifier
*per instance* is a few bytes in a record that has room, and is plainly worth it. A standing
inverted index from disk to instances is the expensive half, since it costs a pointer per instance
