rather than a byte or two — and the alternative is to scan the extent table when a disk dies, which
is a pass over 171 GB of RAM. That is seconds, once per disk failure. So what decides it is the
disk failure rate an SN sees and whether repair may wait seconds to begin, neither of which is a
memory-budget question.

#### 14.1.4 Why the SN's table has to be in memory at all

**Not for read latency — for the loops that walk it** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17). RAM-residency is
**required by the fast-twitch SN/EN sync (§13.1) and by the GC that replaces missing instances**. Those
do not look up one extent; they sweep the table, repeatedly, and compare it against what the ENs report.
A disk-backed structure with a cache serves point lookups well and sweeps badly, and sweeping is what
this tier does.

That is worth stating because the obvious prior art went the other way — Colossus keeps metadata in a
key-value store rather than in memory — and the difference is not a disagreement about latency. It is
that **the sweep is the workload**, and a design whose reconciliation and repair loops are continuous
cannot page its own working set.

⚠️ **The open risk is the DN, not the SN** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17): **how much of the DN needs to be
in RAM is not known.** §14.2 has it disk-backed and unbounded in object count, which is the right shape
for a tier whose size is set by a customer's object count — but a directory listing, a keyed lookup and
the self-hosting bootstrap all touch it, and nothing has established what fraction has to be resident
for those to be quick.

### 14.2 DN: unbounded in object count, disk-backed

The SN's problem is bounding a single stream. The DN's is the opposite: nothing
bounds the number of objects.

At the §4.7 budget of **300 B per user object**:

| Objects | Logical | At 4× compression |
|---|---|---|
| 10^9 | 300 GB | 75 GB |
| 10^12 | **300 TB** | **75 TB** |

The ratio that matters is against the object's own data. **Metadata equals data at a
payload of 300 B**, so:

| Object payload | Metadata as a multiple of data |
|---|---|
| 30 B | **10×** |
| 300 B | 1× |
| 3 KB | 0.1× |

Below a few hundred bytes an object costs more to describe than to store, and §1
expects those in enormous numbers — so the DN tier can exceed the EN tier in
*logical* size. That is why DN state is disk-backed and cached, not resident (§5.1).

In *physical* bytes it is far less alarming, because self-hosting (§5.5) runs that
metadata through the same pipeline as everything else. Object metadata is unusually
compressible — sibling names share prefixes, timestamps cluster, flavor and framing
repeat across every object in a directory — so at a conservative 4× and 8+4 erasure
coding, 300 logical bytes becomes ~75 physical and ~113 billed. Against a bare
4-replica copy at 1,200 bytes, **self-hosting makes the metadata tier roughly an
order of magnitude cheaper than storing it uncompressed and replicated.**

The asymmetry is still worth stating plainly: **SN state is bounded per stream
by construction; DN state is bounded by nothing.** Only the DN tier has to be a
paging, caching store — and, since §5.5, only the DN tier is stored in DeLawson
itself.

### 14.3 What actually binds

Two independent ceilings on one object:

- **Record number**: 2^64 records, from the 8-byte record number.
- **Capacity**: if an object's stream list is allowed ~2^31 entries at the §14.1
  one-stream ceiling of 51 PiB, then 2^31 × 2^56 B ≈ **2^87 bytes**.

These meet at an average record size of 2^87 / 2^64 = 2^23 = **8 MB**. Below
8 MB average the record number runs out first; above it, byte capacity does.

Since records are expected nearer 100 bytes than 8 MB, **the 8-byte record
number binds by a factor of ~10^5**. An object exhausts its record numbers long
before any list approaches its limit. The structure is not strained; the address
space is.

### 14.4 Correction to earlier drafts

An earlier version argued that 32 MB extents and large streams were in tension,
concluding the physical extent limit had to rise toward 4 GB. That assumed a
stream's extent list had to stay in the tens of megabytes, sized for cheap
consensus replication. The real constraint is one SN's RAM, ~10^4 times larger,
which dissolves the problem: the 32 MB limit stands.

A second draft then over-generalized RAM-residency to *all* metadata. §14.2 is
the correction: it holds for SNs and fails for DNs, because object count is
unbounded while extents per stream is not.

A third draft tied stream size to *P*, the rings per machine, by assuming one stream
per ring. Rings serve many streams; *P* is a concurrency and failover parameter and
has nothing to do with stream capacity, which is bounded by the machine's extent
budget (§5.8.1, §14.1).

What survives from all of this is the observation that shrinking extents moves
addressing information up from the extent's sparse index into the stream's extent
list. That trade is real; it just lands well inside budget.

---

### 14.5 Do the metadata tiers fit in the cost budget?

§1.2 wants everything but disk, electricity and rent inside ~5%. The metadata tiers
are the part of that most likely to surprise, so it is worth a check.

Take an EN of 150 disks with a server costing 8 disk-equivalents (§5.3.1): 158
disk-equivalents, holding 3 PB. One SN machine drives ~76 PB of EN capacity (§5.10.1),
so it accounts for ~25 such ENs — call it 1.5 server-costs for the extra RAM, or 12
disk-equivalents.

| | Disk-equivalents |
|---|---|
| 25 ENs | 3,950 |
| 1 SN machine | 12 |
| **SN tier share** | **0.3%** |

Comfortable, with two orders of magnitude of headroom against the 5% budget. The
reason is structural: an SN's memory maps a fixed *count* of extents, and each extent
stands for 32 MB of disk, so the metadata tier scales with the storage it describes
divided by 32 million.

⚠️ The DN tier does not follow that logic. DN cost scales with **object count**, which
nothing bounds (§14.2), so a tenant with a trillion tiny objects buys DN capacity
rather than disk. The 0.2% above is the SN side only, and the DN side cannot be
computed until object-count expectations are pinned. This is the same asymmetry as
§14.2 and §14.4, arriving in the cost model.

### 14.6 The data structures that will hold all this

**Everything in the implementation today is temporary** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17). What replaces it,
per tier:

| Tier | Will hold its metadata in |
|---|---|
| **DN** | a **B-tree**, with a read and a write lock **per node**, so a walker locks a parent and then a child |
| **SN** | **segmented arrays** with a deleted list and a free list, and **hash tables that grow smoothly by linear hashing** — the hash tables being those same segmented arrays |
| **EN** | extents kept **serialized**, with lookup tables beside them; in memory the serialized extents sit in segmented arrays too |

**The segmented array is one primitive serving three tiers**, which is the part to notice before three
copies of it get written (#59).

#### 14.6.1 Why growth without copying is the requirement, not a preference

§17.5i measured a placeholder failing in exactly the way these structures are chosen to avoid. An
in-memory hash table doubling under a lock took successive trials from 2.88M creates a second to 1.67M,
and the slowest request in each from 348 ms to **1.82 s** — a metadata create waiting seconds behind a
rehash. The conclusion recorded there was that **the index must grow incrementally**, and this is what
that means concretely:

- **Linear hashing grows one bucket at a time**, so the work is amortized per insert instead of arriving
  as one stop-the-world copy. There is no moment when a create waits for the whole table.
- **A segmented array grows by adding a segment**, so nothing already in it moves. Pointers and indices
  into it stay valid, which is what lets the hash table *be* the array rather than own a copy of one.
- **A free list and a deleted list are what make reuse possible without compaction**, which the current
  structures avoid needing only because nothing is deleted yet.

So there is a measurable prediction attached to this work: **re-running the create benchmark after it
should show the cliff gone** — three trials in one process staying within a few percent of each other
instead of falling by 40%, and the slowest request staying in the tens of milliseconds. If it does not,
the structure is not doing the thing it was chosen for.

#### 14.6.2 An id is the reference, not a pointer

**All three structures reference things by id — `ExtentId`, `StreamId`, a node number — rather than by
pointer** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17). Two reasons, and they are independent, which is why the decision
is easy:

- **It is how you build these shapes in Rust at all.** A B-tree whose nodes point at each other, or a
  table whose buckets point into an array, is a graph with aliasing that ownership rules make painful
  and `unsafe` makes dangerous. An id is a plain number: the structure holding the things is the arena,
  and a reference into it borrows nothing. This is why the segmented array is the right primitive rather
  than an incidental one — **an id into it is stable across growth (§14.6.1), so the id is the index.**
- ⚠️ **And it costs 4 bytes instead of 8.** §4.6.4 already fixes references at 4 bytes for
  addressability; this doubles the argument. At §14.1's ceiling of 1.7 × 10^9 extent references per SN,
  every reference held as a pointer instead of an id costs an extra **6.8 GB** of a 171 GB budget —
  **4% of the machine, per reference stored** — and a record holding several multiplies it. **Derived.**

The two reasons pull the same way, which is worth noticing because they usually do not: the safe thing
in Rust is normally the slower or fatter thing, and here the safe representation is also the smaller
one. §15's self-concatenation test depends on the same 4 bytes, since 31 doublings is what fits in
2^32 references.

#### 14.6.3 One shared lock per process, and a short list of what takes it exclusively

**The expected shape is a global shared/exclusive lock per process** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17).
Everything ordinary runs under the **shared** side; a named and rare set of operations take it
**exclusively**, and taking it exclusively stops the process.

**Separate free and deleted lists are what keep create and delete on the shared side:**

| Operation | Lock | Does |
|---|---|---|
| create | **shared** | takes a slot off the **free** list |
| delete | **shared** | puts a slot on the **deleted** list |
| GC | **exclusive**, occasionally | moves the deleted list to the free list |

⚠️ **The two lists exist so that reclamation can wait for a moment when it is provably safe.** A slot
just deleted may still be named by an id some other thread is holding — §14.6.2 makes ids the way
everything references everything — so handing it straight back to the free list would let a create
overwrite a slot somebody is about to read. **Exclusivity is the proof that nobody holds one.** That is
the same argument epoch reclamation and hazard pointers make, arrived at from the other end: rather than
tracking which ids are live, wait until no thread can hold any.

So the design buys reclamation safety without per-slot reference counting, and pays for it with a
periodic process-wide stall. Which makes two things load-bearing:

- **The list of exclusive operations must be short and written down.** Bob's C++ experience is the
  reason this is stated as a rule: *whether* something is lock-free and *how wide* its implicit locks
  are is exactly what goes wrong quietly. A caller cannot see, at the call site, that the thing it just
  did serializes the process — so the set that does must be enumerable rather than discovered.
- **Growth is probably on that list too, and probably need not be.** §14.6.1 chose segmented arrays and
  linear hashing so growth adds a segment or splits a bucket instead of copying — which means growth may
  be able to stay on the shared side, publishing a new segment atomically. Whether it does is the
  question #59 exists to settle, and it is the difference between an occasional stall and a frequent one.

**The shared side looks affordable, on evidence already collected.** §17.5d measured a single shared
relaxed counter increment against per-thread counters at 13 million calls a second on sixteen cores:
**12.83M against 12.71M round trips, inside the noise.** A shared-lock acquire is that plus a compare, so
the reader side of a global lock is not obviously the thing to fear. **What to fear is an unexpected
exclusive acquisition**, which no amount of cheapness on the shared side helps with.

#### 14.6.4 Two more consequences worth stating now

- **Locking a parent then a child is the discipline, and it constrains the B-tree's shape.** A read and
  write lock per node with hand-over-hand acquisition is what lets many readers descend while a writer
  splits a node elsewhere — and it means every operation must acquire locks in one direction only, root
  downward, or two operations meeting in the middle deadlock. §17.12.1 has already paid for that lesson
  once, at a smaller scale.
- **Keeping extents serialized means the memory form and the disk form are the same bytes.** So an EN
  writing its journal (§8.1.5) writes what it already has rather than serializing on the way out, and
  reading one back is a lookup into bytes rather than building an object graph. The lookup tables are
  what make that navigable, and they are the thing that has to be rebuilt on load — not the extents.

#### 14.6.5 The SN's extent array, indexed by `ExtentId`

**Designed by Bob on 2026-08-17**, with the ordering notes below worked out here. This is the concrete
form of §14.6.2's "the id is the index", and it exists because `ExtentId` is **permanent** — never
reused, so deletes leave holes and a naive array grows with the highest id ever issued rather than with
the extents that are actually there.

**A record has a normal fixed size**, plus a flag and a pointer to an extra block for the **unusual**
cases. There are many ways to be unusual and the total is kept small; being **beyond the end of the
array** is one of them, budgeted at about **1/20th of extents**.

| Piece | What it is |
|---|---|
| the **array** | mostly compact, indexed by `ExtentId`, rebuilt compact at startup |
| a **squatter** | a live extent whose id is past the end, placed in a hole and flagged as owning a different id |
| the **hash table** | `ExtentId` → slot, for exactly the squatters |
| the **free list** | slots a create may claim |
| the **recycle list** | slots that are finished with but may still be under a reader's eye |

**Lookup compares the id against the bound.** Below it, index the array directly — and the flag is
tested only to notice that a *dead* id has landed on a slot belonging to someone else. Above it, probe
the hash table. §14.6.3's point holds: the comparison was needed anyway to reject an id beyond the
highest ever handed out, so a correctly-mapped extent pays nothing for the scheme.

⚠️ **Internal references are always the final `ExtentId`, never the squat slot.** This is the decision
the rest depends on. Nothing anywhere points at where a squatter physically sits — the hash entry is the
only thing that does — so relocating one is a copy and a hash edit, with no reference anywhere to chase.
The alternative, letting internal references name slots directly, saves a probe on 1/20th of lookups and
buys an obligation to rewrite every stream's extent list on every move.

##### 14.6.5.1 Growth hands each new slot to whoever owns it

**The array is grown before it is needed**, not when a create finds the free list empty. Growth walks
the newly covered ids and does one of two things with each:

- the id is **in the hash table** — so the extent that really owns it is squatting somewhere. Copy it
  into its own slot at last, and put **the slot it vacated** on the recycle list.
- the id is **not** — put **the new slot** on the recycle list.

**So growing by K ids yields exactly K recycled slots either way**, which makes the growth lead easy to
size: allocation rate times the gap between write-lock windows, plus slack.

**Reclamation is the O(1) part.** The recycle list becomes claimable by attaching its head to the tail of
the free list, under the write lock — **one splice, however many slots are pending**. This is §14.6.3's
deleted-list argument with its cost made explicit: exclusivity is the proof that no reader holds a slot,
and the proof is bought once for the whole batch rather than per slot. Which is why cleanup does not
have to be aggressive: **being lazy costs memory and never costs work**, and an SN's space is expected
to fluctuate daily and weekly anyway.

⚠️ **The stale hash entry retires with the slot, not at the copy.** A reader reads the bound and then
dispatches on it. If growth copies the squatter, publishes the new bound, and drops the hash entry
straight away, a reader still holding the *old* bound probes the hash afterwards, misses, and concludes
the extent does not exist. Deferring the drop to the same write-lock window that splices the slot fixes
it with no new mechanism, and the alternative — making a reader re-read the bound on a miss — is more
moving parts for the same guarantee.

Two properties worth having in mind while reading the above:

- **An extent is copied at most once per run.** Its final slot never changes once the array covers its
  id, so there is no chain of relocations and the lifetime cost is bounded by one pass over the array.
- **Growth converts the oldest squatters first**, since it covers the lowest ids past the old bound and
  those were issued earliest. Squatter lifetime is therefore FIFO and bounded by growth cadence.

⚠️ Growth is **O(K) record copies**, not a pointer publish, so it wants to stay incremental — a segment
at a time rather than a doubling — which is what §14.6.1 already wanted for its own reason.

##### 14.6.5.2 What this buys, and why no runtime shrink is needed

**Resident size tracks the live extent count rather than the highest `ExtentId` ever issued**, which was
the entire problem. New extents fill holes, freed slots return to circulation, and the array grows only
when the holes run out — so the machinery for shrinking an array in place, and the reader-coordination
it would need, is never written.

**Restart re-compacts**, and the startup path is the compaction. ⚠️ **But compactness should not depend
on restart timing**: an SN restarted at its weekly peak stays inflated for a week, and it is the one that
most needed compacting. The startup path already builds the compact array from the on-disk list, so it
should be callable without restarting — a recompaction on the same batched exclusive pass as everything
else in §14.6.3.

**The hash table is used by the outside, and the inside mostly avoids it**: a user presenting an original
`ExtentId` for a squatting extent pays a probe, while internal work goes through the array. At the 1/20
budget that is one lookup in twenty, against roughly 16 bytes per entry — under 1% of the array's memory
for the table itself.

---

## 15. Testing at scale

The sizing claims of §14 are about metadata volume — B-trees of 10^9 entries,
checkpoints of hundreds of GB, failover that must materialize them. Provisioning
exabytes of disk to test any of that would be absurd. It is also unnecessary.

### 15.1 Self-concatenation

Because extents are reference-counted (§4.6.1), **an unkeyed stream can be
concatenated to itself.** Each concatenation appends its own extent list to its end,
which doubles both the number of extent references in the list and the reference
count on every original extent. The bytes on disk do not change at all.

So *n* operations produce 2^n references over constant physical data:

| Doublings | Extent references | Logical size | Physical data |
|---|---|---|---|
| 10 | 1,024 | 32 GB | 32 MB |
| 20 | 1.0 × 10^6 | 32 TB | 32 MB |
| 31 | 2.1 × 10^9 | **64 PiB** | **32 MB** |

Thirty-one doublings from a single extent reaches a stream larger than §14.1's
ceiling, on 32 MB of real data. It works because unkeyed appends land at the end and
never disturb existing cumulative counts (§3), so records *N*..2*N*−1 legitimately
repeat records 0..*N*−1 and every addressing invariant still holds.

### 15.2 What it exercises, and what it does not

Genuinely tested:

- B-tree descent, split, and memory footprint at 10^9 entries
- The Raft snapshot/log/state-machine cycle (§4.4) on a full-sized checkpoint
- Materialize time and failover (§5.8.1) — the numbers there become measurable
- Reference counting under extreme fan-in, and every path that must handle it
- **Copy-on-write compaction** (§4.6.1), because *everything* is shared, so no
  compaction may ever rewrite in place. A bug there is impossible to miss.

Not tested — worth being explicit, since the technique is tempting to over-trust:

- Fan-out breadth and placement diversity (§5.10): all references point at the same
  few ENs, so neighborhoods, domain spreading, and repair remain untested
- Disk capacity and bandwidth behaviour under real load
- Compaction across *distinct* data, and compression-ratio variety

It is a metadata-scale test, not a data-scale test. Both are needed; this one is
nearly free.

**The reference width already accommodates this.** References are 4 bytes (§4.6), so
2^32 references are nameable and 31 doublings from a single extent sit just inside the
limit. A 32nd doubling would overflow — which makes the test method reach almost
exactly as far as the design does, and no further. Convenient rather than
coincidental: both limits come from the same 4-byte field.

The same technique works one level up. **Concatenating an unkeyed object to itself
doubles its stream references**, which exercises the DN-side stream list and its
paging path (§14.2) at scales no real object would reach during development.

### 15.3 The shape of the suite: unit tests are the bulk

**The bulk of the tests are unit tests, and the whole suite runs in under a minute, because
it is run before every push** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17). That is the entire reason for the
time limit: a suite nobody waits for is a suite nobody runs, and a suite nobody runs is not
protecting anything.

The three kinds are not three flavours of the same thing. They differ in what they cost to
*keep*, which is what decides how many of each there should be:

| Kind | Breaks when | Costs | How many |
|---|---|---|---|
| Unit | its own code changes | almost nothing to keep | as many as possible |
| End-to-end | *anything* changes | slow to run, and constant maintenance | **one** |
| Benchmark | anything changes | slow, and maintenance | a few, and discardable |

⚠️ **An end-to-end test's real cost is not that it is slow — it is that it is end-to-end.**
It touches everything, so everything that changes breaks it, and the maintenance bill
arrives for ever. A unit test depends on one piece of code and therefore only breaks when
that piece is modified, which is the one time a test *ought* to break.

So the standing end-to-end budget is **one test that executes every command once**. That
catches the failure a unit test structurally cannot — a command that does not run at all,
or a path that nothing wires together — and it stops there. Anything more is bought with
maintenance that would be better spent on unit tests.

#### 15.3.1 What makes a test a unit test

Three properties, and they are requirements rather than preferences:

- **It is single-threaded.** No cluster, no background threads, no waiting for anything.
- **It calls the relevant code directly** — not through a request, a process, or a running
  process of any kind.
- **It depends on almost nothing**, which is what makes it stay passing while the rest of
  the system is rebuilt around it.

**Touching the disk is not what makes a test end-to-end** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17). A test
of the log writer writes log files, because files are what that code does, and a temporary
file is a direct call rather than a whole system. The rule that matters is the one above it:
depend on little, and call the code rather than a cluster. What a unit test may *not* read from
disk is a **configuration** (§15.3.2) — not because it is a file, but because it is a
dependency on the deployment instead of on the code.

⚠️ **The real code usually has to change to make this possible** (Asserted, Bob,
2026-08-17). Logic that exists only inside a request handler cannot be called by a unit test —
so the code is packaged to be callable, and the test is not bent around the code. This is a
claim about how the *system* is written, not about tests: work that can only be reached
through a whole running cluster is work whose shape has not been factored yet.

#### 15.3.2 Tests are real code, so they do not repeat themselves

Unit tests need configuration, and they may not read one from disk. **So there is one shared
routine that builds a default configuration in code**, with the knobs a test cares about
overridable, and the same for every other setup that more than one test needs.

The duplication rule that applies to the system applies to its tests unchanged: two copies of
a configuration literal in two test modules is the same defect as two copies of anything else,
and it has the same symptom — adding one field means editing every copy.

#### 15.3.3 Benchmarks carry their numbers, and are versioned

Benchmarks are the other end-to-end thing, kept for a different reason: **run occasionally, to
notice that something has regressed.** Two rules follow from their being expensive to keep:

- **The latest numbers live in a comment beside the benchmark that produced them**, so the
  figure and the thing that measures it cannot drift apart. `DESIGN.md` argues about the
  numbers; the comment is where the current ones are recorded.
- **A benchmark is versioned when its numbers move significantly — about 5% or more.** A
  change that size is either a regression or a new baseline, and either way the old number is
  no longer what "unchanged" means.

And **a benchmark that has finished the tuning it was written for is often better discarded
than kept** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17). Its value was the tuning, which has already been
banked in the code and in this document; what remains is a maintenance cost. Keep the ones
that guard a number worth guarding.

Every benchmark is subject to §17.5i: **three trials, and report the spread**, because one
sample cannot say whether a 5% move is a regression or noise.

---

### 15.4 Where this is, how big it is, and who it is for

**There is more than one use case, and shared AI memory is one of them rather than the one**
(Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17). Worth stating because §1.0 argues the AI-memory case at length and a
reader can mistake emphasis for exclusivity:

| Use case | What it wants |
|---|---|
| **Shared AI memory** | **size rather than speed** — a slow shared memory, and large |
| **Models**, stored and retrieved | 50 TB objects, which is what §1.4's large-object work is for |
| **What Hadoop is used for** | bulk analytics over many objects |

That AI memory wants size and not speed is the part that changes how other sections should be read:
it is not a latency-critical workload dressed up as a storage one, and a design decision that trades
a little latency for a lot of capacity is trading in the right direction for it.

**The project is about the scope of Hadoop** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17): the basics of the store are
CRUD, directories, concatenate, and keeping the data durable — and then there are user accounts, and
then there is Compute. ⚠️ **Compute is deliberately out of the picture at present** (Asserted, Bob,
2026-08-17), because *the store itself is a big enough can of worms* — so §5.12 is a placeholder to be
left alone rather than a section to grow. That is the measure to keep in mind when reading sections that go into tenths
of a percent: the whole is large, and most of it is not built.

⚠️ **And the current state is early**, whatever the depth of this document suggests: *"we're rapidly
putting pieces in place and rolling marbles through them, which is a milestone but one far away from
shipping"* (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17). §17 records real measurements of real code, and every one of
them is of a placeholder standing in for the thing that will exist.

**The operational assumption follows from the scope.** Bob can watch a first large deployment; **after
that, whoever deploys DeLawson keeps it running themselves** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17). So the design
cannot assume a privileged operator who knows where the bodies are buried — which is the standard the
log tool is already built to (§17.5h: nobody should have to log into a machine to read a log) and the
standard the rest of the operational surface has to reach too.

## 16. Open questions

Roughly in order of how much else depends on them.

1. **The bootstrap root**: what exactly it holds, and how it is made durable and
   strongly consistent *outside* DeLawson (§5.5.1, §5.5.3). It must anchor the
   key hierarchy as well as the object hierarchy.
   ⚠️ **Partly answered by separating two roots that this entry conflated** (§5.5.6): the
   *object-locator* root stays in DN0's Raft state, and the *topology* root — machines, ring
   membership, tenant ids and ranges — is KS's, because a ring's membership cannot live in that
   ring and DN0's state is unreadable until KS has already come up. What remains open here is
   the object-locator root's exact content and how DN0's Raft state is operated.
2. **Ring reassignment, fan-out mutability, and cluster topology** (§13, §5.10.3).
   How a stream moves from a failed ring to a fresh one that may not be able to
   reach its ENs; whether fan-out sets are mutable; and where the failure-domain
   hierarchy that §5.6 depends on is stored — ⚠️ **not the bootstrap root, as this entry
   guessed: it is KS's topology root** (§5.5.6), cached everywhere and invalidated by a topology
   epoch. Reassignment and fan-out mutability remain open.
3. **Fan-out policy and EN sizing together** (§5.10.1). G, the sharing factor, is
   what gives repair and balance room to move, and EN capacity is what makes G
   affordable. One decision, not two.
4. **Soft allocation of SN memory between streams and extents** (§14.1.1). The 1/3
   : 2/3 split encodes a workload mix that varies wildly by tenant, so it must
   rebalance — and when a machine's mix drifts past what it was assigned, streams
   have to migrate, which is reassignment arriving from workload drift rather than
   failure.
5. **Shared-extent and shared-stream consequences** (§4.6.1): copy-on-write
   compaction, and billing attribution between a clone and its original. The cross-ring
   version of the same question is **closed**: a cross-ring clone copies rather than shares
   (§5.1.1.2), because aliases cover the case that made cross-ring sharing attractive — and
   where sharing is wanted anyway, §5.11.3.4's two-level count handles it.
6. **The DN-side stream-list entry has no budget** (§14.1.2). Sizings currently use
   the 200 B stream record as a loose upper bound; a real figure would shrink every
   stream-list number severalfold.
7. **Digest-based instance confirmation** (§13.1.9). A per-disk hash tree would make
   steady-state cost proportional to divergence rather than instance count, and
   divergence is normally zero.
8. **The maximum sync message size** (§13.1.5), which sets how much bucketing either
    sync pair needs.
9. **How widely an SN's streams spread across DNs** (§13.1.5). It swings the DN→SN
    digest from 0.4 MB to 85 MB per pair, and it is not determined by anything decided
    so far.
10. **Should streams carry a creation timestamp too?** (§4.6.3) Bob's expectation is
    yes, not yet thought through. Two asymmetries make it a different problem from the
    extent case rather than the same one: a stream is not itself encrypted, so a stream
    timestamp would be for id-reuse safety only and would not select a key; but
    "rewriting" a stream to escape a wrap means re-identifying it in every object that
    references it, where rewriting an extent is something compaction does anyway. So the
    wrap obligation is cheap for extents and expensive for streams — an argument for
    giving streams a *wider* timestamp rather than an equal one.
11. **How a DN range splits** (§5.11). The only place fullness forces movement. It should
    reuse the keyed-object split of §10, but the interaction with in-flight writes to the
    range is undesigned.
12. **What ring unavailability *p* actually is** (§5.11.1). ⚠️ **Partly answered, and the answer
    changes the question** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17): **the system does not work if a ring is
    unavailable**, so *p* is not a quantity to accept and design around — it is a quantity to drive to
    nothing. The design response is to **switch to a new primary in less time than a timeout**, so that
    an unavailable ring is never observed as one, and **ring size is the lever**: seven members, going
    to nine if seven does not deliver no-long-downtime. What remains open is the measurement that says
    which it is, and what *p* residually is once failover is that fast — which is what the locality
    argument and the availability contract actually need.
13. **Hedge delays per tier** (§9.5). The *percentile* is settled at p99.9+ (§1.4.1), but the
    absolute delays differ by orders of magnitude between an EN granule read, a metadata
    lookup and a client-to-FE request. Also: may a ring's hot backup serve hedged metadata
    reads, and what staleness does that admit?
14. **The give-up budget for seal-short** (§9.5, §13). It must sit far below a 40-second TCP
    retry or one dead EN stalls a writer for a timeout.
15. **Read hot spots** (§13.1.2, §1.4.4). Free-space-weighted placement balances space and
    is blind to read load. Colossus runs a balancing custodian, which suggests this is real.
    Adding instances to hot extents would fix it without relocating anything, but nothing is
    designed.
16. **Where the hot-object cache lives** (§9.6.1) — an EN cache of ciphertext adds no new
    plaintext location, while an FE cache of whole objects removes a hop but does.
17. **The broadcast tool for Compute** (§9.6.2): tree fan-out, how a job's vertex set is
    discovered, and what happens when a forwarding vertex dies mid-distribution.
18. **Compute allocation** (§5.12). Not Virtual Clusters, but nothing yet in their place, and
    §12 means whatever appears has to be billable.
19. **Telling a job whether its remainder fits** (§5.12.2). Phase 2 is a memory workload or a
    storage workload depending on the filtering ratio, differing by the iteration count. That
    looks like the most useful thing DeLawson could tell a scheduler, and nothing computes it.
20. **Does the flat-network assumption hold at the intended scale?** (§5.12.3) Affinity is
    unnecessary only while intra-cluster network is flat, which costs ~6% of an EN and is tight
    against a strict 5% overhead target. If a cluster ever spans an unflattenable boundary,
    topology and affinity both return.
21. **Pick the repair window, then the replica count** (§4.3.1.1). *p_gone* = 10^-4 implies a
    58-hour window; a 1–4 hour window costs 0.04–0.18% of fleet read bandwidth and makes three
    replicas sufficient. So four instances is a decision to repair slowly, not a reliability
    necessity — and the window is the number to set deliberately.
22. **Deployment increment size** (§13.2.3). Expected loss from a failed rollout scales as
    D^-4, so ~1% increments instead of 5% is a sixteen-to-six-hundred-fold reliability
    improvement for no design change. Needs to become policy, and it interacts with the
    utilization ceiling of 1 - 1/D (§5.11).
23. **How much fleet bandwidth repair may take** (§13.2.1). Recovery at full tilt stops all
    customer work; at 10% it takes five days. The split is a business decision nobody has made.
24. **Soft-delete authority split** (§8.4.2). The window is only a safeguard if the principal who
    deleted cannot also shorten or waive it. Needs a concrete authority model; everything else about
    soft delete is bookkeeping.
25. **The hard-delete brake** (§8.4.1b). A cluster-wide switch halting all hard deletion, usable by
    someone who knows only that something is wrong. It is what makes three days sufficient, since
    diagnosis does not fit in the window.
26. **Aggregate retention against the repair reserve** (§8.4.3). The opt-out makes the punishing cases
    self-select out, but a tenant with month-scale data and no opt-out sits at 10% and exceeds a 5%
    reserve alone. Retention needs admission control, jointly with the utilization target and D.
27. **The directory as the unit of policy** (§8.4.3). Expiry grouping, soft-delete opt-out and default
    locality are all converging on the directory. Better to design that scope once than to let three
    mechanisms each invent their own.
28. **Name the durability tiers honestly** (§12.7.2.1). "Usually available, always reliable" hides that
    1.333× also survives only a 25% disaster against 2.333×'s 57% — and large correlated events are the
    dominant loss mode. A customer-facing tier list should state disaster tolerance, not just availability.
29. **Turbo codes' disaster tolerance** (§4.3.2.1, §4.3.3.2a). The storage cost of not licensing is priced
    at ~$0.24/TB-month; the *reliability* cost is not. §4.3.3.2a gives the procedure — two failure models,
    Monte Carlo or pattern-counting, expressed as "equivalent to 3× or 4× replication at what loss rate" —
    and the candidate to evaluate is a (5+1)×(12+3) matrix. Arithmetic, not research, and it should be done
    before the choice is made on price.
30. **The 1.333× guarantee is tight against the 10% outage case** (§12.7.2.1a). The LRC tolerates at most
    11.7% of fragments by the Singleton-like bound, and the worked scenario is a 10% loss. Worth confirming
    that maximal recoverability covers the realistic patterns, since the margin is thin.
31. **Why the price undercuts B2 threefold** (§12.7.2.2). Either disk density and cost discipline are a
    real advantage, or the efficiency chain is optimistic. B2 runs a lower-overhead code, so it is not the
    coding. Worth resolving before the number is quoted to anyone.
32. **Truncation above the durable watermark on handover** (§8.1.1a). This, not exactly-once semantics, is
    what erasure coding actually requires — an instance holding an unagreed suffix must discard it. Raft log
    truncation in another guise, and unspecified.
33. **Bound and timeout on the out-of-order cache** (§8.1.1a-4). Together they set how far ahead a single
    writer may pipeline, and a gap that never fills must not pin cached data indefinitely.
34. **Which corner of the ingest trilemma the shared-memory case takes** (§8.6.2). Parallel bandwidth,
    dense stable object offsets, and a timestamp-monotone extent list are not simultaneously available.
    §8.6.6 proposes the sealed-prefix-plus-growing-frontier shape as the default, but §1.0's case has not
    been made to choose, and the choice is visible in the API. Related: whether the frontier's stream count
    is user-visible, since an object's total record count is unknown while it is open.
35. **When coalescing should re-frame** (§8.2.1). Matching the dominant read format takes translation off
    the read path, but nothing tracks what the dominant read format is.
36. **Waste from a large append at a nearly-full extent** (§8.1.1c). The 32 MB logical bound (§8.1.1a-2)
    caps it, but a 32 MB append arriving at an extent with 1 MB left still seals that extent 31 MB short.
    Lands in §12.7's garbage term rather than in silent padding.
37. **Does shared AI memory need latency this design deprioritizes?** (§1.0.2) Near-real-time is
    comfortable; millisecond index lookups are not what §1.4 optimizes for. If the motivating use case
    wants them, that is a conflict to resolve rather than assume away.
38. **A time-based sealing trigger** (§9.7.1). It would bound the durability-timestamp table, which a
    slowly-written extent grows to 0.8% of its size, and open extents are expensive anyway — but hourly
    sealing of a slow stream makes nine times as many extents, and extent metadata is priced. A three-way
    trade, undecided.
39. **Time-range queries on keyed objects** (§9.7.2). Record number is not monotonic in time there, so the
    query is a scan over candidate extents rather than a binary search, and its cost is unworked.
40. **Governance and licence** (§1.0). An open-source data store needs a licence choice, a contribution
    model, and a position on whether a hosted service competes with its own users. None decided.
41. **What FE-layer retention means** (§8.4.1c). DN, SN and EN retention is a deferred decrement; FE
    holds no durable state, so its window presumably means declining to issue the hard delete until its
    timer expires. Worth stating, since a layer that gets this wrong silently leaves the protection.
42. **Retention window versus the repair reserve** (§8.4.3). Window × churn consumes the 1 − 1/D
    headroom that durability depends on, so windows must be admission-controlled rather than freely
    chosen. A 30-day window at 100%/yr churn already exceeds a 5% reserve.
43. **Measure the space-efficiency chain** (§12.7). Every factor is a guess and they multiply: the
    difference between 58% and 55% billable is a 5% swing in revenue per disk bought. The
    undeletable-garbage term is the one most under the design's control, via compaction policy.
44. **Expiry-aware placement** (§8.5.1). Grouping objects by declared expiry so extents die whole is
    the strongest lever on the efficiency chain, worth ~30× the entire extent-size range. Needs a
    placement policy, an API field, and a decision on how hard to discourage "never".
45. **A lifetime dimension in the price list** (§8.5.3). Short-lived data skips erasure coding and so
    costs 2.7× more per byte-day. Correct, but it means price cannot be one figure per byte.
46. **A guaranteed repair-bandwidth floor** (§4.3.4.1). Repair below the failure arrival rate makes
    loss certain rather than unlikely. The floor is ~7.6 GB/s per 100,000 disks — cheap, but it has to
    be reserved rather than left to compete with foreground traffic.
47. **Treat utilization as a durability limit** (§4.3.4). A full cluster cannot repair, so 1 − 1/D is
    not a capacity guideline. Needs enforcement, and an answer for what happens when a tenant's growth
    would cross it.
48. **Defence against logical corruption** (§4.3.4). Erasure coding faithfully preserves corrupted
    data. Scrubbing catches bit rot, not a bug that wrote the wrong bytes correctly.
49. **What disaster size to design for** (§4.3.3). Overhead = 1/(1−s) makes this the single largest
    cost-versus-reliability decision in the system: 33% survivability at 1.50×, 50% at 2.00×. It
    should be settled before the erasure code is chosen.
50. **Do real disasters respect the domain hierarchy?** (§4.3.3) The guarantee depends entirely on it.
    A cross-cutting failure mode returns loss to the binomial regime, where a 5% event loses hundreds
    of terabytes outright instead of ~3 extents.
51. **Measure the disaster frequency exponent α** (§4.3.3.1). Every expected-loss figure depends on it,
    5×- and 10×-per-halving differ by ~6×, and for α > m the integral diverges and needs a floor.
52. **A second cluster** (§4.3.3.1). Expected loss is of order the whole-cluster disaster rate for every
    in-cluster code, so geo-replication is the only answer to the top of the distribution — and nothing
    in this document addresses it.
53. **Is durability a per-customer billable tier?** (§4.3.3.3) Write-off fractions span 1/1000 to
    999/1000, a 250× spread in effective loss rate on identical storage. Overhead = 1/(1−s) makes the
    knob natural and §12 bills it for free, but nothing offers it.
54. **Do local codes actually lose on disasters, or only in the worst case?** (§4.3.2.1) Guaranteed
    tolerance is 7.5% against MDS's 33%, but maximal recoverability plus a good domain-to-local-group
    mapping may recover most real patterns — worth analysing before writing off the construction or the
    patent question.
55. **Placement retry behaviour in a lopsided cluster** (§5.6.3). Free-space weighting
    and domain constraints interact: a markedly emptier domain attracts weighted picks and
    then rejects them, which is worst right after adding capacity. Bounded, but worth
    measuring.
56. **Primary EN selection and handover** (§8.1.1). The 3-of-4 intersection makes handover
    safe, but who chooses the primary, and how a new one is appointed when it fails, is
    undesigned.
57. **SCN width, scope, and validity window** (§4.6.3). The width and the 10-minute cap
    must be chosen together; a Raft log index is a natural per-ring counter, but what an
    SCN is scoped to is unsettled while objects span many rings.
58. **Expected object count** (§14.5). DN cost scales with object count rather than
    bytes, so the DN tier's share of the cost budget cannot be computed until this is
    pinned — it is the one part of §1.2 still unquantified.
59. **Why nesting forces serialized planned disruptions** (§5.6.5) — the
    arithmetic is verified but this operational constraint is asserted, and it
    determines how the cluster is actually operated.
60. **Choosing P, the rings per machine** (§5.8.1). Not a tuning knob: it trades
    core utilization and failover speed against stream-list size, and it multiplies
    with the unmeasured extent-entry size — the stream list grows as the *square*
    of that entry size across the plausible range.
61. **Transactions and long consistent reads** (§5.7). Getting them would drop the
    ring from 3× RAM to 2×, the single largest cost saving identified so far. §5.8
    makes the required read duration much shorter than ten minutes, so this looks
    more attainable than when first raised. **And there are two more, unrelated
    arguments**: §9.1.3.1 shows consistent read is what turns a paginated read of a
    large object from serial into parallel, since a consistent view makes chunk
    boundaries computable rather than discoverable; and §3.0.2 finds that **updatable
    secondary indexes need transactions**, since an appended row spawns index updates
    that must not half-happen. Three unrelated reasons for one feature.
62. **Raft ring sizes and slack** (§5.6.1): how many members for an SN ring, for a
    DN ring, for KS. ⚠️ **A working figure exists** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17): **seven members, and
    nine if seven cannot deliver no-long-downtime** — chosen for availability under failover (question
    12) rather than for durability. What is open is whether seven suffices, which is a measurement of
    failover time and not an argument.
63. **Where the live counters live** (§5.5.2). §4.5 shows the recursion cannot run
    away, so this is now a write-amplification question only: keep the
    authoritative count on the SN and let the DN cache it lazily, or accept one
    metadata write per data write.
64. **Bounding open logs per stream** (§4.2). RAM bounds the extent list; nothing
    bounds the logs, and each costs EN replicas and network.
65. **Background loop scheduling** (§13.3): prioritisation and rate limiting
    against foreground traffic, and whether the rewrite-shaped work — compaction,
    re-encoding, re-keying, garbage reclamation — is scheduled as one pass or many.
66. **Where the live counters live** (§5.5.2). §4.5 shows the recursion cannot run
    away, so this is now a write-amplification question only: keep the
    authoritative count on the SN and let the DN cache it lazily, or accept one
    metadata write per data write.
67. **The metadata key** (§5.5.4): `(parent dir id, name)` recommended over full
    path, so directory rename stays O(1).
68. **Do inline and packed remain distinct regimes?** (§11) Self-hosting makes
    inline objects pack automatically inside metadata extents, which may leave the
    explicit packed regime with nothing to add.
69. **Metadata-tier placement policy** (§5.5.3): more redundancy, maximal spread,
    replicas retained rather than erasure-coded?
70. **Remaining directory semantics** (§5.1): listing huge directories,
    permissions, quotas.
71. **The keyed `first_key` in the extent entry** (§14.1, §5.10.4). The only field
    whose size is unknown, and the stream list grows as the *square* of the entry —
    so a bounded key prefix with disambiguation-by-read looks strongly preferable to
    inlining an arbitrary key. Also: confirm the 60 B estimate by measurement.
72. **Local-index namespace and lifecycle** (§5.10.4): per-stream or per-ring, and
    how a slot is retired without silently re-pointing the extents that name it.
73. **Compression block size vs index granularity** (§7.1, §1.4.2). Now a throughput trade on
    both sides: coarse granules compress better and bill less, fine granules cut read
    amplification, which is a 50× throughput factor for point reads.
74. **Keyed objects** generally — the split-on-overflow B-tree shape of §10 needs
    its own pass.
75. **The packing threshold** (§11) — half of *which* maximum? Presumably ~16 MB
    physical.
76. **Packed-object billing attribution** (§11, §12) — per-object physical size is
    not additive under shared-extent compression.
77. **Billing policy** (§12.9): garbage, transient double footprint, shared-extent
    attribution, instantaneous-usage contract, reporting granularity. Slack itself is
    settled at 2× (§4.7).
78. **Key custody within KS** (§7.3): how the daily master keys are themselves
    protected beyond the unlocking key, and whether customers may supply their own.
79. ~~**EC vs read locality**~~ — moot: EC groups whole extents (§4.3.2.3). Formerly: align the fragment stripe to the granule, or
    keep a full replica?
80. **Compaction policy** (§10) — now partly a pricing decision.
81. **Membership and leader election** (§13).
82. `Nul` and `\0` framing were both listed originally and are folded together
    (§8.2). Confirm no distinction was meant.
83. Does a tombstoned unkeyed record number stay readable as "deleted" forever?
    Reclaiming it would renumber, so presumably never — worth stating
    deliberately.

84. **Whether the stripe of a `(12+3)x(5+1)` turbo code is 90 cells or 108** (§4.3.3.2e). The 4/3 rule
    reproduces 8 and 20 exactly but needs 108 to reach 144; 15 x 6 is 90, which wants 120. It decides
    where the code reaches designed reliability.
85. **Whether 4-instance collapses at the EN level or the disk level on one machine** (§5.6.8). Four
    instances on four disks of one machine protect against the commonest failure there is; collapsing to one
    gives that up. The difference is 4x in space.
86. **The hint window's real value** (§10.1; and now §9.1.3.5.2). 10 minutes is a guess; it should be
    derived from how far a
    tail-following consumer may lag before falling back to a key lookup.
87. **The SSD seek/scan break-even** (§7.1.1). It spans 4 KB to 320 KB across defensible assumptions —
    the widest uncertainty in the document, and it sets index density, compression block size, and the
    staging bypass threshold.
88. **How inline tiny object bodies are kept out of Compute-readable snapshots** (§12.8.4). Exclude them,
    or encrypt them under a key Compute lacks. §11 inlines them and §12.8 reads the snapshot on Compute.
89. **Padding versus size-binning for EC groups** (§4.3.2.3, §13.5.1). Whether an unfilled cell is padded
    to a fixed EC unit or matched by size offline, and what the residual waste is in §12.7's chain.
90. **What retires a snapshot schema version** (§13.5.5). Several jobs read one artifact, and old
    snapshots must stay readable by newer code; nothing says for how long.
91. **Whether the append-rate ceiling should be surfaced** (§8.1.1a-8). A single unkeyed object appends at
    ~200 MB/s. That is discoverable by benchmark and surprising if undocumented.

92. **Where recompression runs** (§7.2.2). It needs significant CPU *and* a node running only signed
    executables, and no machine type currently has both: ENs have no CPU budget, Compute runs user code.
    Since §10 makes compaction the home of recompression, EC re-encoding, key rotation, media migration and
    code promotion, this decides whether compaction is a background loop on an existing tier or a machine
    type of its own.
93. **What verifies executable signatures, and what happens when verification fails** (§1.5). Code signing
    is now load-bearing rather than operational: it is the entire justification for ENs holding keys. A
    machine that cannot verify its own executables must not receive keys, and nothing says how that is
    enforced or who notices.
94. **What is in the erasure-code catalog, and what each entry recommends itself for** (§4.3.2.5). Not
    "which code" — a list, with a few recommendations per use case, each justified by the fields §4.3.2.5
    enumerates. Turbo codes suffice for shipping, so this is not a release gate.
95. **What the batch API for small metadata requests looks like** (§1.4.0). Batching is known to work —
    batches of 1,000 are what produced the 2M QPS figure — so the question is not whether but how it is
    expressed: how a caller groups requests that may target different objects, different DNs, and different
    SNs; what partial failure means when 1,000 lookups share one message; and whether the batch is a client
    convenience or a wire-level primitive. §9.5's hedging interacts, since a batch's latency is the maximum
    over its members (§1.4.1) and one straggler delays a thousand answers.
96. **How much of the ~32,000 instruction-slots per batched lookup is real work** (§1.4.0, §1.4.0.1). The
    ping floor is under 1,000, so the gap is 32x — but the figure is wall-clock per request, and question 98
    may account for most of it as waiting on the log. If it does not, a random lookup over 20 M objects
    costing eighty cache misses' worth of time is worth understanding. Not blocking: the target is met.
97. **io_uring for EN-to-SSD** (§1.4.0.1). Untried, with a positive prior: deep queues of independent
    device reads is the case it is built for, and §7.1.1 expects §1.4's request pattern to keep SSD queues
    deep. Distinct from the network path, where batching already subsumed it.
98. **Whether the batched metadata path is CPU-bound or log-bound** (§1.4.0.1). At one durable write per
    1,000 requests, 2M QPS is 2,000 log writes/sec, so the ceiling may be the device rather than the CPU.
    Until this is known, the ~32,000 instruction-slots per request is an upper bound on work and not a
    measurement of it — and it decides whether question 96's headroom exists.

99. **Random-access memory efficiency, which every metadata bound rests on** (§1.6.2). The ~40M lookups/s
    ceiling assumes ~15% of peak bandwidth for random 64-byte access. That single assumption sets the
    denominator for every metadata fraction-of-bound figure in the document, so it should be measured on the
    actual box rather than believed.
100. **Writing down the essential work per operation** (§1.6.3). Fraction-of-bound means nothing until the
    numerator's denominator is defined: what a lookup, an append, a repair and a compaction *must* do. This
    is a documentation task with teeth — naming the essential work is what exposes the inessential — and it
    gates every measurement issue.

101. **`E`, the expected number of reads over an object's life** (§7.1.3). It is the term that decides
     whether compression pays for itself, it is a workload property rather than a hardware one, and nothing
     currently measures it. §13.5's snapshots are where it would come from, and §12.6.1 already argues the
     billing model is diagnostic of workload — so the data may already be there.
102. **Whether compression may run on ENs after all** (§7.1, §7.1.3, §7.2.1). §7.1 forbids it from a
     line-rate figure of ~21 cores, but each byte is compressed once cluster-wide by the primary
     (§8.1.4.1), which makes an EN's share ~0.1 of a core at the sustained fill rate. Either §7.1's rule
     restates as "not at line rate", or the sustained-rate case needs a reason it is wrong. This decides
     whether #22's missing compaction machine is needed for compression as well as for recompression.

103. **How promptly EC groups are formed** (§8.1.4.4). Common extents cannot be released until parity exists,
     so staging retention equals group-completion latency. Data accumulates in under a second, but §13.5.1
     forms groups in a daily job — which would need ~5.5 TB of staging per EN against the ~1.8 TB §8.1.4.5
     sizes for endurance. Prompt online grouping, more instances up front, or a bigger device: pick one.
104. **Whether regrouping is worth its parity rewrite** (§8.1.4.4, §13.5.1). If groups are formed promptly and
     optimized later, the optimization means recomputing parity over a whole group. That may cost more than
     the co-deletion and size-binning it buys.

105. **Which constants are functions of the cluster's chosen communication time** (§1.0.5). Diameter is a
     definition, not a bound — but §13.1's one-minute liveness loop, §9.5's timeouts, §5.7's election
     timeouts and §8.1.1's watermark round trip all assume round trips far below their own periods. Those
     assumptions should be collected and expressed against the chosen minimum communication time rather than
     left as constants that happen to work terrestrially.
106. **A cost model for a platform where mass and heat rejection are scarce** (§1.0.5.1). §1.2's basis is
     disk, electricity and rent; in orbit, power is abundant and launch mass and heat radiation bind. §12.1's
     principle is unaffected, which is the point of it being a principle — but §12.7's whole chain to a price
     per byte would need rebuilding. Not near-term unless StarMind is.
107. **Whether a read's latency tier is visible to the caller** (§1.0.3.1). §9.8's user-settable timeout is
     the actionable half — a caller can bound exposure without knowing the tier in advance — but it still
     cannot *choose* the fast path. Candidates: an advertised tier per object, or a fast-path-only mode that
     fails rather than waits. Note §9.8 already makes the latter nearly free, since a degraded read fails
     anyway.
108. **Whether a user-triggered whole-group repair is charged** (§9.8.1). A long timeout means one caller
     pays latency for work that benefits every future reader. Charged, unpriced, or credited — and if
     charged, it is the one read that is not flat.
109. **Whether §9.8's hot bump accumulates** (§9.8.1). A single +1 global read may leave a heavily-read
     degraded group below the bar, starving it while demand mounts. Accumulation makes read demand a real
     weight; no accumulation keeps §13.4's ordering bounded. A decaying accumulation is the obvious
     compromise and is not obviously right.

110. **How a scheduled EN decommission gets a deadline out of a threshold system** (§13.4.3.4). Every other
     repair purpose is "sooner is better"; vacating a machine that leaves on a date is not. Lowest door
     unconditionally, or a door that descends as the deadline approaches. This is the one admission-control
     mistake that loses data rather than delaying repair.
111. **The sufficient-bandwidth allocations, as a partition** (§13.4.3.4). Not independent knobs: if they sum
     above the total, the floors they appear to guarantee are nominal. Needs the list of purposes, their
     values, and a validator on the sum. §9.8's hot repair should be one of them (§13.4.3.5).
112. **The size of the repair allocation *A*** (§13.4.3.5). Doors at 1% and 9% remaining need *A* ≳ 100× the
     largest single repair cost, or a global solve jumps every door at once. That is ~5,200 outstanding units,
     ~166 GB in flight per SN, which is reachable only if repair operations complete slowly. Measure the
     completion latency before setting *A*.
113. **Whether the GC repair sweep and the verification sweep are one pass** (§13.4.3.3, §13.1.10). Both walk
     every extent and every EC group at ~20-200 s per SN. Two passes is twice the memory traffic for no
     benefit; fusing them couples loops with different natural cadences.

114. **What an SN does when the repair coordinator is unreachable** (§13.4.4.3). Falling back to the minimum is
     the safe answer, but only if the minimums sum within the cluster total — otherwise a coordinator outage
     oversubscribes the network. Needs the fallback rule and a validator on the sum.
115. **How stale a work report may be** (§13.4.4.3). Proportional shares are only as accurate as the sweep that
     discovers an SN's backlog, which is 20-200 s (§13.1.10). Tolerable for a slowly-moving level; possibly not
     at the onset of a disaster, which is when proportions change fastest and when getting them wrong costs the
     most.
116. **The values of the per-SN minimum and maximum** (§13.4.4). The minimum is bounded by the partition
     constraint above; the maximum is set by how much repair an SN can schedule before damaging its own
     foreground work, which is a measurement rather than a policy.

117. **Whether the bandwidth allocation must be multi-dimensional** (§13.4.5.1). Georeplication consumes WAN
     bandwidth plus one local write, where repair consumes the intra-cluster cross-section. A scalar bin cannot
     express "plenty of WAN, no local write bandwidth". Arbitrate a vector, or admit against the scarcer
     resource with the other as a constraint.
118. **Shared-extent billing** (§13.4.5.5b, §12.9). Already listed as open policy; georeplication failover makes
     it load-bearing, since immediately after a copy two objects reference one set of extents and they may belong
     to different tenants. Charging both double-bills, charging neither loses revenue, splitting requires knowing
     the sharers. Needed before georeplication ships.
119. **What georeplication's unit and policy are** (§13.4.5). Per object, per directory, or per stream; which
     clusters pair with which; whether replication is symmetric; and how a reader chooses a replica. None of
     this is designed, and it is now a ship gate.
120. **Whether compressed blocks ship as-is across clusters** (§13.4.5.2). They can when media classes match,
     saving WAN bandwidth; they cannot when they differ, since §7.4.2 makes compression block size durable and
     media-specific — which needs recompression, and §7.2.2 has nowhere to run it.

121. **Bill predictability under sharing** (§12.6.3.2). A tenant's charge falls when a stranger copies an object
     sharing their extents and rises when that stranger deletes. Total revenue is invariant so this is not a
     correctness problem, but §12.6 promises a simple presentation, and it has to survive a customer asking why
     their bill moved when they changed nothing.

122. **How a job's parallelism profile is obtained** (§5.12.4.1). "Fewest concurrent jobs that saturates" needs
     to know how wide each job can run, not just its total cost. Declared by the submitter, measured from
     history, or discovered by ramping — and a declared value is an adversarial input under §5.12.5's pricing.
123. **Overrun policy for the compute bank** (§5.12.5.1). Admission tests an estimate. Killing at the estimate
     makes estimation adversarial; unbounded debt invites abuse; letting the balance go negative and refusing new
     starts needs a bound on how negative.
124. **How large a simultaneous burst is acceptable** (§5.12.5.1a). Σ rates ≤ capacity settles solvency; Σ
     ceilings settles nothing about solvency and everything about the worst-case transient, which is served rather
     than refused but drains over `Σ ceilings / capacity`. That is a product decision about acceptable burst
     latency, not an arithmetic one.
125. **Feasibility checking for periodic reservations** (§5.12.6.1). Admitting one means finding the peak of a sum
     of periodic step functions, exact only over the least common multiple of all periods — large once hourly,
     daily and weekly mix. Quantize to a slot grid and check one LCM window, or restrict admissible periods to
     divisors of a day. The second is much cheaper and constrains the product.
126. **A cap on the reservable fraction of the cluster** (§5.12.6.2). At a peak instant best-effort work gets
     `cores − Σ scheduled(t)`, which may be zero, making the bank's accumulation rate briefly worthless. Bounding
     the reservable fraction fixes that and costs reservation revenue. Where the line goes is a product decision.

127. **Whether any object class needs guaranteed-prompt destruction** (§8.4.1b, §8.5.1b). §8.4.1b delays
     reclamation up to three days for soft delete and §8.5.1a's delete limit defers further under load, so
     DeLawson promises "not before" and not "not after". Compliance-driven deletion wants the opposite, and
     nothing says which class an object is in — plausibly the same distinction as the soft-delete opt-out. Note
     the dithering that originally motivated this question was rejected; the question survives on its own.
128. **How the compute spot price is computed and published** (§12.1.1.3). It must be derived from observable
     utilization and predictable enough to plan against, or it gives customers no way to shift load and fails at
     its only job. A published forward curve, a posted current rate, or an auction — and the choice determines
     whether §12.6's simple presentation survives.
129. **Where an object's ACL is fetched from** (§9.1.3.5, §5.1, §9.1; #81). It was a detail while every read
     walked the DN anyway; the hint capability makes it load-bearing, because it decides whether a hint
     saves two round trips or one. §5.1 puts an ACL reference in the DN's object record, which would keep
     the DN on the authorization path for ever; §9.1 counts the authorization hop separately from the DN
     hop, which implies it is held or cached elsewhere. One of the two has to give.
130. **The cluster-wide daily key the hint capability needs** (§9.1.3.5, §7.3; #82). §7.3's hierarchy is scoped
     by SN and day on purpose, so a key any FE can verify with is a new scope rather than an existing key
     reused. Small, but it needs a custody story of its own and it widens §7.3.1's blast radius argument.
131. **The snap rule's interaction with a record that spans extents** (§9.1.3.4, §8.2.3). Snapping forward
     is defined on record boundaries, and §8.2.3 lets a record span appends; whether a boundary search may
     have to cross into the next extent — and therefore onto another EN — decides whether resolving an
     offset start is one EN round trip or two.
132. **Whether the entry limit should be in entries or in bytes** (§9.1.3.7). Entries are what a caller can
     reason about and what the continuation is expressed in; bytes are what actually has to be bounded, and
     the two differ by whether an extent has 4 instances or 15 fragments after erasure coding (§4.3.2). The
     10,000 default is derived from a byte target, which is a hint that the byte form is the real one.
     §8.1.6.2 adds a wrinkle either way: whichever unit it is in, the limit is an index-and-count sharing one
     type, so its maximum is one or two below the type's.
133. **What the short extents from truncation-sealing cost an SN** (§7.2.4, §8.1.7.4, §14.1; #56, #83). Sealing on
     truncation is what turns the IV rule into an invariant, and it makes primary stability a driver of
     **extent count** — which is what bounds an SN's memory. Nothing yet says how often a handover
     happens, so nothing bounds the growth. #56 has to settle handover regardless; what is new is that
     handover frequency now lands in a second budget, and a flapping primary is a metadata cost and not
     only an availability one. §8.1.7.4 arrives at the same budget from a second direction: a single
     instance may request a seal, so a flapping EN can produce short extents across every extent it
     holds. The SN records every seal and is therefore where both are damped, but the threshold or rate
     limit is unchosen.

134. **What a partial seal answers** (§6.4.1). A keyed object with many unsealed extents may seal most and
     fail one. "Ok" is wrong, and a bare failure discards the work that succeeded. §9.1.3's shape — say what
     was done and what to ask for next — looks right, and idempotence is what makes retrying the whole
     request cheap, but neither the answer nor whether the operation is resumable is chosen. Unkeyed objects
     do not have the problem, since they have one open extent.

135. **Whether a certificate may name a bearer with no standing** (§5.9.1a, §9.1.3.5). ⚠️ **Narrowed by
     §9.1.3.5's revision**: the hint certificate now carries authorization for `(tenant, extent)`, so a
     bounded revocation lag is already accepted and "may a capability authorize" is answered yes. What
     remains is the harder half — sharing with an **outside party**, who is not the named tenant and has
     no ACL entry anywhere. That is S3's presigned URL, and it gives up the one thing tenant-binding
     still buys: a leaked certificate is useless to anyone else. So it wants a separate mechanism with
     its own name, and what is open is whether DeLawson wants the feature at all, who may issue one, and
     how issuance is audited.
136. **Whether a tenant needs any representation beyond a path** (§5.9.1a, §12). Nothing in
     authorization requires one once policy attaches to directories, which suggests "tenant" is a
     billing concept rather than a security one. But §12.8.3's quota accounting and §12.6.3's shared-cost
     division both talk about tenants as if they were entities, and whether a path with a quota and a
     bill attached is enough has not been checked against them.

137. **What a machine's identity actually is** (§7.3.2.2, §5.5.6.3, §1.5). §7.3.2.2's automatic recovery
     from quorum loss rests on "a quorum of those machines is up", which is meaningless if an attacker can
     stand up processes claiming to be members. So machine identity has to be cryptographically
     established — and the credential cannot be behind the key it is trying to obtain, which rules out
     the encrypted half of KS's own state. §5.5.6.3's signed half is the right home, and §1.5's code
     signing is adjacent and equally unspecified (#23), but nothing says whether identity is a per-machine
     keypair, hardware-backed attestation, or something issued at provisioning.

138. **Whether master keys are threshold-shared across the KS ring** (§7.3.2.7). It is the only
     structural answer to a tampered member being re-keyed automatically: shared k-of-n across members,
     one compromised machine leaks a share rather than every key. Affordable, because a key fetch is once
     per SN per day per EN (§7.3.1) rather than per request, so multiplying it by k participants costs
     messages where there is no throughput requirement — and it would want the same k as §7.3.2.5's
     recovery shards, since both ask how many custodians can be compromised at once. ⚠️ Against it: it
     puts subtle machinery in the component that must never be wrong, where a bug is unrecoverable in a
     way a bug elsewhere is not. If it is declined, §7.3.2.7's attack is an accepted risk whose controls
     are physical security, attestation and audit — none of them cryptographic.

139. **Where the `updatable` flag is declared, and what a shared stream does about it**
     (§9.1.3.9, §5.11.3.4). ✅ **The substance is settled**: streams carry flags, one of them disallows
     updates, and with tombstones retaining their original logical length the prefix sum is tail-only and
     may be exact — so a bare object offset becomes a descent rather than HDFS's walk (§9.1.3.8). What is
     left is placement. The guarantee is about an *object* while enforcement must be per *stream*, so the
     natural reading is declared at creation and carried onto every stream the object is given. §5.11.3.4
     lets a stream be shared, which leaves the awkward case: a shared stream with the flag set constrains
     every referrer, and one without it cannot serve an object that wants the guarantee. Also open, and
     more likely to be got wrong: **§10's compaction must preserve the widths of tombstoned records**, and
     the natural implementation closes the gaps instead — which is sharpest where §9.1.3.10's
     `deletable` cleanup pass *is* a compaction, so the two flags' cleanup passes have to agree
     and each one's obvious implementation violates the other.

140. **Which tier holds a stream's promise flags, and how the two are reconciled** (§4.1.2, §9.1.3.9,
     §13.1). Declaration is the object's business, so the DN's; enforcement and the cleanup pass are the
     SN's, since the SN owns the extents whose tombstones are compacted and whose lengths are summed. That
     puts one fact in two places, which §13.1.3's DN→SN loop then has to reconcile — and §13.1.7 fixes the
     loop inventory at one per tier boundary, so this needs to ride the existing loop rather than wanting
     a new one. Whether the cursor is purely SN-side, and what a reader is told while the two disagree,
     are both open.

141. ✅ **Where the coding rules live** — **answered: §18.** They now have a section, with four
     occupants: *make the logic simple* (§13.2.5.1, §4.1.1.0), *structural rather than careful*
     (§17.12.1), *make the compiler catch it* (§8.1.6.1) and *decompose the state* (§18.1). What remains
     open is only whether more are implicit and unnamed; the guess when the section was created was that
     it would have occupants immediately, and it had four.

142. **Why the same lookup benchmark differs 23% between sessions** (§17.19.2). Three trials back to back
     spread 0.6%; the same measurement four days apart differs by 23%, on one box, against builds proven
     equivalent, with the hit/miss defect explaining only 3% of it. Until something explains the rest, no
     cross-session performance comparison in this document is worth more than ±25% — which is wide enough
     to hide most of what §16's performance questions are asking about. The object count differed (17 M
     against 20 M, favouring the *newer* run), so the candidates are outside the code: CPU frequency
     behaviour, what else was on the box, page-cache and allocator state, or the object population's
     layout in memory (#88, and #87 for the run that failed partway). Worth pinning down because it
     sets the resolution of every measurement here.

143. **What protects the unlock verifier from a bit flip** (§7.3.2.8, §7.3.2.3). A corrupted verifier
     **rejects a correct key**, turning a recoverable outage into an apparently unrecoverable one — the worst
     direction for a check to fail in. It lives in the KS ring's snapshot and log, which is where a rare
     corruption sits unnoticed for years, and an orbital deployment makes bit flips a design input rather
     than a curiosity. ⚠️ Checking it against a copy is not the same operation as checking a key against
     it, so replication of the verifier needs its own answer: several copies and a vote, an error-correcting
     encoding, or accepting a key that matches *any* stored copy — which trades a false rejection for a
     weaker check.

144. **Which primitive signs a hint certificate** (§9.1.3.5.3, #93). The requirement is statable and the
     choice is not: an unforgeable tag over a short message, verifiable by any FE from a key it already
     holds, cheap on every hint read (§7.2.1 makes that easy), and versioned so it can change. ⚠️ Bob
     notes not knowing what the signing key would be nor what protocols are available. Two things that
     *were* part of this entry are now settled: §7.2.4's key-and-salt restriction is handled by the salt
     the certificate carries regardless, and read against write is **two keys selected by a plaintext
     flag** (§9.1.3.5.3). What is left is only the primitive — and the two-key form narrows it, since
     whatever is chosen has to be cheap to hold twice.

145. **Whether anything needs a security boundary within one tenant** (§9.1.3.5, §5.9.1a). The hint
     certificate binds the **tenant**, on Bob's judgement that no use case has an adversary inside one —
     which is an assumption, not a property of the model: §5.9.1a's directory ACLs name principals, so a
     tenant whose principals have different grants has an internal boundary the certificate would not
     enforce. ⚠️ **And it is load-bearing**: §8.1.1a-10's motivating case is a scheduler minting hints
     once and handing them to many vertices, which works because the binding is coarse. Narrowing to a
     principal enforces intra-tenant policy and costs that. So this stays open as *the price of the first
     use case that needs it*, and the answer will be to narrow the binding rather than to patch around it.

146. **Whether an alias may be appendable, and who pays if it is** (§5.1.1.3, §5.1.1, §12.6.3). Bob wants
     it for many workers sharing one object while each keeps private scratch, and it has a second argument
     nothing to do with that: it keeps the worker boundary *between* tenants, so §16.145's assumption
     holds and §9.1.3.5's certificate can go on binding the tenant. ⚠️ The sharp objection is billing —
     write access through an alias is spend authority on another tenant's quota, and an alias is
     deliberately not a counted reference, so §12.6.3 cannot attribute it. Either the owner accepts that,
     or an alias becomes something §12 can count and stops being free. And ⚠️ the case may not need it:
     §5.1.1.3 prices inverting the alias — private scratch, owner concatenates (§8.6.1) — which is faster,
     since shared appends meet §8.1.1a-8's one-disk ceiling. What decides it is whether the shared object
     needs **immediate** visibility or eventual assembly.

147. **Whether billing should count only canonical paths** (§5.1.1.1a, §12.6.3, §5.1.1.3). Bob leans yes:
     an alias is not a new set of references, so data written through one bills to the owner whose canonical
     path it sits under. That **computes** — an earlier draft wrongly said it could not — and what is open is
     whether it is the right policy, since granting write through an alias then means granting spend on your
     own quota. Note what canonical-paths-only still counts: several streams referencing one extent and
     several objects referencing one stream (§4.6.1) are genuine references and are divided by §12.6.3. It is
     only the alias that is not one.

148. **Whether `realpath` is a user-visible operation** (§5.1.1.1b, §5.1.1.1a). Canonical paths now decide
     who is billed and what the scrub examines, so *"what is the canonical path of this"* becomes a question
     with consequences — and POSIX exposes exactly that. ⚠️ Against it: a canonical path names a directory in
     **another tenant's** tree, so answering reveals structure the owner may not have shared. The likely
     resolution is a scoped answer — the canonical path as far as your own grants reach, and told that it
     continues — but that is a guess, and the leak is the reason to settle it before building it.
