149. **Whether the FE assembles a multi-DN batch, or the caller does** (§9.1.3.12, §9.1.3.2). The cheap
     round trip that §9.1.3.12 needs anyway produces exact counts for every name, and those let **either**
     party slice the remainder into requests that will each fit. The FE doing it suits a caller that wants
     one request and one answer; the caller doing it suits one with many batches in flight, which can
     pipeline across them and has the context to order the work. ⚠️ Note §9.1.3.1 named this as a problem
     with no fix — batch lookups cannot be pre-sliced because the answer size per object is what is being
     asked about — and the counts are the fix, for whichever party holds them. So the question is only who
     is served, not whether it can be done.

150. **A directory-wide object-info, which BatchObjectInfo is not** (§9.1.3.12). A batch carries an explicit
     list; enumerating a directory instead discovers names as it goes, so it cannot route or budget up
     front the way §9.1.3.12 does, and it inherits §5.1.1.1a's alias questions about what "everything in
     a directory" even means. Bob expects such a command eventually; it is not this one.

151. **What gives a batch name locality** (§17.24.5, #75). A hash spreads a batch over every DN by
     construction, so at a hundred DNs a hundred-name batch is 63 requests and batching has bought
     almost nothing — the thing §1.4.0 built it for. Contiguous ranges are the obvious answer, but they
     raise their own: a caller has to *know* to name things that land together, which means either the
     namespace shape leaks into the routing (a directory's objects share a DN, and a hot directory is
     then a hot DN) or the caller is given a way to ask. ⚠️ Note this is not fixed by §16.149's
     caller-side assembly — a caller sending D requests costs the FE tier D too, so it is more messages
     and not fewer. Locality is a routing property, not a fan-out one.

152. **What a shared stream's sizes mean for one object** (§17.25.1, §11). ⚠️ **Answered by
     §17.25.5**: nothing, and the case is load-bearing rather than an edge. Kept here because the
     storage shape that fixes it is still open, under §16.153. §11 lumps small objects
     into common streams, and a stream's totals are then the *stream's*, not any one object's — so a
     listing would report the same size for every object in the lump, wildly wrong for all of them.
     Per-object accounting inside a shared stream is a different thing to store and nobody has asked
     for it yet; the large-object case, which is what the system is for, is exactly served by the
     per-stream figures. ⚠️ Note the creation date does not have this problem: an object already
     carries its own.

153. **What the small-object regimes need from the metadata, and whether the tax is billed**
     (§17.25.5, §11, §12.2). Bob has settled the shape: the first append's seal flag decides the
     regime, once and for life — sealed means inline or a common-stream range by size, unsealed means
     a dedicated stream. The EN packs tiny appends regardless, and the SN rewrites small sealed
     objects, so a missing flag costs metadata and never data. Two things are open. **Where an inline
     object's size and creation second live**, since it has no stream to hang them on and the DN
     knows them exactly. And ⚠️ **whether the metadata tax is actually charged**: §12.2 prices a
     minimal stream at 300 B of SN RAM, 1.5 MB disk-equivalent, break-even at ~375 KB — and measures
     the 1 KB case as underbilled 375×, so today the tax falls on the operator. A flag whose omission
     costs the user nothing is a flag nobody sets.

154. **Whether lumped reads are row-limited, and what that costs in compression** (§17.26, §17.28).
     ⚠️ **Reframed**: the question was how to scope a common stream, and §17.28 finds the scoping
     already settled — streams are single-tenant (§5.11, §17.28.1), so that billing can charge whole
     extents rather than ranges of them, which has nothing to do with reads. What is actually open is §5.1.1.1a's boundary *inside* a
     tenant, and there the choice is row-limited reads (which force a block per object, so tiny
     objects compress alone) against an extent-scoped certificate (which forces a common stream per
     authorization domain). §17.28.3 proposes a shared per-stream compression dictionary as the way
     to have both, and names the two things to check: the client must fetch the dictionary, and a
     dictionary leaks statistics about what trained it.

156. **How a batch create says which names it did not make** (§17.31.1). Its answer is a count, so a
     caller learns how many objects were newly made and not which — and cannot distinguish a name
     that already existed from one that failed. One DN made that tolerable; several make it worse,
     and the current answer is to fail the whole batch on any DN's refusal. ⚠️ A header of the shape
     `batch-object-info` grew (§17.23) would fix it — asked, made, and an index — but a create's
     natural unit is the name rather than the entry, so it is not the same header.

**Closed** since earlier drafts:

- how frequently DN metadata is resident in RAM — it does not need measuring, because the inline
  cutoff is taken at its limit and the limit is the safe end (§17.27, §17.25.6);
- the unkeyed overwrite/addressing contradiction (§3);
- logical vs physical extent size, which is compression (§6);
- the metadata topology, now three explicit node types (§5);
- whether the DN tier is self-hosted — it is, with a bootstrap root (§5.5);
- where the bootstrap root lives — DN0's Raft persistent state, since ring state is made
  durable by Raft rather than by DeLawson (§5.5.1);
- whether summary maintenance can run away under self-hosting — it cannot, by
  the tail-only rule (§4.5, §5.5.2);
- the hedging percentile — p99.9 or beyond, from the throughput priority (§1.4.1);
- whether DeLawson needs co-partitioning affinity — it does not, because the intra-cluster
  network is flat and affinity only avoids network (§5.12.3);
- whether `count` is exact and cheap — exact and synchronous for unkeyed
  objects, lazy for keyed ones, again by §4.5;
- the supposed 32 MB-vs-large-streams tension, based on a wrong constraint
  (§14.4);
- who may authorize deleting a stream — the `DnId` is part of the stream's name, so
  there is exactly one owning DN by construction (§4.6.3);
- whether key derivation survives stream reassignment — it does, because the extent
  names its creating SN and its creation day (§4.6.3, §7.3.3);
- which offset an append may report — it follows from the object flavour, and
  compare-and-append is therefore unkeyed-only (§8.1.1a-7);
- whether to defer the object offset until sealing — no; no system does it, and the
  reasons are structural, not merely conventional (§8.1.1a-9);
- how zero-width fixed-length rows break the fixed-offset check — they no longer do,
  because offsets are assigned in a canonical length-stuffed space (§8.2.2);
- whether logical offsets survive re-framing during coalescing — they do, for the same
  reason (§8.2.2, §8.2.1);
- whether EC splits extents into fragments — it does not, so reads never touch EC
  (§4.3.2.3);
- whether an all-SSD fleet changes the codec choice — it does not, because repair
  bandwidth is network-bound either way (§4.3.2.2a);
- whether mixed-media extents are supported — they are not, because compression block
  size is a durable property and EC needs byte-identical instances (§7.4.2);
- what the minimum viable cluster is — one machine, because an unenforceable placement
  rule is simply not enforced (§5.6.7);
- whether toggling a placement rule across its threshold causes churn — it cannot,
  because placement is never revisited (§5.6.7);
- whether placement needs a general solver on the common path — no; the solution is
  persisted in the instance list order and the steady state is verification (§5.6.9);
- what the 4/3 slack is for — cheap solving and routing around bad domains, not a
  durability reserve (§5.6.1a);
- whether EC verification fits a one-minute loop — only incrementally; the unconditional
  pass rides the hourly instance sync (§13.1.10);
- how the repair work list is found when an EN is dead and cannot report — by a scan
  bucketed by EN, needing no reverse index (§13.1.10.1);
- whether the fast loop needs a re-replication timeout — it does not, since
  unavailability duration is a priority input (§13.4.2);
- whether billing may read live metadata — it may not; reproducibility requires an
  immutable retained input (§12.8);
- whether daily snapshots make storage billing a sampling exploit — they do not, because
  soft delete outlasts the interval, provided the opt-out still leaves a tombstone
  (§12.8.2);
- whether SN knows an extent's sealed physical size — it must, for three independent
  reasons (§13.5.1);
- where decryption happens — **on the EN** (§5.9.2), which is licensed by §1.5's real
  boundary: keys live where the executables are signed, and ENs run no user code;
- whether ENs need keys at all — they do, and they cache SN-master keys and derive extent
  keys from the creation timestamp, as §7.3 already had it (§5.9.2, §7.3.1);
- whether end-to-end encryption is offered — not by DeLawson, but users may encrypt
  before sending and pay for it in physical bytes (§7.2.3);
- which AEAD, and whether encryption fits the EN's CPU budget — AEGIS-128X2 at ~20 GB/s
  per core, so line-rate encryption is 0.63 of a core where compression would be ~21
  (§7.2.1); KS uses 256-bit;
- whether a separate checksum layer is needed — no, the AEAD tag is the checksum, and it
  makes every stored block self-verifying before EC uses it as a repair source (§7.2.1);
- whether staging may live in DRAM — no; durable means durable with the power off, which
  also removes the motive for power as an explicit failure domain (§8.1.4.5);
- whether the erasure code is a single choice — it is a **catalog** with recommendations,
  and turbo codes suffice for shipping, so the patent is not a release gate (§4.3.2.5);
- whether reads should be billed by latency tier — mostly moot: §9.8 removes the expensive
  read entirely, so read billing can stay flat (§9.8.1);
- what a read does when a cell needs reconstruction — it does **not** reconstruct; it repairs
  the whole group if the timeout allows, else flags the group hot and fails (§9.8);
- what the portable, user-visible durable name is — the **path**, since `DnId` and `SnId` are
  cluster-local and cannot survive georeplication (§4.6.3, §13.4.5.3);
- how a replica avoids colliding with the destination's local namespace — a **dedicated
  directory** per source, making cross-cluster translation one prefix substitution (§13.4.5.4);
- whether a replica is ever promoted in place — **no**; georep directories stay read-only
  permanently, and a writable version is made by copy-by-concatenation (§13.4.5.4, §13.4.5.5);
- how a promoted replica avoids offset-level split brain — the question does not arise, since
  nothing is promoted (§13.4.5.4);
- whether copy-on-write needs new machinery — it does not: a shared sealed base plus a private
  log is §4.2 (§13.4.5.5);
- how a shared extent is billed — **cost divided by the number of billed references**, exactly,
  with each sharer paying its own reference's metadata cost in full (§12.6.3, §12.6.3.1);
- whether cross-tenant sharing can be gamed to cut a bill — it cannot; total revenue is invariant
  under any regrouping of references (§12.6.3);
- how DN finds what to expire, given metadata on disk — a **secondary keyed index on expiry
  second**, scanned by prefix; the heap-refilled-by-sweep alternative lost on a correctness hole
  (§8.5.1b, §8.5.1b.0);
- whether hard deletes should be dithered to flatten the midnight spike — **no**; the
  outstanding-delete limit defers under load and costs nothing when idle (§8.5.1a);
- whether the several deletion smoothers might compound — moot, there is now only one (§8.5.1b.2);
- whether the throughput targets are per box or per cluster — **per box**, and both have
  already been reached on this box, so they are a floor rather than a stretch (§1.4.0);
- whether the 200k/2M pair is two requirements or one — one, on messaging: the 10x gap
  says nine tenths of the unbatched cost is per-message overhead (§1.4.0);
- whether io_uring is wanted for the network path — **no**; batching amortizes the same
  syscall overhead, gave all the gains, and io_uring measured as a regression (§1.4.0.1);
- whether the measured throughput figures were in-memory-only — they were not: they include
  a durable log write per message, encryption, and message compression (§1.4.0.1);
- where initial compression happens — in the **`delawson` client library**, which is DeLawson
  code, so it is upstream of the internet link and costs the cluster nothing (§8.1.4.1);
- whether four dedicated replicas are written before EC — no; the four ENs' common extents
  are the protection, and migration writes only the 1 or 2 instances the scheme needs
  (§4.3, §8.1.4.4);
- whether recompression must be deterministic across instances — no, because exactly one node
  performs it and the second instance is a byte copy (§8.1.4.4);
- why a read request would be logged at all — because §12 requires metering request rate,
  so the log write is the billing record rather than overhead (§1.4.0.3);
- whether a read may name only an extent — **no**; the ACL is the object's and no reverse edge
  recovers it, so every read names the object and a narrowing is an optimization on top (§9.1.3.4);
- whether putting the stream in a hint makes it authorizable — **no**, and §4.6.6 said so wrongly:
  an asserted pairing is only as good as the caller, and `stream → object` is still the DN's
  (§9.1.3.5, §4.6.6);
- what binds a hint to an extent — an unforgeable **certificate** over `(tenant, extent, write?)`,
  verified at the FE, with the directory's policy read when it is **minted** rather than when it is used
  (§9.1.3.5);
- whether a hint may be opaque — **no**; it stays plaintext with the capability appended, so an
  operator can act on a hint quoted in a bug report (§9.1.3.5);
- which space a range budget is in — the caller picks one of **records, logical bytes or compressed
  bytes**, and the answer reports all three (§9.1.3.6);
- what a budget smaller than one block returns — **one block**, since anything else is a livelock;
  the overshoot is bounded and reported (§9.1.3.6);
- whether extent detail wants an operation of its own — **no**; the entry limit makes it opt-in, so
  `object-info` is extended instead (§9.1.3.7, #61);
- whether an extent offset may be written twice — **no, ever**, because key-and-IV reuse over
  different plaintexts is catastrophic rather than degrading, so **a truncation seals the extent**
  (§7.2.4, §8.1.1a);
- whether the IV should carry a truncation epoch instead — **no**; it would need agreement across
  instances in the write path, and a missed bump fails silently, where sealing cannot be violated
  by anything (§7.2.4).

---

## 17. The implementation, as it stands

Implementation began 2026-08-16 with two processes — the `laws` client and KS — plus the
`common` library they share, checked-in configuration, and a single-box harness. This
section records the decisions that writing them forced, which §5 and §7 did not specify.

### 17.1 Layout

| Directory | What it is |
|---|---|
| `common/` | configuration, wire protocol, daemon lifecycle, placement-rule report |
| `laws/` | the client: a CLI over a library, holding no persistent state |
| `ks/` | the Key Store daemon; the template the other machine types are copied from |
| `config/` | the checked-in cluster and per-service configuration |
| `scripts/` | `start-laws`, `stop-laws`, `bench-laws` |
| `run/` | created by `start-laws`, one directory per process, not checked in |

DN, SN, EN and FE do not exist yet. A client command with no service to reach fails locally
saying so, rather than pretending.

### 17.2 Configuration is three layers

- **Cluster** — one file, identical fleet-wide: KS's address and the port base, the
  failure-domain levels, ring size, timeouts, the roster, and the per-media-class table of
  §7.4.1. The roster says *who may exist* — identity, kind, failure domain, media class —
  and carries no addresses.
- **Service** — one file per machine type, holding only what that type owns.
- **Process** — one small file per process, written by `start-laws`, saying who the process
  is, which port it was given, and where the other two files are.

Two decisions inside that:

- **Identity and port come from the process file, not from argv.** A process's whole
  assignment is then one file that a harness or a deployment system writes, and nothing
  depends on how it was invoked. The only command-line argument any daemon takes is the path
  to that file.
- **No process's address is checked in except KS's.** Whatever starts a process hands it a
  port; the process announces that port to KS and asks KS where its peers are (§17.7). So an
  address exists in exactly one place at a time and two copies cannot disagree.

### 17.3 Lifecycle: ready is a file, stopping is a request

- **Ready means the `ready` file exists**, written after the listener is accepting, holding
  the pid and the bound address. That is the whole readiness contract, and it is what the
  harness waits on.
- **Stopping is a request, not a signal.** `stop-laws` sends `shutdown` so that a process with
  state to flush gets the chance, and escalates to `SIGTERM` then `SIGKILL` only for one that
  will not answer. It works on either build flavour because it stops processes by pid.
- **Cold start order is by machine type** — KS, DN, SN, EN, FE — which is §5.5.1.1's order,
  and shutdown is its reverse.

### 17.4 Every call is asynchronous

**Decided: nothing in any service is lock-step** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-16). A request carries
a 32-bit id and a response echoes it, so a caller may keep any number of requests outstanding
on one connection and a service may answer them in whatever order it finishes them. Whole
frames are written under one lock, so frames never interleave.

**Asynchrony is what makes transport coalescing possible**, which is where the throughput comes
from (§17.5): if a caller could have only one request outstanding there would never be two messages
pending to carry in one syscall. So ids are not a convenience, they are the mechanism.

**Where an answer is computed is per message type, and it is a measurement rather than a
decision** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-16). Handing a request to a worker costs a queue hop and a
wakeup; answering it on the connection's read loop stalls the next read for as long as it
takes. Ping is cheap enough that inline plainly wins and is what the code does; anything that
touches a disk plainly does not. The middle is unknown, so it is a per-operation knob.

**Measured, 2026-08-16**, by flipping that knob for ping (`inline_ping`) against the other half of
the question — who decides when to send (`batch_sender`). Round trips per second:

| Shape | Read loop, direct | Read loop, sender | Worker, sender | Worker, direct |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 conn, 1 in flight | **59,900** | 47,700 | 36,100 | 40,600 |
| 1 conn, 64 in flight | 1,651,000 | **1,784,000** | 1,158,000 | 123,000 |
| 8 conns, 64 in flight | **6,633,000** | 4,381,000 | 2,535,000 | 240,000 |
| 16 conns, 256 in flight | **12,399,000** | 8,407,000 | 2,906,000 | 211,000 |

Two designs are crossed there. **A batching sender** is a thread per connection that loops: write
everything queued, and let the next batch be whatever piled up while that write was in flight. It is
self-clocking — batch size rises with load and falls to one when idle, with no timer and nothing to
tune. **Direct** means whoever produced the answer writes it, and flushes when it knows nothing more
is in hand.

What the four columns say:

- **Answers produced off the read loop need a sender.** A worker cannot see what else has arrived, so
  writing its own answer means one syscall per message — the worker/direct column is flat near 200k
  however much load arrives. Give those answers to a sender and the same work reaches 2.9M, **14x**.
- **Answers produced on the read loop do not.** The read loop already knows when nothing more is in
  hand, so a sender only adds a queue hop and a thread: 12.4M becomes 8.4M.
- **Except when threads are idle.** At one connection the sender wins (1.78M against 1.65M), because
  it puts framing and writing on a second core while the read loop parses. It loses once connections
  outnumber cores.
- **The hop itself is ~8 µs**, from the top row where there is nothing to coalesce.

> **The dispatch decision is not "threads or an async runtime". It is whether the design still lets
> answers pile up before they are sent.**

Anything that hands each message to a scheduler and writes each answer when it completes pays the
worker/direct column, whatever the scheduler is.

**So the policy is adaptive, and it is the default: a connection writes directly until an answer is
produced off its read loop, and hands its writer to a sender from then on.** The read loop knows at
dispatch which it is about to do and is the only thread that switches, so the switch needs no
agreement with anyone — it happens before the first off-loop answer exists. Anything already
buffered is flushed before the writer moves, so the switch cannot reorder answers. In the steady
state it costs one relaxed load per answer:

| Shape | Adaptive, nothing leaves the read loop | Direct | Adaptive, everything leaves it | Sender |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 conn, 1 in flight | 60,200 | 60,400 | 36,300 | 35,500 |
| 1 conn, 64 in flight | 1,677,000 | 1,669,000 | 1,143,000 | 1,148,000 |
| 8 conns, 64 in flight | 6,675,000 | 6,623,000 | 2,551,000 | 2,592,000 |
| 16 conns, 256 in flight | **12,661,000** | 12,633,000 | **3,059,000** | 3,070,000 |

**Measured, 2026-08-16.** Adaptive lands on whichever fixed policy is the right one, within noise,
and KS reports how many connections switched — 0 in the left pair, one per connection in the right.

**Connections scale to the core count and then stop**, which is where this box's ceiling is. At 256
in flight each, with ping answered on the read loop:

| Connections | 4 | 8 | 16 | 24 | 32 | 48 | 64 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Round trips/s | 6,746,000 | 9,463,000 | **12,658,000** | 12,470,000 | 12,266,000 | 12,191,000 | 12,120,000 |
| Average latency | 152 µs | 216 µs | 323 µs | 492 µs | 667 µs | 1,007 µs | 1,350 µs |

**Measured, 2026-08-16.** 4 to 16 is close to linear; past 16 — this box has 16 cores — throughput is
flat and latency grows in proportion to the connection count, which is a queue getting longer and
nothing else. The server's own accounting agrees that nothing degrades: **0.58 µs of core per message
at 16 connections and 0.60 µs at 32**, so the same work is being done, there is simply no more
machine. KS took ~7 cores of the 16 and the client the rest, so ⚠️ **the knee at 16 is the box, not
the design, and it cannot be attributed to either side until the client runs elsewhere.**

⚠️ **The switch is one-way, so one off-loop answer commits the connection for its lifetime.** A
connection that does a single metadata lookup and then a million pings runs the rest at sender speed,
which the table above prices at about 30% off direct. Switching back would mean quiescing the sender
to take the writer from it, which is real work for a case nobody has yet.

**A third of the message path was allocation.** Framing a message allocated twice — once to encode
the body, once to prefix the length — and answering allocated a third time. Encoding into a
thread-local scratch buffer and backfilling the length instead was worth **58%** at 16 x 256
(7.9M to 12.4M) and helped every column. Worth stating because it is the shape of most of what is
left: the message path is short enough that an allocation is a large fraction of it.

### 17.5 The first measurements: a ping to KS0

Loopback TCP, this box (16 cores, client and server both on it), release build, `bench-laws`, ping
answered on the connection's read loop. A ping asks for a reply of a stated size, filled with random
bytes, so **message size is a knob rather than a constant** — zeros would let compression and a
page-sharing kernel cheat, and a per-reply generator would measure the generator, so one random
block is made at first use and replies are slices of it.

**Batching here means per-connection coalescing at the transport, not a batch message.** Every
request is separate and independently answerable; what changes is how many are pending when a
syscall happens. Both sides buffer and flush when they have nothing left to answer or to read, which
adds no latency: the flush happens exactly where the alternative was to block. Nagle stays off,
because the decision of when to send is made in DeLawson and not in the kernel.

Requests in flight per connection, against connections:

| Connections | 1 in flight | 8 | 64 | 256 | 1,024 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 59,000 | 396,000 | **1,483,000** | 2,088,000 | 2,393,000 |
| 8 | 244,000 | 1,635,000 | 5,471,000 | 7,015,000 | |
| 16 | | 2,644,000 | 6,446,000 | 8,185,000 | |
| 32 | | | 7,297,000 | | |

Round trips per second. **Measured, 2026-08-16**, before §17.4's allocation fix, which later lifted
the 16 x 256 corner to 12.4M; the shape is what matters here, not the absolute numbers. What it
says:

- **Depth is worth 25x on one connection**, 59k to 1.48M, with average latency going 17 µs to 43 µs.
  Nothing about the work changed; the only difference is how many messages a syscall carries.
- **One connection at 64 in flight reaches the prototype's ~1.4M ping** (§1.4.0). That is the bar,
  and coalescing is what clears it.
- **More connections still help on this box**, to ~8.2M at 16 x 256 — which qualifies an earlier
  expectation that one connection per address was optimal because it batched most. Depth is indeed
  what matters most, and a single connection gets most of the way, but it does not win outright
  here. ⚠️ The client is on the same box as the server, so every client thread costs a core the
  server could have used; the honest reading is that this box saturates around 7-8M with either
  shape, and which is optimal cannot be settled without the two on separate machines.
- **Latency is the price and it is proportional**: at 16 x 256 the average is 500 µs. §1.4 wants
  throughput first, so that is the right trade, but it is a queue and it should be sized as one.

**The 8.4M corner of that table was checked rather than trusted**, because it is six times the prototype's ping and
a surprise in the favourable direction deserves more suspicion than a disappointment does. KS counts
the requests it answers, and over a 1 s warm-up plus 3 s measured run it answered 33.97M against the
client's 25.3M measured — the difference being one warm-up second at the same rate. So the messages
are real and the arithmetic is right.

What it cost, from the KS process's own CPU accounting: **27.5 s of core time for 34M messages, or
0.81 µs of server core per message** — about 2,400 cycles at 3 GHz. Against §1.4.0's instruction
budget that is a few thousand instructions of *message path* per message, versus the < 1,000 that
the ping's actual work costs. The server used ~6.5 of 16 cores; the 16 client threads used most of
the rest, which is more evidence for §17.5's caveat that the client is the co-resident cost.

⚠️ **This is not the prototype's ping, and the gap is mostly things this one does not do.** §1.4.0.1
records that the measured prototype path included a durable log write per message batch, encryption,
and message compression. None of those are here yet. So the honest claim is narrow: **the message
path alone, stripped of everything that will later share it, costs about 0.8 µs of core per message
and reaches millions per second.** Expect that number to get worse as the omitted work returns, and
treat 8.4M as a ceiling on this box rather than a result to defend.

**But logging and encryption were not the majority of the prototype's cost** (Asserted, Bob,
2026-08-16), which leaves the 6x mostly unexplained by omitted work. Bob's own guess is the async
runtime: that prototype was Rust on Linux **using tokio**, and this is not. §17.4's measurement is
the part of that guess this box can test — dispatching each ping through a worker instead of
answering it on the read loop caps throughput at ~200k, a 38x loss, because a scheduled handler
flushes its own answer and the connection stops coalescing. That is the same shape a task-per-message
runtime has by default. It is evidence for the hypothesis and not a verdict on tokio, whose scheduler
is far better than the one measured here; what it does establish is that **per-message dispatch, not
the work, is what a small request pays for.**

Then message size, holding 64 in flight:

| Reply bytes | 1 connection | body MB/s | 8 connections | body MB/s |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 1,483,000 | — | 5,471,000 | — |
| 1,024 | 952,000 | 974 | 1,710,000 | 1,751 |

And with one request in flight, where the round trip is the whole cost:

| Reply bytes | Round trips/s | Average latency | body MB/s |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 55,800 | 18 µs | — |
| 64 | 54,600 | 18 µs | 3 |
| 1,024 | 54,200 | 18 µs | 56 |
| 8,192 | 40,300 | 25 µs | 330 |
| 65,536 | 9,900 | 101 µs | 650 |
| 524,288 | 1,400 | 721 µs | 726 |

**`M`, the per-message overhead, is 15-18 µs** unbatched — the ~15 µs issue #5 calibrated for a
*Unix-domain socket*, not the ~40 µs it guessed for TCP loopback. **Size is free to about a
kilobyte** and costs from there: 8 KB costs 28% of the round-trip rate and past that it falls roughly
as 1/size, so the cost model turns from per-message to per-byte somewhere between 1 and 8 KB. That is
the number to know before choosing any granule or batch size.

### 17.5a Every message is encrypted, and batches are the unit

**Decided: everything sent is encrypted, and the unit of sealing is the batch**
(Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-16). Not the message: whatever one write carries is compressed and
encrypted together, so a nonce, a tag and a compression attempt are paid per write rather than per
message — and a batch of small messages has repetition that no one of them has.

What goes on the wire is therefore a segment:

```
u32 length | u64 counter | AEGIS-128X2( u8 form | [u32 length | message]... )
```

- **The cipher is AEGIS-128X2**, which §7.2.1 already chose for extents and messages both.
- **The nonce is a connection prefix, a direction byte, and the segment counter.** The connecting
  side picks the prefix and states it before anything is sealed; the direction byte is why one
  prefix suffices for both ways. No two segments under one key can then share a nonce.
- **The length and counter are authenticated** as associated data although they travel in the
  clear, and a segment that arrives out of order does not open — the counter must be the expected
  one.
- **Compress before encrypt**, for the reason §7 gives: ciphertext does not compress. The form byte
  says which was done, and it is inside the sealed region.
- ⚠️ **The key is currently one pre-shared test key in the cluster configuration.** That is a
  stand-in, not a hierarchy: KS handing out message keys is what replaces it, and until then a
  cluster's processes all share one key.

#### 17.5b What encryption and compression cost

Release build, loopback, this box. "Round trips" is per second; "wire" is how much smaller the sealed
bytes were than the plain ones, which KS counts.

| Shape | Plain | Encrypted | Encrypted + lz4 | Wire, with lz4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 16 conns x 256, bare ping | 14,381,000 | 14,423,000 | 13,024,000 | **5.5x smaller** |
| 8 x 64, 1 KB random reply | 3,080,000 | 2,565,000 | 1,566,000 | 1.0x |
| 8 x 64, 1 KB repetitive reply | 2,897,000 | 2,807,000 | **3,379,000** | 93.6x smaller |
| 8 x 64, 16 KB random reply | 76,200 | 60,600 | 54,500 | 1.0x |
| 8 x 64, 16 KB repetitive reply | 78,500 | 61,200 | **146,700** | 230.2x smaller |

**Measured, 2026-08-16.** Four things worth keeping:

- **Encryption is free on small messages and costs about 20% on large ones.** A bare ping is
  unchanged inside the noise; a 16 KB body drops from 1,249 to 992 MB/s. Both ends run on this box,
  so that is a sealing *and* an opening — AEGIS is doing roughly 10 GB/s per direction, which is
  what §7.2.1 assumed when it called encryption nearly free.
- **Headers compress even when bodies cannot** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-16). A batch of bare pings
  is almost entirely framing and identity, and it compresses **5.5x** — with no user data in it at
  all. That is the case for compressing batches rather than messages, in one number.
- **Compressible bodies pay for themselves twice over**: 230x less wire and 2.4x the throughput at
  16 KB, because bytes not sent are also bytes not copied.
- ⚠️ **A failed compression attempt is expensive.** With random 1 KB bodies, lz4 finds nothing and
  costs **39%** of throughput for it. So compression is not a switch that is simply left on — it
  samples first.

#### 17.5c Sampling: judge a batch by pieces of it, from end to end

**A large batch is judged before it is compressed.** A few kilobytes are taken from it, compressed,
and the rest is attempted only if that much shrank. Two rules make it worth doing:

- **Only when the sample is small against the batch** — an eighth or less. A wasted sample then
  costs an eighth of the attempt it was meant to avoid, and a batch smaller than that is cheap
  enough to compress outright.
- **The sample is several pieces spread from the first byte to the last**, not a prefix. A batch is
  whatever happened to be pending, and it will hold a mixture of message kinds; a prefix judges all
  of it by whichever arrived first (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-16). The pieces are concatenated, which
  hides redundancy spanning the gaps between them, so the sampler is pessimistic rather than
  optimistic — the safe direction.

| Shape | No compression | lz4, always | lz4, sampled | Wire |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 16 conns x 256, bare ping | 14,353,000 | 13,187,000 | 13,166,000 | 5.5x smaller |
| 8 x 64, 1 KB random | 2,741,000 | 1,546,000 | **2,477,000** | 1.0x |
| 8 x 64, 1 KB repetitive | 2,808,000 | 3,302,000 | 3,256,000 | 93.8x smaller |
| 8 x 64, 16 KB random | 60,700 | 54,900 | **60,600** | 1.0x |
| 8 x 64, 16 KB repetitive | 61,200 | 141,500 | 141,000 | 230.2x smaller |

**Measured, 2026-08-16.** Sampling gives back nearly all of what a failed attempt cost — the 16 KB
random case is back to the no-compression rate exactly, and the 1 KB case is within 10%, which is
the sample itself at 4 KB against a 64 KB batch — while keeping the whole of the gain where there is
something to find.

**Decided: compression is on by default** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-16). What the table shows on
loopback is the worst case for that choice, because loopback makes bytes nearly free and CPU the only
scarce thing — and even there the cost of leaving it on is 8% on bare pings and nothing at all on
large incompressible replies, against 5.5x to 230x fewer bytes when there is anything to find. On a
real network those bytes are the scarce resource, so the balance only improves. ⚠️ The residual 10%
on 1 KB incompressible bodies is the sample itself, and it is the number to watch if a workload
turns out to be mostly small and mostly incompressible.

**What the padding cost had to be measured separately**, because a reply body has to come from
somewhere: the generator runs at **10.2 GB/s** producing words and **11.1 GB/s** filling a buffer,
which is 0.78 ns per 8 bytes and 1.5 µs for a 16 KB body. Worth knowing before reading any
large-reply number as a measurement of the wire.

⚠️ **Three measurement flaws found while getting here, all of which flattered compression.** Reply
padding was a slice of one block, so every reply was the same bytes and a batch of them compressed
41x; giving each reply a different offset made them overlapping windows, which also compressed; and
the repetitive padding was built a byte at a time, which measured the loop rather than the wire. The
rule that fell out: **a benchmark's own inputs need the same suspicion as its outputs**, and the
check that caught it was counting bytes in and bytes out rather than trusting the throughput.

### 17.5d Logging: two files, and a histogram deciding what reaches the second

Every process writes two rotating logs into its run directory:

| | Carries | Reaches back |
|---|---|---|
| `ks0-0000000.log` | every line | hours |
| `ks0-info-0000000.log` | a target share of them, a tenth by default | days |

Both are configured by size and count, oldest deleted; the same bytes therefore cover a much longer
span in the info log, which is the point of having two.

A line is:

```
n,2026-08-16 23:31:32.538104,pid=64967,tid=64967,file=common/src/server.rs,line=360,listening,address 127.0.0.1:9601 workers 16
```

Level as one letter, the time to the microsecond in UTC, the process and kernel thread ids, where in
the source it came from, and then **two messages: a constant and the values**
(Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-16). The constant is what a histogram groups on, exactly, so grouping needs
no guess about where the words stop and the values start — which is what grouping on a prefix of a
rendered message could never do. `logi!("answered", "op {} status {} …", …)`, and the constant may not
contain a comma, since it is a field. **The identity, host and version are written at the top of
every file** rather than on every line, so a rotated file still says what it is. **Kernel thread id
rather than a name**, so a line matches what `perf`, `gdb` and `top` say.

⚠️ **There is no request id on the line, and there should not be** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-16).
Only code serving a request has one; a compaction, a sync loop or a repair does not, so a fixed
field would be empty for most of what a storage system does. Where a line belongs to a request, the
id goes in the message with the rest of that line's values.

**Separate the values with commas as well**, and order them low-cardinality first — the low ones are
what a reader greps for. The file's first line is the same shape, at level `h` with constant `opened`,
so nothing reading a log needs a special case for it.

**How much reaches the info log is a rate, not a rule about levels.** A running histogram counts
each site; rare sites pass through whole, and the busy ones are sampled at a stride recomputed so
the total comes out near the target share. Sampling rather than suppressing means the info log still
shows what the busy traffic looks like. Counts are halved at each recount, so the answer follows the
workload rather than being set by whatever happened first.

**A third kind of line: at most one a second, whichever message got there first, carrying how many
times the site said nothing.** For a place that would otherwise say the same thing millions of times,
a sample says what is happening and the count says how much of it there was:

```
n,…,line=783,pinged,reply size 0,skipped 2252071
n,…,line=783,pinged,reply size 0,skipped 2296037
```

It logs at `notice` — being rate-limited already, it is not the chatty kind. The count is a value, so
the histogram takes no notice of it, which is right: what varies per line is not what a kind is
grouped by.

⚠️ **The count is one shared counter, and an earlier version of this section claimed that would be too
expensive.** It is not: measured with everything else held still, per-thread counters gave 12.83M round
trips a second against 12.71M for one shared relaxed increment — a difference inside the noise, at 13
million calls a second on sixteen cores. The per-thread machinery was written, measured, and deleted.
What had looked like its cost was the per-request `answered` line, which the ping path also goes
through; attributing a 6x drop to the counter was a guess, and the guess was wrong.

#### 17.5d.1 Many lines in the code, few in the log

**Write a new line at `notice`, and demote it only once a histogram proves it noisy**
(Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-16). The aim is *more* logging sites in the code and *fewer* lines in the log,
and those are compatible because most sites are rare — so the levels are a demotion path rather than a
taxonomy:

| Level | Where a line goes | What it means |
|---|---|---|
| `notice` | both logs, always | where every line starts |
| `info` | the full log, sampled into the info log | proven noisy once |
| `debug` | nowhere, unless the level is turned down | proven ruinous |

**The pass is periodic and cheap**: every year or so, run the histogram, look at the top of it, and
demote what is loudest. The rows carry the level, the file and the line, so the histogram is both the
evidence and the worklist — and demotion to `info` does not lose the line, it only stops it filling the
log that is kept for days.

Today that has happened exactly twice, which is the discipline working: the per-request `answered` line
is `info` because it was measured at 270,000 in a run, and the ping's line is `debug` because it cost
85% of throughput. Everything else — including a *failed* answer, which is rare and wanted — is
`notice`. The consequence is the right shape for the log that lives longest: **the info log keeps every
problem and a sample of the successes.**

**And there is a level above `info` for a line that must always be in both**: `notice`, from syslog's
ladder. That answers a question worth stating, since `debug` is normally off and `info` is normally
the floor — the levels are `d i n w e`, `info` is the default floor, and `notice` means *ordinary but
not chatty*. Warnings and errors are also flushed to disk immediately, where everything else waits
for a batch.

#### 17.5e What a log line costs, which at these rates is a great deal

One `info` line per ping, at 16 connections x 256 in flight:

| | Round trips/s |
|---|---|
| No line (the level filters it out) | 12,933,000 |
| One line per ping, written as it happens | 373,000 |
| One line per ping, batched | 1,899,000 |

**Measured, 2026-08-16.** Two things follow, and the second is the one to remember:

- **Logs are written in batches** — a 64 KB buffer per file, flushed when it fills, every 200 ms, at
  rotation, and immediately for anything at warning or above. That is worth **5x** over a write per
  line, and it is the same argument the message path makes: a syscall per small thing dominates the
  small thing.
- **A line rate-limited to one a second costs 2.87 ns when it is not the one written**, and the
  ping keeps 13,169,000 round trips/s with one in it — inside the noise of the 13,235,000 it runs at
  with nothing. So the whole of the useful signal, one line a second saying what the traffic is
  doing, is available for nothing. The suppressed path is two relaxed loads and a compare; the
  second comes from a ticker rather than a clock read, which is what makes it 3 ns instead of 30.
- **A line the level filters out costs 0.52 ns** — about two cycles, since the macro tests the floor
  before it evaluates anything, so neither the arguments nor the formatting happen. At 16 x 256 the
  ping runs at 13,235,000 with its debug line filtered out against 13,213,000 with no line at all,
  which is to say the difference is not measurable. That is what makes it reasonable to leave debug
  lines in a hot path.
- ⚠️ **Even batched, a line per message costs 85% of throughput.** The line is about 105 bytes
  against a ping's 20, so logging one produces five times the bytes the work does — 507 MB of log in
  three seconds. There is no version of per-message logging that is cheap at millions of messages a
  second, so the hot path logs at `debug` and is off by default. The knob stays so the measurement
  can be repeated rather than remembered.

### 17.5f The roster says how many of each, and the harness starts them all

`start-laws` starts whatever the roster lists, so several of a kind needs no new mechanism: each
gets the next port, its own run directory and configuration, and registers itself with KS. A roster
line may say `count = n` for n processes of one kind, named `EN0`, `EN1` and so on in roster order,
or `identity` for a single named one; numbering runs on across lines, so a second group of a kind
does not collide with the first. `stop-laws` reverses cold-start order and, within a kind, stops the
highest-numbered first, which leaves KS0 last because everything is found through it.

The single-box roster is one KS, one DN, one SN, **four ENs** and one FE. Rings are one member for
now, so the three ring-hosting types are one apiece; four ENs is the number of instances an extent
has, which is the count the placement report has an opinion about. All four are on this box, so they
share every failure domain and the rule stays unenforced — but giving four ENs distinct racks in the
roster is now enough to see it become `enforced at rack`, which is the smallest demonstration that
the report is measuring the cluster rather than restating the configuration.

### 17.5g Objects: create, look up, and what both cost

**Built: `create`, `batch-create`, `object-info` and `batch-object-info`**, over the path a client
actually takes. A create is `laws` → FE → DN → SN; a lookup is `laws` → FE → DN. Deliberately naive
where naivety is honest for now: **every object gets its own stream**, with no inlining of small
objects and no coalescing of several objects into one stream, both of which would hide what a create
costs. Nothing is persisted, and nothing is deleted, so no index here has to survive churn.

Who indexes what follows §4.6.3: **DN indexes objects by name and owns the `StreamId`; SN looks a
stream up by `(DnId, StreamId)`** and allocates neither (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-16). Both tables are
sharded by 64 locks, which is what lets sixteen cores create at once.

**Names are taken before streams are named.** A create that loses a race to the same name must not
leave a stream behind, because nothing deletes streams — so DN inserts the name first, asks the SN for
a run of streams for the names it actually took, and fills the stream ids in when the SN answers. A
duplicate create then costs nothing and leaks nothing.

Over 20 million objects on one box:

| | Rate | Note |
|---|---|---|
| create, one per request | 142,000 /s | two chained hops each |
| create, 1,000 per request | **2,564,000 /s** | 20 M objects in 7.8 s |
| `object-info`, one per request | **263,000 /s** | random names over 20 M |
| `batch-object-info`, 10 | 1,595,000 /s | |
| `batch-object-info`, 100 | 3,958,000 /s | |
| `batch-object-info`, 1,000 | **5,113,000 /s** | |

**Measured, 2026-08-16**, release build, 16 clients x 16 in flight, client and server on the same box. DN
holds 20 M objects in **2.3 GB**, about 116 bytes each including the name and the table, and SN holds
20 M streams in 0.85 GB — so the lookups are random over far more than cache, which is the point of
creating that many.

**Against §1.4.0's bars, this is the same workload**: ObjectInfo over 20 M objects with metadata in
RAM, 200k unbatched and 2M+ in batches of 1,000. Both are cleared — 263k and 5.1M — but the
comparison is not yet fair in three ways, all of which make DeLawson's number flattering: there is no
durable log write, since nothing is persisted; the client shares the box; and an object here is a name
and a stream reference, not the full metadata record §4.7 budgets. The right reading is that the
*message and index path* is in the right place, and the write path has not been paid for yet.

Where the cost falls, from each process's own CPU accounting:

| | Lookups/s | FE core per lookup | DN core per lookup |
|---|---|---|---|
| one per request | 263,000 | 31 µs | 11 µs |
| 1,000 per request | 5,106,000 | 0.8 µs | 1.4 µs |

Unbatched, **FE costs three times what DN does**, which says the forwarding tier — not the index — is
what a small metadata request pays for. Batched, the whole cost collapses by a factor of forty and the
balance inverts, because a batch amortizes the forward and leaves DN doing the only real work there
is: 20 million random hash lookups a second across 64 shards.

#### 17.5g.1 A line per request is affordable; keeping it for hours is not

**Every request through FE, DN and SN logs one `info` line.** What that costs:

| | Line written | Line filtered | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| create, 1,000 per request | 2,851,000 /s | 2,820,000 /s | none |
| create, one per request | 115,000 /s | 140,000 /s | **18%** |
| `object-info`, one per request | 212,000 /s | 260,000 /s | **19%** |
| `batch-object-info`, 1,000 | 5,481,000 /s | 5,474,000 /s | none |

**Measured, 2026-08-16.** A batched request pays nothing, because the line is per *request* and the
request carries a thousand objects — the same amortization the batch exists for. A single-object
request pays 11 to 13%.

**Decided: the lines stay, unless something forces them out** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-16). The reason
is live-site argument rather than accounting: *"SN is taking 50 seconds to do an object info" — "no it
is not, SN never received the message"*. That question is unanswerable without a line per request on
each side of every hop, and it is the question that actually gets asked when a cluster misbehaves.
Rate-limited sampling is the fallback for a path that turns out not to afford it, not the default.

**Decided: the line is written when the answer is sent, and carries how long the request took**
(Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-16). That is the only moment which knows the duration, and the duration is what
the argument is about — so one line per request per process rather than one on the way in and another
on the way out. It lives in `Reply::send`, which is the single place every answer passes through,
so a machine type gets it without writing anything: five hand-written log sites went away when this
arrived.

**The clock is read once per batch, not once per request** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-16). A batch arrives
at one moment, so the segment's arrival time serves every message in it — and it is the honest start
for a duration, being when the bytes reached this process rather than when a thread got round to them.
A request that waited behind others in its batch says so, which is exactly what a live-site argument
wants to know.

Two things were tried to make the line cheaper and **neither was measurable**: holding the subject
inline instead of allocating it, and the clock read itself. What the 19% actually buys is the ~125
bytes of line, which is why §17.5g.1's remaining lever is the length of the header rather than anything
around it. The simpler code stays in both cases.

**So each line carries what the argument is conducted in.** The correlator is not a request id — §17.5d
says why there cannot be one for every line — it is the name, and where the name stops, the stream
range:

```
SN  answered, op create-stream status ok    in    10 us  about count 1 from 1 for dn 0
DN  answered, op create        status ok    in  1750 us  about /bob/notes count 1 streams from 1 on SN0
FE  answered, op create        status ok    in  3816 us  about /bob/notes dn DN0
DN  answered, op object-info   status ok    in    40 us  about /bob/notes
FE  answered, op object-info   status ok    in   109 us  about /bob/notes dn DN0
DN  answered, op object-info   status not found in 31 us  about /bob/nothing
```

FE to DN is matched by name; DN to SN by the stream range, because SN does not know names and should
not — it indexes by `(DnId, StreamId)`. Read the pairs: a lookup took 109 µs at FE of which 40 µs was
DN, so the hop is 69 µs and neither side was slow. That is the shape of the answer to the question
this logging exists for.

⚠️ **What is not affordable is keeping it.** At §1.4's target rate and a ~125-byte line, a process
writes **28 MB/s, or 103 GB an hour** — so the 512 MB of full log that §17.5d's configuration keeps
wraps in **18 seconds**, and the info log's tenth of it lasts a quarter of an hour rather than days.
Three things follow, and they are policy rather than code:

- **The retention targets and the line rate have to be set together.** Hours of full log at target
  QPS is a few hundred gigabytes per process; that is affordable on a storage machine and absurd on a
  front end, so the sizes belong per machine type rather than fleet-wide, which is a change to where
  §17.5d put them.
- **The header is most of the line.** Level, time, pid, tid, file and line are ~85 of the ~125 bytes,
  so what a shorter or binary header buys is not a few percent but most of the volume.
- **28 MB/s of log competes with the workload it is describing.** On an EN that is disk bandwidth the
  storage pipeline wanted, which makes the log's share a budget like any other.

⚠️ **Three serializations had to be removed to get here**, and each was invisible until the rate was
high enough to expose it. They are worth stating because they are the same mistake in three costumes:

1. **FE forwarded by blocking a worker.** A request waiting on another process held a thread, so FE
   could have only as many forwards in flight as it had workers, and adding workers did not help.
   §17.4's rule — every call asynchronous — turns out to apply to *serving* as much as to sending: a
   handler now takes a `Reply` it may carry into the answer it is waiting for, and what is in flight
   is a table entry rather than a thread. Worth 50k to 61k on its own, and the structure everything
   else needed.
2. **Each peer request wrote its own syscall**, under one lock, so requests between two processes
   never coalesced. Giving peer connections the same batching sender the answers already had — one
   piece, shared, rather than two — took single lookups to 158k.
3. **One connection between two processes is one read loop on the far side.** However many workers a
   tier has, it cannot outrun a single thread reading its requests. Processes now keep a fan of
   connections to each peer, and the last plateau went with it.

### 17.5h Reading the logs without logging in

A log nobody can read is a log nobody keeps. But the machines hold signed code
only, so reading them is not a matter of shipping a script — it needs deciding
who runs the reader. **Both, and one implementation** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-16):

| Reader | Answers | Good for |
|---|---|---|
| The process itself, over three operations | its own files | the ordinary case, no deployment, already signed and already there |
| `logs`, one standalone signed binary | any files it is pointed at | a process that has died, is wedged, or is too busy to answer — which is when logs are most wanted |

Both are the same library, so neither is a second implementation of anything. **Three answers are
enough to stop anyone wanting a shell**:

- **histogram** — what this process is mostly saying,
- **grep** — whole lines mentioning a thing,
- **lines** — a range by time, or the last few.

The histogram row is `000000123,i,file=…,line=…,constant`, sorted by frequency — and it sorts by plain
text order because the count is zero-padded, which is why it is.

**It is read from both ends** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-16). The busy end says what is happening most,
which is the obvious use. **The rare end says what happened once, which is the needle in the
haystack** — and
it finds that needle *without anyone knowing what the needle is*, which no grep can do. So every row
comes back rather than the busiest few, since truncating to the top would throw away exactly the half
that finds a rare thing. All three answers take a time range as well, because a rare event is looked
for in the minute it happened.

**It has nothing to tune.** A row per place in the code that said anything, the constant whole,
nothing truncated and no knob:

```
000000001,n,file=common/src/server.rs,line=365,registered with KS
000000042,n,file=common/src/server.rs,line=433,switched to a batching sender because an answer will not come from the read loop
000268456,i,file=common/src/server.rs,line=496,answered
```

**Rarest first, busiest last** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-16), because a histogram often runs past a
screen and what a terminal leaves in front of a reader is the end of it — so the end should be the
summary, and the rare rows are where someone who scrolled up, or piped it to `head`, is looking.

**Two cheap queries beat one query with a knob.** The row's fields are spelled exactly as the lines
spell them, so everything after the count and the level is literally a substring of the lines it
counted — the answer to "what is it mostly saying" is also the argument for the next question:

```
laws log-grep --to DN0 "file=common/src/server.rs,line=496,answered"
  i,…,file=common/src/server.rs,line=496,answered,op batch-create,status ok,about /bench/200 …,us 27242
```

Earlier versions folded a character width, and then a count of values, into the grouping. Both were
answering the second question inside the first one, which is why neither was needed.

⚠️ **This puts a requirement on the code that writes the lines: an outcome worth finding needs its own
constant.** The first attempt logged every answer with the constant `answered` and the status as a
value — so a duplicate create and a lookup of a missing name, deliberately hidden among 270,000
successes, did not appear in the histogram at all. They were inside the big row. Giving a failed
answer its own constant makes them a row of their own:

```
000000001,h,file=,line=0,opened
000000001,n,file=common/src/server.rs,line=369,registered with KS
000000002,n,file=common/src/server.rs,line=511,answered with a problem      <- the needle
000000048,n,file=common/src/server.rs,line=439,switched to a batching sender because …
000268709,i,file=common/src/server.rs,line=506,answered
```

and the row leads straight to them:

```
laws log-grep --to DN0 "line=507,answered with a problem"
  i,…,answered with a problem,op create,status bad request,about /bench/1,us 30
  i,…,answered with a problem,op object-info,status not found,about /nowhere,us 26
```

**So the rule for writing a line is: constants separate kinds, values carry detail.** A status that
distinguishes a failure from a success belongs in the constant, not only in the values, or the
histogram cannot see it — and the whole point of the rare end is to see what nobody thought to search
for.

**Reading is deliberately serial and takes as long as it takes** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-16). It is
competing with a server for the same CPU and the same disk, so it reads one file at a time and one
block at a time, holds only what the answer needs, and the caller waits — the client allows half an
hour. Nothing about it is parallel, and that is the design rather than an omission.

**And the files are compressed**, which follows from nobody reading them directly: the only consumer
is a tool that can decompress. Each block is independent, so a torn last block from a process that
died ends a walk instead of failing an answer, and the extension says which a file is — `.logz`
compressed, `.log` not. **Measured: 74 MB of lines in 9.9 MB of file, 7.5x** (Bob's guess of "more
than 6x" was right), and `status` reports the ratio a run achieved rather than leaving it a guess.
28 MB/s of lines becomes 3.7 MB/s on the disk, which turns §17.5g.1's 18 seconds of full log into a
couple of minutes for the same bytes.

⚠️ **Compression buys retention and not speed**, which had to be measured twice to get right. A first
comparison showed a ping 13% faster with compressed files and was wrong: turning compression off also
divided the block by the ratio, so the two arms differed in how *often* they wrote. Holding the block
equal, compression is neutral — 2.31M round trips a second against 2.28M, inside the noise — and
nothing waits for the device anyway, since a write lands in the page cache
(Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-16).

**What the block actually decides is how often a write happens, and that is the lever:**

| Block of text | Writes at 275 MB/s of lines | Bytes per write | Ping |
|---|---|---|---|
| 40 KB | ~6,900 /s | 40 KB | 1,930,000 |
| 280 KB, compressed | ~1,000 /s | 37 KB | 2,240,000 |
| 280 KB, plain | ~1,000 /s | 280 KB | 2,300,000 |

The two configurations that write a thousand times a second score the same whether they write 37 KB or
280 KB; the one that writes seven thousand times a second loses **15%** of a ping. So bytes are nearly
free and syscalls are not — which is why **the block is the same amount of text whether or not it is
compressed**. `min_write_bytes` is the floor a device wants of a write; the ratio is what makes the
block big enough that writes are rare.

**Compressing also buys throughput, but only where the log rate is extreme** (Asserted, Bob,
2026-08-16, and measured): a ping with a line per request runs at 2,205,000 a second with compressed
files against 1,955,000 with plain ones, **13% faster for writing a seventh of the bytes**. At object
rates — 200,000 lines a second rather than two million — it is a wash, within noise either way, because
the CPU of compressing costs about what the I/O saves. So retention is what compression is for; speed
is a bonus that arrives only at rates where the log is a torrent.

**How much text a block gathers is derived from the disk, not configured** (Asserted, Bob,
2026-08-16). A device wants a write of at least its break-even, and compression means the text has to
be that much larger — so the block is `min_write_bytes x compress_ratio`, and both come from the
media-class table:

| Log disk | Wants a write of | Block of text | Which writes | Fills at 28 MB/s in |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| SSD | 40 KB | 280 KB | 37 KB | 10 ms |
| HDD | 2 MB | 14 MB | 1.9 MB | 500 ms |

⚠️ **The table gained a `min_write_bytes`**, which is the *whole* break-even rather than the half that
`min_read_bytes` is: a short read still delivers the bytes asked for, while a short write pays the same
seek for less work.

**The 200 ms flush timer is the other bound, and on HDD it usually wins** (Asserted, Bob,
2026-08-16): a 14 MB block needs 70 MB/s of lines to fill inside the timer, so below that the log is
written every 200 ms in whatever size has accumulated. Measured with the log disk set to HDD, the
blocks came out **0.7 to 1.0 MB** rather than 14, which is the timer deciding. The two bounds do
different jobs — the timer decides how stale a file may be, the block whether a write is worth making —
and whichever comes first is the right answer. The ratio barely notices: 7.5x at 280 KB blocks, 7.6x
at a megabyte.

⚠️ **A reader can only read whole blocks, so a delayed write may have to become several of them**
(Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-16). HDD's 14 MB of text is larger than the 8 MB a block may be, so what is
pending is cut into blocks — always at a line boundary, since a line split across two blocks is a line
no grep would find. Without that, the compression simply gave up on every block and wrote the text as
it stood, which is the kind of failure that looks like it is working.

### 17.5i Measure three times

**Any timing is measured at least three times** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-16). One number is not a
measurement: the spread is what says whether a difference between two configurations means anything,
and this project has twice drawn a conclusion from single samples that repeats then overturned — an
"11% slower" that was noise, and a "13% faster" that was a different variable. The benchmarks do three
trials by default and print each one, then the mean and the spread.

It paid for itself immediately, because the spreads are not all alike:

| Measurement | Spread over three trials |
|---|---|
| ping, 16 x 256 | **1.9%** |
| object-info, one per request | 2.8% |
| create, 10 objects per request | 0.7% |
| create, 1,000 objects per request | **51%** |

⚠️ **That last row is not noise, it is the placeholder index growing.** Successive trials in one
process ran 2.88M, 2.56M and 1.67M objects a second, with the slowest request in each going 348 ms,
727 ms, 1.82 s. In a *fresh* process every trial gives 2.79M to 2.81M — a 0.9% spread — so what
degrades is the table, not the message path.

**And with the table out of the way, the create path does 3.79M objects a second** — three fresh
processes gave 3,864,000, 3,760,000 and 3,738,000, a 3.4% spread, with the slowest request 67 to 85 ms
rather than 348. That is the number worth keeping (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-16): it says the message path
— `laws` to FE to DN to SN, encrypted, compressed, logged a line per request — is **not** what the
2.8M was limited by. It also confirms the diagnosis: **a hash table doubling under a lock is a latency
cliff, and a create can wait seconds behind one.**

**Not fixed, deliberately** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-16): the in-memory table is a stand-in for the
disk-backed index of §14.2, and the goal here is messaging overhead rather than a metadata structure
that is going to be replaced. What the measurement is worth is the requirement it puts on whatever
replaces it — **the index must grow incrementally**, because growth that copies everything under a lock
turns a metadata create into a multi-second stall. Two things follow for how numbers here are quoted:
a create rate belongs to a stated table size, and it should come from a fresh process.

(An attempt to stagger the shards' initial capacities so they would not all double at once made no
difference at all: hashbrown rounds capacity to a power of two, so every shard ended up the same size
anyway. Recorded because it looked obviously right and was not.)

### 17.6 The harness reports what it cannot enforce

One box is one domain at every level, so it satisfies no spreading rule. That is legal — §5.6.7
skips a rule it cannot enforce — but `start-laws` prints the report anyway, and `laws placement`
computes it on demand: per rule, how many distinct things it wants, the coarsest failure-domain
level that has that many, and a loud line when no level does. A rule wanting one of something is
reported as vacuous rather than as enforced.

### 17.7 KS is also the registrar

**Decided: KS holds the process registry, and its port is the one fixed address in a cluster**
(Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-16). That is why KS is the first daemon built rather than FE: it is what the
others need in order to find anything, and it is already the one type that must come up first for
keys. It is also why cold start is acyclic — KS's own address cannot come from a registry, so it is
configuration, and nothing else needs to be.

Built, and the division of labour is deliberate:

| Who | Decides | Because |
|---|---|---|
| Whatever starts a process | which port it gets | it is the thing that knows what else it has already placed on that machine |
| The process | announcing that port to KS | only it knows it came up |
| KS | `identity → (machine, port)` for everyone else | it is the one address that was already known |

So `start-laws` hands out ports from `ks.port_base` upward, writes each into that process's own
configuration file, and the process registers it once it is listening. **A registration announces a
port; it does not invent an identity** — KS checks what registers against the roster and refuses an
identity that is not there or a kind that disagrees, so a misconfigured process is a reported error
rather than a peer that quietly exists.

Two consequences worth stating:

- **Ready now means findable, not merely listening.** A process writes its `ready` file after it has
  registered, so a harness that waits for ready knows the process can be reached by name.
- **Shutdown must not depend on lookup.** `stop-laws` talks to each process at the address in its own
  run directory, and stops the registrar last, so stopping a cluster does not become
  order-dependent on the thing that resolves names.

The registry is in KS's memory for now, so a KS restart makes every other process re-register.
Putting it in KS's Raft state, and deciding whether a registration is a lease that expires, are
tracked in the issue for this work.

### 17.8 Append: three hops, and the first bytes to reach an EN

Built, 2026-08-17. `laws append /notes/first --data "…"` works, which makes this the first
operation that reaches an EN and the first that needs an extent.

| Hop | Asked | Answers |
|---|---|---|
| FE → DN | once per append | which stream the object is: `(DnId, StreamId)` and its SN |
| FE → SN | **once per extent** | the extent that stream is appending to: an id, its second, and its four instances |
| FE → primary EN | once per append | the receipt, once a quorum of instances has the bytes |
| primary EN → the other three | once per append | applied, or not |

**The middle row is the one that had to be got right.** §8.1.3 says the SN places instances and
then gets out of the write path, which it cannot do if every write consults it — so FE remembers
the open extent per `(DnId, StreamId)` and asks the SN only on a miss. Measured: five successive
appends to one object produced **no** requests to the SN at all. An FE holding that is still an FE
that holds no state, because losing it costs one ask and nothing else.

**An EN learns of an extent from the first append that names it.** The SN chose the instances and
recorded them; telling the ENs in advance would be a round trip that buys nothing, since the
append itself carries the extent's whole name. So there is no create-extent operation on an EN,
and there does not need to be one.

**The instance list travels with the append**, because the primary is what broadcasts and the SN is
not there to be asked again. The primary assigns the offset, applies locally, and issues
`apply-append` to the other three at once — all of them before any of them answers, since a quorum
is straggler tolerance only if the writes go out together (§8.1.2).

**Three of four, counted apart from what it means.** The arithmetic is its own type: it says
`Durable` when two secondaries have applied, `Lost` when enough have failed that the rest cannot
make up the quorum, and nothing at all thereafter — so the reply is sent exactly once and the
counting is unit-testable without a connection to answer down. One slow instance is invisible;
two failures settle it immediately rather than after a timeout.

**A second is part of a name, in both directions.** The SN refuses to issue a second earlier than
one it has already used, since the second selects the key and reaching back asks for one that may
be retired. And an EN refuses an append naming a different second for an extent it already holds,
rather than merging two extents that share an id.

⚠️ **The receipt's offset is a compressed position, and the design wants a logical one** — see
§8.1.6 and #48. It is correct only because nothing compresses yet.

**What is deliberately not here**: implicit create (an append to a name that does not exist is
`not found`), sealing and the extent size cap, record framing and therefore record numbers,
EN-internal staging, the per-disk journal (§8.1.5), and any way to read the bytes back. The
instances are chosen round robin, which on one box satisfies no spreading rule — `start-laws`
says so, loudly, and that is the honest state of it.

**And the tests are where the strategy of §15.3 first applied.** Twenty-nine new unit tests, none
of which start a process: the offset arithmetic, the quorum counting, the extent naming, the
instance choosing, and the argument parsing are each reachable directly, which is what §15.3.1
means by packaging the code so a test can call it. The whole suite is 67 tests in 0.8 seconds.

### 17.9 Read: framing, record numbers, and an append that makes the object

Built, 2026-08-17, on the same day as append. `laws append /notes/journal --data "…"` creates the
object if it is not there, and `laws read /notes/journal --record 0` gives the record back.

**A read is by record number, because that is the only durable reference** (§8.1.1a-9). So records
had to exist before a read could, and three things arrived together: framing, record numbering, and
the read path.

#### 17.9.1 Framing is declared at create and travels with every request

All five framings of §8.2 are built: `nul`, `lf`, `crlf`, `length` and `fixed:WIDTH`. The object
declares one at creation and `object-info` reports it, and it travels with every append and every
read — because the primary EN is what counts the records and what parses them, and an instance that
decided a framing for itself would be deciding something the object did not.

**The client frames the record it is given**, which does two jobs at once:

- **It checks what only it can check.** A terminator framing forbids its terminator inside a record
  (§8.2.3 rule 3), and the client is the last place holding a record *as a record* — after that a
  stray `\n` in `lf` data is not a violation anybody can detect, it is simply two records.
- **What it sends always ends on a record boundary**, so a writer using `laws` never meets the
  awkward corners of §8.2.4.

`fixed:WIDTH` is checked the same way and locally: a five-byte record for a `fixed:4` object fails in
the client without a round trip.

#### 17.9.2 Records are numbered by the append that closes them

An extent numbers its records from zero and the SN says what stream-local number its first record
has — so a receipt reports `(stream, record)`, the durable reference, and then the extent, second and
offset as the hint tier of §8.1.1a-10.

A record may span appends (§8.2.3 rule 2), so the primary keeps the bytes of an open record and an
append is told how many records it *closed*, which can be none. **Both gates of §8.2.3 are built**:
an append is answered when a quorum of instances has applied it **and** its record has finished, and
either can arrive first. The block rule of §8.2.4 is enforced where the append lands — a block that
closes a record and then ends inside another is refused, and refused before anything is written.

#### 17.9.3 What a read costs today, and what it will cost

| Hop | Asks |
|---|---|
| FE → DN | which stream, and how it is framed |
| FE → SN | which extent holds that record, and where its instances are |
| FE → primary EN | the record |

⚠️ **The read goes to the primary, not to any instance**, and §9.1 says why: not because a
secondary's bytes differ below the durable length — they do not — but because a secondary may hold a
**stale durable length** and would answer against the wrong watermark. Since nothing seals yet, every
extent is unsealed and every read goes to the primary.

⚠️ **And the EN parses the extent from the beginning every time**, because there is no sparse index
(§9.3) and no seal. So a read is O(extent) rather than O(one granule), which is the placeholder to
remember when a read rate is quoted.

**What is deliberately not here**: reading by key (`--key` answers `unimplemented`, since keyed
reads need the key ordering of §9.2), scans, counts, and the sparse index.

⚠️ **And the shape of `read` is the record-oriented one**, which §9.1.2 shows is the shape that
forces an FE to see plaintext. A block-oriented read — the client asks for the block and extracts
locally, keeping the CRC check end to end — is the other half of #63, and the client should be able
to ask either way rather than the wire API choosing for it.

#### 17.9.4 The order the rest arrives in

Bob's sequence, 2026-08-17, and each step is a knob turned small rather than a new mechanism:

1. **Done**: an append that creates its object, and a read that gets the record back.
2. **Done: extent sealing**, with the limit shrunk to 4 KB so it happens constantly — see §17.11.
3. **Next: shrink the extents-per-stream limit**, so a stream fills and the DN allocates another —
   driven by the previous stream reporting that it sealed. That needs #56 first, because a DN
   allocating a stream is a round trip and several appends will want it at once.

The point of the order is that each step turns a configured limit into a constantly-exercised path,
which is the same trick the small log files play: make the rare case the common one on one box.

### 17.10 One request does the work; the rest are given its answer

**When several requests need the same new thing, one of them makes it and the others queue behind it
and get that same thing** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17). Three places want this, and they are the same
rule with different costs:

| Who | Needs | Cost of making it | So the queue is |
|---|---|---|---|
| SN | the next extent for a stream | a counter and an instance list | **the stream's lock** |
| DN | a new stream for an object | **a round trip to an SN** | an in-flight table (#56) |
| DN | the object for a name | a round trip, once per name | the name being inserted first |

**Built, at the SN**: the stream's lock is held across the naming, so a burst of appends to a fresh
stream — or to one that has just sealed — produces one extent and not one apiece. Sealing and opening
happen under the same lock, which is what makes a second request that finds the extent already sealed
get *the extent that replaced it* rather than an error.

**Built, at the DN, for names**: whoever inserts the name owns the object and asks for its stream;
anyone else finds the name already there and never asks. Same rule, and it is why a create that loses
a race does not leave a stream behind.

⚠️ **The lock is only the right queue while the work is arithmetic.** Opening an extent today is a
counter increment, so a waiter blocking for it costs nothing. **A DN allocating a stream has to ask an
SN**, and blocking a worker per waiter on somebody else's round trip is exactly what §17.4 forbids —
so that one needs an in-flight table where the first request registers what it is doing and the rest
attach to its answer. The distinction is worth stating because the two look identical in a design
sketch and are not the same code.

And the same caution applies to the SN once opening an extent is recorded durably rather than in
memory: the moment it becomes a Raft round trip, the lock has to become an attachment.


### 17.11 Sealing, and what a burst of writers found

Built, 2026-08-17. The seal limit is configuration (`extents.seal_bytes`), and the single-box cluster
sets it to **4 KB** so that sealing is the common path rather than one nothing reaches.

**The primary decides, and says so in the answer.** When a block will not fit, the extent is closed and
the append is answered `Sealed` with what the extent came to — a record count and a length. Not a
failure: the writer is being told where to go. The FE then reports that to the SN, which records it and
names the next extent **in the same round trip**, since whoever saw the seal wants both.

| Who | Does |
|---|---|
| primary EN | closes the extent, answers `Sealed` with its record count and length |
| FE | forgets the extent it cached, reports the seal, takes the next extent, sends the append again |
| SN | records what the extent came to, and names the next one — under the stream's lock (§17.10) |

**An extent with a record still open cannot seal**, whatever the cap says, because an extent holds
whole records — so the open record finishes there and the seal happens after it. That falls straight
out of §8.2.4 and needed no special case.

**Reads span extents.** A stream keeps its sealed extents in record order, so locating a record is a
search over a sorted run; anything at or past the open extent's first record is routed there, because
how far *that* one reaches is the EN's to say and not the SN's.

#### 17.11.1 What eight concurrent writers found
