Three hundred and twenty records from eight clients into one object that did not exist yet, which is
worth doing precisely because it is the case single-threaded testing cannot reach. It failed, in three
ways, and all three are worth recording because none of them is exotic:

- ⚠️ **An append arriving while the object was half made was told "that object has no stream yet".**
  The DN takes the name first and asks for the stream after (§17.10), so for the width of one round
  trip an object exists with no stream — and a second writer's append hit exactly that window and
  failed. **Seven records were lost this way.** The fix is §17.10's rule applied to lookups: a lookup
  that finds a name taken but its stream unnamed **parks behind whoever is naming it** and is answered
  when the stream exists. A lookup can therefore be answered by another request's completion, which is
  why `object-info` now defers.
- ⚠️ **One retry was not enough.** An append that stepped into a fresh extent could find *that* one
  already full, because other writers fill extents while one append is being placed. Retrying a fixed
  number of times is right, but the number is not one — and the case that must not be retried is
  distinguishable rather than a guess: **an extent that sealed with nothing in it** is one this block
  could not fit even empty, which is the block's fault and gets `bad request`.
- **A counter counted the wrong thing.** Every append that found a sealed extent incremented the count
  of sealed extents, so an EN reported five where the SN reported three. Only the block that *closes*
  an extent is closing it; the rest are being turned away.

After all three: **320 of 320 records durable, readable, and numbered without gaps**, across four
extents with three seals, and the tiers agree — the SN counts four extents and three seals, the EN
counts four extents, 320 appends and three seals, the DN counts one object and nothing waiting.

The interleaving is a writer-visible consequence worth stating: record 0 came from client 7. Several
writers appending to one object get **at-least-once ordering by arrival**, which is §8.1.1a's
assigned-offset mode working as designed, and a reason a writer wanting its own order wants its own
object.

#### 17.11.2 What the SN can and cannot see

**The extent-create *request* rate climbs towards the append rate when the ENs are busy, while the
actual number of extents created stays exactly what it always was** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17). Every
append that is in flight when an extent fills gets `Sealed`, and each of them asks the SN for the next
extent — so the requests multiply with the number of appends in flight, and the SN collapses them all
into one extent under the stream's lock (§17.10).

Measured on one box, 160 appends of 44 bytes at a 4 KB seal limit:

| | SN requests | Extents created | Requests per creation |
|---|---|---|---|
| One append at a time | 2 | 2 | **1** |
| Eight writers at once | 9 | 2 | **~4** |

**Measured, 2026-08-17.** Eight concurrent writers is a shallow queue; the ceiling is one request per
append, reached when every append in flight hits the same seal.

⚠️ **So three things must not be read off the SN, and one may be:**

- **Not the append rate.** Appends never reach the SN, by design (§8.1.3). The only append-shaped
  traffic it sees is the seal burst, and that measures **how many appends were in flight**, not how
  many there were.
- **Not a workload change.** A jump in extent-create requests is not a user doing something new. **It
  is a symptom of the ENs being busy** — deeper queues mean more appends caught by each seal. Reading
  it as offered load would send an operator to look in the wrong tier.
- **Not extent-creation cost.** The requests multiply; the creations do not. An SN doing four times
  the request rate is doing the same amount of work.
- **The read rate, though, it does see**: one `locate-record` per read, since nothing caches where a
  record lives. That part of its traffic *is* proportional to reads.

Two consequences for what to build, and both are §17.10's rule in new places:

- **The FE should collapse the storm** — one seal in flight per stream, with the other appends
  attaching to it rather than each asking the SN (#57). The requests exist only because eight
  coordinators independently discovered the same fact.
- **The FE should cache where a record lives** for reads (#58). A sealed extent is immutable, so its
  record range never changes; §9.1 already says a warm client goes straight to the EN.

### 17.12 A stream seals too, and the DN gives the object another

Built, 2026-08-17, which completes §17.9.4's sequence. `extents.per_stream` is the limit — **3** on the
single-box cluster, so a stream fills every few kilobytes — and what happens when it does:

| Who | Does |
|---|---|
| SN | seals the last extent, finds the stream has all the extents it may have, and answers `Sealed` with what the **stream** came to |
| FE | drops the extent it cached and asks the DN to extend the object |
| DN | seals that stream in the object's stream list, names the next one, has an SN record it, and answers with it |
| FE | starts the append again on the new stream, which has no extent yet |

**An object is a list of streams, each with the object-local record number it starts at.** That is what
makes an object's numbering continuous across the streams it is made of: a sealed stream's record count is
known (§6.3), so the next stream starts at first + count and never moves.

**So a read asks a different question of the DN than an append does.** An append asks for the object's
*last* stream (`object-info`); a read asks which stream holds *its record* (`locate-stream`). Same answer
shape, and the same number of hops as before — the DN was always in the read path, it just used to have only
one stream to answer with.

⚠️ **The DN can answer for the sealed streams by arithmetic and cannot for the last one**, so a record at or
past the last stream's first record is routed there and the SN and EN say whether it is really present. That
asymmetry is §6.3's definition showing through: a sealed stream's count is a fact, an open one's is not.

**Extending is collapsed the way §17.10 requires**: the first append to find the stream full sets a flag on
the object and asks an SN, and the rest park behind it and are handed the same stream. Because asking an SN
is a round trip, they park rather than hold a worker — which is what #56 asked for, arriving here first.
`extend-object` therefore defers, and so does `object-info`, since it may be parked behind the same work.

#### 17.12.1 What it took to work

400 appends of 44 bytes: **2 streams, 5 extents, 4 sealed extents, 1 sealed stream, and every record
readable — including 269 and 270, which are the last of one stream and the first of the next.**

Three bugs found on the way, and the shapes are more instructive than the fixes.

**`Sealed` leaked to the client.** Three separate places ask the SN about an extent — opening one, sealing
one, and retrying after a seal — and each has to handle "the stream is full too". One did not. The lesson is
not about sealing: **a status every caller must handle wants to be impossible to forget**, and three
hand-written checks is three chances to miss one.

⚠️ **A self-deadlock, from a method that takes a lock the caller already holds.** The extension path decided
what to do with the object's shard locked, and one branch called a helper that locks the same shard to
describe the object. Rust's mutexes are not reentrant, so that branch wedged a worker thread — and under
eight writers it took them all, one at a time, until the DN answered nothing and every client timed out.
**It looked like a performance problem and was a liveness one.**

⚠️ **A missed wakeup, from releasing the lock between deciding to wait and waiting.** The same path chose to
park behind an in-flight extension, released the shard, and *then* put its `Reply` on a queue — so an
extension that finished in that gap woke nobody, and the request waited for ever. The fix is structural
rather than careful: **the waiters live in the object, under the shard's lock**, so deciding to wait and
waiting are one step. A separate table of waiters cannot be made safe by ordering the two operations
correctly; it can only be made safe by not having the gap.

Both of the second two are §17.10's pattern being got wrong in the same function, and both are invisible to
a single writer. The run that found them was eight.

### 17.13 The FE asks once per extent, and reads of sealed data ask nothing

Built, 2026-08-17, closing #57 and #58. §17.11.2 measured the problem: eight concurrent writers turned
2 extent creations into 9 SN requests, and every read cost one more. Both were the same mistake — several
coordinators independently discovering the same fact.

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| SN requests, 200 appends over 3 extents | ~1 per append at the ceiling | **4** — a stream, an open, and two seals |
| SN requests, 100 reads of sealed extents | 100 | **0** |
| SN requests, 10 reads of the extent still open | 10 | 10 |

**Measured, 2026-08-17.** So the append side is at its floor — one request per extent created, plus one
for the stream — and the read side is at zero for everything sealed.

#### 17.13.1 One request in flight per stream, and the rest join it

Opening the first extent and replacing a full one are the same operation, so they collapse together: a
stream either has an extent to use, or has a request in flight for one, or has neither and the asker
becomes the one asking. **The third case is the only one that talks to the SN.**

The decision is a method on what the FE remembers about a stream, and the reply is queued **inside the
same lock that made the decision** — §17.12.1's missed wakeup is the reason that is stated as a rule
rather than left to care. Being a method rather than a passage inside a lock block also makes it four
unit tests instead of an integration test: one append asks and the rest join; several appends that saw
the same extent fill still ask once; an append late to a seal uses whatever replaced it.

#### 17.13.2 Why a sealed extent is rememberable and an open one is not

**A sealed extent's record range never changes.** So when the FE reports a seal it keeps what the extent
came to, and a read of any record in that range goes straight to the EN. Nothing invalidates it: if
compaction later rewrites the extent, §4.6.3 gives the rewrite a **different identity**, so a stale entry
fails loudly rather than reading the wrong bytes.

⚠️ **The extent still being appended to is deliberately not remembered.** It reaches further with every
append, so how far it reaches is not a fact to keep — and a read of the tail is exactly the read that has
to reach the primary anyway (#54). That is why the third row of the table above did not move, and it is
the right answer rather than a gap: **the cache holds only what cannot go stale.**

The FE's `status` now reports what it is remembering — open extents, known sealed extents, and appends
waiting for an extent — because a collapse that is not working looks exactly like one that is, except in
those three numbers.

#### 17.13.3 A wire contract with no test, found by breaking it

Rewriting the append path reordered the arguments of `append-extent`, putting the framing after the
instance list instead of before it. **It compiled, and the primary would have read the framing out of the
first two instance numbers** — silently interpreting "EN2" as a framing. Nothing caught it but reading the
code again.

That is precisely the gap §15.3's one end-to-end test exists to fill, and it is worth naming as a class:
**the argument order between two processes is a contract that no unit test on either side can check.**
Both sides pass their own tests while disagreeing. The candidates for catching it are the end-to-end test
(#45) or giving a request shape a name both sides share rather than a position both sides count.

### 17.14 Several front ends, each with its own clients

The single-box cluster now runs **four FEs**, and a client is **pinned** to one with `--to` rather than
round-robined across them (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-17). Pinning is what makes an FE's memory worth having:
a client that goes somewhere else next time is a client whose coordinator knows nothing about it.

**What the SN sees scales with front ends, not with clients.** 200 appends from eight clients, two pinned
to each of four FEs, into one object across three extents:

| | SN requests |
|---|---|
| One FE | **4** — one stream, one open, two seals |
| Four FEs | **13** — one stream, and four × three extents |

**Measured, 2026-08-17.** Which is the floor and the expected shape: §17.13's collapse is per FE, so each
front end discovers each extent once. *n* FEs cost *n* requests per extent and clients cost none, so the
metadata tier's load is set by how many coordinators there are — a number the operator chooses — rather
than by how many writers there are, which is a number the customer chooses.

#### 17.14.1 A read-only front end has to be told, and now is

Running more than one FE immediately exposed something one FE could not: **an FE learned where records
lived only by being the one to report a seal**, so an FE that had never written to a stream asked the SN
about every read for ever. Measured before the fix: reads through the writing FE, 0 requests for 40 reads;
reads of the same records through another FE, **40 requests for 40 reads, and 40 again on the second
pass.** It never warmed up, because the answer it got carried no record count and a range is not something
to guess.

**The fix is one number in the answer.** An SN naming a *sealed* extent now says how many records it
holds, so any FE can remember it — the count is zero for the extent still being appended to, whose reach
changes with every append and is therefore not a fact to keep.

| Reads of sealed records through an FE that never wrote them | SN requests |
|---|---|
| First pass, 40 reads | **1** |
| Second pass, 40 reads | **0** |
| Ten reads of the tail, in the extent still open | 10 |

**Measured, 2026-08-17.** So a reader pays one request per extent it reads from, ever, and a reader of the
tail pays one per read — which is the case #54 is about and caching cannot fix.

⚠️ **The general shape is worth naming, because it will recur.** A cache that is only filled by the write
path serves writers and starves readers, and the two look identical from the writing side — every
measurement passes. What made it visible was running more than one of something, which is the same reason
§17.11.1's bugs needed eight writers: **a single instance of a thing cannot exhibit the disagreements
between instances.**

### 17.15 The CRC, as far as it can go before compression exists

Built, 2026-08-17. `laws append --crc` computes the CRC of the framed block and sends it; the FE carries
it; the primary EN stores it with the block and broadcasts it to the other instances. `status` on an EN
reports how many blocks it holds a CRC for.

**Everything the design asks for except the checking**, and that is not an omission: §7.5.3 puts the
check where a compressed block becomes logical bytes again, and **nothing compresses yet**. So there is
nowhere honest to check it.

⚠️ **A check at the EN would have worked today and been wrong tomorrow**, which is worth recording as a
kind of mistake rather than as a fact about CRCs. An EN currently holds exactly the bytes the writer
sent, so an EN-side comparison would pass — and would fail on every append the moment the client
started compressing, because the stored bytes would no longer be the bytes the CRC covers. **A check
that only works while a feature is missing is worse than no check**: it passes its tests, and it breaks
when something unrelated is switched on.

The implementation is the dependency, not a copy: `crc64-nvme` from
[crc64nvme](https://github.com/bobjen/crc64nvme). Two things about taking it that way are worth noting:

- **The catalogue's check value is a test here**, because the polynomial has two forms and the wrong one
  produces plausible values that agree with nothing. It was written from memory first, in the reflected
  form of the catalogue's constant, and failed — the authorized implementation's constant is
  `0x9a6c9329ac4bc9b5` and the check value then matched. That test now says this build agrees with Azure,
  with Cosmos, and with the crate.
- **The chaining convention is the crate's**, not the one a table-driven implementation uses: the seed
  is the previous *finished* CRC, so `continuing(0, bytes)` is `of(bytes)`. The unit test that caught
  this was written against the wrong convention, which is the useful direction for a test to be wrong in.

**And the shared append shape came out of §17.13.3's lesson.** Adding the CRC meant adding a field to a
message two processes each parse by counting positions — the exact contract that had already gone wrong
once. So `common::wire::AppendBlock` is now built and read in one place and used by both the FE and the
EN, which turns that class of mistake into a compile error. Its round trip is a unit test; the positions
are nobody's business.

### 17.16 The client compresses, and the tiers below stop understanding records

Built, 2026-08-17. `laws append` frames the record, computes its CRC, **compresses out of place**,
re-checks the buffer against the CRC, and sends the stored bytes. `laws read` gets the **whole block**
back, decompresses it, checks the CRC, and takes the record out. Nothing in between looks inside.

**Measured here, by content:**

| 50 records of 901 logical bytes | Stored | Ratio |
|---|---|---|
| highly repetitive | 2,150 | **21x** |
| random | 45,050 | **1.00x** — stored as it stands, not larger |
| 50 short records of ~68 bytes | 3,090 for ~3,400 | ~1.1x |

**Measured, 2026-08-17.** The middle row is the one worth having: a block that does not compress is
stored uncompressed rather than bigger, so incompressible data pays nothing. And the last row is the
finding — **per-append compression of small records buys almost nothing**, because 68 bytes is too
little for a compressor to find anything in. That is an argument for §8.1.4.4's coalescing rather than
against compression: the win is there for a block of many records, and a single small append is not
one.

#### 17.16.1 What compression took away from the tiers below

⚠️ **An EN can no longer see a record**, and that turned out to be most of the change:

| Before | After |
|---|---|
| the EN parsed the block by framing to count records | **the writer counts, and the counts travel with the block** |
| the EN enforced §8.2.4's block rule | **the client enforces it** — the EN cannot see a boundary to check |
| the EN kept the bytes of an open record | it keeps **a flag**; the writer holds the bytes |
| a read returned one record | a read returns **the whole block** holding it (#63) |
| `read-extent` took a framing | it does not: the framing has left the wire below the client |

So the EN became a tier that deals in bytes, offsets and counts, and that is a simplification rather
than a loss — it is what §9.1 already said the division should be. **What it costs is that the EN now
trusts the writer** about what a block contains. A writer that lies corrupts its own object and no
other, which is the same bargain the CRC already makes.

**And the logical/compressed distinction became real, which fixed #48.** A receipt now reports the
**logical** offset and length — what the writer wrote — while the extent's stored end is a separate
number the tier keeps to itself. Two appends of 301 logical bytes landed at logical offsets 0 and 301
while occupying 13 and 301 stored bytes. Before compression those numbers were equal and the receipt
was wrong in a way nothing could detect.

#### 17.16.2 A bug that only appears after the first seal

**Three numbering spaces meet on the read path** — a caller counts records from the start of the
object, a stream counts from its own first, and an extent counts from its own — and the FE is the only
party that knows all three. The first version of this returned the block's first record in the
*extent's* numbering to a client counting in the *object's*.

⚠️ **Everything worked until the first seal**, because until then all three origins are zero. Then 139
of 200 reads failed. The lesson is not about numbering: **a conversion between two spaces that agree at
zero is untested by anything that never leaves the first extent**, and the single-box cluster's tiny
seal limit is what made it show up at all. Had the limit been the design's 32 MB, this would have
shipped.
### 17.17 An offset is written once, and the check is a refusal rather than a repair

§7.2.4's rule went into the EN, and what it took is instructive about where the rule actually bites.

**The primary was already safe by accident.** `take` hands out `extent.end` and moves it forward, so
an offset is used once as long as nothing moves `end` backwards — and nothing did, because truncation
did not exist. **The secondary was not.** `apply` took the offset the primary chose and did
`end = end.max(offset + stored)`, which accepts a block at *any* offset, including one already
written, and silently kept both. That is the catastrophic case of §7.2.4 sitting in the one path where
the offset arrives from another machine rather than being chosen locally.

**So the check lives on `apply`, and it distinguishes three cases** rather than two:

| At that offset | Answer | Why |
|---|---|---|
| nothing | store it | the ordinary case |
| **the same bytes** | **ok, stored once** | an append this instance already has, arriving again. The primary is owed the same answer it got the first time, and nothing changed |
| anything else | **refuse** | two plaintexts under one key and IV |

⚠️ **The middle row is the one worth having thought about.** Without it the retry that §8.1.1a-3 makes
harmless would start failing, because a retry *is* an overlap — so a check that only asked "is this
offset free" would have turned exactly-once into an error. The distinction is bytes, not offsets.

**And truncation is one operation with sealing, not two.** `truncate` discards everything at or above
a compressed offset and seals, and the two cannot be called separately, for §17.12.1's reason: a rule
that depends on remembering to do the second thing is a rule that will be broken. It refuses three
ways, and each refusal is a different invariant checking this one:

- **a cut inside a block** — §8.2.4 makes splitting an append impossible, and a durable watermark is a
  block boundary by construction, so a cut that is not one did not come from a watermark;
- **a cut that would leave a record open** — §8.2.3 keeps whole records in an extent, and
  `INCOMPLETE-RECORD-NOT-DURABLE` means a watermark never lands mid-record, so this too says the
  caller is confused rather than sealing something invalid;
- **a cut past everything held** — the same confusion in the other direction.

**Sealing is unconditional, including when nothing was discarded**, and the reason is a whole-extent
argument rather than a per-instance one. A handover seals the extent at one agreed length (§8.1.7), so
an instance that happens to hold nothing above it is still part of a sealed extent. Sealing only the
instances that lost bytes would leave the others appendable, and a new primary taking its end from one
of *those* would hand out an offset another instance has already written — which is the original bug
wearing a different hat.

⚠️ **Nothing calls `truncate` from the wire yet, because primary handover is unspecified** (§16.32,
#55). The primitive is deliberately ahead of its caller: the invariant it carries is most of the reason
handover cannot be written casually, so it should exist before the protocol rather than after. What is
enforced today is the `apply` refusal, which is on a live path, plus seven tests naming the two
invariants they check.

### 17.18 A read becomes a range, and one shape replaces two

§9.1.3.4's start and §9.1.3.6's budget went in, along with the answer that says what it covered.
Four things are worth recording, and two of them are about what the change *revealed*.

**The point read did not survive as a separate thing, and should not have.** `laws read --record N`
now sends a range of one record, so there is one code path where there were two. The old point read
found the block *covering* a record by `first_record <= N < first_record + records`, and that
predicate **cannot find a block that completes no record** — the block wholly inside one record that
§8.2.4 explicitly permits. So the old path could not read a record larger than one block at all. The
range walk orders by **offset** instead and carries every block from the one where the record starts,
which fixes it as a side effect of being written properly.

⚠️ **Two stopping rules, and the order of the test is both of them.** The budget is checked *after* a
block is taken, so one block always comes back — a smaller budget returning nothing would be a
caller retrying for ever and never learning it asked for too little. And stopping is only permitted
with no record open, so `next` is a real record number rather than the one the request started at.
**That second rule is §8.2.3's durability gate arriving on the read path**, for the same reason: half
a record is not a record, so a range that ended on one would hand back a continuation that makes no
progress. Neither rule is optional and neither is obvious from the design text, which is why they are
here.

⚠️ **The FE's numbering conversion had to stop patching a position.** It added the extent's origin to
argument index 1, which was the block's first record. When the answer grew a header saying what it
covered, index 1 became a **byte count** — so the patch would have corrupted a measure and left every
record number unconverted, and the existing test would have gone on passing because it asserted the
patch rather than the meaning. §17.13.3's lesson again, arriving through a different door: the shapes
now live in `common` and both ends read them rather than counting.

**And `more` is a statement about the tier that answered, not about the object.** An EN sets it from
its own blocks because an extent is all it knows; only the FE knows there are further extents, so it
widens the claim using something the EN cannot see — whether that extent is sealed. Overstating it
costs one round trip that answers "no such record"; understating it would lose data silently, so the
asymmetry decides which way to err.

⚠️ **What is not built, and why each is blocked rather than skipped:**

| Not built | Because |
|---|---|
| **stream and extent narrowing** (§9.1.3.4) | an asserted narrowing is only as good as the caller (§9.1.3.5), so it waits on the capability (#78) and its key (#82). Sending it before then would be building the unauthorizable version |
| **logical-offset starts**, both forms | they need a prefix sum of logical lengths, which §4.5 keeps lazily and no tier can answer today. Well-formed requests for something unbuilt, so they return `unimplemented` rather than a wrong answer |
| **crossing extents in one request** | the answer already says where to carry on, so stopping at an extent boundary is a correct paginated answer. A 1,600-record object over two streams and five extents scans in **five** requests, one per extent |

**Measured, on the single-box cluster**: 1,600 records appended across 2 streams and 5 extents,
scanned in 5 requests, every record number contiguous and matching its contents — including across
both the extent seals and the stream seal, which is the conversion §17.16.2 records getting wrong.

### 17.19 The lookup benchmark was measuring misses, and that is the smaller finding

Bob asked for `object-info` to be re-benchmarked before #79 grows what it returns. It did not need
re-running — §17.5g's numbers were undisturbed, since `dn` and the FE's forwarding path were untouched
by §17.18 — but *checking* that turned up three defects in the benchmark itself.

⚠️ **`bench-info` had never once hit an object.** `bench-create` puts the trial number in the path,
because a second trial reusing the first's names creates nothing and measures the refusing; `bench-info`
did not, so it looked up `/bench/0` while the objects were at `/bench/1/0`. **Every lookup in every run
ever recorded missed**, and the `--prefix` help text describing the shared naming was what both halves
were meant to implement and only one did.

⚠️ **And the hit counter double-counted, which is why the miss was invisible.** It chopped the answer
into pieces of five arguments, and the row had grown to **eight** when §17.12 added the stream's first
record — so it reported two objects per object. The two bugs concealed each other: names never matched,
so nothing was found, and the counter would have exaggerated anything that was.

**Both are one mistake with two faces, and it is §17.13.3's.** Four places counted the positions of that
answer independently — the DN built it, the FE read it for a stream, `laws` read it to print, and the
benchmark chopped it to count — and two of them were wrong. The row now lives in `common` as `Described`
(§17.18 did the same for the range shapes), so the count comes from parsing rather than from an assumed
width, and the name comes from one function both halves of the benchmark call.

#### 17.19.1 What it cost the numbers: about 3%, and in the reassuring direction

**Re-measured, 2026-08-20**, release build, 17 M objects, 16 clients × 16 in flight, 3 trials:

| | Rate | Spread |
|---|---|---|
| unbatched, **hitting** | **203,900 /s** | 0.6% |
| unbatched, missing — what was being measured before | 197,100 /s | 2.0% |
| unbatched, missing, **pre-§17.18 client** | 199,500 /s | 0.6% |
| batched 1,000, hitting | **4,269,000 /s** | 0.5% |

Three things follow, and the first is the one worth being relieved about:

- **A hit is ~3% *faster* than a miss**, because a miss formats an error message while a hit fills a
  fixed row. So §17.5g's figures were very slightly **pessimistic**, not flattering — the defect did not
  inflate the claim.
- **§17.18 cost nothing.** The pre-session client and the current one measure the same miss rate to
  within 1.2%, inside the trial spread. Worth checking rather than asserting, since §17.18 rewrote the
  FE's read path and put a new field on every lookup.
- ⚠️ **The unbatched number now sits ~2% above §1.4.0's 200k bar rather than 30% above it.** That is a
  materially different claim, and §1.4.0's "both are cleared" should be read as *just* cleared for the
  unbatched case.

#### 17.19.2 The real finding: between-session variance dwarfs within-session spread

⚠️ **§17.5g measured 263,000 /s and the same benchmark measures 203,900 /s today**, on the same box,
against a build proven equivalent, with the hit/miss difference accounting for only 3% of it. So a **23%
gap between sessions** sits alongside a **0.6% spread within one**.

| | Spread |
|---|---|
| three trials in one session | **0.6%** |
| the same measurement four days apart | **23%** |

**That says §17.5i's rule is measuring the wrong thing.** "Measure three times" was adopted because one
number is not a measurement and the spread says whether a difference means anything — but three trials
back to back share everything that varies slowly: page-cache state, CPU frequency, whatever else is on
the box, the object population's layout. **A 0.6% spread invites confidence that the 23% shows is not
there.**

Two consequences, and neither is about this benchmark in particular:

- **A quoted figure needs its session recorded**, which §0 already requires for numbers and §17.5g did
  do. What it also needs is that **comparisons across sessions be treated as ±25% until something
  explains the difference** — so §16's performance questions cannot be settled by a 20% improvement
  measured on a different day.
- ⚠️ **#79's benchmark must run both arms in one session.** Its whole purpose is to test §9.1.3.7's
  claim that asking for no extents costs what it costs today; a before-and-after separated by days
  cannot see a 20% regression, let alone attribute it. The zero-extent and extents-requested arms have
  to be measured back to back against one running cluster, and the *baseline arm re-run at the same
  time* rather than quoted from here.

⚠️ **What causes the 23% is not established** and should not be guessed at in this document; #88 holds
it. The object count differed (17 M against 20 M, which should favour today's run), so the likely
candidates are outside the code.

### 17.20 object-info grows levels, and the DN answers the two it owns

§9.1.3.7's answer shape went in, along with the entry limit, for the detail the DN can supply without
asking anyone: **streams and counts**. Extents wait on an SN hop per stream (§9.1.3.3), capabilities on
#82's key, and stream flags on §4.1.1 existing at all — so a caller asking for those is told **which**
by name rather than handed an answer that quietly omits what it asked for.

**The answer is a shape, then the object, then its streams**, and the order is the point: the header
says how many rows follow before a reader starts reading them, so nothing counts positions or infers a
count from a length. `Shape`, `StreamRow` and `Described` all live in `common` (§17.19's lesson).

⚠️ **Which it is comes from whether the plain row parses at the front**, not from a flag. A request that
asked for nothing gets the bare eight-argument row exactly as before — **byte for byte**, which is what
keeps every existing caller working and keeps §17.5g's baseline comparable. A request that asked for
something gets a shape in front. That is §13.2.5.1's rule inside a request rather than a config file:
the new thing defaults to the old behaviour.

#### 17.20.1 Three things the implementation had to get right

**The counts are exact while the detail is capped**, which is §9.1.3.2's whole point: the stream total
is the DN's own, so it costs nothing and is always right, while the rows stop at the limit. A caller
learns *how many there are* in the same answer that tells it *how many it got*.

**The continuation is a record number and it must advance.** `next` is the first record of the stream
after the last one described, and a test walks the loop to exhaustion asserting `next > at` each time —
because a continuation that does not advance is a livelock, and it is the same failure §17.18 guarded
against on the read path.

⚠️ **And a growing stream reports `UNKNOWN`, not zero.** How far the stream being appended to reaches is
not the DN's to say (§6.3), and a sealed stream holding nothing would be a real zero — so the two cannot
share an encoding. §8.1.6.3 had just settled that a sentinel goes at the top of the range for a count,
and this is the first place it was needed: **#90 is the same mistake already in the code**, where an
open extent reports zero records for the same idea.

#### 17.20.2 Two caps, and the smaller wins

`info_entries` is the DN's configured limit and a request may name its own; the answer honours whichever
is smaller. **A request may ask for less and may not ask for more**, which is §9.1.3.7's rule and the
only sane direction — a caller knows its own buffer and the operator knows the fleet's.

The test cluster sets it to **3**, low on purpose so that paging is the common path rather than the rare
one — the same reasoning as `extents.per_stream` in §17.12, and for the same reason: a limit that never
binds is a limit that never gets tested.

⚠️ **The knob's placement in `dn.toml` cost a restart to find.** A top-level key written after a `[knobs]`
table parses as a member of it, so the first attempt failed with *unknown field `info_entries`, expected
`workers`* — TOML's rule, not a bug, and worth knowing before the next machine type grows a knob.

---

## 18. Coding rules

§16.141 recorded that these had no home and sat wherever the argument that produced them happened to
land. There are now four, which is enough to collect: they are about **how code should read and be
shaped**, which is neither the test strategy (§15.3) nor what is built (§17).

Each is stated where it was argued and summarised here. **The summary is not the definition** — the
sections are, and they carry the reasoning that makes each rule more than a preference.

| Rule | Argued | In one line |
|---|---|---|
| **Make the logic simple** | §13.2.5.1, §4.1.1.0 | reduce the depth of negations; name things positively; a name is never a negation |
| **Structural rather than careful** | §17.12.1 | if a rule can be broken by forgetting, change the shape so forgetting is impossible |
| **Make the compiler catch it** | §8.1.6, §8.1.6.1 | wrap same-typed values when a mix-up would be silent; group parameters when a signature has a run of them |
| **Decompose the state** | §18.1 | m + n things is far less code than m × n |

⚠️ **They are not independent, which is itself an instance of the last one.** "Structural rather than
careful" is often achieved by "make the compiler catch it", and both are ways of making the logic
simple. Where they conflict — §13.2.5.1 works through a case where naming positively costs a negation
at the enforcement site — the rule higher up the list wins, because the lower ones exist to serve it.

### 18.1 Decompose the state, because m + n beats m × n

**When there are lots of states, look at whether they decompose into small independent things**
(Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-19): *"handling m+n things is a lot less code than m*n things. Usually you can
decompose them all the way down to a bunch of almost-independent booleans but not always."*

**The saving is not linear-versus-quadratic in the running code; it is in what has to be written and
what has to be tested.** A mode enum with m × n cases needs every case written, read, and covered. The
same information as two independent fields needs m + n pieces of handling and the product falls out.

#### 18.1.1 Where this design already does it, mostly without having named it

| | Decomposed as | Rather than |
|---|---|---|
| what an `object-info` answer should carry (§9.1.3.11) | **six independent bits** in one flag field | a ladder of detail levels |
| a stream's capabilities (§4.1.1) | independent booleans — `updatable`, `deletable` | a mode enum over their combinations |
| which detail a tier can answer (§17.20) | **one bitmask per tier**, and a set difference for the rest | a table of supported combinations |
| nonce distinctness (§7.2.4) | day × SN × extent × block, each independent | anything that had to enumerate the product |
| a range budget (§9.1.3.6) | **one measure of three**, never two | a cross product of bounds |

**The nonce case is the one worth pausing on**, because there the decomposition is doing *correctness*
work rather than saving code: each dimension is independently unique, so the product is unique without
anybody enumerating it. §7.2.4's whole argument is that the one place the decomposition fails —
truncation reusing an offset — is the one place the rule breaks.

**And the budget case is the rule applied in the other direction: by removing a dimension.** §9.1.3.6
refuses to let a request bound two measures at once, so what could have been a 3 × 3 space of
combinations is 3. The reason given there is that a caller cannot know the compression ratio in
advance — but the *shape* of the fix is this rule.

#### 18.1.2 The almost in "almost-independent": normalize rather than validate

⚠️ **The bits are rarely quite independent, and what to do about it matters.** `Detail::Extents` implies
`Detail::Streams`, because an extent's record numbers mean nothing without the stream containing them.
Three ways to handle that, and they are not equally good:

| | Cost |
|---|---|
| **reject** the incomplete combination | a `BadRequest` for something the caller obviously meant, and a case to document and test |
| **ignore** the missing bit | the answer omits something the caller needs, silently |
| ⚠️ **normalize** — complete the implication on the way in | **no illegal combination exists to reject or test** |

**Normalizing is what `Want::of_args` does**, and it is the better answer for an *implication*. It
converts a disallowed-combination problem into no problem, which is the same move as
§17.12.1's structural-rather-than-careful: the bad state stops being representable rather than being
checked for.

**That does not dissolve every dependency.** A genuine *exclusion* — two bits that must not both be set
— cannot be normalized away, and there the combination has to be refused and tested. The distinction is
whether the dependency says *and also* or *not both*.

#### 18.1.3 The practice first, then the surprising arithmetic, then the tool

**Ordered by how much each is worth** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-19), because the ranking is not obvious
and the tool is the least of the three:

**1. The practice: break things into almost-independent dimensions with a small feature list each.**
This is the valuable part, and it pays whether or not anything is generated from it. A knot of
conditions nobody has separated cannot be reasoned about, tested systematically, or even counted; the
same knot as eight dimensions of two or three values each can be. **Most of the benefit is in the
decomposition, not in what is done with it afterwards.**

**2. The arithmetic, which is genuinely surprising.** All *pairs* over n dimensions can be covered in a
number of test cases that grows only **logarithmically** in n — not with the number of pairs, which is
quadratic. The floor is set by the largest two level counts rather than by n at all: with every
dimension binary, four rows is the minimum and a dozen or so covers dozens of dimensions.

> ⚠️ **And it works only because each test case is *complicated*.** One row that sets every dimension at
> once covers a value-pair for **every** pair of dimensions simultaneously. A suite of simple tests that
> each vary one thing needs a number of cases proportional to the *pairs*, which is the quadratic figure
> the whole result avoids.

**That cuts against the instinct to keep every test minimal**, and it does not contradict §15.3's "unit
tests are the bulk" so much as add a second kind beside it: many small tests that each pin one
behaviour, plus a few deliberately tangled ones that exist to cover combinations. The two are
complementary, and only the second kind gets the logarithm.

**3. The tool, which is *sometimes* useful** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-19) — **particularly where there is
a big knot of loosely connected things.** `jenny` generates n-way covering arrays over
almost-independent dimensions and can list, avoid and negative-test the disallowed combinations
([tool](https://github.com/bobjen/jenny), [description](https://burtleburtle.net/bob/math/jenny.html)).
⚠️ **Provenance, as with §4.1.1.1's `ENABLE NOVALIDATE`: it is Bob's own.** The
disallowed-combination handling is what makes it usable on a real system, where dimensions are
almost-independent rather than independent — and negative-testing those combinations is the part
easiest to skip by hand.

##### The two knots in this design

**Bob names them: the append interface, and the properties of streams** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-19).
Both are loosely-connected conditions that accumulated rather than being designed as a set.

**The append interface**, from §8.1 and §8.2: the framing (five values), fixed-offset against
assigned-offset, whether a record spans appends, whether the block ends on a boundary or holds none,
whether a CRC came with it, whether compressing helped, whether the extent is full, whether a record is
open, whether the extent is sealed, whether this is the first append to it. **Ten dimensions, one with
five values and the rest binary:**

| | |
|---|---|
| the full cross product | 5 × 2^9 = **2,560** |
| all pairs | of order **ten to twenty** rows |

**Derived**, and it is the ratio rather than the exact figure that matters: two orders of magnitude, for
a suite that catches every two-condition interaction. §17.12.1's `Sealed`-status leak was exactly that
kind of defect — one caller of three failing to handle a state.

**The properties of streams** are the newer knot and the one this session grew: `sealed` (§6.3),
`updatable` and `deletable` with three states each (§4.1.1.1), a storage class (#74), a soft-delete
opt-out, a declared expiry, whether extra structure is present (§4.1.2), whether the stream is shared
(§5.11.3.4), and whether it is an object's first or last. **That is a cross product in the thousands and
a pair-covering suite in the tens.**

⚠️ **It is also the knot most likely to grow**, since §4.1.1 exists precisely to be added to — which is
the argument for decomposing it now rather than after the next three flags arrive.

#### 18.1.4 Where DeLawson has an m × n problem it has not decomposed

**This is the useful direction to point the rule**, and #67 already wrote the observation without
naming it:

> Six of them interlocked inside one function: the block rule (§8.2.4), seal-on-a-record-boundary
> (§8.2.3), records spanning appends, the two durability gates, tenant purity of a block (§9.1.2), and
> who decompresses. **Each is right; the interaction is where the bugs were.**

Six almost-independent conditions is 64 combinations if they were independent, and they are not — which
is exactly the shape jenny exists for. §17.12.1's three bugs were all interaction bugs, and #67 already
concluded that a spec would have found the missed wakeup "by construction".

⚠️ **And `INVARIANTS.md`'s term index turns out to be a first cut at which of these are not
independent**, which was not why it was built. Invariants sharing a term are the ones liable to
interact:

| Term | Invariants naming it |
|---|---|
| `record` | nine |
| `extent`, `watermark`, `seal` | five to nine each |

**So the pairs worth covering are the pairs within a term group**, not all ~4,600 pairs over 96
invariants. That is a much smaller set, it is already computed, and it is the natural input to a
covering-array generator — which makes the term index a testing artefact as well as a navigational one
(#92).

#### 18.1.5 Where the tool does not fit, which is often

⚠️ **There are lots of ways a covering array can fail to be appropriate** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-19),
and the practice of §18.1.3 survives all of them while the tool does not. Two failures are worth
writing down because they are the ones this design will meet.

##### It handles nested dimensions badly

**A covering array wants a flat set of dimensions, each with a fixed list of values.** Nesting breaks
that: dimension B exists, or means anything, only when A takes a particular value. This design is full
of it:

| Nested thing | Exists only when |
|---|---|
| a framing's **width** | the framing is `FixedLength` (§8.2) |
| the **cleanup cursor** | a capability flag is mid-withdrawal (§4.1.2) |
| **EC parameters** — the code, the group shape | the storage class is erasure-coded rather than 4-instance (§4.3) |
| an extent's **log** and everything about it | something has updated or deleted from it (§4.2) |
| the **offset** in a range start | the start is `RecordThen` and not `Record` (§9.1.3.4) |

⚠️ **And nesting is worse than exclusion, which is the part that surprises.** §18.1.2's disallowed
combinations can be excluded, and jenny handles that. A nested dimension's out-of-scope combinations are
not disallowed but **meaningless** — a width when the framing is `lf` is not wrong, it is nothing — and
there is no value to put there that carries the right meaning. Two ways out, both lossy:

- **Flatten into the parent**, so `framing` becomes `lf, crlf, nul, length, fixed:1, fixed:8, fixed:4096`.
  Correct, and it inflates the parent's level count — which raises the *floor* on rows, since that is set
  by the two largest level counts (§18.1.3).
- **One array per branch**, which keeps the level counts small and **loses every pair that crosses
  branches.**

The last row of that table is in code written this session: `Range::args` pads the unused second number
with zero, because the wire is flat while the meaning is nested. That padding is the same problem in a
different place, and it is why `Start` is a kind plus two numbers rather than a variable-width thing.

##### And the knot keeps growing after the suite is written

**Once a suite has been generated and run, features and dimensions keep arriving.** Regenerating is the
obvious response and it is the wrong one, because a generated suite that has been *run* is worth more
than the array it came from:

| Regenerating loses | Because |
|---|---|
| known-good status | every case becomes unvalidated again |
| the reason a case exists | a case that once caught a bug is gone, along with whatever comment said so |
| any readable diff | the whole suite changes, so nothing can be reviewed |

**The practice instead: add the new feature to several random existing cases, and add new cases only
when forced** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-19) — *"rather than rerunning the tool or using the options in the
tool to extend the test suite."*

⚠️ **That is an admission worth noting, since it comes from the tool's author**: even the tool's own
extend mode loses to hand-editing here, because the value being protected is the suite's stability
rather than its optimality.

**Why *random* matters**: the existing cases already spread the other dimensions well, so a handful of
random hosts covers most pairs involving the new feature. Adding it always to the same few, or to
adjacent ones, would correlate the new dimension with whatever those cases happen to hold — and the
pairs it then misses are not random but systematic.

**And "forced" means an exclusion no existing case can host** (§18.1.2). If the new feature is
incompatible with what every existing case does, there is nowhere to put it and a new case is the only
option. That is the one time the suite has to grow.

⚠️ **Stated honestly: this trades guaranteed pair coverage for suite stability**, and it is a judgement
rather than a theorem. What it buys is that the suite keeps its history; what it costs is that coverage
becomes probabilistic at the edges.

##### The same shape as a decision already made

**§5.6.9 settled that placement is a solver whose answer is persisted, so the steady state is
verification rather than re-solving** — and re-running the solver would cause churn for no benefit
(§5.6.7 adds that this is why oscillation causes none). **A covering array is a solver output with
exactly that property.** Generate once, persist, maintain by hand, and never re-solve. Fifth instance of
the pattern in this design, and the first outside the running system.

### 17.22 The DN fans out, and one ask per SN rather than one per stream

#79's second half: `object-info` answers `Detail::Extents` and `Detail::Instances` by asking the SNs.

⚠️ **The DN drives it, not the FE, and an earlier draft of this plan had that wrong.** The reason given
for the FE was that only it knows all three numbering spaces (§17.16.2) — **which is false**. The FE
knows them because it is *told*; the **DN holds the object→stream map natively**, so it can convert
stream-local extent records to object-local itself. And since it also holds every stream of every object
in a batch, it is the tier that can group by SN before asking.

**So `Op::ObjectInfo` stays purely forwarded and the FE needed no changes at all** — which is the other
sign the DN was the right place.

#### 17.22.1 One ask per SN, because §1.4.0 says where the cost is

⚠️ **`list-extents` takes several streams, not one** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-19): *"a DN asking about
several SN streams should use the batch SN stream info... to make BatchObjectInfo truly batch."*

**One ask per stream would put the fan-out exactly where §1.4.0 measures the cost.** That section finds
nine tenths of an unbatched request's cost is messaging, and a `batch-object-info` over a thousand names
can hold a thousand streams — so a per-stream ask would turn one batched request into a thousand
unbatched ones, one tier down.

**The limit is shared across the whole ask**, since §9.1.3.7's limit is one number over the answer. A
stream reached after it runs out is **still answered** — `given` zero, and `next` where it was asked to
start — so a caller learns the count and the resume point rather than inferring that it was skipped.

**And the answer is interleaved**: a stream row, then the extents it says follow, repeated. Two blocks
would make a reader attribute extents to streams **by position**, which is §17.19's defect exactly. Each
`ExtentRun` also names its stream, so nothing depends on the SNs answering in the order asked.

#### 17.22.2 Three bugs, and a live run found all three

**The unit tests passed throughout.** Every one of these needed a cluster.

⚠️ **The limit was spent twice.** The DN charged the object and its stream rows against the cap, then
passed the **whole** cap again to the SNs — so a configured limit of 3 produced an answer of 6 entries.
Fixed by sending what the stream rows did not spend. The tell was in the output: *"6 entries"* under a
limit of three, printed right next to itself.

⚠️ **A truncated answer said "nothing more".** `Shape.next` was computed from the *stream* level, so an
answer that described every stream reported no continuation — even when a stream's extents had been cut
short. The continuation has to come from whichever level actually truncated: the first stream, in record
order, whose run says extents remain. Without it a caller stops one page early and silently.

⚠️ **And `then_some` is not a guard.** This line panicked with *attempt to add with overflow*:

```
(short && run.next != UNKNOWN).then_some(run.next + row.first_record)
```

**`then_some` evaluates its argument eagerly**, so `UNKNOWN + first_record` — `u64::MAX` plus a record
number — was computed whatever the condition said. It reads like a guard and is not one; `then` with a
closure is.

**Two things worth taking from that third one.** §8.1.6.3's sentinel at `MAX` made the mistake **loud** —
an overflow panic rather than a continuation of 1,114 that would have sent a caller to the wrong record
— which is the reservation earning its keep on its first outing. **And it is an argument for #86's
newtype**: `ROff` would own this arithmetic and return an error on a `NONE` operand, so the guard would
not be something to remember. §8.1.6.2 claimed the type should own the boundary arithmetic; this is what
it looks like when it does not.

⚠️ **Also worth noting how the panic presented**: the callback thread died holding the `Reply`, so the
client saw a **timeout** rather than an error. Nothing in the DN's own log said anything — the counters
showed the request simply never answered — and the panic was in `stderr.log`. A worker that dies holding
a reply is indistinguishable from a slow one, which is a monitoring gap rather than a bug (#95).

#### 17.22.3 What it answers now

Measured on the single-box cluster, 1,501 records over two streams and five extents, `info_entries = 6`:

| | |
|---|---|
| first page | the object, both streams, and **three** extents of stream 1 — six entries, and *"ask from record 1115"* |
| resuming there | stream 2 and **both** its extents, at object-local records 1,115 and 1,456 — four entries, *"nothing more"* |

**The conversion is the part worth checking**, and it holds: stream 2's extents are stream-local 0 and
341, reported as 1,115 and 1,456. The open extent reports its counts as unknown rather than zero, and
every extent carries the whole name — `(SnId, ExtentId, creation second)` — plus its instances, which is
what #61 asked for. **What is still missing from a usable hint is the capability** (#78), waiting on
#82's key.

### 17.23 The batch limit measures the cost of a name before it commits to it

**Built for #80's second half.** §9.1.3.7's entry limit applies to `BatchObjectInfo` as much as to
`ObjectInfo`, but the batch has an extra property to preserve: the answer must stay readable positionally
(§17.12 padded a missing name with zeros so it did), and a truncated answer cannot.

**So the answer leads with a header** — `info::Batch { asked, given, entries, next }`. `asked` and `given`
are the name counts, `entries` the entries spent, and `next` is an **index, not a name**, because the
caller already holds the list. A caller resumes by slicing its own request.

#### 17.23.1 Measure, then commit — not the other way around

⚠️ **§17.22.2's bug was spending the limit twice**: the DN charged itself for the object and its streams
and then handed the *whole* cap to the SNs. The batch loop is the same shape one level up, and it avoids
the bug by construction:

```
for each name:
    (entries, args) = piece(name)      // what this name would cost
    if committed > 0 and committed + entries > limit: stop here
    commit it
```

**Two rules make that correct.** It stops **at a name boundary**, never inside one, so the answer stays a
prefix (`A-BATCH-ANSWER-IS-A-PREFIX`). And it **always returns at least one name** even if that name alone
exceeds the limit — the same rule as `ONE-BLOCK-ALWAYS-RETURNS` (§8.1.5) and for the same reason: a limit
that can return nothing is a limit that can make forward progress impossible.

#### 17.23.2 A batch answers the cheap levels only

`BATCH_ANSWERS` is `Streams | Counts`, against `ANSWERS`' `Streams | Counts | Extents | Instances` for
the single case. Asking a batch for extents is `Unimplemented` rather than silently ignored, because
§9.1.3.12's fan-out is what makes extents affordable in a batch and it is not built (#96).

#### 17.23.3 ⚠️ The benchmark was measuring truncation, not lookup

**With the test cluster's `info_entries = 6`, `bench-info --batch 100` reported 2,464,449/s** — and the
answer covered six of every hundred names. **That 6.0% is 6/100**: the limit doing its job, and the rate
measuring the 94% it declined to do.

**The benchmark now counts three things, because two was not enough:**

| | |
|---|---|
| **asked** | names put on the wire |
| **answered** | names the server *looked at* — from `Batch.given`, or one per reply for a single lookup |
| **found** | names that named an object |

⚠️ **A miss is not a truncation**, and conflating them was the first thing this got wrong: counting a
single lookup as answered only on `Ok` made every miss look like the limit truncating, reporting 0.2%
answered when the true figure was 100%. `bench-info` now warns only when `answered < asked`, and names the
knob to raise (#97).

**And the test cluster's limit went to the design default of 10,000** (§9.1.3.7). Six was chosen to
exercise truncation, but a config-level limit poisons every measurement taken against that cluster, while
a **request-level** `--limit` exercises the same path on demand — `object-info --limit 1` still answers
*"0 streams described, 1 entry, ask from record 0"*.

**The honest baseline, release build, 2,000 objects, one stream each:**

| | |
|---|---|
| `bench-info --batch 100` | **4,296,330 names/s**, spread 1.5% |
| `bench-info --batch 1` | **123,081/s**, spread 1.6% |
| the same batch at `info_entries = 6` | 5,703,769/s — *faster*, by answering 6% of it |

That last row is the point: **the truncated configuration looked 33% better.** A benchmark that counts
requests rather than work done rewards declining the work, which is worth remembering for #79's
re-measurement and #88's variance hunt.

#### 17.23.4 A partly-given name is a continuation, not a completed one

⚠️ **Found while closing #80, and it is §17.22.2's bug again one level up.** The batch header said *"nothing
follows"* whenever it had reached every name asked about — but a name is not necessarily *finished* just
because it was *reached*. A name given its object row and none of its streams, because the limit ran out
inside it, left the answer incomplete while the header claimed otherwise.

**So the continuation distinguishes three cases**, and only the first may say nothing follows:

| | `next` |
|---|---|
| every name reached, each described whole | nothing follows |
| stopped before the end of the list | the **next** name's index |
| ⚠️ reached the end but the last name is partial | **that** name's index, not the one after it |

**A caller resuming at the third case re-asks that name**, and its own `Shape.next` says which
object-local record to resume from — which is how #80 specified it: *"the continuation is the next name,
with an extent range only in the mid-object case."*

**Only the last name given can be partial.** An earlier one stopping short would have spent the whole limit
and ended the loop, so `whole` is a single flag over the loop rather than a per-name field on the wire.
That is §18's decompose-the-state rule paying off: one bit, not one per name.

### 17.24 A batch across DNs, and the routing that decides what it costs

**Built for #96, on §9.1.3.12's design.** Two things had to exist first, and one of them was a
surprise.

#### 17.24.0 There was no name-to-DN routing at all

⚠️ **`Process::pick` is round robin**, and every DN-bound request used it. With one DN that is
invisible; with two it means **a create lands on one machine and the lookup that follows it asks
another**, so half the objects are lost the moment a second DN exists. The fan-out had nothing to fan
out *to* — it had to be built on routing that was not there.

`common/src/routing.rs` is the crude version: a hash of the whole name over the DNs in the roster.
It is wrong in every way #75 is about — a DN cannot be added without moving names, a range cannot be
split — and right in the one way that has to hold first, `A-NAME-HAS-ONE-OWNER`. Everything that maps a
name to a DN goes through it, so #75 replaces one function.

`Process::owner` now routes `create-object`, `object-info` and single-name lookups. ⚠️ **`batch-create`
still uses `pick`** and therefore still creates on the wrong DN (#98).

#### 17.24.1 Two defects the single-DN cluster was hiding

**Both were in code written and tested the same day**, and neither was reachable with one DN.

| | |
|---|---|
| a **missing name** in a levelled batch got a bare object row while every other name got a shape first | so a reader counting arguments walks off by five and attributes rows to the wrong name — §17.12's failure exactly. A miss now carries `Shape::plain()`. |
| a **summary** — counts, no rows — reported `nothing more` | while holding undescribed streams, contradicting the batch header that had just told the caller to come back to that name (§17.24.2) |

#### 17.24.2 A shape says where a listing would resume, not whether rows were asked for

`Shape::next` was set only when stream rows were wanted. But §9.1.3.12's summary asks for **counts and
not rows on purpose**, and the answer has to say *"three streams, none described, a listing starts at
record 0"* — which is the whole reason the summary is useful. Reporting `nothing more` there made a
summary indistinguishable from a complete answer, and made every per-name line in a merged batch
disagree with the header above it.

> **So `next` means "where a stream listing would resume", not "where the rows you asked for ran out".**
> One rule, true of a summary and a truncation alike.

#### 17.24.3 The reservation needs no round trip

⚠️ **§9.1.3.12 says the summaries are what tell the FE how much to reserve, and that is one step too
many.** A summary costs *exactly* one entry per name — the object's own row, by
`A-NAME-COSTS-AT-LEAST-ONE-ENTRY` — and the FE knows how many names it routed elsewhere before it
sends anything. So the detailed ask can be given `limit − (names elsewhere)` **with no measuring round
trip at all**, and round one is: full ask to the lead DN, summary to every other, all at once.

**What the summaries are actually for is round two.** They report each name's exact stream count, which
is what sizes the upgrade — §9.1.3.2's counts, one tier out.

**Measured on the three-DN cluster, six one-stream objects, so a full name costs two entries:**

| limit | what came back |
|---|---|
| 12 | all six in full, 12 entries, nothing more |
| 8 | the lead DN's two names in full, four summaries reading *"0 streams of 1 described"*, exactly 8, carry on at name 1 |
| 10 | slack of 2 spent upgrading the **two names nearest the front**, exactly 10, carry on at name 3 |

**Round two takes a contiguous run from the first unfinished name, not the cheapest names going.** The
continuation points at the first unfinished name, so a caller coming back for name 5 asks again *from*
5 — detail fetched for name 9 in the meantime is work nobody will read.

#### 17.24.4 ⚠️ Every estimate here is allowed to be wrong

The DN's limit is the authority, a DN may answer shorter than asked, and #75 will make ownership move.
What stops any of that from being a correctness problem is one property:

> **Assembly walks the caller's order and stops at the first name it does not have.**

A bad estimate then costs a round trip and never an answer attributed to the wrong name
(`A-BATCH-ANSWER-IS-A-PREFIX`). That is what makes it safe to guess at all — and a refusal from a DN
fails the whole batch rather than being reported as those objects not existing, which would be a wrong
answer rather than a partial one.

#### 17.24.5 ⚠️ Hash routing makes a batch cost D messages, which is the whole cost

⚠️ **Retaken after #98 and #106** — the first figures here were void, because `bench-create`
scattered objects round-robin while `bench-info` looked them up by owner, so most lookups missed
(§17.30.3). These are one session, 100,000 objects, **every lookup found**:

| | `--batch 100` | `--batch 1` |
|---|---|---|
| one DN | 3,479,408/s | 130,825/s |
| three DNs | **2,037,511/s** | 109,226/s |

**A batch got 41% slower by having three DNs to spread over.** The void figure said 46%, so the
conclusion was right and the number was luck.

⚠️ **But the single-name column decomposes it, which the first version missed.** A one-name lookup
does not fan out — it goes to one DN either way — and it is still **16.5% slower** on three. That is
two extra processes competing for one box's cores, not routing. Against a contention-adjusted
baseline of 2,904,963/s, the fan-out itself costs **30%**.

**So the effect is real and was overstated by a third.** One request became three, and §1.4.0
measures nine tenths of a request's cost as messaging, so multiplying the messages multiplies nearly
all of it.

⚠️ **It gets worse, and not gently.** A hash spreads *n* names over *D* DNs, so the number touched is
`D(1 − (1 − 1/D)^n)`:

| DNs | DNs a 100-name batch touches |
|---|---|
| 3 | 3.0 |
| 10 | 10.0 |
| 100 | **63.4** |
| 1000 | 95.2 |

**At a hundred DNs a hundred-name batch is 63 requests, and batching has bought almost nothing.** The
thing §1.4.0 built batching for is gone at the scale the system is for.

> **So #75's ranges are not only about splitting and moving.** A hash guarantees maximal fan-out — it is
> the *worst* case for a batch, by construction. Contiguous ranges let names that are asked about
> together live together, which is the only way a batch of a thousand stays one request.

**And that reframes §16.149.** Caller-side assembly does not fix this: the caller sending D requests
costs D to the FE tier as well, so it is more messages, not fewer — better latency, worse load. What
fixes it is **locality**, which is a routing property and not a fan-out one. §16.151.

### 17.25 A stream's sizes, and why a physical one is never stored

**Asked for by Bob, 2026-08-20**, for `batch-object-info` and for the `dir` that does not exist
yet: *"users like seeing when their objects were created and how big they are."*

#### 17.25.0 #94 first, because the logical length was not being carried

**The SN recorded a compressed length and no logical one**, so `list-extents` answered
`logical: UNKNOWN` for every extent and one of §9.1.3.6's three budgets could not be planned. The
number was already on the write path — the EN accumulates `logical_end` per extent — and the seal
report simply did not carry it.

**It is a shape now, not a third bare number** (`range::Filled`), which is what #94 asked for:
§8.1.6 exists because a logical length and a compressed one are easy to confuse, and three numbers
in a row in a seal message is precisely that. ⚠️ **And the types caught it immediately** — the first
build after `Filled` became `{ records, LOff, COff }` failed in two services on exactly the
substitution §8.1.6 was written about.

> **The type discipline also made it free.** Both spaces are 32-bit, so all three measures are the
> 16 bytes the two of them took, and `Sealed` did not grow by a byte. Storing them as `u64` would
> have cost **13.6 GB of an SN's memory** at §14.1's 1.7 × 10^9 extents — which the size test caught
> on the first attempt.

#### 17.25.1 What the DN keeps, and what it is allowed to be wrong about

`Held` — the DN's per-stream record, and its largest structure — gained a creation second, an extent
count, a logical length and a compressed one.

| | |
|---|---|
| `created` | the DN's own, so **always exact**. It hands out the stream. |
| `records` | exact once sealed, **`UNKNOWN` while growing** |
| `extents`, `logical`, `compressed` | exact once sealed, **as-of while growing**, `UNKNOWN` until an SN has been asked |

⚠️ **Why `records` alone does not go stale.** §4.5's exact record count is what addressing runs on,
so a stale record count is a **wrong read**; a stale byte count is a slightly wrong listing. The
asymmetry is the point, not a compromise.

**40 bytes to 56, and four fields for the space of two**, because `records` stopped being an
`Option<u64>` in the same change: a sentinel in a space that already reserves one costs 8 bytes where
a discriminant cost 8 plus padding (`EVERY-SPACE-RESERVES-A-SENTINEL` paying for itself in a place
that was not the reason for it). Six `u64` and two `u32`, no padding — and the size test says so
rather than just asserting 56.

**The SN is the authority** and the DN caches: only the SN owns the extent list, so the totals come
back on a `list-extents` answer and are written to `Held` before the answer goes out. A sealed
stream cannot change, so **one refresh is right for ever**; `Held::learned` refuses to move a number
backwards, because two answers can cross in flight.

##### ⚠️ Two limits found by running it

| | |
|---|---|
| **the staleness floor is one extent** | the SN sums *sealed* extents only. The open extent's size lives at the EN, so an object still inside its first extent reports **0 bytes** — measured: 60 records read as `0 bytes so far`, and 4,094 appeared only when the extent sealed. §17.25.4 has the home for it. |
| **the cache only refreshes when somebody asks for extents** | so a listing that never asks reports `UNKNOWN` for ever, and the feature that motivated the storage does not benefit from it. §17.25.4. |
| **a shared stream's totals are not one object's size** | §11 lumps small objects into common streams, and then every object referencing that stream would report the *stream's* size as its own. §16.152. |

#### 17.25.2 Physical length is calculated, never stored

⚠️ **Bob, twice, and both halves matter** (2026-08-20): physical bytes are *"what they look for for
billing"*, and they *"should be calculated from compressed length and storage class, not actual"*.

**So there is no fourth number anywhere** — not on the wire, not in `Held`, not at the SN. A stored
physical length is a derived value that goes wrong the moment a storage class changes, and the class
is what the factor belongs to.

##### And the class's intent, not the copies that exist

> *"If the extent is supposed to have 4 instances, it doesn't matter if it has 3 or 5 at the moment,
> the user gets billed for 4."*

**The second reason is the stronger one**: *"you can always get a snapshot of the SN's metadata but
some ENs are offline."* Reading the live instance list would put **every EN on the billing path** and
make a bill depend on the repair queue. Charging the class means billing runs off SN metadata alone
— a whole tier off the path, and a figure that is consistent in time because one snapshot produces it
(`BILLING-CHARGES-THE-CLASS-NOT-THE-COPIES`).

#### 17.25.3 A double, because the next scheme need not be a ratio

**Erasure coding's factors are not whole numbers**: 3 data plus 1 parity is 4/3, 3 plus 4 is 7/3,
5 plus 1 is 6/5. An integer multiplier was wrong before it was written.

⚠️ **And a `f64` rather than a rational, on Bob's call**: *"we don't have any fibonacci-like things
yet but it's easy to imagine them showing up."* A ratio of two integers is exact for every scheme
that exists and assumes the next one is also a ratio — an assumption with nothing behind it. The
double costs nothing worth having: 53 bits of mantissa is exact on byte counts to 9 PB, and past
that the relative error is around 10^-16 against a bill nobody computes to the byte.

**It is honestly inexact and the tests say so.** `4.0 / 3.0` is a shade under 4/3, and only the
round-up lands a three-megabyte stream on 4,000,000 — a factor a shade *over* would charge one byte
more. Rounding **up**, because a fragment that is not a whole one still occupies a whole one, and
because a bill that rounds down is a bill nobody is paying.

**Measured end to end**: an object with two extents, one sealed, reported *"2 extents, 4094 bytes so
far, 4094 stored, 16376 billed"* — 4,094 × 4 copies. The same line came back from the DN's cache
with no SN asked, which is what makes it affordable in a listing.

### 18.2 A parameter may be a fraction, and a fraction beats a percentage

**Yes, a parameter can be a double** (asked by Bob, 2026-08-20). Nothing in the config layer stood
in the way — TOML has floats and serde wants nothing extra — but `extents.expansion` is the first
one, so there is a test whose whole job is to fail loudly if that ever stops being true.

**And when a parameter is a proportion, it is a fraction in [0, 1], not a percentage** (Asserted,
Bob):

> *"I don't like percentile parameters because you end up multiplying by 100.0 in one place and
> dividing by 100.0 in another when you could have just multiplied by a probability once."*

⚠️ **The two conversions are the defect, not the notation.** They are written in different places by
different people, so nothing checks that both exist, and the failure mode is silent: a value 100×
out is often still a plausible-looking number. A fraction multiplies once, at the point of use, and
there is no second place to get wrong.

**It also composes.** A fraction of a fraction is a multiply; a percentage of a percentage needs a
divide nobody remembers. `0.99` reads as a probability and can be used as one — in a comparison, as
a weight, as a rate — while `99` has to be told what it is every time.

**A configured number is written as it will be used.** ⚠️ Which is why `expansion = 1.3333` is a
worse way to say 3-data-plus-1-parity than letting the code compute `4.0 / 3.0` — the written form
carries four decimal places of precision and the divide carries fifteen. **Say the thing that is
known; let the code do the arithmetic.** Neither is exact (§17.25.3), and that is fine; one is
needlessly less exact than the other.

#### 17.25.4 The sync loops are where the refresh belongs

⚠️ **A seal-time refresh was the wrong answer** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-20): *"there will be a DN/SN
sync occasionally (once a day? once a week?), which is an opportunity to report the current lengths
of unsealed and recently-sealed streams."*

**§13.1's loops already carry exactly this traffic, and both of §17.25.1's limits have a home in
them:**

| Limit | Loop | Cadence |
|---|---|---|
| the DN's cached sizes only refresh when somebody asks for extents | **DN → SN**, which already enumerates every stream a DN references (§13.1.3) | a day to a month |
| the SN cannot see the open extent's size, so a small object reads as 0 bytes | **SN → EN, instance state**, the only loop that talks to the tier holding the bytes | ~1 hour |

> **Neither needs a new mechanism, and that is the point.** A seal-time round trip would sit on the
> path an append is blocked behind (§17.22's `extend-object`), and it would cover **only** sealed
> streams — while the sync covers the unsealed ones, which is where staleness actually lives.

**And it costs nothing measurable.** §13.1.3 prices the DN → SN sweep at 156 MB daily for
7.8 × 10^6 distinct streams; three more numbers per stream is 24 bytes on a record that sweep already
carries, against a loop whose own justification is a 10^13 leverage ratio on leaked streams. The
sizes ride along.

⚠️ **Which fixes the staleness contract as a cadence rather than an accident.** §17.25.1 says the
sizes are "as-of" for a growing stream; the sync says as-of *what*: the last sweep. A growing
stream's listed size is a day old, a sealed one's is exact, and nothing has to be asked at the moment
a listing is rendered — which is the only way a `dir` over a million objects can be cheap.

#### 17.25.5 ⚠️ §11's regimes break most of this, and they are expected rather than hypothetical

**Bob, 2026-08-20**, on the four regimes of §11 as they will actually arrive:

> *"Extremely small seal-after-append single-append objects will get inlined in the DN metadata, and
> larger but still small ones will become a range offset in a common per-tenant SN stream. Append will
> have a seal-after-append flag, and there will be a simplified user interface for giving an append
> that creates and seals its own object. A second append to an open object triggers a dedicated SN
> stream for that object even if the first append went to a common stream."*

**§16.152 asked whether a shared stream's sizes mean anything for one object. This answers it: no, and
it is not an edge case** — §11 calls lumping "the load-bearing case", the one that keeps stream counts
proportional to bytes rather than to object count. So everything §17.25.1 stores is, for the regimes
below, either absent or wrong.

##### What each regime does to a per-stream size

| Regime | What breaks |
|---|---|
| **Inline** | ⚠️ **there is no stream at all**, so there is no `Held` and nowhere for `created` or the sizes to live. And the sizes are *exact and free* here — the DN holds the records — so this regime wants them on the **object** record, not the stream one. |
| **Lumped** | ⚠️ the object is a **range within** a shared stream, so the stream's totals overstate the object's size by the lumping factor — §13.1.3's expected case lumps ~128,000 objects into one stream, so a listing would report every one of them as **128,000× its true size**. |
| **Packed** | the same, one tier down: a shared *extent* with a directory of its occupants |
| **Dedicated** | the only regime §17.25.1 is actually correct for |

> **So a size is a property of an object's *range*, not of the stream that range sits in.** That is the
> shape the storage has to take, and `Held` as it stands cannot express it.

##### And a third numbering space, which §17.16.2 has already been paid for once

A lumped object's records sit at some **stream-local** offset that is not zero, while `Held` carries
only `first_record`, the *object-local* number of the stream's first record — an encoding that assumes
stream-local zero **is** the object's start. §17.16.2 is what happened the last time a conversion like
that was skipped: 139 of 200 reads returned the wrong record, and it was invisible until the first
seal because all three origins are zero while an object fits one extent. ⚠️ **A lumped object makes
