them differ from the first record written**, so the same bug would present immediately and everywhere
rather than rarely.

##### The one thing that gets *easier*

**A seal-after-append object is exact from the moment it exists.** §17.25.4's staleness and #100's
"a small object reads as 0 bytes until its first extent seals" both come from an object being open —
and the two regimes where a small object's size matters most are precisely the two that **seal at
creation**. So that gap narrows to objects that are *medium* (too big to lump, small enough to sit in
one extent) and still being written, where *"so far"* is an honest thing to say.

**And the flag is what makes the regimes decidable at all.** A DN cannot choose to inline or to lump
unless it knows at append time that nothing more is coming — the decision is not reversible after the
bytes have gone somewhere. So `seal-after-append` is not a convenience on the append path; it is the
input the placement decision runs on, which is why the single-call create-append-seal interface and
the small-object regimes are one feature and not two (§16.153).

##### The regime is decided once, at the first append, by the seal flag alone

⚠️ **An earlier draft of this section read promotion as a fork — span both streams, or move the first
append. Neither** (Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-20):

> *"Let's have inlining and range-of-common-stream both be only when the first append seals the
> object. Then the rule of a dedicated stream on second append becomes a rule of dedicated stream if
> the first append does not seal the object."*

**So there is no promotion at all.** The decision is made at the first append, from one bit, and never
revisited:

| First append | Regime |
|---|---|
| **seals the object** | inline, or a range in a common stream, by size |
| **does not seal it** | a dedicated stream |

> **An object is therefore in exactly one regime for life, and the shared-range encoding never
> coexists with a multi-stream object.** That is what the fork was really about, and it is settled in
> the direction that keeps every case simple rather than the one that avoids a copy.

##### Which unifies the numbering, rather than adding a space to it

§17.25.5 above worried that a lumped object needs a stream-local base alongside `Held.first_record`'s
object-local one. It does — but **never both at once**, and that collapses:

| Regime | Conversion |
|---|---|
| dedicated, stream *i* | `object_local = stream_local + first_record[i]`, and the stream's own records start at 0 |
| lumped | `object_local = stream_local − base`, and the object has exactly one stream, so its own records start at 0 |

**One signed offset does both**, positive for a dedicated stream and negative for a lumped range. Not
a third numbering space after all: the same conversion with a sign, which is §18.1's rule paying out —
the two states were never independent, so `m + n` is one field rather than two.

##### Three safety nets, so the flag is an optimization and not a correctness requirement

**A user who does not set the flag must not lose data or waste disk**, and three things arrange that
(Asserted, Bob, 2026-08-20):

| | |
|---|---|
| **the EN packs tiny appends into a common extent regardless**, *"if the data gets that far"* | so there is **never** disk waste from missing the flag — the data placement is always right |
| **the SN is strongly encouraged to rewrite small sealed objects** as inline or a common-stream range | so the metadata placement is right *eventually*, and the flag only makes it right *immediately* |
| meanwhile the user **sees a stream + extent metadata tax** | which is what makes the flag worth setting |

> **The layering is the design.** Data is placed correctly always; metadata correctly eventually; the
> flag buys immediacy. Nothing about a missing flag is unrecoverable, which is what lets the fast path
> be a hint rather than a contract.

##### ⚠️ And the tax has to be billed, or nobody pays it

**§12.2 has already priced this, and it says the tax does not currently exist.** A minimal stream is
200 B of stream record plus a 100 B extent reference — **300 B of SN RAM**, and RAM against disk is
~5,000, so **1.5 MB of disk-equivalent**. Break-even is a **~375 KB** payload.

So a tiny object with a dedicated stream costs the operator more in metadata than in data, by a wide
margin — and §12.2 measures the 1 KB case as **underbilled 375×**. ⚠️ **Today that is a cost to the
operator and not a tax on the user**, which means the incentive to set the flag points the wrong way:
the cheapest thing for the user is the ruinous one for the operator, which §12.2 already names as the
workload pricing selects for.

**Billing therefore has to charge for metadata records and not only for bytes**, which is a real
addition to §17.25.2's model: physical bytes from the compressed length and the storage class are the
*data* half, and a per-stream and per-extent charge is the other. Without it "users will see a
metadata tax" is not true of anything the system computes (§16.153).

#### 17.25.6 The inline cutoff is calculable, and it comes out at the size of the pointer

**Bob, 2026-08-20**: *"The cost of DN metadata depends on the fraction of time metadata is in RAM.
Once you know that you can calculate where the tradeoff is for keeping the data inline vs as a range
in a shared stream."* So the boundary between §11's first two regimes is **not a tuning knob to be
guessed at**. Here is the arithmetic.

##### The compaction terms, which have closed forms

**A shared stream is rewritten when it is 1/3 garbage** (Asserted, Bob, *"going by memory I didn't
redo the logic"*). Redoing it: of the objects live just after a compaction, a third have died by the
next one — that is what makes the third of garbage — so an object survives each cycle with
probability 2/3 and is copied when it does.

| | |
|---|---|
| Expected copies | Σ (2/3)^k = **2** |
| Total writes | 1 initial + 2 copies = **3** |

**Which generalizes: compacting at garbage fraction *g* writes each object `1/g` times, and holds
`1/(1−g)` bytes per live byte.** (Derived. Check: *g* = 1/3 gives 3 writes and 1.5× space, and Bob's
memory is right — reading "rewritten 3 times" as three writes rather than three *re*-writes.)

⚠️ **That is the whole compaction tradeoff in two terms pulling opposite ways**: tolerate more garbage
and writes fall as `1/g` while space rises as `1/(1−g)`. Where to sit depends on the price of
bandwidth against the price of space, which is a separate calculation this one does not need.

##### The cutoff

Costs per byte, in disk-byte-equivalents, with *r* = **5,000** for RAM against disk (§12.2, Cited),
*E* the storage class expansion, *G* = `1/(1−g)` = **1.5** the garbage amplification, *R* the metadata
a range costs that an inline object avoids, and **_f_ the fraction of time DN metadata is resident**:

| | Cost of an *n*-byte object |
|---|---|
| **inline** | `n·(E·G + f·r)` — its bytes are DN metadata, so they pay the RAM term |
| **ranged** | `n·E·G + R·(E·G + f·r)` — its bytes are ordinary data, and the range record is the metadata |

Inline wins while `n·f·r < R·(E·G + f·r)`, so:

> ### `n* = R · (1 + E·G / (f·r))`

⚠️ **§17.27 takes this at its limit and stops there** — `inline ⟺ n < R`, with no *f* to measure. What
follows is why that limit is the *safe* end rather than merely the easy one, which is the part still
worth having.

**With *E* = 4, *G* = 1.5, *r* = 5,000 and *R* = 56 bytes** — today's DN stream record (§4.7.1), which
is exactly what a range costs and an inline object does not pay:

| *f* | Cutoff |
|---|---|
| 1 (always resident) | **56 B** |
| 0.1 | 57 B |
| 0.01 | 63 B |
| 0.001 | 123 B |
| 10^-4 | 728 B |
| 10^-5 | 6.8 KB |

##### What the formula says

> **Inline an object when it is smaller than the record that would otherwise point at it.** The limit
> as `f·r → ∞` is exactly *R*, and the whole `E·G/(f·r)` term is the correction for metadata that is
> *not* resident.

**And it is remarkably insensitive.** Across four orders of magnitude of *f* — from always-resident to
one part in a thousand — the cutoff moves from 56 to 123 bytes. It only runs away when DN metadata is
nearly always cold, and then it does so fast.

⚠️ **Which makes *R* the lever, not *f*.** The cutoff is proportional to the range record, so
**shrinking the DN's stream record lowers the cutoff** and inlines fewer objects — correctly, because
a cheap pointer makes pointing cheap. §4.7.1 is the relevant number: 56 bytes against a 4-byte design
budget, so a DN stream record that met its budget would put the cutoff near **4 bytes** and inlining
would be for almost nothing.

##### ⚠️ *f* is per-object, so the cutoff is too

**The fraction of time a byte of metadata is resident is not one number for the fleet.** A DN holding
100 TB of metadata in 256 GB of RAM has *f* ≈ 0.0026 *averaged*, giving a cutoff near 80 bytes — but
a hot object's metadata is resident and a cold one's is not, and the formula says a hot object should
be inlined at a smaller size than a cold one.

> **That is exactly what the SN's rewrite pass is positioned to use** (§17.25.5): it decides regimes
> *after the fact*, when access frequency is an observed quantity rather than a prediction. The
> cutoff formula is what tells it which comparison to make.

**And *f* is a measurement nobody has taken** — ⚠️ **nor will anyone**, since §17.27 takes the limit
and closes the question. Were it ever needed it would be, per §18.2, a **fraction in [0, 1]** and not a
percentage: a parameter multiplied by 5,000 in exactly one place.

## 17.26 Sharing an extent puts an authorization boundary inside it

**Bob, 2026-08-20**, on §11's lumped and packed regimes: *"This is a use case where a user would be
allowed to read some records in an extent but not all of them."*

⚠️ **That falsifies a stated assumption.** §9.1.3.5 accepted the extent-scoped certificate partly on
this ground:

> *"I don't know of a use case where there is a security boundary between a tenant and itself, so the
> security aspect isn't bothering me so far."*

**There are now two**, and one of them Bob introduced himself:

| | |
|---|---|
| **within a tenant** | §5.1.1.1a's writable aliases exist so that *"many workers on a gorilla"* can each have *"their own private scratch space"*. That is a boundary between a tenant and itself, by construction. |
| **across tenants** | an inline object's records end up in a **metadata extent shared with thousands of other objects' metadata** (§11) — though see below, this one turns out not to bite |

### 17.26.1 Three things assume the reader may see the whole block

**The leak is not in the capability alone.** Three separate mechanisms in the read path each assume
that whoever may read one record may read everything alongside it:

| | Where |
|---|---|
| the certificate is **extent-scoped** — `(tenant, extent, write?)` | §9.1.3.5 |
| a read **returns the block**, and the client picks its record out of it | §17.5's read path; `Piece` carries `bytes` |
| the CRC is **over the block**, checked end to end by the client | §8.1 |

> ⚠️ **So trimming the answer is not available.** Removing another object's records from a block breaks
> the CRC the client is about to check, and the EN cannot re-cut a compressed block because **the EN
> never decompresses** — that is the property that makes the whole read path cheap (§17.25's *"nothing
> in between ever looked inside"*).

**The block must therefore be clean by construction**, not cleaned on the way out.

### 17.26.2 Two ways to make it clean, and the cheap one keeps everything

| | Cost |
|---|---|
| **a block never spans two objects**, and the certificate carries a **range within the extent** | ⚠️ a tiny object gets a block of its own, and a block is the compression unit (§7.2) — so tiny objects can no longer be **compressed together**, which is a large part of what lumping was for. Plus the FE must check a range, and §9.1.3.5.4's signed form has to carry one. |
| **a common stream never spans an authorization boundary** | more common streams — one per domain rather than per tenant — and a domain with few tiny objects gets an under-filled stream, which is §12.2's metadata tax again |

**The second keeps every mechanism above intact.** Blocks may be shared freely, compression works
across objects, the CRC stands, and the extent-scoped certificate is *exactly right again* — because
everything in the extent is readable by the same set.

> **So the fix is in placement, not in the read path.** Lump by authorization domain rather than by
> tenant, and the boundary never lands inside an extent in the first place.

⚠️ **And that only works while domains are coarse.** §5.9.1a makes authorization directory-shaped and
Bob has *"no use case demanding per-object authorization"* — so domains are few and large, and one
common stream apiece is affordable. **If authorization ever becomes per-object, this degenerates into
a stream per object, which is precisely what lumping exists to avoid**, and the first row becomes the
only option (§16.155).

### 17.26.3 Inline objects are safe for a different reason

**A metadata extent is shared across tenants, which sounds worse and is not.** An inline object's
records are bytes in a DN metadata object, and a user never reads that extent — the **DN** reads it,
and the DN is the authorization point. The user's read is answered from the DN's own metadata, so
there is no extent-scoped certificate in play and nothing to over-grant.

> **The regimes divide on who holds the bytes, not on how small the object is.** Inline is safe because
> the DN mediates; lumped and packed are exposed because the point of them is that the **EN** serves
> the bytes directly.

### 17.26.4 What the range-bounded certificate would need, if it comes to that

§9.1.3.5.4 anticipated this exactly (Bob, 2026-08-19): *"If I ever need authorization for a record
offset or logical offset or compressed offset, it would be the extent offset since the hint is by
extent, and ObjectInfo does give enough information to deduce offset within an extent."*

**Both signed-form rules already permit it**, which is worth checking rather than assuming:

- **the signed form is closed** — every field must be in the answer, the request, or ambient. `object-info` reports each extent's base offsets, so a range within an extent is computable by the caller and the closure holds.
- **identity, never a derived position** — refined by Bob to *a position may be signed if its space is pinned by an identity in the signature*. The extent **is** in the signature, so an extent-local range is pinned and does not drag §17.16.2's three numbering spaces inside the certificate.

So the mechanism is available and consistent; it is the compression cost in §17.26.2's first row that argues against reaching for it.

### 17.27 Decided: inline while the data is smaller than the reference to it

**Bob, 2026-08-20**: *"It's easiest then to inline only if the data is smaller than the stream range
reference, and not worry about how frequently the metadata is loaded."*

> ### `inline ⟺ n < R`

**§17.25.6 derived `n* = R·(1 + E·G/(f·r))`; this is that formula's limit, and taking the limit is the
decision.** The residency fraction *f* does not have to be measured, so §16.154 closes and #104 with it.

#### 17.27.1 The error is one-sided, which is why the limit is safe to take

⚠️ **This is not an approximation that could land either way.** The correction term `E·G/(f·r)` is
**strictly positive**, so the true cutoff is always *at least* *R*:

| | |
|---|---|
| `n < R` **under**-inlines | by at most the correction — 0.1% when metadata is always resident, 12% at one part in a hundred, and materially only when metadata is nearly always cold |
| what under-inlining costs | a 56-byte range record pointing at an object slightly smaller than 56 bytes |
| what **over**-inlining would cost | user bytes in RAM-backed metadata at **~5,000×** disk (§12.2) |

**So the rule errs in the direction where a mistake is cheap**, and the expensive mistake is
unreachable by construction. That is the whole argument for taking a limit rather than measuring.

#### 17.27.2 And the rule has no free parameters

**`n < R` is stated in terms of the thing it is compared against.** *R* moved on 2026-08-20, from 40
bytes to 56, when the DN's stream record took a creation second and a stream's sizes (§4.7.1) — and a
rule of this shape needed no re-derivation and no re-measurement, because the quantity it depends on is
the one it is already reading.

> **A cutoff written as a constant would have been silently wrong that day.** §4.7.1's placeholders mean
> *R* is still fourteen times its design budget, so it will move again — and when the segmented array
> and the B-tree land and *R* approaches 4 bytes, this rule will correctly stop inlining almost
> anything, with nothing to change.

**What §17.25.6 is still for** is the argument above: it is what proves the limit is the safe end rather
than the convenient one, and it is where to look if *R* ever becomes small enough that the correction
stops being a rounding error.

### 17.28 Why streams are single-tenant, which is not a read-authorization argument

**Bob, 2026-08-20**: *"For #105, if read is limited to just the correct rows, I forget what the motive
is for not combining all tenants in the same common stream."*

**It is recorded, and it predates the question** — §5.11 and §12.4.3, both Asserted by Bob on
2026-08-17 and 2026-08-19. Read authorization was never the reason:

> *"Single-tenancy is what makes §7.3.3's key derivation, §12's attribution and the plain statement
> 'this stream belongs to a tenant' all simple, and pricing gives them up for nothing."*

**The attribution clause is the load-bearing one** — §17.28.1 works out why, and it is a bigger number
than that sentence suggests. The pricing clause is what makes the trade free. The only thing multi-tenant streams buy is an answer to the
zillion-tenants-with-one-tiny-object abuse, and §12.4.3 already buys that with a base tenant charge —
so the benefit is nil and the cost does not need weighing.

⚠️ **And the exposure is one object per tenant, ever.** §12.4.3: lumping puts a tenant's *later* small
objects into common streams they already own, so single-tenancy bites only at the **first** one.
Combining tenants would save on the order of a kilobyte of metadata per tenant — not per object.

#### 17.28.1 The strongest leg is billing, and it is stronger than §5.11 states it

⚠️ **A draft of this section had this backwards.** It argued that §12's attribution no longer needs
single-tenancy, because §11's lumping makes many *objects* share a stream, so #102 must attribute per
**range** regardless. That conflates two consumers with different granularities, and Bob's version is
the right one (Asserted, 2026-08-20):

> *"The most persuasive argument to me at the moment is to keep single-tenant streams, for billing:
> I can bill whole extents instead of ranges of extents."*

**Billing needs tenant granularity, not object granularity.** #102's per-range sizes are for a
*listing* — what one object costs its owner to look at. A **bill** never has to descend below the
stream, because the stream belongs to one tenant and therefore so does every byte in every one of its
extents.

##### What whole-extent billing actually costs to compute

**It is already computed.** §17.25.1's `Totals` is the SN summing its sealed extents per stream, so a
bill is:

> **sum each stream's compressed total, multiply by the storage class's expansion (§17.25.2),
> attribute to the stream's tenant.** No extent is divided, no object is visited, no range arithmetic
> happens anywhere.

⚠️ **And the sweep is `O(streams)`, not `O(objects)`.** §13.1.3's expected case is 10^12 objects in
7.8 × 10^6 streams — so ranged billing would be **~128,000× the work** of whole-extent billing, on the
one sweep that has to run over the entire fleet on a billing cycle. That is the argument, and it is
much larger than "attribution is simple".

##### It also settles whose garbage is whose

**A stream carries up to a third garbage before it is compacted** (§17.25.6), so a tenant's
whole-extent bill includes the garbage their own deletions left. That is the right answer — the
operator is holding that space — and it arrives **for free** rather than as a rule.

⚠️ **Multi-tenant streams would have to decide whose garbage it is**, which has no good answer: the
space exists because of one tenant's deletions but sits between another's live records, and the
compaction that reclaims it rewrites both. Single-tenancy makes the question not arise, and it aligns
the incentive — the tenant who creates the garbage is the one paying to hold it.

**So the conclusion stands on a broader base than §5.11 gave it**, not a narrower one. Key derivation
and the pricing floor are the other two legs; this is the load-bearing one.

#### 17.28.2 ⚠️ The premise is not free, which is the part worth pricing

*"If read is limited to just the correct rows"* is **exactly §17.26.2's first branch**, and §17.26.1 is
why it costs something: trimming on the way out is unavailable — the CRC covers the block and the EN
never decompresses — so row-limited reads require **the block not to span an object**.

**And a block is the compression unit.** `compress_block` is 256 KB on HDD and 64 KB on SSD, against
lumped objects of tens to hundreds of bytes. So a tiny object in a block of its own is compressed
**alone**, and small inputs compress badly — which gives away much of what lumping was for.

| | Keeps | Costs |
|---|---|---|
| **row-limited reads** | one stream per tenant; the scoping question dissolves | tiny objects compress alone |
| **extent-scoped certificate** | shared compression across objects | a common stream per authorization domain, not per tenant |

#### 17.28.3 A shared dictionary gets both, and is the thing to try first

**Compress each block against a dictionary trained on the stream**, rather than against its neighbours
in the same block. Every block stays independently decompressable and independently CRC-checked, so
§17.26.1's three mechanisms are all intact — and the cross-object redundancy that a 200-byte block
cannot find on its own is in the dictionary instead.

**That collapses the table above**: row-limited reads *and* most of the shared compression, so the
scoping question dissolves and nothing is given up for it.

⚠️ **Two things to check before believing it:**

- **the reader needs the dictionary**, which the client does not have — it decompresses, not the EN (§8). So it is a per-stream artifact to fetch and cache, small and stable but another thing on a cold read's path.
- **a dictionary is trained on data, so it leaks statistics about it.** Within one tenant that is nothing. It is the reason the dictionary must not be shared across a tenant boundary even if the blocks could be — which, given §5.11, is not a constraint that binds.

## 17.29 An extent does not know where it starts

**Bob, 2026-08-20**, reading `sn`'s `Extent`. Four corrections, and the first one is not the
tidying it looks like.

### 17.29.1 A stream offset in an extent has no correct value

`Extent` carried `first_record`, *"the stream-local number of this extent's first record"*.
⚠️ **Nonsensical, and not because it was derivable** (Asserted, Bob):

> *"You can concatenate the same extent to multiple streams."*

**So one extent has as many first-records as there are streams referencing it**, and the stored
one recorded whichever stream created it. Every other reference reads a number that is wrong,
silently, and reads wrong records with it. That is a correctness argument, not a size one —
`REVERSE-EDGE-IS-A-COUNT` and §4.6.1's shared extents were always going to collide with a field
that assumes a single referrer.

**What the extent stores instead is how many records it holds**, which *is* intrinsic. Position
becomes the stream's: `Stream::sealed_from` walks the list accumulating a running total, and the
new `Placed { extent, first }` is what anything answering *about an extent in a stream* returns.

> **The signature is the argument.** `Extent::args(first)` now takes the position from its
> caller, because the extent has no opinion about it.

⚠️ **The cost is that finding an extent is a walk rather than a search.** It was already a walk —
`locate` used a linear `find` — and §14.1.1's 128 MB stream against 32 MB extents is a handful of
entries. A stream with millions would want a sparse checkpoint every *k* extents, one `u64` per
*k* rather than per extent (#107).

### 17.29.2 `u32` ids are safe because the id was never the name

An extent is `(SN, id, second)` (§4.6.3), so an id only has to be unique among the extents **one
SN makes in one second**. 4.3 × 10^9 is not close to that, and the monotonic counter would need
to wrap inside a single second to alias anything.

### 17.29.3 The instance list names disks, not ENs

⚠️ **An EN serves several disks, and a disk moves between ENs** — a rebuild, a chassis swap,
capacity balancing — without any extent on it changing. So the durable fact is *which disk holds
this instance*; which EN to ask is a lookup against a mapping that changes underneath it.

`placement::en_of` is that lookup and is the identity function, because the code still runs one
disk per EN and numbers them the same (#108). **Everything that turns an instance into a process
goes through it**, so the real mapping replaces one function. The EN's own broadcast filter is the
place that would have broken quietly: it removed itself from the instance list by comparing raw
numbers, which with several disks per EN would have had it send itself its own append.

### 17.29.4 What it saved

`Sealed` went **80 bytes to 64** — a `u32` id, a `u32` record count in place of a `u64` one, and
no stored position. At §14.1's 1.7 × 10^9 extents per SN that is **27 GB of an SN's memory**, and
it takes the list from twenty times §4.7's reference budget to sixteen.

### 17.29.5 ⚠️ The parameter changed meaning and the literal did not

**A live run caught this, and no test did.** `Extent::args` used to take the record count and read
the position from the field; it now takes the position and reads the count from the field. Two
call sites passed a literal `0` — correct as *"this extent's count is not known"*, and wrong as
*"this extent starts at record 0"* — and it type-checked.

The symptom was an append to the second extent of a stream reporting record 9 instead of 66. **The
`Placed` type is the fix that stops it recurring**: the position is no longer something a caller
can pass by accident, because it comes back from the thing that knows it.

> This is §8.1.6's argument arriving somewhere new. Two `u64`s, one meaning a count and one a
> position, exchanged silently — which is the case #86's `ORoff`/`SRoff`/`ERoff` exist to make
> impossible, and this one is not covered even by those, since a count and an offset in the *same*
> space share a type (§8.1.6.2).

## 17.30 One name, two routers: how appends were silently lost

⚠️ **Five appends to one object produced two records, and every one of them reported success**
(#106). Found by running the thing, not by any test.

```
laws create /h --flavor unkeyed
for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do laws append /h --data "seq $i"; done
  → record 0, record 0, record 0, record 1, record 1
laws read /h --record 0  → seq 3
laws read /h --record 2  → not found
```

### 17.30.1 The cause: half the routing was converted

§17.24.0 replaced round-robin DN selection with `Process::owner`, because *"a create lands on one
machine and the lookup that follows it asks another"*. It converted `FE::handle`'s forwarding path
through a new `destination`, and **missed `FE::resolving`** — the path every *coordinated*
operation takes, which is to say every append and every read.

**So the object had two routers.** `object-info` went to the name's owner; `append` went to
whichever DN came up next. With three DNs:

| | |
|---|---|
| each DN made **its own object** under that name, with its own stream numbered 1 | so the SN held three stream keys, one per DN |
| each append was the first into *its* DN's stream | which is why the record numbers read **0, 0, 0, 1, 1** — three DNs each answering 0, then two answering 1 |
| the read went to the name's owner | and found only the third of the appends that had gone there |

**The pattern in the numbers was the whole diagnosis**: three zeros then two ones, over three DNs,
is one append per DN per round.

### 17.30.2 ⚠️ It was introduced by the fix for the same bug

§17.24.0 exists *because* round-robin loses objects. The commit that said so converted one call site
and left the other, **and turned the test cluster to three DNs in the same change** — so it created
the conditions for the bug it was fixing, in the act of fixing it.

### 17.30.2a ⚠️ The test goes where the bug is, not around the outside

**A first attempt at this wrote an end-to-end script** — start a cluster, append *n*, read back *n*.
Bob's correction (2026-08-20): *"end-to-end tests are expensive to maintain, they are good to run
one-off, but ideally there would be a unit test covering the spot where the bug is. Bugs usually
aren't in generic glue code."*

**And the spot is nameable.** The bug was not in appending, or in resolving, or in any of the chain
the script would have walked. It was one call site choosing a DN the wrong way. So:

> **`Process::pick` now refuses to return a DN.** A DN is chosen by the name it owns, and the
> generic round-robin helper — which is exactly where the mistake was cheap to make — can no longer
> make it.

**The one caller that still needs the old behaviour says so at its call site**: `batch-create` calls
`any_of`, named separately and documented as #98's debt, rather than hiding inside the helper
everything else uses. So the remaining offender is greppable instead of indistinguishable.

⚠️ **And the rule is a free function, `pickable`, so the test tests the rule rather than a copy of
it.** A first draft of the test restated the refusal inline because `Process` needs a socket — which
would have passed for ever regardless of what `pick` did. A test that restates a rule catches
nothing when the rule moves.

**The second bug of the day got the same treatment.** §17.29.5's `args(0)` was in the *answer*
`open-extent` builds, not in `open`, which was right — so the test asserts what the answer's third
field says after a seal, which is the argument that was wrong.

### 17.30.3 ⚠️ And it invalidates §17.24.5's measurement

§17.24.5 reports a batch lookup as **46% slower over three DNs than one** and reasons from it that
hash routing multiplies messages. **That number was taken on this cluster**, where `bench-create`
still scatters objects round-robin (#98 — `batch-create` is the *third* call site, still unconverted)
while `bench-info` looks them up by owner. Most lookups were missing, so the figure measures a
cluster that was not finding its own data.

**The analysis survives and the number does not.** A batch whose names span *D* DNs really does
become *D* requests, and `D(1 − (1 − 1/D)^n)` is arithmetic rather than measurement.

⚠️ **Retaken after #98** (§17.24.5): 41% rather than 46%, of which **16.5 points are two extra
processes on one box** and not routing at all. The first version attributed the whole gap to fan-out
because it had nothing to subtract with — and the single-name arm, which cannot fan out, is what
supplies the subtraction. **A one-armed benchmark cannot tell its effect from its overhead.**

## 17.31 A batch create is grouped by owner, and its answer is a count

**#98, the third and last call site.** §17.24.0 converted `object-info`, §17.30 converted the append
and read path, and `batch-create` was left sending every name to one DN — harmless with one and
wrong with two, since a create landed where a lookup would not go.

### 17.31.1 Simpler than the lookup fan-out, and worth saying why

| | `batch-object-info` | `batch-create` |
|---|---|---|
| an entry limit to divide | yes (§9.1.3.7) | **none** |
| detail levels to negotiate | yes | **none** |
| the answer | a row per name, which must come back **in the caller's order** | a **count** |

**So there is nothing to budget, nothing to size, and nothing to put back in order.** The FE groups
by owner, sends one request per DN, and the counts add. No `Spread`, no second round, no prefix rule.

⚠️ **The answer being a count is also its weakness.** A caller learns how many objects were newly
made and not *which* — so a partial failure names nothing. That was already true of one DN; spreading
over several makes it worse, which is why **a DN that refuses fails the whole batch** rather than
being quietly subtracted. A short count that cannot say what it is short of is not a partial answer,
it is an unusable one (§16.156).

### 17.31.2 The shape moved to `common`, which is the rule that made this cheap

The FE now has to cut a create request into objects, and §17.13.3 says no two processes count
argument positions independently. So `Wanted` — name, flavour, framing — moved out of `dn` into
`common::info`, with one `ARGS` and one `all_of_args`.

**And `all_of_args` refuses a trailing part-object rather than truncating**, which the DN's version
did not: a batch that does not divide is one somebody built wrong, and creating the whole ones would
leave a caller's list and the objects that exist disagreeing silently.

### 17.31.3 The escape hatch went with the debt

§17.30's `pick` refusal needed an `any_of` for `batch-create` while it was still round-robin. #98 was
that debt, so `any_of` is gone and `pick` refuses a DN with nothing to route around it.

> **Three call sites, converted over one day, in the wrong order** — the generic helper was made safe
> *before* the last caller was fixed, so the hatch existed for one commit. Doing it the other way
> round would have needed no hatch, and there would have been nothing to remember to remove.
